1933-05-06.text: Geneva, May 30 (AF)—Germany officially raised the question of her right to equality in armaments, both in the air and under the sea, at the world disarmament conference today. The German delegate introduced amendments to the British disarmament plan which were regarded as tantamount to serving notice that unless military and naval airplanes and submarines are abolished, the German government will want air fleets and submarine fleets. These amendments, which caused something of a sensation, created the impression at the conference that Germany expects to participate in the conference of the big naval powers slated for 1935.

London, May 5 (Py—America’s first big move for giving the world economic conference a constructive sendoff by means of a tariff truce failed today to gain the support of the British government. With other countries awaiting Britain's lead, there appeared no hope tonight of making effective an armistice in the economic warfare among the nations. No outright refusal of cooperation came from Downing Street, where Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald held two long sessions with his cabinet, but it was understood that Sir Robert Vansittart, permanent undersecretary of foreign affairs, had informed Norman H. Davis, President Roosevelt’s negotiator, of the inability of the British government to agree to any immediate truce, or even to a truce from the opening of the economic conference, unless Britain's tariff position is protected by safeguards. A tariff truce with reservations, according to an aut

Washington, May 5. ()—A forewarning of German insistence upon removal of the bonds imposed by the victors of the World War tonight raised new obstructions in the path to united international action against the depression at the world economic conference in London. This new controversial issue appeared with the arrival of the German government's representative, Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, who lost no time in asserting that the present world crisis is not based on economics but on moral factors. "All forces are used to keep down the defeated," he said. The declaration of the Hitler representative, president of the German Reichsbank, left little doubt of the attitude he would take in his forthcoming talks with President Roosevelt, but American officials believed his host would use every effort to keep the conversation on an economic plane. The day's swiftly mingled events both here and abroad serv

New York — Further gyrations in dollars held the spotlight in the financial markets today. The dollar dropped to a new low since leaving the gold standard in the earlier dealings then rebounded toward the close. The pound sterling, after rising as high as $4.06 in London, was quoted up to around $4.05 here, then fell back to $3.9912, or only 1% cents above Friday’s final price. The French franc jumped up .05 of a cent to 4.75 cents, indicating a discount from gold parity in the dollar of close to 18 per cent. But then the franc fell back to 4.65 cents, or .14 of a cent under Friday’s final level, which was accompanied by echoes here of the inflation talk heard recently in some quarters of Paris. The gyrations in the dollar, in terms of other currencies, was attributed both to withdrawal of foreign balances, on depreciation uncertainty, and to heavy bear selling by European speculators. W

London, May 65. (P) The American dollar again held the limelight in the exchange market today by a sharp fall which at one time carried it to $4.01 in relation to the pound, thereby giving sterling the highest value it has had since September, 1931, shortly after Britain abandoned the gold standard. From an opening of $3.92 to the pound, the dollar slumped 9 cents, although it recovered to close at $3.97.

GENEVA May 5—(AP)—Amendments to the British proposal on naval armaments were introduced by Germany today in the world disarmament conference in terms which created the impression here that the Hitler government expects to participate in the projected conference of great naval powers in 1935. The projected naval parley of 1935 will be a sequel to the London conference of 1930, at which the German government was not present. The British proposals, which have been accepted by the conference as the basis of further discussions, call for no reductions in the fleets of the five great sea powers, but merely ask for the completion of the London treaty through the full adhesion of France and Italy. "Germany has not abandoned hope that the conference will decide on the complete abolishment of submarines," the German amendments set forth. "If, however, it is decided that submarines cannot be renoun

LONDON, May 6.—Li Chang Yun, who claimed to have reached the age of 256, is dead at his home in Kaihsien, Szechuan Province, China, the Daily Express said today. Li outlived 23 wives and left a widow of 64... He stated that his beard did not turn white until a century ago.

LONDON, May 5.—UP)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald declared tonight that the delicate war debts problem must be settled before the end of the forthcoming world economic conference, convening here June 12. He anticipated a debts conference would be conducted simultaneously at London with the economic parley. MacDonald asserted that both he and President Roosevelt had agreed that the success of the world economic conference largely would depend on a satisfactory settlement of the war debts question. Surprise Declaration. His address was a discussion of his Washington conversations with Mr. Roosevelt and other American leaders. Inasmuch as the prime minister announced in the House of Commons yesterday that debts could not be discussed at the world economic conference itself, his surprise declaration tonight was taken to mean that the debt conversations would occur concurrently here. “The

1933-05-26.text: United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, May 26.—-(UP)—Horatio Bottomley, one of the most amazing figures of modern England—editor, silver-tongued orator, millionaire, convict, pauper—died in a free ward of Middlesex hospital today. Bottomley, “the man who might have been prime minister,” died behind a screen that sheltered him from the stares of his fellow charity patients. He was operated on a week ago. At 73, a flabby old man, he was unable to fight very hard. His last public appearance came a few weeks ago when he applied for, and was refused, an old age pension of $2 a week. Bottomley was brought up in miserable poverty. He was an office boy at ten in a lawyer’s office. His acquisitive cockney mind absorbed a tremendous amount of legal information. He became a court reporter, and was a good one for five years. At 23 he became a financier. His companies flared like skyrockets across

London, May 26 (JP) — Great Britain joined with President Roosevelt today in common attitude toward European security demands. In an historic pronouncement in the House of Commons, Sir John Simon, Foreign Secretary, announced Britain's unequivocal support of the United States’ attitude on “security pacts” and informed the continental powers that Britain would assume no further obligations than she has already taken to protect them from the war. Sir John paid eloquent tribute to the offer of the United States to modify its old policy of neutrality—affecting the freedom of the seas doctrine—as a contribution to world peace.

London (AP)—The new American policy of co-operation with other nations to avert any threat of war was hailed as an important step today by Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary, and Sir Austen Chamberlain, one of his predecessors in that post. Sir John, speaking in the House of Commons, asserted the new American doctrine as explained by Norman H. Davis, American ambassador at large, at Geneva, amounted to abandonment of the idea "of standing with folded arms as a mere spectator from afar, of struggles between two other states, one of which was in the wrong." The secretary informed the House that Britain intends to assume no new continental commitments.

GENEVA. (®). Any hard and fast definition of an aggressor nation would be only a trap for the innocent and a protection for the guilty, the delegate of Great Britain told the disarmament conference. This attitude, set forth by Capt. Anthony Eden, British foreign undersecretary, threatened to upset the harmony which has prevailed since the American policy of co-operation was expounded by Norman H. Davis, ambassador at large. It is necessary to know the background of each case of aggression in order to determine which party is responsible, Captain Eden said. The definition of an aggressor suggested by President Roosevelt is any country whose armed forces are found within the territories of another country in violation of treaties. A more elaborate definition of the aggressor has been approved by the security commission of the conference. It accepts the Roosevelt definition, but adds to it

Washington, D. C.—(AP)—President Roosevelt today called in his delegation to the London economic conference and a staff of experts to draft a program of action. Bernard M. Baruch, New York financier and economic authority, joined the White House parley, but he emphasized before it started that he was not a member of the American delegation. The president set aside most of the morning for his talk with the delegates and experts. There was no indication of immediate action on his part, although he scanned closely reports from overseas. Besides Secretary Hull, the chairman of the delegation, the following were present: James M. Cox, former governor of Ohio; Senator Pittman of Nevada and Representative McReynolds of Tennessee, all delegates, and Raymond Moley, assistant secretary of state; Herbert Feis, James P. Warburg and William C. Bullitt of the State Department, and Rexford Tugwell, ass

GENEVA, May 26 (U.P)—Japan today demanded the scrapping of the 5-5-3 naval ratios of the Washington and London naval treaties. Naotake Sato, Japanese delegate, announced at a meeting of the general commission of the world arms conference that Japan's adherence to the proposed arms convention depends on acceptance of an amendment deleting mention of the naval tonnages allotted by the Washington and London treaties. Japan has made no secret of her desire for the right to a larger navy. Under the treaties, she is restricted to three tons of naval vessels for each five tons possessed by the United States and Great Britain.

WASHINGTON, May 26 — President Roosevelt conferred with his economic experts today to put the finishing touches to the American program for the World Economic conference which opens in London June 12. With the President were four members of the American delegation of seven and several state department advisers who have been assisting him in his economic conversations with foreign representatives. Bernard M. Baruch, New York banker and close associate of Mr. Roosevelt, was present. As the group assembled the White House indicated the President was cheered over Sir John Simon’s statement in the House of Commons clarifying British support for American peace proposals. A spokesman for the President said that any developments anywhere that gave promise of concrete results in London or Geneva were welcome and extremely gratifying to the President. The belief persisted that Mr. Roosevelt would

London, May 26 —-(AP)—- Horatio Bottomley, 73, founder of the weekly "John Bull" and one time popular figure in English public life, died today. A spectacular career in British politics, finance and journalism crashed in 1922 at Old Bailey Court when he was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for converting to his own use £5,000 of funds he had helped raise for war purposes. Released from Maidstone jail in 1927, he was a broken man. His health had declined and his fortune was gone. He appealed for an old age pension of a few shillings a week, He refused aid, however, from a man who had exposed his frauds and to the end said, “let no man

1933-05-23.text: | BUDO, May 23, (—The British government, replying today to President Roosevelt's message to the world, declared that it “entirely shares the president's view

WASHINGTON (UP)—O. M. W. Sprague, former economic adviser to the Bank of England and Harvard professor, Tuesday accepted the position of economic adviser to the United States tendered him Monday by President Roosevelt. Sprague is expected to be made executive assistant to Secretary Woodin. WASHINGTON, (UP) —Prospective appointment of Prof. O. M. W. Sprague, one of the world’s foremost monetary authorities, as economic advisor to the U. S. government, was expected Tuesday to expedite efforts to stabilize American currency. Well-informed quarters believed Sprague's appointment would be announced by Secretary of Treasury Woodin. Thus another college professor—this one from Harvard—would be added to President Roosevelt's “brain trust.” Sprague recently has been advisor to the Bank of England. He was called there in 1930, helped guide Britain through the trying period when it left the gold st

- LONDON, May 23. (4)—Robert W. Bingham, new United States ambassador, riding behind prancing king horses in an open royal carriage went to Buckingham Palace this morning, officially met King George and presented his credentials. Ray Atherton, embassy counsellor, and chiefs of the embassy departments accompanied the ambassador. The king, on account of an attack of rheumatism in one arm, still was unable to wear a uniform, and His Majesty, Mr. Bingham and the other members of the party were dressed in formal morning clothes. After the formal presentation, the king and the ambassador chatted. The royal carriage waited in the courtyard of the palace to take the Americans back to the embassy.

LONDON, May 23—(P)—Sources close to the Chinese government have approached Sir Miles W. Lampson, British Minister to China, seeking British mediation to stop hostilities with Japan in the Peiping area, it was said officially today. Lampson, the announcement said, has informally discussed the Chinese suggestion with Japanese officials.

The United States won an important point in its disarmament formula today when the steering committee of the armed conference agreed to the proposal of Norman H. Davis, that discussion of the armed reduction phase of the British plan begin immediately. Despite unfavorable criticism in the French press, the French foreign office paid high tribute to America’s disarmament stand as outlined by Davis yesterday. Although some disagreement in the French government circles over Premier Mussolini’s four-power peace pact was reported, Premier Daladier discussed the treaty before his cabinet and indications pointed to progress. Premier Mussolini in Rome told the Fascist grand council that success of his plan is “imminent.”

LONDON, May 19 (INS)—Robert W. Bingham, new American ambassador to Britain, formally presented his credentials to Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, at the foreign Office today. Bingham, attired in formal morning clothes, was accompanied by Ray Atherton, counsellor to the United States embassy. Before going to the foreign office, the new ambassador received the embassy staff. Arrangements are being made for Bingham to drive to Buckingham Palace some time next week for formal audience with King George. The ambassador will be conveyed from the embassy to the palace in one of the elaborate scarlet and gilt semi-state coaches with outriders and footmen in attendance, specially sent by the king. It will be the first time since the regime of former Ambassador Houghton that an American ambassador has been taken to the palace in a royal coach.

WASHINGTON, May 23.—P}— American officials are pleased at informal agreement by France, England, Germany and Italy on the “Mussolini-peace pact to preserve the peace for a decade at least: — While regarded as essentially an European affair, the American administration believes the pact helpful in the general drive to reduce armaments and achieve economic stability, particularly since it appeared here to go a long way to meet France’s demands for assurance of security in exchange for disarmament.

GENEVA, May 23 (U.P.)—Pressing on after his oratorical triumph of yesterday, Norman H. Davis, chief United States delegate to the disarmament conference, forced delegates of the leading European powers to agree today to discuss disarmament at once, leaving discussion of security to a special committee. The general steering commission of the conference decided to take notice of French claims by discussing reduction of war materials and security on alternate days before the full commission. This compromise was aimed at satisfying both the United States and France. The commission was asked to take up war materials at its meeting this afternoon, and to discuss possible acts of consultative pacts and the definition of an aggressor nation tomorrow afternoon. At Davis’ suggestion, it was agreed to devote tomorrow morning to private negotiations calculated to lead the way to agreements. France w

1933-08-11.text: Violence broke out again today in the turbulent mine fields of Illinois and Indiana. One man was killed and two were wounded in two outbreaks between mining factions. John Hilltrop, 27, Table Grove, Ill., was shot in a soft drink parlor brawl in London Mills, Ill., early today. He and seven other members of the Progressive Miners union participated. William Cragg, a United miner, is being held, At Clinton, Ind., two employees of the Bunsen No. 4 coal mine were shot by picketers when they approached the mine. It was the second time gunplay had broken out at the mine within a week. A picketer at the mine was shot Tuesday. Picketers also shot at other miners but no casualties were reported. Officials of the mine said that a full force of 250 men was at work today.

ROME, Aug. 10. (?)—A Roman triumph, a custom not followed for many centuries, will be revived Saturday to give Gen. Italo Balbo and members of his trans-Atlantic sea-plane squadron a rousing welcome home. It will have another purpose too—to pay tribute to Premier Mussolini as the inspiration for Italy’s renaissance in aviation. It will compete in enthusiasm with the receptions given the fliers in Chicago and New York and in other places along their route. General Balbo advised the air ministry today that he plans to bring his armada to Ostia, Rome’s new port, from Lisbon, Portugal, 1,300 miles away, without stopping. Their arrival in Italy is set for Saturday evening. Returning from Ostia, the premier and General Balbo will be driven through the central passage of the Arch of Constantine, just outside the ancient coliseum, which thousands of Americans have visited.

TOKYO, Aug. 13 (P)—Testimony that fears of “America’s ambition” were the motive for the assassination of Premier Suyoshi Inukai and other terroristic acts was given today by Lieutenant Horishi Yamagishi, leader of ten naval officers who are being tried in a naval court on charges of responsibility for those events. The court heard testimony adduced to prove that Yamagishi was commander of the group of naval officers who entered Inukai’s home, and that he gave the command “Fire!” when the shots which killed the premier were discharged. The courtroom was ordered to be cleared after the lieutenant made his statement regarding fears of America and the proceedings, which are being held at the Yokosuka naval base, were continued in secret. Yamagishi told the tribunal that he and his co-defendants feared that the United States would attempt what he described as further domination of Japan and t

MULHOUSE, FRANCE, Aug. 10.— Armed French troops were again stationed today on the German frontier near here as a precaution against alleged aggressions of German nazis such as occurred early this year at Huningue. Small detachments from the Mulhouse garrison were sent to Huningue, Kembs and Chalampe, where only isolated customs posts were previously maintained. At Chalampe the troops occupied defensive works along the Rhine. At Kembs they are guarding the electric plant and the span over the Alsace canal. At Huningue they are watching the bridge where Chancellor Hitler’s Brown Shirts staged an anti-French demonstration late in February shouting taunts. The troops were sent at the request of the border population. More than 200 nazis were reported to have marched to the middle of the Huningue bridge February 21, singing “Deutschland Über Alles.” France made protests to the League of Natio

SHANGHAI, China, Aug. 11 ()—The Yellow River, called “China's sorrow,” took an additional toll of life and property in north Honan province today when it rose ten feet, its highest point in a decade, and burst over its dikes. Thousands of miles of farm lands were flooded and hundreds of houses were destroyed. The number of deaths was not learned. In previous floods recently thousands have perished.

Istanbul, Turkey, Aug. 11 (AP) — Raymond S. White, an American teacher of the Smyrna international college, was wounded in the foot last night by Turkish gendarmes who mistook him for an escaped brigand as he was motoring at high speed from Bergama to I n n e a c e s

MARSEILLES, France, (RP) — Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi, new holders of the world long distance flight record, were back on home soil Friday after their flight from New York to Rayak, Syria. They arrived here just before midnight, to be met by a cheering crowd which included air ministry officials and Louis Bleriot, designer of their plane. Joseph Le Brix. “We are not tired but we are glad to be back in France,” said Rossi. “We have no plans, but shall go to Paris in a few days.” They will receive at Paris a 1,

The Associated Press — VIENNA, Austria, Aug. 11 Two Hitlerites were arrested in Linz today and charged with planning to assassinate Prince Ernst Rudinger von Starhemberg, leader of the Fascist Heimwehr (Home Guard).

1933-12-14.text: LONDON. (AP). A check for $7,500,000 is expected to be handed over to the United States in Washington Friday by Great Britain as a token payment on its war debts, it was authoritatively stated. PARIS. (UP). France will temper its third successive war debt default Friday with a note to the United States government, carrying further the defense made at the time of the last default, June 15. The note will explain that the French had hoped a revision would be reached before payment was due. WASHINGTON. (AP). Acting Secretary Morgenthau announced the Austrian government has notified the United States a Jan. 1 installment of $460,093 on its relief debt to this government will not be paid.

(By The Associated Press) European capitals hummed today with talk of disarmament and the possibility of reshaping the League of Nations. Interest centered in London and Berlin. Italian Under-secretary of State Fulvio Suvich faced at least two brilliant social events in connection with his visit to Berlin. They were official dinners at which President Paul von Hindenburg and Chancellor Adolf Hitler were to preside. In this manner the way was to be paved for brass-tacks talks: What concessions Germany would demand if she re-entered the League of Nations; just what the Nazis want as a basis for a world accord on disarmament. Busy Signor Suvich hoped to finish with Il Duce’s business in Berlin soon, it was said in Rome, that he might hurry on to England. Premier Mussolini, it was said, would like to have his ideas on reforming the League presented in both London and Berlin before his repres

LONDON, Dec, 14 — Trawlers, freighters and great ocean liners fought today through the roughest seas and highest winds of years in the English Channel and North Sea. On land many persons perished from cold and roads at some points were made impassable by ice and snow. An unknown steamship estimated to have a crew of 12, and to be of 600 tons’ burden, sank off the Sussex coast in seas so high that lifeboats were unable to approach. In contrast to some less severe storms, that was the only casualty reported on the sea. As the storm progressed many ships fled to port, and the English Channel services were cancelled after vain efforts to reroute traffic by safer paths. Lifeboats did heroic work off the English coast going to the aid of small distressed craft. Atlantic liners were hours late in arriving at their ports. A 70-mile wind howled in the English Channel and churned up the seas to al

By The Associated Press A northeast gale continued to whip the English coastline and five additional deaths were reported there while the United States took stock of havoc wrought by the elements. Twelve of those who died in England perished when a cargo steamer was wrecked off the coast of East Suffolk. Snow is predicted for England while parts of the European continent have below zero temperatures. The cold wave caused 11 deaths in France. The French rivers began to freeze, Traffic on the upper Seine was stopped. An increase in the cold was expected. A few snowflakes fell in Paris. In the United States the wintry-like weather that began earlier in the week held its grip, particularly in the east, where snow is predicted Thursday. A blizzard hit in upper New York.

Furious gales swept the British Isles Wednesday and sent to destruction a cargo steamer with all hands while a lifeboat fought through the surf of the East Suffolk coast in a futile effort to reach the ship. A dozen lives were thought to have been lost. On this side of the Atlantic a gale pounded the Nova Scotia shore, and heavy loss to fishermen’s gear was feared. While most of the United States reported normal winter temperatures, the northeastern seaboard was frozen with temperatures as low as 10 degrees below zero in Maine. Along the northwestern States fringing Canada the mercury hovered just above zero. More than three inches of rain fell in parts of southern California, Los Angeles suffering floods four feet deep in some sections. The near zero wave in France had moderated, and snow covered the central part of that country as the temperature rose toward the freezing point.

Washington, Dec. 13. (/P)-The administration expressed its apparent satisfaction with the dollar's exchange level today, by again quoting a price of $34.01 an ounce for newly-mined domestic gold. This figure, repeated for the 11th time, was announced as the dollar showed new strength on the London market, opening at $5.03 1-2. The bar gold price on the basis of the opening pound rate was $31.74. The gold program, meanwhile, was subordinated in immediate interest to the 1935 budget preparations going on at the White House and treasury. Though figures were guarded closely by Lewis W. Douglas, director of the budget, the discussions drew attention to the present condition of the treasury. The deficit since the fiscal year began July 1 was $872,783,591 as compared with $1,211,443,000 at the same time a year ago. Ordinary expenditures were $1,283,560,000 and receipts $1,259,549,000, while eme

London, Dec. 13 (AP).—A French nobleman was missing tonight, more than 36 hours after he had embarked on a flight across the stormy British Channel, but another aviator for whom fears had been expressed landed safely at Le Bourget field in France after spanning the channel. Vicomte Charles De Manneville started from Croydon airport Tuesday morning and was last heard of when his plane, in which he flew alone, was reported over the Lympne air base near the channel 45 minutes later. A. Henshaw, British flyer, set out today for Paris from Heston airdrome. No definite news had been received of him until tonight when he set his plane down at the field outside Paris.

Washington—U.P.M—The acting secretary of state, William Phillips, today informed the British embassy that extradition papers for John ("Jake, the Barber") Factor, would be held up until Factor has testified in the Touhy gang kidnapping case in Chicago. Factor’s extradition to Great Britain to face charges of the alleged fraudulent sale of securities has already been granted by federal courts. He is the principal witness in the case against the Touhy gang, however, and the delay was granted so that he might testify at the trial. Under the extradition treaty the United States has the right to withhold issuance of extradition warrants for 60 days for cause. The British embassy was notified, as a matter of courtesy, that the warrants would be issued as soon as Factor had testified at the trial.

1933-08-08.text: NEW YORK, Feb. 18. (AP)—President-elect Roosevelt will confer with Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, Monday on war debts and the world economic situation. Ambassador Lindsay reaches this country on Monday from London where he has been in consultation over the forthcoming American-British war debts and economic conference. "I told Secretary Stimson over the telephone last night," Mr. Roosevelt said today, "that if it is decided entirely appropriate by the state department, to save time and an additional trip, I would be glad to see Ambassador Lindsay when he arrives in New York on Monday. Mr. Stimson said he would communicate with the ambassador."

Berlin, Aug. 7.—(AP)—The French and British ambassadors were told today by the German foreign office that their governments’ “mixing in the German-Austrian impasse was inadmissible” when they handed the Wilhelmstrasse identical notes saying that German propaganda activities in Austrian politics violated the spirit of the four-power peace pact. An official communique by the Wolff agency stated the French ambassador, Francois Poncet, called with reference to the four-power agreement and said that according to the view of the French government, German propaganda with reference to Austria in recent days was not compatible with treaty conditions. Teuts Stand Pat The French diplomatic representative was told that the Berlin government failed to see any reason for application of the four-power treaty in this instance and that Germany regarded as inadmissible this interference in the German-Aust

LONDON, Aug. 8.—Germany by a blunt rebuff of joint British and French representations brought the problem of Nazi activities in Austria nearer a crisis today. Great Britain and France, through their embassies at Berlin, made oral protests, in what were described as most friendly terms, against Nazi propaganda against Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss of Austria. The German foreign office promptly countered with a public announcement of the representations, with the comment that there has been no violation of the treaty cited and hence the representations were inadmissible.

Portishead, Eng., Aug. 8, (LP) Twelve seaplanes of the Balbo Squadron were sighted at 6:45 a.m. EST by the S. S. Seringa, 400 miles off Cape Race, a wireless message from the ship reported. Shoal Harbor, Nfld., Aug. 8, U.P. General Italo Balbo led his 24 seaplanes from the placid waters of this harbor at dawn today on one of the final and most dangerous legs of the greatest mass flight of airplanes in history. The fleet was bound for the Azores Islands, a distance of 1,200 miles, all over water. The fleet already had negotiated the dangerous North Atlantic in its flight from Orbetello, Italy, to Chicago and New York, and the men were supremely confident that no accident would interfere with the successful completion of their magnificent adventure in Rome. The start was carried out with efficient, military routine. At 2 a.m. the crews boarded the planes and in a few minutes the roar of th

HORTA, Azores, (U.P)—The Italian air armada, en route back to Italy from Chicago, arrived in the Azores today after a 1200 mile flight from Newfoundland. The sixth, seventh and eighth triads of the 24 planes landed here at 1:12 p.m. EST, to be welcomed by an enthusiastic populace, the salute of cannon and ringing of church bells.

FIELDS OF SOUTHWESTERN PENNSYLVANIA, The action was taken in a rising vote after Edward F. McGrady, labor advisor of the National Recovery Administration, delivered a stirring appeal to the men to support President Roosevelt's recovery program. McGrady flew to the coal fields from Washington at the request of General Hugh S. Johnson, recovery administrator. Several hundred persons, many of them strikers, milled about the streets as the decision was reached. The men have been on strike for more than two weeks, defending recognition of the United Mine Workers of America. Opposition to the return to work plan failed to materialize after McGrady’s appeal, brought directly from the administration in Washington.

Horta, Azores. (4) - General Italo Baibo's Italian air armada of 24 seaplanes successfully completed today the longest hop of their long journey from Rome to Chicago and back again. The general led his ships from Shoal Harbor, Newfoundland, to the Azores, whence he and his men received an unparalleled welcome.

HAVANA, Aug. 8.—(P)—Strife-torn Cuba today counted the cost of a widespread strike in terms of a mounting death toll and a tense political situation complicated by demands for President Machado’s resignation and his efforts to re-establish peace by armed force. Machine guns and heavy guards at public buildings were withdrawn after upwards of 20 persons were killed and 120 wounded during a demonstration last night which followed a report that Machado had quit, but hundreds of army reserves were held ready in their barracks today for any emergency. The A B C Opposition Society had broadcast a report that the President had agreed to withdraw, whereupon thousands rushed into the streets in a hilarious mood. Thousands gathered at the capitol. Fifty uniformed policemen hurried to the scene, to be joined by mounted officers. In a blaze of rifle, pistol, and submachine gun fire, scores fell, dea

1933-08-19.text: POONA, India, Aug. 19 (AP).— The Mahatma Gandhi began the fourth day of his “fast unto death” today disdaining the offer of the British government to free him from prison if he would quit his civil disobedience campaign. Official doctors watched the health of the Mahatma but issued no statement on his condition.

VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Aug. 17: Two bald eagles, measuring nearly 7 feet from tip to tip, attacked Henry Lehr, a fisherman, near Burnaby today when he disturbed them while walking across a field. Although he defended himself with a stick, one of the birds bit him on the leg. Lehr summoned police who shot both birds as they nested on the ground.

Poona, India.—(AP)—As the Mahatma Gandhi entered the third day of his “fast until death,” the government of India announced today that it was prepared to liberate him if he abandoned civil disobedience. The Mahatma began to show signs of weakness, although his voice remained strong. Reports from Yeroda jail, where he is serving one year for his disobedience campaign, were that he had started saving his strength by remaining in bed, attended only by his secretary. A government communique said the administration was satisfied that the facilities allowed the nationalist leader were ample to enable him to conduct such work in behalf of the untouchables as was reasonable in the circumstances. If the Mahatma feels that life ceases to interest him, and if he feels that he may not do his work without let or hindrance, then the government is prepared to set him at liberty, the communique said, pr

ROME, Aug. 19 (CP)--The International Institute of Agriculture today forecast a drastic price rise in wheat as a result of a world-wide wheat crop shortage. The institute estimated the northern hemisphere’s wheat harvest will be nearly 8,000,000 (m) metric tons below the 1932 level. (8,000,000 metric tons is equivalent to 293,949,333 U. S. bushels). “The crop across the Atlantic is exceptionally small,” the institute statement said, “due to drought which damaged crops in both the United States and Canada. Production of wheat in North America in 1938 corresponds to the quantity necessary to meet internal consumption. It must not be expected the new crop will add any exportable surplus to the heavy stock of previous crops.”

BUCHAREST, Aug. 18. (#)—King Carol, already suffering from an attack of the flu, has contracted the measles, apparently from close contact with his son, the Crown Prince Michael, who has been a measles patient several days. Physicians issued a bulletin saying that the king's condition was generally good. Dowager Queen Marie returned today from her northern trip.

ANFF, Alberta, Aug. 19.—(UP)—International repercussions may ultimately wreck President Roosevelt’s recovery program, experts at the Institute of Pacific Relations declared today. Economists studying the possible effect of the NRA and the agriculture adjustment program on world trade believed that although the initial effect would be beneficial, price rises might come so rapidly in the United States as to initiate a new depression. Price Rise Menace Discussion of the new American program was led by Dr. Harold Moulton of the Brookings Institution at Washington after the question of its world effects was raised at numerous round-table discussions. “The danger of the American program lies in the rapid rise in prices,” Moulton said. “To protect American industry it may be necessary to raise tariffs again. While the revival of American business cannot help benefiting other nations, new tariff

Bumper European Wheat Outlook (By The Associated Press, Rome, Aug. 19—Prospects of a bumper wheat crop in Europe led the International Institute of Agriculture to warn that the European demand for wheat from Russia and as exporters would drop about 98,000 be under last year’s needs.

BERLIN, Aug. 19.—(AP)—Berlin's Nazi group leader, Karl Ernst, announced today that he would call on United States ambassador William E. Dodd next Tuesday and offer apologies for the attack by a Nazi storm trooper on Dr. Daniel Mulvihill, of Brooklyn, N. Y. Dr. Mulvihill was struck in the face because he failed to salute parading Nazis last Tuesday night. The trooper who hit him has been arrested.

1933-08-30.text: HONGKONG, China, (UP) The U. S. S. Sacramento and the H. M. S. Wishart left here today for Foochow, capital of Fukien province, to protect American and British citizens reported endangered by Communists nearing the city. United States citizens had already been warned to leave Foochow, it was reported, before arrival of the Communist hordes. Three Japanese warships were dispatched to Foochow yesterday from Formosa. Considerable doubt was expressed in official circles here that the Communist bandits had, as reported, captured Yenping in Fukien province.

EXMOOR COUNTRY CLUB, Highland Park, Ill., Aug. 30. (AP)—Brushing aside her opponent with a game that shattered par by three shots, Enid Wilson of England entered the quarter-finals of the women’s national golf championship today with a 4 and 3 triumph over Mrs. Harley Higbie of Detroit. The English champion was never headed as she won the first hole with a birdie four, made the turn in 36, three under par, and ended the match on the 15th with a half in birdie fours. Pumping out tremendous tee shots with her man-sized woods and pitching dead to the pin with magic approaches, she was an easy master of par and Mrs. Higbie, although the latter was only two over par herself. Charlotte Glutting of West Orange, N.J., conqueror of Miss Wilson last year at Salem, survived with a 3 and 2 victory over Peggy Wattles of Buffalo, and will meet the English champion in the quarter-finals again tomorrow.

LONDON, (UP). Thomas A. Le Breton, Argentine ambassador to France, signed the world wheat agreement on behalf of his government after a delay that caused fear the price raising pact might collapse because of Argentine abstention. After Le Breton had signed the agreement, he, Frederick E. Murphy, chief American delegate, and Stanley Bruce, Australia, initialled a gentlemen’s agreement designed to serve as a cornerstone for the main treaty. Twenty-one nations signed.

HAMILTON, Bermuda, Aug. 20—Former President Gerardo Machado of Cuba sailed late today for Canada after British police refused him permission to go ashore during a stopover of several hours. Asked what he would do if he had a chance to live over again, his sight fears rule in Cuba, General Machado said he would do exactly the same thing again. An interview was given by him indirectly through his former secretary of treasury Octavio Averhoff. Others in the Machado party found from the Bahamas to Montreal were former Secretary of Agriculture Eugenio Moiinet and Machado's aide-de-camp Manuel Mireno. None was permitted ashore. They expected to remain in Canada two or three months.

ATHENS, Aug. 29 (4)—The appeal court approved today the application for formal sanction of the detention of Samuel Insull, former Chicago Utilities operator, in connection with American extradition proceedings. Insull arrived shortly before the beginning of the hearing at 10:15 A. M., escorted by two plainclothes policemen. After his identity had been established, several questions were put to him regarding himself, his wife, and son. When asked about his nationality, Insull replied that he was British and was born in London, but acquired American citizenship in 1896. He said he did not know his present status because the American government has cancelled his passport.

PARIS, Aug. 28 (AP).—Premier Edouard Daladier’s visit to intricate fortifications along the German frontier after proclaiming that France guarantees Austria's independence aroused keen interest in political circles today. The hundred million dollar fortification visited by the premier was erected in the last three years along with a 125-mile front between the Rhine and Luxembourg on the German frontier. Trenches link a series of shellproof vaults from one to 16 miles apart. There is an elaborate system of underground barracks connected by tunnels from which army officers believe a continuous barrage could be put down. Although France wishes only peace and intends to pursue a policy of international cooperation, the premier declared, it is a duty “to assure our own liberty which will be better respected when it is known we are capable of guaranteeing it.” “We must also be on guard,” he sa

COPENHAGEN, Aug. 28 (#)—Police stationed a guard today in front of the hotel where Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh are staying, and the men assigned had plenty of work keeping back a crowd of autograph hunters. The rooms occupied by the Lindberghs, who arrived Saturday after completing a flight over the north Atlantic route by stages from the United States, were guarded as though they contained the crown jewels.

INNSBRUCK, Austria, Aug. 30,— All Austria's borders were closed today after an audacious jail delivery in which three men chloroformed two warders and rescued Franz Hofer, Nazi chief of the Tyrol-Voralberg district. Seventy Nazis in the Innsbruck neighborhood were arrested as soon as news of the rescue reached police. Hofer was imprisoned as an enemy of the government of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, whose determined fight to keep Austria free of Nazi influence has brought the country into a critical situation with Germany. Early today two men clad in the uniforms of officers of the Heimwehr—the home guards, with which Dollfuss is combating Nazi activities—appeared at the prison dragging a third man between them. The masqueraders announced they had a prisoner, and the door was opened by two warders or guards. The intruders then seized the warders, chloroformed them and forced the wife o

1933-08-16.text: SHEERNESS, Kent, Eng., Aug. 15.—(#)—One of the strangest tragedies in British military annals occurred today when a London girl, Jean Chesterton, 17, who was rowing in a boat with her sister off Leysdown Beach, was shot dead by a machine gunner in a Royal Air Force auxiliary plane. The gunner mistook her boat for a target. The girls were a quarter of a mile from the shore searching for a child's ball which had floated from the beach. Five planes roared overhead and began shooting at a string of buoys. One of the gunners, mistaking the rowboat for a buoy, killed the girl instantly. The sister rowed frantically to shore. The planes were manned by territorials—volunteers—in annual training.

Sheerness, Kent, England, Aug. 15. (P)—Jean Chesterton, a 17-year-old girl, was shot to death by a Royal Air Force machine gunner today when she rowed out into the sea to recover the lost ball of a child. The gunner mistook the boat rowed by Jean and her sister for a target and fired upon it from an auxiliary plane.

LONDON — Great Britain will build 100 fighting airplanes, the fastest and most efficient in the world, and a new force of seaplanes if the disarmament conference fails, the Daily Herald asserted today. The Daily Herald forecast that disarmament failure would precipitate a race for aerial armaments. The new airplanes, the newspaper said, would cost $2,250,000 and would be equipped with late model machine guns and motors such as those with which Britain has won recent Schneider cup speed races, capable of more than 250 miles an hour.

LONDON, Aug. 16.—For the first time in the history of the Metropolitan police, three women have been named members of the Scotland Yard staff of detectives. Experimental tests of their aptitude for criminal investigation proved successful.

POONA, India, Aug. 16.—After the Mahatma Gandhi announced he was starting a fast until death, the government came forward with an offer which it was expected would impel him to abandon the plan. The government was willing to provide the Nationalist leader with facilities enabling him to continue, under certain conditions, his campaign to better the status of India's most lowly caste, the Untouchables. Thus far the Mahatma has not actually missed any meal, and it was expected he would eat as usual this evening. The little nationalist leader, who was arrested August 1 at the outset of a new disobedience campaign and committed to Yeroda jail here for a year because he refused to obey a command to cease political activities, threatened to start the fast unless he was given full rights as a state of political prisoner. At present he is treated as an ordinary prisoner, and certain privileges h

OTTAWA, Aug. 15. (#)—Alan Winslow, noted United States world war aviator and author of several books on aviation, died today. Death was due to injuries suffered when Winslow fell from a third floor window of a hotel here Saturday. Apparently becoming faint, Winslow had sought to open the window and fell out. Winslow, 87 years old, served in France with the Lafayette escadrille and lost an arm in action. After the war he was associated with the United States government’s foreign service.

POONA, India, Aug. 16.—(UP)—The Mahatma Gandhi’s fast, which began at noon today, ended suddenly a few minutes later, when he received permission from the government to continue his campaign in behalf of the “untouchables” in whatever manner he saw fit. The government laid down only minor restrictions for the campaign, which Gandhi insists upon managing from his cell in the Yeravda jail. Gandhi had insisted that the fast, his second this year, would be continued “to the death” if the government failed to relent. The government had insisted that he divorce his propaganda in behalf of the unfortunate outcasts of India, from politics.

Lo (A?) elas cr an alleged attempt to assassinate an American ambassador and consul were disclosed today in testimony at the trial in a naval court of ten officers charged with killing Premier Suvoshi Inukai and other terroristic activities in May 1932. The projected assassinations were designed to provoke friction between Japan and the United States and in this way encourage a nationalistic and militarist revolution, Lieut. Kijo lio, one of the defendants declared in giving testimony. When the alleged planning to kill the American ambassador was made, Ito testified, the ambassadorship was vacant, Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes having departed for the United States and Joseph C. Grew, his successor, not yet having arrived in Japan. It has previously been testified by Lieut. Horishi Yamagishi, leader of the ten officers on trial, that fears of what he termed “America's ambition

1933-08-23.text: WASHINGTON, Aug. 22 (P)— Importers cited the poetry of the Stein Song of Old Heidelberg and the pathos of the man who wants English ale for his stomach’s sake, in pleas before the tariff commission today for a 50 per cent cut in the duty on foreign brew. They noted many a statistic, too, to prove the way of the beer and ale importer is unduly difficult, Then they asked that the United States make a “friendly gesture toward 25 beer-producing nations" by reducing the tariff on imported beer from $1 to 50 cents per gallon, or from $31 to $15.50 per barrel. The commission, which had ordered the inquiry, gravely received the testimony, which eventually will go before President Roosevelt for final decision under the flexible provision of the 1930 tariff act. Commissioner Thomas Walker Page of Virginia said he had been opposed to the investigation at first, but that correspondence had convinced

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Aug. 22.—(A)—The Irish Free State government tonight banned the blue shirt national guard organization of Gen. Eoin O'Duffy by proclamation and set up a military tribunal to operate under the public safety act. This action was in line with predictions which followed a number of parades throughout the Saorstat last Sunday. President Eamon De Valera declared Sunday night that if reports were received that the demonstrations were made by uniformed men an outlawing proclamation would surely follow. The military tribunal was established with Col. Francis Bennett as president and a personnel the same as when the tribunal operated during the administration of former President William T. Cosgrave. Will Not Dissolve. O'Duffy, who had declared previously that the national guard “will neither dissolve nor allow itself to be driven underground,” said when informed of the pr

London. Aug. 23 ()—The world wheat conference was unable today to determine the level of international wheat prices at which importing countries should begin to reduce tariffs. The conference adjourned to meet again tomorrow. By the terms of a draft agreement submitted by wheat exporting countries to the importing nations, the importers would undertake to cut down tariffs on wheat once the world price went above a stipulated level. At today's session the conferees could not agree on what this level should be.

London, Aug. 23 (UP)—Prospects of a world agreement to restrict export of wheat in the interest of higher prices are improved, Frederick E. Murphy, United States delegate to the World Wheat conference, announced today as committees drafted reports. Findings of the committees, one technical, the other advisory, are to be submitted to a meeting of the full conference tomorrow. In anticipation of the meeting, some delegates telephoned their governments today for final instructions.

POONA, India. —(4”)— Mahatma Gandhi broke his fast, which is in its eighth day, shortly after he had been unconditionally released from custody today by the government. The Mahatma had grown weaker yesterday, but his condition had not yet become critical. Gandhi is engaged in a “fast unto death” because authorities refuse to grant him concessions in Yeroda jail for conducting his campaign for the untouchable class. He was removed to the civil hospital Monday.

POONA, India, (UP)—Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, weak and ill after fasting for a week, was released unconditionally from his one year prison sentence Wednesday. He was taken from the civil hospital, where he had been under treatment, by ambulance to Parnakutti. Gandhi broke his fast before he left the hospital and participated in prayers offered by his followers. Gandhi received word of the remission of sentence at the hospital, where he was taken from Yeravda jail Sunday when his condition became alarming. Gandhi's latest tour in jail was the result of his renewal of his civil disobedience campaign. He organized a march through the country with 31 followers, to preach disobedience of laws as a means of forcing home rule. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, and his followers to six months. Gandhi was offered his freedom if he would remain in Poona and refrain from conducting civil disobe

Paris, Aug. 22.—(/P)—Suddenly renewed fear of armed conflict along the Austro-German border became today one of the dangers complicating little Austria's political and economic plight. Reports from Austria said six or eight thousand exiles, many with shotguns and rifles, were strung along the frontier, creating a menace of guerilla warfare and even organized invasion. When the fast growing Austrian Nazi party, agitating for union with Germany and declaring allegiance to Chancellor Hitler, was ordered outlawed by the Dollfuss government, many were exiled or fled to Germany to escape arrest. May Boost Army To meet this new crisis, France has approved the plan of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss to increase his present army of 22,000 to 30,000, the limit authorized by the Saint Germain peace treaty. It is believed Great Britain and Italy likewise will sanction the increase.

VIENNA, Aug. 23.—(UP)—Austria prepared an army of 1,000 picked sharpshooters today which is to be sent to the German frontier in fear of an attack by exiled Nazis, working in cooperation with Hitler storm troopers. The frontier already is heavily guarded. Military intelligence reports that the Nazis planned a series of border raids, and perhaps an invasion in force, early in September, caused Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss to order the new force of two battalions of the Heimwehr to prepare for action. European powers were considering the addition of 8,000 men to the military forces allowed Austria under the St. Germain treaty. It was hoped the men would be ready to go to the border early in September, after they have been organized and instructed in special duties. Frontier incidents have been frequent. Only a fortnight ago a frontier policeman was shot and killed from ambush. This led to

1933-08-21.text: REYKJAVIK, Iceland, Aug. 21.— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh obeyed a rule of the air and lent a helping hand to a comrade in distress when he aided a young British pilot, John Grierson, in salvaging parts from the latter's plane, wrecked yesterday in an attempted takeoff for Greenland. Grierson left England August 5 on the first leg of an intended flight by stages to New York. A wave broke over one of the floats and wrecked the craft. Grierson was not hurt. The American aviator, who is engaged in a northern air mapping tour, conferred aboard the supply ship Jellinge, which today awaited sailing orders from New York.

LONDON, Aug. 21. — (J.P) -- The world wheat conference, opening today with 29 producing and exporting nations represented, made rapid progress in its first session, and adjourned at 1:30 p.m. practically in agreement on procedure. Even with agreement conceded among the chief exporting nations—the United States, Canada, Argentina, Australia and Russia—a fight was foreseen with importing nations. A two-year agreement is sought. The International Institute of Agriculture at Rome, in a pessimistic forecast, Saturday, predicted a shortage of 293,949,333 bushels in this year's North American wheat crop, with resulting higher prices.

REYKJAVIK, Iceland, Aug. 21 (UP).—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh discussed their next move today, as the supply ship Jelling which has accompanied them on their exploratory air cruise prepared to leave for the United States. John Grierson, former British royal air force pilot, ended his flight to the United States when his plane capsized as he was taking off for Greenland. Grierson’s plane was believed too badly damaged to be repaired.

| Vienna, Aug. 21 (UP)—Great Britain, France and Italy have agreed to take ‘certain’ military action to preserve the status in Austria if either German or Austrian Nazis attempt to forcefully overthrow the government of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, a reliable diplomatic source said today. The governments, it was said, have decided to inform Germany in friendly conversations of their decision. In considering the increasingly serious diplomatic problem of Austria versus Germany, it was asserted, the three allied powers thought both of the immediate future and the ultimate solution of Austria’s difficulties. To this end, it was said, they have considered the possibility of a Danubian economic federation. Chancellor Dollfuss’ airplane flight to Rome Saturday was understood to have followed immediately upon a cabinet meeting at which Dollfuss announced the allied powers had reached agreemen

Poona, India, Aug. 20, (4)—The condition of Mahatma Gandhi from his self-imposed ordeal of fasting has grown so bad that he was removed this afternoon from Yeroda jail to the civil hospital where facilities for medical attention are better. Friends were extremely anxious about the Mahatma’s increasing weakness on the fifth day of his present hunger strike. Gandhi meanwhile was adamant in refusal to accept the government’s conditions under which it offered to release him for continuance of his campaign on behalf of the Indian untouchable class. His fast was undertaken to obtain privileges which would enable him to carry on this work. It was believed an acute attack of kidney trouble caused the move to a hospital. Late tonight it was said that Gandhi had not spoken or written since his removal to the hospital. The political situation is unchanged, it being pointed out that the Mahatma stil

MOSCOW, Aug. 21.--(AP)—Approximately 100,000 children, ranging from kindergarten age to 16 years, are being used for the harvest in north Caucasus, Ukraine and mid-Volga regions to ‘protect the Socialist crop.” The children, a Kharkov dispatch said today, are being organized by the Communist political sections, which now exercise rigid control over all agriculture, into “light cavalry detachments.” Both boys and girls are called on to watch sharply to prevent grain thefts and her depredations in these troublesome areas and also to retrieve grain left in the fields by the harvesters. Thousands of them have built huts in which they live in the fields of the collective farms. They are fed by the government. Virtually all of them are children of collective farmers belonging either to the Octobrists, the young Pioneers or the young Communists. To the Octobrists—children from six to ten years

VIENNA, Aug. 21,— Political circles, taking cognizance of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss' hurried visit to Italy for a conference with Premier Mussolini, inclined to the belief today that the chancellor has abandoned his policy of friendship with Germany. Rather, these quarters think, Dollfuss is trying to win the Italian premier to concerted action by big European powers against what the Austrian government characterizes as German interference with Austrian internal political affairs. Broadcasts in Germany of what the government considered anti-Austrian propaganda resulted in representations by the governments of France, Great Britain, and Italy. Germany replied that the incident was closed. Many Austrian newspapers have demanded the administration bring about an intervention of the League of Nations, but Dollfuss so far has refused to adopt such a course.

POONA, India, Aug. 21.—Mahatma M. K. Gandhi's wife, Kasturba, was released unconditionally from jail today. She went immediately to a hospital where Gandhi is ill as the result of his latest fast. Gandhi was removed to the hospital from jail yesterday, because of the better facilities for treatment. He reiterated his determination to fast until he dies unless he was released unconditionally or permitted in his own way to carry on from jail his campaign in aid of the untouchables.

1933-08-14.text: Cincinnati, O., Aug. 13 (AP)—A pretty 18-year-old girl, born amid the roar of a British barrage near the World War battle lines in Belgium, was not to be daunted today when three hold-up men confronted her. Daughter of a Belgian mother and of a German soldier who was away fighting at the time of her birth, Rose Ruda had too much spirit to submit helplessly as the trio robbed the restaurant where she worked. So Rose walked to the kitchen, obtained a revolver placed there for just such an emergency, and fatally wounded one of the robbers before she herself was shot in an arm. A short time later she helped capture the man she had shot when he was brought to a doctor's office where Rose's wound was being treated. The wounded robber, John Phillips, 23, of Cincinnati, died in General Hospital with a bullet in his chest, four hours after he and two companions took $50 from the restaurant and si

DUBLIN. (UP). Rumors that President De Valera intended to proclaim an Irish republic, and perhaps to force an early parliamentary election with the republic as the issue, brought increased tension to the political crisis after a weekend of riots. De Valera announced he would appoint a military court of five officers, empowered to impose the death penalty for attempts against the government.

London, Aug. 12.—Douglas Fairbanks, Hollywood film star, flatly denied rumors he plans to become a British subject in an interview published today by the London Daily Sketch. “The rumor I am proposing to become a British subject is all nonsense,” the paper quoted him as stating. “I am an American and shall remain an American,”

Dublin, Irish Free State, Aug. 13.—(P)—Nervousness and tension relaxed in Dublin today as the threatened clash between General Owen O'Duffy's blue-shirted national guard and authorities failed to materialize. It has been feared that disorders might occur in connection with the memorial ceremonies at the cenotaph in Leinster Lawn for Arthur Griffith, Michael Collins and Kevin O'Higgins, national heroes of early Free State history, since O'Duffy had planned to parade his men in uniform and President De Valera forbade it. The government prepared for any eventuality. One scuffle occurred as six blue shirts left their headquarters in uniform after midday and were attacked by a crowd. Police rescued the six, somewhat battered, and escorted them back to their headquarters. Ceremony Off Formal functions at the cenotaph were abandoned for the first time since the memorial was erected.

Berlin, Aug. 14—(AP)— Amazement was expressed at the American consulate general today at the severity of the sentence imposed on Thorsten Johnson, American seaman charged with having called Chancellor Hitler a Czech Jew. The consulate expects shortly to send a representative to Stettin, where an emergency court rules that Johnson must serve six months. “Before Johnson's trial,” a consulate spokesman said, “we were in contact with the state's attorney at Stettin and received a distinct impression that the case was not regarded as serious, especially as Johnson claims he merely said, ‘Hitler is a Czechoslovak and the Jews don’t like him.’ “But even if he said that Hitler is a Czech Jew we consider six months imprisonment grotesque.”

ROME, Aug. 13.—(AP)—Air Marshal Italo Balbo and his hundred fliers who returned yesterday from their record mass flight to Chicago were accorded a triumph today such as emperors received when the city was mistress of the world. In the presence of a vast throng packed between the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill, the heroes of the double-Atlantic flight paraded afool under the historic arch of Constantine while cannon boomed and thousands of Fascist women threw flowers and laurel leaves in their path. Amid volleys of cheering they first passed beneath arches formed by Fascist banners. Premier Mussolini, wishing the airmen to receive the undivided plaudits of the multitude, did

ORBETELLO, Italy, Aug. 14. (UP)--The 23 ships of the Balbo squadron which survived the historic flight to Chicago and back reached their base at Orbetello today and were reviewed by King Victor Emanuel. The flying boats were drawn up in parade formation, and the king passed along the line in a motor car while the crews stood at attention on the great wings. Victor Emanuel congratulated the flyers and led a parade through the streets to the city hall, where an informal demonstration took place. The squadron then was released on a two months furlough in recognition of their special service.

ROME, Aug. 13—The Italian mass flight to America and return was a "consecrated fascist revolution in the skies of two continents," Premier Mussolini declared today in addressing the Balbo aviators after a triumphal procession under the historic Arch of Constantine. The duce, garbed in the uniform of commander of the black shirt militia, conferred the title of air marshal upon Air Minister General Italo Balbo, leader of the transatlantic expedition, and promoted each flier one grade in recognition of the epic achievement. The fascist chief, addressing members of the squadron lined up at attention on the Palatine hill, predicted that "many years will pass before the air corps of other countries" equal the feat which was finished yesterday with the arrival of the air armada at Ostia. Mussolini embraced and kissed Balbo on both cheeks and handed him the hat of an air marshal after the leader

1933-12-13.text: London, Dec. 12. (AP)—Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, who claims to be the illegitimate son of the late Duke of Clarence, was committed for trial at the next session of historic old Bailey court after he had pleaded not guilty today to "demanding money from the king with menaces." He was remanded to jail after a hearing December 4 on a charge of attempting to extort money from King George V. Haddon reserved his defense when it was announced today that he must stand trial. "I never had any criminal intention," he declared. The 43-year-old jobless engineer wrote a letter to the king last June in which he said he was forced to wash his own dirty linen in a backroom "and that of the royal family in public for a living." Haddon wrote he would have been satisfied with £600 annually, or about $3000, and "enough money to start a modern boarding house." This and other similar letters were admitted as

SANTA CLAUS, Ind., Dec. 15. —(P)—Having overcome both politics and congress, Santa Claus is back again at the big job of keeping alive in the minds of the tots of the world a myth that is centuries old. Letters from Palestine, Egypt, the Philippines, Canada, Australia, England and most of the United States again have swamped Postmaster James F. Martin, first assistant to old Saint Nick. It is with increased happiness that Martin and the dozen families that reside in this quaint village in the southern Indiana hills go about their Christmas work this year. Some time ago, it appeared probable that the only Santa Claus in the world would disappear from public notice. First the congress was going to take the Santa Claus post-office away. Then, with the change of political parties in power, it appeared that Postmaster Martin, who has been the country’s real Santa Claus for many years, would b
BOSTON, Mass., Dec. 12.—James Roosevelt, son of President Roosevelt, is a patient in the New England Baptist Hospital because of a slight intestinal disorder.

London, Dec. 12 —(4)— Queen Mary, considered an excellent judge of dancing, has passed favorable judgment on two American dancers, The pair, Fred Astaire and Clair Luce, entertained yesterday in a command performance. The queen commented enthusiastically to her companions during their performance, The show in which the dancers were presented was arranged for the benefit of the king's pension fund for actors and actresses.

MOSCOW, Dec. 13.—(U.P.)—Ambassador William C. Bullitt today presented his credentials to President Mikhail Kalinin and for the first time in 16 years normal diplomatic relations between the United States and Russia were formally resumed. Pledging “close collaboration in world peace” and the establishment “not merely of normal but of genuinely friendly relations” between the two nations, Ambassador Bullitt was impressively received in the historic Kremlin. He announced immediately after the ceremony that the United States embassy would be in full operation by February and that the American consulate would be established within a short time.

BRUSSELS, Dec. 12.—(A#”)-— The Belgian cabinet decided today to maintain its previous attitude concerning its war debt to the United States—that of default. It made no provisions for the payment falling due Dec. 12.

BERLIN, Dec. 12—(ch)—Springing to their feet four times with military precision to vote “yea,” more than 650 Hitlerite solons, with a handful of non-Nazis in mufti, organized the new Reichstag today in seven and one half minutes. They elected officers, empowered the speaker to appoint committees and call the next meeting, listened to a snappy two-and-one-half minute acceptance speech, shouted ‘Heil Hitler!” and then adjourned. The proceedings moved like clockwork. Whether they wore the brown of the storm troopers, the black of the select troopers, the steel gray of the steel helmeters, or the light gray of the air ministry, the legislators rose each time at the exhortation of Reichstag President and Prussian Premier Hermann Goering as though they had practiced the act.

PARIS, Dec. 13—France will enter its third successive war debt default Friday with a note to the United States government, it was learned today. A note has been drafted carrying further the defense made at the time of the last default, June 45; The note informs the American government that France will not pay the $19,154,046.82 due as interest on the war debt. It will explain that the French had hoped a revision would be reached before the payment was due. Therefore, the note says, France feels obliged to defer payment, though it remains desirous to settle the entire problem of intergovernmental debts whenever the United States believes settlement feasible. It was one year ago today that the government of Edouard Herriot was overthrown by the chamber of deputies for advocating payment of the December 15 war debt installment, and there has been no change in sentiment.

1933-11-24.text: London, Nov. 24—(4:4)—The Duke of Atholl, one of the leading figures of the British peerage, was fined £25 (currently about $132) today for contravention of England's 110-year-old lotteries act. Sir Rollo Graham Campbell, chief metropolitan magistrate, who presided over the hearing on the original summons, handed down his decision in the Bow Street police station. The 66-year-old Scottish warrior’s attorney, Norman Birkett, declared he would appeal the case to a higher court.

LONDON, Nov. 24—Sir John Simon announced in the House of Commons today that Great Britain has suggested to France the desirability of direct disarmament negotiations with Germany. The British foreign minister said the government flatly rejected the suggestion that a disarmament convention should be drawn up without Germany, and then presented to the Reich for signature. “Germany is not a target for dictation,” he declared. “She is a partner in the discussion. We shall never get anywhere unless we try to look inside the German mind.” Simon said he believed bilateral discussions through “the regular diplomatic channels constituted the best method of negotiation at present. Referring to the position of France in the disarmament problem, Simon said, “We already have made it plain to the French government that if they saw their way clear to enter into closer communication with Germany, they h

Washington, D. C.—(AP)—A price of $33.76 an ounce for R. F. C. purchases of domestic newly mined gold was established for the fourth time today. Meanwhile, the world price of the metal was less than that figure for the first time in several days. At London it was $33.48 on a basis of sterling opening at $5.31 to the pound.

LONDON, Nov. 24.——C?—One thing George Bernard Shaw likes about Adolf Hitler is the German chancellor's “expression of intense resentment.” “That,” the Irish dramatist told the Fabian Society last night, “is what every statesman ought to have.” It was Shaw's annual oratorical “night out” and he appeared to make the most of it. He eulogized Joseph Stalin and Premier Mussolini along with Hitler. He referred to President Roosevelt, too, as a man “trying to get something done.” “One thing about Hitler commends him to me from the very start,” Shaw said. “That is his face. “What is prominent in the expression on that face? It is the expression of intense resentment—and that is the expression every statesman ought to have. “English statesmen never show resentment in surroundings which ought to make them mad with fury. BOSTON, Nov. 24.—Bruce Barton, New York advertising executive, urged “deflation of governmental ballyhoo,” in a speech prepared for delivery before the New England conference today. He expressed the belief that the whole recovery program of the administration “has seriously handicapped itself by its own ballyhoo.” “The NRA is a sound and inspiring effort,” he said, “but why was it necessary for General Johnson to surround himself with a brigade of publicity men? Why the tumult and the shouting? Why the parades? “When you say to the American public, ‘We are going to try, slowly and earnestly, to restore purchasing power and get people back to work,’ they are willing to tighten their belts and go along with you. But when you say: ‘March up Fifth Avenue, and everything will be all right’ when you promise to get millions back to work immediately and then have to confess that you are far shor

PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 23.—James P. Warburg, vice-chairman of the Bank of Manhattan Company and recently financial adviser for the government at the London Economic conference, has joined the group opposed to the administration's monetary policy. Speaking before the American Academy of Political and Social Science here last night, Warburg opposed the commodity and price-raising plans of the administration. Dr. Cyril James, assistant professor of finance at the University of Pennsylvania also was in opposition. Professor Irving Fisher of Yale, and Senator Elmer Thomas of Oklahoma, the other speakers, upheld the President. Tells of Resignation Warburg disclosed for the first time that he resigned during the progress of the economic conference because his views conflicted with those of President Roosevelt. He advocated immediate return to a gold standard as did Doctor James. Professor Fisher an

London, Nov. 24 (UP)—The dollar continued a strong tone at the market opening today. The pound sterling opened at $5.205, down 4 cents from the close yesterday, and down 11 cents from yesterday's opening.

His attorney gave notice of appeal. 1933-11-27.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 27.—(4)—On the return of Acting Secretary Morgenthau from his Warm Springs conference with President Roosevelt, the administration today held the gold price for the sixth day at $33.76 an ounce—well above the London figure. On the basis of sterling opening at $5.24 to the pound, the London price was $32.83.

LONDON, NOV. 27. (AP).—A Reuters (British) news dispatch from Harbin, Manchuria, today said it was feared many were killed and wounded when bandits fired upon the 600 passengers of the Trans-Siberian express after having derailed the train near Tsitsihar. The dispatch also said many of the survivors were kidnapped.

LONDON, Nov. 27. (AP)—A gloomy outlook for wheat still prevails, the world international wheat commission found when it met today to review the developments of the past two months. The 25 delegates agreed that Russian exports have not been a depressing factor although the Soviet still refuses to accept the quota offered by the big four— the United States, Canada, Argentina and Australia. Abraham Gourevitch, the Russian delegate, said: "We actually are keeping within the quota offered us because prices are so poor. It is true our crop is not as good as expected earlier in the year but there is no necessity for hurrying into an agreement to restrict exports. For the present, the Soviet Union is selling other products and cannot be blamed for the conditions now obtaining." LONDON, Nov. 27.—()—Russia’s determination to play a lone role in world markets, current "distress selling," bumper Eur

LONDON, Nov. 27— (AP) — Russia’s determination to play a lone hand in world markets, current “distress selling,” bumper European crops and the difficulty of getting accurate information on the operation of the new wheat pact were problems tackled with fresh vigor by the world wheat commission today. At this meeting, Russia was expected to be less obdurate toward the effort to bring her into the gentleman’s agreement for the international control of wheat exports than she was two months ago when the agreement for the year 1933-1934 was drawn. There was no indication, however, that Russia would be ready to give up her demand that her quota of 37,000,000 bushels be doubled. Wheat export quotas for other leading wheat producers, as fixed last summer, were Canada, 200,000,000 bushels; Argentina 110,000,000; Australia 105,000,000 and the United States 47,000,000.

By United Press PARIS, March 14.—France is preparing to pay her defaulted December 15 war debt installment to the United States, it was reported reliably today. The payment may be made without a new debate in Parliament, it was said.

PARIS, Nov. 27—(P)—A fast-emptying treasury, widespread protest meetings and miners’ “work and bread” demonstrations greeted the new cabinet of Premier Camille Chautemps today. The members took office early this morning after formal presentation to President Albert LeBrun. No sooner had they officially entered office than Finance Minister Georges Bonnet told Bank of France officials that the government could meet its debts only until December 15. To meet the situation, the cabinet began preparing a program contemplating saving 6,000,000,000 francs (about $400,000,000) through economies and tapping new resources to raise more funds. At the same time, it was made known the cabinet planned to demand a decree of power to cut the pay of functionaries—a matter which has been a bone of bitter contention in the chamber of deputies. PARIS, Nov. 27 — Camille Chautemps today formed the fifth cabinet of the year, and decided to stake its life in the chamber of deputies this week on an appeal to all parties to pass the budget as a matter of national emergency. It was practically identical with the moderate left wing cabinet of Albert Sarraut which was overthrown in the chamber on the budget issue Friday morning. There was but one important change. Paul Marchandeau, of the Chautemps radical socialist party was made budget minister in place of Abel Gardey, member of the left democratic group which is the senate wing of the radical socialists. Important government obligations maturing within the next few weeks made it necessary to act promptly on the budget, and find means to overcome a prospective 1934 deficit of 6,000,000,000 francs ($373,000,000) before the fiscal year ends December 31.
