Two coast guardsmen, unheard from since Sunday when they left Ontonagon, Mich., in a 35-foot picket boat for Bayfield, Wis., on Lake Superior, and believed lost, were reported safe by coast guards at Madeline Island not far from their destination. Their craft, its hull punctured, was towed to the island by a lightship. Many Great Lakes ships remained at hastily taken anchorage, delaying their trips for better weather. The Norwegian steamer Flaks went aground near South Haven, Mich. and t

LONDON, Nov. 17.—(#)—Speedy selection of a place agreeable to Germany for new disarmament discussions will result, it is hoped, from a meeting at Geneva to which Sir John Simon and Capt. Anthony Eden hurried today. It was generally indicated that Great Britain's emissaries were ready to represent the government as willing to consider concessions to Germany in arms. On the way to Geneva, it was understood Sir John, who is foreign secretary, and Captain Eden, under-secretary, would confer with Joseph Paul-Boncour, French foreign minister. M. Paul-Boncour planned to join their train and accompany the British pair southward, it was said. Meanwhile, some political commentators here referred today to a rumor that Germany threatened to denounce the treaty of Versailles unless she obtains concessions as supplying one reason for the urgency of the Geneva gathering, but no substantiation was forth

VALENTIA, Irish Free State, Nov. 16 (#)—Hope was virtually abandoned Thursday for 27 men in the crew of the British freighter Saxilby, of whom nothing had been heard since their last despairing SOS as they took to the boats of the storm-battered vessel Wednesday morning. One by one searching vessels gave up the quest after reaching the spot, about 300 miles off the Irish coast, whence the last signal came, without finding a trace of the Saxilby or its lifeboats. The captain of the British freighter St. Quentin, which battled the storm near the place where the Saxilby was last reported, advised his owners by wireless Thursday night that a temporary steering apparatus had been made and the ship was proceeding under her own steam and expected to reach Cobh Saturday night.

By The Associated Press. The hope that disarmament conversations may be redeemed from the doldrums occasioned by Germany's withdrawal was revived Thursday in four European centers, Authoritative circles in London said Great Britain was ready to listen to Chancellor Hitler's arms demands and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon was instructed to proceed to Geneva to survey possibilities of beginning new conversations in which Germany could join. Four-Power Powwow There was talk that Italy, France, Great Britain and Germany might send representatives to a four-power conference to be conducted perhaps in Rome or London on a date not yet chosen, Sir John was due to confer with Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour of France in Geneva Saturday and it was said a new French arms proposal, with an apparent lessening of the tension between Germany and France, had accelerated disarmament hopes, Semi-of

LONDON, Nov. 17--Disarmament negotiations must be pushed vigorously despite dislocation caused by Germany’s withdrawal, King George said today in a speech on the prorogation of parliament. The speech was read in the House of Lords and Commons by Lord Sankey, the Lord Chancellor. Parliament’s adjournment will be a brief one. It will meet again Tuesday. The king, discussing domestic problems, referred warmly to the fortitude of British people that had strengthened the financial structure.

London, Nov. 17 (4)—With the blessing of King George, who expressed the hope before parliament that disarmament difficulties could “be surmounted”, two British leaders left for Geneva today to seek in a three-power parley a formula for Germany’s return to arms discussions. “My government have throughout taken an active part in the disarmament conference,” said His Majesty, and the British draft presented March 16 was adopted as the basis for a proposed convention. “I earnestly trust that the difficulties which have since arisen may be surmounted. “The withdrawal of Germany a month ago from the deliberations at Geneva necessarily dislocated the program, but work for international disarmament between the nations must be vigorously pursued.” Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary, and Captain Anthony Eden, under-secretary for foreign affairs, will confer in Geneva with the French foreign min

London, Nov. 17 (®).—Parliament was prorogued until the opening of the new session Tuesday, after the reading of a speech by King George today in which he expressed hope that world disarmament difficulties can be overcome. "My government have throughout taken an active part in the Disarmament Conference," His Majesty said, "and the British draft presented March 16 was adopted as the basis for a proposed convention. "I earnestly trust that the difficulties which have since arisen may be surmounted. "The withdrawal of Germany months ago from the deliberations at Geneva necessarily dislocated the program, but work for international disarmament by agreement between the nations must be rigorously pursued. Regarding Britain’s general situation, King George said, "the continuous willingness of my people to bear heavy sacrifices made it possible for this country almost alone among the great coun

London Nov. 17—()—That Great Britain is ready to bow to Chancellor Hitler’s ultimatum and discuss concessions to Germany in the matter of armaments was indicated Wednesday night in authoritative circles. This report, coming on the heels of instructions that Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon proceed to Geneva as a move to get Germany back into the arms conference, was viewed as an explanation for renewed activity here to save the disarmament talks from a breakdown. Must Make Gesture It was admitted in informed quarters that the British government realizes the futility of this activity unless the European nations are ready to make a gesture to Germany. Sir John and Captain Anthony Eden, under-secretary for foreign affairs, may leave for Geneva today. It was believed that the only act to be achieved there is the selection of a four-power meeting place acceptable to Germany in view of her ave

1933-04-20.text: The first official departure of the United States from the gold standard in more than fifty years was felt today throughout the world. London.—Britain’s reaction was puzzlement and extreme anxiety. The dollar value dropped heavily—at one time it was $3.90 to the pound. The British government rejected the theory that the United States took the step to provide itself with a bludgeon for the MacDonald-Roosevelt negotiations. Paris. — Stocks jumped upward and the dollar closed on the bourse at 22.46 francs, the lowest in more than seven years. Berlin.—A high financial authority said that in the long run present fluctuations should not touch the dollar value, for the United States is the world’s creditor. The dollar dropped. Rome.—Large groups of American tourists called at banks and travel agencies seeking advice. The dollar dropped. Vienna.—American travelers got 19 percent less for their d

London, April 20 (4)—Puzzlement, coupled with extreme anxiety, was the British reaction today to the American imposition of the gold embargo and the statements from Washington that the United States was off the gold standard. The immediate result was a heavy fall in the value of the dollar as compared with the pound. It was quoted at one time at $3.90 to the pound, a slump of 43 cents under the closing figure of Tuesday. Government quarters were beset with uncertainty as to just what President Roosevelt's move meant and economists were equally bewildered. Two things did emerge clearly from Downing Street: The president's official position is that Mr. Roosevelt's action was not, as some suggest, for the purpose of bludgeoning Prime Minister MacDonald on the eve of the White House conversations and secondly, there is no disposition on the part of England to try to debase the value of the p

London, April 20 (4)—The chiefs of the Soviet Russian trade delegation to London were recalled to Moscow today “for consultation” and will start for home next Monday. This action follows the conviction of five British engineers tried in Moscow on sabotage charges, and the imposition of an 80 per cent embargo against Russian importations into England, a measure resorted to by the government in protest against the sabotage case. Asked if there was any question of the delegation not returning to London, a Soviet official said: "All I can say at present is that the delegation is going home to make a report—a not unusual thing from time to time." LONDON, April 19.—An 80 percent embargo on Russian imports was proclaimed today through King George as a result of the trial in Moscow of six British electrical engineers. Shortly thereafter, however, there were authoritative indications that the action might be revoked if prison sentences of two of the Britons would be commuted to banishment from Russia. Soviet Ambassador Maisky, chairman of the Russian trade delegation, and his chief assistants conferred with Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, and the Board of Trade today in an effort to avoid a break because of the crisis. The British labor ranks, aroused by the threatened rupture, summoned leaders of trades unions to a conference with the Labor party and Laborite members of parliament to consider the whole question of the embargo. WASHINGTON, April 20 (UP)--Speaker of the House Rainey today charged a “planned and concerted effort" on the part of “nations tied up with the English pound” to attack the United States world monetary position. Abandonment of the gold standard, he added, was a “weapon of defense.”

BY United Press LONDON, April 20. — Alexander Ozersky, head of the Soviet trade delegation to Great Britain, has been ordered to Moscow “for consultation,” the Soviet embassy announced today. ‘This was generally interpreted as the first move toward a Soviet embargo on British goods, in retaliation for the British embargo declared yesterday.

Sir Josiah Stamp, director of the Bank of England and one of the most powerful figures in British finance, told the United Press in an exclusive interview today. The American dollar dropped rapidly again today, but British economic and financial experts, recovered from the first shock of American abandonment of dollar parity, were optimistic that it would bring the international monetary problem to a quick head and induce a speedy international agreement on monetary stability. Paris April 20 French financiers feared today France eventually will be obliged to follow the United States off the gold standard, She already is on a gold bullion basis, releasing only bars. Bankers say that further restrictions are likely because Great Britain is draining French gold. The Bank of England got most of the $117,000,000 in gold France lost in the past four months, The Bank of France is extremely cautious. Bankers said contrary to custom, it issued no advice in the present situation but adopted a “wait and see” policy. One leading banking expert said: “This is the most far-reaching financial event of the past century, far greater than England’s desertion of gold. 1933-03-23.text: LONDON, (UP).-- The government has instructed Sir Esmond Ovey, ambassador to Moscow, to demand unconditional release without trial of four Britishers held there on sabotage charges, it was understood today. The demand would be made of Maxim Litvinov, Soviet foreign commissar, on the ground that the men are absolutely innocent. The question of severing diplomatic relations in the event developments warrant was being considered. Suspension of negotiations for a trade agreement with Moscow already has been announced.

The Senate confirmed the appointment late yesterday without discussion and by unanimous consent after Senator McNary of Oregon, Republican leader, withdrew an objection that had blocked consideration earlier.

By the Associated Press LONDON, March 22.--"An almost miraculous change,” has occurred in the United States since the inauguration of President Roosevelt, Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain said in the House of Commons tonight. Mr. Chamberlain referred to economic conditions throughout the world as well as in the United States, and his remarks were optimistic. “Looking over the world,” he said, “one can see indications that the industrial situation is likely to improve within the next few months.” Recent improvements in the United States, he asserted, have been reflected on this side of the ocean. “A few weeks ago,” he told the House, “anyone looking at the situation in the United States could have done so only with a feeling of gravest anxiety. Today, thanks to the initiative, courage and wisdom of the president, a change has taken place which is almost miraculous. “Confide

WASHINGTON, Mar. 22-17) — Robert Worth Bingham of Kentucky, President Roosevelt's choice for the major American diplomatic assignment, ambassador to Great Britain, today was confirmed by the Senate within a few hours after his nomination was approved by the foreign relations committee. Confirmation of the Louisville publisher's name came without discussion and by unanimous consent late in the day after Senator McNary of Oregon, the Republican leader, withdrew an objection that had blocked consideration a few hours earlier. McNary had objected to taking up the nomination in the absence of Senator Borah of Idaho, ranking Republican member of the foreign relations committee, which had held up action a week while it looked into some speeches made by Bingham in Scotland in 1927. Later in the day, when Senator Robinson of Arkansas, the Democratic leader, for the second time asked that Bingham'

WASHINGTON (UP).—The Senate without debate put its stamp of approval on the appointment of Robert Worth Bingham, Louisville, Ky. publisher, to America’s first ranking diplomatic post, that of ambassador to Great Britain. The distinguished Kentuckian is expected to sail soon for London, where he succeeds Andrew W. Mellon. His post is one of predominant importance, due to the impending war debt negotiations, the world economic conference, and other pressing international problems on which the United States and Britain hope to find solutions that will help restore world stability. The new ambassador is publisher and president of the Louisville Courier Journal and the Louisville Times. In 1907 he was elected mayor of Louisville and four years later he became chancellor of the Jefferson circuit court.

LONDON, March 23.—(#)—Lieutenant Norman Baillie-Stewart of the Seaforth Highlanders, accused of selling out his country for 50 pounds, testified in his own defense Thursday afternoon at a court martial trying him for betrayal of military secrets to a foreign power. Norman Parkes, his attorney, led him through the strange story about the girl named Marie Louise who, he says, sent him money in the mail after he had spent a night with her while he was on furlough in Berlin. The prosecution, which rested Thursday morning, presented several letters from the girl. It was contended that “Marie Louise” was an alias disguising the identity of a foreign agent. The money contained in at least two of the letters, said the prosecution, was Baillie-Stewart’s payment for the betrayal of military secrets.

- BERLIN, (UP). The aspirations of Chancellor Hitler's Nazis for a political union of Germany and Austria were emphatically proclaimed at the opening session of the Prussian diet. The spokesman for union was Wilhelm Kube, the Nazi floor leader. Midst the greatest enthusiasm he saluted eight Austrian Nazis who were in the gallery, and declared: “As the leader of the Nazis in this house and on order of Chancellor Hitler, I, as a Prussian, say that we Prussians are pan-Germans, that we shall continue to be so, and that we shall have obtained our goal only when all Germany, including German Austria, is united with our fatherland in one great state which can then serve Germany's mission in the world.” The well-oiled Nazi parliamentary machine functioned perfectly, disposing within forty-three minutes of a diet program that ordinarily would have necessitated weeks of deliberation. 1933-06-05.text: S. S. President Roosevelt at sea June 5—The view that the London economic conference offers a chance to cut ‘dead wood’ from tariff hedges, that encircle many countries was put forward today. As the vanguard of the United States delegation sped eastward, led by Secretary Cordell Hull, delegation quarters urged that tariff problems be approached with this understanding. Offers Prospect That the field offers a prospect of readjustments of mutual benefit without imposing corresponding sacrifices. Authorities asserted that the attitude of “give and take” in tariff bargaining is exaggerated since much can be done with little giving. Trade agreements reached at the British imperial conference at Ottawa are not regarded as a handicap to this process of pruning, notwithstanding the known protectionist policies of British delegates.

LONDON (UP) — If both Great Britain and France fail to meet the June 15 payments on war debts owed the United States, there is every likelihood that the remaining European debtor nations will join in a general default, a United Press survey indicated Monday. The survey showed that at least five of the 15 debtor nations already had decided not to meet the payment. The remaining 10 will take the cue from the decision of either France or Great Britain, but four of this group may be classed as probable non-payers on the basis of present indications. The survey revealed the tottering condition of the $22,188,486,000 war debt structure built on post-war funding agreements. With a powerful section of the press clamoring for default, Great Britain was still postponing a final decision, hoping for an 11th hour moratorium offer from President Roosevelt. {Associated Press} Labor News NEW YORK, June 5—(#)—From a jumble of facts and prejudices delegates to the four-nation wheat conference now meeting in London want to draw a single design for controlling wheat production. When they again take up plans for helping ailing agriculture started in Geneva and temporarily laid aside last week they will plunge deeper into problems tinged with nationalism. Representatives of the United States, Argentina, Australia and Canada have indicated a desire to agree on acreage restrictions so that wheat prices will be increased. Behind any plan, however, they may reach, are problems of other farmers that scarcely can be ignored.

(Copyright, 1933, by United Press.) ABOARD S.S. PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT, En Route to London. June 4—(UP)—The United States delegation to the world economic conference in London will start to gain prompt action on a few major points in order to stimulate genuine accomplishment, it was learned today. Secretary Hull and his associates may seek direct action on a general agreement to lower tariff barriers and encourage trade, on one hand, and an agreement for the stabilization of currencies on the other.

Moscow, June 5—James Mattern, United States aviator bound round the world in a solo flight, landed in Moscow this afternoon dog tired but “feeling fine.” He was exactly 51 hours and 37 minutes out of New York City, (this put him almost three hours ahead of the Post-Gatty round the world flight record he is trying to beat). Mattern landed at 7:57 A. M. (EST) swooping down on the muddy field from a sky darkened by angry clouds. He said he would remain in Moscow a short time and then press on toward Siberia. After taxiing his ship to a standstill the Texan was gathered up by half a dozen Soviet aviators and tossed into the air several times in the most enthusiastic reception ever given an American airman here. MOSCOW, (U.P)—James Mattern, clipping three hours off the round-the-world flight record to this point, dropped down to a skillful landing at the Moscow airport Monday and prepared to make his way across Siberia with a few hours delay. The dauntless Texan, despite bad weather over the Atlantic which forced him to come down and waste almost a whole day on an island off the south coast of Norway, speeded on with such purpose on his solo flight that was 51 hours 31 minutes out from New York in 1931 in eight days, 15 hours and 15 minutes. They were 54 hours, 34 minutes out of New York when they landed here. They stayed nearly 12 hours, whereas Mattern planned to resume within three or four hours toward Novosibirsk, 1700 miles distant. Mattern drove his red, white and blue monoplane the 1100 miles from Oslo, Norway, in seven hours averaging 157 miles an hour. With only three hours’ sleep since

Oslo, Norway, June 5 —-(AP)— Jimmie Mattern, the grinning Texas airman the world has feared lost, was flashing toward Moscow in his red-white-and-blue plane, "Century of Progress" today after a surprise landing on a small island 70 miles southwest of Oslo. Fighting storms and fogs, which forced him 300 kilometers off his course, the dauntless flier from San Angelo, Texas, fought his way through successfully to land safely on Jomfruland Island, on Norway’s south coast, at 4:15 A. M. (BST) yesterday. The first news that Oslo heard of the landing came when the lighthouse keeper telephoned from his post on the island that Mattern had landed on the beach there and was safe. Plane Rendered Aid A private plane was sent there to give him any aid necessary and at 9 P. M. (BST) yesterday, he hopped for this city. (My 20 AGRO Fra) Naples, Italy, June 5.—A lava wave from Mount Vesuvius was halting a few feet from the precipitous edge of the valley of Inferno today, and as the flow gradually stopped it was believed danger to the town of Terzigno was over. The fireworks display, with shooting flames and rocketing burning stones, still continued.

1933-06-03.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., June 1.— Mr. Roosevelt has been for six weeks trying to find a Republican. He wanted to put him on the economic conference and send him to London. Well, he finally located one, Senator Jim Couzins of Detroit, and he only admitted to being one, just to get the trip. I tell you it takes bribery to get a fellow to write Republican after his name nowadays. Well, they are leaving with high hopes. And it would be wonderful if they could do something besides just seeing the King when he delivers his address. Yours,

BEVERLY HILLS, Cant. June 1.—"Farm prices have advanced 17 percent in the last month." Now that's better news than a speech on "good relations" by Mussolini and Hitler combined. Our new ambassador to England got so elated over the Prince of Wales introducing him that he turned over America to England to be used as they saw fit. It takes a strong man to remember what country he is representing when the wine and the flattery start flowing. If the Republicans ever decide to enter another presidential candidate better hire this little wop, to run for 'em. He is the best bet I see right now. Yours, WILL.

LONDON, June 28 (AP) -- King George V observed his 68th birthday anniversary today but rheumatism in a shoulder prevented him from attending a glittering military pageant in his honor. Rather, the Prince of Wales was deputized to represent his majesty at the trooping of the color. Except for the rheumatic attack, the king is in good health, and many prayers were offered for his continued well being.

| London, June 2—(4)—Unless the nations lay aside prejudices and make mutual concessions for agreements, the world economic conference which begins here June 12 is sure to fall, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told the British house of commons today. “Then indeed it would have been well if the conference never had been held,” he declared in an address which set forth the hopes and fears of the British government for the approaching parley. Failure of the conference might bring despair, the chancellor said “of emerging in our own time from depression, hardship and suffering.” Countries which have adopted an aggressive attitude toward Great Britain need expect no quarter from his government in the continuing economic warfare, he asserted. “Much as we regret the economic warfare which has arisen between us and other countries,” he said, “We must maintain that warfare as lo

CONFERENCE—Mr. Roosevelt may surprise you yet with a swift visit to the London Economic conference. Nothing will be said openly about it for a while yet, but he will go suddenly in July if the situation over there demands his presence. That means if the conference bogs down and he sees a chance to save it by a personal appearance he will call for a cruiser and set sail. The way things look now there is a good chance that he will make the trip. The Conference is headed for the bog. That is not pessimism but realism. The nations are assembling with strong nationalistic fervor running high in all their home capitals. They are not in a conciliatory mood. Beyond that, they face more difficulties than any international conference of modern times. The thing which might keep Mr. Roosevelt from going is the possibility that even he could not resume the conference. The conference delegates did not

SHANGHAI, June 2.—(/)—Glenn Mortimer Hargrave, of Bridgeport, Texas, was arrested here today and charged in the American court of China with the murder of Leslie Bell, a British businessman living in Shanghai. On May 31 Hargrave allegedly assaulted Bell in a street in downtown Shanghai, striking him in the face. The authorities charge that Bell died as a result of the blow. Hargrave is a motorcar salesman. He was previously in Shanghai in 1929 and 1930 as a member of the Fourth Regiment of the United States Marines.

New York, June 3.—()—The world this week has been racing through the pages of the world’s most complicated mystery story—“The Mystery of June 12.” The mystery lies in the attitude of the nations at the London Economic Conference, and new clues have popped up on the plans of North China, in Washington Senate chambers, in European chancellories and on a liner in mid-Atlantic. World statesmen have nine days to study those clues. Then they must assemble, June 12, to offer their solution. This week’s news from China had its bearing on their solutions. China and Japan announced the signing of a truce. It creates a demilitarized zone south of the Great Wall but remains notably silent concerning political control north of the Wall. But Gen. Feng Yu-Hsiang announced plans to war on both Japanese and Chinese who had signed the truce. Japan suggested he might be counting on Russian aid. Such consid

1933-10-26.text: KOBE, Japan, ()—Sixty-six persons, including an English woman, were feared to have perished Friday when the coastwise steamer Yashimamaru foundered in a typhoon, off Suma, near Kobe. Owners of the vessel said records showed 51 survivors of the crew of 58 and 49 passengers were reported. The typhoon carried death to fishing fleets. Several ports reported craft foundered and missing with crews that totaled nearly 100.

Geneva, Oct. 26—()—The disarmament conference today adjourned until Dec. 4 after hearing friendly references to Germany during the discussions. The adjournment decision was in line with a recommendation of the steering committee which met yesterday. Capt. Anthony Eden, British foreign office under secretary, said during the discussion that it was quite clear that the withdrawal of Germany could not be without effect on the work of the conference and it would cause some dislocation. "But," he added, "The British government feels this should not be allowed to stop the work of the conference. We must look forward and not indulge in recriminations."

GENEVA, Oct. 26.—(AP)—The world disarmament conference adjourned today to December 4 with expressions of determination that the work continue and of hope that Germany return to it. “Any failure owing to timidity or a lack of will,” said Arthur Henderson, British president of the parley, “would be a confession that the nations represented are not prepared to discharge the obligations which the conference already has accepted. “This is a responsibility no government would care to assume before its own people and before the world. “The moral and political consequences of such a failure would be too grave for the future of the League of Nations and the cause of world peace.”

(By The Associated Press) In the wake of a storm that whistled out over the Atlantic, temperatures dropped to new October lows in several parts of New England today. In snow-blanketed sections of northern New York the mercury slipped close to the zero mark. At Saranac Lake in the Adirondacks, it topped at eight degrees—the coldest October day there in ten years. Owl's Head, a den under snow drifts three feet deep. Elsewhere in the United States temperatures rose rapidly. From the Mississippi valley west to the Rockies, October's traditional bright blue weather returned after a brief eclipse. Several southern cities early today reported unusually cold weather. The thermometer registered 48 degrees below zero at Vicksburg, Miss. Dixie came out from under its overcoats and blankets later in the day, and normal weather was predicted. WASHINGTON (4) — Today's newly mined gold price was announced by the treasury as $31.54 an ounce, 18 cents higher than yesterday's quotation. The price was 35 cents greater than quotations this morning on the London Gold Exchange, converted into dollars at a rate of $4.75 to the pound. While the increase in the London figure over yesterday was ten cents per ounce, the advance in the treasury quotation was nearly double that. Government financial experts sifted economic elements of the commodity price bulge prompted by costlier gold today seeking the factors to guide future steps toward a managed currency. Only one day's practical experience was at hand, but that was favorable to the Roosevelt price-lifting program. Paris, Oct. 26.-Senator Alpert Sarraut, called “the father of the French colonial empire,” decided definitely today to accept the premiership of France. After obtaining enthusiastic endorsement of his program to balance the budget at a conference with radical socialist supporters, he expected to see President Lebrun early in the afternoon and immediately organize a cabinet. M. Sarraut was tendered the office yesterday over a half dozen others mentioned to succeed Edouard Daladier who resigned with his cabinet after a vote of no confidence in the chamber of deputies. A firm stand for gold against inflation and devalorization formed the cardinal point in the program drawn up by M. Sarraut. He definitely adhered to the radical-socialist wing and told the party at the meeting that he refused to go to the right and that his and M. Dalaciens party would remain a bulwark.

K.A. Sarraut. Onward successful today in forming a cabinet to succeed Edouard Daladier’s defeated government, immediately announced that France would enter no separate disarmament negotiations with Germany. The new cabinet will seek its first vote of confidence in the chamber on the broad outline of mass economies in the budget, as vitally necessary to preserve the country's credit intact. He will face the chamber next Tuesday. Whether he will long survive—or whether any government will survive until a worse financial situation forces a strong cabinet—was doubted by many. Sarraut’s ministry differs little from that of Daladier, in which he was minister of marine. At least six members of the old cabinet will retain their posts, it was understood. MOSCOW, Oct. 26.—(AP)—Maxim Litvinoff, commissar for foreign affairs, left Moscow tonight for Washington, where he will confer with President Roosevelt regarding American recognition of Soviet Russia. The commissar’s departure was attended by a great air of mystery and secrecy because of his desire to travel incognito. His private car was attached to the Berlin train. Its route was by way of Warsaw, Poland. Only a handful of people, all of whom were minor foreign office officials, saw him off. Travelling with him were C. Oumanski, chief of the foreign office press section, and Ivan A. Divilkovski, secretary of the foreign office collegium. Litvinoff refused to break his silence regarding his plans, or even to indicate anything at all about his itinerary or the date he expected to arrive in America. 1933-02-16.text: The shock which President Hoover expressed when he was told of the attempt on the life of his successor was echoed in every capital of the world. From London to Mexico City, government heads, some of whom have themselves been assassin's targets, sent messages expressing horror at the crime and gratification that the president-elect had escaped. Everywhere the newspapers, expressing the feelings of the people, deplored the attack. In many countries where high hopes are held for the Roosevelt administration, there were expressions of relief that he had been spared. The police in Italy, informed of the assassin's statement that he had tried to kill King Victor Emmanuel twenty years ago, were unable to find this man's name in their records.

Hartzell, deported from England for his alleged activities in connection with a mythical estate of Sir Francis Drake, was arrested when he arrived on the Champlain today and later announced that he would waive extradition and go to Iowa in custody. NEW YORK, Feb. 16. (p)—Dacae Merrill Hartzell, deported from England as an undesirable alien, was arrested at quarantine on a mail fraud charge as he arrived today on the new Champlain. A reception committee consisting of a district attorney, three post office inspectors and a deputy United States marshal rode down the bay to meet Hartzell and served a warrant which charged him with using the mails to defraud and conspiracy. The officers found him in the chief purser’s office, where he was virtually being detained. He had been accompanied across the ocean by G. W. Ray of Birmingham, Ala., who is vice consul for the

NEW YORK, FEB. 16. (AP).—Oscar Merrill Hartzell, deported from England as an undesirable alien, was arrested at Quarantine on a mail fraud charge as he arrived on the liner Champlain. He is accused of collecting more than $1,000,000 from persons in the Middle West, by describing himself as the rightful heir to an allegedly mythical estate of Sir Francis Drake, estimated, according to Hartzell’s description, at more than $22,500,000,000. Post office inspectors said he promised to return the money of investors a thousand-fold. The donations to Hartzell, post office inspectors said, came from about 10,000 persons scattered through the Middle West, New York and Pennsylvania.

ROME, Feb. 16—(U.P)—Italian police checked the record of known anarchists today to determine whether Guiseppe Zangara, attacker of President-elect Roosevelt, might have been connected with attempts against the life of King Victor Emmanuel. One of the attempts caused the death of 23 persons. There have been two attempts against the king. The first was in 1911, and the second on April 12, 1928, at Milan. Terrorists placed high explosives in a lamp post in the second attempt, designed to explode when the king passed in the royal carriage. The King passed five minutes ahead of schedule and escaped, although 23 persons were killed when the lamp post was blown to bits. Police did not apprehend the perpetrators of the attempt against the King at Milan.

BUCHAREST, Feb. 16.—(UP)— Roumanian troops fired with machine guns on 4,000 workers barricaded in the state railway shops here, killing four workers, wounding a dozen others, and forcing the immediate surrender of 2,500. The others remained barricaded within the shops. The workers seized the shop in protest against the arrest of 11 of their leaders.

Ithaca, N. Y., Today.—()-— Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt, wife of the president-elect, today was escorted by a policeman out of the way of an oncoming string of railroad cars that had come within 20 feet of her at the Lehigh Valley station shortly after her arrival here this morning. She had just alighted from her special train and was standing on one of the tracks. Neither Mrs. Roosevelt nor any of the other members of the party noticed the string of cars being backed in their direction by an engine, until Motorcycle Policeman Edward J. Moore took Mrs. Roosevelt's arm and moved her off the tracks.

A new cold wave swept down from Northern Canada toward the middle west today as the nation barely recovered from the worst blizzard in 34 years. South winds that brought relief from temperatures ranging downward to 5 degrees below zero shifted to the northwest. The United States weather bureau at Chicago predicted the mercury would drop to 10 below there by tomorrow. Reports from northern states said the new storm was “the worst in years.” Temperatures dropped in a few hours to low levels of a few days ago. Central states, which suffered the heaviest toll in the 150 casualties of the first storm, will bear the brunt of the new frigid spell, the weather bureau said. Another heavy snowfall will accompany the storm, predictions said. Temperatures in St. Paul dropped again to below zero after the first day in a week above that point. BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., Feb. 11.—See in all the newspapers about making Mr. Roosevelt a president, instead of just a man that sends plans up to Congress for the fun of having them vetoed. Now you will hear the wail go up, “We are not ready in this free country for a Mussolini.” Say Mussolini could run this country with his eyes shut, in fact that’s the way our Congress has been running it. Mussolini, with no money, no natural resources, no nothing, has kept his country going, while with us, with a surplus of everything under the sun, are mangy with representatives and liberty. But we can’t digest either one of ‘em. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

1933-06-30.text: London, June 29—An eagerly-awaited British compromise plan for solution of the stabilization crisis of the world economic conference was chucked overboard in a meeting this evening with European gold bloc countries, and responsibility for a way out was laid on Washington’s doorstep. The British and the representatives of the gold bloc decided to appeal to Washington for assistance in overcoming the stabilization problem. The British compromise had been offered to meet an ultimatum by the gold standard nations, headed by France, which demanded currency stabilization as the price of their remaining in the conference. Prior to the meeting between the British and the gold nations there was a lengthy conference of British leaders to discuss the compromise plan offered by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald; the details of which were not published. London, June 30.—The expectation prevailed in some world economic conference quarters Thursday night that the Washington government would co-operate in checking the gyrations of the dollar and thus save the parley from the threat of a breakdown over the vexing stabilization issue. The belief was that America would take this action while still holding fast against immediate pegging of the currency. The hopes that the conference had been saved were voiced at the end of a strenuous day in which countries forming the European gold bloc fought tirelessly behind the scenes for protection of their currencies, threatening to quit the conference if Great Britain and the United States refused to co-operate. LONDON, June 30—American and Canadian wheat negotiators, seeking an agreement to restrict wheat acreage and so raise prices, formally threatened today to dump their 500,000,000 surplus bushels of wheat on the world market if Australia refused to co-operate. Figures were presented to Stanley Bruce, chief Australian negotiator and former prime minister, to show the amount of wheat that the United States and Canada could dump on the world market in case of a wheat war. Bruce at once cabled the Australian government, presenting the sat in full and giving the figures so that they could be considered (turn to Page Fifteen—No. 4)

LONDON, June 30.--(U.P)—Latest developments in the world economic conference include: Delegates hold anxious consultations, awaiting President Roosevelt's response to appeal for action on currency. Federal Reserve Bank of New York considers plan for buying dollars abroad to check fluctuations. Dollar gained in all foreign exchanges. France makes implied threat of trade retaliation unless dollar is stabilized. Daladier tells Parliament at Paris he plans a self-sustaining French Empire if the conference fails.

London, Today.— (7) — The world economic conference waited tensely today for word that would save the great party from the rocks of monetary controversy, as the American delegates and Assistant Secretary of State Raymond Moley gathered at the American embassy to consider the American stand toward regulation of dollar fluctuations. The American delegates remained silent about whether they met to consider word from President Roosevelt. But an authoritative source said American adherence to a plan under which the conference could progress was under consideration. Important American quarters indicated that Mr. Moley, as the President's personal representative, had received authority to agree to a plan of preventing erratic gyrations of the dollar which are threatening the gold currencies. 1933-10-27.text: By The Associated Press Winter staged a rehearsal along the New England seaboard yesterday, sending temperatures in many localities down to record October lows, Unsettled weather prevailed in the Middlewest and South. In the Adirondacks temperatures of eight degrees above zero were recorded following a 24-hour snow. It was the coldest day in ten years. In New England In Massachusetts and other New England states the temperatures mounted into the upper thirties during the day. New Jersey had the coldest October 26 in the history of weather bureaus with readings of 27 at (Continued on Page 2)

SUNNINGDALE Eng., Oct. 29-- The condition of the Prince of Wales, who has not been in the best of health for several days, was reported unchanged today. He is staying at his country home here. It was stated officially today that the Prince was remaining in bed while the chill which troubled him pursued its normal course.

CHICAGO, Oct. 27.—UP—Col. William Francis Forbes-Sempill, scion of British nobility and famous flier, and Charles Dollfuss, noted French aerialist, were critically injured today in an automobile accident after a safe trip of thousands of miles aboard the Graf Zeppelin.

Washington, Oct. 27—Unconfirmed rumors in diplomatic circles caused Secretary Hull to be asked at his press conference today whether the British war debt negotiators were dissatisfied with their progress and contemplated returning to London. The Secretary of State referred his questioners to the treasury, where officials were not readily available to talk of the matter. Sir Arnold Lindsay, the British ambassador, had conferred at length with Secretary Hull in the morning. The debt discussions have been held off and on at the treasury department, as well as informally elsewhere. Treasury officials subsequently declined to comment on debt developments beyond saying that another meeting with the British negotiators was scheduled for early next week.

Paris, Oct. 1 (AP)—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh are slipping secretly into Paris to avoid another tumultuous hero’s welcome, traveled today over familiar streets, completely unobserved by Parisians whose cheers of years ago abashed the modest flier. No crowds swarmed at the doorstep when Lindbergh left the Hotel Crillon guardedly and went by automobile to Les Maures to inspect the plane which brought the couple through a storm from Inverness, Scotland. Mrs. Lindbergh likewise rode up the bustling Champs Elysees packed by a work-a-day crowd despite leaden skies without even the chauffeurs in the surrounding traffic jam recognizing the eagerly-peering young woman as the famous ocean-flier’s wife. She was the curious one this time, watching the oblivious crowds on either side of the famous tree-lined thoroughfare which glistened with rain.

MOSCOW, Oct. 27.—(P)—Maxim Litvinoff, to whom all Russia looks for the attainment of American recognition, was on his way to the United States today in an atmosphere of utmost secrecy. A peep beneath a scarcely-raised blind from a window of his train was the only parting view of his associates the foreign commissar was seen to permit himself. And the crowds which gladly would have cheered him off on the all-important journey to Washington were barred from the railroad station. Hours after he had slipped away behind closely drawn shades on the Berlin train, it was impossible even to learn whether his English-born wife had accompanied him. To the time of his unheralded departure, he refused to break the silence in which he has locked his ideas about the forthcoming negotiations. Similarly tight-lipped were his associates in high government circles. They would discuss neither his plans for

Paris, France, Oct. 27.—(U.P.)— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh was back at the scene of his world triumph today struggling vainly to be a private citizen instead of a hero worshipped by excitable Parisians who had not forgotten his New York-Paris flight of 1927. Missing for many hours in a storm that raged along the British and French coasts, Lindbergh and his wife flew from Inverness, Scotland, to land secretly at the naval seaplane testing station near Paris and go unobserved to the Crillon hotel. While they slept, airport attaches flew over Great Britain and France watching anxiously for them. They awoke today to find thousands of Parisians, deserting their jobs, massed outside their hotel in the historic Concorde Square where Louis XVI was guillotined. Dismayed, the Lindberghs at once changed to a room facing on a side street and seemed at a loss as to what to do. There was no doubt that

| BY MARY ANIGHYD United Press Staff Correspondent (World Copyright, 1933, by U. P.) PARIS, Oct. 27,—(UP)—"We're going home soon, and we're not flying—once is enough,” Mrs. Chas. A. Lindbergh told this correspondent today as she sat wistfully in her apartment at the Crillon Hotel, almost a prisoner of surging crowds waiting outside to cheer her and her famous husband. The attractive wife of the world’s most famous flyer is homesick, frankly and thoroughly. For this reason, she is eager to leave this famous European capital, where her husband won world fame. She can't even buy Paris gowns because Col. Lindbergh points out that they have no room for more baggage. Anne Morrow Lindbergh and the colonel were almost fugitives today from the acclaim that has followed them from here to China. 1933-07-28.text: London—(AP)—President Roosevelt, in a dramatic message to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, today ripped the labels of “failure” from the world economic conference which many delegates were busily affixing by their speeches at the final plenary session. The president's note, which Secretary of State Hull read to the assembled delegates, came as a climax to a morning of speeches, most of which were critical. The session was adjourned until 3 p.m. as soon as the communication was read. Mr. Hull was scheduled to speak during the afternoon meeting. Far from the bickering and squabbling of London during the last six weeks, Roosevelt gave the delegates a perspective of the work they have done here and told them that “results are not always measured in terms of formal agreement.” With an interchange of views comes a better understanding by nations of the problems of other countr

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif.— Well, the London conferences closed yesterday. It just disbanded yesterday, but it ended the day it started. You will hear a lot of 'em say that it didn't accomplish anything, but it did. They stayed in session till every nation got thoroughly disgusted with each other. There is no place in the world better to find out shortcomings of each other than a conference. Now every delegation goes home and tells tales on the others. Of course, we leave as the principal villain. We were supposed to bring the pie that they were to cut. When we didn't bring it, the banquet was a total loss. Where is the next conference? We just love to confer. Yours, WILL.

London, July 27—The world economic conference adjourned for an indefinite period today as a message from President Roosevelt full of faith in its ultimate results dispelled prevailing pessimism. “Results are not always measured in terms of formal agreements,” the American president said in a communication which pledged his country’s efforts for world recovery. “They can come equally from a presentation of each nation’s difficulties and each nation’s methods to meet its individual needs.” Join in Fervid Plea After receiving this note of confidence and hope, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, the conference chairman, and Secretary of State Cordell Hull terminated the six weeks’ efforts to defeat hard times by international action on a high note of idealism. They joined in a fervid plea that the efforts to remedy world ailments be carried on tirelessly in a spirit of good will and mutual unde

Dublin, Ireland (AP) — The wheels of the plane in which the Australian aviator, Capt. Charles T. P. Ulm and three companions planned to fly to North America, sank in the sands at Portmarnock airdrome, near here, today, resulting in injuries to five persons. Planks were being put under the plane to raise it but the machine slipped, pinning three persons under the fuselage. They and two others, also hurt, were taken to a hospital.

WASHINGTON, (Special) — The Roosevelt administration decided yesterday to go ahead with its domestic wheat program without waiting for an international grain agreement. Simultaneously with the recess of the London wheat conference, Secretary Wallace announced the amounts that each state and county would be allotted to grow next year of the 456,198,588 bushels of wheat that has been estimated as the amount that will be needed for domestic consumption. Wallace said that within 10 days he would proclaim the percentage of acreage reduction that would be required of farmers in order to qualify for benefit payments of up to $136,000,000 under the voluntary domestic allotment plan. Previously, he had announced that he would require an acreage reduction up to a maximum of 20 per cent with the final figure to await the outcome of the London wheat conference. After that meeting recessed until Augu

ROLAND GARROS STADIUM, AUTEUIL, France. (/P) — England blasted France’s hopes of keeping the Davis Cup today with a clean sweep of the first two singles matches in the challenge round of the international tennis battle. Fred Perry, British No. 1, overthrew the great Henri Cochet in a stirring five-set struggle, 8-10, 6-4, 8-6, 3-6, 6-1, for the main thrust after Henry W. Austin easily disposed of the newcomer, Andre Merlin, 6-3, 6-4, 6-10.

| LONDON, July 28.—(UP)—The geological museum was handed back to the fossils today as delegates to the World Economic conference departed for home, leaving behind the remnants of eight tons of documents issued by the secretariat during their 46-day visit. Speculation as to the future, particularly as to the possibility that the recess taken yesterday because of the long deadlock on currency problems, might mark the final breakup, was given a new turn. It was suggested authoritatively that the world war debt negotiations impending at Washington early this fall might be made the occasion for a conference of representatives of leading powers that would amount to a tabloid economic conference. These representatives could decide either to reconvene the conference or to abandon it. By autumn it was believed the currency situation might be clarified.

London, (AP)—The following is the text of a message sent by President Roosevelt to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, chairman of the world economic conference, today: “I want you to know my sincere admiration and respect for your courage and your patience as its (the conference’s) presiding officer. “I feel that because of it the nations of the world can continue to discuss mutual problems with frankness and without rancor. “Results are not always measured in terms of formal agreement. They can come equally from a free presentation of each nation’s difficulties and each nation's methods to meet its individual needs. We in the United States understand the problems of before the conference met and we trust that other nations will in the same spirit of goodwill view our American policies which are aimed to overcome our unprecedented economic situation at home. “Such an interchange, especiall

1933-07-12.text: London, July 12 (AP)—The American federal reserve board, it was understood in authoritative quarters today, has vetoed participation by the United States delegation at the world economic conference in discussion of a resolution calling for central bank cooperation. This resolution was backed by the European gold bloc and has been under consideration by the subcommittee on permanent monetary problems. It was stated that Senator Pittman of Nevada told the subcommittee that the federal reserve board felt that the resolution was “premature.” This development immediately created a sensation. Some members of the committee asserted this attitude killed further consideration of Senator Pittman’s important resolution calling for, among other things, eventual return to the gold standard, reduction of the gold cover to 25 per cent, and optional use of silver for one-fifth of that cover. American qu

LONDON, (?). The world economic conference decided to wait for action on the American dollar. After a fortnight of bitter controversy, the conference found itself back where it was when the clash of the gold and non-gold groups disrupted it a fortnight ago, save for this vital difference—the gold representatives were no longer threatening to wreck the conference. The most vital monetary problems still were as far from solution as previously, but the opposing groups agreed to drop all dangerously contentious subjects and proceed on a few mostly secondary topics in the hope the conference could be kept alive until the dollar quiets down and real steps to bring out order in the world currency situation may be taken. The question of adjournment was said not to have been mentioned in the day's committee meetings, but important conference circles were inclined to agree that the present schedul

LONDON, July 12 —(U.P)—Hope that he may negotiate in secret the agreements that proved impossible in the deadlocked World Economic Conference led Cordell Hull, chief American delegate, to intimate today that he would defer his return to the United States until August and put off British-American war debt negotiations until September. Hull already has engaged in talks with some delegates, and Dr. Herbert Feis, chief economic adviser to the State Department, last night discussed with Tomas A. Lebreton, chief Argentine delegate, the possibility of an Argentine-American trade treaty. Rep. Samuel D. McReynolds, Dem., N. C., plans to introduce in the conference tomorrow an American Federation of Labor resolution, drafted by James Wilson, Federation attache to the American delegation, calling for world reduction of working hours—a plan which coincides with President Roosevelt’s domestic policy.

PARIS, July 12.—Europe’s economic war, with tariff bombardments and retaliation in the form of restrictive customs regulations, is proceeding briskly despite the London economic conference and the recent tariff truce, a United Press survey showed today. France is waging tariff wars with Germany and Portugal; Poland is waging a tariff war against Germany and so is Roumania. The bombardments in each instance affect every country that competes with the warring ones in its export trade. France Hits Germany. French regulations effective today raise tariffs on 100 products imported from Germany, including chemicals, cotton linters, paints, glassware and machine tools. This followed Germany's boosting of tariffs on French products. Portugal has just raised the tariff on French goods by 20 per cent. This war was started when France raised tariffs on Madeira and Port wines; Portugal in turn raise

LONDON, July 11.—UP—Great Britain jubilantly visualized a return of prosperity today. Unemployment figures published last night were the lowest since December, 1931, totaling 2,438,108, or 144,771 fewer than a month ago and 309,235 fewer than at this time last year. Improvement has been most noticeable in steel, shipping and shipbuilding, textiles, construction, road transport and distributive trades.

Plymouth, England, July 12— Laurence A. Steinhardt, new American minister to Sweden, arrived today on his way to Stockholm by way of London and intimated strongly that he bore President Roosevelt’s views to the American delegation at the World Economic Conference. Steinhardt, arriving in the French liner Île de France, was questioned on the chance he might be the successor of Prof. Raymond Moley, of the Roosevelt brain trust, as a bearer of word from Washington. The day before he sailed, Steinhardt had a long talk with Mr. Roosevelt.

SHEDIAC, N. B., July 12.—(#)—The Italian air squadron led by General Italo Balbo arrived Wednesday afternoon at Cartwright, Labrador, ending its flight from Iceland, according to a wireless report received here. The information of completion of the flight from Reykjavik to Labrador port, a distance of 1,500 miles and the longest stage in the entire trip from Italy to Chicago, was received at the Italian air base here. The fleet of 24 seaplanes descended at Cartwright at 1:30 p. m. Atlantic standard time (12:30 p. m. eastern standard time). According to the time given in the wireless message the 1,500 miles were

HALIFAX, N. S. (Special) — Bound north over the air trails, the flying Lindberghs halted last night in this port. Bright sunlight sparkled on the harbor and a brisk southeast wind was blowing as the black-barrelled, red-winged monoplane settled on its white pontoons and taxied to a mooring at the Royal Canadian Air Force base at eastern Pass Bar. Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and his wife arrived at 5:50 p. m., Atlantic Standard Time, (4:50 Eastern Standard Time), two hours and 36 minutes after leaving North Haven, Maine, their first stop on an aerial route survey to Greenland. “It was a very nice trip,” said the transatlantic airman’s petite wife and flying companion as small aircraft of every description clustered around their seaplane even before it was moored. “Everyone else seems to know more about this trip than we do,” Colonel Lindbergh said, laughing, as he came ashore. “As a matt

1933-01-05.text: CHERBOURG, France, Jan. 5 —(Thursday)—(#)—The luxurious liner Atlantique was wrecked by fire Wednesday in the English Channel while proceeding to Havre for overhauling without passengers. The loss of lives was placed early this morning at 17. Latest available figures here showed 228 persons were aboard, of whom 211 arrived here during the night on four rescue vessels. The victims either suffocated at their posts of duty or drowned when a lifeboat upset. All those rescued were exhausted when they were brought here. All their possessions had been lost. Still Burning The wreck still was burning this morning and it was being blown in a northerly direction in a rough sea. The vessel was owned by the Compagnie De Navigation Sud-Atlantique of Paris. Leon Meyer, French minister of the merchant marine, arrived here this morning. In an address to the crew of the ill-fated South Atlantic liner, he

WASHINGTON, Jan. 5. (AP)— Indications were seen today that some Senate leaders might support proposals to renew war debts discussions with those nations which have met their payments, particularly Great Britain. Such evidence was found in speeches by Robinson of Arkansas, and Reed of Pennsylvania, during the course of the Senate’s first wide open airing of international relations this session. Touched off by Johnson of California, who arraigned France and other defaulting nations, the sharp debate reached its height yesterday when Senator Borah, Idaho Republican, determinedly urged that President Hoover and congressional leaders approve any agreement made with Premier Laval in 1930 for debt revision. Reed, a staunch supporter of Mr. Hoover, gave indications of a more friendly attitude toward Great Britain. Both, however, agreed that it would be impossible to treat with France at least un
New York, Jan. 5. (AP)—Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon sailed early today on the White Star liner Majestic for London to return to his diplomatic post there.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Jan. 4. (PP) The labor party decided tonight to give its support to President Eamon de Valera in the election January 2. Announcement of the labor party's support of the president followed by a few hours the decision of Frank MacDermott, head of the Farmers League, and former President William T. Cosgrave that the time until the election was too short to complete preparations for forming a national party to oppose the president. Until tonight's action, the position of the seven labor members of the Dail Eireann, on whose votes Mr. De Valera’s majority has depended for several months, has been uncertain. These seven members as well as other members of the labor party have opposed the president's policy on civil service pay reductions.

Queenstown, Ireland. Jan. 4 (UP)—The S. S. Manhattan of the United States Lines arrived today twelve hours late, reporting a seaman killed and twelve persons injured during a terrific three-day gale which battered the liner. Tremendous seas broke over even the top decks, staggering the ship. Passengers were hurled from the decks. The water even entered the cabins. Much chinaware and other movable objects were broken. The man killed was John Hill, whose neck became entangled in a winch rope which slipped.

CHERBOURG, France, Jan. 4.—The magnificent South Atlantic liner Atlantique tonight drifted a smoking wreck in the English Channel off the Isle of Guernsey, a tomb for 30 of her crew reported by the captain to be missing, either burned to death or asphyxiated at their posts in a fire which swept the vessel with lightning rapidity this morning. There were conflicting reports about how many were aboard as the vessel was en route to Havre without passengers for overhauling, but 119 men reached Cherbourg tonight in three vessels while the rest of the crew, believed to number 800, was en route to Brest. The steamer Pollux tonight reported the Atlantique afloat 24 miles off Casquets, west of Alderney. She was so hot that it was impossible to board her. The ministry of Merchant Marine announced in Paris that the damage was so great the ship must be considered lost. Captain Schoof, master of the

| CHERBOURG, France, Jan. 4. | (UP)—The $18,000,000 liner Atlantique, one of the most luxurious of French passenger ships, was adrift and on fire without a crew today, probably a total loss. Fire broke out off Cherbourg with a skeleton crew of about 200 men but no passengers aboard. The Atlantique had been taken off the south Atlantic run for her first overhauling since her maiden voyage in September, 1931. The crew took to the lifeboats when it became evident that they could not check the fire.

CHERBOURG, France, Jan. 5 The superb 41,000-ton French passenger liner Atlantique, gutted by fire and with loss of lives at present placed at eighteen, was burning herself out today 70 miles off Cherbourg. The French mine-layer Pollux reported the huge ship was drifting rapidly northward toward the Welsh coast and was within five miles of Portland Bill. The fire was diminishing but flames were still visible, while a strong wind was increasing, the Pollux reported. A ship bearing Captain Schoofs, master of the Atlantique, left at 10 a.m. to direct salvage operations if possible. Other ships in the vicinity radioed that the wreck was listing badly to the port side, while the bow was rising indicating a leak. It was declared impossible to board her. Try to Save All. London, Dec. 26 (UP) — Plans which would give Great Britain absolute control over all shipping in the English Channel within less than half an hour after a declaration of war have been elaborated and secretly rehearsed off little frequented spots of the coast for a year, it was learned today. Two developments in the use of Britain’s small but highly efficient fleet of bombing airplanes will enable the plan to go through successfully in case of need, experts are confident. Wireless Control. For months experiments have been conducted secretly and with remarkable success, in the wireless control of bombers over the channel, it was learned. By United Press LONDON, Dec. 25. A dispatch to the Exchange Telegraph from Hongkong said that 26 persons were killed when eight airplanes of the Nanking government bombed Foochow this afternoon. The bombing was part of a recently-developed internal political struggle in China, marked by the establishment of an independent government in Fukien province, of which Foochow is the capital, in defiance of Nanking. Not since the old Peking government rested on the bayonets of Marshal Wu Pei-Fu has there been so much unrest in China. Long hidden because of fear of Japanese intervention, it has now flared up with the Fukien outbreak, which is communist in nature. Backed by the 19th route army, which won fame against the Japanese at Shanghai in 1932, the regime of Foochow is out to break the personal dictatorship of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek. It is represented as the movement of a new party co

EL FERROL, SPAIN, Dec. 26 (7) — It was said in official circles today that the Spanish cruiser Jaime I has received orders to proceed to Havana, Cuba, to protect Spanish interests if necessary. It was said the cruiser would set out shortly. The recent political disturbances in Cuba, which resulted in the deaths of several Spanish citizens, caused the Spanish cabinet last week to consider the Cuban situation. At that time, it was said in Madrid that Spain might ask the United States to intervene under the Platt amendment for the protection of the lives of Spaniards and Spanish property. By the Monroe Doctrine, the United States has warned European nations against armed invasions of any American republic.

Paris, Dec. 26 (UP) — Mme. Blanche De Paunac, France’s seeress extraordinary, came out of her annual Christmas silence today to predict that 1934 will be a year of peace and returned prosperity. Next September, Mme. De Paunac said, would mark the opening of a new era of prosperity for the United States—an era whose start would spread out from the United States to the whole world. Great attention is paid to Mme. De Paunac by those who pay attention to seeresses. She won fame by predicting in midsummer of 1918 that the World War would end with an armistice November 11. Rising from her self-induced hyp- Adolf Hitler's power unbroken. But, she added, in 1905 it would be broken. NO political revolutions of moment. The deaths of a famous general and two French statesmen. Restoration of a king who ran away from his throne. A great, mysterious French air catastrophe—A group of planes to leave fo

Paris, UP)—France counted 196 dead today after a train wreck—and Christmas became for most of the nation a holiday of despair. The accident — the worst in France's history — came Saturday night when the speeding Strasbourg flyer telescoped the wooden coaches of the Nancy express in a fog at Lagny, 17 miles from here. Both trains were filled with holiday-bound passengers. The dead included the French statesman Paul Morel, former cabinet minister, and his wife. Many Critically Hurt, How great the death toll will be is not known even yet for many persons lay critically injured in hospitals and dawn found rescue workers still probing the tangled and splintered wreckage. Railroad authorities set the official death list at 196 of whom 160 lay in the black-draped Eastern railway station—now a temporary morgue. Of the 160, police still were unable to identify 37. Authorities feared at least ten

SHANGHAI, Dec. 26 (WP)—The Nanking imperial government staged “a terrific three day aerial bombardment of the rebel city of Foochow, causing considerable loss of life and much property damage, delayed official reports revealed today. The bombardment started on Saturday and reached its climax on Christmas Day, the Japanese telegraphic station was informed. The Nationalist military forces directed their attack at the centers of confrontation of the revolutionary “people's government” of Fukien and of the 19th Route Army engaged in the revolt. Reports indicated that the populace of Foochow was in a state of panic, to the extent that 10,000 people were reported to have fled the city.

TOKYO, Dec. 26. (—Emperor Hirohito opened today a diet session at which are expected to be approved the largest peacetime defense appropriations in Japan's history. Thousands stood in brilliant sunshine along the route taken by the procession of state from the palace to the parliament building. There the emperor, reading from a prescript, declared the session open. The legislative program, drafted by a cabinet dominated by the ministers of war and navy, calls among other things for army and navy appropriations of 938,000,000 yen (about $281,400,000).

Rome, Dec. 24 (P)~-All Italy paused to pay tribute to motherhood today before turning to the celebration of Christmas. Thirty thousand prizes were distributed over the nation to mothers of large families, to newlyweds, and parents of their first child in observance of mothers’ and infants’ day, which with Premier Mussolini's drive to increase the population, has become one of Italy's most important occasions. At Rome, fathers of large families also shared in the awards. They received passes on street cars valid for one year. Ninety-three “champion” mothers, who yesterday were received by Mussolini, were escorted in automobiles through lines of an applauding public this morning to the Augusteo theater, where they were honored guests in the day's principal ceremony. The Crocunes, or tiny black shirts of Balilla organization, and the Piccole Italiane, corresponding girls' group, massed at t

1933-02-15.text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 15 (AP).—A “ruthless policy” by Great Britain to drive down gold dollar prices in an effort to win war debt cancellation or reduction was charged today before the senate finance committee by Rene Leon of New York, formerly technical advisor to the house coinage committee. Leon, in appearing before the committee in its study of economic conditions, joined a number of other witnesses in advocating monetization of silver. He suggested purchase of 400,000,000 ounces or more by the treasury and the issuance of silver certificates. He said that through the British exchange equalization fund for purchasing gold currencies in the open market, England had “the control of dollar exchange and consequently the control of American prices.” “That which Britain would not for one minute countenance from America she practices every minute upon America with disastrous consequences to ever

London, Feb. 14. (4%)--In Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay's safe-keeping on the high seas tonight was the outline of the British policy for the Anglo-American War debts talk at Washington. The liner Majestic sailed from Southampton today, with the ambassador maintaining what he called the “golden standard of reliance.”

WASHINGTON, Feb. 15. (UP) Charges that Great Britain is “attempting to keep world prices down so as to reduce debtors’ capacity to pay.” were made before the Senate prosperity seeking committee today by Rene Leon of New York, monetary expert. Leon charged that Britain was using such a “ruthless policy” in order to obtain readjustment of her war debt on a reduced basis. Leon, a retired financier and recently technical advisor to the House coinage committee, asserted Britain is carrying out such operations through a 150,000,000 pounds ‘secret exchange equalization fund,” purchasing gold currencies in the exchange markets and thus obtaining “control of the dollar exchange and consequently the control of American

MENA, ARK.—John Tomlinson, who boasted he had voted for every Republican nominee for president since the party was founded in 1856, is dead at the age of 98. Born in England, he came to the United States when he was 8 years old.

Daytona Beach, Fla., Feb. 15 (4#)—Inability of mechanics to complete extensive adjustments to Sir Malcolm Campbell’s trim racing car prevented the 48-year old British driver from making an official assault today on his own world land speed record of 253 miles an hour. Following a test run yesterday, in which he estimated he attained a speed of between 230 and 240 miles an hour, Campbell said several major adjustments would be necessary to the car before he could race again. Mechanics worked all night on the machine and today parts of the 2,500 horsepower car were strewn about its garage. They said it would be impossible to assemble the machine in time for further trials today so Campbell definitely abandoned plans for test runs at low tide, which occurs late this afternoon. The major job confronting the mechanics was changing the gear ratio, which necessitated tearing much of the mechani

LONDON, Feb 15--(L P)——Britain, the United States, France and Italy are drawing up an agreement to prohibit export of arms to Bolivia and Paraguay, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary announced today in the House of Commons. Efforts of the powers to persuade cessation of the warfare between the two republics in the Gran Chaco region have failed.

TOKYO (4)—Japan served notice today that it has ceased negotiations with the League of Nations on the Manchurian dispute, but its expected withdrawal from the league membership was not looked for for about a month. The Tokyo stock exchange was closed at noon today and the exchanges of Osaka and Nagoya also were shut, owing to a severe slump in prices due to indications of increasing anti-Japanese sentiment at Geneva. It was learned on high authority that the government feels withdrawal from the league would be the turning point in the empire's history. Before the ultimate decision is made, the council of elder statesmen, the nation’s most distinguished personages, the heads of branches of the imperial family, and all living ex-premiers will be summoned for consultation. GENEVA, Feb. 15 (UP).—Japan’s threatened withdrawal from the League of Nations may involve the United States and other powers in a serious dispute with Japan over possession of the 1600 islands in the Pacific which form a “bridge” of 2500 miles east and west between Japan and the United States. The islands, formerly German, are held by Japan under mandate from the League of Nations, acting as custodian for the victorious powers in the World War. Nobody in Geneva believes Japan would relinquish the islands when she quits the League, although she would have no legal right to retain them. The islands are too valuable for strategic reasons. They control American communications in the Far East. The United States has never recognized the League mandates as giving the islands to Japan and theoretically still claims a share.
