WASHINGTON — The disposition in many quarters today was to regard Neville Chamberlain’s “no swapping” war debts statements as the views of one cabinet member and not definitely indicative of the final position the British government will assume in the forthcoming discussions. Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told American correspondents in London Wednesday that Britain does not regard the debts talks in March as a “great swapping deal.” He said the “conception of concessions by Great Britain in return for the scaling down of war debts is not a British concept. Not long afterwards, Senate leaders issued a plain warning that the British cannot expect debt adjustments without giving compensations. No Alternative In a formal statement, Chairman Borah of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said that if Britain will not consider other world problems in connection with debts “we hav

A debate broke in the Senate today with Senator Robinson (R.. Ind), demanding that the state department “apprehend” under the Logan Act, William C. Bullitt, who has been reported negotiating on debts abroad. Reading from press accounts of Bullitt’s visits to Berlin, London and Paris, supposed to be in connection with war debts, Robinson said Bullitt was making a “laughing stock” out of the American people. “It is high time the American government asserts who he is,” he said. “He is going about in disguise and when not in disguise he is going under an assumed name. “He seems to have no credentials,” Robinson added. “He is not representing the American government. He seems not to be representing the President-elect. He certainly is not representing the Senate or the House, both of which have gone on record against further reduction of the debts.”

Long Beach, Calif, Feb. 2—(AP) Witnesses ranging in rank from an English lord to a rowboat seaman were summoned today for the opening of the trial of William James Guy, Welsh soldier of fortune, charged with the murder of Captain Walter Wanderwell, globe-trotting adventurer. All of today and tomorrow probably will be taken in the selection of the jury. Superior Judge Robert Kenny of Los Angeles will preside over the trial. Wanderwell was shot to death the night of last December 4 in the unlighted passageway to his cabin aboard the yacht Carma on the eve of its intended departure on an around-the-world cruise. The Carma, owned by Wanderwell, was tied up at a local dock here and aboard were a strange crew of adventurers, including writers, lecturers, waitresses and seamen. All had signed on as members of the crew. Among the witnesses summoned are Mrs. Aloha Wanderwell, the widow, and Lord

London, Feb. 1, (#). — Britain's clear-cut stand for settling the war debts without “swapping” economic concessions with the United States, or pledging return to the gold standard except on definite conditions, was outlined with outspoken frankness today by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain as the guest of the American Correspondents’ Association of London. Chamberlain told the American writers that he did not come to make a speech on war debts, and his talk dealt in the main with an analysis of the world economic depression, the solution of which, he said, was largely dependent on the return of confidence everywhere. But, following the British luncheon custom, the chancellor said he was willing to answer questions, and the reporters, availing themselves of a rare opportunity of cross-examining the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, shot them thick and fast. When the barr

Peiping, Feb. 2 (UP) — Diplomatic quarters were concerned today over indications that China as well as Japan may withdraw from the League of Nations due to dissatisfaction with the league's handling of the Manchurian dispute. Foreign Minister Lo Wen Kan was understood to have informed British Minister Sir Miles Lampson that China would quit the league unless the league refused to recognize Manchukuo. Sir Miles was said to be gravely concerned over China’s resentment of the British attitude at Geneva.

LONDON, Feb. 2. — (INS) — The duke of Manchester, ninth holder of a title dating back to more than two centuries, was ordered committed to prison for 42 days for non-payment of a hotel bill. The order was issued when the duke, who married Kathleen Dawes, an Anglo-American actress, in Greenwich, Conn., in 1931, failed to appear in Margate county court on a judgment summons issued by the North Foreland Hotels, Ltd. The duke also was fined 10 pounds (about $34) for failing to appear on

Berlin—(—Chancellor Hitler's first appeal for a parliamentary majority in elections set for March 6 found Germany seething today with political animosity. All outdoor communist demonstrations were reported banned in the greater part of Germany. The tense situation reached a climax with Hitler's announcement of two four-year plans of national regeneration—for the “salvation” of the farmer and the worker. The Telegraphen-Union Press association heard that orders were issued to Prussian police to prevent communist demonstrations during the election campaign. The national communist newspaper Rote Fahne said the ban was invoked to curb election campaigning. The communists held one-sixth of the seats in the Reichstag which was dissolved yesterday. Confident of Victory The Nazi leader was supremely confident of victory after his cabinet, in which nationalists far (Continued on Page 3)

1933-02-19.text: By The Associated Press New London, Wis., Feb. 18.— Thousands of pounds of milk splashed on highways of Winnebago and Waupaca counties and fists flew today as large groups of farmers participated in a milk sales strike. Tempers of hundreds of highway pickets grew more surly and farmers trying to smuggle milk to market received rough treatment. The strike increased in effectiveness, leaders said, and became general over Dodge county where it was estimated that half of the 300 cheese factories, condenseries, creameries and receiving stations had been closed. Here pickets had a tussle with Chief of Police Harry Macklin, brushing that officer aside and trading punches with him when he tried vainly to save a truckload of milk. At many places in Winnebago, Waupaca and Dodge counties timber barriers blocked highways and farmers allowed none to pass without a search of authorities and trucks for

Rome.—-(AP)—The entire Italian press engaged in an attack on France today, charging an alleged ultimatum to Austria concerning an arms shipment from Italy was “camouflage” to take attention from anti-Italian military preparations. Denials that the arms were shipped to Austria for war purposes there were coupled with counter charges that France was arming Czecho-Slovakia and Jugoslavia. The Giornale d’ Italia of Rome and Premier Mussolini's own newspaper, Popolo d’ Italia of Milan, were the most outspoken. The so-called ultimatum, demanding the Austrian government get rid of the arms and supplies within two weeks, was published. Great Britain was reported to have approved the action by France on the grounds that the concentration of arms violated the post-war treaty with Austria. (A Paris dispatch said the note to Austria was presented February 11 and was mainly in the nature of a request

(Copyright, 1933, by Associated Press.) Doorn, Holland, Feb. 18.— Wilhelm II, former emperor of Germany, reflected in the solitude of his banishment upon the American discussions concerning technocracy, has arrived at the conclusion that the technocrats are wrong in conceding the supremacy of the machine. The rule of the machine, he believes, can and must be broken by the same human mind which called the machine into being. Only then can the problem of unemployment be solved. The former monarch's views were carefully laid down in the form of a letter written to his life-long friend, T. St. John Gaffney of Summit, New Jersey.

TOKYO, Feb. 18.—Nothing short of a miracle can prevent the withdrawal of Japan from the League of Nations as a result of the League’s censure of the Japanese Manchurian policy, a high official indicated today. Meanwhile it appeared unlikely that Yosuke Matsuoka, Japan’s chief delegate at Geneva, would be able to make his proposed trip back to Tokyo by way of the United States, where he hoped to talk with Franklin D. Roosevelt or other members of the new administration. A government spokesman said that a summons to Matsuoka to return by Siberia, the shortest route, in order that he might assist in preparation for Japan's secession from the league, probably would make it impossible for him to visit the United States. This matter is not wholly settled, but the cabinet may decide to consult with the Geneva representative before taking final action. In this event, he would be called home.

Geneva, Feb. 18—Colombia appealed to the League of Nations today to intervene in its dispute with Peru over possession of the upper Amazon port, Leticia, invoking article XV of the league covenant, whereby the league would seek a settlement by conciliation. Colombia's appeal was conveyed in a three-page message, setting forth the situation and accusing Peru of taking action in violation of its league engagements. A special league council session was convoked for next Monday afternoon to hear appeals.

GENEVA, SG, Feb. 18. — The Japanese delegation today prepared a declaration rejecting the Manchurian report which, their spokesmen say, will be delivered to the League of Nations secretariat as soon as the committee of nineteen presents the report to the assembly on Tuesday. The Manchurian report, made public yesterday, condemned Japan's military activities in the province and reaffirmed China’s right to sovereignty. It bound the powers not to recognize the State of Manchukuo. In the face of Tokyo reports, league chiefs were discussing measures to be taken if and when Japan withdraws her delegation from Geneva.

PEIPING, CHINA, Feb. 18.—(#)—A major battle between Chinese and Japanese armies at Kailu, northern gateway of Jehol province, appeared imminent after the receipt today of a Japanese ultimatum. It ordered Chinese forces immediately to evacuate the city. The Chinese decided to ignore it, it was stated at Manchurian headquarters here despite a Japanese threat of attack at once if the demand was not complied with. An army of 30,000 to 50,000 volunteers has been concentrating in the Kailu region to block the Japanese invasion of Jehol from that point. Kailu is at the start of a main communication route to the city of Chihfeng and the capital, Jehol City, some 200 and 300 miles, respectively, to the southwest. The Japanese already have made at least a half dozen airplane bombing raids upon Kailu from their military base at Tungliao, 20 miles eastward across the Manchurian border. A series of t

COLUMBUS, O.—(P1)—On the basis of reports that adoption of the Blaine repeal resolution was virtually assured in the lower house of congress, Governor White today said he was prepared to forward a special message to the Ohio legislature on the prohibition issue. He said such a message would be sent to the general assembly, Tuesday or Wednesday, provided congress finally approved the repeal resolution. His message, the governor indicated, would ask support of the McCrystal resolution, providing for a referendum vote in Ohio in November on the question of repealing the prohibition amendment to the state constitution, and that the legislature set up machinery for a state prohibition convention. Definite recommendations regarding a state convention, he said, would be without pending receipt of the report by his commission on state liquor control.

1933-06-16.text: WASHINGTON, June 15 ()— it became apparent today that American collections on the $144,000,000 war debt installments due would aggregate less than 9 percent of the total. The amounts to be collected either announced or indicated were: Great Britain $10,000,000; Italy about $1,000,000; Czecho-Slovakia $200,000, possibly less; Finland $148,592. Definite defaults were: France $40,738,000; Belgium $6,325,000; Roumania $1,000,000; Poland $3,559,000; Lithuania $132,073. Defaults were indicated by Yugoslavia, $275,000, and Estonia $284,322. The following were in doubt: Hungary $28,260; Latvia $118,961. Thus, if collections were made from all the countries still in doubt the total will be less than $23,000,000. With Yugoslavia and Estonia defaulting, as is probable, the total would be $12,187,000. Meanwhile, the administration kept its eye on congress for any further outbursts of disapproval at

Washington, June 15. — (P) — Europe paid a little more than 8 per cent of the 144,180,000 war debt instalments that fell due today and the countries immediately fell into line behind Great Britain to seek a review of the debt agreements from President Roosevelt. One after another, the diplomatic representatives of the debtor nations called at the state department to present the decisions of their governments, until finally the line-up showed payments from six nations, defaults by five and probably defaults by three others. The conference monetary committee, headed by James M. Cox of Ohio, worked on the currency issue while American and British representatives conferred at the Bank of England on temporary exchange stabilization of the dollar and pound. The monetary committee decided to recommend that the conference set up two committees, one to consider temporary measures for monetary reconstruction, another to consider permanent measures. (By the Associated Press) London, June 15—The Americans won a major victory in the world economic conference today, ending its second disturbing crisis, by breaking down French opposition and electing James M. Cox, former governor of Ohio, to the chairmanship of the vitally important monetary committee. This ended a day in which the Franco-American controversy had replaced war debts as the conference's chief irritant and final settlement of the chairmanship gave a distinctly brighter aspect to the big world conclave. Cordell Hull, United States secretary of state and head of the American delegation, said this evening he was more hopeful than at any time, and expressed the view the parley now was getting down to business. The situation facing the monetary committee, however, remained an enigma, with conflicting interpretations among the various groups. French quarters endeavored to make t

LONDON, June 16 (#)—In the midst of solemn deliberations by the economics commission of the world economic conference today, the chairman, Premier Colijn of the Netherlands, announced that 4 pounds, 10 shillings, had been found, and that the owner could have them by applying to him. The delegates, many of whom previously had slumped in their seats, promptly sat up.

gathered © London, and three things are in their minds concerning this country. First, how to get rid of the war debts, in a nice way that will seem like doing Uncle Sam a favor and make him seem a worse Shylock than ever if he objects. Second, how to regulate Uncle Sam’s dollar for him, that it may not become too cheap, and make it easy for the outside world to buy goods here. Third, how to tear down this country’s tariff wall, and obtain free markets for foreign goods produced by cheap labor based on a lower standard of living. Europe has a low opinion of American common sense and statesmanship. If she carries out her present plans, she will have established the soundness of that opinion. LONDON, June 16.—(4)—Germany asked the world today for an African colonial empire. A memorandum prepared by Dr. Alfred Hugenberg, German minister of economics, for the economic committee of the world economic conference, said there were two possible ways of increasing Germany’s capacity to meet her international debts—first, by giving her an African empire where large public works schemes could be carried through; or, second, by opening other new territories “to this people which has not enough space in which to live.”

London, June 16 (®)—The world economic conference began its serious labors today with unanimous agreement on five points and disagreement on eight others. Apparent accord has been indicated by an analysis of speeches, on: 1. That stabilization of currencies is necessary; 2. Trade barriers—tariffs, quotas, exchange restrictions—must be lowered; 3. Monetary and economic remedies for the crisis are interwoven; 4. The gold standard is the best; 5. The world is at a crossroads. Points of apparent disagreement: 1. When stabilization should take place—some said immediately, others just an indefinite time; 2. Raising wholesale price levels; 3. Public works programs; 4. Restriction of production, such as the wheat crop acreage; 5. Creation of an international credit institution; 6. Remonetization of silver; 7. 1933-08-31.text: London—(UP)—Norman H. Davis, American disarmament delegate, will confer with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald on September 5 or 6 and reveal a new disarmament plan sponsored by President Roosevelt, it was reported Wednesday. Davis, it was said, would seek MacDonald’s support for the plan preparatory to introducing it at the disarmament conference when it reconvenes at Geneva in October. Davis, who sailed from New York Wednesday on the liner Washington, is due to land here September

London, Aug. 20.--Argentina's signature to the international wheat agreement today put the finishing touch to a pact which the negotiators assert will rehabilitate the wheat industry and thereby do more toward restoring world prosperity than could any other single factor. Wheat experts assert that unless the world’s impoverished wheat farmer is put on his feet there can be no universal prosperity. Frederick E. Murphy, Minnesota representative, is one of those who hold this opinion, but he said today that the agreement need not be expected “to work a miracle overnight.” Argentina became the twenty-second nation to sign the pact, the general purpose of which is to reduce production by the great wheat nations and stimulate consumption in the importing countries. The delay in the signature of Argentina, which is one of the major wheat-producing nations, had caused much uneasiness among the n

Exmoor, Highland Park, Ill., Aug. 31.—(AP)—Enid Wilson, champion of England, and Virginia Van Wie of Chicago, American titleholder, reached the semifinals of the national women’s golf championship today and will meet tomorrow. The international duel of the champions was set as Miss Wilson defeated Charlotte Glutting of West Orange, N. J., 2 and 1, and Miss Van Wie turned back a spirited challenge by Mrs. Leona Cheney, San Gabriel, Calif., 1 up. Helen Hicks of Inwood, N. Y., and Maureen Orcutt, Haworth, N. J., reached the other semifinals match. Miss Hicks defeated Lucile Robinson, Des Moines, 4 and 3, and Miss Orcutt, coming back to win three of the final five holes, with a medal finish of 36, eliminated Mrs. O. S. Hill of Kansas City, 4 and 3.

NUREMBERG, Germany, Aug. 31.—Triumphantly dominant over Germany's destinies, 350,000 Nazis jammed Nuremberg today for a four-day party convention that may write a flaming page in Europe's history. With Europe alarmed at the virility of the Nazi movement and the bluntness of his talk, Chancellor Adolf Hitler, revered almost as a god, is due to make two speeches and issue a party proclamation. In addition, Hitler's chief expert on foreign affairs, Alfred Rosenberg, will deliver a report on foreign policy that offers hope of liquidating the Austrian crisis or the threat of further isolating Germany from the rest of Europe. Hitler arrived last night after an automobile journey from Munich. All along the road he was acclaimed like a conquering general. Crowds gathered at the roadside to cheer him hysterically while bells rang in his honor. Hermann Goering, Prussian minister of interior; Paul

THE HAGUE, AUG. 31. (AP).--J. H. Van Royen, Dutch minister to Washington died suddenly at his villa today. He had planned to return to Washington in October after spending an annual leave here. He became minister to America in 1926. He was 61 years old and had had a long and distinguished diplomatic career.

Bolzano, Italy. — Franz Hofer, Austrian Nazi chief rescued from prison at Innsbruck by three men who chloroformed his jailors, arrived here today after a gruelling trip across the Alps. Hofer, Nazi chief for the Tyrol-Vorarlberg district of Austria, was suffering from a gunshot wound in the knee, suffered when a policeman shot at the rescuers’ motor car when it failed to halt at his command on the Brenner pass road. The Nazi chieftain’s rescuers carried him most of the way after that, abandoning their stolen motor car and fleeing on a mountain path toward the Italian frontier. Hofer had hoped to start at once by airplane for the German Nazi convention at Nuremberg, but seeks his extradition and it was believed he would be de-

Cannes, France, Aug. 31.—(P)— Mr. and Mrs. James J. Walker left today to spend a month in Evian, a resort in southern France, where Mrs. Walker, the former Betty Compton, has been ordered by her doctor because of delicate health. A close friend of the former New York mayor paid the Walkers had expected a baby, but that hope was destroyed following a severe intestinal illness which she suffered recently.

TRENTO, ITALY, AUG. 31. (AP).—Seven mountain climbers were killed yesterday and Tuesday in the Italian Dolomites, according to reports reaching here today. Five were Germans, one of them a woman, one was a Czech and the other a Italian priest.

1933-01-27.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Jan. 27 (P)—President Eamon De Valera’s prospects for forming his first independent government appeared bright today as additional returns from Tuesday's election showed the Fianna Fail to have a clear majority over all other parties. With 35 seats still undecided, the Fianna Fail had 60, Cumann Na nGaedheal (Ex-President Cosgrove’s party) 35; Independents 7; Labor 7; Centre Party 8, and Independent Labor 1. Although recording gains, there was still a feeling in some quarters that final returns will show De Valera is unable to carry on without the aid of the small Labor party, which supported him during the past year. When De Valera dissolved the Dail January 3, he was confident of winning a clear majority for the first time in the 10-year history of the Free State and release from the dependence of Labor's vote, as he has had for the past year.

Empire do not constitute a barrier to possible trade concessions by Great Britain to the United States in return for reduction of the war debt, according to an authoritative interpretation. Chamberlain Speech. There was no intimation here that the recent speech by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, in which the British debt policy was outlined was a direct move for such bargaining between this country and America, but one of the fundamental objectives of England's swing from free trade to tariff last year was to be able to use the tariff as a bargaining weapon. Dublin, Jan. 27 (UP)—Eamon De Valera’s Republican party approached a clear majority in the New Dail today, needing only 20 of 39 outstanding seats to insure control even without support by the Labor party. At noon, De Valera had 57 seats, and other parties combined had the same number. With seven Labor seats counted on to support the Republicans, De Valera needed only 13 more to ensure a coalition majority. Without Labor's support, the Republicans needed 20 seats to reach 77, a majority. There are 153 seats in the Dail.

New York, Jan. 26. (4)--A hero of the sea came to port today with 22 men he saved from a sinking British freighter in mid-Atlantic, but he would have none of the credit for the feat, which old seamen had hailed as “remarkable.” The slim young master of the American Merchant, 36-year-old Giles Chester Stedman, stayed in his cabin while harbor craft of all kinds sent up a cacophony of noise New York's welcome of whistles. He went about his routine duties while the ship headed toward a pier loaded with cheering crowds. He talked quietly of the rescue, but he insisted the credit belonged to others. It was the accuracy of a radio direction finder, he said, that enabled the American Merchant last Friday to locate the battered Exeter City, after her bridge had been carried away, and her skipper, third mate and two members of the crew had been swept overboard by a 50-foot wave. LONDON, Jan. 44.—(AUF)—The Evening Standard, in a purported trans-Atlantic telephone interview with Henry Ford, quoted the manufacturer today as saying the stoppage in his Detroit plant was due to the efforts of certain bankers to gain control of the Ford concern. ‘The newspaper quoted Ford as follows: “Certain of my competitors are operating against me, supported by their bankers, with the object of preventing another Ford car from leaving the factory. “They have succeeded for a few hours but I will fight them and prove that production cannot be stopped. I am going straight out to clean up the whole affair.” DEARBORN, MICH., Jan. 27.—(U.P)—Henry Ford’s trans-Atlantic telephone interview with the London Evening Standard was confirmed by his office here today. Ford refused to amplify his statements.

Washington, Jan. 27—Offering a resolution for Congress to reaffirm its expressed opposition to war debts revision, Senator Robinson, Republican of Indiana, told the Senate this afternoon that the Democratic leader Robinson of Arkansas had violated Senate rules yesterday by inviting the British ambassador into the legislative chamber. Twice this week Robinson had clashed in the Senate with the Democratic leader, Robinson of Arkansas, over the debts question. His resolution “from one adopted by Congress in December 1931 in ratifying the Hoover moratorium. It recorded Congress against any debt revision.”

The "most-favored" nation agreements between England and other countries would not be violated and no previous diplomatic dealings between the United States and England would prevent such bargaining. England's departure in the past years from its centuries-old free trade policy has put it in a position to welcome President-elect Roosevelt's proposed tariff bargaining policy in the forthcoming war debts conference. Dublin, Irish Free State, Jan. 27 (Friday) (4P)--—- Election returns from 112 contests for the 153 seats in the Dail Eireann showed early today that President Eamon De Valera's party was running in an independent majority combination with the Allied Labor party; however, the De Valera supporters were ahead of the opposition. With 41 seats still undecided, the party standing was: Fianna Fail (De Valera party) 56; Cumann Na nGaedheal (the party of former President William T. Cosgrave) 34; Independents 7; Labor 6; Center party 5, and Independent Labor 1. At this stage of the tabulation Mr. De Valera’s own party had exactly half the seats decided. The supporting six seats of Labor gave him, however, a handy margin.

1933-01-19.text: PARIS (#) — More than a dozen French airplanes were engaged today in searches over French territory in Africa and the Alps region for Lady Mary Bailey and Bert Hinkler, two of the British Empire's foremost fliers. Planes were starting from various points in Algeria and Morocco to search for Lady Bailey, wife of a South African millionaire and mother of five children, who has been missing four days on an England-South Africa speed flight. French authorities said other planes would explore forest regions in the vicinity of Dijon and the French Alps for Bert Hinkler, missing 12 days since he began an attempt to recapture the England-Australia speed record.

He believes, as he well may, that he may find his most important work still ahead of him. COLUMBUS, C., Jan. 19.—(?)—Don't correct yourself when you say “It is me.” That expression has the approval of the dean of English at Ohio State University. “There’s too much of the schoolmaster in the American language,” says Dean George H. McKnight. “‘It is me’ is a natural use of the expression and is much to be preferred over ‘It is I.’

(By Associated Press) LONDON—Several snakes at the London Zoo are regarding spectators with a glassy stare. They lost their eyes in accidents of various kinds—and the keepers fitted them with glass ones. The only trouble is that every time the snakes shed their skins, the eyes pop out and have to be fitted back in again. Try that on a boa constrictor!

London, Jan. 18.—(#)—A dozen planes, mostly French military machines, will start Thursday from various French African points to search for Lady Mary Bailey of whom nothing has been heard since she left Oran, Algeria, Sunday on the second leg of a flight to Cape Town. It was understood that any search from England would be deferred pending the result of the French operations.

London, Jan. 18.—(P)—The Royal Astronomical Society’s gold medal will be awarded this year to Dr. Vesto M. Slipher, director of the Lowell Observatory, Flagstaff, Ariz, it was announced today. He will receive the award for his spectroscopic researches on planets, stars and nebulae. Dr. Slipher will be invited to deliver the George Darwin lecture of 1933. Discovery at Flagstaff of a newly found body in the solar system designated as “Planet X” brought worldwide attention to Dr. Slipher in March, 1940. Dr. Slipher insisted the trans-neptunian object could only be a major planet, of which existence of eight were known previously. He said it was 41 times 33,000,600 miles from the earth. Miller's $342,000 damage suit against the cowboy actor. Carles H. English, counsel for Miller, who seeks the sum from Mix for alleged abrogation of a contract for appearance with his 101 Ranch show, protested vigorously against the juror’s hand-shaking. He described it as “highly improper” but no action concerning the incident was taken by the court. Miller, on the stand almost continuously on the third day of the trial, was a cool witness, but wearied from the tireless direct and cross examination. PARIS, Jan. 19—(UP)—The air ministry tonight announced Lady Mary Bailey, British flyer missing since Sunday, had been found alive on the banks of the Niger river in Africa. Lady Bailey landed safely, with only an hour’s gasoline supply left. The English woman left Oran, Algeria, at 1:50 p.m. last Sunday for Niamey, French West Africa, on the second phase of her England-to-Capetown, South Africa, flight in an effort to beat the record recently set by Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison, another well-known English flyer.

1933-03-21.text: ROME, Mar, 20. (4#)—The new Mussolini peace plan will not be limited to Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy, but will embrace the whole continent and even the United States to a certain extent, Premier Ramsay MacDonald said in an interview today. The British premier made the statement before leaving for Paris where he will urge Premier Edouard Daladier of France to approve the projects. Mr. MacDonald refused to divulge any details but said ‘our whole idea is to open up the possibility of complete agreement, not between two, three, four, five or six powers, but all nations concerned.” An official Italian announcement yesterday said “collaboration of the four powers” was proposed in Premier Benito Mussolini’s plan but no details were made public. PARIS, March 21. — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of England arrived in Paris today bearing the text of the four power peace pact proposed by Premier Mussolini, and immediately placed the project before Premier Edouard Daladier of France. At the British embassy, MacDonald conferred with Daladier, Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, and Joseph Paul-Boncour, foreign ministers of France. The French government, it was learned, will not commit itself definitely until Daladier has undertaken prolonged study of the Italian plan, in company with experts, after hearing MacDonald's outlined explanations of the real significance of various clauses. French opinion is inclined to distrust some of the proposals, but it is not believed that Daladier will reject the plan outright. Instead, he is expected to express a willingness to cooperate in discussions among the four powers involved, France,

London — () — A charge that Lieutenant Norman Baillie-Stewart of the British army had “sold his country for the sake of £59,” was made Monday by Major H. Shapcott, the prosecuting officer, in opening a court-martial against the young officer. The lieutenant has been a prisoner in the Tower of London for several weeks. The general nature of the charges revealed that Baillie-Stewart, 24-year-old officer of the Seaforth Highlanders, allegedly planned with a German, suspected of being a foreign agent, to procure and communicate army secrets which might be useful to an enemy. Major Shapcott produced a letter addressed to Baillie-Stewart, signed “Marie Louise” and mailed at Berlin. It was said to have contained ten £5 notes. The prosecutor said he would mince no words, and declared the accused had sold his country for that amount, Army Data Sold? The main charge is that between Aug. 1 and Nov.

LONDON, March 20.—(P)—A tall good-looking Scots youth, a lieutenant in the aristocratic Seaforth Highlanders, went on trial today before a court-martial composed of his brother officers on ten charges involving the sale of military secrets which might prove useful to an enemy country. “I am not mincing words,” said Major H. Shapcott, the prosecutor, with a finger levelled at the defendant, Lieutenant Norman Balllie-Stewart, the son of a lieutenant colonel, “The prosecution contend that Lieutenant Balllie-Stewart sold his country for the sake of 50 pounds or more.” (By current exchange 50 pounds is $173.) In a two and a half hour speech Major Shapcott outlined the government's case—a case built upon an exchange of letters between Lieutenant Balllie-Stewart and persons in Berlin and on other evidence as yet undisclosed. | LONDON, March 20.—(P)— Negotiations for renewal of a commercial treaty between Great Britain and Soviet Russia have been suspended, the House of Commons was informed today. | “In the present circumstances,” said Captain Anthony Eden, Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, “Negotiations for renewal of the treaty which expires next month could serve no useful purpose.” The announcement followed the recent brisk diplomatic exchanges in connection with the arrest of several British subjects representing a British commercial concern in Russia. The prisoners are charged with sabotage.

London, Mar. 21. — An intimation that the third degree had been applied to Lieut. Norman Baillie-Stewart when army officials at Aldershot began an investigation of his alleged wrongful acts was put forth by his counsel in the course of today’s session of the young officer's court martial. Lieut. Baillie-Stewart, an officer of the Seaforth Highlanders, is being tried on charges of betraying army secrets to a foreign agent. Lieut. Col. F. N. Syms, who conducted this preliminary questioning of the accused officer, denied on the witness stand, however, that there was anything in the nature of a third degree in the course of this questioning, or even that Lieut. Baillie-Stewart was cross examined. Lieut. Col. Syms was questioned at length by Lieut. Baillie-Stewart’s attorney on cross examination with particular reference to the accused officer's explanation that 90 pounds he had admitted havi

READING, March 20—(#)—After it was learned that several cases of scarlet fever had developed over the week-end, Albright college today was ordered closed for two weeks. All classes were dispensed with and regular sessions will not be held until April 3, it was announced by Dean George W.

MOSCOW, March 21.—(A.P.)—The British government's action in breaking off trade negotiations with Soviet Russia is expected in foreign quarters to bring repercussions in the impending trial of four British subjects here on espionage charges. While the action was viewed as an attempt to bring pressure for the unconditional release of the prisoners, some foreign quarters were inclined to believe it only would stiffen the Russian attitude. Strong resentment was caused here by the implied feeling in England that the arrested men will not obtain a fair trial. The four British prisoners and 35 others, all employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Co., are to be tried within a month on charges of 'wrecking activities' in connection with electrical stations in several cities. The company has been engaged in supplying and installing electrical appliances in Russia for 10 years and its contract was nea

1933-03-29.text: Brussels, Belgium, March 28.— Fifteen persons were killed today in the wreck of an imperial airways passenger liner near Essen, Eleven of the victims were English.

LONDON, Mar. 29—(4)—The question of a final settlement of the war debt owed the United States again became the chief business before the British government today. The subject was up for discussion at today’s cabinet meeting even before the expected arrival tonight of Norman H. Davis, who has been named special ambassador for the United States in Europe by President Roosevelt. Important action was expected in parliamentary circles to result from the discussions between Davis and government chiefs. Reports emanating from abroad that two cabinet members have been appointed to handle the debt question were denied in authoritative quarters. Latest reports from Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay, who has been carrying on preliminary conversations with President Roosevelt and Secretary of State Hull, suggested some time in April would be the earliest a debt commission could open a conference in Wash

Brussels, March 28.—(4) The City of Liverpool, a tri-motored airplane of the British Imperial Airways, burst into flames and crashed today near Eesen, killing 15 persons, everyone aboard her. The cause of the accident was not definitely established. The ship, bound from Cologne, Germany, to Croydon, England, by way of Brussels, had stopped at Haeren airdrome here only a short time before the crash. One explanation advanced was that one of the three motors exploded, setting fire to the plane. Witnesses said the great ship dropped like a spent rocket. Apparently four of those aboard jumped, for their bodies were found some distance from the wreckage. It appeared that the others had been burned to death. There were no Americans aboard.

| By The Associated Press | London, March 29.—Trial of one of the strangest cases in the annals of the British armed services concluded yesterday in a finding of not guilty on three of ten charges brought against Norman Baillie-Stewart, lieutenant of the Seaforth Highlanders accused of selling military secrets to a foreign agent. No announcement was made of the decision of the court martial concerning the remaining charges, but military custom made it clear that the findings would be other than not guilty. Otherwise they would have been made public. The case now goes to higher military authorities. If the decisions of the court martial are confirmed by the army council and approved by the king, the war office will announce the penalty to be imposed. San Pedro, Calif., Mar. 20. (AP) George Bernard Shaw, white-whiskered Irish dramatist, sailed for New York last night on the Empress of Britain, traveling by way of the Panama Canal and nearing the end of an around the world cruise. While the hypercritical iconoclast left in his wake in southern California a number of screen celebrities who were impressed by his visit despite his caustic remark that he would return sometime and “show you how to make pictures,” there was at least one person who had come in close contact with the dramatist who saw nothing unusual in Shaw's brief sojourn. When the airplane carrying Shaw from San Simeon to Los Angeles was forced down on the beach yesterday near Malibu, George Gray O'Connor, a sophomore at the University of California at Los Angeles, happened along in his dilapidated automobile. Mr. and Mrs. Shaw accepted O'Connor's invitation for a bouncing

LONDON, March 28. (AP) — The court-martial which tried Lieutenant Norman Baillie-Stewart, young officer of the Seaforth Highlanders, on a charge of selling military information to a foreign agent, late today found him not guilty of three charges, as instructed by the judge advocate in summing up the case. It was announced that the court was closed and that the decision of the court will be submitted to higher authorities for consideration.

Dagenham, Eng, Mar. 29.—(#)— A three day strike over wages at the Ford Motor Company plant was settled this afternoon when representatives of the strikers agreed to accept a new minimum wage rate. The strike affected 7,000 men. Work probably will be resumed tomorrow. The new scale represents an increase over that to which the workers objected.

LONDON, March 28. (U.P)—Lieut. Norman Baillie-Stewart, 24, of the Seaforth Highlanders was found not guilty of three of the ten charges against him today by a court-martial which tried him for allegedly betraying his country’s military secrets to a German agent. In accordance with court-martial procedure, it was understood he was held guilty on the other seven counts. Sentence will be pronounced later.

1933-05-02.text: London, (AP) - Special dispatches received today by British newspapers from the United States, saying that President Roosevelt may attend the world economic conference, considerably surprised members of the mission of Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large. (The Washington government made no announcement that Mr. Roosevelt intended to go to London.) No American officials in London believed that the president was making any such plan, but the special dispatches provided a sensation for afternoon newspapers. It was said that one of the foreign statesmen who recently went to Washington to see Mr. Roosevelt urged him to come to London on the ground that it would add to the prestige of the conference. The two outstanding foreign statesmen who have seen President Roosevelt recently are Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and Edouard Herriot, special French envoy. The infere

WASHINGTON, May 2.—Speculation as to the possibility of President Roosevelt making a speedy trip to the world economic conference in London persisted today in the face of White House denials. "Too silly for words" was the reply from official quarters to questions whether Mr. Roosevelt contemplated using the swift 10,000-ton cruiser Indianapolis for an overseas voyage. "The President may make, however, several short cruises on the Indianapolis which now is completing her trial runs. As a matter of fact he may go from Baltimore to Marblehead, Mass., by sea next month from which latter place he intends starting out on a yachting trip to Eastport, Me." WASHINGTON, May 2 (AP).—President Roosevelt is trying to arrange to get to Chicago to open the World Fair in June. He plans to spend most of the summer away from Washington. His trip to Chicago is only tentative, at present, because he has agr

(United Press Staff Correspondent). (Copyright 193%, By United Press.) LONDON, May 22—Grave danger to United States trade was seen today in the terms of an Anglo-Argentine trade agreement just concluded between the two countries. The text of the treaty, exclusively obtained by the United Press, revealed reciprocal trade and monetary exchange advantages between England and Argentina which were regarded as a serious setback to the United States unless President Roosevelt launches a prompt and powerful counter-offensive against what already has developed into a new Anglo-American struggle for the rich market.

WASHINGTON, May 14. Increasing emphasis was placed today by officials upon the American drive for a truce on tariff barriers pending outcome of the London economic conference. While the White House preparatory discussions widened with arrival of the first Latin American government, it was hopeful on the tariff question, anxious that no new trade obstacles should bounce up to put fresh hazards in the now partially smoothed course for the economic parley. Phillips refused to see failure for the plan in the non-agreement of representatives who met as the conference organizing committee in London Saturday. They, he said, are without authority to commit their governments.

- HENDON, England, May 2—P— Pilot Officer Viscount Kenbworth, eldest son of the Earl of Lytton, and aircraftsman Ralph Harrison, were killed last night in a practice flight for the Hendon air pageant. The viscount, who would have been 30 years old May 13, was a member of parliament. His father is best known as chairman of the League of Nations committee which investigated the Sino-Japanese

Washington, May 5. (UP)—James M. Cox, former governor of Ohio, will be one of the leading members of the American delegation to the World Economic Conference in London, it was reported in authoritative circles today.

MUKDEN, May 2 (AP)—Kidnappings at the rate of ten a day—1,200 in four months—have been reported in south Manchuria to Japanese police since January 1. The figures were announced today. Several victims of the Manchurian banditti, including American and British citizens, are still held captive. A letter from Dr. Neils Nielsen, American missionary from Minneapolis who is being held, warned other missionaries in this area that their safety was endangered. Dr. Nielsen, writing to his wife here, said he was well, but that remarks of his captors indicated that other missionaries were in peril.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS WASHINGTON, May 2.—The name of James M. Cox, 1920 Democratic presidential nominee, today was tentatively put on the list of the American delegation to the London economic conference by observers here. President Roosevelt is casting about for his delegation which will be called up to go into action on June 12. Secretary Hull is regarded as the most probable choice for chairman. Raymond Moley, assistant secretary of state and chief economic adviser to the President, and Chairman Pittman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, are regarded as certain choices.

LONDON. (UP). Widespread fears were felt in London that the German Reichstag would renounce military clauses of the Versailles treaty when it convened Wednesday in special session to discuss the Geneva disarmament crisis. The possibility of reoccupation of the Rhineland by allied troops was being openly discussed in Great Britain. British public opinion was wrought to high pitch by the possibility of German renunciation of the Versailles treaty, which imposes rigid military restrictions upon the Reich. Norman H. Davis, American ambassador at large, having won a signal victory in the adoption of the economic truce by the organizing committee of the world economic conference, was prepared to leave for Geneva in hopes of saving the disarmament conference, disrupted by Germany's demand for the right to re-arm. BERLIN. (UP). The German government believes that a compromise can be arranged to

WARRENTON, Ga. May 13.—(P)—A mob abducted a wounded negro last night after a gun battle in which his brother and a white planter were killed and today his body was found at a roadside just outside the city. The negroes, Lamar Kinsey and Will Kinsey, were tenants of the planter, Charlie English, and the fight took place at their home. Sheriff George P. Hagan said he learned the battle occurred when the planter went to question them about trouble with his nephew. English and Lamar Kinsey were killed instantly in an exchange of shots. Will Kinsey, wounded, was brought here by relatives. Dr. W. A. Davis said he treated him in his office and left him with a deputy sheriff. Later J. A. Bray, druggist, said he saw a mob enter the physician's office, bring Kinsey out, shove him into an automobile and drive off.

LONDON, May 18--The cornerstone of the world economic conference was laid today by the adoption of the American tariff truce, which was declared immediately effective in the eight key nations represented on the conference organizing committee. The text of the truce will be sent to other nations by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald who will ask them to adhere to it until June 12, when, upon the opening of the conference, the United States will formally propose that the armistice be continued throughout the parley. First Achievement The moratorium on tariff changes was the first big achievement of President Roosevelt's ambassador-at-large, Norman H. Davis, who came to London two weeks ago expecting to get the truce approved in two days. Instead, he has had to employ all the arts of diplomacy to conciliate the special problems and conflicting interests of European powers, but in the end he ac

LONDON, much pleased, hears that President Roosevelt will go to England to attend the economic parley, “making a record crossing on the United States cruiser Indianapolis.” The President announces that he has “no present intention” of attending the conference. Perhaps he remembers what happened after President Wilson made such a trip, visiting en famille at Buckingham Palace, and getting his portrait substituted for Garibaldi’s in many Italian homes. That Buckingham lodging and Garibaldi substitution cost this country many billions of dollars, to say nothing of the depression. There was recently a conference in Washington concerning billions that Europe owes us. Mussolini did not come, the president of France did not come; the King of England did not come. They sent somebody, although they owe us. Is there any particular reason why President Roosevelt should go? He has work to do here, a

Paris, May 13.—(®—France and Great Britain were united today to face a disquieting situation created by the armament aspirations of Chancellor Hitler of Germany. Indications that these countries were ready to send their armies back into the Rhineland if Germany seeks greater disarmament than permitted under the Versailles treaty raised the question of whether the United States would be willing to resume its military post on the Rhine river. Foreign Minister Paul Boncour made clear in his statement that France and Great Britain are ready to return to the sanctions of the treaty if forced to.

Berlin, Germany, May 13.—Chancellor Adolph Hitler will appear before the Reich next Wednesday to present a conciliatory compromise plan for world disarmament which may lead to an international armed agreement at Geneva. This was learned by I. N. S. today as reports from London and Paris disclosed keen sentiment in favor of enforcing the penalty provision of the Treaty of Versailles "to the hilt" in the event Germany insists upon rearming. Hitler will not only explain Germany’s views of disarmament, but will call upon other countries for a complete clarification of the European political situation. His address promises to be one of the most important delivered before any parliament since the World War. He will announce the aims of Germany's new Nazi government and declare that before the World Economic Conference meets in London there must be an international understanding through "the tr

ENTOWN, Ga., May 13. UP Will Kinsey, negro tenant farmer about 25 years old, was taken from the office of Dr. A. W. Davis and shot to death by a mob of approximately 40 men last night after he had figured in a shooting affray in which his brother, Lamar Kinsey, and Charles English, well known white farmer, were slain. Will Kinsey was taken by the mob after the physician had dressed wounds he received in the gun battle, it was said. Dr. Davis said he was not in the office when the negro was taken and that he left him in the hands of a deputy sheriff. The shooting resulted from a quarrel between the two negroes and John Pierce, English’s nephew. Pierce, owner of the land on which the negroes were tenants, went to the negroes’ home, a quarrel ensued, and one of the negroes threatened to strike Pierce with a plow fender. Pierce notified his uncle and the shooting took place when he approache

1933-05-30.text: (Associated Press Staff Writer) WASHINGTON, May 31—(?)— The United States delegation headed today for the World Economic conference at London with one final, terse instruction from President Roosevelt: Get fast action and cut the speeches short. On that, the diversified group of spokesmen and technical aides set out to translate into accomplishment Mr. Roosevelt’s bold bid for world concord, stabilization of currencies, lower tariff barricades, higher prices, more credit, employment and business. The delegation left Washington at 7:55 a.m. for New York to embark in the early afternoon for Europe. Behind their campaign at the conference opening June 12 were the painstaking consultations with foreign leaders at the White House and State Department, upon which the President had staked much of his hope for success. Their Main Objectives The delegates take with them today these major internat

By The Associated Press Washington, May 30—Senator Couzens of Michigan today accepted appointment by President Roosevelt as a member of the American delegation to the London economic conference. He is the first Republican to be named the other members selected so far being Secretary Hull, Senator Pittman, of Nevada, and Representative McReynolds, of Tennessee. The delegation sails tomorrow afternoon from New York for the British capital.

GENEVA, May 29.—The disarmament conference appeared headed for a bitter fight today on the question of adjournment until conclusion of the World Economic Conference at London. Newspaper reports from Washington today said President Roosevelt opposed adjournment unless an agreement were reached on disarmament before June 12, the day the World Conference is scheduled to meet. League of Nations headquarters buzzed with excited discussion of the reports at once. Norman H. Davis, chief United States delegate, conferred with Joseph Paul-Boncour, French foreign minister just back from Paris, where he had a week-end consultation with his government on the tangled disarmament and Mussolini Peace Treaty situations. Davis was believed to have urged Boncour to announce at the earliest moment the extent of the reductions to which France would agree, so that agreements might be reached before the World

WASHINGTON, May 29.--A-- President Roosevelt gave his final instructions Monday to the American delegation leaving on Wednesday for the London economic conference. It was said at the White House after the parley that the delegation still consists of only four, but there was an indication that a fifth might be added, probably a Republican member of the Senate. R. W. Morrison of San Antonio, Texas, appeared certain to be a member of the delegation when he entered the White House meeting. It became known at the same time that Senator LaFollette, Republican, Wisconsin, had declined an invitation to serve on the delegation. He is the second Republican who has refused a place, Sen. Johnson of California having also declined. James M. Cox, of Ohio, a member of the delegation, was not present at the White House conference but he will sail with the group.

London, ~~ (Ar) -- The opening ceremony of the world economic conference June 12 will be short and businesslike, and the parley itself may last only six weeks instead of the six months previously estimated. This is in accordance with the latest plans of League of Nations officials, who have taken active charge of preparations for assembling representatives of the sixty-six nations participating. King George’s opening address will be brief, outlining in broadest terms hopes for the return of world prosperity. The opinion is growing here that after the first phase of the conference in London, lasting perhaps six weeks, there will be an adjournment and the work of committees may be carried on at Geneva parallel with the league assembly there in September. The opening day's program is expected to include a formal proposal for a tariff truce by the United States.

LONDON, May 30—(AP)— Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain sidestepped repeated efforts in the House of Commons today to obtain a statement of the government’s policy on the war debts. The interrogation of the chancellor and its meager results were accepted as confirmation that the debt problem is a matter for cabinet executive decision. Mr. Chamberlain said he never had heard of a suggestion that the question be left to the free vote of the House of Commons, as reported by several British newspapers. “I cannot say at present whether I shall be able to make any statement on the debt matter before the adjournment for Whitsuntide,” he told the House. This adjournment will be taken Friday. Specifically, Mr. Chamberlain had been asked concerning the $75,950,000 payment due the United States June 15. Replying to a query about whether saving was possible as the United States governme

LONDON, May 30—i4%—Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain refused today to disclose Britain's war debt policy to the House of Commons. The Chancellor successfully parried all efforts to obtain from him a statement about the $75,950,000 payment due the United States June 15. He said he never had heard of a suggestion that the question be left to the free vote of the House of Commons.

Washington, D. C.—(AP)—A few hours before America’s spokesmen leave Washington to grapple with the world besetting economic problems at the London conference, President Roosevelt today awaited an answer from Senator Couzens (R.-Mich.) as to whether he will join the delegation. Eager that the Republican Party be represented in the group which will speak for the United States, Mr. Roosevelt has invited the wealthy Michigan legislator to join the delegation. It was understood, too, that he was still seeking a Republican member of the House to become a delegate as well. He will have to decide quickly, however, for the delegation leaves Washington early tomorrow and sails from New York in the afternoon. Meanwhile, the administration prepared to combat the amendment which the Senate Foreign Relations Committee unanimously attached to the arms embargo resolution. It would compel the president,

1933-05-03.text: Paris.-(AP)—The ministry of finance has prepared to impose shortly a 15-per-cent surtax on American goods, The decree, it was learned, is ready for signature, to be issued when the dollar approaches 20 francs, which officials expect. This surtax already is effective on British and Japanese goods because of depreciated exchange. It cannot be increased without parliamentary authority, which Premier Daladier was reported contemplating, Hand-in-hand with the surtax movement is an agitation by French holders of American gold bonds to have the government protest to Washington in connection with reports that their coupons will not be payable in gold, The financial press says the government is likely to intervene and remarks that French bonds held in the United States are being paid in gold, as stipulated. Two government issues due June 1, will be honored in this way. Few American bonds are held

Geneva, May 4—Germany through her delegate to the world disarmament conference today disavowed the “opinion that Germany wishes to avail herself of disarmament to proceed with re-armament at the highest possible level.” Count Rudolf Nadolny, the German representative, proposed the British arms plan be changed to provide a maximum calibre of 105 millimeters for mobile guns and to abolish all tanks. “There are still great difficulties but they are not insuperable,” Count Nadolny declared after explaining that if the German proposals are rejected, his nation should be allowed all land, naval, and air armaments deemed necessary for defense by other countries. “The German government has sufficiently proved its good will,” he continued.

Southampton, May 3—(P)—A cheering crowd on the dock greeted Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald when he returned today from his economic discussions with President Roosevelt in Washington. Mr. MacDonald declared on landing that he was pleased with all of his conversations with Mr. Roosevelt, which he described as most successful.

GENEVA; May 3.—A compromise has been reached with Germany on her unqualified demands for arms equality, which threatened to wreck the world arms conference, Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain announced today. Eden told the general commission of the conference that the Germans were willing to withdraw all their amendments to the British plan tending to exclude the militarized German police from calculation in Germany's armed strength. They stipulated, however, that Germany be allowed to possess a certain percentage of militarized police, any surplus over which would be counted as full-time soldiers. Other delegations agreed to the compromise, Eden said. The conference was enthusiastic over removal of one of the more serious problems raised by the German amendments.

| SOUTHAMPTON, Eng., May 3— (P)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald came home “very, very pleased” today from his economic discussions with Pres. Roosevelt in Washington in which, he said, he encountered an attitude of cooperative good will to which the difficult problems of the world must yield. The prime minister was greeted by a cheering throng awaiting him on the dock as the Berengaria pulled into Southampton water. He described his trip as most successful and said he was most pleased with all of his conversations with the American president.

Dublin, May 3—(U.P)—The government of President Eamon De Valera today abolished the oath of allegiance to the British crown. The action climaxed a long controversy started soon after the De Valera regime came into power and designed to sever all ties with Great Britain. The Free State government became involved in a bitter economic war with England because of its program. The Dail originally passed the oath abolition bill, but it was defeated by the senate. After the De Valera government was reaffirmed in the last general election the measure was revived and put through the Dail again. The constitution provides that such action may become effective after a certain delay, even if the senate continues to oppose it.

TOKIO WUP—Sir Miles Wedderburn Lampson, British minister to China, is attempting to arrange direct Sino-Japanese negotiations to end fighting along the Great Wall, the foreign office disclosed Wednesday. His attempts have found small favor with Japan, however, it was revealed. The government is hesitant to undertake negotiations, it was said, pending assurance of Chinese officials they will cease counterattacks.

| LONDON, May 3 ()—The Cabinet was summoned to Downing Street unexpectedly this morning owing to “the pressure of domestic business.” The regular Wednesday session had been postponed until tomorrow so Prime Minister MacDonald, due home today from his conversations with President Roosevelt in Washington, could be present. | It was understood that Parliamentary affairs necessitated the meeting despite the Premier's absence. | A revolt against the government by tariff diehards, it was believed in some political circles, had alarmed national government leaders to the extent of summoning the Cabinet. This meeting, it was believed, was for the adoption of a policy which will result in a vote of confidence if the critics of the trade agreements with Argentina, Denmark and Germany start their bombardment of the government again today. 1933-03-11.text: Paris, March 11. (UPI—The American dollar returned to parity here today when the banks of France, and England and the federal reserve joined to check speculation. The banks agreed to furnish dollars to the shorts in the dollar so that they could make deliveries, it was estimated European groups and individuals stand to lose $1,000,000 through their short operations. Without the aid of the banks, given to curb undue speculation, the losses would have been much greater.

Commissioners appointed. BERLIN, March 9.—Chancellor Hitler's control over the free states and republics of the German federation was tightened today as his minister of interior, Dr. Wilhelm Frick appointed national socialist federal police commissioners for Wuerttemberg, Baden, Saxony and Schaumburg-Lippe. Bavaria is now the only state retaining authority over its own police. Pre-election warnings of Nazi leaders that a federal commissioner would take charge in Bavaria brought responses from Bavarian Populists that any such move would be resisted by force.

TOKYO, March 11.—While a victorious advance guard of the Japanese army occupied a key portal of the Great Wall of China, the Japanese cabinet today approved a decision to resign from the League of Nations. Admiral Viscount M. Saito, prime minister, immediately submitted the documents of withdrawal to Emperor Hirohito. Japan’s memorandum of resignation includes announcement of her determination to keep the mandated islands, former German possessions in the Pacific. Under the procedure contemplated, Emperor Hirohito will refer the decision to the Privy Council, and will then approve it. In addition to the memorandum of the mandated islands, Japan has prepared a memorandum to the League regarding participation in the Labor Bureau and the World Court.

(Associated Press Leased Wire) TOKIO, March 11.—The question of war or peace in north China proper hangs in the balance today with the Japanese army, firmly implanted on the great wall of China, awaiting Chinese moves. These will determine the answer, a war office spokesman said. With Marshal Chang Hsiao-Liang abandoning the struggle, and Marshal Chiang Kai-Shek taking charge, a new situation has developed. "The key to the future is in the hands of Chiang Kai-Shek. If he seriously attempts to recapture any portion of Jehol, it means war on a national scale, in which event there is no reason Japanese operations should be restricted by the great wall," the war office spokesman said. (Any Japanese movement south of the wall would immediately strike the Peiping-Tientsin treaty area in which there are 3000 Americans, including 13800 marines and soldiers.)

BERLIN, March 11.—(#)—While the Polish government denied troop concentrations in the vicinity of Gdynia and the free city of Danzig, the Taegliche Rundschau, organ of former Chancellor Kurt von Schleicher, claimed today it was reliably informed that not only were Polish troops being concentrated at various German border points but that unusual military activity was manifest throughout the Polish corridor. Under the alarming headline—“Danzig in Danger”—the newspaper said: “Nearly 300 military planes (Continued on Page 12.)

Berlin, March 10.—()—Chancellor Adolf Hitler in an appeal to the German nation tonight ordered his Nazi storm troops to remember their discipline, refrain from molesting business life and to prevent any attacks upon foreigners in Germany. (Several complaints have been made at the American embassy in Berlin recently that Nazis had interfered with the rights of Americans. The American ambassador was assured that the rights of foreigners would be protected), While the chancellor was making public his views his confidential man, Hermann Goering, minister without portfolio, told an audience in Essen that the police never would be used ‘as protective troops for Jewish merchants,’

Berlin, March 11.—(4)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s broom will be wielded more vigorously than ever tomorrow when two more elections will be held throughout the reich. These are the provincial and municipal-communal elections. It is estimated that the fate of 200,000 office holders will be at stake. Approximately a million candidates are running. In Berlin, where the communists hitherto have been dominant, 7,405 candidates are running for 225 municipal offices and 780 other jobs in greater Berlin's twenty districts. A Big Cleanout. The fate of anti-national socialist councilmen and other officials may be imagined from a speech delivered yesterday by Herman Goering, minister without portfolio, at Essen. “This coming Sunday there will be a big cleanout and it will only be the beginning,” Captain Goering said. “The German communes, once the strength of the German people, are ruined and overburd

Washington, March 11. (#)— The Roosevelt economy bill hit a stormy road in the House today with Democratic ranks on the loose for and against it. In caucus the Democratic leaders fell short by 14 votes of binding their great majority to support the president. The leadership was able to get the bill up as soon as the House met. However, by a vote which directed opposition. Thus with spirited evidence on the Republican side no apparent diminution of confidence among those close to the president that he would get the extensive power requested over the veteran and payroll expenditures. In his special message yesterday he asked it to enable a one-half billion dollar cut in federal expenditures to make a balanced budget in the next year. The Democratic caucus vote was 174 to 108 in favor of being bound by 188 required to put it over.

1933-04-13.text: (By the Associated Press) London, April 13—Lieut. Norman Baillie-Stewart, convicted by court martial of violation of the Official Secrets Act, was sentenced today to dishonorable discharge from the army and to five years penal servitude. The young officer of the aristocratic Seaforth Highlanders, member of a distinguished military family, was charged with having sold military secrets to a foreign nation. During the court martial, the prosecution charged that he had “sold his country for 50 pounds or more,” receiving the money in the mail from Otto Waldemar Obst of Berlin. His defense was that the money had come from a German girl named Marie Louise, whom he had met while he was on leave in Germany. He denied betraying secrets of the army. The king himself confirmed the findings of the court, but Baillie-Stewart will escape the shame of being “drummed out” of the army, for that old ceremo

William H. MacDonald, the only one of six accused employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Company to plead guilty when the trial began yesterday, amplified previous testimony to the effect that he acted under the instructions of L. C. Thornton, another defendant, in gathering military and economic information which subsequently was sent to England. As today’s session began MacDonald caused something of a sensation by declaring that he had made incriminating statements at the time of his arrest because of the methods of the Russian secret police. The first witness recited a detailed story that MacDonald had bribed him to act as a spy, and the young Englishman confirmed almost all of this testimony. The other Englishmen on trial—Allan Monkhouse, Charles Nordwell, L. C. Thornton, A. W. Gregory and John Cushny—all pleaded not guilty. Eleven Russian employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical company, for which all of the Englishmen worked, pleaded guilty. Boston, April 13.—(f—A heavy easterly storm buried large sections of New England under snow today that ranged in depth up to 28 inches, disabled hundreds of miles of telephone and telegraph wires, felled trees and poles, broke power lines, delayed transportation and washed out railroad tracks. One automobile traffic death, that of William Ahern of New Britain, Conn., was attributed to the blinding snow. Near Northampton, Mass., an automobile and a trolley crashed during the storm and four men were injured. Thousands of school children enjoyed an unexpected holiday as a result of general closings of schools. Farmers in sections of Connecticut, where crops had begun to sprout, feared that serious damage might result. The on-shore gale piled up high tides and surf along the coast. Certain southern and coastal sections of New England escaped the snow but were drenched by rain.

New York, April 12 (4) With an hour of final jabbing at the foibles of the world in general and America in particular, George Bernard Shaw left the country today implying he probably never would return. Just before the Empress of Britain steamed off on the last lap of its round-the-world cruise, Shaw received 65 newspaper and magazine writers in the ship's salon. Like the walrus in “Through the Looking Glass,” he was willing to talk about “shoes and ships and sealing wax, and cabbages and kings” —and also about “Al” Smith, Hitler, and Irishmen. He thrust at all of them with rapier-like comment. He pretended never to have heard of former Governor Smith. He likened Hitler to “an officer in the army who defeats his career by cheating at cards.” He said his chief interest in New York was to “get out of it.” “One of America’s troubles,” he declared without a smile, “is that it has too many Ir

MOSCOW, April 13.—The British secret service was accused today of carrying on extensive spying activities in Soviet Russia through a high official of the British Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Co.; The allegations were in a signed confession by William H. Thornton, one of the six Metro-Vickers employees on trial charged with sabotage. It was read by Ludwig C. A. K. Martens, associate judge, who was once deported from the United States. Thornton admitted he wrote the confession and then promptly insisted it was not true. His repudiation was another of the surprises which have kept the audience at the trial on edge. At the day session, William MacDonald, another of the accused, withdrew the plea of guilty he entered yesterday, but then proceeded under cross-examination to admit substantially the major points of a confession he made. MacDonald, British engineer who pleaded guilty yesterday to espionage, sabotage and bribery charges, produced a sensation today by testifying to a hostile courtroom that he made damaging confessions at the time of his arrest ‘because of the circumstances of the investigation’ by the Russian secret police. Five other British engineers and a dozen Russians, including a woman, are being tried on similar charges. Moscow, April 13. (#8).—In a dramatic reversal from the witness stand, W. L. MacDonald, British engineer on trial with five compatriots and eleven Russians in the sensational Metropolitan-Vickers case, today repudiated his confession of guilt to charges of espionage, sabotage and bribery. The youthful British engineer, who at the opening of the trial yesterday admitted his complicity in a plot to wreck Soviet industry “in anticipation of impending war,” made a fruitless attempt to withdraw his plea of guilty and became enmeshed in a tangle of contradictions and disclaimers.

1933-04-05.text: LONDON, (P) — Premier Ramsay MacDonald will sail for the United States next week to discuss debts and disarmament it was learned on the most reliable authority today. Premier MacDonald will spend a few days in Washington, where he visited President Hoover in the last administration, discussing current problems with President Roosevelt, and laying the groundwork for the coming world economic conference, it was understood.
