YINGKOW, Manchuria, April 3. UPR—F. L. Pearce, 30, third engineer of the British steamer Nanchang, returned here safely today after being held with three British officers by Chinese pirates since last Thursday. Pearce was released by his captors who demanded ransom as the price of liberty for C. Johnson, W. W. Hargrave and A. D. Blue. The four British nationals were seized after the pirates had attacked the vessel, anchored here. The pirates demanded $1,000,000 cash ransom for the release of the three officers. In addition, they demanded trench mortars, rifles and ammunition enough to equip an entire regiment. Immunity also was stipulated in the fabulous demands which the pirates communicated in a letter delivered through their liberated captive.

LONDON, April 5.—Sir Esmond Ovey, recalled British ambassador to Moscow, said today the Russian government has worked itself into a state of “morbid hysteria” in fearing a world conspiracy against it. Sir Esmond is not expected to return to Moscow. Attacks Soviet Officials In a white paper which was before the House of Commons today, Sir Esmond vigorously attacked the Soviet officials for the manner in which they have treated six British prisoners who are facing trial in Moscow on charges of espionage. The ambassador asserted a ‘reign of terror’ existed in Russia and that it was “inconceivable that the Soviet government can produce any evidence of criminal malpractice” on the part of the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Company through its six British employees who face charges punishable by death. The General Electric Company of America was declared ‘seriously worried’ about its position

LONDON, APT 8. The arrangements are being made for Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald to visit Washington during the Easter recess of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister could sail either on the Olympic, leaving April 12, the President Roosevelt a day later, or the Berengaria April 15. The British Parliament will be in recess from April 13 to April 20. On account of his disarmament plan, which the disarmament conference will consider at Geneva late in April, and the other important European problems in which he is taking a leading role, it is expected Mr. MacDonald would make the American trip as soon as possible. His daughter, Isbel, is expected to accompany him.

LONDON, April 5.—-(UP)—The British government was on the threshold of complete severance of trade relations with Russia today. The House of Commons had before it an enabling act to permit the cabinet to prohibit importation of Soviet products of all categories—a complete embargo. Passage of the measure — and there was no doubt that it would be passed despite a vocally strong but numerically weak opposition — will result in the proclaiming of the embargo April 17, when the present British-Soviet trade agreement expires. The embargo will be in retaliation for the arrest in Moscow of six English employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Co. for alleged sabotage. The United Press learned that the government did not intend to rush the enabling act through Commons in a single session, but that debate would continue Thursday.

LONDON, April 3.—The British government debated today the grave possibility of a diplomatic break with Russia. The cabinet assembled to receive the formal report of Sir Esmond Ovey, ambassador to Moscow, called to London to relate in person the situation arising from charges of espionage brought against six British subjects, for which they are to stand trial in the Soviet capital. Restrictions on the importation of goods from Soviet Russia will be proposed by the government, Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today. MacDonald said he would present tomorrow an enabling act governing imports from Russia. MacDonald said the government desired to rush the bill, passing it through all stages on Wednesday.

London, April 5 - An almost open threat of a rupture in Anglo-Soviet relations was made in the House of Commons today by Sir John Simeon, foreign secretary, in moving to second reading the bill giving the government power to place an embargo on Soviet imports. Sir John addressed the House with emphasis and fervor on the arrest of six British employees of the Metropolitan Vickers Electric Co., in Moscow and their subsequent treatment. His remarks supplemented a British white paper distributed today, revealing the course of the case and the diplomatic protests made by Britain. “His Majesty's government,” he said, “do not in the slightest desire to disturb friendly relations— (Continued on Page Ten)

1933-01-28.text: WASHINGTON, JAN. 28. (AP).—Ambassador Lindsay of Great Britain headed southward by plane this forenoon to accept an invitation to confer with President-elect Roosevelt at Warm Springs prior to his return to London on Tuesday to advise his government on the impending war debts discussion. Sir Ronald was looking forward to the chance to sit with the next president in his Georgia cottage and eager to get the most definite information obtainable for Great Britain’s guidance in the bargaining on debts to be undertaken soon after March 4. Arrangements for the meeting, undertaken at the instance of the president-elect, were made through the department of state. There was no inkling there, however, as to exactly what Mr. Roosevelt had in mind,

Boston, Jan. 28.—()—Bare-stick a schooners and battered ocean greyhounds beat their way to storm shattered ports yesterday as the worst northeaster in recent years roared down the New England coast. Many sections of Cape Cod were cut off from communication with the rest of the world and scores of families along the Massachusetts coast abandoned their homes to the early morning tide. At Halifax, N. S., the disabled freighter, City of Delhi, was being tossed helplessly in high seas before a 75-mile gale.

Warm Springs, Ga., Jan. 28. —(AP)—Franklin D. Roosevelt, president-elect and private citizen, tonight made plans to receive Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, and set a time for a conference tomorrow to talk over relations between the two countries. In this unprecedented bridging of the gap between administrations on foreign affairs, President-elect Roosevelt took the initiative with the full co-operation of the outgoing secretary of state, Henry L. (The London Standard statement quoted Mr. Ford as saying “the actual truth is that certain bankers are trying to obtain control of the Ford concern.” A member of Mr. Ford's staff said, however, the motor magnate had told him that was not exactly correct). DUBLIN, Jan. 28. — Victory of the Irish Republicans in the general election for a new Dail was assured on the basis of returns available today, President Eamon De Valera said in a victory message to the public. “The national policy is now definitely determined,” the message said. “May we not appeal, then, to all citizens of goodwill to cooperate in the task of restoring our country to its former greatness and making it a worthy home for all our people? “The dead who died for Ireland will attend us in our efforts. Our exiled people will sustain us with their thoughts and prayers. The whole world will wish us well.

NEW YORK, Jan. 28. — A new storm area, centered off the Virginia Capes, moved northeastward today along a coast not yet recovered from an earlier storm. The New Jersey and Long Island coasts were battered by heavy seas for the third straight day. Unprecedented tides were reported in New England, New Jersey and Long Island. Storm warnings were posted from Atlantic City south to Savannah, Ga. In the Boston area, hundreds were marooned when high tides isolated several districts. Shipping was delayed. The Coast Guard picked up two barges of three which were under tow of the tug, Anamony, missing since Tuesday when they left Hampton Roads, Va. The tug and the third barge, each manned by a crew of three, were still missing. Six men on the two recovered barges were taken ashore safely. The Coast Guard rescued three men and a woman from the sinking barge, Morris R. Shaw, off Cape May. The barge

WASHINGTON, Jan. 27.—(?)—An attempt to place congress once again on record against reduction of the war debts was headed tonight towards a senate committee pigeonhole. It was offered to the senate today, accompanied by loud criticism of yesterday's visit of the British ambassador to the senate floor in violation of the rules. For the third time in a week the senate's two Robinsons clashed verbally over the situation. The ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, it became known soon after, will leave Tuesday for London to familiarize himself with the war debt negotiation intentions of his government, and to report the information concerning the March discussion. Advisors Confer. Preparation for this event went on quietly today at the state department, where Professor Rexford G. Tugwell, an adviser of the president-elect, made a round of visits to department experts and technicians. Professor Raymo

- Madrid —(AP)— Lady Mary Bailey, the British flier who was lost and found last week in her flight from Croydon to Cape Town, was reported lost again today. On Thursday she landed because of engine trouble at San Xavier, on the way back to England. She took off when repairs were made but there has been no word from her since 10 a.m. Friday.

1933-09-15.text: TORONTO, Sept. 15.—Captain James Mollison, British trans-Atlantic flier, arrived here today from Montreal to meet his wife, Amy Mollison, and make final plans for a hop that may take them from some point in Ontario to Europe. Mrs. Mollison is to arrive from New York later in the day. Mollison said the choice of a take-off site rests with his wife who has been flying in the United States and Canada for several weeks.

ISTANBUL, SEPT. 14. (AP).—A heavy loss of life and property was feared as a result of an earthquake today at Hassankale, in Erzerum province, near the Turkish-Soviet border. Details were lacking because all lines of communication were broken, but it was believed the toll of lives and property in nearby villages also was great.

STOCKHOLM. (7) Colonel Lindbergh revealed in his first formal interview granted to Swedish reporters that he and his wife will travel further in Europe before returning to the United States. Good-humoredly answering or evading questions, Colonel Lindbergh said they planned to sail home to avoid winter flying and that plans for the North Atlantic air route which he set out to survey were progressing, although much meteorological study yet was required to ensure safety. The colonel invited newspaper men to a reception at the Royal Automobile Club where he and his wife are staying. Although he dropped his customary reserve, he smilingly stipulated that he should not be quoted. He appeared amused at the report he might buy a home near Copenhagen for use when the air route is established.

Tokyo, Sept. 14.--(4)--A report that he will work to establish a new basis of understanding with the United States was published today as Japan's new foreign minister, Koki Hirota, expressed belief the future is bright for friendly relations with that country's three strongest neighbors. These three nations are the United States, China and Russia. Treaty Asked The newspaper Nichi Nichi said Hirota intends to seek the negotiation of a new treaty with the United States embracing either a pact of non-aggression or of arbitration.

PORTLAND, Me., Sept. 11.—(AP)— Maine, stronghold of prohibition since the middle of the last century, swept into the repeal column tonight to make the 26th in the march of states favoring the overturn of National Prohibition. The vote in 512 out of 632 precincts was: for 91,809; against 45,124. PORTLAND, Me., Sept. 11.—(AP)— Prohibition Maine, with the admittedly wet cities yet to be heard from, rolled steadily toward repeal tonight. More than one-third of the state's precincts showed a majority of nearly two to one for the convention delegates unofficially pledged to vote for approval of the 21st, the repeal amendment. The vote from 326 of the state’s 682 precincts was: For—38,426. Against—20,635. | ‘Washington, Sept. 15 (INS)—President Roosevelt today postponed a scheduled week-end trip on the Potomac in the expectation of receiving a bituminous coal code tonight. Working under a virtual ultimatum from the White House to agree today or receive an imposed code of fair competition, operators, union labor heads, and N.R.A. officials were desperately trying to bring long negotiations to a close. The president was not only represented as being determined to bring the industry under the N.R.A. but he was closely watching the Pennsylvania strike situation, where bloodshed already has resulted. Havana. — (AP) — Additional machine guns were mounted and the soldier guard was increased today at the National hotel, where 500 former army officers have been besieged several days in defiance of the new government of President Ramon Grau San Martin. Later, light artillery pieces were brought up and trained on the hotel. The president denied a report that Col. Horatio Ferrer, who has been acting as spokesman for the officers, would be arrested. Ferrer was the secretary of war in the cabinet of President Carlos Manuel de Cespedes. The guards said they had received instructions not to permit anyone to enter the hotel except “the American ambassador.” (The United States envoy is Sumner Welles).

Havana, Sept. 14—()—President Grau San Martin worked today on a manifesto in which his confidants expected him to demand dictatorial powers for combatting disorders. Opposed by veteran political leaders, plagued by labor troubles, and unable to pacify 500 officers who insist his predecessor be reinstated, the executive was said in palace circles to be ready to cite state reasons for iron hand policies. Police reserves, meanwhile, were held in readiness here. They were armed with rifles, but no reason for the action was announced. At the same time rumors circulated that the army faces dissension in its ranks. Two soldiers died violent deaths in the last 24 hours, one a suicide and the other the victim of unidentified machine gunners. Students Are Wounded Several unidentified persons attacked the ninth police station and gravely wounded a student on duty there. Strikes continued in Antilla

1933-06-06.text: Paris, June 6.—The French cabinet approved today the text of the proposed four power pact to guarantee the peace of Europe, and instructed Ambassador Dejouvenel in Rome to initial the document. The four power pact, proposed by Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy, establishes Great Britain, France, Italy, and Germany as arbitrary guarantors of European peace. It recognizes the principle of armament equality, establishes standardized armies, but specifies that any revision of European frontiers must be accomplished within the covenant of the League of Nations. The cabinet decided that Premier Edouard Daladier would head the French delegation to the world economic conference.

While the exploits of the American Jimmy Mattern stirred the world today, Spanish, British and Italian aviators were completing plans for trans-Atlantic flights. Capt. Mariano Barberan and Lieut. Joaquin Collar announced they will be ready in two or three days for a projected hop from Seville, Spain, to Havana. The famous flying Mollisons, Capt. James A. Mollison and his wife, Amy Johnson, will start from London for New York on Wednesday if the weather is land. From New York they plan to fly to Baghdad and thence to Orbetello, Italy, 100 Italian aviators are tuning up more than a score of planes for a mass flight, by stages, to Chicago, to start in a few days.

(by The Associated Press) S. S. President Roosevelt at Sea, June 6—Stabilization of currencies is described as probably the most vital problem facing the economic conference at London. American delegates and experts are devoting their final days afloat to intense study but American plans for dollar stabilization are closely guarded, pending developments at home and abroad. Currency First It is pointed out, nevertheless, that little progress in whittling away tariff barriers is likely until stabilization of currencies is effected. There is much interest in a suggestion that the world banks' functions be expanded to assist in ending gyrations of exchange rates, possibly through arranging for some European central banks to keep foreign currency reserves with the world banks.

LONDON, June 6 (AP)—Viscount Snowden, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, believes “the weight of argument favors” making the June 15 payment of $75,950,000 interest on war debts Great Britain owes the United States. In a special newspaper article today he pointed out “there is a strong moral case for complete relief from the American debt,” but argued that it is dangerous for any government to repudiate its bonds and more dangerous for Great Britain than any other. “The honor of Great Britain is worth 12,000,000 Pounds,” he wrote, after asserting that British default would more likely force the United States from the world economic conference than drive it to debt revision.

ROME, June 6. — (AP) — Henry De Juvenel, the French ambassador, received instructions Tuesday from Paris to initial the latest text of the Mussolini four-power peace pact, and thus the principal obstacle in the way of execution of the agreement was removed. Simultaneously the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Graham, received similar instructions from London. The Italian government is ready to sign, and the German ambassador, Ulrich Von Hassel, is awaiting authorization from Berlin. The ambassadors forwarded to their governments Monday night the final text of the pact, which was agreed upon after long discussions in the last few days. These discussions centered principally on article three, which refers to disarmament and to the arms.

S. S. President Roosevelt, at Sea, June 5.—(#)—A flat 10 per cent cut in all nations’ tariffs was disclosed officially today by the United States delegation as an idea being strongly pushed for action at the forthcoming world economic conference in London. A spokesman for the American group heading for the British capital on board this ship expressed belief such a reduction would be proposed and achieved at the conclave opening a week from today. If this alone resulted in the tariff field, he said, the conference would not be a failure. It was conceded objections would be raised immediately on grounds the proposal is unscientific, since tariff barriers are of varying height, but it was pointed out reciprocal agreements could be reached subsequently to meet specific circumstances. LONDON — James and Amy Johnson Mollinson again postponed the take-off of their London-New York flight today because of unfavorable weather conditions over the Atlantic. They plan to fly first to New York, then to Aleppo, Arabia, and thence back to London.

1933-09-13.text: LONDON, Sept. 13—A diamond valued at $91,600 was stolen today from the show window of a Hatton Garden diamond shop in a “smash and grab” raid. The street, world famous as a diamond market, was crowded with workers on their way to office. The thief smashed the plate glass window and grabbed the stone. Four men participated in the theft. They escaped by automobile. The stone was called the Polar Star. It weighed 33 3/4 carats and was one of the world’s famous stones. It was the property of Samuel H. Harrig and Sons, leading jewelers and bullion merchants.

LONDON, Sept. 13. (P)—A rare diamond known as the Polar Star and valued at $100,000 was stolen today from a shop in the heart of the diamond trade district in the most amazing of a series of recent daylight "smash and grab" raids. Shortly after a window had been decorated at the store of Samuels, Harris & Son in Hatton Garden, a young man broke the glass, twisted the protecting grill with a piece of iron, snatched the diamond, and sped away in an automobile. The robber was believed by authorities to be a connoisseur because he made no attempt to take other valuable jewelry. The stone was unmounted and of 32.7 carats. Shortly after the robbery, employees of the house said that the stolen diamond was the "polar star" but a member of the firm later corrected this, asserting that the "polar star," a stone of forty carats, had been sold some time ago. TOKIO, Sept. 13.—Navy Minister Mineo Osumi told the United Press in an exclusive interview today that Japan will demand a naval ratio for nearly approximating that of Great Britain and the United States at the next international naval conference. International observers saw in his flat statement a possibility of unlimited naval competition after the London naval treaty expires in 1935 unless Japan’s demand is met in a new treaty. Osumi left no doubt of Japan’s dissatisfaction with existing treaties that limit the Nipponese navy to three vessels of war to every five for the United States and five for Great Britain. The minister did not say what ratio Japan will demand. Unofficial reports here were that the Japanese will ask 7.3 ships for each 10 owned by the other two great powers, rather than absolute equality. Now Building. PARIS, Sept. 13. — General John J. Pershing observed his 75th birthday today quietly. He read telegrams of congratulation and hoped to find time to write his daily stint of the second war book on which he is working. Work in connection with the battle monuments, which has brought him to France regularly since the World War, has now been virtually completed, leaving the one-time commander of the A.E.F. more leisure.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Sept. 15 (AP)—Increased admiration for Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh was expressed by Swedish aviators today after he had tested a Swedish army plane in a variety of ways, including loops and spins. The machine was one over which aviation circles have divergent opinions.

By the Associated Press GENEVA, Sept. 12—The world awaits anxiously the results of the great economic experiment now being carried on in the United States, seeking lessons which may be profitable, Joseph Avenol, new secretary-general of the League of Nations, said tonight. It was M. Avenol’s first interview since assuming office. The secretary-general, one of the leading international financial and economic authorities and the secretary of the world economic conference, said the transformation in the American economic system affects the interests of the entire world. “At the world economic conference,” he added, “the United States was able to measure the international repercussions of its policies.” Indications are increasing, M. Avenol continued, that at the international disarmament conference supreme efforts will be made to negotiate some kind of treaty. “To this conference,” he said,

LISBON, Portugal, Sept. 12. (AP)—Ten bulls broke loose today in the nearby village of Sobral and charged into the crowd at the annual summer festival, injuring 20 persons, three of them probably fatally. The bulls smashed articles in china shops, fancy stalls and cafes, and wrecked the bandstand. A barber killed one bull with a razor and the others were rounded up.

The approval of only seven more states was needed Wednesday to remove the 18th amendment from the constitution. Substantial returns from Colorado, Minnesota and Maryland which voted Tuesday indicated good majorities for repeal. They were the 27th, 28th, and 29th states to join the unbroken wet parade. With more than three-fourths of the state’s precincts counted, repeal led in Colorado by more than two to one. With more than half of the precincts counted in Minnesota, the repealists were maintaining the same lead. Hugenberg introduced the politically explosive subject of the former German colonies during his presentation of Germany's opinion on the cause of and remedy for the world depression. BOSTON, June 17 — Boston paused today in its celebration of Bunker Hill Day to give a tumultuous welcome to President Roosevelt on his first trip to New England since his inauguration. Not more than 1,000 spectators were at South Station when the President’s train arrived at 7:32 a. m. (EST), but by the time he detrained, two hours later, the crowd had swelled to at least 19,000. A tremendous chorus of cheers greeted Mr. Roosevelt as, smiling and waving his panama hat, he left his private car and boarded the automobile in which he was to go to Groton to visit his sons, Franklin, Jr., and John, students at Groton school. After that the President was to motor to Marion, on Buzzard's Bay, board the 45-foot schooner yacht Amberjack II, and start a leisurely cruise up the New England coast to his summer home on Campobello Island.

1933-12-09.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 12.—(UP)—The government today held the price for newly mined American gold at $34.01, the price in effect since Dec. 1. Today's Washington price was $1.76 above the world price set in London today. The London price today was 126 shillings 4 1-2 pence, down 7 1-2 pence from yesterday. On the basis of the London opening for the pound sterling (85.10 1-2) this was equivalent to $32.25 a fine ounce. The dollar remained at 60.70 cents.

McCormick of Chicago. The Duc de la Tremoille, of Pree, burned to death. The Hon. James H. R. Rodney, brother of the Eighth Baron Rodney, died of injuries received when he jumped twenty feet from a window to escape the roaring flames. Rodney’s wife, the former Frances Strickland Oldham Lovell, of Poi, was injured critically when she jumped with him. She suffered injuries to her back. McCormick and his wife, who was the French Countess de Fleurieu, escaped in night dress. The Rodneys and the Duc de Tremoille were week-end guests of the McCormicks. Filing of the suit confirmed reports of a permanent separation and set at rest numerous rumors of a reconciliation. Whitchurch, Hampshire, England Dec. 9 —(AP)— Two house guests of Mr. and Mrs. L. J. McCormick, of the prominent Chicago family, were killed by a fire which destroyed the McCormick country home early today. The dead are the Duke De La Tremoille, French Cavalry officer, and Capt. J. H. B. Rodney of London, the husband of the former Frances Strickland Lovell, daughter of R. P. Oldham of Seattle, Washington. Mrs. Rodney was injured by a 20-foot jump to escape the flames. At the Royal Hampshire hospital, Winchester, to which both she and her husband were taken, and where the Captain died, it was stated she was in a very serious condition. | WHITCHURCH, Hampshire. England. Dec. 9—A sudden fire roared through the country home of Mr. and Mrs. Leander J. Emer, prominent Chicagoans, early Saturday, casting tragedy over a week-end house party by causing the death of a duke of France and a British army captain, and left the mansion virtually in ruins. The victims were the Duke De La Tremouille, a French cavalry officer and premier duke of France, and Capt. H. B. Rodney of London, brother of a British peer. Mrs. Rodney, the former Frances Strickland Lovell, daughter of Representative Oldham of Seattle, Wash., was gravely injured in a 20-foot jump to escape the blaze. At the Royal Hampshire hospital in Winchester, where she and her husband were taken, and where the captain died, an operation was performed upon her for serious spinal injuries. Hospital authorities said later her condition was critical.

New York, Nov. 16, (Pl)—The United States dollar weakened further in foreign exchange trading today, dropping below 59 cents in relation to the French franc. The franc opened at 6.65 cents, up 3 points from yesterday's close and a new high for the present currency. The British pound sterling jumped to $5.47, another new peak since 1914, an increase of 8 cents overnight.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 9.—(P)—The administration's offer for all gold newly mined in the United States was $34.01 an ounce today for the eighth successive time. It represented continuation of the same price level two days longer than any previous figure has been maintained. London’s price for bar gold was $32.61 on the basis of sterling’s both opening and closing at $5.15¼ to the pound. As the same RFC quotation was repeated, the treasury estimated that money in circulation in the United States November 30 was $5,740,774,218 as compared with $5,634,603,143 a month ago and $5,647,586,816 a year ago. On the basis of an estimated population of 126,056,000, the November circulation averaged $45.54 per capita as compared with $44.73 in October and $45.11 in November a year ago.

1933-11-18.text: Geneva, Nov. 18—(AP)—The possibility of a rift between France and Great Britain on the question of disarmament developed today. Apparently apprehensive that the return of Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, would involve withdrawal of Great Britain from the accords concerning Germany reached at Paris and Geneva, Joseph Paul-Boncour, French foreign minister, convoked a press conference to announce that France's position remains unaltered. “The departure of the Germans from the disarmament conference changes nothing in France's position,” declared Paul-Boncour. “We want to proceed making a disarmament convention but on the basis of accords previously reached. “However, we are ready to talk.”

The verdict carries mandatory death sentence. The case went to the jury about 4 p. m., Friday.

Simultaneously Finance Minister Georges Bonnet warned that a double drain of gold and treasury funds is sapping French finances which may hold out, he said, until January 1 ‘but “inflation with a consequent devalorization” will follow unless the budget—the bugaboo of three ministries—is speedily equalized. (United Press Staff Correspondent) Moscow, Nov. 17—A holiday atmosphere pervaded Moscow tonight when word swept through the Soviet Russian capital that United States recognition official had been accorded. President Roosevelt's pronouncement ending 16 years of broken relations between two of the world’s greatest powers was cheered by Russians and foreigners alike in cafes and hotels in the nation’s capital. Reports that recognition was expected late today spread swiftly through the nation hours before the word came through from Washington that it actually had happened. The people remained hopeful but tense. A last minute slip-up was feared. Recognition by America—the industrial ideal of the new Russia—had been awaited so long, that any premature celebration it was felt might spoil it. VIENNA, Nov. 18 (AP).—Rudolph Dertil, who shot and wounded Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, Oct. 3 was found guilty today and sentenced to five years in jail. Dertil’s conviction followed a brief minute appearance by Chancellor Dollfuss himself, now recovered from the two small calibre bullet wounds he received from the pearl-handled revolver of the former army bugler. Dollfuss merely testified that Dertil ambushed him in the parliamentary building.

United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, Aug. 26—U.R)—A world agreement to limit wheat exports, signed and awaiting ratification of parliaments of some subscribing countries, was hailed today as the first world wide recovery act, calculated to lead the way to general economic recovery. The agreement, child of the abortive world economic conference at London, is designed to insure fair prices to farmers for their wheat, and, through a two year agreement to limit exports, eliminate the present world surplus of 440,000,000 bushels. It binds the exporting nations—the United States, Canada, Australia, Argentina and Russia, along with the smaller Danubian nations—to export not more than a total of 560,000,000 bushels in the 1933-1934 crop year. The pact was formally signed at a special meeting tonight by representatives of 23 of the 31 nations which participated in the conference session. Those nations which abstained were Estonia, Latvia, Holland, Finland, Denmark, Turkey, Portugal and Lithuania. LONDON, Aug. 26.—A rumor that King Carol of Roumania intended to marry Mrs. Magda Lupescu, his former mistress, early in 1934, was relayed today by the Daily Express Vienna Correspondent. Mrs. Lupescu, a Jewess, intended to join the Greek Orthodox Church, the report said, and would be adopted by some Roumanian prince so that she would have a social position fitting the consort of a sovereign.

- NEW YORK: (UP) — Inflation activity, purchase of government securities by the federal reserve board and an agreement on the wheat recovery price at the London conference started a new bull movement in stocks and commodities today. Stocks gained one to more than six points with better volume. The grain were strong. The dollar was at 70 cents in terms of gold currencies.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 26 (UP).—A formal announcement today by Secretary of Agriculture Wallace was expected to speed an international wheat acreage reduction program to return prosperity to grain farmers on the four corners of the earth. Wallace, credited with bringing agreement at the London wheat conference through threats of dumping United States surpluses, intends to ask United States wheat farmers to reduce their crops by 15 per cent, the reduction which will go into effect throughout the world. The history-making undertaking the government hopes, will go far to reduce the 64,000,000 bushel world surplus of wheat. For their part in the program, farmers in this country will receive about $125,000,000 in government bonuses. The money will come from a processing tax of 30 cents a bushel on domestic wheat.

1933-01-14.text: Geneva, Jan. 13.---() —- Debate on establishment of a 40-hour working week without reduction of wages continued today at the International Labor conference. Arthur Hayday, representing British workers, declared employers must share in the sacrifice necessitated by the present crisis and accept a reduction in hours without a cut in pay. He expressed regret that the United States is not participating officially in the meeting. Need U.S. "America’s attitude and opinions are of tremendous importance to the world," he said, "A brave man cannot beat a squaw on the banks of the Mississippi without the whole world feeling the effects."

LOS ANGELES, Jan. 13 (7)--Victor McLaglen, the man of hard boiled demeanor on the screen, today with 150 other aliens took the oath of American citizenship in the federal court here, The actor renounced allegiance to King George V of England, and said “that while he fought four years for England in the World War, he was glad to be an American now.”

Tokyo, Jan. 14.—()—Sir Francis Lindley, ambassador from Great Britain, informed the Japanese government Friday that British interests in north China are threatened by the tense situation growing out of the Japanese occupation of Shanhaikwan. Yen, chief Chinese delegate at the League of Nations, notified that body today that reports that the Nanking government had appointed someone to negotiate with Japanese authorities regarding Shanhaikwan hostilities were false. TOKYO, Jan. 14—(?)—President Hoover's reference to the grave dangers of a foreign invasion if the Philippines were freed was described by a foreign office spokesman today as “nonsensical” if he meant such a menace came from Japan. The spokesman added such intimations disclosed a total misunderstanding of Japan’s fundamental policies in Eastern Asia.

Shanghai, Jan. 14. ()—Lieut. Christy Mathewson Jr., son of the famous baseball player, continued to improve today in his recovery from injuries received in an airplane accident last Sunday, but physicians said he faced three months' detention in the hospital. Attendants said his suffering was “intense” at present. Young Mathewson’s bride of only two weeks, the former Margaret Phillips, was killed in the accident in which she started on her first flight with her husband, an instructor in a Chinese aviation school.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 21 (#).— The American Railway Association announced today that loading of revenue freight for the week ending January 14 were 506,322, an increase of 70,670 over the preceding week but 66,327 below the same week of 1932 and 218,890 under 1931. Miscellaneous freight loaded during the week of January 14 totaled 159,855, an increase of 19,375 over the preceding week but 28,225 under 1932; coal 117,334, increase 14,268 over the preceding week but 1,767 under last year.

1933-12-16.text: LICHFIELD, England, Dec. 16—(U.P)—Douglas Blood, 5, was burned to death today when he tried to send a letter to Santa Claus by pushing it up the chimney of an open fireplace. Knowing that Santa always came down the chimney, the child tried to “mail” the letter by sending it along this Kris Kringle route. The flames ignited the letter, which blew back in the draught and set fire to his shirt. He died before the three other children with whom he was playing, or his mother could subdue the flames.

Washington, Dec. 13.—The government today again offered a price of $34.01 an ounce for newly mined domestic gold. London's price for bar gold was $32 an ounce on the basis of sterling opening at $5.075-8 to the pound. The dollar later strengthened to range around $5.04 to the pound.
By The Associated Press LONDON, Dec. 16.—Sir Henry Dickens, the sixth son of the novelist Charles Dickens, was seriously injured today when struck by a motorcycle. He was 85.

LONDON, Dec. 16.—Postmaster General James A. Farley charged today that British newspapers were giving a “grotesque” impression of President Roosevelt's activities. Objecting, at an American Embassy Press Conference, to European criticisms of the President, Farley said: “European newspapers convey a grotesque impression of the United States going to pot under President Roosevelt, whereas real improvement has been achieved.”

Halifax, N. F.--(AP)--Seventeen seamen of the American fishing schooner Ellen T. Marshall were rescued today, two were known drowned and seven were missing after the schooner burned near Seal Island, eighteen miles west of Cape Sable, N. S. A ship rescued eight of the survivors from their lifeboats, eight more made Pease’s Island safety, and one got ashore on Seal Island. The schooner was abandoned by her crew of twenty-six at 7 o'clock last night when she burned to the water's edge. The crew escaped the flames in eight dories. One of the dories was reported at Seal Island to have reached the surf, only to overturn. One of the occupants reached shore and the succor of Seal Island fishermen. The other two drowned. (By The Associated Press) TOKYO, DEC. 16—HIROSHI SAITO, THE YOUNGEST MAN EVER PICKED FOR THE POST, WAS SELECTED TODAY AS THE NEW AMBASSADOR TO WASHINGTON, SAITO, NOW JAPANESE MINISTER TO THE NETHERLANDS, WILL SUCCEED KATSUJI DEBUCHI, WHO RESIGNED AND RETURNED TO TOKYO THIS WEEK. SAITO WILL BE FORTY-SEVEN YEARS OLD THIS MONTH.

ALMENS, Dec. 15.—Broken despite the Greek government's concession that he will not be expelled before January 31, Samuel Insull took to his bed tonight because of ill health. If physicians say he is too ill to travel there is a possibility the former Chicago utilities operator may be able to remain in Greece longer than the end of January—a month after the expiration of his police residence permit. As the 74-year-old man, who twice has beaten attempts to return him to America to face charges in connection with the collapse of the light and power interests, dejectedly discussed the latest developments in his case today, it appeared that his health might not continue to withstand another strain.

Paris, Dec. 14—(P)—The French Cabinet was expected in political circles today to state a firm united front with Poland and the Little Entente against Premier Mussolini's attempt to reorganize the League of Nations and against Chancellor Hitler's demand for German equality in armaments. A session was arranged after a conference between Dr. Eduard Benes, Czechoslovakian foreign secretary, with foreign minister Joseph Paul-Boncour and other leaders here. Cognizance also was taken in planning the meeting of a communication received from Warsaw today which made it clear that France and her allies are united in policy. 1933-09-10.text: (By The Associated Press) Gandau, Germany, Sept. 9— Capt. Paul Koenig, commander of the German super-submarine, Deutschland, which made two crossings of the Atlantic in 1916, one to Baltimore and the other to New London, Connecticut, died today at the age of 66.

Paris, Sept. 4 (4)—Information received in French diplomatic circles from London today said Great Britain expects to base further war debts discussions with the American administration on a suggestion to pay 10 per cent of the amount owed. It was learned authoritatively that France wants to negotiate on the same basis, which corresponds to the reduction in reparations from Germany as agreed upon at Lausanne last year. France formally defaulted last June 15 in the $40,000,000 debts installment due then. It was understood the administration hoped an arrangement might be completed permitting the government to pay the $19,000,000 due last December. At that time a note was said to indicate a desire for a 80 per cent discount in the French debt, (At the same time Great Britain made known that it would pay $10,000,000 in silver, at 50 cents an ounce, on the $75,950,000 owed. WASHINGTON, Sept. 9—The navy department plans to send the dirigible Macon into New England and probably into Canada to aid in the search for four missing men in two of the James Gordon Bennett race balloons as soon as the weather in those sections clears up. At the department, officers said that it would be useless to send the Macon to join the search instituted by Canadians until the weather cleared so that the dirigible’s officers could obtain good visibility. The navy has no planes near the regions over which the American balloon, piloted by Ward T. Van Orman and carrying Frank T. Trotter, and the Polish entry carrying Captain Francizek Hynek and Lieut. Znigniew Burzynski, were believed to have drifted. An officer, authorized to speak for the navy, said orders to the Macon would be sent as soon as reports of weather conditions indicated that flights should be worthwhile. CHICAGO, Sept

Sudbury, Ont.,—(AP)—Ward T. Van Orman and Frank A. Trotter, American balloonists who participated in the James Gordon Bennett cup race from Chicago and who had been missing more than a week, were found today between Sudbury and Abitibi Canyon in northern Ontario. They were ill from the hardships they had undergone in the bush country. In order that the outside world might learn of their plight the two balloonists cut down a telephone pole, knowing that repairmen would be sent out to fix the damage. They attached to the pole the following note: “This telephone pole was cut Sept. 10, by U. S. Goodyear balloon team of W. T. Van Orman and Frank Trotter in the hope that repairmen would aid us in getting to civilization from here. We will continue south along the high voltage line. Please come after us. We have a gun and some food, but are both sick evident from ptomaine poisoning. Fir

St. Paul, Minn., Sept. 11—(AP)—Two small safes containing $100,000 in currency and securities were seized by eight gunmen who held up employees of the railway express agency today. The robbers, who executed their daring theft beneath the concourse of the union station, escaped. The holdup occurred a few feet from the train that was waiting, with steam up, to take the shipment of valuables to Minneapolis. Well Laid Plot The eight bandits sprang from the dim light under the station as the truck containing the shipment drew to a stop. Three of them brandished sawed-off shotguns. Two were armed with automatic pistols. In the truck were T. J. Mangan, St. Paul, a guard, and B. Motes, Minneapolis, the messenger. Both were ordered out of the truck. Mangan coolly surveyed the men and a large dark sedan, until the leader of the gang ordered him and Motes to face a wall. Takes But Few Seconds Two b

WASHINGTON, Sept. 11.—(4 --President Roosevelt let it be known today that his attitude toward the new Cuban government headed by Dr. Ramon Grau San Martin depends on whether it has the support of the people there. While keeping the strong navy forces rimmed about the island in readiness to protect American lives in event of outbreaks there, it was said at the White House that the President is ready to support that government in Cuba which is the choice of the people and can maintain order. So the present attitude remains one of watchfulness, If the new president and his forces are able to keep order, it appears that the Roosevelt administration will not hesitate to proffer recognition. There is no certainty that this test has been met yet, however.

By the Associated Press Maine, dry for more than 75 years, drew the attention of the whole nation today as she balloted on the proposal to wipe prohibition from the national constitution. Twenty-five other states had voted previously and all approved repeal. Tomorrow Colorado, Minnesota and Maryland will have their turn at the ballot boxes. Thirty-six states must signify their approval before the 21st amendment, which would nullify the 18th, can become part of the constitution. At least 39 will have held their elections by Nov. 7.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 9 (P)—The American Railway Association today reported carloadings for the week ending Sept. 2, totaled 666,952 cars, the highest for any week this year, and an increase of 34,654 over the preceding week. The total also was a gain of 105,327 cars above the corresponding week last year. All commodities showed increases over the preceding week except livestock and forest products.

Washington — (®) — President Roosevelt and O. M. W. Sprague, financial advisor to the Bank of England, were brought together today by Secretary Woodin in a conference to which significance was attached immediately in view of international efforts underway toward currency stabilization. While there is hope of bringing this about as early as possible, some doubt was expressed in official quarters that this might be attained before convening of the world economic conference on June 13. Nevertheless a concerted effort is in progress to achieve this stabilization at the earliest date. It appeared that Mr. Sprague was considering this problem with the administration, although his visit to the White House was described merely as one to pay respects.

Geneva, May 20—The long awaited definition of how far America will go in a consultative pact to guarantee the peace of Europe will be delivered to the general commission of the disarmament conference Monday, the United Press learned authoritatively today. United States Ambassador Norman H. Davis received an eight page cable from the state department in Washington setting forth in detail the type of treaty the United States would be willing to sign. American willingness to enter such a pact, however, is predicated entirely upon thorough disarmament by the European powers. Davis, it was understood, will urge the Europeans Monday to reduce their military establishments, stressing the necessity for rigid international control of armaments after a non-aggression, consultative treaty is signed. The statement of definition will be issued simultaneously in Washington and Geneva when Davis begins

Moscow, May 21 A definite bid for the establishment of normal relations between Soviet Russia and the United States was sounded editorially today in the publication, “For Industrialization,” the organ of the commissariat of heavy industry. The editorial at the same time laid down the principle that formal diplomatic recognition is the price the United States must pay before it can hope for any improvement in economic intercourse between the two countries. Deliberately holding out bait for such a catch by hinting broadly of profitable business to be enjoyed by America once a normal relationship is established, the article declares that “the time has come when the question of the relations toward the Soviet Union has become the acid test of the wisdom of American political and business circles.” Referring to speculations abroad as to whether President Roosevelt's di- “We are not interested

GENEVA, May 20 (#)—Bolivia today rejected recommendations by the council of the League of Nations for the settlement of the dispute with Paraguay over the Chaco territory. The Bolivian delegate declared that Paraguay had violated the covenant of the league by its recent declaration that a state of war existed and asked the council to apply the penalties provided in Article 16 of the covenant against Paraguay. (Article 16 provides for financial and economic sanctions as well as possible military sanctions by members of the league against a nation declaring war in violation of the covenant.)

This reply placed beyond all doubt the fact that the four "Class B," 10,000-ton 6-inch gun cruisers in the program will be completed. The British were understood to have accepted the reply as final and to have dropped the matter of deferring construction of this class pending a new naval conference. British and American representatives at the Geneva Naval Conference now are concentrating on the more dynamic issue of Germany's demand for rearmament. MANSFIELD, Sept. 26—Search for Victor Palmer, 20, of Cincinnati, last of five prisoners who made a daring escape from Mansfield Reformatory yesterday, was to be broadened today to cities throughout the state. Palmer last night eluded a heavily armed posse of guards, police, and captain sheriffs in a wooded area. The latter, all sentenced from Cincinnati, were Charles Foote, 19, serving a term for robbery; James Roa, 18, automobile theft; Eugene Monn, 18, robbery; and Steve Mommich, 20, burglary. The youths escaped shortly after the dinner hour by sawing through an iron bar in a ventilator shaft in an old power house. Mommich and Foote were captured within 15 minutes after their escape. The other two were captured about three hours later, hiding out in the woods. None offered resistance. According to Supt. T. C. Jenkins, the five fashioned a key to gain entrance to an engine room at the i

ROME, Sept. 26 (UP). — Reports seeping in from mountain towns showed 12 known dead and 60 injured in an earthquake that struck Italy and portions of Jugoslavia today. It was feared the casualties would prove more numerous, because small towns where communication is most difficult were the worst sufferers. Panic prevailed all through the night in a great section of central Italy bounded by Rome, Ancona and Pescara in which almost the entire population camped outdoors to avoid danger from crumbling buildings. From Jugoslavia came reports that many persons were feared drowned between Ljubljana (Laibach) and Kranj, in the northwestern corner of the kingdom.

Lyons, France—The condition of former Premier Edouard Herriot, ill of a kidney infection, grew worse today. His temperature rose to 101 and his kidneys were not functioning. Herriot was ordered to take a long rest, and it was indicated that he would be unable to resume his chairmanship of the important chamber of deputies foreign affairs committee at the assembly of parliament in mid-October.

Geneva, Sept. 25, (AP)--Fifteen years after “that fratricidal crime, the great war,” the world still confronts the menace of war, Premier Johan Mowinckel, of Norway, declared today when, as president of the council, he opened the sessions of the League of Nations assembly. His solemn warning spurred activity among the world statesmen gathered here to advance the cause of peace. Of first importance were efforts to bridge the chasm between France and the new Germany of Chancellor Adolf Hitler. Norman H. Davis, United States disarmament negotiator, had dinner tonight with Baron Konstantin von Neurath, the German foreign minister. Mr. Davis continued the work of Franco-German mediation already started by Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary. Dr. Mowinckel’s warning of the menace of war, coupled with the negotiations to achieve concrete results in disarmament by composing the differe

MOSCOW, Sept. 25—Applauded by thousands of watchers lining the waterfront and bridges of the narrow Moscow river, Colonel Charles Lindbergh brought his transatlantic hydroplane to a perfect landing on the dangerously limited surface today after an overland flight from Leningrad. With Mrs. Lindbergh he received greetings of civil aviation officials, attended a banquet in their honor, and then went to the opera. Two Soviet planes escorted Lindbergh as he approached the city. The American couple was welcomed by high officials, civil aircraft representatives, and members of the domestic and foreign press. The spectators paid tribute in spontaneous applause. Lindbergh waved his hand in response. A banquet was tendered them by aviation authorities and the Soviet tourist agency, which is arranging their tour of Russia. The Lindberghs were expected to remain in Moscow for several days.

VIENNA, 4.P)—Austria’s political crisis was intensified today with Archduke Otto a candidate for the robe from which he has made an open bid for power in accepting honorary citizenship of three towns, offered to him by letter to his refuge in Belgium. Son of the late Emperor Charles of Austria-Hungary, who died in 1922, Otto, now approaching his 21st birthday, has been reared by his ambitious mother, Empress Zita, to be emperor of Austria and king of Hungary. With the blessing of the Roman Catholic Church and the approval of the Austrian government, the “emperor king” made an open bid for the restoration of the Hapsburg dynasty with himself as ruler. Aligning himself with Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss against the Austrian Nazis, Otto declared Nazism to be un-Austrian, treasonable and criminal.

MOSCOW, Sept. 26—All German newspaper correspondents today were ordered to leave Soviet Russia within three days because of the recent arrest of Russian newspaper men at the Leipzig Reichstag trial and other incidents. All Russian newspaper men will be recalled from Germany, it was announced. The four Germans affected by the order here represent the Wolff Agency, the Kölnische Zeitung and the Tageblatt and Lokalanzeiger of Berlin. (Attending the trial of five men, alleged communists, before the supreme court at Leipzig in the Reichstag incendiary trial, several Russian newspaper men were detained by police. They were released subsequently.)

1933-11-21.text: TOKYO. (Tuesday). UP. Former Premier Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki, foremost Japanese defender of the London naval treaty, escaped injury when two youthful ‘patriots’ assaulted him with a dagger. Armed with knives, the assailants forced their way through a large crowd in front of the Ueno railway station in the northern part of the city and had almost reached Wakatsuki when police intercepted them. They seized one, but the other escaped. The arrested man was identified as Susumu Noguchi, a well-known boxer, long contender for the Japanese welterweight championship. Baron Wakatsuki had just returned to Tokyo from a speech-making tour in northwestern Japan. He was crossing the station plaza and about to enter his motor car when the attack was attempted. Although he had not mentioned the London naval treaty in his recent speeches, he has been the target of denunciations by reactionary elements in

TOKYO (#) — The “patriotic” assassination campaign against proponents of the London naval treaty of which Premier Yuko Hamaguchi was the first victim in 1931, struck again today—this time unsuccessfully. The target was the 67-year-old former premier, Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki, who was chief of the Japanese delegation at the London parley in 1930. The instrument of intended attack was a ranking Japanese welterweight, Susumu Noguchi, armed with a dagger instead of his fists. With a companion identified by police as Karulo Matsui, a former soldier, Noguchi had almost reached the Baron when police intercepted them.

London, Nov. 20 (?)—Prof. J. H. Jones, University of Leeds economist, told the American Chamber of Commerce today that the danger to Europe of President Roosevelt's depreciated dollar policy was so great as to justify cooperative action by continental gold standard countries and subsequent cooperation with the sterling group. Jones said that “Roosevelt’s difficulties are only beginning,” and declared he personally had a real fear that France and other gold standard countries would be driven off gold by American gold buying. This buying he said was dangerous not on account of the loss of gold on account of the flight of European currencies to sterling. The economist said “jointly the European countries may be able to withstand the American onslaught, but individually they may not.”

LONDON, Eng., Nov. 21 — For the first time in his memory, King George V of England was subjected to the attack of a heckler today as he concluded his address opening the winter session of the British parliament. As Peers stood with eyes lowered, John McGovern, socialist member of the parliament who has frequently been expelled from the house for violent attacks on his colleagues, shouted: "What about measures for the abolition of the means test and unemployment test?" For a moment the group was shocked into silence. Then, as other members of the house standing near attempted to quiet him, he broke into another wild harangue directing his attack upon the nobles who had turned out in a gorgeous array to hear the king speak.

LINDBERGH, Horta, Azores, Nov. 21 (AP).—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh flying their big sea-monoplane covered more than 900 miles from Lisbon today to land safely here today. The flight from Lisbon had occupied just five minutes less than nine hours, putting their flying speed something over 100 miles an hour. Previously they were sighted at Saint Michael's in the Azores group.

GENEVA, Nov. 20, (7) -- Leaders who have sought for weeks to find some basis for agreement on disarmament virtually decided today to suspend their efforts for two months. An official announcement of the recess was expected to be made at a meeting tomorrow. Whether a program of work to be conducted in the interim will be announced was problematical.

Geneva. Nov. 21 (AP)—A clash between French and Italian representatives marked a meeting of disarmament leaders today at which suspension of the arms parley until January was decided on. The Italians argued for complete cessation of the conference’s subcommittees during the suspension of efforts to reach an agreement on disarmament. Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour of France insisted that the committee meet as usual. As usual, the American representatives abstained from participation in the discussion which ensued up until the time a recess later in the day was called. The meeting was held in the midst of discussions in authoritative quarters of a new world disarmament conference aimed to reorganize the League of Nations, revise peace treaties, and deal with the disarmament crisis and the great political problems troubling the world. 1933-11-20.text: Chesterfield, Eng., Nov. 19.—(A4) Fourteen men were killed in an explosion in a coal mine near here today. Seventeen others scrambled to safety when the blast trapped their companions 1,000 feet underground. Four of them were slightly injured, After three hours of feverish digging, a hastily assembled rescue squad found the 14 entombed miners dead from firedamp. Rescuers said the roof of the mine had crashed behind the men as they stood at the coal face, completely cutting off escape. Prince George motored from Chatsworth this afternoon to offer in person the sympathy of his father, King George.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 19.—Having broken by his heroism the mob spirit of 32 Chinese sailors who threatened his life in a mutinous uprising as the ship was about to leave for the Dutch West Indies, Capt. B. G. Protheroe, of the British oil tanker Calm, today went about the prosaic work of signing up a new crew. The mutiny, brewing in the forecastle while the ship plowed toward Los Angeles harbor from South America, burst last night in a wild melee on the steel decks of the vessel. Dodges Meat Cleaver As Captain Protheroe stepped from his cabin, a Chinese fireman, Geong Boo, slashed at him with a meat cleaver. Ducking and backing away from each charge, the captain reached his cabin, seized his revolver and forced the enraged Chinese to surrender his weapon. Rome, Nov. 20—(AP)—Belief that Italy would withdraw from the League of Nations unless France consents to a four-power disarmament conference in Rome was expressed in well-informed circles today. The possibility became the subject of unofficial discussion after it became known that the fascist grand council will be convoked December 5 to discuss the continuance of Italy’s membership in the League. Such a development was strongly suggested yesterday as the rumble of opposition to the League deepened with three newspapers hinting at the possibility of Italy’s withdrawal. One was Premier Mussolini’s Popolo D’Italia. The others were the Corriere Della Sera of Milan and the Gazetta Del Popolo of Turin.

MOSCOW, Nov. 18.—(AP)—All Soviet Russia, from a chubby red-cheeked girl tending a tramcar switch in one of Moscow's downtown squares to high government officials, hailed news of American recognition today in a burst of popular enthusiasm. Morning newspapers gave the most prominent display to texts of the exchanges between President Roosevelt and Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinoff at Washington. Five and six columns on page one were devoted to a presentation of the official communique from the American capital. And there were large pictures of both the president and Litvinoff. Comment Is Lacking Comment however was lacking, as the newspapers had only time to hurry the big news into print after it was received from the United States late Friday night. Most of the newspapers used the same headline—‘Establishment of normal relations between the Soviet government and the U.S.A.’ But if there w

Madrid, Spain, Nov. 20.—(2)—With seven already known dead and 300 injured, further outbreaks were feared today as a result of Spain’s first constitutional election. Incomplete returns from yesterday's balloting indicated a sweeping rightist triumph. Far fewer disorders than had been anticipated developed, but extreme vigilance was continued because of fears that there might be some dissension on the part of troops headed by leftist officers. Troops in Madrid, Barcelona and Seville were ordered held in readiness for any emergency, it was learned on reliable authority. In the first national election in which women ever had participated, approximately 12,500,000 voters were qualified to ballot to select 473 deputies for the first regular congress of the second republic. It will convene Dec. 8. The first congress merely drew up a constitution.

BERLIN. 7. In the throes of the most bitter religious struggle since the Reformation, Germany witnessed a significant celebration of Martin Luther's birth 450 years ago. The celebration, in honor of the founder of Protestantism, was under the auspices of the new Hitlerite regime and the services took on a marked political character. The political aspect and the magnitude of the ceremonies, however, were eclipsed by the startling and unprecedented step made by the Roman Catholic Church in announcing virtual solidarity with non-Nazi Protestant pastors against the radical factions of the Nazi Christian Church. The fabric of the church itself was torn asunder last week by a demand of Dr. Reinhold Krause that the Old Testament be discarded and that a militant and heroic Jesus be substituted for the traditional meek and gentle Christ. The Corriere Della Sera of Milan and the Gazetta De Popolo of Turin said editorially that the Fascist grand council would be convoked December 5 to "examine Italy’s relations with the league in view of the departure of Japan and Germany and the fact that the United States and are not members." The grand council is the highest constituted body in the kingdom, Mussolini’s Popolo did not mention the League of Nations by name, but said the grand council would discuss Il Duce’s recent references to the international situation in his speech before the national council of corporations, in which he said the league had lost its effectiveness and "its very principle is absurd." 1933-12-28.text: A wave of bitter cold, accompanied by raging winds that brought deaths on the Great Lakes and blizzards in New England states, swept across the United States last night on the course of snow storms that piled high drifts in a dozen states. Accidents caused by the storms were estimated at several score, including eight fishermen lost on Lake Michigan and others missing. The majority of the deaths were from automobile accidents. Temperatures plunged far below zero in the Midwest. Chicago had a 16-degree drop in five hours, with 10 below predicted. The city reported 63 inches of snow. New York had 10.3 inches of snow in seven hours that tied up shipping for hours, kept airplanes at home, delayed trains and buses. A terrific windstorm sunk the 100-foot fishing smack, “Martha,” near the harbor at Michigan City, Ind., and carried four fishermen to their deaths. Four men were drowned when the t

- WASHINGTON, Dec. 26.—The government held its domestic gold buying price unchanged at $34.06 an ounce today with a resumption of business after the Christmas holiday. There was no price established in London for gold today, because of the holidays. The dollar remained at 60.69.

The northern states were numbed by a bitter blast out of the Arctic Wednesday. From Montana to New England and down to the Mason and Dixon line the raw zero weather stretched, with the eastern states shrinking under a deep coverlet of snow while the bleak western prairies of Canada calked windows against a 30 below zero wind. By a vagary of nature, mile high Denver shed its overcoats in a sudden advent of springlike weather. There the temperature rose to 52, and unseasonable warmth spread over Colorado, Wyoming and New Mexico while their neighbors north and east were frigid. Over New England and the North Atlantic seaboard a biting gale whistled, pounding shipping. The Portland, Me., fishing boat Bluenose was missing with two men aboard. It was this same storm that sent eight Lake Michigan sailors to death off the Michigan and Indiana shores Tuesday. Eight foot snowdrifts locked the Verm

WASHINGTON, Dec. 28—()—The RFC again offered today $34.06 an ounce for newly mined domestic gold. This price was repeated for the eighth time as the dollar showed strength abroad. Bar gold in London was worth $32.16 an ounce on a sterling opening of $5.0912 to the pound.

NEW YORK, Dec. 28--(AP)—Americans who want to speak good English would do well to follow President Roosevelt. His speech is an example of the best “American English” spoken in this country. So says Prof. Lee Emerson Bassett of Stanford University, president of the National Association of Teachers of Speech, which opened its annual convention yesterday. He described the President’s speech as a standard form of English, yet lively and varied and with excellent pronunciation and enunciation. “His is an example of what our speech can and should be—the speech of an educated and cultured man.”
LONDON—Henry Watson Fowler, who compiled the pocket Oxford dictionary, died at the age of 75 at his home in Hinton St. George, Somerset.

| BOSTON (AP) — The coldest weather for the day in many years gripped various parts of New England today and while the temperature dropped only to four degrees above zero here it was 21 below in Concord, N.H.; where it broke a record of 63 years. | Bolsters Mill in Oxford County, Maine, apparently was the coldest place in that state with a temperature of 42 below but elsewhere in Maine zero and sub-zero temperatures were plentiful and general. * In Manchester, N.H., the mercury got down to 21 below. At Keene, a temperature of 28 below made it colder than any Dec. 28 in 13 years, while at Montpelier, Vt., it was 30 degrees below. Two New Hampshire communities, Pelham and Franklin, reported 28 below. Practically everywhere the day's minimum reading represented the coldest weather of the present season. In Berkshire County, 14 below was recorded at Dalton and Great Barrington. Greater Bosto

By The Associated Press. PARIS, Dec. 26—Former Premier Edouard Herriot resumed today his campaign for a reversal of the French attitude on the war debt with the assertion that “the position we have taken has isolated us.” In Agence Economique Financière, M. Herriot, champion of payment declared: “IT am for as close contact as possible with the United States of America.” “I can not cease,” he said, “to denounce the danger of the attitude France has assumed toward the American debt.” In separating from England in the manner of payment “we committed a grave mistake,” Herriot declared. He urged Frenchmen to reflect upon “what might happen in case of a European war. While England was making a “token payment” on her debt to the United States, Dec. 15, France defaulted for the third time.

This quotation for the newly mined domestic metal was set last Friday and represented a new high. Just previously the RFC price had been lifted 25 cents. PARIS, Dec. 7.--(UP)—Signs that the new year might bring a complete new deal in world politics multiplied in European capitals today. Activities in Rome, Paris, London and Berlin indicated that such a new deal might involve the death of the Versailles treaty, the rebirth of the League of Nations and a disarmament treaty on new, business-like lines. Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy was at the center of the work. The United Press was informed on high authority today that Mussolini believes he has the pledged support of Great Britain and France for his long dreamed plan for reorganizing the League of Nations. It would be a reorganization that would end the domination of Britain and France in the league council and would end the power of small nations to paralyze league acts by veto. As a supplement to his plans for league reorganization Mussolini pictures the possibility of a seven power e

EEE UL (lS ES EE PASO -— Within two weeks France will go off the gold standard and return to her bi-metal system of two years ago and England will adopt the controlled monetary policy of the United States, Senator J. Hamilton Lewis of Wisconsin predicted here today. He hinted that a new adjustment of the entire war debt question would result. The senator also said that it is likely "the United States will unite with its controlled gold standard."

LONDON, Dec. 8—(AP)—A miniature manuscript, only fifteen-sixteenths of an inch by eleven-sixteenths, dated 1567 and containing Petrarch’s sonnets, brought $225 at an auction here. Some authorities consider it the world's oldest miniature book.

NATAL, Brazil, Dec. 6.—Triumphant at the end of another trans-Atlantic flight, Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh rested here tonight after a nonstop dash from Bathurst, British West Africa. They reached Natal at 3:01 p. m. local time (11:01 p. m. C. S. T.) to receive the roaring applause of thousands gathered at the waterfront to welcome them back to the western hemisphere. With the Colonel at the controls their red, low-winged seaplane was sighted coming in last from the northeast shortly before 3 p. m. He swooped his big ship low over the harbor and after circling the port and dipping his wings in salute to the throng below, turned the blunt nose of their plane into the wind and settled to a graceful, easy landing on the rippling waters of the cleared bay. They made the 1,870-mile flight over the ocean in 16 hours, cruising at a rate of slightly over 100 miles an hour, with a welcome

GLASGOW, Dec. 7. ()—Another big shipment of scotch whisky for the United States will leave here this week-end aboard the American steamer, Winona County, it was announced today. The shipment will comprise between 25,000 and 30,000 cases. Loading of the liquid cargo, destined for New York, was begun yesterday.

GLANCE BAY, N. S., Dec. 6.——(#’)—Trapped by fire, a man and wife and two of their four children, for whom they sacrificed their lives, were burned to death early today as flames destroyed their two-story frame home. The dead were Sam Aucoin, 38, Mrs. Addie Aucoin, 36, Josie, 11, Harold, 7. The four bodies were found within a few feet of the front door through which the mother and father carried two of their children and then raced back in an effort to rescue the others. They battled their way through smoke and flames within sight of the front door when they were halted by flames and overcome by smoke. The bodies were close together, the mother clasping the body of Josie while Harold was held by his father.

London, Nov. 1. (UP)—An unknown buyer, believed to be from the continent, acquired 74 gold bars worth 193,000 pounds sterling or $925,435 as the London open market gold rate was raised sharply to As in the case of yesterday's heavy gold purchase, there was speculation as to the destiny. It had been announced at Washington that the United States was not yet buying gold in the world market. Washington, Nov. 1. (UP)—The government today raised its price on newly mined American gold to $32.26 an ounce from the $32.12 level of yesterday. The price was an advance of 14 cents an ounce. Today's Washington price was 67 cents above the world price set in London.

Oxford, England — Prof. Frederick Soddy, who blames the money system for multiple world ills, declared President Roosevelt's currency-controlling program would be fruitless unless measures are instituted to control banking, too. Havana, Cuba — Carlos Mendieta, veteran Nationalist leader, was prominently mentioned for the presidency as the downfall of the Grau regime appeared near. Athens, Greece — “I will start to work and talk later,” smiled Samuel Insurr, Sr., when questioned about plans for the future now that a Greek court again has refused to allow him to be extradited to the United States. Graf Lends in Spain Seville, Spain — The Nomadic Graf Zeppelin landed for a brief stay before continuing its homeward jaunt to Germany. LONDON, Oct. 31.—(#)—The probability of Anglo-American co-operation in a monetary truce was widely discussed today in financial circles here. Official London, however, was silent on such reported moves in Washington, but high circles were said to believe this week would see a climax in negotiations of the British war debts mission at the American capital. Some newspapers believed the debt discussions might soon be abandoned. In the absence of any definite move by the United States to purchase gold in the world market, London's financial section continued to be puzzled over the new American gold policy. In governmental quarters, authoritative sources carefully indicated the caution with which the British government would be involved in any Anglo-American monetary plan. Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, a British treasury expert, went to Washington with the sole purpose of discussing debts. Howeve

LONDON (UP)—British officials generally believe that hope of an agreement with the United States on revision of the British war debt must be abandoned, political writers of Tuesday morning newspapers said in apparently inspired articles. As a result, the correspondents said, Britain would make a token payment of around 2,000,000 Pounds ($9,580,000) when the next instalment became due Dec. 15 and President Roosevelt would accept it. Taken at their face value, little surprise was expressed here. When Sir Frederick Leith-Ross left for Washington to initiate the negotiations, it was said frankly that there seemed little hope of settlement now.

Tokio, Nov. 1 (UP)—Aggressive little Sadao Araxi, Japanese minister of war, today informed the world that his nation had no intention of “waging war” on Soviet Russia. “I hope all misunderstanding on this score will be removed completely,” the leading militarist of the island empire said. Preparedness, he intimated, compels Japan to build its army to parity with Russia and its navy to approximate the United States naval strength.

PARIS, Oct. 31: (@)—Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet commissar for foreign affairs, left Paris by automobile today, presumably for Cherbourg to take the S. S. Bremen or possibly the S. S. Berengaria. His movements still were covered with secrecy as they have been since he left Moscow last week to pass through Berlin and appear in Paris yesterday 24 hours after he was expected.

ATHENS, Oct. 31—(AP)—The appellate court, holding that Samuel Insull was guilty of no fraudulent intentions, refused again today to grant the United States’ request that the former Chicago utilities operator be returned to face charges of violating bankruptcy laws. The verdict, as read by the presiding officer, pointed out that possibly the letter of the law had been violated in financial acts attending the collapse of the utilities empire, that Insull’s 74 years were acknowledged by the judges, and that the decision to reject the application was reached after examining the extradition treaty. When he was told by the presiding judge that he was a free man, Insull smiled broadly and cordially thanked the court while his friends and the audience burst into enthusiastic applause.
