1933-12-29.text: By the ASSOCIATED Press The cold grew more intense today eastward from Lake Huron over New England, Pennsylvania and New York. New snow flurried west of Lake Michigan. Official thermometer readings went down to 34 below zero at Canton, N. Y., 32 below at Greenville, Me., 16 below at Albany, N. Y., 30 below at Montreal. Official readings showed 46 below at Mt. Washington, N. H., and several points in Vermont; 45 below at Fort Kent, Me., and 15 to 32 below over Massachusetts. With 17 below, Boston had the coldest day in its history. It grew moderately colder in Virginia and the Carolinas. Washington, D. C., had 10 above and Philadelphia 6, with much lower unofficial temperatures in the suburbs. It was milder from the Ohio valley southward and much warmer over the northwest and upper Missouri valley. It rained heavily in eastern Texas, and more lightly in Louisiana and along the North Pacif

WASHINGTON. (UP) — The government held its domestic gold buying price unchanged at $34.06 an ounce today as it tried to corner nearly sixty million in gold bullion and gold money believed to be in private hands. The U. S. price is $1.92 above the world price set at London. The dollar remained at 60.69 cents in relation to gold. The gold buying program went ahead coincident with the order of Acting Secretary of the Treasury Morgenthau requiring all gold outside of federal reserve banks to be exchanged for other forms of money at the old statutory price of $20.67 an ounce. WASHINGTON. (Special) — Acting Secretary Morgenthau, with President Roosevelt’s approval, has issued a rigid command for payment into the treasury of gold coins, bullion and certificates. Virtually the only important monetary exception to the order was gold held by Federal Reserve banks and the Reconstruction Corporation

WASHINGTON, Dec. 29.—(UP)—Initial liquor import quotas for Great Britain, France, Spain and Portugal have been exhausted, and no more permits for shipments from these countries can be issued at this time, the Federal alcohol control administration stated.

London, Dec. 29 (AP)—President Roosevelt’s three-point program for peace enunciated last night in Washington provided front-page headlines for afternoon newspapers here. The Evening Standard, independent, one of the newspapers which commented most fully, said in part: “The new peace plan enunciated by President Roosevelt provokes the reflection that his political realism, admirable as it is in its operation at home, does not extend beyond the borders of his own country.” The Standard said it had little faith in one of those general declarations by nations, of which we have had so many. “The newspaper pointed out that the nations, by the Kellogg-Briand pact, already have renounced war as an instrument of national policy. The time,” the Standard comments, “they are to declare, their armed forces will not cross their own borders.” With this note, there seems small hope that Roosevelt's form

Tokio.-- (AP) —Japan's beloved little crown prince received a name today. In a ceremony which lasted two hours, his father announced his full name as Akihito Tsugu No Miya, which means “prince of the august succession and enlightened benevolence.” If the infant born amid great rejoicing seven days ago lives to succeed Emperor Hirohito, he will be known as Akihito.

HAMBURG, Germany, Dec. 29, (AP)—The Hamburg Fremdenblatt, a usually well-informed newspaper, printed today the reported content of a memorandum France will offer Germany, providing for a short-term militia of 200,000 men, light defensive weapons and international control of armaments over two four-year periods. Under a Paris dateline, the newspaper said: “French plans for conclusion of an international disarmament treaty anticipate two disarmament steps in four years. “During the first step, all European armies shall be placed on a militia basis, with eight or nine months enlistments. “Germany would in this period be granted a militia of 200,000 (Continued on page six),

TOKIO, (.P)—-The infant son of Emperor Hirohito and Empress Nagako, born a week ago, Friday was given the name of Akihito Tsugu-No-Miya, which freely translated means “bright and magnanimous prince of the realm.” The emperor chose the name for his first son from the list submitted by the ritualists just a week after the birth in accordance with the ancient Shinto rites.

PARIS..(P)—French statesmen were deeply moved by President Roosevelt's speech outlining America’s foreign viewpoint, the United Press was advised officially today. “France agrees on every point, and is grateful for this evidence of a perfect communion of ideas,” said foreign undersecretary Francois De Tessan after a thorough study of the speech in consultation with Premier Camille Chautemps and Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour. “M. Paul-Boncour was particularly moved and characterized the speech as magnificent.” French government leaders were particularly pleased at the President’s statement that 90 per cent of the world’s people were satisfied with present national boundaries. “Making an official statement in the name of the French government I am pleased to report France's happy reaction and full support of every point of the President’s speech,” said De Tessan. “Without adhering t

1933-12-21.text: SEATTLE, Dec. 21 (*#).—The crack Canadian National Liner Prince George was abandoned by her crew shortly after midnight this morning on Vadso Rock in Far Northern British Columbia waters, after its 12 passengers had reached shore safely in lifeboats. Running aground about 11 P. M. (Pacific Standard time) last night, frantic calls for immediate assistance were sent out, and within a short time the vessel's plight became serious. The passengers and part of the crew were ordered to the lifeboats. With the weather not severe, the lifeboats found their way safely to Anyox, a mining center four miles away, wireless messages picked up here said. "All passengers and baggage landed safely." "Vessel punctured badly No. 1 and 2 holds. Do not expect to float vessel without assistance." Within a short time, another message picked up at Vancouver, B.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 21-- (AP) — President Roosevelt tonight ordered government mints to coin silver on a fifty-fifty basis with producers. His proclamation, formally ratifying the London silver agreement, provided that half of the annual production of 24,000,000 ounces of silver shall be returned in dollars to the producers and the other half kept by the treasury in reserve. This will give a price, estimated at the White House, of 64 1-2 cents an ounce for silver—or half of the legal price of $1.29 an ounce—and considerably above the current market price of about 43 cents. Mr. Roosevelt stipulated in his proclamation that: “The present ratio in weight and fineness of the silver dollar to the gold dollar shall, for the purposes of this proclamation, be maintained until changed by further order or proclamation.” The London silver agreement proposed by Senator Pittman, (D., Nev.), at the econo

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif. — Just had a long talk with a mighty well-informed man, Mr. Hutchinson, Fox Film Co., man in London. Said the English just stocked up on our securities during all these low prices. There is a real weather vane. There is nothing with his feet on the ground (and as much of ’em) as an old conservative Englishman. He sees further than our rich men, that’s why they are coming out of their mess ahead of us. Another thing too, the fellow sitting off looking at you can tell better how you are doing and what your prospects are than you can yourself. Hutchinson says England looks on us as a bad boy, who has been out on a toot, but will sober up, change some of his ways, and be a better boy for it. Yours, WILL.

Dec. 19. — Chancellor Hitler of Germany sent a new arms demand program to the French government today, but the demands failed to change the Franco-German deadlock. The matter is said to be in the hands of the authorities unless Hitler backs down in his desires. Simon, the British foreign secretary, was expected to visit here Thursday to discuss the French stand in conversations with the French minister, Joseph Paul-Boncour, and possibly Premier Daladier, to close the gap assuring that Hitler will concede if the French are not too exacting. M. Paul-Boncour, it was said, will reply that he is willing to listen to a lessened program which he can submit to the Council of National Defense and the cabinet and the French allies, but will be unwavering in his determination that the allies must stand together and Hitler must submit to a plan of arms supervision. HULL, Eng. Dec. 21—-(AP)— Seven lives were lost today when the trawler Kurd collided with and sank the Swedish steamer Castor off Flamborough Head in a dense fog. The trawler rescued the captain and five members of the crew of the Castor. The Swedish ship went to the bottom within two minutes after the collision.

LONDON, Dec. 21. (UP)—Sir Henry Dickens, 84, only surviving son of the novelist, died at St. Luke's hospital today. He succumbed to injuries received Saturday when he was knocked down by a motorcycle on an embankment. It was a coincidence that he died just at the Christmas season, the traditional English celebration of which was immortalized by his father. Chelsea streets in recent weeks have resounded with Christmas carols, mainly by school children, often within earshot of the dying man.

LONDON, Dec. 21.—(#)—Sir Henry Dickens, 85, son of the novelist, Charles Dickens, died today from injuries received several days ago when he was hit by a motorcycle on the Chelsea embankment. The Central Shoe Store's end sale ends Saturday. Buy shoes, galoshes, hosiery now, at nice

LONDON, Dec. 21 (AP) -- Sir Henry Dickens, 85, son of the novelist Charles Dickens, died today from injuries received several days ago when he was hit by a motorcycle on the Chelsea embankment. Sir Henry lapsed into unconsciousness at 2 a.m., surrounded by his family, at the hospital to which he was taken Saturday following the accident. Four specialists made a stern fight to save his life but his injuries were too severe to prevent his death at the advent of the season which his father had pictured as the happiest and jolliest period of the year.

1933-02-10.text: NATAL, Brazil, Feb. 9 (CAP) - Captain J. A. Mollison, the only man who has flown alone across the North Atlantic from east to west, arrived here today early on a calm hot afternoon with the end of a solo flight from England. Thousands cheered as he brought his monoplane "Heart's Content" down to a good landing. The little ship had averaged about 116 miles an hour. "Well," he said, as he climbed out to shake hands with the governor of the province, and the mayor and the rest of the reception committee, "that was easier than the North Atlantic, but I had good weather most on the way. She's a sweet little ship." He seemed anxious to hurry through the ritual of welcome and after it was over he sent off his wife, Amy Johnson, who holds a few flying records herself. He did not look very tired after the flight across the ocean. After a light meal he said he would stay here overnight and leave f

Istres, France, Feb. 10 (AP)— Lucien Boussoutrot and Maurice Rossi, French fliers, hopped off at 7:48 a.m. (2:48 a.m. eastern standard time) today for Buenos Aires. They hope to break the world’s long distance flying record of 5,340 miles set Wednesday by two British officers, O. R. Gayter and G. E. Nicholetts, on a flight from England to South Africa. The French aero postal company reported the plane passed between Valencia and Tarragona, Spain, at 12:10 p.m. (7:10 p.m., EST), flying low. It was sighted by a seaplane off the Balearic Islands at 11:05 a.m. (6:05 a.m. EST.)

LONDON, Feb 10--Sir Ronald Lindsay, ambassador to the United States, will sail for New York on the steamship Majestic Tuesday if the cabinet 'big five's' plans for the debt conference in Washington are completed in time. Another conference between President-elect Roosevelt and Sir Ronald was expected to take place as soon as the ambassador arrives in Washington.

MIAMI, Fla., Feb. 9.—Washington is waiting for England’s proposition concerning the war debts. Mr. Rainey, of Illinois, says one billion, or ten cents on the dollar, the most probable proposition, is “sheer nonsense.” Mr. Rainey must prepare for another shock for the proposition may include payment in depreciated British or other currency, and possibly part payment in silver, at a price about double the present value. Would it not be simpler to say to our European friends “go ahead and default, it will be worth ten billions plus interest to know that your promise to pay is worth nothing.” One thing is certain; any political party accepting a ten percent debt settlement would not stay in power long. NATAL, Brazil (4% -—- Captain James A. Mollinson, British speed pilot who completed another trans-Atlantic flight yesterday, hopped off at 7:30 A. M. (2:30 A. M. eastern standard time) today for Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Capt. Mollison flew here yesterday from Thies, Senegal, completing a flight from England in three days and ten hours. He made the first westward flight across the North Atlantic last Fall.

"Our negative reply is almost a foregone conclusion but we must proceed with the utmost prudence," said a government spokesman. Foreign Minister Yasyua Uchida today instructed Yosuke Matsuoka, the special Japanese counsel at Geneva, to submit the draft of his reply to the league committee of nineteen to Tokyo before handing it to the league officials. Hence, Japan's answer is likely to be postponed two or three days while the cabinet studies the matter. STRASBOURG, France, Feb. 10 —(#)— More than a hundred persons were reported to have been killed today in the explosion of a huge gas storage tank at Neunkirchen steel works in the Saar valley. A number of the injured had been taken to hospitals. The police cordon was extended to include nearby tanks for fear of another explosion, and the authorities contemplated evacuating the lower part of the town because of the danger of gas poisoning. A second explosion at 7:15 p.m. dumped additional debris into the flattened area.

AMSTERDAM, Feb. 10—(UP)—A death-scattering bomb of 100 pounds, dropped today from a Dutch naval seaplane to the deck of the cruiser De Zeven Provincien, controlled by a mutinous native Sumatran crew, and the mutineers surrendered in the face of a vastly superior naval force. The bomb exploded, killing 18 men and wounding 25. Three of the dead were European enlisted men. The bomb started a fire aboard the ship. All the wounded men were natives, the Ministry of Defense told the United Press. All officers taken prisoners when the mutineers put out to sea Sunday were well. The cruiser is enroute to the naval base at Tandjogpriok, Batavia, with a loyal crew in charge. The Dutch warships met the mutiny ship, spread out in battle formation, and the commander radioed demanding unconditional surrender. 1933-01-08.text: MAURIV, Jan. 3—-(A’)-—-A wave of unrest sweeping through the young republic of Spain left a toll of 18 persons killed and a large number wounded today while an unestimated number were under arrest. Striking suddenly and without warning, the different extremist organizations apparently were operating under a coordinate command. The attacks occurred mainly in industrial centers of the country through the day, Sunday and last night. From Oviedo, in the Northwest, where striking mine workers killed an electrical engineer while he was going home, the outbreaks carried through Sallent, where a civil guard was killed, and on to Lerida and Barcelona, with seven killed in each of the latter two northeast cities. All armed forces were called out to cope with the uprisings. Police hinted that the monarchists, whose abortive revolution was quelled in Andalusia last August, and communists were respon

TOKYO, Jan. 9.—(P)—Marshal Chang Hsiao-Liang, military ruler of North China, was reported today to have intimated his readiness to negotiate an armistice between Japanese and Chinese forces at Shanhaikwan. The Rengo agency and other Japanese news dispatches from Tientsin, China, reported the marshal's apparent readiness and said Japanese expected the parleys to be opened shortly. Rengo dispatch from Chinchow, Manchuria, said the Chinese have expressed their readiness to negotiate an armistice and that General Nakamura, Japanese commander, named Major Chujiro Miura to meet with General Ho Chu-Kuo, the ousted Chinese commander at Shanhaikwan. The parley will open near that city, the dispatch said. (After the battle of Shanhaikwan, Chinese official reports said Marshal Chang served notice on the Japanese that he did not care to deal with them and requested that they send any communications

SHANGHAI, Jan. 9.—()-—-Christopher (Christy) Mathewson, Jr., son of the famous baseball player, was improving today from serious injuries received in a plane accident which took the life of his bride of two weeks. His wife, the former Margaret Phillips, of Philadelphia, was taking off for her first flight with her flying instructor-husband yesterday when the giant two-motored plane suddenly nosedived in the river bank on the outskirts of Shanghai. She died a half-hour later in a hospital where young Mathewson was lying today with two broken arms, a broken leg and other injuries. The couple were married last Christmas Eve in a double-wedding here which was to have climaxed a holiday celebration in the American community, cut short that same day by the sudden death of Colonel Richard S. Hooker, the marine commandant.

By The Associate Press. Shanghai, China, Jan. 7—Despite public clamor for armed action against Japan, indications today after a series of conferences among Chinese military and civilian leaders were that the nationalist government at Nanking would adopt a policy of avoiding any steps aggravating to the Japanese. Chiang Kai-Shek, the strongest military commander of the nation, apparently dominated the discussions which resulted in this decision. No official announcement of the government's policy was made, but it was evident that China desired a quick settlement of the conflict resulting from Japan's occupation of the city of Shanhaikwan. With the national government seeking restraint, the newspapers gave great prominence to extravagant reports of the Shanhaikwan situation. The papers printed statements that the government was making extensive military preparations in anticipation of wide

ROME, Jan. 7.—(UP)—The death of Vladimir de Pachmann, world famous pianist, was announced tonight. De Pachmann, who was 84, was regarded by some as the world's greatest pianist and the most expert interpreter of Chopin.

HAVRE, Jan. 7.—Robert J. Moore, former legislator, pioneer telephone man and hotel operator, died here yesterday of a heart attack. Moore came to Havre in 1903 and later moved to Glasgow, where he installed the first telephone system in that city in 1906. He also installed the first long-distance telephone line between Glasgow and Havre. He was a member of the Blaine County legislative delegation in 1911. A widow and a son survive him.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 9.—Acting with unexpected speed the senate judiciary committee sent a prohibition repeal resolution to the senate today with a favorable report. Vote Almost Unanimous In a single session, the committee voted almost unanimously to report the Blaine repeal resolution, slightly modified to limit the ratification period to seven years. The resolution proposes to repeal the eighteenth amendment, protect dry states from shipments of liquor and permit congress to legislate against return of the saloon. The action was taken in an executive session lasting only an hour and a half at which Chairman Blaine submitted the favorable report from his subcommittee which drafted the measure. There was considerable discussion of the provision for submitting the resolution to state legislatures instead of state conventions but the committee voted to retain it. Plymouth, Vt., Jan. 7.—Calvin Coolidge rested tonight among his native hills. In the quiet country graveyard beside the road that winds past the old homestead of his boyhood, his body was lowered to its last sleep as the shadows of a wintry day crept down the mountainside. Nation Pays Tribute A nation had paid its tribute in simple funeral services in the modest church of Northampton, the city where he began his career as mayor years ago and to which he retired when he stepped down from the highest office in the land less than four years ago. President Hoover, to whom he turned over the reins of government and Mrs. Hoover, men high in world affairs, the friends and neighbors with whom he walked and talked in his daily affairs joined in sorrowful tribute at the church. Then, along highways lined by men and women, standing silently with their heads bowed, he was carried back to the tiny vi

1933-05-18.text: LONDON, May 17.—(/P)—President Roosevelt's peace plan, hailed by Prime Minister MacDonald as a 'monument' which the future will regard as a great landmark in the march of human progress, was considered by the cabinet today. As King George was the recipient of the message, the British reply will go direct from Buckingham Palace to the White House. Prime Minister MacDonald was expected to make a statement before the House of Commons indicating Britain's support of the American proposals. Mr. MacDonald described the Roosevelt message as a great landmark last night at a dinner of the Pilgrims Society, at the same time indicating no reserve in his estimate of the value of the President's declarations. On the contrary, he gave the impression that it was fully in accord with his own ideals. It was apparent, however, that the message was disappointing in some political circles, where it was expe

GLENEAGLES, Scotland, May 18 (P) Enid Wilson today won her third successive British women's golf championship as she defeated Diana Plumpton in the 36-hole final match, five and four. The Diesel gas engine has no spark plugs, the fuel is ignited by the heat from high compression.

London, May 17. — (/) — King George V will make a direct reply to President Roosevelt regarding the British reaction to the American peace plan. The president's message was considered at a cabinet meeting today after which the government chiefs turned their attention to the speech by Chancellor Hitler of Germany. Relief Felt Hitler's response to the Roosevelt project was considered conciliatory and there was evidence of relief in government circles. Prime Minister MacDonald has given whole-hearted support to Mr. Roosevelt's peace appeal and quick action on it by the cabinet was expected. Since the message was addressed to the king, the reply will go direct from Buckingham Palace to the White House.

San Francisco, May 18—(7—Viscount Kikujiro Ishii, Japan's delegate to the London economic conference, expressed hope the world would join in “a war against economic depression” as he paused here today en route to a conference with President Roosevelt in Washington. “My mission,” Viscount Ishii, who arrived from the Orient yesterday said, “is to confer with your government for the purpose of finding out how we may cooperate with you in the war which the nations of the world are now waging. “Your president wants to pool the world’s minds and brain and, I dare say, the world’s hearts as well to find the way out of this appalling situation. Japan is anxious to work with America and other nations for the common good of the world.” Viscount Ishii is Japan’s privy councilor and former president of the League of Nations council. Those who are going there for us have been told confidentially to fix their personal affairs so nothing will interfere during June, July and August. They have been told also their services will probably be required abroad until November. That means those at the top are figuring on a six months conference. The reason for this pessimism inside are the same as those which have gummed all international conferences in the past. The tariff question was shown in Mr. Roosevelt's recent conferences to be almost as difficult as disarmament. Every nation wants tariff reduction—ours not theirs. As a matter of international general policy they think our reductions would be a good thing. The one underlying thing which may make this conference different is Mr. Roosevelt's determination. It is his belief that the World Economic Conference, to be held in London, in June, can be successful only if the present disarmament conference, in Geneva, actually achieves results. BERLIN, May 17 (AP).—Chancellor Adolf Hitler, in an impassioned speech before the Reichstag, today gratefully endorsed President Roosevelt's plan for relieving the international crisis and promised cooperation with Mr. Roosevelt's efforts. The chancellor agreed that without solution of the disarmament problem lasting economic reconstruction is unthinkable. In behalf of the entire nation, and especially the young Nazi movement, he pledged that Germany would go as far as any nation in disarming, even to the extent of scrapping her whole military equipment provided other powers did the same. Germany Ready. Paris.--(AP)--Maintenance of a strong army was the French reply today to Chancellor Hitler of Germany, Premier Daladier, categorically rejecting a further cut in military expenses, declared in the senate that the French army is strong and must be kept strong. This firm stand suddenly squelched talk of a meeting between the premier and Chancellor Hitler of Germany. The government also officially denied that such a meeting was contemplated, The premier told the senate that war economies had been made, but that they had not impaired the army's strength. "I affirm," he said, "that we can have confidence in the army and I affirm that our national defense is assured,"

1933-03-20.text: ROME, March 19 (4)—A Mussolini "plan" to assure an era of world peace was studied in conference of the Italian premier with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and his foreign secretary, Sir John Simon, over the week-end, an official communique said today. Premier MacDonald and Sir John, who had gone to Geneva to break a stalemate in the world disarmament conference, came to Rome Saturday for conferences with Premier Mussolini. While at Geneva Mr. MacDonald offered a new plan for disarmament. The "Mussolini plan" is based on collaboration of the four European powers, France, Germany, England and Italy. It is described as founded on the spirit of the Kellogg treaty and as an international agreement to outlaw war. To French Nation "The communique said the British statesmen would leave Rome tomorrow, going home by way of Paris, where they will submit the project to the French g

(United Press Leased Wire) LONDON, March 20, Harry Hays Morgan, 72, American diplomat, died last night at the home of his daughter, Viscountess Furness. A native of New Orleans, he had been in the consular service in Belgium, Switzerland, Holland, Germany and the Argentine Republic.

WASHINGTON, Mar. 20—(4)—The American government today kept in close touch with developments in Europe as the chiefs of the British and Italian governments sought to bring France and Germany into line on a definite program of peace through disarmament. The United States, while regarding this as a purely European matter which those nations should work out among themselves, prepared to send abroad on Thursday this country’s special ambassador on disarmament and other world problems—Norman H. Davis of Tennessee. Davis will go to London before going to Geneva and will confer with British officials. The big question mark in the European peace equation, as viewed here, centers over France and Germany. Now that Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain has obtained the collaboration of Premier Mussolini of Italy in efforts to gain a reconciliation of the French and German viewpoints, interest ce

WASHINGTON, March 20 (P— Arrangements were made today for Norman H. Davis, special ambassador on disarmament and world economics, to sail Thursday from New York on the Manhattan for London where he will see leading British officials before going on to Geneva. State department officials said they assumed Mr. Davis would see Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon in London. He would then be in a position to exchange views on the efforts to assure European peace by collaboration of the great nations, a move in which MacDonald and Premier Mussolini of Italy have taken a leading part.

LONDON, March 20.——Great Britain has decided to suspend trade treaty negotiations with Soviet Russia, Captain Anthony Eden, undersecretary, announced in the House of Commons today. The decision was reached as a result of the arrest in Russia of six British employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Company, Ltd., charged with plotting sabotage. Eden said that despite repeated requests, the British ambassador, Sir Esmond Ovey, had not yet been allowed to interview the arrested men and had been unable to obtain details of the charges.

An unofficial answer today to the four power peace pact proposal of Premier Mussolini of Italy was a reaffirmation of basic opposition to any fundamental changes in the Treaty of Versailles. No official position will be announced until Premier Ramsay MacDonald of England arrives here at 9 am tomorrow to discuss the Mussolini program, but as the cabinet met today to consider the new developments in the international situation some points of view became definitely crystallized. MacDonald will bring the Mussolini plan for presentation to Premier Daladier. Daladier will not go to Rome as has been rumored, and has received no invitation to do so. Differences Evident The foreign office indicated at noon that its first study revealed several grave difficulties in the Mussolini plan, but that France approaches the problem with the desire to make a maximum effort toward European peace. The French

ROME, March 19.—(U.P)— Premier Benito Mussolini came forward tonight with a bold proposal that the four great European powers—Italy, France, Great Britain and Germany—discard old quarrels and sign a pact in a new spirit of peace and co-operation. Mussolini made his proposal for this new peace pact at a two-hour conference with Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, at the British embassy. He told the British leaders—who dramatically flew to Rome for these week-end conferences—that he was ready to accept the British arms readjustment scheme “in principle,” and then offered his counter-proposal. Kellogg Pact. The treaty as suggested by the “iron man” of Fascist Italy coincided with MacDonald’s arms plan on several major points, it was learned. The accord, which can be styled a “reinforced Kellogg pact for Europe” outlawing war, would be known as a

Latest developments in the European situation follow: A four power peace pact designed by Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy to establish “peace in Europe for at least one generation” was studied today by the governments of Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany. It was indicated the United States would be invited to study the project and perhaps join it in a consultative capacity, although Washington’s previous adamant stand against giving any security pledges to Europe is well known abroad. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, who took his own five-year arms limitation plan on a flying trip to Rome and received Mussolini’s plan in return, was en route to Paris to confer with Premier Edouard Daladier. The French cabinet went over the plan, but it was unofficially indicated France would want more extensive pledges from Britain in return for concessions to Germany and Ita

1933-05-09.text: LONDON, May 9—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today there was every prospect of reaching an agreement between Britain and the United States as to the advisability of an immediate tariff truce. “There have been further exchanges of views with the United States government,” MacDonald said, “and I am now in position to say that, subject to settlement of the actual words, there is every prospect of reaching an agreement between them and as to the advisability of an immediate tariff truce.” Mr. MacDonald said the truce would not prevent continuation of work which Britain now had begun or was developing in accordance with announcement already made in the house. Washington, May 9—(P)—Reports spread over the capital that a deadlock on war debts might undo much that has been accomplished to clear away the causes of friction between nations prior to the London eco

American hopes for an armistice on tariff-boosting to create a favorable atmosphere for the world economic conference in London soared upward today with word of British agreement to an immediate tariff truce. With Great Britain backing the proposal, officials expect complete success. Other major countries have already indicated support. Encouraged despite the ever-present shadow of complications arising out of war debts, the Roosevelt administration went ahead with its conversations aimed at smoothing the way for the London conference now less than five weeks off. Secretary Hull undertook discussions with Finance Minister T. V. Soong of China. Later conversations were to be resumed with Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, the German representative. Tomorrow the eighth of the 11 nations invited by the president for these preliminary talks will appear with the arrival of Alberto J. Pani, Mexican finance

a Bulletin | London, May 9. (AP).—The draft text of the tariff truce agreement between Britain and the United States was dispatched by cable to Washington for the approval of the American ao London, May 9 (AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today there was every prospect of reaching an agreement between Britain and the United States as to the advisability of an immediate tariff truce. "There have been further exchanges of views with the United States government," the prime minister said, "and I am now in a position to say that, subject to settlement of the actual words and while protecting the essential positions of both governments, there is every prospect of reaching an agreement between them as to the advisability of an immediate tariff truce." Mr. MacDonald said the truce would not prevent continuation of work which Britain now had begun or was deve

London, May 9—(A.P.)—The dollar gathered renewed strength on the exchange today on support by big continental interests who became alarmed at President Roosevelt's remarks concerning the currency in his speech to the American public Sunday night. Opening at $3.49 to the pound in sympathy with overnight strength in America, the rate gradually improved as orders came in from the continent to sell French francs and buy dollars for covering purposes. In the absence of recent heavy selling pressure the dollar at noon had gained 7 cents from the overnight close of $3.97.

STRIKING PROGRESS in negotiations toward an international tariff truce and demands for an immediate war debt settlement shared attention today with the rise of the American dollar on the foreign exchanges. LONDON - Britain assured the United States representatives in London that President Roosevelt's tariff plan will be accepted. Prime Minister MacDonald told Commons a debt settlement is vital to prevent failure of the world economic conference. WASHINGTON - The Roosevelt administration, worried by earlier failure of Britain to accept the plan, was cheered by progress in London toward a modified truce pending outcome of the world conference. Roosevelt may ask Congress for freedom to negotiate debts. Meanwhile, he continued economic talks with representatives of China and Germany. PARIS - Huge amounts of gold again flowed back to Paris, but officials denied France and Britain are fighting

BERLIN, May 9,—(U.P)—The ruling Nazi drafted a scheme today for a Reichs Church that would bar all evangelical Christians "of non-Aryan descent" from church membership. The plans of the Nazi party usually become the official plans of the Reich. The scheme aimed at the establishment of an "evangelical Reichs church" for Aryan Christians, and for German Aryan Christians living abroad. It would recognize the sovereignty of the national socialist state and would be "ready to preach the gospel in the Third Reich." It would take in the present Lutheran Church and the Calvinist congregations. The latter, however, would be allowed to maintain special characteristics. The church would be headed by a bishop residing at Wittenberg, where Martin Luther preached. The draft proposed the evangelical congregations adopt a constitution for the new church in accordance with Nazi plans and elect a first bi

- Tokio, May 9.—(A.P.)—Sweeping through the city of Funing, Major-General Teizo Hiraga’s 28th Japanese infantry brigade today attacked Chinese positions at Changli in northeastern China below the great wall, and bitter fighting was progressing, Japanese sources reported. Further to the west Major General Kunizo Matzuda crushed two Chinese centers of resistance with his 11th infantry brigade and was approaching Anshan with the intention of cutting off the Chinese retreat from Chanel. The Shanhaikwan correspondent of the Rengo (Japanese) news agency said that several hours of bitter street fighting preceded the capture of Tsienan, another town in the area, by Major-General Yoshjiaki Takata's 36th Infantry brigade. The bodies of 600 Chinese were found in Tsienan, the Rengo correspondent reported, and the Japanese lost two dead and nine wounded.

Warsaw, May 9, U.R—The Polish cabinet resigned today. The cabinet was formed in May, 1931, with Colonel Alexander Prystor as Prime Minister and has been reconstructed several times. Marshal Joseph Pilsudski, Polish dictator, was Minister of War.

1933-03-08.text: WASHINGTON, Mar. 7.—Swanson in his first press conference as head of the navy today said that he would make every effort to build the American navy up to the limits of the London treaty as soon as conditions permit. Swanson, who attended the disarmament conferences at Geneva last summer, said the United States as well as other nations should benefit by the ratio fixed by the London agreement, whether by increase or a decrease being a matter finally decided by the state. "My view is that the fleet should be built up to treaty limits as quickly as possible," he said, adding that if this work were started it would aid in relieving unemployment. Swanson said the fleet would remain in the Pacific until the situation in the far east had become more calm.

| PARIS, March 8 (4)—Andre Le-fevre de la Boulaye, veteran of the French diplomatic service, today was named ambassador to Washington. He succeeds Ambassador Paul Claudel, who was named to the Brussels post succeeding Charles Corbin, who in turn was appointed to go to London. The official diplomatic shake-up, one of the largest in recent French history, was announced after a cabinet meeting. Charles Alphand, former minister to Dublin, was named ambassador to Moscow. Aime Joseph De Fleuriau, ambassador to London, and Count Francois Robert de Jean, who held the same post at Moscow, will retire. La Boulaye had been assistant director in the foreign ministry. In that position he received President Roosevelt a year ago when the latter was in Paris. The new ambassador is 57 years old. Reports from Paris on February 28, which told of unofficial reports that M. la Boulaye would succeed Ambassado

LONDON, March 8. (#)—Any prospect of former Kaiser Wilhelm II seeking to regain the throne of imperial Germany as a result of recent events there was stated today to have vanished through the former sovereign’s own act. If The London Daily Mail's correspondent at Doorn, Holland, is accurately informed, Wilhelm Hohenzollern has completely and voluntarily abandoned the aim with which he has often been credited — of again wielding power over his own people. Instead he is reported seeking permission to spend his declining years in the privacy of his castle at Homburg Vor Der Hohe, the famous mineral spring resort in Hesse-Nassau. He was 74 years old in January. This request to return to Germany was said to be the special mission undertaken by his second wife, Princess Hermine, when she recently went to Berlin from their residence in exile Doorn. She was reported seeking sanction of the schem

Washington, March 7. (%) — The predictions of naval experts that the United States will be 135 warships below its treaty allotment at the expiration of the London pact in 1936 will not be allowed to come true if Secretary Swanson has his way about it. In his first pronouncement as head of the navy department the former chairman of the senate naval committee in no uncertain terms today said he would endeavor to bring the fighting fleet up to treaty strength. “My opinion is that the fleet should be built up to the ratio laid down in London as soon as conditions permit,” the secretary stated in answer to a query. This was at Mr. Swanson’s first conference with newspaper men since taking over his new post. The London agreement of 1930 made provision for naval equality between the United States and Great Britain, while permitting Japan to build to a ratio of three to five with her two rival n
LONDON, Mar. 71—-(7)—King George and Queen Mary today entertained Andrew W. Mellon, United States ambassador, and his daughter, Mrs. David K. E. Bruce, at a farewell luncheon in Buckingham Palace.

Tokio, March 8 (UP)—A draft of Japan’s formal resignation from the League of Nations has not yet been completed, Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida announced at a cabinet meeting today. Speaking of the foreign situation, Uchida expressed the hope Great Britain would lift the embargo upon shipment of arms to Japan and China last week.

Tokyo, March 7.—(Rengo) A Japanese news agency dispatch said today that a battle for possession of Koupeikow, a pass in the great wall of China between Jehol province and Peiping, started early today. Some Japanese newspapers reported that Koupeikow had fallen. News from the front was that all other passes through the great wall had been captured by the Japanese invaders. The Chinese were stubbornly resisting an attack by General Kawahara’s 16th Japanese brigade on the town of Sanchienfang.

Vienna, March 7.—(A.P.)—The movement for a union of the Teutonic nations, Germany and Austria, a frequent cause of alarm in neighboring countries since the World War, was given new impetus today. Hitlerites held mass meetings throughout the country last night, acclaiming the victory of the former Austrian Chancellor Adolf Hitler in the German elections. Austria and Germany entered into a customs union in March, 1931. It was renounced six months later after France, England, Italy and Czechoslovakia pointed out the peace treaty with Austria after the World War forbade any financial or economic agreement directly or indirectly affecting Austrian independence.

1933-03-27.text: Dagenham, England, March 27 (AP)—Work ceased entirely today at the Ford factory as the result of a strike of 2,000 employees over the question of wages. The dispute started among members of the Amalgamated Engineering Union and efforts of pickets were so effective as day gangs reported that the entire works were at a standstill. The plant is reputed to be the largest motor car factory in Europe and employs 7,000 persons.

WASHINGTON, March 2.—(P)— Simultaneously, the English and French views on economics, which the Roosevelt administration considers is closely linked with European debts, were presented today to the President and his Secretary of State. While President Roosevelt was engaged in a discussion of the French attitude with Ambassador Claudel and Jacques Stern, vice chairman of the finance committee of the French chamber of deputies, Secretary Hull was talking for a second time with Ambassador Lindsay of Great Britain. After their talk with the President, Claudel said they had discussed the forthcoming world economic conference and that the French favored holding it as soon as possible. A little later, Secretary Hull issued a statement saying his conversation with Lindsay, which lasted an hour and a half, was confined to topics contained in the program for the world economic conference. The Briti
GATESHEAD, Durham, Eng., Mar. 27, (P)—Seven persons were killed and 24 injured by a gas explosion in a three-family apartment house here on a street.

LONDON, Mar. 27--(UP)— Strikers picketed the Ford automobile works at Dagenham, Essex county, today, with 2,000 of the plant's 7,000 employees on strike. Strikers are protesting a recent wage cut. Work at the factory was at a standstill.

By United Press WASHINGTON, March 27.—Significant conversations centering around problems to be discussed at the World Economic Conference took place today between President Roosevelt and French Ambassador Claude at the White House and Secretary of State Hull and Sir Ronald Lindsay British ambassador, at the State Department.

London, Mar. 27. (AP)—Lieut. Norman Baillie-Stewart, youthful Seaforth Highlander accused of revealing army secrets to a foreign agent, sat in the Chelsea military court today and heard his mother, Mrs. Elsie Beatrice Wright, and his brother, Lieut. Eric Stewart Wright, give evidence in his behalf. The 24-year-old defendant changed his name from Wright to Baillie-Stewart in 1929. Mrs. Wright’s evidence bore largely upon the young lieutenant’s income, which included an allowance from home of about £9 (about $31); which he had declared was supplemented by money received from a mysterious Berlin girl, Marie Louise, who became infatuated with him. While not brought out in court, it was common knowledge that officers of such crack regiments as his must have private means outside of their pay to keep up the social requirements, meet mess bills and the like. Mrs. Wright knew all about her son's

LONDON, March 27.—(U.P)—George Bernard Shaw must not be permitted to leave America “without being created a Red Indian chief replete with eagle’s feathers, a striped blanket and the tribal title of ‘Heap Big Blather Blather,’” the usually sedate London Morning Post said editorially. Commenting on Shaw's statements on arrival at San Francisco, the Post said the United States was being ‘heavily scourged, first by bank closings, then by an earthquake, now by the fact that Shaw has ‘dodged the immigration quota’ and arrived in the country. “The visitor applied for admission with his usual double knock of incivility followed by asperity,” the Post said. “To capitalize rudeness is a part of Shaw's genius.”

DAGENHAM, England, March (—TY?) majority of the night shift at the Ford factory here went on strike tonight. Hundreds of employees arriving to start work found the entrance picketed. They were informed at a meeting the strike had been decided upon as a protest against wage reductions said to have been instituted during the past week. The reductions were said to range from three pence an hour to 17 pence an hour. (The penny at current rates of exchange is approximately 1.5 cents.) After listening to the arguments of the speakers, a majority of the workers agreed to join the strike.

1933-03-10.text: Boston—An English tea merchant descendant of one whose cargo was dumped into Boston Harbor in revolutionary times, has donated more than half a ton to be distributed to the poor of the city. The merchant who requested his name be withheld said he wished the poor to use the tea to celebrate that historic occasion. Green Bay, Wis.--Since the money pinch started, the public library has been swamped with requests for funny stories, librarians said they were generally just laughing away their troubles with humorous reading.

LONDON—United States official circles in London received information from many sources today that continental exchange speculators, including the so-called "Balkan gang," are organizing a concerted drive against the dollar, beginning as soon as exchange dealings are resumed. The "Balkan gang" suffered heavily in an attempt to depress the dollar in November, 1931. The group had made commitments of $250,000,000 from its headquarters in Vienna. Subsequent recovery of the dollar resulted in huge losses to them.

Vienna, March 9.—(/P)— Steel helmeted army units aggregating two regiments were moved into Vienna tonight as Austria's new dictatorship armed itself to cope with the opposition, which centered in a special session of the diet. Some detachments in motor trucks were moved toward the parliament buildings, where the diet was arguing for its life. Parliament was shelved yesterday when Chancellor Dollfuss assumed dictatorial powers, but Karl Renner, its president, called a special session to defend the constitution. Papers Seized The dictator-chancellor confiscated all copies of two socialist party newspapers which carried Renner's statement, and even as the diet assembled the chancellor mobilized the army and moved troops into town. At the same time, he forbade meetings of the socialist party called in defiance of a decree issued yesterday, outlawing all political gatherings. The diet hall wa

VERO Clix, Mar, 10, (U.P)—Japanese troops, striking hard at a budding Chinese counter-attack, opened an offensive around Kopei-kou, a portal in the Great Wall of China, today. The offensive was aimed at Kopei-kou where Chinese had been reported organizing their forces for a direct charge at Nipponese lines. The Japanese columns were supported by 10 planes which bombarded the Chinese positions on the heights of the rocky terrain. The fighting continued over a wide area. Reports that Tang Yo-Lin, Chinese Governor of Jehol Province, had been executed after fleeing the capital before the Japanese took possession were questioned here today. Military headquarters understood the deposed official took refuge in the mountain village of Fengning, 60 kilometers northwest of here. The report said Tang was guarded by 3,000 troops.

Berlin, March 10 ()—Chancellor Hitler’s merciless campaign against Communism was advanced in the state of Bavaria today by an order from General Franz von Epp, the new federal commissioner, for the arrest of all Communist officials in the state. In Prussia also the anti-Communist campaign continued. Thousands of imprisoned Communists face the possibility of incarceration in detention camps at hard labor. The government, tightening its grip on the independent states, has received the resignations of the cabinets in Saxony and Baden. Karl Scharnagl, lord mayor of Munich, was given indefinitely leave of absence from office. The government board of censors suspended the Berliner Tageblatt, one of the city’s best known newspapers, until March 13 for having published objectionable articles.

PARIS, March 9.—(P)—Former Premier Edouard Herriot, who advocated payment of the American war debt when he was head of the government, proposed today that France pay the $19,000,000 installment due last December, as a gesture of friendship and confidence at this time of financial crisis. In an interview with the newspaper L'Intransigeant he expressed complete confidence in the ability of the United States to overcome its present troubles. “Now that President Roosevelt has shown a desire to discuss the debt issue,” he said, “it is necessary by a single gesture to make the United States know and understand that we would be happy to aid them in overcoming their present difficulties. America is going through a temporary crisis, and will emerge with its customary energy.

—BY MILES W. VAUGHN.— United Press Staff Correspondent TOKIO, Mar. 10.-(UP)—An imperial threat that Japan may drive its war machine into China proper should Chinese troop movements persist in the vicinity of the great wall was intimated today by Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida. Directing the Japanese legation at Peiping to propose creation of a demilitarized zone along the great wall of China to prevent spread of military operations, Uchida warned that future Chinese movements would make China entirely responsible for whatever military action Japan deemed necessary. Existing conditions in that area made it appear inevitable that the warning could not be complied with. Uchida sent the official communique after conferring at length with War Minister Sadao Araki. It urged that the neutral zone be set up immediately. Establishment of a neutral zone has been one of the main objectives in the s

Vienna, March 14.—(AP)—Federal rooms and gendarmes occupied Neunkirchen, near the industrial center of Wiener Neustadt, this morning after a report that unemployed were organizing a hunger march from Ternitz. Machine guns and barbed wire were waved across the highways. Up to 1 p.m., however, no serious clashes were reported. A group of 1,200 marchers were easily dispersed. The situation in Vienna was quiet, and the streets presented a normal appearance. Most of the morning newspapers did not even mention the presence of troops in Vienna. The newspapers, however, are under strict regulation.

1933-09-12.text: EPSOM, ENG., Sept. 11—CAP—Sir Leo Chiozza Money, distinguished economist, author and former member of parliament, was convicted in police court today on charges of annoying a young woman passenger in a southern railway car compartment last month. He was sentenced to pay a fine of £2 10s. He gave notice that he would appeal. The prosecution asserted that Sir Leo followed the girl, Miss Ivy Ruxton, into the compartment, insisted on making conversation with her and finally seized her in his arms and repeatedly kissed her. Sir Leo was quoted as saying that there was nothing in the girl's charges, that they had an amicable conversation in the train and that she offered no objection to his kissing her fingers in a way complimentary to the smallness of her hands, which he admired. “I did not take her in my arms or kiss her at all, other than I have described,” his statement continued.

SALT LAKE CITY, Sept. 11.—(4) Senator Key Pittman (Democrat), Nevada, told a chamber of commerce luncheon audience here today that the silver agreement adopted by the London economic conference paved the way for the United States to take the initiative for remonetization of silver. The chairman of the Senate foreign relations committee and delegate to the London conference stopped here en route to Washington, where he will press his proposal that the president authorize the acceptance of newly mined silver by United States mints and its return to owners in the form of coins, less a charge for minting. In the event the president lacks this power, Senator Pittman predicted that legislation for remonetization of silver will be adopted during the first 30 days of the session. (Continued on Page 2? Col. 7.)

LONDON, Sept. 12—(OP)—A movement to recruit 100 university students as a bodyguard for Professor Albert Einstein began today. Einstein is in refuge on the east coast. Einstein came here after reports that the German Nazi organization "Fiehme" had offered a reward for his assassination.

SUDBURY, Ont., Sept. 12 (4)—Injured and ill from a week of struggling through dense brush but considering themselves “mighty lucky,” two American entrants in the James Gordon Bennett balloon races were ready today to canoe back to civilization. Ward T. Van Orman and Frank A. Trotter were found yesterday, their clothes in shreds, their shoe soles worn thin from walking, and their stamina undermined by a diet of beans and blueberries, by James Barrett, lineman for a hydro-electric company. The pair had cut a pole and the lineman, seeking the cause of the interruption of service, found a note they had left and came upon the Americans in an outpost cabin 40 miles north of Sudbury and nine miles from Thor Lake. After coming down last Tuesday the aeronauts, in the bush for the first time in their lives, had traveled only 16 miles, walking almost continuously in search of help and suffering man

TOKYO, Sept 11 (4)—The state demanded death sentences today for three young naval lieutenants accused of leading seven fellow officers in the assassination of Premier Suyoshi Inukai in May, 1932. Life-imprisonment was asked for three others charged with active participation in outrages accompanying the slaying, six-year sentences for three accused of being accomplices in the conspiracy, and three years’ imprisonment for the tenth. Demands for the unexpectedly heavy penalties brought one of the major climaxes of the court-martial, which began at the Yokosuka naval base Aug. 10, because all Japan wondered whether the government would dare to ask the extreme sentence for the accused, for whose support a powerful and ultra-patriotic movement seeking clemency has developed on the ground that they acted on pure and patriotic motives. Premier Inukai fell mortally wounded before the revolver fir

TORGAU, Prussia, Germany, Sept. 12 (#).—Christine Lies, 46, and her son Walter, 21, were executed by decapitation today for the slaying of the woman's husband. This execution brings the total beheadings in Prussia since February 1 to 38.

Stockholm, Sweden, Sept. 11 () — Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh spent considerable time today inspecting his plane in which he and Mrs. Lindbergh crossed the North Atlantic on an air mapping expedition. It was believed the couple may leave tomorrow, but no hint was given as to the destination.

Monga, Italy, Sept. 12——Three noted racing pilots, Guiseppe Campari and Mario Borzachini, Italians, and Czaichowski, a Pole were killed during the annual running of the Grand Prix de Monza, automobile classic, in which the American, Whitney Straight, finished fourth Sunday. Campari and Borzachini crashed when their cars skidded on an oily stretch at a turn during the second heat and overturned. Two other cars smashed into the tangle, but neither of the pilots, Castel Bareo and Barberi, was hurt. Czaichowski was burned to death during the finals when his car caught fire in the middle of the track. The race was won by Lehoux, a Frenchman, driving a Bugatti automobile. Lehoux averaged 177.6 kilometers (110.29 miles) an hour for the 63 kilometers.

1933-12-08.text: (Copyright, 1933, The Associated Press) NEW YORK, Dec. 7—Eamon de Valera, steel-fisted president of the Irish Free State, today declared in a cable to The Associated Press that England is keeping Ireland within the British Commonwealth by threatening to employ force of arms. The “Irish Mussolini” asserted that but for this threat the Irish people would be free within 24 hours. “While relations between the two countries rest on the basis of force,” continued de Valera, “there can be no real understanding, no real friendship between us and the British people. “For 750 years Ireland has striven to win back her independence. She will not cease now.” The president's message was in answer to a request that he declare his position in view of England's latest refusal to discuss the age-old question of Irish independence. New York, Dec. 8.—(#)—President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State will carry on in his fight for independence despite what he termed England's threats of armed force to prevent a split with the British Commonwealth. In an exclusive cable to the Associated Press yesterday, de Valera recalled that ‘for 750 years Ireland has striven to win back her independence. “She will not cease now,” he added. Although the fighting Irish leader and former professor reiterated his determination to strive for freedom he was silent on what his next move would be. “He expressed bitter dissatisfaction with the recent refusal of Dominions Secretary J. H. Thomas to reply directly to de Valera’s recent question as to what would be done if the Free State should sever connections with the Commonwealth. Mr. Thomas, before the House of Commons, replied with a refusal to discuss what he termed a hypothetical q

ROME, Dec. 6.—The Associated Press learned in highest quarters today that diplomatic conversations have begun in the various capitals of Europe seeking reform of the League of Nations. They began several days before the Fascist grand council declared Italian permanence in the league depended upon radical reform of that institution. Absolute divorcement of the league from the principles of the treaty of Versailles which would eliminate from the league covenant articles which guarantee preservation of boundaries created by that treaty is under discussion, it was learned. The articles provide for use of military and economic forces to squelch cases of aggression. If these articles are eliminated it is believed the United States could be invited to join the league. It was to these provisions that America particularly objected in declining to join Geneva, since it did not wish to be embroiled

North Sydney, N. S., Dec. 7.--(4)— Wireless messages flashed to ships throughout the north Atlantic today warned them to watch for a speedy vessel whose crew turned the tables on its captors, the coast guard, by kidnapping four guardsmen and fleeing out to sea in their seized cutter. "Keep lookout for Kromhout," was the report sent out and on it Canadian coast guard officers pinned hopes of releasing the seamen and recapturing the suspected rum-runners and their vessel. The kidnapping was carried out with striking swiftness just after daybreak, in storm seas, after the coast guard cutter Stumble Inn had captured the Kromhout. The captives were Chief Officer R. M. Muckenzie; Second Engineer J. McIntosh; and Able Seamen W. R. T. Oxford and M.D. MacDonald. Members of the crew of the Stumble Inn said the other boat was loaded with whiskey. It was captured after a chase in which the pursuers

PARIS, (UP).—France will insist upon the sanctity and inviolability of the League of Nations and its covenant, Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour told the United Press today. Ending reports that France was prepared to join other nations in weakening the power and influence of the League of Nations in world affairs, the French statesman insisted that France would remain faithful to the last in its support of the league’s basic principles.

HANOVER, Germany, Dec. 8.—Karl Jatho, 60, who claimed to be the first man ever to fly a motorized airplane, died today. He claimed to have made his flight August 18, 1903, four months prior to the Wright Brothers' feat.

Geneva, Dec. 7 (#).—Reports that a European political conference may be convoked to consider disarmament and the reorganization of the League of Nations reached Geneva tonight but were not confirmed. A League spokesman said the universal interest aroused by the Italian demand, made yesterday, that the League should be readopted to a changing world proves the League of Nations is not dead but, rather is very much alive.

HALIFAX, Nova Scotia, Dec. 7.—(UR)—A sensational battle between an alleged rum runner and the Canadian coast guard cutter Stumble Inn occurred today off the coast of Cape Breton. The rum ship was reported to have kidnapped four of the coast guardsmen placed on board their vessel to bring into port, and made off with them to sea with the Stumble. The report on the battle related that the crew of the cutter seized an alleged rum runner, Kilmut, off Glace Bay. Four of the cutter’s crew were placed on board. A tow line was hitched to the Kilmut and the cutter started for port with the vessel as a prize catch. Guards Overpowered. After covering two miles, the four guardsmen were overpowered by the Kilmut's crew, the report said. The tow line was cut with an axe. The Kilmut turned about and rapidly put to sea with her captives. The cutter maneuvered about and gave chase. Guns on her bow were t

1933-11-10.text: PARIS, Nov. 7. (AP)—France’s debt default policy, officials said today, is unaltered by Great Britain’s decision to renew the token payment. The government might have raised that question of debt negotiations if England had settled, but inasmuch as Great Britain failed to solve the problem, neither the government nor the parliament, the officials added, is likely to change its attitude.

The American dollar, responding to President Roosevelt’s currency policy, plunged to new low levels in London Thursday, as evidences of the plan were seen on other markets. The dollar opened at $4.9814, closed officially at $5.02 to the pound, and in after hours trading skidded to $5.074 on the London exchange. So fast was the descent that the House of Commons, assured by Chancellor of the Exchequer Chamberlain that the independence of the British sterling would be maintained, could not keep up with it. Financial writers watched with great interest the movement of the dollar and the rise in American commodity prices, but professed to see no cause for alarm. Rising gold prices and a decline in international dollar rates caused a rally in stocks in New York, checked somewhat by late profit-taking. Inflationary sentiment predominated and the close was irregular. Bar silver pushed up a full

Washington, Nov. 9. (P)—Weighted by the administration's gold operations, the dollar sank far into new low territory today, putting officials more than ever upon the alert for signs of foreign reprisals. In the absence of any definite agreement with London or Paris on the extent to which the governments there would unprotestingly see the dollar depreciated, there were many predictions that some form of retaliation might soon be attempted. The dollar today fell to $5.05 3-4 in London and $5.15 1-4 to the pound in New York, figures not reached since the uncertain days of 1914. One result was that for the first time the daily fixed price for Reconstruction Corporation purchases for newly mined domestic gold was less late in the day than the dollar value of gold at London. Economists said that every cent added to the dollar and cents exchange quotation for the pound placed Great Britain at a

| Berlin (/P)—Chancellor Hitler, |addressing himself especially once — to German labor, hurled de- fiance at foreign nations today in ja pre-election campaign speech. The German populace gathered through the nation to hear their leader through loudspeakers erected at vantage points everywhere before they go to the polls Sunday to elect a straight Nazi ticket. Hitler served notice that Ger- many would never again gather with other nations around the green table of diplomacy unless her equality were vouchsafed. In a voice that often was at the verge of breaking with emotion he reiterated Germany’s desire for peace and declared the nation wanted nothing except to be left alone and work out its own salva- tion.

STOCKHOLM, Nov. 5, (P) -- The Nobel prize for literature today was awarded the Russian author, Ivan Alexeyevich Bunin, 63 years old. Bunin is a poet and novelist, born Oct. 10, 1870, of a noble family of Voronezh. He won the Pushkin prize, the highest academic distinction under the Czar for his poetry which he started publishing in 1889 and won it again for his translation into Russian of Longfellow’s Hiawatha. His poetry is described as impassive and of classic simplicity. His most recent book “The Well of Days” was recently published in England. An exile from Soviet Russia, he was reported in March of 1920 to be ill and in poverty in Paris.

Rome. Nov. 9, (4P)--A decree authorizing the government to guarantee the principal and a certain modest fixed interest on bond issues of private companies was presented by Premier Mussolini today to the Chamber of Deputies. Its probable result, financial circles agreed, might be a big cementing of all industries. The measure will have the eventual effect of making the government a chancel for all public investments in business since there will be a co-operative control not only over the operations of business but also over the business forces of life. The proposed law would allow the government to guarantee and participate in stock issues of private companies and would transform the whole industrial capitalizing system of Italy. Regardless of the companies’ conditions, stock dividends would be guaranteed to subscribers.

Bombay, India, Nov. 9—A sorrowing young man of 21 occupied the Afghanistan throne today as the nation mourned the death of his father, King Nadir Shah Ghazi, who was slain by a traitor yesterday. Though plunged into mourning, the nation "unanimously declared allegiance to a new monarch, Mohamed Zahir Shah," said a message to the Afghan consulate here. The boy king was married two years ago to a cousin, daughter of Sardar Ahmad Shah Kahan. His father took the reins of government October 16, 1929. He succeeded Amanullah, whose attempts to "westernize" the country met with opposition from certain Afghan tribes. A popular vote sent the late ruler to the throne from which he directed improvements in farming and business. He built roads and bridges and initiated construction of a railroad.

LISBON — () — A ship of death rode into the harbor today manned by only four men. Eighteen members of the crew of the Swedish steamer Elsie had died off the coast of West Africa. They were stricken by Malaria. The Elsie, a 1400-ton ship, brought a cargo of palm oil from West Africa. A number of officers were among the victims.

1933-09-21.text: LONDON, Sept. 20. (AP)—The British cabinet was understood to have reached the conclusion today that a disarmament agreement was imperative for Europe and the world and that failure to reach an agreement would have reaction of an alarming character. The cabinet held a protracted session to consider French disarmament proposals as outlined earlier this week at Paris to Captain Anthony Eden, British foreign office undersecretary.
EDINBURGH, Scotland, Sept. 21 — Sir Alexander Kemp Wright, general manager of the Royal Bank of Scotland and one of Scotland's most prominent men, died suddenly today at the age of

(By United Press). NEW YORK, Sept. 20—Gold soared to new high prices for the century on all markets today, just two years after Great Britain abandoned gold payments and less than six months after the United States officially abandoned the gold standard. Gold in London made a record high at 133 shillings 9 pence ($32.23 with the pound at the London close of $4.82); in Washington, the treasury fixed a price of $32.28, a new high since the treasury has been setting a price for sale of gold to the arts and crafts and for the sale of newly mined gold; in Montreal the price rose to $32.96 per ounce. Higher gold prices were reflected in lower values for the dollar. A spurt in the French franc to 6.15 cents left the dollar at 63.74 cents, a new low since civil war days, when, in 1864, gold soared to $59.91 per ounce and the dollar was worth only 34 1-2 cents in gold.
