By the Associated Press. Leaving Minnesotans new criteria for cold, the big snow hit the eastern states Wednesday night after the warmest February 8 New England ever had. Temperatures fell 50 degrees below zero in northeastern Minnesota and established new all-time low records in the southern part of that state. The storm which preceded the frigidity was above the Appalachians, dooming the balmy breezes which broke heat records : (Continued on page 2)

1933-08-22.text: LONDON, Aug. 21—(AP)—The United States will not resort to dumping to get rid of its surplus wheat if other nations fail to agree on a program to restrict production and exports, Frederick E. Murphy, American delegate, said today as the world wheat conference resumed its work. Representatives of more than a score of nations gathered to continue negotiations begun in Geneva last May and carried on concurrently with the world economic conference during June and July. Mr. Murphy, publisher of the Minneapolis Tribune, asserted there was no idea of upsetting the market by dumping but that the United States would consider means of getting rid of its surplus should the various nations fail to reach an agreement. (Secretary of Agriculture Wallace said last week that unless the nations agreed on a program of wheat acreage production the United States was prepared to proceed with a plan “subsidizin

Paris, Aug. 22. (AP)—Immediate aid to depression-stricken Austria by lifting the restrictions against Austrian exports is being arranged by France and England and probably by Italy, it was learned on high authority today. France proposes to remove or re-adjust her quotas on goods from Austria pending consideration of a vast economic reorganization of Austria and Hungary and the little entente nations, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Romania. The French plan, officials said, contemplates prompt aid as essential to remedy Austria's grave situation, and it is believed here that Italy and England take the same view.

London.—(AP)—Representatives of twenty-nine countries, including the principal wheat exporting nations—the United States, Canada, Argentina and Australia—met here today in an effort to solve the world's pressing wheat problems. The assembly will endeavor to arrive at an international agreement for the adjustment of exports to demand, with the object of eliminating the abnormal carryover which has been depressing the wheat market the last four years. It will also try to increase and stabilize wheat prices at a reasonable level, which will be remunerative to farmers and fair to consumers of breadstuffs. The conference will complete conversations begun by delegates from the chief exporting countries in Geneva May 10 and continued throughout June and July while the world economic conference was in session.

REYKJAVIK, Iceland. (P) John Grierson, British pilot who has been flying in slow stages from England to the United States, wrecked his plane when attempting to take off for Greenland. He was not injured. A wave broke over one of the floats and smashed it. The craft was completely wrecked. The aviator was picked up by a motorboat. John Grierson, of the British royal air force, left Brough airdrome Aug. 5 on the first leg of an intended flight to New York. He reached Iceland by way of the Orkney and Faroe islands.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) London, Aug. 22,—Confronted with a major crisis in German-Austrian relations, France, Great Britain and Italy today sought by means of a Danubian economic federation to maintain Austrian Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in power and limit the Nazi movement that endangers his government. So serious is the situation that Allied governments were talking of the possible necessity of invoking against Germany penalties prescribed by the Versailles Treaty in event blame was placed for any mishap to the Dollfuss regime. Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy is trying to work out a means of economic cooperation between Austria and her neighbors—excluding Germany—which by bringing prosperity, will strengthen Dollfuss and remove for the present the unwelcome possibility of an Austrian-German union. Lifting of customs barriers as regards each other's goods and coordinatio

POONA, India, (#)—The Mahatma Gandhi grew weaker today during the sixth day of his fast in protest against the government’s refusal to grant him privileges to carry on his campaign for the untouchable class. He was taken from Yeroda jail to the civil hospital, still in custody because of his one year jail sentence for civil disobedience. It was believed an acute attack of kidney trouble brought about the removal. The leader had a good night's rest, but nevertheless he was sinking today. He now weighs only 93 1-4 pounds.

Shanghai, — (/P)— Three trainmen whose alleged carelessness resulted in a wreck between Khikiang and Nanchang that caused between 30 and 60 persons to be killed or hurt were executed Tuesday by provincial authorities.

BOMBAY, India, Aug. 22.—(U.P)-- Miss Madeleine Slade, one of M. K. Gandhi's attendants ‘three graces,” was released from prison at Ahmedabad today, and was expected to leave for Poona, where the Mahatma is fasting at the Civil Hospital to which he was taken from the Yeravda Jail. Miss Slade’s release followed that of Mrs. Gandhi, who was set free so she could care for Gandhi, who is fasting ‘to the death” because the government would not let him conduct on his own terms, a prison campaign in behalf of the “untouchable” Hindu outcasts.

1933-03-26.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal, March 25--Bernard Shaw, you let me come to your home in London, talk to you for a time. I always said I never met a man I didn't like. You would all like Shaw if you met him, that is everybody that is fair and honest with themselves. You won't be able to figure him out, and that makes the smart fellows sore. He is one cross-word puzzle that has never been worked. Writers’ animosity to Shaw is that they didn’t think of saying what he has already said. He is away ahead of ‘em. England in all these years don’t know if he is for ‘em or against ‘em, and a fellow Irishman knows no more about him than a Zulu. Now when a guy can do all that and put it over, give him credit. So viva Bernard, look us over, and don't let our hospitality stand in the way of you telling us just about what cage in the zoo we belong. It's bound to do us some good, Yours,

London, Mar. 25--(UP)—Scotland Yard hunted today for “a fashionably dressed woman” reported to have kept watch in a hotel corridor while Confederates stole $70,089 in jewels from the apartment of Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Emery, New York millionaire social registerites. The well-groomed “lookout” for the jewel gang appeared to offer the chief hope of tracing the smooth-working thieves. “The woman, Scotland Yard operatives were told, not only appeared to be keeping watch outside the Emery's rooms in the exclusive Dorchester hotel, but even signalled the thieves when they left the suite. Fingerprints found on glassy table tops may offer another clue in the baffling robbery, but they failed to match any in the records of Scotland Yard, which include most of the known jewel thieves of England, the continent, and Americas. Berlin, March 25.—(?)—Persecution of any man simply because he is a Jew will not be tolerated, said Capt. Hermann Goering, minister without portfolio, in an impassioned address today to foreign correspondents in which he pleaded for fairness in estimating the German situation. He also expressed the opinion that Jews and socialists abroad were rendering their German friends a poor service by making unfavorable reports on German conditions or by holding protest mass meetings. “Every German,” he said, “smiles when he learns that on next Monday prayer meetings will be held in America.” While admitting excesses during the first days of the German revolution, he claimed the government had adopted most stringent measures, including the death penalty, for further transgressions. The many excesses committed during the first days of the national revolution, he said, must be attributed to provocate

PARIS, March 25.—(AP) France intends to open debt negotiations when the new ambassador to America, S. Andre Lefevre de la Boulaye, arrives in the United States April 12, it was said today. Action has been delayed until the new ambassador could become thoroughly acquainted with the subject. A government spokesman declined to say whether the government is ready to grant concessions in return for debt revision. France defaulted last Dec. 15 on a $19,000,000 interest payment on war debts owed the United States. The government of Premier Herriot, who favored payment, fell on the issue. The French Parliament is considering a resolution introduced a week ago by Deputy Rene Richard calling for the payment of the defaulted interest.

- PARIS, March 26.—(P)—The nation tonight awaited further details of reports that skeletons said to have been found in the woods of Newfoundland solved the mystery of the fate of Francois Coli and Charles Nungesser, French aviators who vanished in an effort to fly from Paris to New York in 1927. The ministries of air and of colonies ordered an official inquiry into the reports which said that a resident of St. Pierre and Miquelon, French islands off Newfoundland, had found the skeletons of the famous aviators. Officials were skeptical, but at the colonial ministry it was admitted that the skeletons might be those of the men.

(By The Associated Press) | Sosnowiec, Poland, Mar. 25—A strike of 700 coal miners who remained underground for six days at Klimontow, to prevent employers from flooding the shafts and putting them out of work, was at an end today. Promised jobs by the governor of Kielce, the strikers came out of the pits last night shouting cheers for the government. For four days the strikers had refused to take any food. The mine owners agreed not to dismantle the shafts and announced the shutdown would be only temporary.

- BERLIN, March 25 (#)—Captain Hermann Goering, cabinet minister without portfolio, redeemed his pledge Saturday to permit foreign correspondents to see and talk to prominent arrested communists and other members of the left in order that they might satisfy themselves that the prisoners were neither dead nor injured. The imprisoned men displayed by the police showed no evidence of having been hurt, nor did they make any serious complaints, Captain Goering made the pledge in an interview in which he asserted that he would “never stand for persecuting a man simply because he is a Jew” and that foreigners visiting Germany this summer would enjoy the fullest freedom, Smile at Protests Referring to protest in the United States against alleged maltreatment of Jews, the cabinet minister said: “Every German smiles when he learns that on next Monday prayer meetings will be held in America.” In th

BERLIN, Mar. 25.—(UP)—The Jewish war veterans association today handed the United States embassy in Berlin a statement condemning "exaggerations" in reports on anti-Semitic acts here, and requested that it be cabled to the United States. "Our duty toward our country as well as to the truth leads us to correct reports of alleged anti-Jewish atrocities," the statement said in part. "Maltreatments and excesses have occurred, which we are unwilling to excuse, but such happenings are unavoidable in the case of revolution and the authorities have always energetically intervened wherever feasible. 1933-06-19.text: LONDON, June 19. (®) — Official negotiations for controlled stabilization of the major currencies, which France adamantly insists must be achieved before the world economic conference can make progress on other vital problems, were understood to have come to a complete standstill today. It is understood the French were fostering this program on the ground that no progress was possible on other lines until some form of stabilization had been achieved. The adjournment talk was unofficial but it was so persistent and far-reaching that it was being privately discussed by the heads of the important delegations. In the gold bloc group, which is headed by France, a month to six weeks was mentioned as the probable length of the adjournment. France and her adherents asserted that everything rests with Washington and that there is no use trying to continue the conference until President Roosevelt

LONDON, (UP).— Secretary of State Cordell Hull, head of the American economic conference delegation, sent tariff cut proposals to the economic commission and in an accompanying letter suggested they might "appropriately be included on the agenda of the economic conference," the United Press learned authoritatively today. Senator Key Pittman, member of the American delegation denied in a formal statement yesterday that the proposal for a 10 per cent flat cut in tariffs, extension of the tariff truce, and encouragement of bi-lateral tariff reduction agreements, had been proposed by the U. S. delegation. American sources revealed that Hull submitted the proposal at the request of United States experts without intending it to be regarded as a formal American proposal. Hull did not read the experts’ recommendations before submitting them to the economic commission the United Press was told. A

London, June 18. (4)—An agreement for controlled stabilization of principal currencies, satisfactory to the Washington government, is expected in less than a week in important world economic conference quarters. The Franco-American rift on this point appeared closing as French experts, who had seemed ruffled yesterday over President Roosevelt's disapproval of the first tentative plan, said late today they felt differences could be composed. Oliver M. W. Sprague, executive assistant to Secretary Wovdin, said prospects remained hopeful. Asked if currency control could be made effective in a week's time, he replied it was likely in "less than that." Governor George Harrison, of the New York Federal Reserve Bank, slipped away on the steamship Bremen for New York today after a week's talk with Montague Norman, governor of the Bank of England, and Clement Moret, governor of the Bank of France.

LONDON, June 19, (4)—While sections of the British press were printing sensational stories today to the effect that American delegates to the World Economic conference were disowning the work of their own experts, important American delegation quarters emphatically denied there was a rift within their ranks. Submission of the American agenda proposal for a general ten per cent reduction in tariffs was announced by Chairman Hendryk Colijo at this morning’s meeting of the conference economic commission. This was done despite a statement last night by Senator Key Pittman, American delegate, that the proposal had not been acted on by the American delegates and was not endorsed by them. American delegation headquarters explained that the American ten per cent cut proposal was merely suggested among others to provide a basis for discussion and was not intended to appear as a resolution.

LONDON, June 19 (4)—Flat opposition to President Roosevelt's price raising program was laid by the French before the world economic conference today. They urged the world to adopt governmental agreements regulating the production and exportation of basic raw materials. This policy was set forth in a memorandum presented by Robeh Coulondre, assistant director of political and commercial affairs of the foreign office. Albert Sarraut, minister of colonies, carried the attack against inflation further by declaring before the economic commission of the conference that something tangible along the lines the French had suggested must be accomplished or France would be forced to retire behind tariff walls erected about her great empire. LONDON, June 19.--CP—On his departure for the United States Norman H. Davis denied that he intends to resign as President Roosevelt's special ambassador in Europe. “You can take it from me,” he said as he left for Southampton to sail on the Bremen, “that I am not resigning. I am now going back to see the president at Washington or wherever he may be, but that is not the subject we shall talk about.” After attending the world disarmament conference in Geneva, Mr. Davis conferred here with Secretary of State Hull, chairman of the American world economic conference delegation.

RENO, NEV., June 19.—(?)—The marriage of an English lord, Christian Arthur Wellesley, fourth Earl of Cowley, and a former hat check girl, Mary Elsie Himes, was an addition to Reno’s records today. Lord Cowley, known on the stage as Arthur Wellesley, met the new Lady Cowley, whom he married yesterday, while establishing residence to divorce May Pickard, New York show girl. He obtained a decree Saturday. Lady Cowley, 26, recently employed as a hat check girl at a roadhouse near Reno, divorced Joseph T. Himes, San Francisco bookkeeper, three weeks ago.

London, June 18. — (AP) — The French minister of colonies, Albert Sarraut, served notice on the world economic conference today that unless it could perfect a plan for universal control of production and markets France might have to, curtail back to herself and her colonies. Ultimately, with Mr. Sarraut’s concurrence, the commission decided to adhere to the original program and take up the French thesis as soon as the other is disposed of. Another outstanding development today was the announcement of Dr. W. W. C. Colin of Scotland, chairman of the economic commission, that 4 nations, representing 35 per cent of the world’s trade, already have subscribed to President Roosevelt's call on tariffs.

1933-02-27.text: | PARIS, Feb. 27 (P)—France is ready to participate in any arms embargo proposed by the League of Nations for the Far East, provided the United States and Great Britain also participate, it was learned today in high government quarters. Russian participation would be desirable, but possibly not essential, it was said. The French government is refraining from any initiative in this matter, but will follow the lead of the League.

LINGYUAN, BY COURIER TO CHENGTEHFU, Feb. 27.—(UP)—Japanese airmen, advance scouts of the army sweeping over southeastern Manchuria, today dropped leaflets in English, warning all foreigners to evacuate the province or suffer the consequences. Over this tense city of 27,000, halfway between Chaoyang, which is now in the hands of Japanese, Chengtehfu, capital of Jehol, the Nippon airmen scattered bales of precautionary pamphlets, warning of impending raids by air and land. Reaction to the warning was immediate. It found the staff over the mission a mass of bunting. British and American flags, together with the German ensign, apparently hastily stitched together from bunting, were hurriedly hoisted after the first leaflet was picked up. The residents began digging in. Non-combatants in this city appeared calm as the Japanese drive cigars. There was little military strength evident, because

LONDON, Feb. 27 (UP)—A temporary embargo by Great Britain on the export of arms to the Far East was announced in the House of Commons today by Sir John Simon, foreign secretary. Sir John Simon said that pending international consultations, Britain would not allow further shipment of arms to the Far East.

LONDON, Feb. 27 (#)—Sir John announced pending an international solution of the Far East arms embargo question that the British government would not authorize the issuance of licenses for export either to China or Japan of any arms or war munitions. In making this announcement in an arms embargo debate the opposition had initiated, Sir John said that pending international consideration of the question the government believed any effort and any sacrifice were worth making which would reduce the risk of widening the field of the Far Eastern conflict or lead to a prolongation of bloodshed.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 27.—(4)— Cordell Hull today began a round of diplomatic discussions out of which he will seek as secretary of state under Franklin D. Roosevelt to bring better times to the world by reviving international trade. France and Great Britain, America’s principal war debtors, were the first to send their ambassadors to confer with the Tennessee senator, who will take charge of the state department next Saturday with the change of administrations. Hull took up the debt issue after committing himself to a strong stand on another highly important issue in American foreign affairs—the preservation of world peace. Definite indication of this was given Saturday when, after a long conference with Secretary Stimson at the state department, Stimson sent a cablegram to the league of nations expressing “general accord” with the judgment passed by the league against Japan for its war-like

| Washington, Feb. 27.-(#),—Cordell Hull, secretary of state in the incoming Roosevelt cabinet said after a conference with the British ambassador today, that they had discussed the question of a program that would contemplate revival of business in each and every country — including the United States. As this was the first meeting with the British envoy, Sir Ronald Lindsey, no “specific factors” were gone into in detail Hull said. “It was a preliminary discussion which did not go further than the broad general economic conditions in England and America and other countries to the extent they affected the people in our respective countries together with more or less discussion of fundamental remedies for business recovery,” Hull said.

GENEVA, Feb. 28 (UP).—Peru and Colombia, on the verge of war on the upper Amazon, promised the League of Nations today to halt hostilities pending a settlement. GENEVA, Feb. 28 (UP).—An arms embargo against Bolivia and Paraguay was proposed today by Great Britain.

Shanghai, Feb. 27—(AP)—Seventeen persons, 15 of them girls, were killed and thirty were injured today in an explosion of boilers at the Yunghao rubber factory in the Chinese section of Shanghai. Eighty-one persons were killed last Tuesday at Shanghai when two gasoline vulcanizers in a Chinese rubber factory exploded.

1933-11-16.text: LONDON, (RP) — Twenty-seven men adrift in a stormy sea after abandoning the British freight steamship Saxilby were given up for lost Thursday. The giant liner Berengaria, after a race to the crew’s aid and a search for their tiny lifeboat off the Irish coast, gave up hope and, a day late, continued on toward Cherbourg, France. Nothing had been heard of the Saxilby and its crew for more than 24 hours after the men took to a ship’s boat in a storm. The steamships Manchester Regiment and Boschrijk remained at the scene of the Saxilby’s last appeal for aid, but they saw no signs of the vessel or its crew. The British 8,400 ton cruiser Exeter sped at its maximum of 324 knots toward the British freighter St. Quentin, helpless with broken steering gear 160 miles north of the Saxilby’s last reported position. Throughout Wednesday night the 62,000 ton Berengaria, pride of the Cunard line, raced t

Washington - The administration again held the domestic price of newly mined gold well below world quotations today and watched for the effects of a further dollar decline. The gold price here was announced as $35.56, unchanged from Wednesday and the day before. Meanwhile, gold at London had a dollar value of $35.14, based on the opening exchange rate of $5.47. Declines which took the dollar to $5.50 carried the foreign gold price still higher until the dollar rallied to $5.41 1-2 only to relapse again to $5.44 1-2.

LONDON, Nov. 16 (AP).—Great Britain moved today to get Germany back into the disarmament conference by instructing Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, to proceed to Geneva tomorrow. He is to hold conversations there with Hugh R. Wilson, minister to Geneva and acting head of the American delegation to the disarmament conference, aimed toward giving the parley a fresh start on the basis of an actual draft of a disarmament convention.

New York, Nov, 18 (4)—The flow of capital to London was only momentarily checked today by a lower gold price on this side of the Atlantic, and the British pound sterling surged still higher, reaching new record altitudes since 1914. The dollar declined, as well, in relation to other leading currencies, but foreign exchange dealers said that the demand was chiefly for sterling, and that the British currency was also still in active demand in Paris and some other European continental centers.

Reported Abandoned In Sinking Condition; Little Hope for Men in Storm VALENTINA, Irish Free State, Nov. 15 (P)—The fate of the little British freighter Saxilby, whose crew of 27 was reported to be abandoning ship in a raging North Atlantic storm, was hidden Wednesday night as at least six ships raced to her rescue. The 52,600-ton Berengaria seemed likely to be the winner. The Saxilby's wireless had been silent since morning, when her position was given as 51:50 north, 19:50 west. Wireless messages received close to midnight from officers aboard the Berengaria held out little hope that any of the Saxilby’s crew ever would be found alive.

AMDEN, N. J., Nov. 15.—The fifteenth of Uncle Sam’s 10,000-ton cruisers to be built under the London naval treaty, the Tuscaloosa, slides down the ways of the New York Shipbuilding company into the Delaware river at high tide, noon, today. To Mrs. T. L. McCann, of Washington, D. C., and Tuscaloosa, Ala., was given the honor of sponsoring the vessel for the navy department. A niece of Representative William Bacon Oliver, of Alabama, she is a native of the city for which the ship was named.

LONDON, Nov. 16.—The trans-Atlantic liner Berengaria, after reaching the spot where the British freighter Saxilby last indicated she was in distress and conducting a lengthy search for the 29 members of the steamers’ crew, abandoned the rescue attempt today. Two other ships, the British steamer Manchester Regiment and the Dutch vessel Bosdijk, also arrived on the scene and likewise were unable to find any trace of the men, who had taken to their life boats hours before in mountainous seas. Hope for the rescue of the seamen dwindled rapidly. Those in most hopeful of a rescue pointed out the life boats may have drifted some distance away, and might be sighted later. Others feared the boats may have been swamped by the mountainous seas reported by the Berengaria’s captain as exceptionally high. A second British freighter, the St. Quentin, was battling the seas with a broken steering gear wh

LONDON, Nov. 16 (UP)—Money Barons of Europe, increasingly concerned over the precipitous crash of the dollar in terms of foreign currency and flight of American capital to London, today hastily considered international measures to relieve what was considered an approaching crisis. Among the day’s significant developments were: 1. Continued gyrations of the pound Sterling, which opened at $5.462, 7 cents above yesterday's close, and fluctuated throughout the day in each succeeding sale. 2. The tenth successive decrease in the Bank of France gold reserves, which have lost approximately 2,000,000,000 francs (approximately $130,000,000 at the current rate of exchange) during the past month. 3. Continued drop of the dollar in terms of the franc, which stood at 15.05 to the dollar (6.644 cents a franc) at today’s opening. 4. Reports that London now holds at least $700,000,000 in “exiled” Ameri

1933-05-15.text: New York, May 15. (INS)—Ernest Torrence, motion picture actor, died at the Lennox Hill Hospital here today as a result of complications following a recent abdominal operation. Torrence, who was on his way to his native Scotland for a vacation, was stricken aboard the liner Empress of Britain two days before the ship reached New York from California. George Bernard Shaw was a passenger on the liner. Immediately upon his arrival here Torrence was removed to a hospital, and the operation took place three or four days later. Torrence was a veteran of the concert, operatic, musical comedy and motion picture stages. He made his debut as a concert pianist thirty-five years ago in Edinburgh, Scotland, the place of his birth.

Paris, May 13, WR—A united British, French and American front against German rearmament was sought by Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador at large, when he entered a conference with Foreign Minister Joseph Poul-Boncour today. Government circles displayed the greatest interest in German Chancellor Adolf Hitler's speech before the Reichstag Wednesday. Alarmed by the jingoistic speech of Vice Chancellor Franz von Papen, all three nations were believed to fear that Hitler would announce Germany’s intention to rearm. Reply to anything Hitler may say is scheduled to be made at a meeting to the full disarmament commission Thursday. This meeting was to have been held today but was postponed pending Hitler's speech.

FE ET Seer eee PETAR, London, May 18— (AP)— For- eign Secretary Sir John Simon de- clined in the House of Commons today further to commit himself or the government on the question of intimations that Germany in- tended to rearm. Sir John declared it was neces- sary to await resumption of the disarmament conference commis- sion’s sessions in Geneva. The foreign minister had been asked if he were prepared to make a statement on “the declaration of the German foreign minister that, whatever the result of the disarmament conference, Germany intends to rearm, thereby breaking the terms of the Treaty of Ver- sallies.” “I can make no further state- ment,

Washington, May 14. (#)—The delicate armaments situation entering around Germany has held the attention of American statesmen who regarded it as having an important bearing on the chances of success at the world monetary and economic conference opening at London, June 12. Officials showed keen interest in the announced purpose of Chancellor Hitler, of Germany, to state his government’s armaments policy in a speech at the Reichstag on Wednesday. German objection to features of the British arms reduction plan has blocked action temporarily at the Geneva conference. The part the United States will play in the efforts to surmount the obstacles to real progress toward disarmament will be directed from the White House and executed through Norman H. Davis, President Roosevelt’s special ambassador.

LONDON, May 15 (P)—Efforts were made in Downing Street today to calm the sensation in the Press over the weekend concerning the general European crisis. It was stated that no anxiety was felt in official circles regarding the week’s developments. Several morning newspapers today spoke of the increased tension in Europe, anxiously discussed that they interpreted as gathering war clouds, and viewed as the main danger the growing war spirit in Germany. ‘War Of Revenge’ The Daily Times, after commenting on what it called ‘the inculcation of hatred of the foreigner and of militarism’ in the Hitler regime, called upon Germany “to disprove—if it is possible to disprove—that one of the main objects of Hitlerism is to prepare for a war of revenge.” The cabinet members, including Lord Hailsham, secretary of war, were at No. 10 Downing Street early in the morning but it was declared they attended a

Poona, India, May 14 (/P)--The Mahatma Gandhi today celebrated the seventh day of his "irrevocable" fast by a reconciliation with his eldest son, Hiraldal Gandhi, with whom the father had not been on speaking terms for a long time. The Mahatma displayed quiet pleasure when his son arrived with Mrs. Gandhi at the villa of Lady Thackersey where he has been staying since his release from the Yeroda jail. Gandhi patted his son affectionately on the back, exchanged a few words with him, then smilingly lapsed into silence again. It was evident the frail leader and his son were happy over the reconciliation, and apparently forgot the difference of views which led to their separation. An affectionate greeting was also given by Gandhi to his wife, who had just been released from jail. Because of the arrival of Mrs. Gandhi, the Mahatma did not observe today as a day of silence, according to his cu

TOKYO, May 15 (#)—Lt.-Gen. Yoshikazu Nichi, personally commanding his eighth division, today attacked the town of Nansheng-Chuang, 10 miles northeast of Miyun in North China and about 50 miles from Peiping, and the occupation of Miyun was declared to be imminent. Simultaneously the sixth division swept at the town of Fengjun, west of the Lwan river, and found easy progress along the plains stretching. Reports from all fronts received by the Rengo (Japanese) news agency were that the Chinese morale was collapsing and there were many desertions.

PARIS, May 14—(AP)—The urgent need of disarmament to calm Europe and to facilitate world reconstruction will be urged by Norman H. Davis, ambassador at large, tomorrow when he confers with foreign minister Paul-Boncour upon the situation created by Germany’s armament demands. Mr. Davis, who arrived yesterday from London, will emphasize the need for both political and economic peace, a subject now at an acute state because of the deadlock at Geneva and the approach of the world economic conference at London. It is possible that the American ambassador will discuss French tariff policies as it affects the United States and discriminates such as the preferences given to Italy and to Belgium. 1933-10-11.text: | Cromer, Norfolk, England. — (AP)—Anybody attempting to molest Albert Einstein in his humble refuge on the Norfolk coast may get bullets from guns of his host's game keepers. And if Commander Oliver Locker-Lampson himself is around, any intruder may have to face the revolver which the member of parliament reputedly is carrying while the celebrated mathematician is under his protection... Professor Einstein arrived from London yesterday, fleeing reported Nazi threats against his life, and set about at once in his quiet, tree-surrounded retreat to work on a new mathematical theory—the nature of which was not disclosed—and to prepare for lectures in America next month. Seemingly content, Dr. Einstein said: “All I want is peace. Where could I find a more peaceful retreat than here in England? “At Le Coq (Le Coq-sur-Mer, Belgium) I was always guarded. It was a terrible strain. It interfered

LONDON, Oct. 11 (UP).—An enlisted men’s revolt aboard the battle cruiser Hood, pride of the British fleet and most powerful naval vessel in the world, was reported in naval and civilian circles today. Apparently similar to the serious mutiny in the fleet two years ago, which was politely termed “insubordination,” it was reported to have occurred on the giant warship while she was on her way to the fall naval maneuvers in the North Sea. Destroyers were reported to have taken disaffected enlisted men from the Hood. The vessel was said to have been ordered to return at once to its base at Portsmouth. The 1,341 men aboard the Hood were among those involved in the September mutiny two years ago which caused the fall maneuvers to be abandoned.

| WYNDHAM, Australia, Oct. 11 (AP).—Wing Commander Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith clipped more than 40 hours from the England-Australia flying record when he landed here late this afternoon to the cheers of a mighty throng of welcomers. | The famous airman, hero of a Pacific crossing and numerous other flying feats, left England last Wednesday with the declaration that he was not out to set a new mark.

EL PASO, Oct. 9 (UP).—Mary Pickford, uncrowned queen of Hollywood, will file suit for divorce from Douglas Fairbanks, actor husband, in Juarez within two weeks, Atty. Luis A. Trias said today. Trias said that Fairbanks plans to marry an English actress.

GENEVA, Oct. 9.—(4)—The steering committee of the World Disarmament Conference today voted to resume a full parley Oct. 16, as previously planned. Dr. Rudolph Nadolny, German delegate, said Germany wished to continue discussion of the British disarmament draft, adding Germany was anxious to reach an accord.

GENEVA (P)—The United States, Great Britain and France agreed Wednesday that Germany should not be permitted to re-arm at the present time. Following a conference at which Joseph Paul-Boncour of France, Foreign Minister Sir John Simon of England and Ambassador Norman H. Davis discussed Germany's plea for expansion of her defensive armaments, it was announced the three envoys had agreed there should be no immediate change in the reich status.
By United Press. GENEVA, Oct. 11.—The United States, Great Britain and France agreed today that Germany should not be permitted to re-arm at the present time.

Washington, Oct. 10 (AP)—A plea of radically altered world economic conditions, unforeseen when war debt settlements were made, was advanced today by Great Britain as justification for the reduction she hopes to obtain from the United States. Beyond this, Sir Frederick Leith Ross, spokesman for the London government, emphatically expounded the argument that the loans made to his country before and after the Armistice were not commercial in character, but a matter of necessity and were used for war purposes. With his colleagues, Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, and T. K. Bewley, economic advisor to the British embassy, Sir Frederick called at the treasury. He was met by Dean Acheson, the undersecretary, Frederick Lisesey, assistant economic advisor to the State Department, and Daniel W. Rell, the treasury’s commissioner of accounts and deposits. In Acheson's roomy office, the s

1933-04-19.text: MOSCOW, April 19. (4)—The Central Executive Committee of Soviet Russia was petitioned today to commute to exile for life the prison sentences imposed early this morning on L. C. Thornton and William L. MacDonald, British engineers who were convicted of espionage, sabotage and bribery. Thornton and MacDonald received the only sentences imposed on the five Britons who were found guilty. Thornton was given a three-year prison term and MacDonald a sentence of two years. The pair were held incommunicado in prison. Four other Britons who were tried on the same charges were leaving Russia tomorrow, presumably forever. Three of these—Allen Monkhouse, Joha Cushny, and C. H. Nordwell—were under orders to get out of the country. Albert W. Gregory had been acquitted. They were not allowed to see the two condemned men with whom they had worked for nearly ten years in setting up British machinery in e

By STANLEY P. RICHARDSON Moscow, April 19.—(Wednesday)—(/P)—Two of the six British electrical engineers tried on charges of espionage, bribery and sabotage, early today were given prison sentences, while three were ordered deported and the other was acquitted. Ten of their Russian co-defendants were sentenced to terms up to ten years. One was acquitted. W. H. MacDonald, the only one of the British employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers electrical firm to plead guilty, received a two-year prison sentence. H. C. Thornton, the company’s chief construction engineer in Russia, who was described as a military spy by Prosecutor Andrey Vishinsky, was sentenced to a three-year term. To Be Deported Allan Honkhouse, the Metropolitan-Vickers director in Russia; John Cushny, an engineer, and Charles Nordwall were ordered deported within three days. They will not be allowed to return to Soviet Russia w

London, April 19 (AP)—Great Britain clamped down an 80 percent embargo against Soviet goods today but a few hours after the drastic action had been taken it was authoritatively stated that it might be withdrawn if the Russian authorities commuted the prison sentences of two British engineers convicted of sabotage. Moscow dispatches indicated that the sentences of the two engineers—L. C. Thornton and William A. MacDonald—might be changed to banishment from Russia. Banishment was the court’s verdict in the case of three other British engineers who were found guilty. The British government has contended that its prime concern was the safety of its subjects in Russia. On the basis of current trade figures the embargo, which becomes effective April 26, will bar imports aggregating £9,600,000 (currently $33,600,000) annually. The proclamation was signed by King George at Windsor Castle and pub

LONDON, April 19. (49—Great Britain answered the conviction of British engineers in Moscow by declaring today a partial embargo against Soviet goods which will shut out approximately 80 per cent of Russia’s imports into the United Kingdom. On the basis of current trade figures the embargo, which becomes effective April 26, will bar imports aggregating £9,600,000 (currently $33,600,000) annually. The proclamation was signed by King George at Windsor Castle and was published in the London Gazette. It prevents all importations of Soviet butter, wheat, barley, oats, and maize in grain; poultry and game; raw cotton; petroleum oils; wood and timber, hewn, sawn, planed or dressed; and articles manufactured wholly or partly of wood and timber.

MOSCOW, April 19 (UP).—William MacDonald and W. H. Thornton, British subjects, were lodged behind grim walls of Liubianka prison today, sentenced to penal servitude for sabotage and espionage against the Soviet state. Their four countrymen and co-defendants prepared for a hurried departure from Russia, Allan Monkhouse, John Cushny, and Carles Nordwall were found guilty of the same charges but were sentenced to banishment alone. A. W. Gregord was acquitted. Defense counsel prepared appeal for MacDonald and Thornton to be presented to the presidium within 48 hours, as required by Soviet law. They will ask commutation of the prison terms to banishment. It was undecided whether the banishment sentences imposed against three would be appealed. If the sentences are carried out, MacDonald must serve two years and Thornton three.

(By United Press.) LONDON, April 19. — England struck back at Soviet Russia today for the conviction of five British subjects on espionage charges. King George and the Privy Council declared an 80 percent embargo on Russian imports and the Metropolitan Vickers Company, employer of the convicted men, ordered an immediate appeal on behalf of two defendants who were sent to prison. The partial embargo, amounting practically to a declaration of an economic war, will become effective April 26. Faith In Innocence, Sir Felix Pole, chairman of Metropolitan Vickers, issued a statement reaffirming his faith in his five convicted employees, as appeals were ordered for William MacDonald and W. H. Thornton, the only two sent to prison. The statement echoed a general British opinion that the men had not received a fair trial. The embargo items included timber, petroleum, grain, raw cotton, and butter.

LONDON, April 19 (AP)— Great Britain will begin enforcing an embargo on all Russian goods it does not desire as necessities April 26. A proclamation making this action effective was signed today by King George at Windsor Castle, Economic War. It was authoritatively stated that 80 percent of Russian imports will be affected. All grain, butter, raw cotton, petroleum and timber will be excluded. The proclamation amounted to a declaration of economic war, the second by Great Britain within the last ten months. Soviet retaliations were believed certain, and observers envisaged a complete stoppage of trade. The Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Equipment company, which sent the men to Russia, meanwhile issued a statement continuing its existing contracts in Russia. Observers believed Russian authorities desired above everything else to avoid endangering foreign credit sources. That Russia will o

MacDonald, employee of British Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical company, who pleads guilty of sabotage and military and other spying. He confesses that he and other employees of the British company, after building gigantic turbines, proceeded to destroy that which they had created. For a British concern to sell and take pay from Russia for its installation of machinery, and then for its employees to destroy what they had created, undoubtedly without the knowledge of the British company, is not only shocking treachery, if the man’s confession be true, but bad for British business abroad.
