1933-03-22.text: Paris — (AP) — Tentative acceptance of the peace plan of Premier Mussolini of Italy was understood to have been given today by Premier Edouard Daladier and Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and Sir John Simon, his foreign secretary. The tentative acceptance was said to have been given at the start of an all-day session of conferences at the British embassy. Modification Sought. Mr. MacDonald and Sir John are returning home by way of Paris after conferring last Saturday and Sunday at Rome with Premier Mussolini, at which time the Italian statesman’s plan was broached. France, it was said in government quarters, regards the plan favorably but wants clarification and modification. The French insist that the nature and extent of revision of treaties be defined and that Poland and the little entente be treated as equals, not inferiors. Pl

Croydon Airport, England (UP) — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Minister Sir John Simon arrived by air from Paris today, completing their tour of European capitals undertaken in an effort to establish a new peace pact in western Europe. Premier MacDonald brought with him no assurance that France would support the four power peace treaty proposed by Premier Mussolini to end the danger of imminent international misunderstandings, but he did have an understanding with Premier Daladier that France would consent to enlarge the conversations over the four power pact and would consent to a review of the whole European situation. The powers which would be involved in the treaty as proposed by Mussolini are Italy, France, England and Germany.

Washington, D. C., Mar. 22.—(#)— The nomination of Robert Worth Bingham of Louisville, to be ambassador to England was unanimously approved today by the senate foreign relations committee, which had held up action for a week. Action on the nomination had been delayed last week at the request of Senator Robinson (R., Ind.), who wanted speeches made in Scotland by Bingham some years ago looked into to see if it did not indicate a strong pro-British leaning.

| Paris, March 21.--(AP)—Premier Mussolini's peace plan was accepted in principle today by the French, who made modifications which have been referred to Rome. The moral support of the United States for the four-power peace pact is ardently desired, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain told the press after all-day negotiations with Premier Edouard Daladier and Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour of France. Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, also took part in the conversations. French Desire The French ministers said in a communique that they desire to see the four European powers—France, Britain, Italy and Germany—cooperate to keep peace within the framework of the League of Nations.

Washington, March 22.—(AP)—Efforts of Senator Robinson of Arkansas, the democratic leader, to obtain senate confirmation of Robert W. Bingham of Kentucky as ambassador to England were balked today by objections from Senator McNary of Oregon, the republican leader. The foreign relations committee had unanimously approved the Bingham nomination a few minutes before, but unanimous consent was needed for immediate action by the senate, and with the McNary objection action on confirmation had to be postponed until tomorrow. McNary explained on the floor he was objecting to action in the absence from the senate chamber of Senator Borah (R. Idaho), former chairman of the foreign relations committee.

LOS ANGELES, March 22—(AP)— Charging mental cruelty, H. B. Warner, English-born screen actor, has filed suit for divorce against Mrs. Rita Stanwood Warner in superior court here. The complaint says the couple separated March 4, 1931, and charges that prior to that time Mrs. Warner would stay out until the early hours of the morning and not explain where she had been.

BORDON, March 21.—()—All through this afternoon the doors of the hall at the Duke of York’s military school in Chelsea, where Lieutenant Norman Ballue-Stewart is being tried on charges of having sold his country’s military secrets, were locked and guarded. Secret witnesses were giving evidence. Some of these witnesses are foreign subjects and, according to the prosecution, their lives might be jeopardized if their names were published. Only once during the afternoon were the doors opened and then two women came out and drove away in a taxicab. One of them was weeping. At a public session this morning, counsel for the young lieutenant intimated that third degree methods had been used in the investigation. This was denied by Lieutenant Colonel F. H. N. Syimus, who conducted the preliminary questioning of the accused officer. The lieutenant colonel asserted he did not believe Lieutenant Bal

Paris, March 22,—()—Premier Daladier of France, it was believed today may go to Italy to meet Premier Mussolini of that nation as the next step in efforts to organize a four-power peace club. It was thought the two may meet in northern Italy, as Il Duce still is unwilling to leave Italy. No Plans Made. No plans, it was said semi-officially, had yet been made for the meeting, which was still only a possibility dependent on Signor Mussolini’s reaction to conversations in Paris between Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and French officials. French government circles were increasingly optimistic over the possibility of an eventual accord. “We see a ray of sunshine,” said a government spokesman. France's efforts to widen the scope of the accord is allaying fears of Poland and the little entente, it was said. It remained to be seen, however, on what basis they would participate,

1933-09-18.text: President Roosevelt is warning the world arms conference that he will wash his hands of the whole program unless the dilly-dallying over reaching an armament reduction agreement is ended. Norman H. Davis, the President's special envoy, said on his arrival here today. Davis came from London with Arthur Henderson, president of the Geneva Conference, for preliminary French-British-American talks here before the Geneva meeting. Davis stressed that there is no Roosevelt disarmament plan and that the United States is contributing nothing new to the conversations, standing on the wide proposals it has already made. Davis is visiting Paris to learn what the French and British are willing to do. (Further Details of Disarmament on Page 9)

PARIS, Sept. 18 (AP)——The desire for a three-power front on disarmament motivated French leaders today as American and British representatives joined them in conversations preliminary to the reopening of the arms conference in Geneva next Monday. French newspapers and legislators have pointed to Nazi demonstrations at the border and what they call the possibility of the early completion of a German air fleet as requiring a firm stand against any loosening of pacts governing armaments. Three Objects. From the French point of view, the current talks will have three objects: To compare notes on charges that Germany is rearming; to discuss a course should Germany refuse to accept a control plan which French opinion considers prerequisite to the acceptance of any disarmament treaty, and to get backing for a French proposal for international arms control before armaments are reduced. Ambassado

LONDON, Sept. 18.—(UP)—Norman H. Davis, American delegate to the world disarmament conference, today delivered a message to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald from President Roosevelt, promising full and practical collaboration on disarmament. The message, believed to have been in writing, assured the British premier of the president's unflagging interest in disarmament. It expressed the conviction that an armaments accord was of vital importance to economic recovery. The opinion was expressed that agreement would reduce political tension and increase international confidence. Davis left for Paris after his talk with MacDonald at a breakfast at No. 10 Downing Street. Davis told the United Press he had another message for Premier Edouard Daladier of France, differently phrased because France's disarmament position differs from that of Great Britain. Arthur Henderson, president of the disarma

By the Associated Press Gales pounded the New England coast Sunday, as the tropical storm moved northeastward. The Coast Guard cutter Modoc left Wilmington, N. C., to aid the tanker Fuel Oil, crippled from Saturday's hurricane 70 miles northeast of Frying Pan Shoals. New Jersey and New York City escaped heavy damage. Four were drowned in North Carolina; two in Pennsylvania. Damage in the Carolinas was placed at $2,000,000, with half of it around New Bern, N. C. Latest reports from the Tampico area of Mexico, where a storm struck Friday, said more than 100 were dead.

Havana, Sept. 17.—Beset with growing political and labor troubles in Havana and the interior of Cuba, the weak old government of Ramon Grau San Martin prepared for battle over the conference battle today with its potent opposition factions. Labor troubles still harassed the entire island and Americans in some areas were described as nervous. Commercial forces of Havana represented by 37 business organizations were added to four powerful political groups forming a growing menace to the power of San Martin's government. They announced a plan for a 24-hour general shutdown of business on Tuesday to protest workers' violence. At Havana, anti-American demonstrations were planned, Revolutionary women were the sponsors. Yesterday, 8000 Cubans paraded Havana shouting 'Down with Sumner Welles!' 'Down with American imperialism.'

CHICAGO, Sept. 18, (A?)—Dollar a bushel wheat came back to the grain pits today for the first time since August 11. A wave of buying was caused by a sharp advance of the British pound sterling to $4.76 and by opening strength in securities. The May delivery of wheat boomed up to $1.01½ a bushel at the start, 1½ cents higher than Saturday’s finish. However, the gains were quickly erased by profit taking and within a few minutes prices were back around Saturday’s closing levels. The advance in sterling which carried it within eight points of the normal par value of $4.86 was the chief bullish influence, traders construing it as meaning that inflation would soon be a certainty. Corn and all other grains followed wheat up and down. Some hedging pressure was noted at the advance.

PARIS. (UP) — France threatened today to submit evidence to the disarmament conference that Germany has persistently violated the Versailles treaty by secretly arming. Premier Édouard Daladier, foreign minister, and Joseph Paul-Boncour, in a conference with Capt. Anthony Eden, British parliamentary under-secretary for foreign affairs, and British Ambassador Lord Tyrell made the threat. France is known to have in a strong room of the foreign office information on German armament that has never been revealed. Daladier threatened that if any demand is made on France to disarm before real control of present armaments is tried out, France will reveal the evidence.

LONDON, Sept. 18.—(}—Anglo-American debt conversations are expected in London official quarters to begin in Washington October 5, it was learned today. The first interviews will be between Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, of the British treasury, and representatives of the United States treasury.

1933-01-03.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Jan. 3. (AP).—President Eamon De Valera announced the dissolution of the Dail Eireann today and called for the election of a new parliament January 24. It will meet February 8, just 11 months after De Valera assumed the presidency of the Free State Council, to decide whether his government will continue in power. The action of the De Valera government came as a surprise at a time when seven labor members of the Dail, on whose votes his majority has depended for several months, threatened to bolt. They opposed his policy on civil service pay reductions. Last month the De Valera government decided to postpone an election to fill vacancies caused by the death of two Cosgrave party members. It was believed then that if his Republican party could win those seats he would be ready to go before the country immediately in a general election in an effort to free himself

LONDON, Jan. 2.—At least nine lives were lost, and probably others perished, in a 60-mile gale which swept the coasts of England and Ireland today. Scotland and Northern Ireland were deluged by a fierce downpour which flooded fields and ran creeks and rivers out of their banks. The nine victims drowned when the Aberdeen trawler Venitia was wrecked on the rocky coast off Kincardineshire. Lifebuoys washed ashore revealed the name of the stricken vessel which could not be approached by lifeboats because of the high waves. There were no survivors of the vessel. Lifeboats from both Howth and Clogher Head returned to their home ports on the Irish coast tonight after failing to find any trace of the vessel, which was last seen about seven miles from the Skerries sending up distress signals. High winds in London and other cities felled trees and caused many window panes to be broken. Automobiles

Dublin, Irish Free State, (Tuesday) Jan. 3.—(AP)—The government sprang a surprise early this morning with the sensational announcement it had decided to dissolve the Dail Eireann and to hold the general elections January 24. The decision was taken at a prolonged cabinet meeting after which President De Valera, whose government recently was assailed because of its stand on civil service pay reductions, informed newspapermen that the Dail had been dissolved and that the new congress would meet Feb. 8. Confident of Position The president declared that the country’s attitude toward the government’s program left no doubt that the government enjoys the confidence of the electorate.

PEIPING (%) — Gen. Hsiao-Liang was warned today by ranking Japanese military and naval officials in North China that he would be held responsible for developments arising from the Shanhaikwan incident of the night of Jan. 1 when Chinese and Japanese troops clashed with casualties on both sides. The warning was conveyed in two separate letters, one in the presence of General Nakamura, commanding the Japanese troops in North China with headquarters at Tientsin, and the other from Japanese military and naval attaches here. At noon today the Japanese mission lacked confirmation of reports that the Japanese had entered Shanhaikwan. The latest Chinese official reports said the city was still in the hands of the Chinese, who had “repulsed the Japanese attack.” Future developments remained today subject to keen speculation here. Manchurian headquarters of the Japanese take the view that the clas

New Hamburg, Ont., Jan. 3.—Three boys plunged through the ice of the Nith river Monday and drowned in seven feet of water. Another was rescued by the father of one of the victims who was unaware his own son had been swept under the ice. Those drowned were Fred English, 8 years old; Garfield English, his brother, and Henry Goerts, 10. Henry Goerts Sr. rescued William Penner, 20, who was on the ice with the boys.

PARIS, Jan. 3. Jack Pickford, brother of Mary Pickford, and noted motion picture actor, died in the American hospital here today. Jack Pickford went to the American hospital in Paris early in December suffering from a breakdown with gastro-intestinal symptoms. At the time he was admitted to the hospital it was said he would take a long rest cure. He was 36 years old.

Tokyo, Today.—(/P).--Heavy fighting between Japanese and Chinese troops at Shanhaikwan, where the Great Wall reaches the sea, began Sunday night and continued throughout today, Rengo (Japanese news agency) dispatches said. Japanese reinforcements were rushed there from Suichun, and at 2 p.m. today a Japanese air squadron bombed the walled city of Shanhaikwan. Chinese accounts said the Japanese opened fire on Chinese troops without provocation. The Japanese reported that they had found two bombs in a Japanese police station on Sunday, that thereafter a detachment of troops was sent to Shanhaikwan city to protect Japanese residents and that Chinese fired on the detachment. This morning it was reported that four Chinese troop trains were moving northeastward toward Shanhaikwan to reinforce Chang Hsiao-Liang’s regulars who apparently were holding the walled city against the Japanese attack.

HAMBURG, Germany, Jan. 3. —(#)—Dr. Wilhelm Cuno, former chancellor of Germany and general manager of the Hamburg American Steamship line, died today. The shipping magnate was 57 years old. He died suddenly when he suffered a heart attack as he was about to start with his wife for a vacation ordered by his physician.

1933-02-20.text: (By The Associated Press) New York, Feb. 20—President-elect Roosevelt was ready to talk business today with the British on war debts and world economy recovery. He insisted upon coupling the two. Personally taking over the involved foreign situation, Mr. Roosevelt awaited the arrival of Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, upon his return late today from London. The Lindsay ship is due here at 1:30 p.m. A heavy round of Sunday conferences at the Roosevelt home indicated that imminent action was in prospect. The conferrees all were authorities on economics and resembled a cast Mr. Roosevelt might select to represent this government in the prospective world economic parley. Bernard M. Baruch, Professor Raymond Moley and William H. Woodin, all of New York, and the veteran Col. Edward M. House, authority on foreign affairs, were gathered about the Roosevelt table at one time or anothe

New York, Feb. 19 (®)— President-elect Roosevelt laid the basis for a “new deal” on world economics and war debts in a round of conferences today with his economic advisers on the eve of tomorrow’s meeting with Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador. The significant series of meetings throughout the day at the Roosevelt home on East Sixty-Fifth street included such callers as Bernard M. Baruch, financial authority; Professor Raymond Moley, expert on war debts; William H. Woodin, a close adviser of Roosevelt on economic affairs; and Col Edward M. House, veteran in the field of foreign affairs. These discussions were linked with the sudden invitation by the President-elect to the British ambassador returning from London to see him. All in all, there were signs of new and imminent action in the complicated world economic situation. Whether Mr. Roosevelt has any inkling of a new British

New London, Wis., Feb. 19 (®)—Truckloads of milk were spilled again today on Wisconsin highways as striking dairymen formed tight picket lines in their campaign for higher prices. The market blockade was concentrated around Waupaca County, and little milk reached New London. Nine truckloads of milk, approximating 25,000 pounds, were dumped this morning near Manawa. Order was maintained by picket lines, however, and no physical violence has been reported since yesterday. Frank F. Wheeler, district attorney of Outagamie County, said he conferred last night with Adjutant General Ralph Immel about the milk supply situation, but that no action was planned. While surly-tempered farmers, determined to force price increases, planned to camp all night along roadsides and stop all vehicles transporting milk in this vicinity, there were no indications that the strike sponsored by the Wisconsin Coop

LONDON, (Monday) (®, News has been received here from Sweden that Greta Garbo, film actress, has obtained permission to return to the United States, the Mail said. It is understood, the newspaper added, that Miss Garbo, who returned to Sweden last August, had considerable difficulty in getting the permit, because of a recent action in Hollywood seeking to weed out foreign stars. Greta Garbo left America with the simple announcement she was going “back to Sweden.” Not long ago it was reported in Stockholm that the actress would soon return.

BF CAECRR RATER BONAR PLENTY OF NEWS to start the week. Sir Ronald Lindsay comes back from London as fast as the Majestie can bring him and will talk today with President-elect Roosevelt about European debts and “a new deal” in world economics. The new deal, presumably, will mean that Uncle Sam must get along without his money. Sir Ronald, like all British diplomats, will say more than any one man could understand, so Roosevelt has sent for Bernard M. Baruch to help him listen and answer. And Professor Raymond Moley, very deep, will be there, observing, with William H. Wood—who also knows about money. * * * IN ROME, on the occasion of a saint's beatification, Pope Pius prayed publicly for the souls of Russians, Mexicans and Spaniards—for Russians, repudiating religion and the existence of God; for Spaniards and Mexicans, confiscating the property of the church and without religious leade

New York, Feb. 20—President-elect Roosevelt definitely took negotiations of European debt revision in his own hands today despite the fact that his inauguration is still almost two weeks off. As soon as the steamship Majestic docks this afternoon, he will see Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, who returns from several weeks of conferences with his home office over terms intended to reduce finally England’s $4,500,000,000 debt to the United States. This afternoon’s meeting between Mr. Roosevelt and Sir Ronald will be the second since the election. The first was in Warm Springs, Ga. nearly a month ago, just before the ambassador sailed for final instructions from Downing Street. Never before has a foreign envoy treated directly with an administration still to come into office. President Hoover, however, has turned all of the critical international situations over to Mr. Roosevelt.

LONDON, FEB. 15.—(U.S.)—Agreements from India’s fabulous hoards continue flowing like a yellow river to London and thence to nations of the western world famished for the precious metal. In the last 18 months India has shipped 30,000,000 pounds (approximately $400,000,000 at par) to London. Yet the vast hoards are scarcely touched. It is estimated that India has more than 450,000,000 pounds (approximately $2,250,000,000 at par) hoarded. This is half as much as the United States' entire gold stocks. In the past week $46,195 pounds of Indian gold arrived here, while Britain shipped 409,576 pounds of gold to New York. The flow of gold from India was an important factor in the world scramble for the metal. For centuries, especially the last one, India has been a constant drain on the world’s surplus gold. She bought steadily and piled it up in the form of royal and private wealth. Then, afte

By United Press LONDON, Feb. 20—The United States War Department within the last two weeks has placed orders for 38 bombing planes worth $2,000,000 and 111 pursuit planes valued at $1,700,000, it was learned today. The bombers were ordered from the Glenn Martin Aircraft Co., and the pursuit planes from the Boeing Aircraft Co. REPORTS CONFIRMED

1933-09-03.text: Paris, Sept. 2. (AP)—Britain, France and Italy in identical notes today approved Austria’s plan to raise a special corps of 8,000 men for duty against “terrorist elements” within the country and on the German border. Austria requested the increase in her armed forces recently after propaganda leaflets attacking the Dollfuss government were dropped from airplanes, said by Austrians to have come from Germany, and after a German broadcasting campaign against the Vienna government had got under way. Foreign Minister José Paul-Boncour, in a note published today and dated yesterday, said the French government would raise no objection to the recruiting of 8,000 men if Austria followed the plan which she had submitted to the powers.

Paris, Sept. 2 (P)—France, for the first time publicly, has lent support to Austria’s campaign against the Nazi Party. The French government, acting with Great Britain and Italy, today approved Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss’ request for authorization to raise a special corps of 8,000 men for duty against “terrorist elements” within Austria on the German border. Corps of Exceptional Character Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour, commenting on France’s action, said France agreed to the request “in view of the notably temporary and exceptional character of the corps envisaged and the fact it will be recruited by voluntary enlistment and not surpass the limits of men and equipment fixed by the treaty of St. Germain.” M. Paul-Boncour said that consent was given “for as long as the special conditions exist.” Among the reasons for the special corps given by Chancellor Dollfuss, he said, the Fr
that ocs aaa & ave seeaeer Se & oon = LONDON, Sept. 2.—(#)—Reuter’s News agency reported from Rome that Premier Mussolini today signed a pact of neutrality and non-aggression with Soviet Russia.

Madrid, Sept. 2.—(4)—Unusually reliable monarchist circles reported today that a marriage has been planned between Juan Carlos, 20 years old, heir pretender to the Spanish throne, and Princess Maria, 19, daughter of the king of Italy. The ceremony is scheduled to be held soon, according to these reports, and it will be with full pomp and honor in accordance with the rank of the pretender-ship, with the pope officiating and Premier Mussolini officially sponsoring it. The guests, it is said, will include highest-ranking representatives of the nations, among whom will be the Prince of Wales. Juan Carlos became heir pretender after the marriage of his elder brother, the prince of the Asturias, and Edelmira Sampedro, daughter of a Cuban merchant, on June 21. The second son, Jaime, is a deaf mute, and thus the pretendership went to Juan Carlos.

| By FREDERICK OECHSNER United Press Staff Correspondent NUREMBERG, Germany, Sept. 2—(A.P.)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler today pointed his Nazi followers toward an ideal of a united Germany, purely German in race and culture, ruled from above and pledged to combat Jewry and pacifism. While the rank and file of the “victory” convention drank beer, ate sausages, and cheered leaders at every opportunity, there was being exposed a definite national socialist policy, intended to consolidate the Hitler regime along militant Fascist lines. Hitler himself disclosed the main features in a radio speech and in a proclamation read before a meeting of delegates to the Nazi convention. Most important from the historical standpoint, he sounded the doom, insofar as he can bring it about, of the German federal states, which Bismarck thought were the pillars of the old empire. Bismarck fought to preserve the s

VIENNA—A 22-year-old ex-soldier, incensed over his dismissal from the army for Nazi activities, shot and wounded Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in an assassination attempt Tuesday. The assailant was identified by police as Rudolf Dertil. He stepped up to Dollfuss as the chancellor was leaving his car in front of the parliament building, pretended to hand him a petition and then opened fire. Dollfuss was wounded in the chest and arm, but was able to go home, swathed in bandages, after emergency treatment.

ROME, Sept. 2.—(/)—General Francesco De Pinedo, Italian airman killed today attempting to take off from New York on a projected flight to Bagdad, had been in eclipse for four years. Two hypotheses, one involving money and the other a princess, were advanced to explain his loss of the limelight. According to one theory, De Pinedo dared pay attention to Princess Giovana, now the Bulgarian queen, and King Victor Emanuel requested that he be transferred outside of Italy. The other hypothesis revolves around the fact that De Pinedo neglected to make reports to General Italo Balbo on the money American Italians contributed after his plane burned in Arizona in 1929. When Balbo demanded an accounting, De Pinedo impulsively turned the money over to a fund for aviators’ orphans. He did this without asking General Balbo's permission and thereafter, it was said, coolness developed between the two me

Brooklyn — (4?) — General Francesco De Pinedo, one of Italy’s most famous airmen, met flaming death shortly after dawn today when his huge plane crashed and burned up at the start of a take-off for Baghdad, Iraq. A tremendous load of gasoline, 1,027 gallons, caused his giant red, green and purple plane to swerve from a concrete runway and hit a fence at Floyd Bennett airport. In a second it was a roaring mass of flames, and the flier was burned beyond recognition. The start of what the gallant flier had hoped would be a non-stop record flight became a scene of horror. Spectators shuddered and covered their eyes as they saw fire engulf the airman. Attendants rushed to the scene and tried to pull him out, but the flames forced them back. Michael Hicks Beach, a naval machinist’s mate, was badly burned about the face trying to reach De Pinedo with a fire extinguisher. The plane burned only a

1933-01-13.text: London, Jan. 13 (UP)—Plans for the greatest demonstration of unemployed in British history, far greater than the recent “hunger march” that disorganized London’s existence for nine days, were announced today. Organizers of the demonstration expected that 100,000 persons would assemble to protest the policies of the national government, especially regarding unemployment relief. The demonstration will be held in Hyde Park February 8, the day after parliament reassembles from the Christmas recess and just as the House of Commons starts considering business which will vitally affect the welfare of the nation’s 15,000,000 wage earners. Leaders of the national council of the Trades Union Congress, representing 4,500,000 trades unionists; the cooperative movement, with a combined membership of 7,000,000; and the labor party with a membership of 3,500,000 combined are planning the demonstration.

By the Associated Press. China, Jan. 12.—Opposing military leaders in the Shanhaikwan area were reported to have begun a peace parley at Chinwangtao today but dispatches from Jehol told of troop movements which indicated that the armies were preparing for new campaigns. Japanese planes were said to have reconnoitered Jehol City, once the summer residence of the Manchu emperors and now the provincial capital. The planes circled the capital and flew north over Chaoyang, the second largest city, 1400 miles away and close to the Manchurian border. The same sources reported Japanese troops in Manchuria and southern Jehol were preparing for an invasion of the latter province and that probably there would be sharp fighting. One Japanese expedition from Shanhaikwan was reported marching through Jehol to the town of Lingyuan, 90 miles northwest of Shanhaikwan, on the way to Jehol City.

ATHENS, Greece, Jan. 1d.) —The government of Premier Panayoti Tsaldaris was defeated in parliament by a vote of 109 to 91 this morning, and thus was removed from power after existing ten weeks. Former Premier Eleutherios Venizelos had withdrawn his conditional toleration of the government headed by the royalist leader notwithstanding its denial of a rumored “dictatorship.” Following upon the resignation of Tsaldaris, Venizelos indicated three solutions: First, a coalition cabinet of all parties; second, a new Tsaldaris cabinet on condition the ministers of war and marine were not headed by politicians, or third, a cabinet under a small party leader. Under the last solution the head of the government probably would be George Kafandaris, who was premier in 1924 and was generally regarded as the best financed among politicians.

Tokio, Jan. 14 (UP)—Fear that the Russian steamer Sakkalin may have sunk in the sea of Okhotsk increased today after weak radio messages, indicating the ship was on fire and surrounded by ice floes, ceased. The messages were intercepted by the Hakodate and Oha stations. They were weak and garbled. The messages ceased today. The last known position of the ship was east of the island of Sakhalin, off the northeast coast of Siberia. The number of passengers and crew aboard was not officially determined, although Japanese sources estimated the total at over 200.

Madrid, Jan. 12.—(AP)—A death toll of 70 in the extremist disorders this week in several parts of the young Spanish republic was counted tonight as reports trickled in of a new outbreak at the town of Casa Viejas, where civil guards and assault guards bombed a house in which extremists had taken refuge. Reports reaching Cadiz from Casa Viejas said that the dead and seriously wounded in that region were estimated at this time at more than 650. Communications with that district were almost impossible.

Moscow, June 13—Six prominent Soviet officials were served drastic punishment today by the Communist party's central and central control committees for offenses against the party. Two were expelled from the party, another removed from the central committee, and the other reprimanded. Publication last night of the resolutions of the joint session of the two committees disclosed a new 'right opposition' within the inner councils of Communism. Michael Tomsky, chairman of the state publishing department, Alex Ryhoff, commissar of communications, and Vassili Schmidt, chairman of the state arbitration committee were placed under 'strictest discipline' and warned they were not sufficiently active in the party's fight against anti-Soviet elements. A. P. Smirnoff, vice commissar for agriculture of the Russian Socialist Federated Republic, by far the largest of the seven republics in the union, wa

- Vladivostok, Jan. 13—The Japanese steamer Sakhalin, which sent out distress calls Thursday, is afire in the north Pacific, according to word received today. Two hundred passengers and a crew of about 50 men are aboard. Soviet steamers were reported

PORT ARTHUR, Jan. 12, (P) — The yacht Wild Duck, which bore European royalty and American millionaires on pleasure cruises in the “guy nineties,” was towed out of the ship channel today and scuttled. The 138-foot vessel, once the property of J. P. Morgan, was raised from the spot where it sank during the August hurricane in six days and was sent to the bottom again in about 15 feet of water behind the west jetty guarding the channel's entrance.

1933-01-24.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, Jan. 24.—(A.P.)—Another battle in the long feud between the two outstanding figures in Irish politics—Eamon De Valera and William T. Cosgrave—was being decided today at the polls. A new Dail Eireann was being formed, which in turn will select the head of the government. Tall, dark American-born De Valera and the almost dapper, sandy-haired Cosgrave, each wound up his campaign with jubilant predictions that he would be the dail’s choice for president of the council. The election is upon the principle of proportional representation—the last dail included 153 members and this will slow up the counting, which does not begin until tomorrow. President De Valera, who called for the election in an unexpected political move three weeks ago, is the champion of complete Irish independence which he has extended to the economic field in the past year. He seeks endorsement of

LONDON, Jan. 24—(4)—The condition of John Galsworthy, British novelist and 1932 winner of the Nobel prize in literature, was causing grave concern. Galsworthy is suffering from anemia and was reported decidedly weaker. He was at his home at Hampstead. A heavy cold contracted early in December brought on his present condition.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 24.—()— Attention has been centered on the report of the central control board of Great Britain on what constitutes an intoxicating liquor by the Senate judiciary committee's adoption of its findings. The committee fixed the permissible alcoholic content in the Collier-Blaine beer and wine bill at 3.95 per cent by weight. This percentage was held by the official British commission after an exhaustive inquiry, to be non-intoxicating. The commission found that “any form of alcoholic liquor can cause drunkenness, if such a quantity of it is taken, at once or within a short time, as will lead to the presence of the drug in the blood above a certain proportion, which in the case of the average healthy adult may be put provisionally at from 0.15 to 0.2 per cent.” The smaller percentage, it found, would be produced by a gill and a half of whisky at proof or more than four pints

DUBLIN, Jan. 24.--(UP)—Violence marked the balloting in the free state's general election today. Members of Eamon de Valera’s Fianna Fáil clashed with followers of William T. Cosgrave at Dalkey, a few miles outside of Dublin. Revolver shots were fired, although no casualties were reported. The lord mayor of Dublin, en route to a voting booth, was waylaid by a group of young hotheads in Gardiner Street. He defended himself with his fists until civic guards arrived. The fighting at Dalkey was started by systematic tearing down of Cosgrave posters by Fianna Fáil supporters, who also painted over signs and slogans reading “vote for Cosgrave.”

Washington, Jan. 23, (AP). — New moves in the war debt problem tonight brought Italy and Belgium informally into the rapidly developing discussions following reopening of debt negotiations with Great Britain. Acting without instructions from his government, Ambassador Rosso of Italy made inquiries of the State Department over the prospect of talking debts with the United States. When it paid its debt due last December 15, the Fascist Grand Council in a declaration said it would be necessary to negotiate a new agreement before the next payment is due June 15. Ambassador May of Belgium—which along with France and several other debtors defaulted its December 15 payment—also called at the State Department to inform himself on the status of debt discussions. Czechoslovakia, which paid its December 15 installment, received a full report on the question from its legation last week after inquiri

LONDON (”) — President-elect Roosevelt's intention to reserve to himself the final authority for Anglo-American debt negotiations added weight today to reports that Premier MacDonald himself will head the British delegation to Washington. The Daily Mail said: "It was regarded in official circles as almost certain that Mr. MacDonald will head the British mission and he is expected to leave toward the end of February, accompanied by Neville Chamberlain and Walter Runciman." As head of the national government, Mr. MacDonald was expected to find it even more desirable to lead the British mission since Mr. Roosevelt indicated he will be active personally in the dealings.

Dublin, Jan. 24, UP—The Irish Free State went to the polls today in a general election after a campaign marked by the most bitter animosities since the civil war ten years ago. Both Republican supporters of Eamon de Valera and the party of William T. Cosgrave predicted victory. A record poll was expected, with the result close. The Center party was expected to hold the balance of power, between the Republicans and their opposition. Riots and street fights featured the end of the campaign. Cosgrave had a narrow escape when Republicans broke up a meeting at Tralee. Most members of the cabinet and prominent politicians were reported to have carried revolvers, and the bodyguards of Cosgrave and de Valera were reinforced in the final days of the campaign. Fifty thousand young Irish voters taking part in their first election may turn the tide in favor of de Valera. The women's vote will predom

Washington, Jan. 23 (P)—The supreme court today held international treaties above domestic law, ruling that British and Canadian rum running vessels cannot be seized if they are more than one hour's sailing from the American shore even though inside the 12-mile limit, prescribed by the tariff. The decision, disallowing the seizure of the Nova Scotian runner Mazel Tov off Massachusetts in 1930, possibly averted serious friction with Canada. The latter, through its minister in Washington last December, informed the state department that unless the policy laid down today by the highest court were followed, his government would regard the anti-smuggling treaty with this country as practically nullified. This treaty, put in force in 1924, set the seizure limit at one hour's sailing. That means that a boat capable of traveling but 11 miles an hour cannot be seized eleven and a half miles off s

1933-01-04.text: Cherbourg, France,--(AP)--The crack French liner l'Atlantique, serving in the South American run, was wrecked by fire of undetermined origin in the English Channel early today. Most of the crew was believed to have been rescued by the German steamer Ruhr after abandoning the l'Atlantique, which carried no passengers and was en route to dry dock at Havre for the annual overhauling.

CHERBOURG, Jan. 4.--(INS)- Belief that thirty members of his crew were lost when the French luxury liner Atlantique burned in the English Channel was expressed tonight by Captain Behoot, commander of the ill-fated vessel, on his arrival here from the scene of the disaster. No passengers were aboard the vessel, en route to its home port for overhauling. Cause of the fire is unknown. The crew was rescued by two steamers.

TOKYO, Jan. 4.—(UP)—The government instructed Japanese military and diplomatic authorities in Manchuria and North China today to avoid aggravation of the Shanhaikwan situation resulting from occupation of that Chinese city by Japanese troops. They were instructed to seek a peaceful “localized” settlement. The Japanese legation at Peiping was ordered to negotiate for this purpose with Marshall Chang Hsiao-Liang, the Chinese commander in North China. (A Peiping dispatch today said Marshal Chang requested the Japanese to send communications concerning the Shanhaikwan incident to the Chinese National government at Nanking. It was believed at Peiping that this eliminated any chance for a local settlement.) The vernacular newspaper reported that General Suzuki, in command at Shanhaikwan, had already proposed terms for a truce to General Ho Chu-Kuo, commander of the Chinese garrison which was o

HAMBURG, Jan. 3. — Former Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno, general manager of the Hamburg-American Steamship Line, collapsed on the doorstep of his country home near Hamburg today and died in his wife’s arms. They were just about to leave on a vacation ordered by his physician, and their automobile was waiting for them, the motor running. Dr. Cuno was 56 years old. Death was caused by a heart attack. He had been suffering from a heart ailment for several days and yesterday his physician informed him that he must take a vacation. His death caused universal regret in official, business and shipping circles. Messages of condolence were received at the home from all parts of the world.

CHERBOURG, France, Jan. 4 (AP) — The French liner L'Atlantique, which operates to South America, caught fire from an undetermined cause early today while en route from Pauillac, near Bordeaux, to Le Havre. Abandoning the ship two hours later, the crew of about 240 was rescued by the Hamburg-American liner, Ruhr. The L'Atlantique was proceeding without passengers to Le Havre for overhauling. The Maritime Prefect at Cherbourg sent the Minelayer Pollux to the scene while other boats were held ready to assist, but the liner was believed lost. The L'Atlantique, 41,000 tons and 225 meters long, was launched in September 1931. It was the pride of the South American service in which it had only made 10 trips. It was the second fire occurring on a large French liner within a year. The Georges Philippar, also a new and luxurious vessel but owned by a different line in the far eastern service, burn
ATHENS, Jan. 4.—(#)—The government today ordered payment of 30 per cent of the interest on the American loan of 1929 through Speyer company and the National City Bank of New York.

MONANRNBi, Jan, 8 —(AP)— A graphic picture of the Japanese bombardment and resultant capture of Shanhaikwan was slowly forming today through fragmentary dispatches which trickled in from Shanhaikwan and Chinwangtao. A day of horror preceding the fall of Shanhaikwan was being revealed, in which the casualties were reported to be high. When the Japanese infantry swept into the half-ruined city following a naval aerial bombardment, fierce hand-to-hand fighting resulted in which 300 Chinese soldiers were reported killed. Other advices stated that 2,000 were slain. Advices indicated the Chinese were defeated by force of superior armaments, the reports saying that the Chinese and Japanese infantry strength were about equal, but the Japanese used naval guns, field guns, and air bombers which rained death and destruction, overpowering the Chinese who used rifles, hand grenades, machine guns, and

SPRINGFIELD, I., Jan. 4.—National Guardsmen were ordered today into Christian County, scene of mine strife in which two persons have been killed and 14 wounded since late yesterday. After receiving advices from military observers Adjutant General Carlos H. Black ordered five companies sent to the county from Central and Southern Illinois towns in an attempt to restore order.

1933-04-28.text: Geneva, April 28. (AP)—The United States dramatically allied herself with Britain today at the world disarmament conference when Norman H. Davis announced that the American delegation would oppose any attempt to weaken the draft arms convention prepared by the British. The American ambassador-at-large said he regarded the British draft treaty as a very valuable contribution and a definite step toward the limitation of armaments. He added that the United States looked upon it merely as the first step in disarmament, indicating that others must follow until armaments are brought down to their proper level. Germany had given concrete expression to her demand for equality in armaments when she filed a series of amendments to the draft convention indicating dissatisfaction with the size of the army accorded to Germany. Germany insisted it must get all the weapons of defense allocated to other

| LONDON, Apr. 27.—(AP) — Trade agreements with Denmark, Argentina, and Germany were announced today by the British government to enlarge Great Britain’s foreign markets. Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade, and Julio A. Roca, vice president of Argentina and head of a commercial delegation to Europe, initiated a commercial pact in which “all points of principle” were agreed upon. Subsequent negotiations in Buenos Aires will deal with tariffs, but authentic reports said the understanding involves a loan by British financial houses aggregating $38,000,000 to run for twenty years. Under the Anglo-German reciprocal trade and tariff concessions, the United Kingdom granted tariff changes in a limited field in return for the doubling of quotas for British coal exports to Germany. The Danish market for industrial products will be increased by the Anglo-Danish agreement in return for

PARIS, April 28.—(AP)—France is prepared to take a huge loan from Great Britain to bolster her financial position, it was disclosed today when details of the monetary accord between the two nations became known. A statement will be issued tonight by Georges Bonnet, finance minister, outlining the nature of the agreement, which is increasingly puzzling to financial circles as fresh details leak out. As the price of keeping France nominally on the gold standard and controlling the pound in foreign exchange, it appeared that the British government is ready to become a bondholder to the extent of more than 2,000,000,000 francs ($86,000,000) in French bonds. These bonds would be bought from the holdings in francs of the British equalization fund, instead of converting the francs to gold. Formally, in the conversation process, the gold would be shipped from the Bank of France to supplement Bri

Increasing optimism developed in Washington at the apparently successful efforts of President Roosevelt to clear the road for an actual accomplishment at the Geneva disarmament and London economic conferences. There was indication that the question of war debts was being pushed again into the background for a time as the President continued conversations with Edouard Herriot of France and Premier Bennet of Canada. The Senate approved the section of the administration’s inflation legislation which would authorize the President to reduce the gold content of the dollar. It adjourned until tomorrow, however, By The Associated Press. Geneva, April 27.—The opinion was expressed in disarmament conference circles tonight that in view of recent developments in the United States any nation electing to start a war will have no chance for success if America throws her economic and financial resource

Washington, April 27 (4)— President Roosevelt pushed forward his campaign for world disarmament and economic stabilization today with the French and Canadians, shelving temporarily the subject of war debts with a hint of general revision after the London parley in June. A willingness on the part of the administration to consider debts relief after the economic conference was indicated at the White House but it was emphasized that no debt plan has yet been proposed to the foreign emissaries. Mr. Roosevelt apparently intends to consider this situation after he concludes his search for formulas for economic restoration and disarmament in the pending foreign negotiations. With Prime Minister Bennett of Canada he began today the establishment of his “good neighbor” policy with attention focusing on improvement of trade relations, probably through reciprocal tariff agreements. In this connecti

LONDON, Apr. 28.—(-P)—When representatives of the nations gather here June 12 to discuss world economic conditions, they probably will be asked to consider the feasibility of a general international tariff truce. This was learned from a well-informed source which also was informed the invitations to the conference likely would be issued tomorrow. It was said the agenda under preparation by the conference committee may include a proposal that international tariff barriers be removed temporarily.

Paris, April 27 (P)—Premier Edouard Daladier was said by his friends today to be actively preparing to pay the defaulted debt installment due the United States. He is known to consider assurances of a moratorium on the June 15 payment by President Roosevelt as satisfactory and may decide to pay the defaulted installment immediately after former Premier Herriot’s return from Washington. It is more likely, however, that he will ask the chamber of deputies to approve the $19,000,000 interest which was due last December 15 when that body convenes May 16. Approval of the chamber never was necessary for payments on the debt but such action has been preferred by the government. President Roosevelt’s receptiveness to a consultative pact for the security of peace and general disposition to work with Europe has strongly impressed the government. An official spokesman said it was “distinct evolutio

Rome, April 28—(#)—The Italian air ministry announced today the finding of an Air-Orient passenger plane, which crashed early this week in a sparsely settled district of Calabria. Five of its occupants were dead and three were alive. Search for the airplane, which was en route from Corfu to Naples, had been conducted all week on land and sea. It disappeared on Sunday. The survivors of the crash were seriously injured and suffering from hunger and shock. The large seaplane was a complete wreck.

1933-02-13.text: LONDON, Feb. 13—Premier Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons today the debt discussion at Washington next month would range over the whole program outlined for a projected world economic conference. He did not indicate that the British delegation would be empowered to make definite decisions at Washington. At Washington the unemployment situation was said to have reached an all-time peak. Twelve million American workers are estimated by President William Green of the American Federation of Labor to have been out of work during January. Green said reports from affiliated organizations indicated that unemployment increased 300,000 over the December peak, reaching a new record during January. He added that institution of the shortened work week in some industries had resulted in a lessening of the usual seasonal employment decline. “Unemployment in January was at its all-time peak,” h

London, Feb. 13 (UP)—Great Britain made it plain today for the first time since the war debts crisis arose that she is now ready to give to the United States something tangible in return for revision. The announcement of Premier Ramsey MacDonald in the House of Commons that the government had agreed to discuss economic problems at Washington was regarded as an about face since Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, declared in a speech less than two weeks ago that there will be no “swapping deal.” The change in the government's attitude represents a signal victory for Franklin D. Roosevelt in his first approach to probably the most pressing foreign problem he will be called on to meet when he enters the White House.

London, Feb. 13 ()- Field Marshal Sir William Robertson, one of the most important military leaders among Allied commanders during the World War, is dead. The chief of staff of the British army during three years of that world conflict passed away suddenly Sunday at the age of 75. Sir William had the unique distinction of being the only man in British history to rise from the ranks to receive a field marshal's baton. He received many decorations for service in Indian campaigns and the Boer War as well as in the World War. In recognition of his war service he received a baronetcy and a grant of 10,000 pounds in 1919.

Vienna, Feb. 13.—(%)—The ominous rustle of secret documents again is disturbing Danubian countries. Less than 24 hours after the British and French ministers here renewed a formal request for information concerning a mysterious arms shipment from Italy allegedly to Hungary, it leaked out from diplomatic quarters that the Hungarian military attaché's office in Belgrade had been raided and that the Hungarian minister to Jugo-Slavia had protested. The Belgrade government was reported to have replied it must have been burglars who entered the office. This did not satisfy the Hungarians, however, who pointed out that the intruders did not touch customary valuables such as money and jewelry, and removed only documents which later mysteriously were returned. It was recalled that a widespread espionage plot was uncovered recently in the Rumanian post office and that shortly thereafter martial la

London, Feb. 13 (UP)—Amy Johnson Mollison may attempt a 5,000 mile solo flight from New York to Rio De Janeiro to join her husband, Captain James A. Mollison, on an aerial tour of South America, she revealed today. “Come out if you can by the 26th,” Mollison, who flew the South Atlantic alone last week from America to Brazil, cabled his wife. Mrs. Mollison considered the possibility of shipping her plane, the “Desert Cloud,” to New York and flying down the east coast to Rio De Janeiro. Mrs. Johnson established a new record for an England-Cape Town flight in the “Desert Cloud.” Her husband has flown both the North and South Atlantic in the “Heart’s Content.”

* % LONDON, 1, Feb. 13.—The next war will not be long in coming if the disarmament conference at Geneva breaks down, but the war will be over in a few weeks, Gen. Sir Ian Hamilton told a meeting of the British Legion here. “The next war will take as many weeks as the World War took years,

London, Feb. 13—() — Admiral Sir Henry Hervey Campbell, close friend of King George, died today. He was 67 years old. Sir Henry and the king were midshipmen together on the warship Canada in 1883 and 1884.

Berlin, Today.—(/).—Sanguinary clashes between Chancellor Hitler's National Socialists and their political opponents showed no signs of abatement today with at least eleven persons slain and 23 injured in weekend battles. Slayings occurred in eight different towns and cities in various sections of the Reich. Nazis, who claimed they were fired on from Communist headquarters in Elsleben, raided the building and at least three persons were killed and 15 hurt in hand-to-hand fighting. Communists were reported to have hidden their dead and injured. Two were killed in Bochum and one each in Strassfort, Dessau, Breslau, Dortmund, Stuttgart and Bensheim. Police shot at two women who left their windows open when Nazi storm troops were passing. Since Hitler came into power two weeks ago, citizens in many places have been ordered to keep windows and doors closed while Nazi troops pass in order to p

1933-12-18.text: WESTPORT, IRISH FREE STATE, Dec. 17.—(4)—Blue-shirted General Eoin O'Duffy, United Ireland party leader, was arrested today after a clash between blue shirts and police in a dramatic new climax to Ireland's political warfare. O'Duffy was arrested once, rescued by his followers, and then re-arrested after a hasty flight across a plowed field while his followers fought with those who sought to jail him. Driving toward Westport in his automobile to attend a United Ireland party meeting, the general was stopped by police and told he could go no further. He climbed a fence, escaped across the fields to the other end of town and was met by an escort of 100 horsemen who galloped up. Helmeted soldiers bearing rifles, gas masks and tear bombs patrolled the streets in motor lorries. Police again met O'Duffy, advising him he could not address the meeting, but a crowd of his supporters lifted him on

ROME, Dec. 18—(#)—The possibility of calling a four-power meeting to solve the disarmament tangle, said the strictly supervised Fascist press today, is likely to be discussed by Premier Mussolini and Foreign Minister Sir John Simon, of Great Britain, when the latter arrives early this week. Sir John’s visit to Rome will be the first of several calls at European capitals that he intends to make during the Christmas holidays in line with proposals for direct disarmament conversations following upon the adjournment of the disarmament conference at Geneva. It is known that Il Duce will exert every effort to bring about such a four-power meeting as was discussed in the Fascist press today. He considers it necessary at least as a preliminary to the continuance of the Geneva conference. Authorized information is that unless some get-together can be arranged so that opposing views can be harmoni

YARMOUTH, N. S., Dec. 18 (P— A warm fire and good food today cheered four American fishermen rescued yesterday after two nights and a day at sea in an open boat. The four—Harry Reynolds, John Muise, John Clements and Basil Mulloch, all of Boston—were the last of the Gloucester Ellen G. Marshall’s crew to reach land. With the 22 other members of the crew, they fled the ship when she caught fire Friday night scattering in dories on the tossing sea. Three of the crew drowned when the boat upset, but all of the others were saved.

DUBLIN, Dec. 18—(UFP)—Southern Ireland’s political crisis neared its climax today with Gen. Owen O'Duffy, leader of the fascist blue shirts and outstanding hero of the rebellion against Great Britain, a prisoner of the de Valera government. Defying the ban against his organization, O'Duffy went to Westport yesterday to address a mass meeting of followers. He was halted on the outskirts of town but escaped into a field. With a guard of 100 horsemen he entered the town and went to the meeting, his bodyguard overwhelming a strong police guard around the meeting hall.

London, Dec. 17.—(/P)—Communists who broke through a police cordon in Waterloo Place, near the German embassy, today, were beaten back by officers wielding batons. Several persons were arrested after a lively fight. The demonstrators, estimated to be 200 in number, were engaging in a protest against the Reichstag fire trial in Leipzig, Germany, where five defendants face charges of high treason. The communists later received permission to present a petition, but were unable to see the German ambassador. Later there were other sharp clashes in Regent Street, where a man waving a red flag was arrested. Police Charge There was trouble, too, in Trafalgar Square, where mounted police charged communists. Police established a guard over the German embassy and prepared to stay throughout the night.

TALLIN, Esthonia, Sept. 29 ()-- Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh arrived here this afternoon after an uneventful flight from Moscow. They left there shortly before noon after four days of sightseeing and study of Soviet aviation,

PARIS, Dec. 18.—(A4)—Chancellor Hitler’s demands for a bigger German army and more arms for the nation were pulled to pieces today by the superior war council of France. The military body laid down the foundations for a flat refusal by France of permission for rearmament of Germany. Ministers of war, navy, and air will discuss the proposed reply before the government sends it to Berlin.

LE MANS, France, Dec, 18 — French and foreign aviation enthusiasts gathered here today to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the first flight made by Wilbur Wright in France. The flight was made December 31, 1903. Wright flew 74 miles in two hours 18 minutes and reached the then astonishing height of 460 feet. He won a prize of $10,000 and the Michelin cup for the flight. All those who witnessed the flight from the official stand were alive today except Leon Bolee, the farmer who lent his fields for the exploit of the “Mud American.” Many of the officials were at a ceremony at a local theatre today under the auspices of the Chamber of Commerce.

1933-03-06.text: London, March 6 (AP)—Great Britain’s policy today was “business as usual” while the government here watched with sympathetic interest the firm steps being taken by the Roosevelt administration to deal with America's domestic banking problem. The exchange market in London will continue to deal with all currencies with the exception of dollars. Transactions in dollars were rendered impossible for the time being because delivery of dollars cannot be obtained during the American banking holiday. London banks have arranged to supply American travelers who have letters of credit in dollars with sterling for their immediate use. Japs Suspend Exchange Tokyo, March 6, (AP)—Japanese banks suspended foreign exchange operations today for at least two days. Leaders believe the suspension will continue for the duration of the American banking holiday. Stock exchanges in Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya were cl

Berlin, March 6.—(A.P.)—That the Reichstag in all likelihood will adjourn for two years after a brief session is the opinion in government circles after the national socialist landslide in the Reichstag and Prussian diet elections yesterday gave the national government a decisive majority. The cabinet will meet Tuesday to set the date for the Reichstag convocation. The electoral endorsement of the Hitler government's “nationalistic revolution” with its policy of suppressing communists and socialists leaves no doubt that the next few months will be devoted to wiping out the last vestiges of both democracy and communism. Hitler's Nazis will comprise the largest group ever sent to a German parliament, the final tabulation giving them 288 seats in a Reichstag with 647. Their nationalist allies got 52 seats. They got 17,264,000 and 3,131,000 votes respectively of the 39,290,000 cast. If the c

Berlin—Chancellor Adolf Hitler's command of Germany has been thunderingly affirmed. Returns still filtering in today showed that the Nazi rule was accorded a sweeping victory in Sunday’s election, both in the Reichstag and the Prussian state diet. The national revolution is on its way and will continue, the Nazi leader declared as his party’s poll mounted toward 20,000,000.

Athens, Greece—Martial law and a dictatorship were proclaimed today by General Plastiras after a general election in which the government was defeated. Plastiras said his action was taken to annihilate communism and secure public order.

BERLIN, March 6.—iA’—Seventeen million voters out of 39,600,000 manifested their confidence in Chancellor Adolf Hitler in Sunday's Reichstag election, and demonstrated to President Von Hindenburg that he sensed the desires of the German people rightly when he asked the chief of the Nazi brown shirts to take the helm of the ship of state. Germany now is well on the way to fascist dictatorship. Chancellor Hitler, by the vote of the people, has been given the legal tools to annihilate the last vestiges of the democracy which he considers a failure. The Nazis alone will command nearly 44 percent of the votes in the new Reichstag and can dictate to their nationalist co-workers in the government what must be done to shape a new Germany in accordance with Nazi ideals. As the Nazis in their pre-election campaign left no doubt that the communist deputies would never be allowed to take their seats

ATHENS, Greece, March 6 (P) General Plastiras, who was head of the revolutionary government of 1922-24, set up a military government in Greece today. Yesterday's general election resulted in a slight majority for the party headed by former Premier Panayoti Tsaldaris. General Plastiras asserted that in his opinion this situation did not permit of the establishment of a stable government.

| TOKYO, (4) — Three Japanese armies were turned upon Chinese forces today in a campaign to seize the whole eastern section of the Great Wall of China. The Great Wall, which has been garrisoned by Chinese for more than 2,000 years, is to be transformed into a fortification for the Japanese-sponsored state of Manchukuo. The Chinese were reported making a desperate fight to hold the wall, resisting much more strongly than they did in feeble attempts to halt the victorious sweep of the Japanese over Jehol province. Fanchiakow, one of the three important passes in the wall south of Jehol City, was occupied by the 14th infantry brigade under Maj. Gen. Heijiro Hattori after bitter fighting. The Hattori brigade took Lengkow, another pass, previously after pushing southwest from Lingyuan, central Jehol city.

Berlin, Mar. 6— Germany steered straight toward a Fascist dictatorship today as Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s government emerged victorious in the reichstag and Prussian state diet elections. In both elections, the people of the nation expressed confidence in the Nazi-Nationalist bloc now ruling the nation with an iron hand, giving the government workable majorities in each legislature. Against all other parties, the Hitler-Von Papen-Hugenburg combine gained control of 51.8 percent of the new reichstag seats and 52.3 percent of those in the Prussia diet. Thus the figures bore out the government’s pre-election prophecies, and placed Germany and Prussia under Nazi-Nationalist domination for what may prove a lengthy period. The Nazis gained 92 seats over their previous reichstag representation, making them the largest single party in the nation. The new reichstag will have 646 seats.

1933-05-19.text: Geneva, May 19.—The world arms conference took a definite step forward today when Germany accepted the British disarmament plan which President Roosevelt urged all nations to adopt in his message to the world. Rudolph Nadolny, German delegate, acting on Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s instructions, announced his country’s acceptance after Arthur Henderson, president of the conference, had appealed to Germany and other nations to withdraw their amendments, which were deadlocking the conference. The general commission of the conference convened this afternoon in a tense atmosphere, with its leaders expressing the view that the crisis had arrived and the next few days would mean peace or war for the world. Norman H. Davis, President Roosevelt's special ambassador, had told the United Press before entering the hall: “This is the most critical week of the conference. Either it blows up in our face

Moscow, May 19—4(?)—The Soviet government, it was learned today, will accept the invitation to participate in the London economic conference. Formal announcement to this effect may be expected in a few days. Although the invitation was received several days ago, Moscow so far has withheld acceptance, apparently waiting to gauge the extent of world opinion as to the usefulness of the parley. What concrete proposals the Soviet government will offer has not been revealed. It was considered certain Maxim Litvinov, commissar for foreign affairs, will head the Soviet delegation.

Geneva, May 19 (#)—Germany followed up today the conciliatory remarks in Chancellor Hitler’s Reichstag speech by announcing to the disarmament conference her acceptance of the British plan for an arms convention. “I hope this will be regarded as new proof of German moderation,” Rudolf Nadolny, spokesman for the Berlin government, said in making the announcement. Herr Nadolny’s address, conciliatory throughout, was received with many evidences of approval by the conference, which resumed its sessions full of hope because of President Roosevelt's disarmament initiative and the Hitler pronouncement. The French delegate, Rene Massiglia, declared that the German statement meant that there was now no obstacle in the way of concluding a disarmament treaty. Amid applause, Massiglia pledged France's cooperation to this end. Captain Anthony Eden, British delegate, praised the spirit of the German
