BERNE, Switzerland — King Feisal of Iraq died early today at a Berne hotel from a heart attack. The monarch, who was 48, had been under a heavy strain in the last few weeks because of reports of massacres of Assyrian Christians in his kingdom. When he arrived here, he refused to talk about reports he might abdicate and declared he would return to Iraq upon finishing the cure. He was famous for his exploits with Lawrence of Arabia during the World War. He came here from Baghdad three days ago with the intention of remaining two weeks. His health had been poor for some time, but the sudden turn came as a shock to his entourage.

BERNE, Switzerland, Sept. 8 (UP).—King Feisal of Irak died today of heart disease after a brief illness. Feisal was a descendant of Fatima who was the only surviving child of the Prophet Mohammed. He was one of the few real winners in the World War. He arrived here recently on a vacation that was delayed by the campaign of his army against Assyrian rebels. He was 50 years old. Feisal is succeeded to the throne by his eldest son, the Emir Ghazi, who was born at Mecca 21 years ago.

Berlin, Germany, Sept. 8 — The American embassy revealed today the German foreign office had presented its “deep regrets” for recent attacks upon two Americans who failed to return the Nazi salute to passing storm troopers in Berlin streets. The Embassy made the following announcement: “The German foreign office on September 7th presented orally to Ambassador Dodd, the deep regrets of the German government for the recent attacks upon American citizens, Samuel B. Bossard, of Philadelphia, and the son of A. V. Kaltenborn, a former Brooklyn editor, and informed the Ambassador the cases had been turned over to the police and officials of the Prussian ministry of the Interior with instructions to take the most energetic action possible under the circumstances.”

WASHINGTON—President Roosevelt, today called for a greater effort on the part of the public in relief for unemployed. He warned that there are many areas mingling the relief question with politics and then coming to the federal government “hat in hand” seeking federal funds. The President's remarks, in which he sounded a hopeful note of improved economic conditions, were made on the White House lawn to officials of the 1933 mobilization for human needs conference, He pointed out that it was first the duty of private citizens and private agencies to assist the destitute. That failing, the cities must step in, then the state and finally the federal government, he said. “It is the inherent duty of the federal government to keep people from starving,” Mr. Roosevelt told his listeners, explaining however, that because the federal government provided funds there should be no lessening of effor

Belfast, Maine.—(AP)—A mentally deranged man, who for years had been considered harmless, ran amuck in the business section of the city today, killed three men and critically wounded another, and then blew off his own head. Adrian Jones, the killer, suddenly appeared on Main street in front of the Masonic temple, just after the dinner hour, with a shotgun in each hand. People scurried into doorways and around the corners of buildings. He first shot down Herbert F. Ellis, aged 65, an insurance man. As Ellis slumped to the sidewalk, Jones turned to a man who had been unable to find cover and said: "Well, I've got that fellow all right." Then Jones walked rapidly down the street and turned off on Washington street. Here he entered the offices of a trucking concern operated by W. W. Blazo, aged 75, and his son, Raymond, 40 years old. He poured shots into both and went into the nearby office

Havana, Sept. 8. (P)—The commission of five now in control of the government refused today to consider "a suggestion that they reinstate Provisional President Carlos Manuel De Cespedes, who was ousted by a coup d'état Monday, to preside over a cabinet representing all factions. For two hours the members of the commission conferred with the leaders of the various revolutionary groups. In their refusal to consider the return of Dr. De Cespedes they were supported by Cuban students, who played an important part in the ousting of President Gerardo Machado last month and in the downfall of the provisional government that succeeded him. "There’s nothing new but delay, linger and wait,’’ said Joaquain Martinez Saenz, at the conclusion of the two-hour session. 1933-06-28.text: France’s battle to sustain the franc, principal currency tied to gold since the United States joined Great Britain and most of the nations of the world in the retreat from the gold standard, appeared today to French financial experts to be lost and devaluation was regarded as imminent. Development in the crisis confronting France and the other European nations still tied to gold—Switzerland, Holland and Belgium—moved swiftly with London the scene of efforts to save the gold standard. Enlist Aid of Moley Stabilization was the goal of the gold nations and they considered a dramatic appeal to assistant secretary of state Raymond Moley to enlist his aid in their fight to remain on gold, with the prospect they would like the dollar be stabilized somewhere near its present level. The latter part of the war Germany had chutes and Udet had his only 11 days when his plane was shot down. Had there been no chute there would have been no Udet today. LONDON, JUNE 28. (AP).—The world economic conference radiated the impression this morning that it was waiting on the presence of Assistant Secretary of State Raymond Moley, who popularly was supposed to be bringing from his chief in Washington medicine to cure many ills of the great assemblage. The lobbies were throbbing with steady talk of the man who has been heralded in the press as a mysterious but all-knowing “head of President Roosevelt’s brain trust.” Few men have entered London with such great expectation built on their address. But, if Mr. Moley had concrete proposals or suggestions for removing some of the many controversies which are blocking the progress of the conference they were carefully guarded. Whatever he said, he said in private, and the American delegation remained similarly silent. Almost coincident with the arrival of the assistant secretary of State there was an i

LONDON, June 28.—An appeal to Secretary of State Cordell Hull for aid in currency stabilization having failed, the gold standard countries of Europe met privately today and frantically tried to organize a gold standard defense league. While representatives of the central banks of the continental gold countries met in a committee room of the world economic conference, Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England conferred with representatives of the Bank of France in Threadneedle Street. Esthonia abandoned gold this morning and fears were expressed in many quarters that all remaining gold standard countries would be forced off within seventy-two hours. The effect of developments was reflected on the money market where the pound soared against the dollar, reaching $4.304 at 1:50. Meanwhile, the monetary sub-committee of the economic conference at a public meeting unanimously approved a

London, the sub-committee of Senator Key Pittman’s gold resolution, which provides among other things for withdrawal of the yellow metal from circulation and reducing the gold coverage of central banks to 25 per cent was formally reported this morning by the sub-committee which has been studying it. This sub-committee reported its findings to its parent commission which now will consider the matter.

LONDON, June 28. (U.)—Hope for immediate agreement among four chief wheat producing nations to limit acreage seemed shattered today when it was learned on high authority that Australia would not adhere until European nations also agreed to do so. Stanley Scuce, chief Australian delegate, received new instructions from his government, that he must not commit Australia to any wheat restriction agreement with the United States, Canada and Argentina until European nations had agreed to limit production as it was said.

Geological Museum, London, June 28. (INS)—Arrival in London of Assistant Secretary of State Raymond Moley, who is considered by some European statesmen as the “real voice” of Washington, was signaled today by a renewed drive to persuade the United States to agree to some form of de facto currency stabilization. Behind closed doors, the American delegates to the world economic conference are being told that unless they agree to hitch the dollar to the pound and franc, the parley will fail, and the blame will be placed on the United States. It is patent the stabilization issue was revived to coincide with Moley's arrival in order to impress upon him, and through him upon President Roosevelt, the European contention that the responsibility rests with America. It is considered unlikely that the European campaign will succeed for with wheat at more than a dollar for the first time in three ye

LONDON, June 28—(INS)—Esthonia today joined the international flight from gold, abandoning the gold standard following an all-night sitting of the Esthonian parliament, it was reported in an Exchange telegraph dispatch from Riga. The decision, the dispatch stated, was likely to have considerable repercussions in other Baltic states, whose adherence to the gold basis is proving detrimental to their foreign trade.

1933-01-22.text: London Jan, 21--(AP)—George Moore, famous Irish novelist, died early today. He would have been 81 years old next month. Moore died in his widely known home in Finsbury Street. He was seriously ill only a few days, but his health had been failing due to old age for some time. Despite his advanced years and impaired health, Moore was active in the literary field close to the end. He left an uncompleted task in which he was greatly engrossed—editing and supervising a complete edition of his works. He also left an unfinished “modern” novel, a little more than half of which he had written.

Powered by a joint agreement between President Hoover and his successor-elect, Franklin D. WASHINGTON, Jan. 21—(P)—Washington and London were preparing today to revise downward Great Britain’s $4,500,000,000 war debt to the United States. Secretary of State Stimson called Sir Ronald Lindsay, British Ambassador, to the state department last night and gave him the eagerly awaited news that the United States would be ready to discuss debt reduction shortly after March 4. The British were invited to send a commission to Washington to carry on the negotiations. Stimson’s assurance was based on an agreement made at the White House conference yesterday by President Hoover and President-elect Roosevelt. To Begin Promptly They decided that the Hoover administration should prepare for the debt discussions so that they may begin promptly after Mr. Hoover enters the White House. C., Jan. 21.—President-elect Roosevelt’s agreement to discuss war debts with Great Britain in connection with “world economic problems” was hailed today by Chairman Borah of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee as “a matter of very great and heartening significance.” While Borah was throwing his powerful support back of the incoming policy in a formal statement, some of Mr. Roosevelt’s friends on Capitol Hill interpreted his move as the first step toward joint consideration of the debt and other international problems at the forthcoming world economic conference. New York, Jan. 21.—The 8, 3 American Merchant labored through mountainous seas today with 22 ship-wrecked British sailors, saved by the gallantry and seamanship of her master and crew. Four men were lost, It was a new page in the book of heroic rescues at sea. The scene was the north Atlantic, 1575 miles east of New York. A gale piled up seas as high as office buildings and marine officials ashore could see little possibility of rescue. Still Captain Gites C. Stedman of the American Merchant maneuvered his heavy liner around the stricken freighter, Exeter City, until the 22 seamen were taken off. He ran the American Merchant to the weather side, thus throwing the Exeter City in her lee. Three times the crew fired a life gun before a line was hurled across the Exeter City. The British seamen made it fast and hauled a light cable aboard, thus connecting the two ships. A lifeboat was lowere

LONDON, Jan. 21.—(UP)—Montague Norman, governor of the Bank of England, was married at the Chelsea registry office today to Mrs. Priscilla Cella Maria Worsthorne. The romance of the 61-year-old financier had not been suspected until formal notification of intention to wed was filed yesterday. Mrs. Worsthorne, divorced wife of Alexander Louis Wynand-Koch Worsthorne, is 33.

Washington—(4)—Sen. Borah said today the readiness of President-elect Roosevelt to hear Great Britain's debt case "is a matter of very great and heartening significance" and something Sen. may eventually be accomplished in economic recovery by that means. In a press statement, Borah, chairman of the foreign relations committee, said: "The rigid and rather strained situation with reference to these economic problems, without settlement of which the world can not start to recover, has been greatly changed for the better, and it is of the utmost importance. "I take it that the President-elect is not simply performing an act of courtesy toward a friendly nation, as has been intimated, but that it is his purpose to take up these problems and make a start, if possible, toward their solution."

1933-07-13.text: London, July 13. (AP)—New life was injected into the drowsy world economic conference today by James M. Cox of Ohio when he convinced his colleagues of the steering committee that the parley could usefully continue despite the refusal of the federal reserve board to consider cooperation of central banks. In a fighting speech, which one delegate said, "curled the hair" of leaders of the conference, Mr. Cox gave a clear exposition of American differences and induced the committee to agree to keep working at the problems of silver and commercial indebtedness. Prominent gold bloc delegates had taken the position that the federal reserve board's veto on the discussion of central bank cooperation had effected the point to put an end to all discussion of monetary matters. LONDON, July 12.—(47)—The United States, the American delegation informed the world economic conference today, is unable to consider one of the three subjects left on the financial agenda of the parley—central bank co-operation. Indebtedness, silver and central bank co-operation were left yesterday as contemplated subjects for discussion, along with “any other subjects which may, by general agreement, be considered suitable” for further talks. Senator Key Pittman of Nevada reported to a private meeting of a monetary sub-committee that a pending resolution calling for central bank co-operation has been found unacceptable by the federal reserve board. As word leaked out of this development the conference was thrown into a new uproar the very day after a truce had been called on controversial subjects to open a way for peaceful expiration of the world congress within two or three weeks. LONDON (#) — With the world economic conference apparently drawing to an inconclusive close, the United States is inaugurating efforts to tighten trade bonds with individual nations, particularly neighbors in the western hemisphere. It was learned authoritatively today that behind the scenes of the conference quiet diplomacy is opening the way for negotiating a series of trade agreements when Secretary of State Cordell Hull and his colleagues return to Washington. The first of these is expected to be with Argentina, Canada, Mexico, and various Latin American nations will probably follow. Japanese delegates also have approached Mr. Hull on the subject. One of the features of the parleys has been the close and friendly cooperation of countries of North and South America. This friendship may be continued with the sending of a government official to Montevideo, Uruguay, for a commercial conc

LONDON, July 13.—(U.P)—Again the center of criticism and blamed for continued dissension in the World Economic Conference, the American delegation awaited new instructions from Washington today. This time the instructions concerned the advisability of discussing cooperation of central banks, which would mean in the case of the United States, cooperation by the Federal Reserve Bank with the Bank of England, the Bank of France, and similar institutions in other countries. To the amazement of other delegates, Senator Key Pittman, Dem., Nevada, yesterday refused to discuss this at a committee meeting. It was charged that America had reversed its position again, and further emasculated the conference agenda.

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 13.—()— England and Australia broke even today in the first two singles matches of the European Davis Cup zone tennis finals, the survivor of which plays the United States for the right to challenge France. Pred Perry, British No. 1 player, scored decisively over young Vivian McGrath, 6-2, 6-4, 6-2, after Jack Crawford, Australian and New Wimbledon singles king, rallied to conquer Henry W. (Bunny) Austin, 4-6, 6-2, 6-3, 6-3.

St. Johns, Newfoundland.—(AP)—Unfavorable flying weather along the Newfoundland coast prevented Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh from leaving here for Cartwright, Labrador, today on their aerial mapping expedition. It was cold, wet and foggy when the colonel arose and he said he would not take off until the weather cleared. The famous flying couple had looked forward to meeting the Italian air fleet at Cartwright, but Gen. Italo Balbo led his twenty-four seaplanes southward from that port today for Shediac, N. B.

ST. JOHN'S, Nfld, July 12—(AP)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, en route on an aerial mapping tour over Greenland and Labrador, arrived here at 5:46 p.m., Atlantic daylight time (4:46 p.m., eastern standard time) after a flight of five hours and a half from Halifax, N. S. Lindbergh brought down his big red and black monoplane on Quidi Vidi Lake. He found the weather clear and the visibility good. Later the couple moved their plane from the lake to Bay Bulls big pond, where they were greeted by a large crowd. They were met by Col. L. C. Outerbridge, at whose home they are overnight guests. They planned to proceed tomorrow to Cartwright, Labrador, where the Italian squadron of 24 seaplanes, en route to Chicago, landed late today after a 1,500-mile hop from Reykjavik, Iceland.

1933-10-05.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 5.—Four men faced each other across a table in the treasury department today to determine what Great Britain shall pay the United States on its war debt of more than $4,000,000,000. Even deeper questions of monetary exchange and trade seem bound to enter the talks. Some observers foresee the stabilization of the dollar and the pound as a result of the conversations. Undersecretary of Treasury Acheson and Frederick Livesay, economic advisor of the state department, represent the United States. Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, economic advisor of the British government, and T. K. Bewley, British treasury expert, will present the case for debt reduction. Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, is expected to “sit in” from time to time. WASHINGTON, Oct. 5. (U.P)—The charge that international financiers were supporting the Hitler regime to crush democracy was made before the American Federation of Labor Convention today by a delegate from the British Trades Union Congress. James Rowan, a former British miner, urged united support of labor against Hitlerism and the principles of the German dictator. Rowan told the convention that Professor Albert Einstein's “brown book” revealed that Hitler was financed by industrialists. He recalled the allegation that even Henry Ford had contributed but added that this had been denied by the American manufacturer. “It has not been denied, however,” Rowan added, “that the big European industrialists have contributed. It is my considered opinion that a small group of international financiers are fighting desperately and unscrupulously in this way against the advance of democracy.” A resol

LONDON, Oct. 5—(AP)—Hidden somewhere in the first heavy fog of the season, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh motored today toward Salisbury and west England, presumably en route to Cardiff, Wales, to visit relatives. "Without being recognized the Americans stayed at a hotel six miles from Southampton overnight, after their arrival at Southampton from Stavanger, Norway. They dined with 45 other guests without attracting attention. They started motoring westward at 9 a.m. today. The elements contrived to aid them in their desire to keep their whereabouts secret, for there was a sudden change to foggy weather shortly after they landed and disappeared in an automobile. At the American embassy it was said the Lindberghs did not want the embassy to know where they were going. Furthermore, it was said, the embassy did not want to know because of countless inquiries about them.

SOUTHAMPTON, Oct. 5.—(UP)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh proceeded westward by motorcar today after spending the night at a county hotel near here. It was believed they were going to Cardiff to visit Mrs. Lindbergh's sister Elizabeth, now Mrs. Aubrey Neil Morgan.

LONDON, Oct. 6 — (AP) — London prison farm's smallest inmate has been paroled. Ennis Dillard, 33, of Stark Co., who was released after serving a term for carrying concealed weapons, was so small the prison tailors had to make his clothes to order, and when Ennis needed shoes, he had to be taken to a London shop to be fitted. Dillard is four feet nine inches and weighs 105 pounds.

Vienna, Oct. 4.—A former soldier, firing a little pearl-handled revolver yesterday, came close to killing Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss and plunging Austrian and European politics into new and more dangerous confusion. As it was, two bullets from the gun of Rudolf Dertil, a former corporal in the Austrian army, only grazed the chancellor's left breast and wounded him slightly in the left arm. Dollfuss, after receiving treatment at a hospital, went home within an hour. The question immediately asked: "Was he a Nazi?" still was not definitely answered last night. Socialist newspapers headlined the accusation that Dertil was a Hitlerite, while on the other hand the pro-Dollfuss newspaper Weltblatt identified him as a member of the Schutzbund, dissolved Socialist military organization.

-BERLIN, Oct. 6.—Freedom of the press ended in Germany today with the promulgation of the first of six sections of the new press law. The law, drafted by Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda, declares editors and members of editorial staffs of newspapers, periodicals and news agencies must uphold unreservedly the rightness of the present regime. The section that became law today ruled specifically that newspapers no longer were organs of free opinion but must be classed with the radio, theatre and schools. Newspapers and periodicals comprise public institutions spiritually influencing the nation, the law said. This decree was followed by one prescribing the death penalty or alternatively 15 years' imprisonment for anyone who imported or disseminated periodicals classified as treasonable. The decree prescribed death also for anyone who plotted against the lives of judges, lawy

BERLIN, Oct. 5 UP—A new law making journalists public officials and regulating their rights and duties was interpreted today as ending finally freedom of the press, as understood in America. In their new status German journalists must bow to the so-called “leadership principles,” meaning that they must take orders from the top, which permits no appeal. Chancellor Hitler signed the measure yesterday. It put down iron rules for German journalism, by which Aryanism and Nazi patriotism were made primary professional qualifications.

1933-04-08.text: —The chiefs of the French, Italian and German governments as well as the British have been invited to come to Washington to talk world economic recovery with President Roosevelt. Invitations to Italy and Germany were extended verbally today through the embassies. A similar invitation was extended by President Roosevelt through the French ambassador previously. Each nation has been invited to send the head of its government. In the case of Germany and Italy, this presumably would mean the dictators, Adolph Hitler and Benito Mussolini. For France, it would be Premier Daladier. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain already has accepted a formal invitation and will sail April 15. If the head of the state is unable to come, the three powers have been advised that a member of the government would be welcomed. By The Associated Press LONDON, April 5—Mrs. Edgar Wallace, widow of the author, died early today at her London home after a long illness.

MOSCOW, (UP) — Threats will not influence the Soviet court that will start hearing evidence of sabotage against six accused British subjects on Monday. This was, in substance, Moscow's answer Saturday to the threatened British embargo. The Moscow press vigorously denounced the threat of embargo, significantly indicating that evidence against the accused Britons was strong. Izvestia twice referred to them as “people whom the government considers guilty.” Pravda, in an ironic vein, foresaw the discomfiture of Sir John Simon, British foreign minister who denounced Soviet Justice in the House of Commons, when evidence against his “innocent countrymen” is made public. The principal point of the press argument, however, was that Great Britain could not treat the Soviet Union as though it was a colony. LONDON, April 7. Confident that the threat of economic boycott would have some effect on the Soviet government, the British cabinet was represented today as feeling that it had done everything possible for six British subjects to be tried in Moscow Monday on charges of sabotage until after the revolutionary tribunal reaches a verdict. Official tempers had cooled somewhat following approval by the House of Commons of a measure that gives the cabinet power to declare a complete embargo on Russian importations after April 17, when the present Anglo-Soviet trade agreement expires. The measure was approved on third and final reading yesterday and passed first reading in the House of Lords. It was the second time within ten months that Commons had given the government power to engage in economic warfare.

(International News Service) CANNES, France, April 8.—Betty Compton, former British actress and bride-to-be of former Mayor James J. Walker of New York, is seriously ill with intestinal influenza, it was announced today. Shortly after midnight, it was disclosed, the former stage star was removed from her villa, the Beau Geste, to a private clinic. Miss Compton's illness has indefinitely delayed her marriage with Walker. The nuptial ceremony was tentatively set for April 13.

NICE, France, April 7. (---) Friends expect former Mayor James J. Walker of New York and Betty Compton to be married at the Cannes City Hall April 13, with Michael Arlen and Norman Shearer mentioned as likely witnesses. Arlen's villa is near that of Miss Compton, and Miss Shearer is now visiting at Cap Antibes. Walker has not revealed his plans, but his friends point out that unless he is married April 13 he will be unable to do so before April 18 on account of the Easter holidays.

CANNES, France, April 8. (?).— Betty Compton, friend of former Mayor James J. Walker of New York, was taken seriously ill overnight with an attack of intestinal influenza and it was believed their marriage, which friends said yesterday they expected to occur the morning of April 13, probably will be postponed.

PARIS, April 8 (—Former Premier Edouard Herriot, dominant figure in national and international affairs, has accepted the government's invitation to represent France in the world conference assembling in Washington. He probably will sail on the steamship Île de France April 19. John Krapp of Cortland was in the city yesterday. He recently recovered from a spell of sickness which confined him to his home most of the winter.

1933-11-19.text: The renewal of diplomatic relations between Russia and the United States, announced yesterday by President Roosevelt in Washington, brought forth instantaneous world-wide reaction. From Geneva, where diplomats assembled in an effort to save the disarmament conference from oblivion; from London, Paris, Berlin, Rome and Tokyo, came official and semi-official comments that the American government’s action should result in international benefit. The United States named William C. Bullitt, state department expert on Russian affairs, as ambassador to the Soviet; the Soviet appointee to the United States was not immediately named but two possibilities were deemed outstanding. They are Valerian Ivanovitch Mezhlauk, first vice chairman of the state planning commission, and G. L. Sokolnikoff, member of the commissariat of foreign affairs.

GENEVA, Nov. 18,—After seeking in a long conference with British representatives for a way to resuscitate the disarmament conference, Foreign Minister Joseph Paul Boncour of France said tonight the two governments no longer were agreed on how to handle the problem of German arms demands. As the disarmament deadlock seemed more nearly complete than at any time since Germany left the Geneva council a month ago, the United States arms delegates were invited to explain in a meeting tomorrow their attitude toward the outline which Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, gave on prospects a month ago when Germany quit. Paul-Boncour reported that France will stick by the accords already reached and particularly favors the declaration of Sir John on Oct. 14 regarding a draft convention. Admits Equality. PARIS —()— Two airplanes of an Egyptian squadron of ten flying from England to Iraq fell in flames in northern France Saturday night, two flyers burning to death. A third plane was forced down by bad weather. The pilots of the remaining seven planes, ignorant of the accidents, landed their craft at Le Bourget air field for an overnight stay. The two fatally burned flyers were in a plane which fell near Blangy. Another of the squadron dropped near Gamaches, a few miles farther south, and also burst into flames. The occupants escaped. The third plane was forced down at Orly. There were no casualties.

Pittsburgh —(#)— War between Great Britain and the United States —“by proxy”—is envisioned by author-lecturer John Strachey, of the writing and lecturing Stracheys, as a consequence of American recognition of Soviet Russia. Addressing the League of Women Voters, he predicted a conflict between the two great English-speaking powers, with world markets as the prize, but said the actual armed warfare would be between Russia and Japan. In such a war, he asserted, Britain would back Japan and the United States would support the U. S. S. R. “You can see that coming with Russian recognition,” the writer, for two years a labor member of British parliament, declared, “Undoubtedly the United States will extend credit to the Soviets. Recognition is a smart move and undoubtedly will check Japan for a time. But the outbreak of war is only a question of time.” As to his views on America, Strachey desc

WASHINGTON, Nov. 18.—The invisible man has been running around town during the past few days. He is Henry Clay (not our forefather), who has been handling exchange for the Bank of England. He took the place of Gov. Sprague in London when Sprague enlisted in the new deal. Clay keeps himself from being seen, almost as well as his boss, Montagu Norman. But those who use special glasses have detected motives in his presence here at a time when the Roosevelt gold policy is ruining the British stabilization program. It is understood he is seeking to ascertain how far we are going and what the Bank of England can do to protect itself. It is significant also that we wafted into town the day that Dean Acheson’s resignation was announced from the treasury department. Acheson is supposed to have hinted to the British some time ago that they need not fear the Roosevelt gold-price policy. The natural

Berlin, Nov. 20. — Secret police today ordered the seizure of all property of Dr. Albert Einstein, famed physicist, and Mrs. Einstein by virtue of law for confiscation of communistic property. Legal notice of the action was published in the official gazette Reichsanzeiger which listed “all mobile and immobile goods particularly bank accounts and other deposits to be confiscated in favor of the Prussian state.

Tokyo, Nov. 18 (2) The household announced today that the birth of a child to the Empress of Japan was expected late in December or early in January. Japan is praying for a boy. The possibility of a son to Emperor Hirohito resulted in tremendous joy for the imperial household. The governors of seven prefectures were sent an order, considered a signal honor, to choose and send a tosyō from each prefecture of young women "of the best physical conditions and unimpeachable moral character" as candidates for the position of wet nurse to the expected imperial infant. Only two of the seven were chosen for this illustrious assignment. Thus far their majesties have had four daughters, three of whom are living, but there is no man-child to carry on the dynasty unbroken for ages eternal.

VIENNA, Nov. 18 (P)—Rudolph Dertil, who shot and wounded Chancellor Englebert Dollfuss, Oct. 3, was found guilty today and sentenced to five years in jail. The Chancellor was shot in the arm and breast October 3, but neither of the wounds was serious.

1933-09-07.text: (By International News Service) Alnwick, Northumberland, Eng. Sept. 7.—Viscount Grey of Fallodon, British foreign minister under two kings and the man who sent England to war against Germany in 1914, died at his home today. He was 71. Death followed a lingering illness which became acute a week ago Saturday when intensified by an abdominal complaint. He had been in a coma much of the past week, unable to recognize relatives called to his bedside. Lord Grey, one of the eminent statesmen of his day and described as the last of a line of Victorian leaders, was temporary ambassador to the United States in 1919, an office which marked the virtual end of his public life. --_ - --—--- -— London, Sept. 7.—By a curious coincidence, David Lloyd George’s new book “War Memoirs,” bitterly attacking Lord Grey, was published today, the day of the war-time foreign minister’s death. The former premier in

New York, Aug. 30.--D. J. Moran, president of the Continental Oil Company, declared in a statement today that the 10 cent a barrel price increase on midcontinent and Texas crude initiated this week by the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey subsidiaries "is not high enough." "It is regrettable that leaders in the last price advance seemingly hold the opinion that a 10 cent advance will be enough to meet the code provisions as to hours of labor and employment without evasion," he said. "This company is making effective all provisions of the oil code and on September 2 it will give consideration to a more adequate price for crude, unless it has been fixed by the president prior to that time."

Stanford, Sept. 6.—(AP)—Sam Gaskill, 59, ranch manager, shot and killed George Mulliner, 30, a laborer, eight miles south of Raynesford today during an argument over hogs. Gaskill, who was locked in the county jail here tonight, admitted the shooting, Sheriff L.L. E. Black said, but insisted he fired in self-defense.

PARIS, Sept. 7 (AP)—Henry Cochet, France’s leading tennis star, today announced that he would play against Big Bill Tilden, American professional, in a Franco-American series in Paris starting Sept. 22, but that he would not accept money for his play. In Italy, there are 320 persons to the square mile.

GENEVA, Sept. 7. (UP)—The executive committee of the Jewish conference decided today in favor of an official boycott on German The meeting was an outgrowth of the world congress at Prague, which refrained from taking any action on alleged oppression of German Jews by the Nazi government.

Frank Wilson, president of district No. 13, who with other officials signed the notices, predicted that the 24 Iowa mines now idle because of walkouts would be operating by Monday, "probably before." He said that he thought several groups now out would return Friday. This morning 180 miners returned to work at the Midwest Coal Company at Redfield and 60 more returned at the Smoky Hollow mine near Hiteman. Both are in Monroe County. Polk County miners were still idle, but two operators said their men may return to work Friday. There was, however, no hint of a formal announcement of policy and no certainty that one would be forthcoming when Ford returns, probably the last of the week, from his Huron mountain camp where he has remained secluded for three weeks. Harlingen, Tex. Sept. 1.—(P)—Army ambulance detachments Thursday began a systematic search through hitherto inaccessible sections of the hurricane-devastated lower Rio Grande Valley for injured refugees. It was considered likely additional fatalities would be discovered in remote communities unheard from since the disastrous storm abated. A preliminary survey by the Red Cross, covering that part of the stricken area linked by paved highways, accounted for 24 deaths and hundreds of persons injured. There were found to be 3,750 families destitute, 4,000 homes destroyed and 8,000 damaged. Four persons lost their lives at Harlingen, seven at San Benito, seven at Rio Hondo, one at Port Isabel, two in rural communities and eight at Matamoros, Mexican resort city across the Rio Grande from Brownsville. 1933-03-30.text: NEWCHANG, Manchuria, March 30.—(#)—British gunboats searched off the Manchurian coast today for Chinese buccaneers who kidnapped four British officers yesterday from the British merchant ship Nanchang. Fourteen pirates attacked the British ship, wounded two Chinese members of the crew, and carried off the officers in two junks. The Chinese vessels escaped in shallow water along the coast of the Gulf of Liaotung as the Nanchang tried to pursue them. The pirates boarded the Nanchang as it was waiting for the high tide at the Newchang bar. They fired rifles and pistols with abandon as they cowed Chinese sailors and ordered them to lead the way to the officers’ cabin. There they seized W. E. Hargraves, A. D. Blue, F. L. LONDON, March 30.—Norman H. Davis, special ambassador of the United States in Europe, and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald this morning began a series of talks at No. 10 Downing Street covering the whole range of world problems, with emphasis on the forthcoming world economic conference and disarmament. Mr. Davis arrived in England yesterday from America. He will return to Downing Street this afternoon for a continuation of the conferences and will remain in London over the weekend.

MOSCOW, (UP) -- Sir Esmond Ovey, British ambassador to Moscow, was summoned to London Thursday. The ambassador will leave the Soviet capital Thursday night. His return to London was in connection with the Soviet’s refusal to release British engineers facing trial on charges of sabotage. Foreign Minister Maxim Litvinov warned Wednesday that the Russian government would brook no “coercion” in the affair. Sir Esmond’s recall to London followed startlingly soon after an official rebuff Wednesday to strong British diplomatic representations demanding the release of three British subjects who are to face trial on charges of obstructing public work. The three engineers were representatives of the Metropolitan Vickers firm. Litvinov Wednesday told the British ambassador that any attempt to influence the Soviet’s course of action was useless, because the trial already had been determined upon and

(United Press Leased Wire) BELLSHILL, Lanarkshire, Scotland, March 30. Communists, booing, singing the “Internationale” and waving red flags, tried to break through a police cordon when the Prince of Wales arrived in this mining town today on his inspection tour of unemployment conditions. Police reinforcements routed them.

Dublin, March 30. (UP)—The most violent mob scenes in Dublin in years ended early today after thirty persons had been injured in a riotous attack on Communist headquarters. One demonstrator was shot in the leg. Thousands of men and women, driving against Connolly House in Great Strand Street and the Communist College in Encles Street, smashed through civic guards and set fire to the buildings. Revolver volleys failed to stop the onrush. The mob smashed every window. Sticks and stones flew while beleaguered Communists replied with stones and bottles. The attacks brought a climax to three nights of disturbance.

Little Rock, Ark., Mar. 30. (AP)—Tom Redman makes his own canaries and Mexican finches, the police say. After they had observed him trapping English sparrows on a roof adjoining his room, and later exhibiting in the street birds of brilliant plumage about the size of sparrows, officers followed him home last night in the guise of customers. "I take $11 for that pair," Redman was quoted as telling them when they priced two of his prettiest red birds. The room was filled with cages of birds of all colors. In one cage officers found a half dozen sparrows and nearby an improvised dryer, heated by an electric bulb, in which several birds were drying. The policemen found a pair of rubber gloves and several bottles of dyes and bleaching materials. They arrested Redman for investigation, and quoted him as saying he obtained $1 each for many of the birds; and sometimes higher prices in jars.

By Associated Press London, Mar 30--Sir Esmond Ovey, British ambassador to Moscow, has been summoned to London for consultation, it was stated in Whitehall today. He will return to Moscow afterwards, it was added, The consultation presumably will be in connection with the recent arrest of British technicians in Soviet Russia on charges of sabotage.

London,—(AP)— Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today that Britain favors the American proposal for a tariff truce during the period of the world economic conference, with safeguards for Britain’s special tariff position. With tariff issues paramount in the House, Mr. MacDonald made it clear that, while President Roosevelt, Edouard Herriot of France and he had agreed on plans for convening the world economic conference, the Washington talks had brought no definite agreement in regard to policy. Nor had there been any solutions of world problems, he said, although the exchange of views was “most encouraging.” The Prime Minister announced that war debts had been “frankly examined in all their aspects,” but he said that no fuller statement was possible at the present time, as the problem “necessarily has not yet reached the stage of agreement.”

PARIS, May 3—(AP)—Clinging stubbornly to gold in the face of President Roosevelt's dictatorial monetary powers and the battle between the dollar and the British pound, the French government is planning a 15 percent surtax on American goods should the dollar go as low as 20 francs. A decree imposing the surtax has been drawn up and is ready for signature. Similar measures already are effective against British and Japanese goods, against which France considered former tariff measures ineffective because of the depreciation in British and Japanese currency.

1933-05-01.text: Proxxo, May 1.—(P—The Jap-ese foreign office disclosed today that Chinese leaders were seeking through American and British ministries in Peiping to negotiate a Sino-Japanese armistice. Official reports were received that certain Chinese approached both Nelson T. Johnson, the United States minister, and Sir Miles Lampson, the British minister, proposing that they assist in opening negotiations. A meeting between Sino-Japanese military leaders for the purpose of deciding on an armistice and establishing a neutral zone south of the Great Wall of China is desired. Ho Ying-Ching.

LONDON, May 11 (UP).—Britain will “take any step open to the government” to defend the open door policy in Manchuria, Stanley Baldwin, the prime minister, told the House of Commons today. The announcement was occasioned by press reports that the Manchouku government did not intend to trade with any country that withheld recognition.

1933-08-07.text: LONDON, Aug. 7.—(UP)—Ten steel helmet troopers, wearing the uniform of the German Nazi labor corps, ambushed, shot and killed an Austrian auxiliary policeman near Kutstein, “on the Austrian-Bavarian frontier, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Munich said today. A detachment of the Austrian Heimwehr was sent to the frontier and closed the area to traffic. It was feared the incident might have international consequences because of the current Franco-British representations to Berlin against German propaganda in Austria.

Hyde Park, N. Y., Aug. 6.—()— President Roosevelt and Secretary Hull concentrated today on relations of the western hemisphere, leaving the creased world economic conference to an indefinite future. The secretary of state and chairman of the delegation to the London parley submitted his detailed report and Mr. Roosevelt gave it his approval, but said nothing about the plans for reconvening. He and Mr. Hull are still confident of full accomplishments by the world economic conference, but it appeared today they are going to make sure the other nations will cooperate to the limit when they go into another session. Meanwhile, the president focused the attention of Secretary Hull on the Pan-American parley assembling at Montevideo in December. Already, negotiations are in progress with the leading powers of Central and South America for new trade relations. Mr. Roosevelt also has extended the

ROME, Aug. 7.—(/)—Austria has privately petitioned the governments of England, France and Italy to permit her to increase her military strength, it was declared today on good authority. To grant the permission would have a drastic effect on the enforced disarming of all the former central powers, commentators predicted. Under the treaty of St. Germain universal compulsory military service was abolished in Austria and the army was limited to 30,000 men. Officers must do active service duty for twenty years, and the enlistment period for non-commissioned officers and privates must not be less than twelve years. Austria now wants a much lower enlistment period in order that a greater number of men can serve in the army in successive classes. Thus the trained military would be many times larger without actually increasing the army strength beyond 30,000 in any one year.

New York, Aug. 7.—(#)—Jas. M. Cox, the last American delegate to leave the scene of the world economic conference, returned from London on the liner Europa today and expressed the opinion the conference was “called too soon.” “It was called too soon,” the former governor of Ohio said, “No one could have foreseen the development in it. Therefore no one is to blame. The world was just not ready for it.”

By 2H HBO iatee Freee. THORNSHAVN, Faroe Islands, Aug. 7.—John Grierson, a young British pilot, took off at 9:45 a.m. Greenwich time (4:46 a.m. East Liverpool time) today for Iceland, the next lap of his leisurely flight to New York.

PARIS, France, Aug. 7.—Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi, smashing the world’s distance record for straight line flying, landed at 1:10 p. m. (E.D.T.) today at Rayack, Syria, the air ministry announced. Their straight line distance was unofficially estimated at 5,700 miles from New York to Rayack as compared to the previous record of 5,340 miles from England to South Africa set by two British fliers. The air ministry announced that the air record had been broken, and it was expected the international air federation would take about two days to compute and confirm the official distance.

TOKYO, Aug. 7.—A typhoon in southern Korea last week was reported today to have resulted in 78 deaths, the destruction of 2,634 houses, and the loss of 271 boats. More than 180 persons were said to be missing.

The official explanation was that delay had occurred in the preparation of the French text of the agreement, the purpose of which is to associate importing countries with a broad program to boost prices by cutting production and stimulating consumption. The wheat conference, delegates to which had been scheduled to sign the agreement late this afternoon, adjourned until 8:30 o’clock tonight.

The chief barrier to this agreement had been the question of how high the price of wheat must go before the importers would lower their tariffs. This problem was met by a compromise. LONDON (WP) — The world wheat conference Friday reached an agreement on the “recovery price” at which world tariffs may be altered, and was to reconvene at 5:30 p.m. to initial the draft of its pact. The compromise recovery price was set at 12 gold francs a quintal, equivalent to 63.6 gold cents a bushel, or about 80 cents on the basis of the depreciated dollar. Barring unforeseen difficulties, it was expected the conference would conclude its work Friday night. Representatives of exporting and importing nations held separate meetings before the full conference assembled, to see how far they could go toward accepting a compromise to make possible a world agreement to limit export of wheat during the next two or three years. The wheat exporting countries agreed to accept twelve pre-war gold French francs per quintal as the market price to be reached and maintained for four months, after which the importing countries will adjust their tariffs to permit freer imports. 1933-03-16.text: GENEVA, Switzerland, March 16—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, presenting a new plan for peace and security of the world disarmament conference today, proposed an army of 200,000 men for Germany doubling the maximum limit set by the Treaty of Versailles, The armies of Italy and France would be reduced to the same numerical strength, but France would be permitted an overseas force of 200,000 and Italy of 50,000. This would reduce the French army about one-third, paralleling the proposal of President Hoover. No maximum was suggested for the British army, nor does the plan include any attempt to limit non-European forces.

GENEVA, Mar. 16—(UP)—Warning solemnly against the danger of war, Ramsay J. Macdonald today presented drastic proposals for a disarmament move to the world. He proposed a new all-naval powers conference in 1935, and proposed a British convention looking to the reduction of the army, navy and weapons. “If this is a failure it will drive you speedily to a new catastrophe,” he said pleading for an agreement. In announcing the British plan for a proposed naval conference in 1935, Macdonald said, “It is not our fault if past naval treaties were not general.” The British plans proposed abolition of military and naval aviation, providing a means is found for the safeguarding of civil aviation. It also provides the following: 1--A naval holiday in practically all ship construction until 1935, 2--Future limitation on all mobile land guns over 106 millimeters with extension of existing guns up to 1

WASHINGTON, March 13 (#)— President Roosevelt announced his first diplomatic appointments today in preparation for early resumption of the discussions on world economics, armaments and war debts. To the prize London post he nominated Robert W. Bingham, Louisville publisher and prominent Democratic leader. He selected Jessie Isidor Straus, New York merchant, to go to Paris. He appointed Josephus Daniels, North Carolina publisher, to hold the important Mexico City ambassadorship. Early announcements of the ambassadors to Germany, Italy and Cuba are believed in prospect. With the London and Paris emissaries chosen, the President is ready to go into further detail on the negotiations he has been conducting with England and France on the world economic and armaments conferences. There is every sign he intends to get action on these two propositions before taking up personally the appeals from

Washington, D. C.—President Roosevelt conferred Friday with advisers in a move to co-ordinate the domestic program and the policies of the London economic conference. The president conferred for more than two hours with Acting Secretary Phillips of the state department, Acting Secretary Acheson of the treasury; Bernard M. Baruch, his recovery co-ordinator; Norman H. Davis, ambassador-at-large; and Frederick Livesey, state department economic adviser. Mr. Phillips said the extraordinary session had been discussing the economic conference. The meeting was interrupted by a cabinet session and Mr. Roosevelt summoned the group to return later in the day to renew the conference.

ROME, March 15 ()—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Sir John Simon, his foreign secretary, will meet Premier Mussolini in Rome Saturday to discuss means of salvaging the disarmament conference, it was officially announced tonight. A statement issued at the foreign office said the British statesmen were at the express invitation of Mussolini. They are to leave Geneva, where they are at present, after a week-end with one another Sunday.
London, March 13.—The dollar opened in official quotations today at 3.43% to the pound sterling. This was better than the close on the day before the beginning of the presidential bank holiday.

Washington, Mar. 16.—Imminent action in the world disarmament problem appeared in prospect today as President Roosevelt conferred in quick succession with the ambassadors of Great Britain, France and Germany and his own secretary of state and chairman of this country’s delegation to the Geneva conference.

London, March 15.—()—Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council and acting prime minister, told the house of commons today that the British ambassador at Moscow had been instructed to make representations 'in strong terms' to the Soviet government in connection with the recent arrest of British subjects there. Six British subjects affiliated with the Metropolitan-Vickers company, a British electrical machinery concern, were arrested Saturday and Sunday, along with 25 other employees. They were charged with sabotage.

1933-09-28.text: Geneva, Sept. 27 (7)—A prompt disarmament agreement, Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, plainly told the League of Nations assembly today, is a vital necessity for world political and economic recovery. "A disarmament convention based on concession and cooperation is the greatest need of the world," said Sir John, who added he detected certain signs of a beginning in economic recovery. He coupled this, however, with the warning that such recovery "cannot make strides without political amelioration." Meanwhile, Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss of Austria staunchly proclaimed Austria’s right and "duty" to maintain her independence. This statement, accepted by his hearers as a hint to Germany, brought a wave of applause in the assembly. "We assert more than ever our freedom and independence to the free will of our people," said the chancellor, whose government is now engaged in attempt

Washington, Sept. 28.—(UP)—Secretary of State Hull announced today that Undersecretary of Treasury Acheson and Frederick Livesey, assistant economic adviser to the State Department, had been designated by the administration to conduct negotiations for settlement of revision of the British war debt. The conversations will be held at the Treasury Department. Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, financial adviser to the British government, is expected here Oct. 6 to begin the debt discussions. He will strive for a reduction in his government's $4,600,000,000 funded obligation to the U.S. Treasury. Hull’s announcement that the negotiations would be carried on by the Treasury Department occasioned some surprise. It was recalled that all debt discussions since the financial crisis of 1931 had been conducted by the State Department. The secretary, however, declined to admit that there was any special sign

Washington, Bert. 28,(/P) —Secretary Hull disclosed today that the important war debt conversations to be opened next week with British representatives now on their way to this country will be handled by Dean Acheson, undersecretary of the treasury, and Frederick Livesey, assistant economic adviser of the state department. The secretary of state said it had been unanimously agreed that the conversations be handled in this way when Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, financial adviser to the British government, arrives to begin the talks. He is accompanied by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, and T. K. Bewley, financial expert.

LONDON, Sept. 28—Germany, her every move watched by a circle of unfriendly neighbor states, was believed today to be taking stock of her international position. Official German declarations against boycotting Jewish businessmen in Germany were followed today by reliable reports that Joseph Goebbels, chief German delegate at the League of Nations assembly, sought at a luncheon in Geneva to effect removal of the Polish Jews boycott against German goods. Goebbels, the reports said, asked Polish Foreign Minister Joseph Beck the circumstances under which the boycott would be removed. Beck, it was reported, told the Nazi propaganda minister that the boycott would be lifted by Polish Jews only when Germany removed disabilities from German Jews. Goebbels was reported to have said it was impossible to restore all pre-revolutionary Jewish rights but the government was willing to make concessions i

LONDON, Sept. 28 (P)—While Sir Reginald Wolseley was alive he and his wife couldn't agree on how worthwhile it was to be called “Lord” and “Lady”. He much preferred running an elevator in Waterloo, Iowa; she wanted the honors of the aristocracy. She had her way. But now he is dead, and she who is Lady Wolseley wants to be known simply as Mrs. Marion Raker Wolseley. Yesterday she declared her intention to renounce his title to the baronetcy. She had nursed his mother during her last illness and, carrying out a death-bed wish, went to Waterloo to marry the son. He refused to leave the job he held 14 years and she sailed back without him. He obtained a divorce charging desertion. She returned to Iowa in December, 1931. They apparently patched up their differences; the divorce was annulled, and they left for England. “It's not my money she wants,” said Dick Wolseley, “for I haven't any. She

BPR BHU WIVSIBLY 2480 5 B46B4N (By The Associated Press) Moscow, Sept. 28. — Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and his wife are so impressed by the experimental aviation work that is being carried on in Soviet Russia that they hope to return to this country in a couple of years to see for themselves how the experiments have worked out. The colonel told of this desire at a banquet given in honor of himself and his wife last night. Two United States senators—W. G. McAdoo of California and R. R. Reynolds of North Carolina—were present, and a four-piece orchestra periodically played “Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean.” “This country is peculiarly fitted for aviation development because it is a land of great distances,” Lindbergh said, “and I am impressed with your accomplishments.” The Lindberghs continued their sightseeing today, planning to leave Moscow tomorrow. They refused to reveal their desti

VIENNA, Sept. 28.—(UP)—Suppression of political parties—a move which Socialists say will result in a general strike and perhaps civil war—was regarded as imminent today. The way was paved for general political suppression when the strong Fascist Heimwehr organization of Prince Starhemberg was dissolved as a political force and its members joined Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss’ “Patriotic Front” party in a body. A communique announced the inclusion of the Heimwehr, or More Guard, in the “Patriotic Front,” added: “This makes the further existence of other parties unnecessary.” Anticipating suppression, Socialist leaders called newspaper men to a conference last night and announced: “A general strike, and probably civil war, will result if the government dissolves the Socialist organization, outlaws the trades unions and proclaims a Fascist constitution. “We shall not take such a move lying

GENEVA, Sept. 28 — (AP) — A patched-up disarmament agreement designed primarily for Europe and based on mutual political arrangements, with the United States and Japan both left out of the picture, seemed today to be the tendency of disarmament negotiations. Indications were seen that the American delegation was not fully informed about political details of the forthcoming arms conference, which probably will include a greater consideration of the German viewpoint of equality than is generally realized. Ambassador Naotake Sato of Japan conferred today with American Ambassador-at-large Norman H. Davis. It was learned authoritatively that Japan's position is to allow European powers to reach an agreement if possible and then allow Japan to pass on the results, making reservations to an eventual treaty or refraining altogether from signing if the contents are found altogether unacceptable.

1933-09-30.text: PARIS, Sept. 27.—(UP)—Gustave Le Moine, civilian pilot, claimed a new airplane altitude record today with a flight of 45,264 feet (13,800 metres) over Villacoublay airfield. The existing record of 43,976 feet was made by Capt. Cyril Unwin, British World War ace, September 16, 1932. The record for balloons made by Prof. Auguste Piccard in his stratosphere flight is 10 miles 117 yards (68,153 feet or 16,201 metres). Le Moine flew in an 800 horsepower Poetz plane, equipped with a supercharger. He was up half an hour, using an oxygen tank to breathe.

LONDON, Sept. 28.—Threat of wheat dumping by Russia, endangering the recent world wheat control plan, was brought nearer today when Russia refused a compromise submitted by John McMurray, American delegate to the wheat advisory commission. McMurray tried to effect a compromise between Russian demands and offers of other exporting nations as to Russia’s share of the total world export quota. Abraham Gurevitch, Russian delegate, declined the offer today at a conference with McMurray and the Canadian delegate. Russia demands an export quota of 75,000,000 bushels this year under the world wheat plan, whereas other wheat exporting nations offer only 37,000,000 bushels. It was expected the conference of the advisory commission would be adjourned until November 27. McMurray planned to leave for Washington today on the liner Manhattan.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 28 (P)—An atmosphere of business instead of diplomacy will surround the war debt discussions that begin here next week with representatives of the British government. It was disclosed today they will be conducted by Dean Acheson, undersecretary of the treasury, and Frederick Livesey, an economic adviser of the state department, in the treasury building. The British spokesman will be Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, who sailed yesterday from England. Secretary Hull, in making the arrangement, described Acheson as being as competent as anybody in the government to handle the matter and said he would have Livesey's able cooperation. In putting the negotiations in the hands of the treasury, the government returned to a policy followed in the early days of the debt problem. Under President Wilson, the debts were regarded as a treasury matter. More recently under President Hoover an

ADEN, Arabia, Sept. 29 — (U.P) — Sir Graeme Thomson, called the “greatest officer since Noah,” died today on his way home to London from his post as governor of Ceylon. He was 38. Thomson's efficiency was shown by his record in the World War. He was knighted in 1919 for his services.

London, Sept. 30. ()—The search of Mrs. Eugenia Bankhead Hoyt, Tallulah Bankhead's sister, for an “ideal husband” has had a temporary setback with the announcement that her engagement to a handsome 28-year-old Englishman was broken. Thus her seventh venture into matrimony has been postponed. Her engagement to E. Kennedy McConnell, son of a retired coal magnate, was cancelled yesterday for an unannounced reason. The betrothal was announced Sept. 12. Mrs. Hoyt recently told interviewers that if young McConnell was not an ideal mate she would “have to start seeking again.” Regarding the shattering of the latest romance, she remarked, "I am not terribly disappointed.” She and McConnell first met a number of years ago, but it was not until five years later that they met again, during a Mediterranean cruise on a private yacht. At the time her engagement to McConnell was announced, she said: “I

WASHINGTON, Sept. 30 UR— Henry Bruere, president of the Bowery Savings Bank of New York, has been selected by the administration to act as coordinator. Bruere, officials said, will work under the direction of Lewis Douglas, the director of the budget, in a new agency which will be set up to further the administration’s credit plan. Treasury officials said that Bruere would come to Washington next week to work out with administration leaders the next step in the government’s credit program. Meanwhile, President Roosevelt was understood to be formulating his new monetary policy to be announced soon. This policy was expected to be a sound money pronouncement to reassure business and money lenders of no wild monetary inflation. Choice of Bruere, head of the largest savings bank in the country, and a sound money man, was interpreted that the administration plans on no drastic money inflation.

TICLES, UF 8,000 BCLS. SAAN stayed aloft 12 hours. MOSCOW, Sept. 30. — UP) — Three Russian scientists, exploring the stratosphere 11 miles above the earth in the giant government balloon USSR, today shattered all existing altitude records. Studying their instruments at the comfortable temperature of 71.6 degrees maintained in their gondola, the scientists cruised through space where the temperature was 88 below zero. Starting at 8:43 a. m. from the local airport, they reached at 9:58 a. m. an altitude of 17.9 kilometres (11 miles 204 yards). Soaring rapidly, they surpassed all previous records within 40 minutes after their start. “Feeling Fine.” As cruising about and studying their instruments, the balloonists ascended finally to 18.4 kilometres (11 miles 750 yards) at 2:20 p. m. “We are feeling fine and send best wishes,” they radioed to earth. Twenty minutes later they began to descend

MOSCOW, Sept. 30 () — Three Russian balloonists who took off for a flight into the stratosphere at 8:41 a.m. today reported by wireless before preparing to descend that they had reached an altitude of 19,000 meters, or 11.80 miles, which they claimed to be a new record. At that hour the huge army balloon, which had passed out of sight early in the morning after its takeoff, was plainly visible to the naked eye and appeared as a silvery fleck in a cloudless sky northwest of Moscow. “Please prepare to receive us,” said the final message from the balloonists. It indicated that the bag might land about 31 miles from the capital. An earlier message said they had ascended 17,900 meters, which, if their instruments were correct, surely passed the record of 16,700 meters set by Prof. Auguste Piccard in August, 1932. Hovering over an area near Moscow after having shifted its position in a leisure

1933-10-28.text: WASHINGTON—(AP)—A price of $31.76 an ounce for Reconstruction Corporation purchases of newly-mined gold was announced today at the treasury, 22 cents higher than that of Thursday and 66 cents above the London quotation. The price for the metal had been freshly advanced on the London market, to the equivalent of $31.10 an ounce on the basis of the $4.74 valuation of the pound at the opening there. Higher Daily The Roosevelt administration, with each successive daily quotation, has set the domestic price higher. Wednesday, with the inauguration of this policy, a price of $31.36 was established, and Thursday it was $31.54. These figures compared with the following world prices: $31.09, $31.06 and $31.10. Administration officials would not reveal whether any particular formula had been prescribed for the determination of the daily figure. As on Thursday and the day before, today’s quotation

WASHINGTON (*) — In spite of a decline in the London gold price, the administration today placed the domestic quotation at a new high of $31.82, six cents an ounce above yesterday. The London figure dropped from $31.10 yesterday to $30.57 at the close there today, a decline of 53 cents. While yesterday's domestic price of $31.76 was 66 cents above the world figures, today’s was $1.25 above.

LONDON, Oct. 28.—(U.P)—British-German relations, already strained on the disarmament question, were made worse today by the prospect of a British reporter being tried by the Nazi government on an espionage charge from which the penalty may be death. Noel D. Panter, Munich correspondent of the London Daily Telegraph, was arrested after he reported a storm trooper parade at Kelheim, Germany, as of a military nature. Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador to Germany, protested strongly to the German Foreign Office and demanded an explanation. Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, called Dr. Leopold von Hoesch, German ambassador, to the foreign office and protested angrily against the arrest. It was reported that he spoke bluntly, and told Hoesch that Great Britain would not tolerate a trial. Simon was said to have demanded conclusive proof that suspicions against Panter and the subsequent

JAFFA, Palestine, Oct. 28. (UP) A death list of 30 with more than 100 others injured was reported today as serious clashes continued between police and Arabs demonstrating against increased Jewish immigration. A squad of British airplanes arrived from Egypt, ready for an emergency. Police patrolled the city and all government buildings were under close guard. At 6 p.m. curfew was imposed to prevent further looting of Jewish shops by night.

GOLD WENT UP 22 cents an ounce Friday; price $31.76 an ounce and your Uncle Sam is industriously buying it with his poor depressed paper dollars for 66 cents an ounce more than England's price. First he said, “We don’t need gold.” Now he is bidding against England to get all he can of it. Some wise plan must be back of it, as the clergyman always tells a bereaved family, but it puzzles many. The French stock exchange is worried because a little of the enormous French accumulations of gold is wandering away and fears the France may not stay on the gold basis, without an absolute embargo. MRS. MARIE DELROSSO had twins both girls, but no money. She left one twin in a New York subway station. The other she abandoned in a church. One twin died, as soon as it reached the hospital. The other is suffering from lack of food. The mother MAY be punished, although that would seem like adding insult

Bern, Oct. 28—(UP)—Nool DP. Fanles, British newspaper correspondent held on grave espionage charges, is under strongest suspicion of having attempted to obtain information of a military character in Germany, an official statement said today. Panter, the statement said, was suspected of having tried to get the information through a German journalist living in Munich, who was himself under suspicion—in connection with propaganda abroad regarding atrocities against German Jews, and with obtaining military secrets.

LONDON, Oct. 28.—The British government regards the arrest and imprisonment of Noel Panter, British newspaper correspondent in Munich, as “a grave breach of friendly relations” now existing between Germany and Great Britain. This serious revelation will be the crux of a message delivered by John Simon, British foreign minister, to the German ambassador, Léon Von Hoesch, at a conference last night, according to word in informed circles today. The warning was for transmission to the Hitler government in Berlin, and Von Hoesch, emerging from the meeting, a glum look, promised to relay the message forthwith. Panter, correspondent for the London Daily Telegraph, was arrested in Munich Tuesday and held incommunicado until yesterday, when a British consul was permitted to see him. Charges were not announced yesterday, when it was said the young Briton would be charged with “treason against the

GLASGOW, Oct. 27.—(7)—Eighty more men went to work today clearing brush for construction of the Fort Peck dam project. This brought the number of employees to 230, and 60 additional men are to be hired tomorrow. All are residents of Valley County.

1933-03-01.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, March 1 (AP) - The Dail Eireann today passed by a vote of 75 to 49 a government bill abolishing the oath of allegiance to the British crown. The measure now goes to the senate.

LONDON, March 1—(P)—A Reuters news agency dispatch from Geneva today said the Japanese delegation there had received instructions from Tokyo to remain in Geneva and to continue to collaborate in the work of the disarmament conference. The Japanese delegation at the League of Nations walked out of a meeting of the assembly last Friday after a report had been adopted condemning the Manchurian policy of Japan. Conjecture arose as to whether the Japanese government would participate in the forthcoming world economic conference.

TOKYO, Mar. 1.—The United States was blamed, in part, in a statement by a government spokesman today, for Great Britain's decision to impose an embargo on arms to the Far East. The Japanese government feels deeply the apparent rift in the Anglo-Japanese alliance, but will make no protest against what it feels is an “unwarranted phrase”—the charge in Sir John Simon’s statement that Tokyo has violated the League covenant. It was revealed that Secretary of State Stimson talked with Ambassador Debuchi in Washington Monday, explaining the American policy on the Far East “in a friendly tone,” but offering no concrete suggestions. The government spokesman reiterated that, in its conversations with other powers, the Tokyo government never has given a pledge not to enter North China.
Nanking, China, March 1 (Py) -- It was officially announced today that China was making representations in London in connection with the British arms embargo against China.

New York, March 1 (4—For Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt the social activities incident to the inauguration of her husband will not be confined to next Saturday, Inauguration Day. They will start at 2:30 o'clock Friday afternoon, and between that hour and midnight she will attend two receptions, call with her husband at the White House, receive President and Mrs. Hoover at the Mayflower, attend a formal dinner and a concert, make a speech, and finish the evening at a formal reception. To Attend Church Her program the following day will begin with a church service at 10:15 a.m. and end after midnight at the Inaugural Ball. During the afternoon and early evening she will be hostess at the White House to more than 2,500 guests. The invitation list for tea, started at 1,000, has grown to more than 2,000. Mr. and Mrs. Roosevelt will arrive in Washington Thursday evening. At 2:30 o'clock Friday aft

NANKING, China, March 1.—(/P)—It was officially announced Wednesday that China was making representations in London in connection with the British arms embargo against China and Japan. One section of opinion among foreign residents was expressed in an editorial in the Shanghai Evening Post Wednesday. “As a practical measure to hasten the end of hostilities in the Far East the British embargo is absolutely futile, and as a moral gesture, grotesque,” the newspaper said. “The British policy is to deprive the defender as well as the offender. This embargo, which Sir John Simon described as dictated by complete friendliness for both countries, is in effect an unfriendly act to China, an irritant to Japan and a most damaging blow to the British aircraft industry in this part of the world. It is a colossal blunder and it will have absolutely no effect on the present hostilities.”

BERLIN, Feb. 28 (AP).—Virtually martial law under police regime was decided upon by the German cabinet today. The cabinet, which had been in session since 11 a.m., adjourned at 2:30 p.m. until 6 p.m. It had read a report from Wilhelm Goering, minister without portfolio, upon the fire which damaged the Reichstag building yesterday and the result of a raid last week by police on Karl Liebknecht house, Communist headquarters on Buelowplatz. A military state of emergency was refrained from in order to keep the Reichswehr (standing army) out of political action, but the measures to be decreed will have the effect of placing Germany under a state of emergency with the sole object of meeting Communist danger. Herr Goering reported that material seized in Karl Liebknecht house included forged orders to the police and to Nazi storm troopers and even included instructions for poisoning wells and f

BERLIN, Feb. 28.—A hefty blow was struck at communism in Germany by a decree President Von Hindenburg signed tonight placing the nation under virtual martial law “to protect the people from communist danger.” The decree was approved at a cabinet meeting at which Wilhelm Goering, minister without portfolio and commissioner for the Prussian ministry of interior, reported to his colleagues on the incendiary fire which damaged the Reichstag last night and on the recent raid on Karl Liebknecht house, the communist headquarters in Berlin. The emergency measures taken by the government to cope with the situation fell short of martial law only because of the desire to keep the army out of politics. Extraordinary powers to safeguard against disorder were placed in the hands of police. Meanwhile, communist leaders throughout Germany were placed under arrest. The arrest order affected communist mem

1933-02-05.text: To the News-Republican: Beverly Hills, Cal, Feb. 3—With a million and one home talent problems that ought to be worrying our lawmakers, why are they still excited about the debts? England is paid up till June, so why start worrying now about June? Suppose the unemployed had work till June, the hungry food till June. They could rest mighty easy for awhile. But they haven't got it. But the debts are paid till June. I bet if you diagnosed all our troubles and listened to them in the order of their importance to us right now, you would find debts awful near the bottom. Any problem that is even temporarily settled up to four months ahead is no problem nowadays. Yours.

LYMPNE, England, Feb. 6, (7)— Capt. J. A. Mollison, noted long distance flyer, took off from here at 8:11 a.m. today (2:11 a.m. Alton time) on a 4800-mile flight by stages to Brazil. He planned to reach his goal in three and a half days. His itinerary was not announced.

London —(A)— Margot Asquith, the Countess of Oxford and the widow of the late Prime Minister Herbert H. Asquith, has been forced to sell her beautiful country home in Berkshire. The Countess admitted her present circumstances were difficult but she was not at all unhappy today about her fate. She said only lack of means to retain her beloved home—"The Wharf,” at Sutton Courtenay—induced her to sell it. “But for my writings and small annuities I would have had to abandon my London house, too.
