It is impossible for anyone to realize how difficult it is, after living on the scale I have done for so many years,” she said. The premier's widow said she sold the country home “for a mere song” because of the burden of taxation and the fall in dividends from securities.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 4. (®)— Great Britain was accused in the Senate today of undertaking by “secret diplomacy” in advance of the world economic conference to secure international agreements detrimental to American shipping. The charge was made by Senator Copeland, Democrat, New York, who asserted it constituted “a species of lobbying against Uncle Sam and the interests of the American Merchant Marine.” “It is the most outrageous and selfish national policy ever,” Copeland, a vigorous opponent of proposed cuts in the subsidies paid shipping companies under ocean mail contracts, contended that the “British shipping interests” are “trying to coerce us into action.” His contention was that the British chamber of shipping had recommended to its government that “both pending the conference and at the conference itself” Great Britain should seek to secure the cooperation of as many nations as poss

LYMPNE AIRDROME, England. Feb. 6.—Capt. James A. Mollison left in his baby monoplane today on a journey which he expected to carry him across the South Atlantic to Argentina, northward to New York and back to England via the north Atlantic. Captain Mollison, superstitious like most fliers, wore the same green, white and yellow necktie which he wore on his solo flight across the north Atlantic last year. “No aviator could have crossed the Atlantic from east to west without wearing such a tie,” he explained. He also carried an image of St. Christopher, patron saint of travelers. Captain Mollison left for the continent at 8:15 a.m. He was not attempting any speed record, and was expected to proceed leisurely down the West African coast to Senegal, from where he will attempt a solo flight of 1,800 miles to Natal, Brazil.

CRANWELL, ENGLAND, Feb. 6 —(?)—In an attempt to create a new world record for a long distance non-stop flight, a royal air force long-range monoplane piloted by Squadron Leader O. R. Gayford and Flight Lieutenant G. E. Nicholetts took off at 7:15 a. m. (2:15 a. m. eastern standard time) for South Africa. Cape Town is 6,198 miles from this Lincolnshire town. To beat the present non-stop record of 5,012 miles, made by Americans, Russell Boardman and John Polando, on a New York-Istanbul flight, the British pair must reach the vicinity of Zesfontein in British South West Africa. International aviation regulations require that the record be beaten by at least 62.14. The British fliers have a “robot pilot” or automatic control system in their plane which relieves them from piloting when they desire. A short wave radio set was installed. The plane, with a 530-horsepower engine, is the same used
LONDON, Feb. 4.—(AP)—Former King George of Greece underwent an operation for appendicitis today. The doctors said his condition was satisfactory.

LONDON, Feb. 4.—(4)—Great Britain's debt policy, explained in detail in the recent talks by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain, was expected to remain virtually unchanged after the cabinet is informed Monday of President-elect Roosevelt's views. Unless wholly unexpected news is brought by Sir Ronald Lindsay, it was indicated in high quarters today that the main features of the British proposal would remain intact. WASHINGTON, Feb. 4.—(4)—Investigation by the State Department (Continued on Page Two)

1933-09-23.text: Paris. Sept. 23 (#)—That the United States, France, Britain, and Italy will face Germany with a united disarmament front at Geneva was foreseen by French officials today as a result of a tentative agreement for the limitation and control of arms. The understanding, which awaits ratification by the governments, was reached in conferences by representatives of the first three powers, French sources announced. Obtaining Germany's acceptance of "this common viewpoint," they said, remains the principal obstacle, but hope was expressed a 4-power accord will be completed by October 9 to enable negotiations with Germany to proceed along a "solid front" with reopening of the world disarmament conference October 16. The French were understood to have indicated a willingness to trim their powerful army if the German Reichswehr is transformed into a short-term militia during a transition period prel

London, Sept. 23. (A)—The case of an Indian girl giving birth to a baby before being seven years of age was reported by a Delhi doctor today in the “British Medical Journal” of London. The baby weighed four pounds, three ounces at birth, the doctor reported. Beyond suffering from fright for three days, he added, the mother recovered perfectly and was able to nurse the infant for nine months, when it weighed eleven pounds, two ounces.

Paris, Sept. 22 (4)—Paris police picked up today what they thought was a clue to the Lindbergh kidnapping mystery but ran it into the ground and abandoned it. First they announced they had the name of a man who had a 1,000-pound note identified by the Bank of England as part of the ransom money extorted from Colonel Lindbergh last year. Later they said they were mistaken and no search for the Lindbergh kidnappers was being made. The arrest of three men in Antwerp after trying to cash the British note was reported. One of the men later revealed the note was enclosed in an envelope addressed to a Belgian judge, who thought the matter a joke and tossed the envelope to a clerk who crumpled it and threw it in a waste basket. Investigation by Belgian authorities revealed the 1,000-pound note was stolen from a consignment of money en route from Monaco to Paris. Three men were sentenced for rece

PARIS, Sept. 22.—-(4)—Only one main point appeared today to remain unsettled as a French official reported “substantial progress” toward the forming of a solid front of the United States, France, Italy and Great Britain at the resumption of the world disarmament conference. This official declared the four countries have reached a common ground of understanding concerning the disarmament question. It was learned the outstanding point of sanctions remains to be solved. France has been represented recently as desiring to set up penalties for any nation violating a disarmament agreement.

MANSFIELD, O., Sept. 23 — Discovery of the bodies of a girl and man in a truck standing in a park here today led police to express belief they were victims of a murder and suicide tragedy, the result of a lover's quarrel. The bodies of Mary Trumpower, 21, and Joseph Gordon, 27, were found by Frank Keifer, as he was walking through the park. Coroner James K. Biddie said they had been dead about ten hours. The girl’s body was slumped against that of Gordon in the cabin of the truck. Both had been shot through the head. A revolver with three empty shells lay beside the seat, police said. Parents of the girl told police that Gordon called for her last night while she was entertaining another male acquaintance in her home. Gordon said he wanted to say goodbye, that he was leaving the city. The girl accompanied him in his truck, nothing was heard from them until their bodies were found this mo

LONDON, Sept. 22 (P)— The British Medical Journal's report of a seven-year-old Indian girl giving birth to a child was supplemented Friday night with information that the girl was an unmarried Mohammedan of Delhi, India, 47 inches tall, weighing 48 pounds and was still having her milk teeth. The doctor reported the baby weighed four pounds, three ounces at birth and that beyond suffering from fright, the mother recovered and was able to nurse the infant.

Paris, Sept. 23. (4P)—A close approach to a general agreement between the United States, France, Great Britain and Italy for the limitation and control of armaments, it was authoritatively learned, was made Friday in talks between negotiators of the first three powers.— A French official reported "substantial progress" had been made toward the forming of a solid front of the four nations at the resumption of the world disarmament conference, with the four powers on a common ground of understanding concerning the disarmament question. It was learned that apparently only the outstanding point of sanctions remained to be solved. France has been furthering the setting up of penalties against any nation guilty of a breach of any disarmament agreement which might be reached. Great Britain was understood to be holding back from such a plan. Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large, told bo

PARIS, (U.P)—Germany has begun the long planned direct attack on military clauses of the Versailles treaty in preparation for the Geneva disarmament conference next month, it was indicated today. Success may depend upon the degree to which she can persuade France that she will not secretly build up a war machine such as the treaty forbids. France is convinced that Germany is heavily armed now despite treaty provisions.

1933-09-27.text: LONDON, Sept. 27.—Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, Great Britain's one man “brain trust,” left for Washington today to reopen negotiations for the revision of the British war debt. Sir Frederick, economic adviser to the government, went by motor to Southampton to embark in the liner Majestic, with Sir Ronald Lindsay, ambassador at Washington, and T. K. Brewley, financial counselor of the embassy, as fellow passengers. The debt originally was negotiated by former Secretary of Treasury Andrew W. Mellon and Stanley Baldwin, former British Premier and now Lord President of the Council in the Ramsay MacDonald cabinet. Its present capital value is approximately $3,600,000,000 (B). It provides for annuities between now and 1984 of approximately $9,900,000,000. Officially the British government still thinks the best solution of the present situation would be cancellation of the entire debt. Unofficiall

WASHINGTON, Sept. 27.—(AP)— The United States will press completion of its 32-ship, $238,000,000 naval building program and has so advised Great Britain. The London government had suggested that construction of the four 10,000-ton six-inch gun cruisers included in the program be deferred pending further discussion of possible naval limitations. The American reply, understood to have been given personally to Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, by Norman H. Davis, the American ambassador at large, was described in this statement last night by the state department:

Southampton, Fi Sept. 28, -Pi— Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, chief economic adviser to the government, sailed yesterday for the United States where he expects to see President Roosevelt personally concerning the projected new war debts settlement. “Tam visiting America,” he said. “to observe the feeling toward the question of the war debts and I expect I shall be presented with an opportunity of discussing the position with President Roosevelt, although for the moment he is very busily engaged with internal problems.” Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador at Washington, and T. K. Bewley, Treasury official who has been attached to the Washington embassy, sailed with Sir Frederick on the Mauretania.

Geneva, Sept. 27.—(LP)—The treatment of Jews in Germany is a fit subject for the council of the League of Nations to take up, Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, indicated in a speech to the League assembly today. The council, Sir John said, has a special responsibility "under the minorities treaties for assuring itself of just and impartial treatment for those who by race, language or religion differ from the governing majority." He did not mention Germany specifically. But his remarks were considered a direct reference to the Jewish problem there.

ROME, Sept. 27.--Unofficial reports from the provinces indicated today that between fifteen and twenty persons were killed in the earthquake that shook Italy and northern Jugoslavia. Approximately 200 persons were injured, most of them slightly. Two hundred houses collapsed and 1,000 more were damaged in Chieti province.

ROME, Sept. 26 (4)—Latest reports Tuesday night showed 16 persons killed, approximately 200 injured and hundreds made homeless in the earthquake in the Abruzzi mountain region in the early morning. That district has furnished thousands of emigrants to America. All the dead and most of the injured came from small villages. The larger cities were spared serious victims, although they suffered the loss of many homes. Residents of Sulmona, a city of 19,000, found scarcely a home without a damaged roof. The shock was severe at Abez-bane, but damage was only slight and no one was injured.

(By The Associate Press) RYAN, Sept. 25 -- Directors of Texas A & M College in special session on the campus yesterday voted to fight efforts of Bryan residents to compel the college to admit their daughters this scholastic year. The board planned to advise with the state attorney general's department, employ counsel and oppose the application for a writ of mandamus, filed Sept. 16 with W. C. Davis, district judge, in Brazos County court. Judge Davis indicated today that a hearing on the application, set for tomorrow, might be delayed by application for continuance on the ground that the board desired more time to prepare a defense. J. F. Stanford and others filed the application. Two of his daughters, Evelyn and Alice, were among the 12 Brown girls who signed the petition presented Wednesday. Evelyn married Lee Searcy. She had planned to do post-graduate work at the college. Stanford, a

WASHINGTON, Sept. 26 (4).— R. S. Carey, American vice consul at Tampico, Mexico, advised the State Department today that all Americans residing in the Tampico area are believed to have escaped injury from the hurricane which devastated that city. State Department records list 969 American citizens living in the Tampico district. Carey reported the city is now under martial law.

1933-07-22.text: (Copyright, 1933, by the United Press.) LONDON, July 22.—(U.P)—Nine nations, producers of silver or holders of silver bullion, signed a four year silver control agreement at a secret meeting late today in the suite of Senator Key Pittman, (D.), Nevada, American silver expert at the world economic conference.

Pendine Sands, Wales, July 22—James and Amy Mollison, the “flying sweethearts,” took off at 11:59 a.m. today (6:59 a.m. EDT) in their airplane Seafarer for New York. They arrived in their plane from London only two hours and 29 minutes earlier. They said they hoped to reach New York in about 34 hours. After resting and overhauling their plane they planned to take off for Baghdad, Mesopotamia, trying for the long distance non-stop record.

Roland Garros Stadium, Auteuil, France, July 22.—()—The American doubles team of George Martin Lott Jr. and John Van Ryn today put the United States back into the inter-zone Davis tennis battle with England by defeating Fred Perry and George Patrick Hughes in straight sets, 8-6, 6-4, 6-1. It was the first victory for the Americans who dropped both singles matches yesterday, leaving England with a 2-1 advantage.

London—The plane bearing James Mollison and his wife, Amy Johnson, passed over Fastnet Rock, County Cork, at 2:20 p. m. GMT (10:30 a. m. EDT) today, heading for the north Atlantic on a flight to New York. Fastnet Rock is off Cape Clear, at the southwestern tip of Ireland. The Mollisons got their last sight of land there before striking out on the long over-water flight across the Atlantic. The “Flying Sweethearts” took off at 11:59 a. m. today (6:59 a. m. EDT) from Pendine Sands, Wales, in their airplane Seafarer for New York. They arrived in their plane from London only two hours and 29 minutes earlier. They said they hoped to reach New York in about 34 hours. After resting and overhauling their plane they planned to take off for Baghdad, Mesopotamia, trying for the long distance non-stop record. They said they hoped to be back in England within from seven to ten days.

LONDON, July 22.—(#)—It was said in well informed American quarters today that representatives of the chief silver holding and producing nations had reached an understanding for control of the silver market. United States Senator Key Pittman said he expected to make an announcement later.

London, July 21. (P)—The United States will apply “the precise test of necessity” before raising tariffs under the farm relief and industrial recovery acts, Secretary of State Cordell Hull told the world economic conference today in a final appeal for perpetuation of the tariff truce. As the world congress ended its consideration of trade policies, Secretary Hull presented a tentative resolution setting forth the American position which he urged as a basis for study during the recess which begins next Thursday. The document provided the ground for continuation of President Roosevelt’s tariff armistice and indicated that the United States proposed to raise such import duties as may be made necessary by higher costs through higher wages and shorter working hours. Only as an emergency measure and after due notice to the countries affected. As the United States prepared to enter negotiations

‘SY ine Associated Press) New York was the goal today of two planes, one winging eastward around the globe and the other flying over the Atlantic on the difficult westward crossing between England and the North American continent. It was the last lap of a round-the-world dash for the intrepid Oklahoman, Wiley Post, who pushed off from Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, at 8:41 a.m. (central standard time) for Floyd Bennett field, Brooklyn. Nearly 20 and a quarter hours ahead of the record globe-circling time, Post had within his grasp a new record. With but 2,100 miles of his trip remaining, his backers expect him back late tonight nearly a full day ahead of the time he and Harold Gatty made in 1931. Meanwhile, Jim Mollison and his wife, Amy Johnson Mollison, were en route from England on an over-ocean hop to New York—what they term their “greatest gamble.” The dangerous westward crossing of the

LONDON, July 21.—(AP)—The American team under the leadership of Ely Culbertson stretched its lead in the international contract bridge tournament, for a trophy posted by Charles M. Schwab, to 150 points tonight, leaving the English quartet an almost hopeless task in the remaining 50 boards. The score at the end of the 250th board was United States, 83,200 points; England, 74,050.

1933-06-09.text: LONDON, June 9—(?)—Secretary of State Cordell Hull, head of the American delegation to the World Economic Conference, and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, had a private talk lasting 45 minutes after luncheon today at the home of Ray Atherton, counselor to the American embassy. Considerable secrecy surrounded the luncheon. Where Mr. Hull had been was not revealed until after he had returned to conference headquarters. It was stated that the men renewed their Washington acquaintance. Whether the war debts were discussed was not disclosed.

By Joshen F. H. Baind. United Press Staff Correspondent. London, June 9—(UP)—Stabilization of currencies is the first logical point of attack against the world depression, Secretary of State Cordell Hull, head of the American delegation to the world economic conference, declared today in his first interview with the British press. Reduction of tariff barriers is an essential complementary necessity, he said, and to be effective the two would have to be carried out simultaneously. Depreciation of currencies and increasing tariffs inspired each other, forming a vicious circle, he said. The American delegation approached the conference with very definite ideas of what had to be done to end the depression, but was open-minded toward all ideas, he said. He hoped to confer with Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald either late today or tomorrow and also hoped to talk to statesmen of other countries befo

Geneva, June 2.--Japan threw the disarmament conference into confusion today by assailing the London naval treaty as a provoker of international apprehensions and refusing to renounce bombardment from the air until aircraft carriers should be abolished. In this uncertain atmosphere the formal discussions of arms limitation and reduction were adjourned until July 3. The attack on the naval accord, reached in London in 1930 by the United States, Great Britain and Japan, drew sharp protests from the American and British delegates and from Arthur Henderson, president of the Geneva parley, and British foreign secretary when the agreement was concluded. Aerial Bombing, Hugh R. Wilson, American spokesman, also appealed earnestly but in vain—to the Tokyo delegate, Ambassador Haotake Sato, to reconsider his stand against prohibition of aerial bombing as long as other great powers possess warships

London, June 9—(/P)—The cabinet met for more than two hours today for discussion of the war debt question, but it was understood that the matter was not finally disposed of and that it still was under consideration. Another meeting is to be held, probably early next week, although definite arrangements for it have not been made.

LONDON, June 9. ()—Secretary of State Cordell Hull, chairman of the American delegation to the world economic conference, struck out vigorously today at what he described as attempts by 'minority groups' in various countries to divert attention from the real purpose of the conference to relatively minor issues. Hull, facing a roomful of American and British reporters at his hotel in his first press conference in England, said that in view of the magnitude and difficulties of the economic problems facing the parley he does not consider it within the functions of his delegation to go outside a well-defined list of subjects outlined in the formal program for discussion. He spoke out emphatically when asked about a London newspaper story directing attention to his reference to the Irish Free State as an Irish 'Republic' when he spoke at Cobh en route to England. This reference caused some di

Washington, June 5—(A)—The signing of the four power peace pact in Europe was hailed today by President Roosevelt in a formal statement as a good omen for the Geneva and London conferences. The brief statement by the President follows: “The initialling at Rome of the four power pact between France, Germany, Great Britain and Italy is a good augury. The United States welcomes every effort toward replacing conflicting national aims by international cooperation for the greater advantage of all. This agreement of the principal European powers to work closely together for the preservation of peace should give renewed courage to all who are striving for the success of the Geneva and London conferences.

London, June 9, (UP)—The British cabinet, meeting today to consider the question of paying its June war debt installment to the United States, was understood to have failed to reach any definite decision.

LONDON, June 8.—(@) — Resolutely hopeful but without the conspicuous optimism which has characterized so many missions to international parleys, Cordell Hull, secretary of state, and his colleagues of the American delegation to the world economic conference arrived in London this evening and at once established themselves in 90 rooms of a west-end hotel. Mr. Hull, debarking at Plymouth today from the steamship President Roosevelt, declared that war debts will not be discussed during the world parley which begins next Monday. "We shall not go outside the details of the agenda," the secretary said before he and his party took the train which brought them to London. Fifty huge boxes of archives and records brought by the American group were unpacked at their new (continued on Page 1, Col. 6)

1933-12-04.text: Beehttrst, Gamoria, West Africa, Dec. 4. ~ A glassy sea held Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh at this little British port today after three further attempts to start on a non-stop flight to Natal, Brazil. In the warm light of a brilliant tropical moon and as Europeans and natives watched, Lindbergh tried again and again to get the plane off the water. There was so little wind, and the sea was so smooth that suction held the long pontoons in the water as they glided along with gathering speed at the mouth of the Gambia river. At 5 a.m., there still was no prospect of a wind, and it was understood that Lindbergh would make his next trial tonight. Lindbergh had made five trials in all—two yesterday, to get the plane up. On their projected flight from (Continued on Page Two)

Washington—John (Jake the Barber) Factor must go to London to face charges growing out of his stock market operations there as a result of a ruling by the Supreme Court today. The court held the charges of “receiving money knowing it to be fraudulently obtained” furnishes a sufficient basis for Great Britain extradition proceedings against the wealthy Chicagoan who started his career in a loop barber shop. The ruling was accepted as an important interpretation of the extradition treaties between this country and Great Britain.

LONDON, DEC. 4. (AP).—The British cabinet wrestled nearly two hours in a special meeting today with problems arising from the crisis which has been reached in relations between the Irish Free State and the British Commonwealth of Nations. The ministers had before them a dispatch sent by President Eamonn DeValera of the Irish Free State, to Dominions Secretary J. H. Thomas. In it, it was understood DeValera said he was awaiting a statement as to what would be the British government's attitude toward the declaration of an Irish Republic. It was generally expected in political circles that the cabinet reply to DeValera would be dispatched today and the contents of this answer would be disclosed tomorrow in the House of Commons.

London, Dec. 4.—A public prosecutor read letters in Bow Street police court today in an attempt to prove that Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, 43-year-old engineer, sought to blackmail King George. At the end of the hearing Haddon, who claims to be the illegitimate son of the late Duke of Clarence and hence a nephew of the king, was remanded to jail until Tuesday. The prosecution contends the letters were written by Haddon to the king in an effort to extort money. “There is absolutely no evidence at all to support his assertion.”

LONDON. (Special) — The question of whether Ireland will remain a British commonwealth or secede and become an independent republic, with thousands of Irish in England subject to deportation unless they choose British citizenship, is expected to be presented to the House of Commons tomorrow as a clear-cut issue. Bluff Jim Thomas, secretary for the dominions, and the dour Irish president, Eamon De Valera, have joined in a battle which it is feared will revive the bitter pee of the ancient Anglo-Irish feud. If a free state political crisis is credited, it is believed in authoritative quarters that De Valera will call a general election on a platform of an all-Ireland republic, that is a de jure republic for all Ireland and a de facto republic for 26 counties of the Irish Free State. (The six counties of Northern Ireland are not a part of the Free State.) As secretary of the Dominions, Thom

| NEW YORK, Dec. 3.—()—For the second time in as many days the difficulties of communicating with the smallest and most northerly of the British West African dependencies gave an added touch of secrecy to the flying plans of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh early today. Yesterday word of two unsuccessful attempts of the Lindberghs to take off across the South Atlantic for Brazil from Bathurst, Gambia, was delayed in reaching the outside world because of the operating hours of the cable office at the colonial. When it became known that the colonel planned a third attempt at dawn today arrangements were made to maintain contact throughout the night. The explanation of the lack of word from the West African village generally accepted here was that virtually all of the English population was assisting the colonel until he could lift his plane.

COLUMBUS, Dec. 4.—Youngstown’s gangsters were branded the “toughest in the midwest” today by Prof. David W. Maurer, head of Ohio State University English department, as he made public a partial report of a three-year study of crime conditions. Chicago gangsters, Prof. Maurer found, “aren't so bad.” Cleveland, he said, is a “yap town” in underworld parlance. During his three-year study of middle western crime conditions, Prof. Maurer visited gang meeting places in Chicago, Youngstown, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Akron, Buffalo, Detroit, New York and New Orleans. Coincident with the end of probation, Prof. Maurer blamed the dry era for a major part of gangsters’ activities and predicted that the return of legalized whisky would abolish many of the underworld evils of the prohibition period. The investigator said the “toughest” spot he found was a section of Youngstown known as “the monkey’s nes

Bathurst, Gambia, British West Africa, Dec. 4, (INS)—Again frustrated by a tropical calm which since dawn Sunday had prevented their taking off on their projected flight across the South Atlantic to Brazil, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh today were forced to temporarily postpone their start. A glassy-smooth sea and a windless sky conspired to keep the Lindberghs aground, balking their attempts to get away both this morning and yesterday morning. The smooth sea allowed suction to be created under the ship’s huge pontoons, holding the plane to the water, and lack of wind left nothing for the big wings to grip as Colonel Lindbergh futilely speeded his craft over the water. The Lindberghs were ready to take off shortly after midnight (8:00 p.m. Sunday Eastern Standard Time), but eight hours later there still was not sufficient wind for the take-off on the 1,800-mile hop, the longest o

1933-01-02.text: (By Associated Press) LONDON, Jan. 1.--Six new peers were created in the new year's honor list announced today. Others honored included two men who were elevated to privy councilorships, six to baronetcies, and 28 who were made Knights. Sir Joseph Duveen, art dealer and connoisseur, was named a baron and heads the list of new peers. He became a knight in 1919 and a baronet in 1926. Others who were created barons today are Field Marshal Sir George Milne, Sir Charles Nall-Cain, Sir Rennell Rodd, and Sir Walter Runciman, father of the Rt. Hon. Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade. Sir Walter is a director of shipping lines. Sir George, since 1925, has been chief of the imperial general staff. Sir Rennell served his majesty in several diplomatic roles and a few years ago was a member of the permanent international commission for advancement of peace between the United States and

SHANGHAI, Jan. 1.—(#)—Sharp pessimism concerning possible developments in Sino-Japanese relations during 1933 characterized main articles in New Year's editions of newspapers today. The almost unanimous opinion was brought out in the Chinese journals that, although China faced “the Japanese occupation of Manchuria in 1931 and the hostilities here in 1933, the new year perhaps will witness still greater catastrophes since the Sino-Japanese dispute is nearing a crisis.” The newspapers indicated belief Japan's activities in Manchuria are straining that nation’s resources to the breaking point and that during 1933 “the Japanese must win a decisive victory or break under the strain.” In order to maintain the position Japan has sought in Manchuria, the newspapers set forth, the Japanese must soon seek to occupy Jehol, the province between Manchuria and China proper, and to strike boldly into t

(By United Press). * Shanghai, Jan. 2.—Fighting between Chinese and Japanese at Shanhaikwan, border city at the southern edge of Manchuria, continued at a late hour tonight with 12 Chinese killed and numerous wounded, reports reaching here said. Chinese authorities insisted the Japanese fired on their barracks without provocation. Marshal Chuang Hsueh-Liang ordered the Chinese commanders to avoid aggravations. The Japanese occupied the main gate of the ancient walled city, which is the gateway into China. Shortly thereafter there was heavy hand-to-hand street fighting, the fighting continued during the night. The Japanese claimed that the Chinese had violated the neutrality agreed on after the Japanese occupation of Chinchow and subsequent operations. It was reported that Marshal Chang Hsueh-Liang had concentrated six brigades of troops at the Jehol border fearing Japanese occupation of

) MOSCOW, Jan. 2.—C(P)—It was learned unofficially today that the Japanese government has communicated to the Soviet government a formal refusal to sign a non-aggression pact with Soviet Russia proposed by this government a year ago. Details were not yet available, but it was reported that the main reason for the Japanese refusal was the inability of the two countries to reconcile their opposing viewpoints. Japan was represented as desiring first to settle all differences before signing the pact, and Soviet Russia contending the pact should be signed first as a guarantee that the settlement of such differences would be accomplished by peaceful means.

Moscow, Jan. 1.-(4)—The ending of Soviet Russia's first five-year plan and the beginning of the second plan was acclaimed today by the Soviet press, which without exception devoted entire editions to glowing accounts of the nation’s achievements. With the success they attributed to first efforts to complete the reconstruction of Russia's national economy on a socialistic basis, the newspapers contrasted conditions which they said exist in capitalistic countries and which were painted in the blackest of colors. Every newspaper made the unqualified assertion that the five-year plan was completed in four years. Tzvestia, organ of the executive committee of the Communist party, printed a three-quarter page drawing of Joseph Stalin, president of the east section of the third internationale and general secretary.

New York, Jan. 2 (*)—A warning that the alternative to closer coordination of the social forces in American life might be a dictatorial system in which violence might subordinate technical intelligence, was contained in the report of the President's Research Committee on Social Trends, made public this morning. The committee, appointed by President Hoover in 1920, has spent three years studying changes in institutions. The report said in part: "Unless there can be a more impressive integration of social skills and fusing of social purposes than is revealed by recent trends, there can be no assurance that these alternatives with their accompaniments of violent revolution, dark periods of serious repression of libertarian and democratic forms, the proscription and loss of many useful elements in the present productive system, can be averted." Democratic Regime Might Help In a discussion of

NEW YORK, Jan. 2.—(4)—Slain by the doorman of his garish midtown night club, Larry Fay, high powered Broadway racketeer, was a victim of his own modest gesture at unemployment relief, police said today. Fay, a product of the Hell’s Kitchen district, was shot through the heart last night as he attempted to mollify a man whose salary had been cut to make room for another employee. Police, discrediting reports the shooting may have had the more sinister aspect of a planned underworld execution, set out to find Edward Maloney, a doorman, who disappeared immediately after four shots had cut Fay down. The one-time milk “czar” and taxi-cab operator whose night club enterprises once brought him as much as $10,000 a week, died with three dimes in his pocket. He was said by police to have cut Maloney’s $100 a week salary to $60 in order to take on another doorman at $40. Shortly after 8:30 o'clock

A heavy snow wave swept west as the President’s research committee on social trends, after three years’ study, reported tonight that there “can be no assurance” that “violent revolution” in America can be averted, “unless there can be a more impressive integration of social skills and fusing of social purposes than is revealed by recent trends.” The committee's findings emphasized that the group did not wish “to assume an attitude of alarmist irresponsibility,” but added that it would be “highly negligent” to “ignore imminent perils in further advance of our heavy technical machinery over crumbling roads and shaking bridges.” Silence Is Assent “There are times,” the committee reported, “when silence is not neutrality, but assent.” The research was financed by the Rockefeller Foundation and more than 500 investigators throughout the country took part in it. The findings are published in t

1933-06-25.text: LONDON, June 24 (AP)--A determined drive for the lowering of tariff barriers was planned tonight by Secretary of State Cordell Hull, who emphasized that America’s home program does not clash with efforts toward world cooperation. Whether the world economic conference succeeds in reducing tariffs depended on an important series of secret conversations which Hull plans early next week with Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, Foreign Minister Georges Bonnet of France and other leaders. Hull issued a formal statement saying that the conference's program of international cooperation was “not irreconcilable” with the United States domestic program for an increase of employment and a raising of price levels. He charged that conflict was being fomented by certain forces at every stop, aimed at confusing the conference and seeking to prevent realization of its goals. Hull's statement was designed

BERLIN, June 24—The last obstacle in the way of Germany’s Protestant churches becoming the exponents of a militant racially restricted Christianity was removed tonight with the resignation of Dr. Friedrich von Bodelschwingh from the new post of Protestant reichsbishop. Reliable sources reported that another prominent non-Nazi figure, Dr. Alfred Hugenberg, presented his resignation today to President von Hindenburg as minister of economics and agriculture in the Hitler cabinet. A determined move against the aviation inequality imposed upon Germany by the Versailles treaty was heralded by officialdom and the press in a demand, based on yesterday's reported visitation by foreign airplanes, that Germany be given the right to self-protection in the air. Resignation of Dr. von Bodelschwingh a month after his election by Protestant church groups appeared to assure ultimate victory for the Nazi

Vatican City, June 6. (AP)— The bomb which exploded yesterday in the portico of St. Peter’s was manufactured in Spain and brought here by Demeterio Solamon, who carried a Spanish passport, the authorities declared today after they had arrested Solamon, charging him with planting the explosive. The authorities asserted the explosion was the result of the present strained relations between the Vatican and Spain following the pope’s encyclical of June 3 and the Latae Sententiae excommunications of members of the Spanish government. The bomb caused a panic in a crowd of holy year pilgrims. Four persons were injured but there was little property damage.

WASHINGTON, June 24—(AP)—The nation’s business moved ahead of its planned restoratives last week with freight car loadings—one of the most accepted industrial barometers—showing new and substantial gains. For the seven-day period ending June 17, the American Railway Association announced Saturday, loadings were 587,533 cars, an increase of 23,385 over the preceding week and 69,533 more than in the corresponding week of last year. All commodities except less than carload merchandise increased over 1932. Meanwhile, the Industrial Regulation and Public Works Administrations were mustering their strength to put it behind the upward push which business is already making. Thirty tentative codes providing for increased wages and greater employment were reported Saturday to have been submitted to Hugh S. Johnson, head of the National Recovery Administration, exclusive of the textile code upon wh

WASHINGTON, June 24 (#)— President Roosevelt threw his personal influence behind the cotton acreage reduction program Saturday as administrators of the farm act put final touches on plans for beginning Monday an intensive campaign in southern states to cut down this year’s output of the crop. An important change in the plan was announced by Cully A. Cobb of Atlanta, the cotton production chief. This change provides that farmers will be permitted to offer to destroy up to 50 per cent of the area they have planted to cotton instead of a maximum of 40 per cent, previously announced. The minimum each must offer in order to become eligible to benefit payments remains the same, 26 per cent.

FORT SMITH, Ark, June 24.—(AP)—Two desperadoes who mowed down an officer with a sub-machine gun at Alma last night, appeared at a farmhouse in the Ozark Mountains near Winslow today, beat Mrs. John Rogers with a chain when she refused to give them the keys to her automobile and fled. Heavily armed posses of officers and citizens beat through the underbrush of the hills tonight in the vicinity of the Rogers home. Guards were posted on all roads and it was believed the gunmen were hemmed in. Mrs. Rogers was alone when the men appeared. They called her to the door and pointed their sub-machine gun at her, threatening her with death unless she produced the keys to her car. She refused and one of the men picked up a heavy chain and again demanded the keys. As she refused, the man struck her until she fell, badly bruised and cut about the legs and body. "We'll fix it so nobody can use it," Mrs

WASHINGTON, June 24.—(@)—Pointing the way to the reopening next Tuesday of the investigation into private bank operations, Chairman Fletcher of the Senate banking committee today said the investigators will continue to disclose any ‘unwholesome income tax practices’ that might be found. Referring to the recent acquittal of Charles E. Mitchell, former chairman of the National City Bank, Fletcher said in a formal statement that “public condemnation of devices employed by him and others to escape taxation” made legislative remedies inevitable. Fletcher mapped out the future course of the inquiry and, reviewing its accomplishments, said it “has already imposed many unsound practices in securities markets.” Hopeful for Reforms “It has shown,” he said, “that the stock exchange, while enforcing the most rigid honesty within its own circle, does not yet assume much responsibility for the manner

WASHINGTON, June 24 (4) —Demands for recognition of Russia came from two different quarters today as the capital speculated over the possibility that renewed diplomatic relations might flow indirectly from the world economic conference. Senator Norris (R-Neb) in a formal statement ridiculing America’s failure to recognize the Soviet government, said he was reliably informed Russia wanted to buy millions of dollars worth of American wheat, cotton and machinery which would give employment to thousands of jobless. At about the same time, the United States Board of Trade, headed by Rudolph Spreckels of California, issued a statement requesting President Roosevelt to restore “full diplomatic relations with the Soviet government.” Recognition of the Soviet republic is understood to be an open question with President Roosevelt, with informed quarters of the opinion that no action will be taken

1933-07-14.text: — 7 Oe a re, London, July 14.—The steering committee of the world economic conference decided today to recess the worldwide parley on July 27. All committees were notified to have their complete reports ready by next Friday. The full bureau meeting will be conducted the following Tuesday and the final plenary session will be held on the 27th. It is understood that great care will be taken to avoid a note of discord at the plenary session. There was a clear indication that the conference is expected to resume at a future date. This attitude would permit continuation of the tariff truce which was for the duration of the parley and which many nations desire not to terminate. The plenary session will have to confirm the steering committee's decision to close out the deliberations, but leaders consider this a mere formality.

BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., July 12.—I see by the papers where my old governor friend, Bill Murray of Oklahoma, called out the national guard to keep the folks from voting for beer. Now he will have to call out the United States army to keep the folks from celebrating the voting of beer. The London conference has decided to hold for two more weeks, in order for the hotels to kinder play even on the thing, and give the American delegation a little golf against the Prince of Wales. There is nothing as sad, forlorn and forgotten, in the world as a delegation returning from conference. We have forgot now who we sent over. Yours, WILL ROGERS

(By United Press). London, July 14.——Tactily confessing their inability to make progress, the general staff of the Fevia economic conference—the so-called little bureau or steering committee—today decided to arrange a recess for July 27. Ever since President Roosevelt told the European nations that he would not allow the American dollar to be stabilized until rising prices had advanced to a reasonable level, the parley has been inactive. The gold bloc nations will not allow their money to be depreciated and they insist that the dollar be stabilized regardless of the consequences to the U.S. For the past few weeks, American business has enjoyed a favorable position in world trade due to our prices, which have been attractive, based on the depreciated dollar. The gold bloc nations insist that this position not be changed by stabilization. The result in the parley has been made apparent. No

LONDON, (P) — Great Britain Thursday smashed the United States’ dream of an internationally coordinated public works program to raise employment. In a declaration to the economic committee of the world economic conference, Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade, informed the delegates that England could not and would not join in any further experiments of this nature. A resolution backed by H. Colijn of Holland, not to establish the sub-committee on public works until the monetary commission “is in a position to join us in that work” effectively ended the controversy when it was passed by the commission. It was realized that further steps cannot be taken in the present phase because the gold nations already have blocked discussion by the monetary commission.

London, July 13. —(®)— Great Britain went on record in the world economic conference today as opposed to public works programs a short time after the American delegation had broached a proposal calling for shorter hours of work and increases in wages to compensate for rise of prices as an ameliorative for unemployment. The American resolution, submitted by Sam D. McReynolds of Tennessee, declared unemployment is ‘one of the gravest problems the governments are confronted with at this time.’ Not Wise The British stand, taken in opposition to a French recommendation, came in the economic commission toward the close of the day. It was expressed by Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade. Runciman declared Great Britain had considerable experience with public work schemes, and found them ‘the most unremunerative of all efforts to reduce unemployment.’ He added that his government wo

POONA, India, July 14—(UP)— The Indian National Congress voted today to continue the struggle for freedom from Great Britain through the civil disobedience campaign which has been directed for more than three years by the Mahatma Gandhi. The Congress, after Gandhi had made an impassioned plea, decided to carry on civil disobedience unless the Viceroy receives Gandhi before August 1 and agrees to terms of "honorable peace."

LONDON, July 13 (®)—The American delegation presented a resolution to the economic commission of the world economic conference today calling for shorter hours of labor and an increase in wages in proportion to the rise in prices. Sam D. McReynolds of Tennessee submitted the proposal on behalf of the United States group. Unemployment Problem Its preamble declared that the unemployed situation is ‘one of the greatest problems the governments are confronted with at this time.’ Premier Hendryk Colijn of Holland, chairman of the commission, announced the introduction at a public meeting this morning. “The text of the American resolution follows: “Representatives of the powers participating in this conference, considering that unemployment and consequent great distress are now prevalent throughout the world, considering that existence of this situation is one of the gravest problems with which

Swanage, Eng., July 13.—(UP)—The Prince of Wales made a forced landing in his new airplane today while on his way to Weymouth to open a new pier in the harbor works program there. His pilot descended in a wheat field unable safely to continue because of heavy rain and mist. The machine was not damaged. The prince accepted a lift from a passing motorist, walking across the muddy field to the roadway. He arrived in Weymouth, his hair tousled, his clothing wet and his shoes covered with mud.

1933-10-25.text: GEORGETOWN, British Guinea. —(/P)— Senora Carola Perez Tuesday is caring for seven sons born to her in one delivery. Physicians regarded the septet birth as unique in medical history, and reported mother and babies as doing nicely.

London, Oct. 24 (#)—Observers in close touch with the Russian situation expressed amazement today at a report from New York that $500,000,000 credit was being sought on behalf of the Soviet in connection with President Roosevelt’s overtures looking to possible American recognition—with $450,000,000 wanted for machinery and steel rails and $50,000,000 for cotton. The observers said rails form one of the direst of Russian needs, but pointed out that Russia's most urgent need is for foodstuffs and livestock of all kinds. Independent agricultural economists here say Russia could absorb the whole world's agricultural surplus on long-term credits. Instead, it was noted, American farmers are destroying millions of pigs they could have shipped to Russia and likewise many cattle which could easily be transported on both land and sea. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 24—(4)— The cruiser Chicago, one of the new American fighting ships, was badly damaged, one of her crew was killed, another was missing and two others were seriously injured in a collision today with the British freighter Silver Palm in a fog off Point Sur, 130 miles south of here. A great hole was torn in the port side of the Chicago. The bow of the Silver Palm struck her just forward of the number 1 turret, penetrating the heavy armor plate and bored in until it reached almost to midship. The Chicago’s forward compartment below the water line filled. She began plowing her way toward Mare Island in San Francisco bay for a survey of the damage. The Silver Palm, also badly damaged, turned back for San Francisco. Chief pay clerk John W. Troy, of Newport, R. I., was killed. Lieutenant H. A. MacFarlane, of Hoverhill, Mass., was missing possibly in the mangled section of t

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 25.—(?)—Tales of a mystery ship in the fog about Point Sur, 110 miles south of here, and death to three officers that came in the crash of the U.S.S. Chicago and the British freighter Silverpalm were told today by officers of the cruiser as it prepared to proceed to Mare Island naval yard to get a 40-foot hole in her port bow repaired. The ships collided at 8 a.m. Tuesday while, Vice Admiral Harris Lang, Captain Manley Simons and Captain Herbert E. IVERNESS, Scotland (4) — Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh took off toward the south without revealing their destination. They flew here yesterday from Galway, Irish Free State, and were believed en route to Southampton, England.

New York—(#)—The sudden enthusiasm of some policemen for the study of English got nothing but the Bronx cheer today from certain low elements of the metropolis. “So the cops are going to have a school to learn how to talk nice and pretty,” sneered one gentleman who, loy and man, has known policemen ‘in and out of jail and up one alley and down another going on 25 years. “It’s a laugh. “What's the correct English, f'rinstance, for ‘scram’? That’s a swell five letter word meaning to ‘blow’ or ‘beat it’. “Suppose instead of ‘scram’ a bull would pipe something like this: ‘You dastardly ruffian, begone from this vicinity with alacrity’? I'm askin’ you, what'll it get him? The razzberries, that’s what it'll get him. Sure, it’s elegant English, but it ain't got no hair on it. “But ‘scram’—there’s a word, Pal; there’s a word.” Police Commissioner Bolan in opening a school of correct English for

; BY Vth ree WASHINGTON, Oct. 3--U. S. Treasury, on order of President Roosevelt, fixed the price of its open market gold purchases today at $31.36 an ounce. This was 50 cents above the price fixed in London on the basis of late exchange quotations. The action was designed to carry out Mr. Roosevelt's new program for lifting prices in America by controlling the dollar. The new gold price will be announced daily. The price yesterday was the world price on gold this morning.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 25.—A “phantom” ship drove the U.S. cruiser Chicago off its course and into the path of the British freighter Silver Palm, officers of the warship said today in describing the mid-sea collision which killed three men and injured another. The bodies of Lieutenant F. S. Chappelle, Waterloo, N. Y., Lieutenant H. A. MacFarlane, Haverhill, Mass., and Chief Pay Clerk John W. Troy, Newport, R. I., were carried on the cruiser, which reached port here despite a gaping hole in its port side. The opening extended from the waterline to the top deck. Machinist Joseph A. Oehlers, Camden, N. Y., had an arm amputated in the collision. Captain’s Statement Captain H. E. Kays, commander of the Chicago, said a “large brown ship” appeared suddenly out of the fog on the starboard side of the cruiser, cutting across the bow. He did not know its identity. “We slackened speed and sheared off

1933-10-24.text: INVERNESS, Scotland, Oct. 25 (4 After bucking strong head winds on a flight from Galway, Irish Free State, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed here today in their big seaplane. They remained overnight and plans for tomorrow were not announced.

SLATTIM, Oct 24. — Shattering and blowing, winter roared over the North Pacific today in its 1933 debut. It brought snow, gales, heavy rains, near zero temperatures and rising rivers in Alaska, British Columbia and Washington. In neighboring Oregon Monday summer made a timid bow, perhaps a farewell, sending temperatures up 10 degrees in Portland to a maximum of 72. A gale toppled chimneys, tore off roofs, smashed plate glass windows, and drove a halibut boat ashore in Juneau, Alaska. Temperatures dropped abruptly to 13 degrees above zero. Eleven inches of snow fell at Revelstoke, B. C., a strange sight for October. Nearly an inch fell at Vancouver, B. C. Strong warm winds melted the snows on the Cascade Mountains of Central Washington, sending streams rapidly upward.

GALWAY, Irish Free State, Oct. 24.—Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh is getting homesick. “I'm terribly anxious,” said the wife of the famous American airman after their hop from Southampton, England, “to see my baby....” “Yes, I'll be glad to be back home again.” She insisted, however, the long trip with her husband has not been tiresome and she said she considered Ireland one of the most delightful lands over which they have flown. But perhaps there was a reason: The westerly part of Ireland, Colonel Lindbergh pointed out to his wife, gave him his first sight of land after his historic lone Atlantic crossing years ago. Even the quiet-mannered colonel confessed seeing the land again gave him a “thrill of pleasure.” After their aerial survey of the northern coast of Ireland, the Lindberghs will fly to Scotland.

GALWAY, Irish Free State, Oct. 23 (P)—The air-minded fisher folk of this district gave an enthusiastic welcome to Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh today. The flying American couple made a perfect landing in the great harbor of Galway shortly after 5 P. M., after a five and one-half hour flight from Southampton, England. They will carry on again tomorrow, hopping off at 7 A. M., to view the winding Connemara Coast to its northwest end.

European President Roosevelt's new gold policy was received in a generally sympathetic way Monday, but the American dollar was under pressure on the Paris, London, and Berlin exchanges. In London, selling pressure caused a depreciation of nearly eight cents, with the close at $4.60% to the pound. On the Paris bourse, the dollar opened at 17.90 francs (5.58 cents to the franc) and closed at 17.86 francs (5.59 cents) after touching 17.65 francs (5.60 cents) in a flurry of short selling. In Berlin, the dollar rate was 2.92 marks (34.24 cents to the mark), compared with 2.98 marks (33.55 cents) Saturday. Comment on these fluctuations and the American executive's plan ranged from statements that a rise of prices would make the payment of fixed charges easier to the remark that a stable currency “will be something new in the history of economics.” French monetary and economic authorities haile

WASHINGTON, D. C., Oct. 24.—The United States cruiser Chicago collided with the British Kerr liner Silver Palm while en route from San Pedro to San Francisco with the scouting fleet today, according to despatches to the navy department. Two men were missing and two reported seriously injured in the accident. The port bow of the Chicago was penetrated to nearly the midship line, filling the forward compartment below the water line.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 23.—(U.P)—The Reconstruction Finance Corporation will begin “almost immediately” the first step in President Roosevelt's new move for a “managed currency.” This first step is the purchase of newly mined gold in the United States at prices above the world prices of London and Paris. The immediate effect is expected to be what amounts to renewal of the embargo on all gold exports unless the R. F. C. itself decides to sell—a step unlikely for some time to come. With stoppage of the outflow of newly mined gold, amounting to 25,000 to 30,000 ounces a week, prices are expected to rise. This means automatically that the dollar falls, and the normal result would be a corresponding rise in commodity prices. At the same time, the R. F. C. will be building up a huge gold reserve, such as that now possessed by the Bank of France. This may be used either as a foundation for new issue

Washington, Oct. 24—(C?)—The Navy department received a report today from the cruiser Chicago saying that two officers were missing and a marine officer and some navy enlisted men were seriously injured in a collision today between the cruiser and the British tanker Silver Palm off San Pedro, Calif. The Chicago reported it was struck just forward of the No. 1 turret. The Silver Palm penetrated to amidship line of the cruiser, which was proceeding northward from San Pedro to San Francisco. The missing men were Lieut. H. A. Macfarlane, Haverhill, Mass., and Chief Pay Clerk John W. Troy, Newport, R. I. Those reported to be seriously injured were First Lieut. F. S. Chappelle, a marine officer of Waterloo, N. Y., and Machinist Joseph A. Oehlers of Camden, N. J.

1933-01-12.text: Chinese and Japanese military leaders are reported to have met in the presence of British naval officers, at Shanhaikwan to discuss peace terms, but meanwhile there were indications that troop movements were continuing in the northern Chinese province of Jehol. A Japanese advance on Lingyuan, in southern Jehol about 100 miles from Shanhaikwan was said to be continuing, and Japanese troop movement from Mukden to Chinchow, in Southern Manchuria, also were reported. From Chinchow dispatches described the Japanese movements and circulated to forestall the possibility of a Chinese offensive. These Chinese forces in Jehol was estimated at 130,000 men, including Chang Hsiao-Liang’s regulars and organizations of volunteers. Japanese planes, it was reported, reconnoitered Jehol City, the provincial capital, and Chaoyang, the next largest city, near the Manchurian border.

TOKYO, Jan. 12.—(/)—A Rengo (Japanese) news dispatch from Chinwangtao, China, said Japanese and Chinese military officers met in the presence of British naval officers there today to discuss peace terms. Results of the meeting were not divulged. A Chinese officer representing General Ho Chu-Kuo, Shanhaikwan commander who lost that city to the Japanese last week, was reported to have met with the commander of the Japanese detachment stationed at Chinwangtao. This Japanese detachment is a patrol force regularly stationed in the treaty port under provisions of the Boxer protocol of 1901. The meeting was reported held at the Japanese commander's headquarters. Further parleys were expected.

London, Jan. 12—Ubi—Fear that Beri Hinkler had met disaster, seeking a new record for an England-Australia flight increased today. No word has been received of Hinkler since he left England Saturday. It was hoped that Hinkler might have landed in some inaccessible spot. Leaving England with a 25-hour supply of gasoline, he could have reached the Greek coast before being forced down. But he might have crashed in the Alps, come down in the Adriatic or Mediterranean, or have been forced off his course, perhaps to North Africa.

LONDON, Jan. 11 (#)—Friends feared Wednesday night that disaster had overtaken Bert Hinkler, famous Australian airman, who has been missing five days on a flight by stages from Feltham, England, to Australia. Captain Hope, who is organizing a searching party, said he believed the aviator was dead. The airman took off before dawn Saturday, expecting to make Brindisi, Italy his first stop. He should have reached there Saturday night at the latest. The distance is 1,400 miles. Some of his friends said that perhaps he had more fuel than he had expected and so tried to make Athens without a stop, crashing in the Mediterranean.

11.—(#)—Chinese dispatches said today that 10,000 Japanese soldiers were marching into Jehol, headed for the City of Lingyuan. The attacking force included artillery and cavalry marching from Suichung, north of Shanhaikwan, which is in the hands of the Japanese. Lingyuan is in Southern Jehol. These dispatches, which were not otherwise confirmed, said also that a Japanese landing force had been put ashore at Chinwangtao, a seaport not far from Shanhaikwan, and was patrolling that vicinity.

Shanghai, (AP)-- Japanese airplanes were reported scouting today over Jehol (Cheng-Te), former summer residence of the Manchu emperors and now the capital of Jehol province, and Chaoyang, near the Manchurian border. There are the two principal cities of Jehol, about 140 miles apart. Chinese newspapers, which reported the sighting of the planes, also announced receipt of dispatches from southern Jehol and Manchuria stating that Japanese were engaged in feverish preparations for an invasion of Jehol. Military leaders predicted sharp fighting if a Japanese expedition already in the ancient Chinese province continued an advance toward Lingyuan, about 100 miles northeast of Jehol city. (Lingyuan is about ninety miles northwest of Shanhaikwan and the section of the great wall of China where Sino-Japanese fighting has occurred during the past ten days. The wall forms the southern boundary of Je

PARIS, Jan. 12 U.P)—Japan has placed a new $8,000,000 contract with a French firm for arms and munitions, the Agence Economique et Financier reported today, while other sources reported that the secret shipment of war materials from Europe to the Far East had reached quantities sufficient for war on a large scale. It is no secret here that the United States government has been trying to track down the sources of arms shipments and to determine the amount of war supplies sent to the Far East. Shipments also have been made to South America. Agence Economique et Financier said the $8,000,000 Japanese contract was secured by the Hotchkiss Armament Works. Paul Faure, member of the chamber of deputies, showed the chamber photostatic copies of orders for arms and munitions which included “1,000 kilograms of powder for Mauser rifle cartridges, destination Mauser factory, Leipzig. Madrid, Jan. 12, (4)—Nineteen extremists engaged in anti-government activities were reported to have been killed today when civil guards bombed a house at Casa Viejas where they had taken refuge. The government announced that the house was destroyed by hand grenades and for the present it was impossible to determine whether more than nineteen of the occupants had been killed. During the attack the extremists fired upon the guards, wounding six.

1933-01-26.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, (4)— Incomplete returns indicated today that President Eamon De Valera’s party, the Fianna Fáil, won a decisive victory in Tuesday’s election of a new Dáil Éireann. He may be assured of election to the presidency without needing the votes of any other parties. The Fianna Fáil—the party which has fought for complete independence of Ireland—has never had a clear majority in the Dáil in the ten-year history of the Free State. The Dáil elected De Valera president for the first time last March 9 as the result of a Fianna Fáil-Labor party combine.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Jan. 95.--Counting of the heaviest vote in Irish history began today with indications of an extremely close race between President Ramon de Valera and William T. Cosgrave for the presidency. A definite trend in yesterday's election of a new Dáil Éireann--the Irish House of Representatives which in turn elects the president of the executive council--was not likely to develop until tomorrow. In some scattered districts clerks will not be able to open ballot boxes until then. Rioting, which featured many meetings during the whirlwind three-weeks campaign, carried right through into election day with the biggest free-for-all at a polling booth in Ashburton. Tear gas bombs used by troops, summoned from an army barracks several miles away, finally ended the row. Civil guards previously found they were unequal to the situation. CAIRO, Egypt, Jan. 26. (AP)— A bomb was discovered this morning in the British general headquarters here. Military policemen discovered the bomb on a window ledge near the main entrance. It was immediately removed for examination. This bomb was said to be similar to one

WASHINGTON, Jan. 26.—Great Britain’s acceptance of terms for a war debts discussion was regarded today as having filled in much of the ground that must be built up before President-elect Roosevelt talks with that nation's representative. This attitude was taken generally in many quarters despite the British reservation against deciding in advance of a meeting of all nations to be represented there what subject should be placed on the agenda of the world economic conference, In the weeks preceding the American meetings in March with Great Britain and other debtor nations which have paid promptly, other exchanges undoubtedly will take place, outlining in more detail the ideas of both Mr. Roosevelt and the prospective foreign visitors, Will Do Own Bargaining. DUBLIN, Jan. 26. U.S—The Republican party of Eamon De Valera was leading the Cosgrave party two to one in returns from the election for members of the Dail today. The latest comparative standing of the parties on Dail candidates elected was: Fianna Fail (De Valera) 22; Cosgrave party 11; Independents, 4; Laborites, 1; Center party 1. Both President De Valera and former President William T. Cosgrave carried their home constituencies and were elected to the Dail. Complete results of the election were expected today, or early Friday. The use of the preference system of voting, in which proportional representation is determined by first preference votes, made final tabulation slow.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 26. - Anglo-American conversations on reduction of Great $4,600,000,000 war debt and other economic issues were assured today. Britain in a note to this country has accepted President-elect Roosevelt's invitation to send envoys here early in March. These discussions will inaugurate a parade of European debtors to Washington. Italy, Czechoslovakia, Lithuania, and Finland also have been invited to submit their cases for debt reduction. Latvia is to be given an invitation today. The British note was forwarded to Mr. Roosevelt at Warm Springs, Ga. Administration sources in close touch with the president-elect regarded the British answer as satisfactory, despite its reservations as to the scope of the economic discussions. “It will be recognized,” the note said, “that decisions on matters which constitute the subject of the approaching world economic conference and which affe

Washington, Jan. 25—Great Britain accepted today President-elect Roosevelt’s terms for a discussion of its war debt but made a reservation against deciding what questions will be considered by the world economic conference until there is a general meeting of all nations to be represented there. The British reply was delivered at the State Department while a furious debate rang out in the Senate which indicated that if there has been any yielding in the congressional agitation to cancellation or revision, the effect of the debt situation upon a wide range of world economic problems is crucial to every government and in the course of the discussion at Washington on the debt we shall be glad to take the opportunity of exchanging views with Mr. Roosevelt on those other matters in which the two governments are seriously interested,” said the British memorandum. LONDON (#) — Limiting by Great Britain of the forthcoming Anglo-American conference solely to decisions on war debts today apparently had eliminated any chance of the Washington parley eclipsing the proposed world economic conference in London. In official circles it was conceded Great Britain did not want the scope and purposes of the projected London conference limited, despite President-elect Roosevelt's offer to discuss the general world situation. Premier MacDonald yesterday was elected chairman of the forthcoming economic meeting, which cannot be held before this summer. This was decided yesterday by a preparatory commission which also listed currency, tariffs, prices and movements of capital as among the world problems to be considered at that time.

1933-11-12.text: NEW YORK, UP. A sharp re- bound in the dollar, in relation to other currencies, was halted by a substantial increase in the RFC gold price. The dollar was moving up sharply in London and Paris, when the RFC announced its price at $33.32 an ounce, up 12 cents. The dollar quickly subsided, and closed in New York, virtually unchanged from Friday. The pound sterling was off 1-2 cent at $5.10, but the French franc was unchanged at 6.27 cents. Securities markets were quiet, but U.S. government bonds attracted strong support after their substantial decline of the past two days, in a selling movement evidently prompted by the swift decline of the dollar on Thursday. Much of the selling of the governments was believed to have come from abroad. While there was no indication as to the source of Friday's buying, some quarters suggested the Federal Reserve may have expanded its open market purchases.

Paris, Dec. 12.—(49—A third default on the French debt to the United States was confirmed by the cabinet today. At the same time a firm stand toward Chancellor Hitler of Germany was approved. The government considers itself bound by the chamber’s refusal to pay the United States a year ago. Washington, Dec. 12.—(4)—The war debt payment due the United States from France December 15 amounts to $22,200,926, of which $2,354,438 is principal and $19,855,487 interest.

Berlin, Nov. 11.—-(4)—President Paul von Hindenburg appealed to the German people today ‘to stand before the world as a united nation, united in the will for peace but also in the demand for honor, equality and the respect of others. The venerable former war marshal and president endorsed Chancellor Hitler's stand for peace and honor, asked Germans to do likewise in the foreign policy plebiscite and Reichstag elections tomorrow and brought to an end one of the most remarkable pre-election campaigns in German history.

MOSCOW, Sunday, Nov. 12. (U.P) - Reports, which met with complete silence on the part of the Russian government, reached foreign diplomatic circles last night that a number of Japanese airplanes flying over the Soviet Siberian borders had been shot down eight days ago. The reports were not confirmed early today from other sources. The reports came at the time of a grave situation which was recently outlined by Premier Viashelev Molotov. He warned Japan that the Soviet would suffer no invasion of her territory. Warnings also had been sent to Tokio through the Russian ambassador regarding alleged violation of the Soviet’s borders by Japanese airplanes. The report said that six out of nine planes had been shot down and that 20 Japanese attached to the squadron had been captured or killed. VIENNA. (®) Hammers resounded in the gloomy courtyard of old Vienna's district jail as carpenters built a gallows for offenders against Chancellor Dollfuss’ new martial law decree. The gaunt scaffold, standing where there has not been an execution for almost twenty years, emphasized the government's description of the new order of things as “a new martial law.” The noise of the hammers replaced what otherwise might have been merry-making attending a celebration of the 15th anniversary of the founding of the Austrian republic Sunday. It was to prevent violence in connection with the anniversary observance by socialists or Nazis that martial law was decreed with a communique declaring that violence or inciting to violence would be punishable by the death sentence. But almost simultaneously with the publication of the decree unidentified men killed a home guard auxiliary policeman in Lochau

Berlin — (PF) — Elected by a nearly unanimous ballot, 661 nazis and near-nazis will march into the Kroll opera house on or about December 1 for the opening session of the largest reichstag ever assembled. ‘There is one seat there for every 60,000 votes cast in the election Sunday and hence the largest voting turnout in German history also means the largest number of solons ever elected. Al “Hand Picked.” Despite their number, nothing but a unanimous vote may ever be expected on any measure proposed by the government as all are hand-picked men, “blindly devoted to Chancellor Hitler's policies,” as described on Nov. 11, by Rudolf Hess, official head of the Nazi party. The Kroll opera house will continue as the meeting place of the reichstag because the plenary hall of the reichstag building had not yet been rebuilt following the incendiary fire last February.
