LONDON, JUNE 27, (AP).—Representative Sam D. McReynolds, addressing the commercial policy committee of the world economic conference, today struck back at charges that the United States had gone nationalistic. He asserted monetary stabilization should be undertaken by all nations rather than only three or four. The conference this morning was in the throes of a fresh dramatic development precipitated by the unexpected action of gold bloc countries in trying to force European monetary stabilization, irrespective of American desires or what happens to the American dollar. Representatives of the Central Bank of France, Switzerland, Holland and Belgium met secretly to perfect plans which involve forcing Great Britain to stabilize along with continental countries. From this meeting came a declaration by one of the conferees that gold would be defended to the last ditch. Great Britain was unde

LONDON, June 27—(CP)—Great Britain was understood in well-informed quarters this evening to have refused to commit herself to a new European gold bloc scheme under which British and continental currencies would be stabilized irrespective of the desires of the United States. In responsible British circles this move, headed by France, was described as an effort to split England and America so that they would be unable to deal independently on stabilization. England, it was stated, wants to keep her hands free so she can deal directly with America on stabilization when the proper time comes. Britain’s position at the moment, therefore, is that she is sitting tight. Meanwhile gold bloc bankers were meeting again late in the day to consider what new move they could make to force stabilization.

SOUTHPORT, Eng. June 27— (AU)—Great Britain regained possession of the Ryder Cup, emblem of Anglo-American professional golf rivalry today, defeating the United States, 6 1/2 points to 5 1/2 in two days competition. Syd Easterbrook, British pro scored the deciding victory by defeating Densmore Shute, 1 up, 3 holes, as the climax of one of the most exciting international golf battles ever waged, with the outcome in doubt until the last hole of the final match was completed. The British divided the eight singles matches played today but won the foursomes yesterday, 2 1/2 to 1.

LONDON, June 27. — The world economic conference faced showdown tonight upon the decision whether the principal European powers will follow the American monetary program for breaking the pack of the depression or will leave the United States to pursue her own policy alone. Abandoning all hope of persuading or forcing the United States to stabilize the dollar, representatives of central banks of four continental gold countries, headed by France, exerted pressure on the Bank of England to join the stabilization group. British Refuse Action The British government and Bank of England officials, however, according to authoritative information, refused to be drawn into common action with the gold group, at least for the time being. LONDON, June 26 (#)—Senator James Couzens, American delegate, said Monday it was time the world economic conference made a concrete move to relieve debtors, raise prices and increase the demand for raw materials. Both the Michigan senator and Neville Chamberlain, British chancellor of the exchequer, urged negotiations between debtors and creditors in speeches before a monetary sub-committee. Conference Hits Stride The conference appeared to be hitting its stride at the start of the third week with pronounced progress toward international cooperation to rehabilitate wheat and silver. Australian adherence to the wheat acreage restriction plan, along with Canada and Argentina, the other big exporters, appeared nearer after a conference between Henry L. Morgenthau, Sr., American representative, and Stanley M. Bruce, of Australia. India, world’s largest holder of silver, indicated her adheren

The “Big Four” chief delegates called an “act of Providence” has so altered the wheat situation that the conferees decided today to wait until crop prospects are better manifested before approving or disapproving a plan to restrict wheat acreage. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, in an hour-long discussion of the problem with the leaders of the “Big Four” delegations, asked for and received information as to the near breakdown of the negotiations at the morning session of the conferees. The “Big Four” are the United States, Canada, Australia and Argentina. When he received information concerning the rise in the price of wheat on world markets, presumably because of adverse crop reports, MacDonald professed satisfaction with the progression of the negotiations.

COBH, IRISH FREE STATE, JUNE 27. (AP).—Assistant Secretary of State Raymond Moley, who had intended to land here and fly to London, where he will attend the world economic conference, changed his plans today and decided to proceed to Plymouth aboard the steamship Manhattan. The Manhattan is due to reach Plymouth about 6:30 p. m. today (1:30 p. m. Eastern Standard time) and Moley therefore is scheduled to reach London at 11:30 p. m. (6:30 p. m. Eastern Standard time.) There was a lively scene in the harbor as the Manhattan crept in through the early morning darkness. Reporters clambered aboard from a tender which went down the harbor and Moley talked to them while the steamer made its customary halt before proceeding to Plymouth. To the newspaper men, Moley said: “In pursuance of the plans made before the London economic conference that I go there during the sitting, I am en route to that

1933-02-23.text: DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. Feb. 22. —(?)—Sir Malcolm Campbell, famous British race car driver Wednesday cracked the world's automobile speed record wide open in a thrilling, breath-taking dash over the crystal sands of the beach speedway here. In two blistering runs over the hard packed sands, the intrepid 48-year-old race car driver attained the astounding speed of 272.108 miles an hour over an officially measured mile course for a new land speed record. On the first of two runs across the sand, Campbell was clocked at a speed of 273.556 miles an hour, and on his second trial at a clip of 270.676 for an average two way record of 272.108 miles an hour. On his epochal runs, Campbell exceeded by 21.866 miles an hour his old world record of 253.968 he established here a year ago. WASHINGTON, —(i(#)— Official circles here heard Thursday that Robert W. Bingham, the Louisville, Ky., publisher, definitely had been chosen by President-elect Roosevelt to be ambassador to London. The ambassadorship to London is ranked at the head of the list of diplomatic appointments. Judge Bingham, a native of North Carolina, is publisher of the Louisville Courier-Journal. He is a lawyer, and former mayor of Louisville. He is 61 years old.

London, Feb, 22, (®).—The cabinet decided tonight that Britain cannot act independently for an effective arms embargo on the Far East. Cooperation by other arms exporting countries is essential for any practical scheme, the ministers held. France, Italy and Britain can apply embargo by the simple process of refusing licenses for export of arms, but the official view here is that the procedure in some other arms producing countries, including the United States, is not so simple.

TOKYO, Feb. 23.—Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida instructed Japanese envoys in Washington, London, Paris, Rome and Berlin today to inform the government in those capitals of Japan’s plans in Jehol province and North China. These are to annex Jehol to the state of Manchukuo but not to invade North China proper unless Chinese reprisals force such action. The foreign minister took this course in notifying powers who have various interests and maintain military posts in the Peiping-Tientsin area of North China instead of summoning the various ambassadors in Tokyo, as originally planned. The foreign office pointed out there was “real danger” of attacks on the Japanese garrison at Tientsin and “a massacre” of Japanese in Peiping. The record was made over a measured mile route. He also established a new record of 272.463 miles an hour over one kilometer on the same trials, and 257.295 over a five-kilometer course. Uses Airplane Motor Driving a long, streamlined Bluebird car, equipped with a 2500-horsepower airplane motor, the 48-year-old Campbell clipped 94 of a second off his own previous record of 253.968 for the mile and increased the mark by 18.140 miles an hour. DAYTONA BEACH, Fla, Feb. 28—Three new world land speed records were to the credit today of Sir Malcolm Campbell, the British race car driver, and he thought seriously of trying for two more. With new flying start records for one kilometer, one mile and five kilometers to top more than a quarter of a century of thrilling racing, the 48-year-old Britisher now wants to try for new standing start marks for one kilometer and one mile. Whether he makes any more speed trials now, or decides to sail for England shortly, will depend, he said, upon how soon he recovers from an injured left arm, sprained while making repairs to his giant Bluebird racing car a week ago. (P) A government spokesman said there was “real danger” that Japan would be compelled to take steps to protect Japanese nationals in Peiping and Tientsin, endangered by the impending military campaign to conquer the province of Jehol to the north. The government intends soon to inform the ambassadors of the principal powers interested in China of the policy it will pursue concerning the Peiping-Tientsin area. 1933-12-06.text: NATAL, Brazil. (UP). Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh, flying a true course for 1,870 miles, arrived in their big seaplane in the Natal harbor at 12:55 p. m., e. s. t., after a spectacular flight from Bathurst, British West Africa. The Lindberghs had traversed the South Atlantic Ocean in a straight airline, landing at 1 p. m., sixteen hours out of Bathurst. The flight completed 19,000 miles of aerial touring since their departure from New York, July 9. The Lindberghs came down to a city that had declared an unofficial holiday in their honor. They were greeted by cheering thousands, swarming on every vantage point along the rocky shores. Rowboats, motorboats and launches jammed the river Potengi where it sweeps into the ocean near the new Pan-American naval airport. All business had been suspended since noon, and the entire population joined to make the reception the most notable ever given a v

Washington, Dec. 6,-(4)-The $34.01 an ounce government price for newly-mined domestic gold was posted for the fifth successive time today as the treasury polished plans for big mid-December financing operations. - The London price for bar gold was $32.84 an ounce on the basis of an opening sterling quotation of $5.17 1-2 to the pound. Whether recent stability of the RFC gold quotation was connected with the newly completed plan for meeting $727,000,000 of December 15 government maturities could not be ascertained officially. Acting Secretary Morgenthau has promised to announce the new financing program before the week is out. Treasury officials were pleased, meanwhile, with exchange subscriptions received for 10-12 year treasury bonds from bondholders of fourth Libertys. The exact figure on exchange subscriptions which closed last Saturday was given by the treasury at $99,899,200. “Feder

WASHINGTON, Dec. 6—The government left its gold price unchanged for the fifth time today at $34.01 an ounce. The offer for bar gold in London was $82.84 an ounce on the basis of sterling opening at $5.17 1-2 to the pound. The R. F. C. gold quotation has remained unchanged since last Friday when the highest point to that date, $34.01, was reached.

By International News Service, NATAL, Brazil, Dec. 6—Completing their second flight trans-Atlantic flight, Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh arrived here today from Bathurst, Gambia, British West Africa. The Lindberghs completed their daring venture at 12:55 P. M., eastern standard time. They completed the 3,850 miles separating Africa from South America in fast time and thus climaxed a careful and comprehensive survey of ocean air routes and terminals which previously had taken them across the North Atlantic by way of Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe and Shetland Islands. It was Colonel Lindbergh's third flight across the ocean's expanse and in some respects the least hazardous of the three. The distance covered was little more than half the mileage of his history-making flight from New York to Paris in 1927. Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh first contacted Brazilian territory when they pass

ATHENS, Dec. 5.—It was reliably reported tonight that the Greek government will request Samuel Insull, former Chicago utilities magnate, to leave Greece at the expiration of his police permit December 31, 1933. Insull, it was explained, has no passport. The government was said to be prepared to furnish a laissez passer for any country which Insull desires to enter from Greece. Anxious to Please This action would be the result of the Greek government's decision to do all possible to avoid disturbing friendly relations with the United States, which has made repeated representations desiring his extradition to face criminal charges in Chicago in connection with the bankruptcy of his utilities concern. A member of the Greek senate deposited with that body today an interpellation asking the Greek government what it had decided about Insull’s return. Position Insecure The senator said he belie

Athens, Dec. 6—(#)—The possibility that more chapters may be added to that steadily lengthening story, “the pursuit of Samuel Insull,” was heightened measurably today. Greece, the former American utilities czar's present haven of refuge from extradition, will ask him to leave when his police permit expires Dec. 31, reliable sources said yesterday. But this, it was indicated, should not be taken to mean necessarily that Insull can be returned immediately to Chicago to face embezzlement charges growing out of the fall of his far-flung utilities domain. For, it was said, the Greek government is prepared to equip him with a “laissez passer” (free pass) which will give him entree to other countries. CANTON, Dec. 6—Thousands of men and women walked to work here today as a result of a strike of bus drivers which completely paralyzed the city’s passenger transportation system. The strike was voted early today by members of Bus Drivers’ Union, local 489, after they had failed to reach an agreement with officials of Canton Motor Coach, Inc., over working conditions. The walkout was called at 4:30 a.m., when the first of the 100 drivers were to have started the day’s first coach runs. Approximately 25,000 persons who have been using the buses daily were left without means of transportation. Clyde Howis, vice president and general manager of the coach company, said the drivers demanded ‘excessive’ pay raises and changes in working conditions which the company cannot meet. He said that no attempt would be made to operate buses today. Several weeks ago a strike was averted when the dispute w

Bari, Italy, Dec. 6.—(AP)—Thousands of worshipers paid homage today to the memory of St. Nicholas, traditional original Santa Claus. Pilgrims poured into St. Nicola church throughout the day to bow before a coffer containing his bones. Special services to commemorate the 1581st anniversary of his birth were held throughout Italy.

Borah said, in the talk, that the Prime Minister was optimistic and believed an agreement "would be reached that would make the world economic conference a success." Another visit was paid by Sen. LONDON, UP, Greeted by rousing cheers from a large crowd, the British technicians who were deported from Russia as a result of their sabotage and espionage trial arrived in London. They still showed traces of their experiences in Moscow, but were smilingly astonished at the warmth of their welcome. The deportees, Allan Monkhouse, John Cushny and C. H. Nordwall, were accompanied by A. W. Gregory, another Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical company’s engineer, who was acquitted in the Moscow hearing last week, and Nordwall’s Russian wife, who had never before seen England. The four homecoming Britons stood bareheaded as the crowd sang the national anthem and then happily greeted their anxious relatives and friends. Subsequently, Sir Felix Pole, chairman of Metropolitan-Vickers, accompanied them to a hotel for a quiet reunion with their friends. One of the men would talk about the trial before

Money, its stability and future worth, was at stake in Washington today. President Roosevelt, Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain and their experts were striving to find a way to restore the dollar and the pound to the gold standard, perhaps at a reduced value. Former Premier Herriot of France prepared to enter the discussions with a further plea for currency stabilization as the first requisite to world economic recovery. The Senate was to begin debate on the administration currency and credit inflation plan, designed to raise prices and quicken business. Investors’ faith in the Roosevelt regime and its financial policies came to a test as the treasury offered a $500,000,000 issue of three-year notes at 2 7-8 per cent interest.

CHICAGO, April 24 (P)—All grain swung sharply higher at the start of trading today. Initial gains in wheat were as much as 17 cents a bushel and followed a rise in silver, securities and the British pound sterling. The upswing carried the May and July deliveries of wheat, July corn and oats, and all deliveries of rye to the highest prices of the season.

Washington, April 24 (UP)— The wife of the president of the United States personally prepared the scrambled eggs that the prime minister of Great Britain had for Sunday evening supper. For 20 years, eggs scrambled in chafing dishes at the table have been the principal dish of the Roosevelt Sunday suppers. This same informality prevailed last night, even though the guests happened to be Prime Minister MacDonald and his daughter rather than some old neighbors.

LONDON, April 23 (P)—Faced by a financial uncertainty unparalleled in modern times, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, will present to parliament on Tuesday Great Britain's annual budget, revealing secrets of how more than 700,000,000 pounds (currently about $2,695,000,000) will be raised and spent this year. Even this huge sum makes no provision for the June instalment on the American war debt, but there is no political significance in the omission. It is recalled that the British instalment of $95,550,000 in December was not provided for in the previous budget. Numerous financial factors have been crowding upon the chancellor since the main lines of his budget were approved before the economic mission of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald left for the United States. Rangoon, Burma, Apr. 23 (4)—Mrs. Harry Bonney, who had been missing since she left Alor Star, Malay States, England, was found 30 miles south of Victoria Point, Burma, today. She was not hurt, but her plane had been damaged in landing. Mrs. Bonney was discovered on the Siamese island Baing where she had attempted to land. Because of a terrible storm the plane overturned. 1933-09-20.text: LONDON, Sept. 20.—-(P)—An International legal commission, which has been holding an inquiry into the Berlin Reichstag fire last February, found today that grave grounds existed for suspecting that the building was set afire by the Nazis rather than by the Communists whom the German government has accused. The commission, an entirely unofficial body, pointed out that any view or conviction it might express was formed only on the material it had obtained, and that this material was incomplete. The investigators’ reports said that individual acts of terror ran directly counter to the teaching of the third International.

New York, Sept. 19 (4°)—Denied a place on the regular Democratic ticket, Frank J. Prial, a veteran in the city’s service, threatened on the basis of incomplete returns tonight to wrest the comptrollership nomination away from the Tammany machine. Mayor John P. O’Brien meanwhile held a commanding lead as the organization's designee for the mayoralty nomination. Prial, entering the primary as an independent, had polled 87,915 votes against 65,477 for John N. Harman, the organization's choice for the comptrollership nomination, when 1,625 districts out of a citywide total of 3,794 had reported. Mayor O’Brien, with 1,575 districts tabulated, had piled up a total of 112,681 as compared with 52,510 ballots cast for Congressman Loring M. Black. WASHINGTON, Sept. 20.—-(INS) President Roosevelt confirmed today that the United States intends to go ahead with its naval building program despite suggestions by Great Britain that part of it be held up pending developments in the disarmament situation at Geneva. Although the president said, in response to questions, that the British suggestions had not been brought to his attention by the state department, he added that the naval building program would go ahead. He said contracts for the construction of the vessels had been let and there never has been any question of suspension. The president's statement was regarded in naval circles as nipping in the bud the British effort to retard the American naval building program. MOSCOW, Sept. 25, (4)—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and his wife completed a flight from Leningrad this afternoon, bringing their plane down on the Moskva river.

Madras, India—(P)— Dr. Annie Besant, who was known throughout the world for her leadership in theosophical activities, died here today. On Oct. 1 she would have been 86 years old. The peacefulness of her last few days was in vivid contrast to the storm of her life. She was in a state of half-consciousness for some time, never speaking at length even to her most intimate friends. Dr. Besant had no malady except old age. In 1931 she suffered a fall from which she never recovered. On that occasion she was unconscious. Her theosophist friend, an inner group of the elect sat in a circle about her and restored her to consciousness by concentrated transference of power from themselves to her. Some theosophists expressed the opinion that her last days were

Capetown, South Africa, Sept. 20. (AP)—Bernt Balchen, American aviator, who disappeared yesterday when he was supposed to report for an appendicitis operation finally showed up at noon today at the Volks hospital. Physicians said that the operation is necessary this afternoon. Balchen is here with Sir Hubert Wilkins en route to the Antarctic on an expedition. Magnolia, Sept. 20. (AP) A quarrel which involved thirty cents led to the slaying today of Leonard Mullins near McNeil. J. F. Shaw was held and officers said he admitted the slaying. Both were campers.

MADRAS, India, Sept. 20.—Mrs. Annie Besant, who for years had worked in the interest of the depressed classes of India, died today at Adyar. Mrs. Besant was approaching her eighty-seventh birthday. She was an author and a lecturer on religious, philosophical and scientific subjects and had an international reputation. As president of the Theosophical Society she was sponsor of the young Hindu Krishnamurti, hailed by some of her followers as a new Messiah. She was in a sense the religious leader of 150 Theosophists. As a follower of Charles Bradlaugh she campaigned for Atheism. Then spiritualism interested her, and eventually in 1899 she became a theosophist. She toured the United States with Krishnamurti in 1926, with little success. During one lecture appearance at Minneapolis she told her audience she was a reincarnation of a Peruvian woman born 12,000 years ago, that she was born a se

CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa — () — Lieut. Bernt Balchen, the flier, who arrived Tuesday with Sir Hubert Wilkins suffering from acute appendicitis, has mysteriously disappeared and his present whereabouts is not known. Balchen left the ship on which he and Sir Hubert arrived at 4 p.m. and took a taxi for a hospital to undergo an operation, but he never reached the hospital. Newspapermen who boarded the ship found Sir Hubert and the captain and crew of the vessel still awake, anxiously awaiting news of Balchen. Persons aboard the ship said the airman met a doctor at a hotel in town after asking a taxi containing his belongings to wait for him. Having talked to the doctor awhile, Balchen excused himself and left the room. He did not reappear.

1933-10-04.text: NEW YORK, Oct. 3. (P—A British mission which is seeking to reduce the $9,658,695,000 war debt owed to the United States arrived in New York from London today expressing the belief that there would not be any cancellation of the huge obligation. “From the information I get about the feeling in the United States,” said Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay, one of the members of the mission, “cancellation might come in but it would go out again just as quickly.”

SOUTHAMPTON, ENGLAND, Oct. 4.— Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, who took off from Stavanger, Norway, this morning without disclosing their destination, landed at Woolston airport here late today, after an uneventful flight.

LONDON, Oct. 3—It was reported here today that Scotland Yard had received an anonymous message from some organization telling of an alleged plot to assassinate Prof. Albert Einstein, the scientist, tonight. As a result, special precautions were said to have been taken to guard the professor, who is lecturing tonight at Albert Hall. When informed of the report, Commander Locher-Lam pson, host to Blaustein during the seventh's retreat, said, "Neither LT nor Professor Einstein is afraid. "The professor will go to Albert Hall tonight," he added, "and will make his speech. We don't take much notice of these rumors."

Washington, Oct. 2—-(P)—An advance in world wheat prices from "segment levels" was predicted today by the agriculture department's bureau of agricultural economics. The forecast was based on the "smaller world crop for the current season and the constructive nature of the London wheat agreement." The bureau’s statisticians also mentioned that between 30,000,000 and 86,000,000 bushels of surplus wheat in the northeast is to be exported with government aid, or otherwise disposed of, and this was given as another favorable factor on the market. Continuance of "materially higher prices in the United States than in world markets through most of the remainder of the present season" was predicted.

HASTINGS, England. Oct. 4- (CUP)—The British labor party voted unanimously today not to participate in any war and to resist the outbreak of war with the whole force of the labor movement. The Laborites, who polled 6,638,171 votes out of a total of 21,648,390 at the last general election, were in annual convention here.

STAVANGER, Norway, Oct. 3—Rumor tonight said that Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh who flew here this morning from Oslo, may fly to England on the next lap of their European air travels. Colonel Lindbergh said he expected to take off early tomorrow morning, but declined to reveal his destination.

LONDON (#) — Professor Albert Einstein is confident a better world will emerge from the “present upheavals.” The famous physicist said so last night in an address on science and civilization at Albert Hall, which was heavily guarded by police because of rumors there might be trouble. “Only through perils and upheavals can the nations be brought to further development,” he asserted. “It is in times of economic distress such as we experience everywhere today that one sees very clearly the strength of the moral forces that live in a people.”

Vienna—Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss was wounded in the left arm Tuesday by a gunman who fired two shots at him at the entrance to the parliament building. Rushed to a hospital a few blocks distant, the chancellor was found to have been wounded slightly in the left breast also. This shot ripped through his coat and vest and grazed his body. Drastic action against both Nazis and Socialists was expected to follow the shooting. The assassin was identified by police as Rudolf Dertil, a 22-year-old former soldier. It was intimated he was incensed over his dismissal from the army for Nazi activities, but he denied he was a Nazi. After receiving congratulations from government colleagues on his escape from death, the chancellor called a special session of his cabinet.

1933-06-10.text: London, June 10—Great Britain has informed the United States of her intention of meeting the June 15 war debt payment in full, the United Press was advised today by trustworthy sources. The payment would be made in silver rather than gold. The payment would be charged against the equalization fund established to maintain the level of the pound with other currencies, thus preventing an additional burden on the budget. The argument that a full payment would be a heartening gesture to accompany the opening of the world economic conference was coupled with the traditional honor of Great Britain in meeting her financial obligations at yesterday's meeting of the cabinet, and prevailed, the United Press was informed. Officials declined to confirm or deny the United Press information, but it was indicated the payment would exceed the 2,000,000 pounds sterling token remittance which had gained wi

London, June 10—(7)—An announcement regarding the British war debt installment due the United States next Thursday will be made before the House of Commons and will be made Tuesday by Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer. The Chancellor's statement will be made before the House of Commons and will make clear the government's position regarding the 76,060,000 installment. Until then, it was learned in well-informed quarters, no statement regarding the debt situation will be issued by official sources.

Moscow, June 10.—(Saturday)—(@—Reuters (British) news agency was informed today that Jimmie Mattern, American round-the-world flyer, took off from Beloye, Siberia, at 1:50 a.m. Moscow time today (5:50 p.m. Friday, Eastern Standard Time), for Khabarovsk, Siberia. The agency reported he passed over Irkutsk at 2:30 a.m. Moscow time. — MOSCOW, June 8—(%)—Making a quick recovery from a mishap in the air which almost cost him his life and forced him down in a sparsely settled section of Siberia, Jimmie Mattern, American round-the-world flyer, sped on his way across Russia today and rested tonight in the little town of Beloye preparatory to resuming his voyage tomorrow. Halting only once on the way to Beloye from Belovo, where fumes from a leaking gas line caused him to make a forced landing Wednesday, the airman made Krasnoyarsk in fairly good time. He remained there only long enough to take o

London—The British cabinet was understood tonight to be drafting a communication to the United States on the war debt question after failing to decide whether to pay the $75,950,000 installment due Thursday. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald was declared by American sources to have met a polite but firm refusal when he sought, at a diplomatic luncheon today, to broach the debt question to Cordell Hull, American Secretary of State and chief of the United States delegation.

LONDON, June 10 (AP)—Monetary and exchange control problems came to the fore today in preparations for the world economic conference. With the American monetary and economic officials and experts, the keenest interest was aroused in world financial quarters over a possible call for the American ‘enigma’. De Facto Type Urged. M. W. Sprague, assistant to the secretary of the treasury who, with three other experts, George L. Harrison and J. Crane of the New York Federal Reserve bank and James Warburg, official adviser to the American delegation, arrived today, has said that currency stabilization is more a matter of stabilization of international conditions than international agreement. This statement has led to the belief that control of exchange rates and efforts to smooth out fluctuations and achieve virtual stabilization may be the best that can be hoped for.

London, June 9—7P.—Undaunted by the war debts glaring him in the face, Secretary of State Cordell Hull, head of the American delegation to the world economic conference, today went quietly about his preliminary discussions, including his first meeting here with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Although Mr. Hull and Mr. MacDonald met at a private luncheon for 45 minutes before a British cabinet session at which the debts were discussed, it was emphatically asserted in high American delegation quarters that the debt topic was not raised. At the cabinet session, which lasted for two hours, no decision was reached on the $75,950,000 installment due the United States next Thursday. Default Is Doubtful, The debts are the liveliest subject in the British press, which displays a tendency to regard default as unlikely. Regarding the British disinclination to contemplate debt and economic

LONDON, England, June 10 (INS)——-Assembling for the opening of the world’s economic conference on Monday, players in what promises to be the world’s greatest “poker game” poured into London today, each carefully concealing his cards. From all quarters of the globe they came, but each delegation waits until it could glimpse the cards held by the other. This atmosphere of mutual caution will be fully revealed when the conference is opened in a series of speeches by the principal delegates, which are expected to consume the greater part of the first week. So far, more is known about the American position than about the aims of any other country.

Washington, June 10 — An oral communication on war debts from the British government, presumably either a proposal for partial payment or for payment in full in silver, was being studied today by President Roosevelt. The communication was presented by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, and was represented as being of great importance.

1933-06-29.text: pniieeemniimmmie 235-2) <3)--2 United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, June 29—(UP)—France brought the World Economic Conference to a grave crisis today with an ultimatum that if a currency stabilization agreement were not effected within one week she would propose the conference adjourn indefinitely. The seriousness of the situation was emphasized by a later American announcement that there was no prospect of even temporary stabilization of the dollar in the near future. It was reported in the conference lobbies that Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister and chairman of the conference, fearing disaster, had sent a personal message to President Roosevelt urging that he take immediate steps toward stabilization for the sake of the conference. It was disclosed that Washington had tentatively offered France dollar stabilization “on conditions” believed connected with war debts, but Fran

London, June 28. (Py—A precipitant drop in the dollar today forced the bitter stabilization controversy in the world economic conference nearer a showdown. The dollar declined to $4.85 in the after-closing trading on the London market, as compared with yesterday's closing figure of $4.237 to the pound. Balked in their persistent efforts to obtain stabilization of the American dollar, the delegations of France, Switzerland, Holland and Belgium were seeking financial support from the Bank of England. One high official of the conference, and a representative of the gold standard bloc, asserted privately that the conference was nearing a crisis this weekend, and that if no new American tack were taken as the result of the arrival of Raymond Moley, American Assistant Secretary of State, the President's emissary, the gold bloc would renew its campaign for adjournment. Mr. Moley maintained a di

London, June 29.—(U.P.)—Gold standard nations of Europe at a secret meeting late today drafted a plan for co-operation between themselves and the United States and Great Britain to eliminate speculative dollar fluctuations without interfering with President Roosevelt’s price-raising program. The new plan of the gold nations will be submitted to President Roosevelt through the United States delegation to the conference.

LONDON (AP)—British delegates were authoritatively stated Thursday to have prepared a compromise plan that hoped would overcome the monetary stabilization issues and obviate the possibility of gold bloc countries withdrawing from the world economic conference. The plan was scheduled for discussion tonight between representatives of gold standard economies and Britain. Assistant Secretary of State Raymond Moley caused a sensation in conference lobbies by suddenly making his first appearance and entering the British conference. The British compromise plan was understood to be an attempt to reconcile the conflicting policies of countries on gold and those which abandoned it, notably America.

London, June 29—The gold bloc nations served a currency stabilization ultimatum on Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today and immediately thereafter the American delegation held an important meeting on the stabilization issue. The British press reported that the Americans had sent a cable to President Roosevelt suggesting that there was urgent need for a definite pronouncement on this question and asking when the President considered such a pronouncement timely. As American framers stated that a communication had been sent to Mr. Roosevelt, but the account of this communication, published by London newspapers, was denied. The ultimatum provided a new and grave crisis for the world economic conference. The gold nations headed by France declared that they would withdraw from the conference unless something was done immediately to achieve stabilization of currency. Virtually all the conferen

London —(?)— Australian opposition to the American program of wheat acreage reduction, with the view of raising the price of the world’s principal staple commodity, manifested what American quarters termed “a definite softening” today. Stanley M. Bruce at a meeting of the representatives of the United States, Canada and Argentina called especially at his request, made it clear that he and the Australian government grant the necessity of acreage reduction. He also expressed the belief that the Australian states, in which the power of co-operating with the project rests, may be brought around to a similar view providing certain conditions are met. The central Australian government intends threshing the matter out further with the states at a meeting Friday afternoon.

LONDON, June 28. — (U.P) — The British, spurred into action by the swiftly tumbling dollar, have thrown in their lot with the European gold standard bloc and agreed to peg the pound sterling with the French gold franc, it was reported in world economic conference quarters tonight. This report was supported by word from trustworthy sources close to the Bank of England, who informed the United Press that the Bank of England and the Bank of France representatives, in a meeting tonight, agreed to peg sterling to the franc. The move was described as an effort to support gold currencies on the continent. Defense League. Word came during a day in which the falling dollar slowly forced the British to yield to pressure from the gold standard countries, led by France, demanding Britain join the continental "gold standard defense league" against the dollar. The dollar closed at $4.323 to the pound,

London, June 20—Prof. Raymond Moley conferred with Prime Minister MacDonald for an hour today and it was understood he would attend the next meeting of the steering committee. He is expected to make an important move in the committee toward meeting the European currency demands. After the meeting with MacDonald, Moley told the United Press that they had “exchanged viewpoints.” Asked if they had discussed currency stabilization, he said “no,” but he was not emphatic and quickly changed the subject. There was reason to believe MacDonald was dissatisfied after the conference, possibly because he could not get much-needed immediate reassurance from Moley on stabilization. Moley was calm and taciturn, MacDonald betrayed annoyance, flying into a rage when he saw reporters tackling Moley a few steps away.

1933-06-24.text: Portland, Me., June 23 (AP)— Stephen T. Early, secretary to President Roosevelt, denied today that the chief executive would go to London. Rumors that the President would dash across the Atlantic on the cruiser Indianapolis in a bold attempt to swing the world economic conference into line with his views have been current and have as often been denied.

Pulpit Harbor, Me., June 23. (/P)--Elated over the progress of the London conference, President Roosevelt let go today and shot his schooner up the Maine coast far ahead of schedule under a driving northwest wind and bright sun. Pulling into this isolated harbor at the tip of North Haven island in Penobscot bay, Mr. Roosevelt took occasion to speak through his secretary, Stephen T. Early, for the first time on his vacation jaunt. He's Well Pleased The statement of Early expressed the president's satisfaction over the present trend of the events at London and denied fresh reports he was going to the London parley. Early’s statement, thrown aboard (Continued on Page 2)

London, June 24 (/P)—Considerable uneasiness existed today at headquarters of the American delegation to the world economic conference as to whether fresh instructions Stanley M. Bruce, Australian minister to London, received from Canberra last night mean that his government will join other great wheat producing countries in the American scheme for the restriction of production. Mystery surrounded the nature of the communications to Mr. Bruce who declined to discuss the matter with newspapermen. Americans were continuing their drive over the week-end to obtain Australian adherence. ‘Australia is the only nation lacking among the major producers, including Canada, Argentina, and Russia, which already have given the stamp of general approval to the plan. The American delegation today indicated they believe Australia would come in. The week-end found a decidedly more optimistic atmosphere s

London, June 24.—(AP)—A drive for an international accord to raise prices in harmony with the American recovery program was under way in the world economic conference tonight as Secretary of State Cordell Hull assailed the sources of suggestions that internal and inter-governmental schemes of action were in conflict. The parley finished its first fortnight with several leading delegates expressing determination to bring it down to brass tacks in order to discover which way it is going or can go. As a result of this week's serious rift over monetary stabilization and French charges that the United States is blocking agreement here in order to help its own domestic campaign against the depression, Secretary Hull again defended his government's position in a declaration to the press. Not So There is 'no basis and no logic' in the thought that America’s do. (Continued on Page 3.)

| London, June 23. (4)—The troublesome currency issue was temporarily buried tonight as the world economic conference plunged into other work with France proposing an immediate truce in quota restrictions, While providing against any further use of the quota system as a weapon to curb importation, the plan would permit France to continue indefinitely the enforcement of the quotas it has already adopted. The move was interpreted as a counter-stroke to the American demand for elimination of import discriminations. British and French delegations insisted that international agreements could not be completed until dollar stability was achieved, but finally joined today in a unanimous agreement to table the currency question, Prime Minister MacDonald, chairman of the conference, asserted that the failure of the American government to agree to an immediate fixing of the dollar value was a “setb

PARIS, June 24 — Approving a wheat subsidy plan by the overwhelming vote of 530 to 3, the chamber of deputies today dealt a drastic blow at international trade—one expected to have grave repercussions among delegates to the World Economic Conference at London. The Bill’s provisions are: 1—Foreign wheat imports into France are forbidden, even under the present temporary admission plan which is abolished. This means that France is unlikely to import a single bushel of wheat for at least a year. 2—A bonus of approximately $1 a bushel is granted to French wheat exporters. 3 —The legal price of wheat in France is 115 francs ($490) a quintal (3.67 bushels). This is $133 a bushel. Anyone who sells or buys wheat at a lower price is liable to prosecution. 4—Owners of ten quintals (36.7 bushels) or more of wheat flour must declare whether it is domestic or foreign. A credit of 400,000,000 francs (

Hoylake, England (7P)—The Hon. Michael Scott, 55 year old internationalist and member of a prominent Scottish family, today captured the British amateur golf championship for the first time, defeating Thomas A. Bourn, 4 and 3, in the 36 hole final match.

LONDON, (UP).—Resumption of the world disarmament conference at Geneva today was officially postponed until October. The postponement was announced by League of Nations officials participating in the world economic conference. The steering committee of the Arms Conference will meet June 27, after which the general commission will assemble for one day, on July 3, to announce the postponement. The uncertainty of the world situation during the economic conference negotiations convinced Arthur Henderson, president of the Arms Conference, that it would be better to postpone arms discussions until after the economic conference ends, and also until after the end of the September meeting of the League of Nations assembly.

1933-06-14.text: LONDON, June 15--Great Britain has settled Thursday's $75,050,000 war debt installment due the United States on a 10 percent basis, according to a report today in well-informed world economic conference quarters. These sources predicted Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain would make an announcement along this line shortly in the House of Commons. It had been expected that a definite statement on the situation would be made by Chamberlain before the House of Commons this afternoon, but it was learned that his statement may be deferred until evening.

LONDON, June 13 (AP)—The development of a European bloc of debtor nations to force America to settle the war debts question immediately was predicted today by close observers at the world economic conference as leading delegates took the floor to expound the views of their governments. Sensation followed sensation in the morning session, which met in a state of excitement as a result of the war debts crisis with which the British cabinet was struggling today. First, Secretary of State Hull who was to deliver the first speech did not appear, and Premier Daladier of France took his place. Hull Speech Delayed. The word from American delegation headquarters was that there had been a delay in preparing Mr. Hull's speech. It was denied that the debt crisis had anything to do with the delay, although it was understood

Focuses LONDON, June 14.—(#)—Ignoring critics who have bitterly assailed the American currency and war debt policies, Secretary of State Cordell Hull called on the world economic conference today to stand against economic nationalism by all-nation participation in the American proposed tariff truce. Presenting the eagerly-awaited American views of the conference, Mr. Hull did not so much as mention the war debts, which have constituted the main target of attack against America. It had been thought in some conference quarters that he could not ignore them because they had been given such great emphasis by the spokesmen for other nations. Three points were stressed by the chief of the American delegation. He called for removal of "all excesses in the structure of trade barriers." He urged the conference to face the "vexed problem of a permanent international monetary standard and lay down

London, June 13 — Great Britain has sent to Washington a proposal for settlement of the June 15 debt installment which it believes acceptable to President Roosevelt, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told the House of Commons tonight, arousing hope that the issue which has acutely disturbed the world economic conference would soon be amicably adjusted. Declaring that a full statement In well informed quarters, however, it was asserted that the proposed terms of settlement was by payment of 10 per cent. with the understanding insisted upon by President Roosevelt that this ratio should not constitute a precedent for a final settlement of the whole problem. (A British note offering a partial payment of the $75,950,000 war debt installment due Thursday was submitted to the State department at Washington today. An informal proposal somewhat to the same effect on the part of It

WASHINGTON, June 14, P— President Roosevelt today received a $10,000,000 payment by Great Britain as an “acknowledgement of the (war) debt pending final settlement.” Great Britain in her note asked for a review of her debt agreement and Mr. Roosevelt suggested that she send representatives to Washington to discuss this “as soon as convenient.” He informed Great Britain that he had no power to reduce the level of the British debt and would submit any results from the negotiations to Congress for its information and action.

(UP Staff Correspondent) LONDON, June 14, (UP)—The United States called on the world today to banish economic nationalism, break down trade barriers, establish a genuine monetary system and put an end to the tragic burden oppressing all nations. Secretary of State Cordell Hull faced an expectant international audience at the world economic conference and offered his country’s whole-hearted cooperation to end economic wars. He asked the conference to create a ‘will and a determination’ to follow such a course. Definite plans would come later, While he spoke, Washington and London were arranging what was believed to be a mutually satisfactory compromise on the troublesome British war debt problem. Hull pointedly ignored the injection of the debt issue into the conference by previous speakers, He warned the conference against selfish obstruction by any nation of its work, asserting that any

LONDON June 14—(P)—Cordell Hull, American Secretary of State, solemnly warned the World Economic Conference today against selfish obstruction of the Conference work. Hull urged the lessening of trade barriers and general adherence to the existing tariff truce. ‘The whole panic-ridden world is looking to this conference for leadership with a program of ‘basic relief’,' he said. ‘The success or failure of this conference will mean the success or failure of statesmanship everywhere and a failure at this crucial time would long be conspicuous in history.’ Applauded Loudly Hull, wearing morning suit and swallow-tails, was applauded loudly and lengthily as he went to the rostrum. He spoke slowly and evenly, without gestures and with clear-cut enunciation and good emphasis. The assemblage listened with deep interest and many bent forward on their elbows to catch every word. Hull raised his voic

(By Associated Press) LONDON, June 14—A proposal for a world pact of economic non-aggression was made at the world economic conference by the commissar of Russian Foreign Affairs. The commissar said that “lengthened credits, normal condition for Soviet exports and other favorable conditions were necessary.” He said Russia could absorb $200,000,000 worth of ferrous metals, $100,000,000 of textile and rubber industries and $400,000,000 in machinery, all of which would be bought from other countries.

1933-04-16.text: MOSCOW, U. S. S. R., April 15. (?)—Allan Monkhouse, chief of the six British engineers on trial here on charges of espionage, sabotage and bribery, dramatically protested to the Soviet court today that the whole trial was a “frameup against the Metropolitan-Vickers company engineers based on evidence of terrorized prisoners.” “After listening to the statements of Soviet citizens yesterday and the day before,” he asserted at the opening of today’s session, “it is perfectly clear to me that this case is a frameup against the Metropolitan-Vickers company engineers, based on evidence of terrorized prisoners.” “I know from my own experience when I was arrested and subjected to 18 hours continuous examination—” he continued. But at that point he was interrupted by Presiding Judge Vassili Ulrich. The judge ruled Monkhouse, who spoke in English, had no right to make the declaration at this time.

Southampton, England.— (AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald sailed at noon today on the S. S. Berengaria for the Washington conference. Messages of good will from President Roosevelt and King George were delivered to the British statesman as he left port. With him were his daughter Isobel and four economic experts.

London, April 15.—Germany, through her London embassy, today formally protested to Great Britain against remarks made by Germany during Thursday’s debate on foreign affairs in the House of Commons. Details of the protest have not yet been made public; Berlin dispatches indicated offense had been taken particularly in connection with an impassioned speech by Austen Chamberlain, former foreign secretary.

Southampton, England, April 15; W.2)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald is confident that his forthcoming conversations with President Roosevelt would result in good for the world, sailed for America today aboard the liner Berengaria. Just before the boat shifted her gangplank, MacDonald dispatched this cable to Mr. Roosevelt, “I am leaving in wonderful weather which I take as a good omen.” His cable was in response to one from Roosevelt which was handed to him when he embarked. Roosevelt messaged: “We are greatly looking forward to your being with us and wish you a good voyage.” MacDonald spoke feelingly of Roosevelt and of his “courage and

By The Associated Press. WASHINGTON, April 15.—Leaving his domestic program to those pressing it to maturity, President Roosevelt today began pointing for his international conferences to begin late next week with Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain. No doubt was left as to the paramount importance attached by him to moves planned for reciprocal tariff treaties, aimed at the diminishing of trade barriers and the stabilization of international exchange. The Senate devoted another day to wordy farm bill debate, while the House was in recess. Senators and representatives in committee and in private concentrated on the Muscle Shoals, relief, securities regulation and other legislation, but made little advancement. Roosevelt remained away from his White House desk, secluding himself to make ready for the significant world discussions. Raymond Moley, assistant secretary of state, one of

Moscow, April 15.~~-(4P)-—Allan Monkhouse, highest ranking of the six British engineers on trial for spying and sabotage, provided a double sensation in court today by charging that the case was a frame-up and then failing to follow through with a detailed explanation of his accusation. At the morning session Monkhouse interjected an unhesitating statement that the case was a "frame-up based on evidence of terrorized prisoners." The court shut him off before he had his full say. When he was called to the stand as the first witness of the night session he failed to renew his demand for permission to make the declaration.

WASHINGTON, Apr. 15 (UP)—The desirability of discussing economic problems with Russia before the world economic conference was understood today to be influencing the administration's While officials would not go so far as to predict that Russia would be recognized before the London meeting June 15 they admitted that possibility. New data on Russia's economic condition and the prospects of United States-Russian trade, it was understood, were given President Roosevelt last night by Col. Hugh Cooper, engineer and economist. He has spent much time in Russia where he helped build huge hydro-electric plants, Cooper talked also with assistant Secretary of State Moley, one of the President's principal advisors. Authorities familiar with Russia say that the Soviet Union is such a weighty factor in world commerce that its cooperation would be necessary in any broad international plan of recovery.

LONDON, Apr. 15. (U.P)—Automobile parties searched in the Sahara Desert today for Captain W. N. Lancaster, famous British flier, unreported since he took off from Reggan, Africa, Wednesday in his attempt to lower the record for a flight from London to Cape Town, South Africa. CALCUTTA, Apr. 15. (U.P)—Captain Robbiano of the Italian army took off today for Victoria Point, Burma, en route from England to Australia. He is attempting to establish a new record for the flight.

1933-04-14.text: Moscow, April 14. (4P)—Russian testimony to support charges of bribery and sabotage was presented today at the trial of six British engineers accused of bribery here against the Soviet government. One witness told of taking a bribe of $1,500 from L. C. Thornton, one of the defendants. Another said he had been paid $500 by W. H. MacDonald, another of the accused, to deliver plans for the power plant in the Urals. A third Russian witness said C. Nordwell had paid him $2,500 and given him a fur coat to damage a turbine at the Ivanovo power plant. The last charge was made by A. L. Labanov, chief of the electrical department of the Ivanovo plant. Labanov also is a defendant in this trial. Nordwell’s name was brought into the proceedings for the first time when the witness told of the $2,500 bribe. Labanov recently conversed in detail with Nordwell but Nordwell denied every word of it. The blo

Washington, D.C. (AP) - President Roosevelt is planning to take to the open sea again this summer on a cruise up the New England coast. James Roosevelt, his eldest son, is arranging for the use of a 45-foot boat owned by Paul D. Rust Jr. of Massachusetts. As on last summer, when he guided a 40-foot yawl around the cape, Mr. Roosevelt intends to have only his three boys, James, Franklin and John, with him, together with George K. Briggs, a Marblehead yachting enthusiast. It is the hope of the president to begin his sea trip from Marblehead, Mass., the latter part of June, depending on the adjournment of congress by that time. The cruise will end at his Campobello, Maine, summer home. The sloop which Mr. Roosevelt will use is known as the Amberjack II.

MOSCOW, Russia, April 14 (P) Direct evidence of bribery was presented today against three of six Englishmen on trial charged with sale and bribery. William T. Thornton, William MacDonald and Charles Nordwall, all employees of the British Metropolitan-Vickers company, were accused by Russian witnesses of giving them bribes of 3000, 1000 and 5000 roubles respectively for activities in wrecking machinery. Thornton admitted giving the money, but said it was a loan, not a bribe. MacDonald admitted everything. Nordwall made a blanket denial of all the charges.

Thornton, one of the six British engineers on trial for sabotage and espionage, sat in the witness-stand of a packed courtroom and denied, item by item, a confession which he said had been wrung from him by Russian police with questions and accusations. BOSTON, April 13—(AP)— A spring storm, leaving in its wake much as three feet of snow today, brought death and untold property destruction to New England. The deaths of four men, three of them in motor accidents and injuries to many other persons were attributed to the storm. Power lines, telephone and telegraph systems, shade trees, and fruit orchards went down under the weight of the heavy, clinging snow. Sprouting crops on farms were snow-blanketed, roads and streets blocked, traffic was impeded, dozens of communities were cut off for hours from wire communication, hundreds of automobiles and trucks stalled in the snow, train, bus and street railway schedules were disarranged. In the howling wind, the Yawl Sinaea of Marblehead en route for Philadelphia, went aground four miles west of Mattituck Point in Long Island Sound.

(Copyright, 1933, by the Associated Press) LONDON, Apr. 14—(4)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald leaves England's shores tomorrow on a three-fold mission which may crown his long career by opening to the peoples of the world a road to solution of their crushing economic and political problems. By his talks with President Roosevelt around the White House fireplace, MacDonald hopes to further these three objectives: To strengthen Anglo-American friendship by a candid discussion of everything from economic nationalism to war debts; To arrive at a common policy on such subjects as tariffs and monetary problems in order to pave the way for a successful world economic conference in London; To outline the aspects of the threatening European political situation which will arouse American cooperation, not in alliances or European entanglements, but in a neighborly helpfulness for their solution. Berlin, April 14, (4).-—Criticism of Germany in the British House of Commons so aroused the ire of the German government today that legations Leopold von Hoesch was ordered to protest to Great Britain. The long distance wires were kept busy when the decision was being made that the Ambassador must protest in the name not only of the foreign office but of the entire cabinet. The telephone had to be used because many members of the cabinet are not in Berlin. Chancellor Adolf Hitler and Joseph Goebbels are taking a vacation in Bavaria. In the House of Commons Sir Austen Chamberlain, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, asserted that this is no time for revision of the treaty of Versailles because of the present state of mind in Germany. “This new spirit of German nationalism,” Sir Austen said “is the old Prussianism with an added savagery of racial pride and exclusiveness.”

MOSCOW, U. S. S. R., April 14. (AP)—A specific charge of bribery was flung today from the witness stand in the trial of six British engineers and eleven of their Russian associates on charges of espionage against the Soviet Union. Alexey Dolgov, chief of inspection of the Soviet department of imports, said a bribe of 3,000 rubles (about $1,500) was given him by L. C. Thornton, one of the British defendants. Dolgov said he considered this a bribe to influence him to conceal a defect in the machinery being installed in Russia by the Metropolitan-Vickers company of England, which employed the defendants. 1933-12-01.text: An outspoken defense of the American monetary and naval building policies and the declaration that the United States is operating an “equalization fund” for the protection of the dollar were made tonight by American Ambassador Robert W. Bingham in a Thanksgiving address. He stated that the United States has no hostile intent, to buy and sell gold “as might seem beneficial to British finance and industry,” and said the United States established a similar fund, but smaller, with a like purpose and hope. Later he explained to the Associated Press that his remarks referred to the $50,000,000 Reconstruction Corporation fund for buying newly mined gold and to nothing else. Important Speech. His address was regarded by many as his most important speech on Anglo-American relations since he took over the post. LONDON, Nov. 30.—() The Daily Express, often outspoken in its criticism of American affairs, paid tribute to President Roosevelt today with an editorial headed, “Here Is a Man.” “In America,” it said, “Roosevelt stands up to furious onslaughts. “The Wall Street banks line up against him. His old friends and colleagues desert in droves. Their flight is shameful. “The president is tackling a job which would be enough to break most men's hearts. “Roosevelt keeps his nerve. He carries on and he will carry through. “Other news from over there concerns a fresh wave of lynching. A country which lets criminals ply their trade unchecked and then takes the law into its own hands and goes mad wants a brave, strong man for its head in a crisis. “Americans are lucky to have found him.”

| BATHURST, Gambia (British West Africa Colony), Dec. 1—UR— Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, here today after a flight from Praia, Cape Verde Island, still were considering whether to fly home via South America or to return by steamship. Lindbergh said he had not decided definitely.

LONDON, Dec. 1 (4)—The report of an unofficial coroner today had accused Richard III of the murder of two boys who died 450 years ago and absolved Henry VII of the stigma of guilt. In a paper read before the Society of Antiquaries last night, Professor William Wright, dean of the London hospital, described research in which he had removed from their burial urns in Westminster Abbey the bones of the "little princes in the tower," found evidence they had been murdered by Richard III and that they were not so little. A scar on the facial bones of Edward Prince of Wales, eldest son of Edward IV, led Professor Wright to conclude that the boy and his brother, the fifth duke of York, had been slain. The first objectives of the raids were the Dublin flat of General Eoin O'Duffy, blue shirt leader, and the suburban home of Ernest Blythe, former minister of finance in the William T. LONDON, Nov. 30 (#)—Ambassador Robert W. Bingham told the American Society in London at their Thanksgiving Day dinner today that the United States established about a month ago a fund similar to Great Britain's equalization fund. Mr. Bingham expressed the hope that the operation of the fund will prove as beneficial to the United States as the British fund has proved beneficial to Britain. Concerning the British fund, the purpose of which is to control fluctuations in the pound, the ambassador remarked that it is “now said to be in excess of 300,000,000 pounds” (currently about $1,551,000,000). He said the American fund was “being operated in the same wise and intelligent way” as the British equalization account, through which the English government has been buying and selling in the market for some months. Mr. Bingham also commented upon the fluctuations of the dollar in relation to ster

ISTANBUL, Turkey, Dec. 1 (AP).— Seventeen persons were drowned, 150 were missing and damage estimated at $225,000 was done at Samsun today by a storm which raged violently along the whole Black Sea coast. Huge waves destroyed 57 fishing and motorboats, according to reports reaching here from the stricken area. Large sections of the city of Samsun were under water. Residents took shelter in the mosques. Many houses were destroyed.

Paris, Dec. 1 (UP)—France’s default on the December 15 war debt payment to the United States became a virtual certainty today with the government of Camille Chautemps preparing to face the chamber of deputies of the budget for 1934. There is no provision in the budget for making the payment, which calls for $19,154,046, as a half year’s interest on the French war debt for the fiscal year 1933-1934. Not only is there no payment provision, but Frenchmen seem more than ever convinced that the debt should not be paid. When the first default was made last December 15, many Frenchmen believed the government acted unwisely. They watched Great Britain, Italy and other countries make their full payments and believed they would be granted a new deal before last June’s instalments became due. 1933-02-07.text: LONDON, Feb. 7 (UP).—Reliable sources put their stamp of authority today on reports that Great Britain would seek to settle the American war debt immediately with a single payment. The new British debt commission was expected to offer flat payment of about one-third of the sum now allocated for settlement in the next 50 years, The proposal for an immediate settlement of the debt, as explained in well-informed quarters, would mean an offer of outright payment of $1,250,000,000 to $2,000,000,000. The present outstanding debt is about $4,302,450,000. Great Britain has paid $2,007,348,298, most of this before the 1923 British debt commission obtained the new funding agreement under which $4,600,000,000 was to be paid over a period of 62 years. The sums mentioned ranged from $1,250,000,000 to $2,000,000,000 for wiping the World War debt slate clean, the Associated Press learned in well-informed quarters. No Hint Given. Three British planes which started from England yesterday and today were zooming southward to trans-equatorial points in quest of new records. Capt. J. A. Mollison left Agadir, Morocco, on the third leg of his proposed three and a half day flight to Natal, Brazil. The only man to make the westward north Atlantic passage by plane alone expects to complete his last 3,000-mile ocean leg tomorrow, hopping off from French Senegal. He stopped to refuel last night at Barcelona, Spain, and was headed to Filla Cisneros, a Spanish African coast town, today. The British Royal Air Force fliers, Squadron Leader O. R. Gayford and Flight Lieut. G. E. Nicholetts, shooting for a new long distance world record, were across the Sahara desert and going strong in their dash to Cape Town from Cranwell, England. WASHINGTON, Feb. 7.—Representative Rainey of Illinois, the Democratic leader, expressed to newspapermen today the opinion that “the American people will never stand for the British lump sum proposal whereby Great Britain would cut three fourths of her debts away.” Rainey made his assertion shortly after Representative Collier (D. Miss.) had told reporters he was “always ready for a cash compromise.” “But I wouldn’t think much of changing the amounts and leaving the payments over a long period,” Collier said. “I do not see what the United States would gain by that.” Collier said it was not clear to him whether British discussions contemplated a cash settlement but that he presumed that a cash payment was meant in the suggestions of a lump sum settlement. LONDON, (UP).—Parliament reconvened today with growing agitation among its members in favor of a lump sum payment to end the war debt to the United States. The lowest lump sum payment suggested was 100,000,000 pounds sterling and the highest 200,000,000 pounds. At current rates, the lower sum would be roughly $340,000,000, which amounts to approximately 74 cents on the dollar on the $4,500,000,000 (present value) which Britain still owes on the funded debt figure. If the $95,500,000 which Britain paid under protest last December 15 is deducted from the lump sum payment, as is proposed, the ratio to the dollar would be even less. Payment of a lump sum, settling the entire debt, would eliminate interest and service charges. By The Associated Press. LONDON, Feb. 6.—Sir Frederick G. Hallett, noted for his research in cancer, died today after a long illness. He was 73.

DON, Feb. 7.—UP—The government will be asked to offer the United States as a final settlement of the British war debt a lump sum of 100,000,000 pounds, equal to about one fourth of a cent on the dollar of the amount outstanding, when parliament reassembles this afternoon. The suggested lump sum payment would be worth about $560,900,000 with the pound at par, but only about $343,000,000 at the current rate. More liberal Britons have suggested $686,000,000 as a reasonable settlement figure. Impatience with the government's delay in filing a request for final settlement of the war debt is growing in parliament and an attempt will be made to induce the government to move without further delay for Washington negotiations.

LONDON, Feb. 27.—Sinclair Lewis, who hasn't been noted in the past for his aid to Anglo-American friendship and fellowship, appeared in the unaccustomed role today of ambassador of good will, hands-across-the-sea and all. Only England and America, working together, can save the world from war, he told surprised interviewers when he arrived here from the continent. British critics have not been overly kind to the winner of the Nobel prize for literature, whose jibes some years ago at the lack of heat in British homes and the scarcity of ice in London cocktails did not rest well with Britons. But Lewis was all for amity this trip. 1933-11-29.text: Washington, Nov. 28 (AP)— President Roosevelt’s gold buying plan was given a spurt today after a week’s price standstill, to top London’s gold quotation by the biggest margin since its inauguration. The RFC offered $33.85 an ounce for the newly-mined domestic metal, an increase of nine cents over yesterday’s figure and the first boost since a week ago—before Acting Secretary Morgenthau conferred with Mr. Roosevelt. The London gold price was $32 on an opening sterling quotation there of $5.10 to the pound. During the week of unchanged RFC gold prices, the dollar and government bonds were off, while public controversy over the administration monetary program mounted. But in recent days, the dollar strengthened abroad and government bonds climbed. In some quarters today's advance was considered to serve as a reply to criticism of the President's program. — London.--(AP)—Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, a middle-aged, well-dressed man, was charged in Bow Street police court today with an attempt to blackmail King George V. Haddon told the Scotland Yard inspector who arrested him: “ I do not see why I should be hounded for being the illegitimate son of the Duke of Clarence.” The Duke of Clarence was the eldest son of King Edward VII, then Prince of Wales, and the title became extinct when he died in 1892. The specific charge made in court was that Haddon had written a letter “demanding money from the king with menaces and without reasonable or probable cause.” Haddon replied to the charge: “ I deny that. I pleaded for the right to live, as the letters I wrote to the king show.” The hearing was short and was adjourned to December 4, with Haddon remaining in police custody.

LONDON, Nov. 29. (AP)—A revolutionary price-fixing scheme, proposed by French and German delegates, is in the hands of a subcommittee of the world wheat commission today. This committee is to investigate the price-fixing plan and other proposals viewed by the commission, which adjourned last night, as too radical for immediate action. With the United States, Canada, Australia, Hungary, the United Kingdom, France and Germany represented, the committee is expected to meet in London in about two weeks. Meeting in January Another group, formed to consider measures for increasing wheat consumption, is to meet in Paris in January. Then, after having prepared recommendations on various proposals relating to the world wheat situation, the committees will report to the full commission at London in January. LONDON, Nov. 29.—Nila Cram Cook, American girl who tried to sink her personality to become one of Mahatma M. K. Gandhi's three graces, has appeared at a luxurious hotel at New Delhi, India, "with a heart leaping for thrills," the News Chronicle said today. Miss Cook disappeared from Gandhi's headquarters in October, and was clocked on a pilgrimage through the country, walking barefoot from city to city, and resting by roadside at night among the low caste "untouchables." According to the News Chronicle, Miss Cook announced at New Delhi: "I want to speed—fly—dance." She revealed, the newspaper reported, that she "escaped" from Gandhi's household and found her way to the American mission house at Muttra. "I took my vows too lightly," she was quoted as saying. NEW DELHI, India, Nov. 28.— (?)—Nila Cram Cook, a former follower of Mahatma Gandhi, who recently disappeared from his seminary, arrived here today from Muttra with a determination to turn her back on that “rigid life” and realize her “new dreams.” “I don't care what others say,” Miss Cook, who became a Gandhi disciple months ago, declared. “My heart is leaping for thrills. I want speed. I want to fly. I want to attend orchestra dances.” Describing the Mahatma as a tyrant in enforcing his rules, the young American woman said: “One day Gandhi stated that he had not put a fence around the cantonment, and any girl could leave; so I took the hint and left while the others were busy at their prayers.” She said efforts had been made to persuade her to return, but that “I am finished with it; I took the seminary vow too seriously.” She said she slept on a bed of bricks without blankets for eigh

NEW DELHI, India, Nov. 29. (®) — Nila Cram Cook, who fled Mahatma Gandhi's seminary in search of thrills, has been offered a movie contract, it became known today. The young American woman revealed that before coming here she had received a proposal from a motion picture company at Bombay. At the time, however, she explained, she did not make up her mind because she was still under the spell of the Mahatma. “I want speed. I want to fly. I want to attend orchestra dances,” she said. On Bed of Bricks The bed of bricks on which she told of sleeping in the seminary contributed to her change of heart. “The flutter caused in meeting a man with beautiful eyes and brows,” had something to do with it, too. PARIS, Nov. 28.—(AP)—France is ready for arms talks directly with Chancellor Hitler of Germany through ambassadors, Foreign Office officials indicated today, but all decisions, they think, must be made in consultation with others of the war-time Allies. Premier Mussolini's pressure to utilize the four-power peace pact signed by France, Germany, Italy and Great Britain, and the British disposition to mediate, it was said, tend toward direct negotiations because France is anxious to avoid little group meetings where she would be urged to sign on the dotted line.

Berlin, Nov. 29.—(7)—A clear path to a 100 per cent Nazi Germany is seen by Chancellor Adolf Hitler as a result of the indorsement of 93 per cent of the electorate given him in the unusual election of November 12. While the Reichstag still will contain a sprinkling of nonparty members, for all practical purposes the Nazis are in absolute control. The Reichstag will be not a deliberative body, but a rubber-stamp institution. Even before the election result was known, Hitler had instituted the arrangement of putting special "SA" and "SS" men (brown and black storm troopers) into all government offices. Their job is to watch both the bureaucracy and local or state leaders who might have ambitions of their own—with a view to making them toe the Nazi mark. 1933-02-22.text: DAYTONA BEACH, Fla., (UP).— Sir Malcolm Campbell drove his mighty Bluebird racing car through a dangerous haze at Daytona Beach today to break his own world speed record. Defying unfavorable conditions to "please the crowd," the famous British speed driver sent his machine along faster than man had ever traveled on land to average 272.108 miles per hour on the regulation two runs over the measured mile. His old record set here last year was 253.968 miles an hour. The times made by Campbell today as compared with his record times last year were: South run, into wind, 1932, 267.459 mph.; today 273.556, North run, 1932, 241.773; today 270.676 Average for two runs, 1932, 253.953; today 272.208 (record).
