A tropical hurricane, the third to batter the eastern seaboard within a month, lashed the coast from the Virginia Capes to northwestern New England today, leaving death and destruction in its wake. Offshoot of a storm that took a toll of 32 lives in Tampico, Mexico, and then sped northward, the gale ripped through Norfolk, Va., and surrounding territory, killing at least two persons, demolishing homes, inundating towns, and cutting two municipalities off from communication with the world. The full force of the storm was not expected to be felt until late afternoon, but the early morning hours found Norfolk’s lower business section under two feet of water. Two houses of Willoughby Spit, six miles from Norfolk, were swept away as wind and rain turned Chesapeake Bay into a maelstrom. Morehead City and Beaufort, N.C., were cut off from communication by the storm. Points along the New Jersey

PARIS, Sept. 16 (4)—French and British leaders will discuss with American Ambassador-at-large Norman H. Davis early next week a French disarmament plan said to be based on a scheme of international arms control and the limitation of military forces to the present level. The conversations are preliminary to the reopening of the arms conference.

Tokyo, Sept. 16, (UP). Japan will strive for friendly relations with her three great immediate neighbors, United States, Soviet Russia and China, as a first step in solving complex international problems, Koki Hirota, new foreign minister, said today. He told the United Press he would retain Katsuji DeBuchi as Japanese ambassador at Washington. In a formal statement Hirota expressed confidence that Japan's policies in the far east would soon be understood by other world powers.

Havana. Sept. 16.—Americans women living at Santiago were removed from the city today to the Shelter of Puerta del Sal, across the bay, due to disturbed conditions in the interior. Americans at Cienfuegos also were believed threatened by labor troubles in that vicinity. Meanwhile the new government of President Grau San Martin attempted to cut off the lights at the National hotel, where several hundred former army officers remain defiant of the new regime. Army officers asked the Cuban Electric Company to shut off the lights, but the company refused for the time being on the ground that the entire Vedado suburb also would be deprived of lights. Soldiers began digging a trench in an attempt to reach the water main supplying the hotel.

1933-09-08.text: CHRISTON BANK, England (A.P.)—Viscount Grey of Fallodon who, as Sir Edward Grey, the British foreign secretary, gave Germany the ultimatum plunging Great Britain into the World War, died today at the age of 71. He virtually retired from public life in 1916 because of failing eyesight and had been seriously ill for more than a week. As foreign secretary for the eleven years from 1905 to 1916, Viscount Grey was fated to play a leading role in the destinies of Europe. He never wavered in his stand on behalf of Belgium after exhausting every effort to avert the war.

Daily Herald asserted today that the German Nazi organization “Fehme” had placed Albert Einstein, world famous scientist, on its “death list” and had offered $4,555 to the man who “silenced” him. Precautions have been taken, the newspapers said, to guard Professor Einstein, who is staying with his wife near Blankenberghe, Belgium. Mrs. Einstein, the Herald reported, was alarmed but Einstein was unconcerned and said: “I do not fear danger.”

London, Sept. 87)—An official dispatch from Bagdad today said that Crown Prince Ghazi, son of the late King Feisal of Iraq, had been crowned as his father's successor there today. King Feisal died early today at Berne of a heart attack.

Boston, Sept. 8 (UP)—Coast guards along the New England seaboard today began search by ship and airplane for four men missing in two balloons which left Chicago Saturday in the James Gordon Bennett race. With a thoroughness reminiscent of the recent hunt for the missing sloop Postscript, aboard which were several young friends of President Roosevelt, coast guards dispatched all available cutters, patrol boats and speed boats, and one plane. More craft are expected to join the search later. One of the missing balloons, the Goodyear IX, carried Pilot Ward T. Van Orman, three-time winner of the Bennett trophy, and Frank A. Trotter. The other carried the Polish airmen, Captain Francizek Hynek and Lieutenant Zbiginew Burzynski. Three Lost in Autogiro Chicago, Sept. 8 (UP) —Coast guard patrol boats and several airplanes started out over Lake Michigan at dawn today in a search for H. W. “Pud” M

PORES. HLS, N. £., Sept. 4. -(UP)- Lester Stoefen, giant Los Angeles tennis star, today reached the semi-finals of the National championship by a 4-6, 6-4, 3-6, 8-4 victory over Bryan Grant Jr., of Atlanta. Stoefen’s victory placed him in the semi-finals along with Fred Perry of England, who gained the round of four with a 6-4, 6-4, 6-0 victory over Adrian Quist of Australia. Grant, conqueror of defending champion Ellsworth Vines yesterday, put up a stubborn fight against Stoefen, but in the end wilted under the Californian’s tremendous service and volleying. The semi-final round was three-fourths filled when Jack Crawford, Australian ace, defeated Clifford Sutter of New Orleans, 6-3, 6-3.

MADRID (UP).—The cabinet of Premier Manuel Azana resigned today under pressure of opposition elements led by Alejandro Lerroux’s radical party, which contended the Cortes as at present constituted does not represent the popular will. The resignation was accepted by President Niceto Alcala Zamora. A coalition of Republican parties to replace Azana’s Republican-Socialist cabinet was suggested as a possibility, with a recess of the Cortes pending a decision on elections. If the other parties cannot agree, it was believed Azana might continue in power, with perhaps some cabinet changes.

TOKYO, Sept. 7. (UP)—Emperor Hirohito today sanctioned withdrawal of the sixth division of the imperial army from Manchuria, it was officially announced. The sixth division will return to Japan. It will not be replaced. The sixth participated in the Jehol province campaign. Announcement of the recall was made after the emperor received Prince Kanin, chief of the general staff, and was taken to indicate that present peace in Manchuria is expected to continue.

BERNE, Switzerland, Sept. 8— (INS)—King Feisal of Iraq, one of the most romantic figures of the east, died suddenly today of heart disease at his hotel. Although he had suffered from a heart complaint for some time, and on his present visit here was taking the cure, the monarch’s death came as a shock to the members of his entourage. King Feisal, who was 49, was the third son of El Husein Ibn Ali, king of the Hedjaz. He was crowned ruler August 23, 1921. He led a life crowded with adventure, and was an intimate of Col. T. E. Lawrence, (Lawrence of Arabia) during the latter's fighting against the French in the World War. Iraq, kingdom of Mesopotamia, in southwest Asia, is under British mandate. Heirs to the throne is the crown prince Emir Ghazi, just as popular in his native land.

1933-08-06.text: New York, Aug. 5. AP Secretary of State Hull returned from London today and went immediately to Hyde Park to see President Roosevelt, with no intention of resigning "now or hereafter." The secretary, who is chairman of the American delegation to the world monetary and economic conference now in recess, arrived on the steamer President Harding and was taken to the Summer White House in an automobile. Hull met reporters at quarantine with a prepared statement in which he said that "to preach the failure and futility of the world economic conference at this premature stage, would be to preach a gospel of despair." Later, he stood in the writing room of the ship and answered questions. "The conference, despite any confused reports about its status," he said, "is still alive and has a thoroughly virile and comprehensive organization to direct its affairs during the recess period." New York, Aug. 5.—A statement that “all Europe is ready for war” was made by Henry Morgenthau Sr., yesterday upon his return from abroad. A delegate to the wheat conference in Geneva and later an expert with the Americans in London at the economic parley, the former ambassador to Turkey said war is brewing in Germany. He declared that the policies of Chancellor Hitler, if successful, will work for a general war, and that if these policies are unsuccessful civil war will result within that nation, and spread over the continent. Asked how Europe could prepare financially and physically for another war, Morgenthau replied: “By martial law. The nations of Europe can easily confiscate enough to carry on war. It is most pathetic, as the masses of the people want peace—but the leaders want war.” Morgenthau said all the nations of Europe are conserving their resources. “The unwillingness on the

NEW YORK. (UP). Secretary of State Hull, mildly optimistic over the results of the world economic conference returned from London and promptly departed by motor for D.C. to report to President Roosevelt. Appearing somewhat worn, the secretary met newspaper reporters in the writing room of the liner President Harding as it came up the bay and denied reports he contemplated resigning because of asserted differences with the administration. Speaking of the London conference, the secretary said: “Despite any confused reports about its status, the conference is alive and has a thoroughly virile and comprehensive organization to direct its affairs during the recess period. The conference can be depended on to go forward in the future with such progress as the nature and extent of difficulties would permit. These difficulties have been piling up in every part of the world for 12 years with the

Burlington, Ja., Aug. 5.—Two men burned to death and a third was seriously injured in a fire that broke out at 3 a.m. today, in a garage on the edge of the business district. Harold Rust, 23, of Little York, Ti, and Joe Schneider of Burlington died of suffocation and burns and Albert Rust, older brother of Harold, was badly burned before being helped out of the garage through a window by firemen. He was in serious condition in a local hospital. The fire was believed to have started in the office located under the men’s sleeping room.

TOKIO, Aug. 5. UP—A typhoon raked South Korea Friday night, taking a toll of life and causing property damage estimated at 700,000 yen. Eleven persons were known dead, 16 were injured, and 116 fishermen were missing. More than 1000 houses were ground into matchwood by the terrific wind. Approximately 50 boats were carried away. Flood waters inundated 300 residences.

COPENHAGEN — Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh have flown across the great inland ice cap of Greenland and were safe today at Eilace, on the coast of the sub-arctic island. They landed beside the Danish expedition ship named Godthaab. The famous flying couple made the flight from Holstenborg, on the western coast of Greenland, where they had been making aerial surveys. They arrived at Eilace at 6 p.m. (EDT) Friday, after an uneventful flight, meagre messages from government officials said. The inland ice cap covering is a vast blanket of snow and glacier rising in places to an altitude of 8,600 feet. It has long offered a fascinating and dangerous field for famous Arctic explorers, some of whom have spent years attempting to see the vast inland peaks over which the Lindberghs flew in a few hours. The highest peak is believed to be Petermann, not far from the eastern coast of Greenlan

GANANOQUE, Ont.— (4) —Ontario provincial police said today that Gordon Dignem, native of Wolff Island, had confessed sending Mrs. Cleveland E. Dodge, wife of a New York financier, a letter threatening destruction of her estate and injury to "one very dear" to her if she declined to pay the writer $1,000. The confession, police said, had been obtained by New York State police at Watertown where Dignem was held following his arrest Friday night at Clayton, N. Y.

1933-04-03.text: Paris.—(AP)—The big four directorate idea in the European peace pact proposed by Premier Mussolini of Italy has been quashed, government quarters said today following a three-hour cabinet meeting. The government announced it was preparing a reply to proposals made by Great Britain and Italy. The plan also envisaged France and Germany as directing powers. A memorandum, which is to be approved at a cabinet meeting Wednesday, was understood to be in a highly conciliatory tone and the government hopes it will advance negotiations. The memorandum, quarters close to the government said, will seek elimination of mention of treaty revision, which was endorsed in the Mussolini plan and remained in the revised British text. The French insist that vaguer phrasing should be substituted, including all problems but specifying none. The present French proposal is that the four powers discuss affairs co

LONDON, April 3. — Miss Emilia Tersini, an English girl, was awarded a judgment of 4,260 pounds (approximately $14,300) today in her breach of promise suit against Primo Carnera, the prize fighter. Carnera did not appear in court. Miss Tersini brought a suit against Carnera a year ago. In 1930 there was a report that they were to be married, but Carnera and his manager, in Minneapolis, denied it.

By Herbert Moore, United Press Staff Correspondent. London—(U.P)—Sweeping trade reprisals against Russia, including possibly a total embargo on imports to Britain, were proposed by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald today. After summoning the British ambassador home from Moscow for consultation, the government decided on this further drastic step in protest against the arrest and impending trial of six British subjects in Moscow on charges of sabotage. In announcing his decision to the House of Commons, MacDonald said he would present an enabling act governing Soviet imports tomorrow and that it was proposed to rush the bill through all stages Wednesday. Britain already has suspended negotiations for a new trade treaty when the present one expires Easter Monday, so that the prospects of any trade between the two powers after that day appeared remote, unless the Soviets should about-face

Salford, England, Today.--()-- Authorities were investigating today to determine whether Albert Voss, English passenger aboard the ill-fated airliner City of Liverpool, may have set a fire, while mentally deranged, which sent 45 persons to their death Tuesday when the plane crashed in Belgium. Coroner A. H. H. Flint, who will direct an inquest into Voss’s death, said, however, it was difficult to reconcile such a theory with the fact that Voss's 16-year-old schoolgirl niece, Miss Lottie Voss, was aboard. Flint said he understood that some time ago Voss attempted suicide. Apparently Voss fell from the diner nearly two miles before it crashed near Essen.

(The Associated Press) Paris, Apr. 2.—The Mussolini four-power peace plan was said in official circles to be gaining ground. The new draft was said to be based on British views. M. Paul-Boncour in turn handed the draft to Premier Daldier. The French government was still divided on the question, but the premier was understood to be more friendly to the plan as Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain and Premier Mussolini contributed concessions to the French views. France and her eastern allies of the Little Entente, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and Rumania, have expressed disfavor of some phases of the plan, particularly as concerns treaty revisions. Before Cabinet Tomorrow The premier today conferred with President Lebrun on the British redraft in a special Sunday audience. The cabinet will consider the draft tomorrow and, if after further negotiations the plan is adopted, it is believ

LONDON, April 3.—(UP)—Residents of Garditi, Wales, have received reports that Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh plan to live near Cathedral City, in Llandaff, The Daily Mail reported today. It was pointed out that Mrs. S. M. Morgan, Mrs. Lindbergh's sister, has a home near there.

PARIS, April 3.—(P)—Counter-proposals to the Italo-British four-power peace plan were drafted at today’s cabinet session. They were based on the French insistence that the project must protect Poland and the Little Entente, which should be consulted in affairs interesting them. The cabinet definitely rejected the idea of any four-power directorate which would seek to impose its will on the rest of Europe. The main idea of four-power collaboration already had been accepted by France as a basis for discussion. This acceptance was decided on March 21, when suggested modifications of the Mussolini scheme were sent.

PURNEAH, India April 3. — A British expedition which is here to attempt a first flight across Mt. Everest, the world’s highest mountain, made a test flight today in that region. Two planes which carried the party were reported to have reached a height of 35,000 feet, nearly 6,000 feet above the top of the mountain. They said it was necessary to reach that height approximately in order to make the passage.

1933-08-01.text: BOMBAY, Aug. 1—CUP—British Indian officials, including the Earl of Willingdon, the viceroy, decided at a meeting today to release Mahatma M. K. Gandhi after serving him with an order restricting his movement and forbidding him to collect on civil disobedience activities. Should Gandhi disobey such an order, he would be subject to a formal sentence of two years’ imprisonment. Reports here showed that as soon as news of Gandhi's arrest at Ahmedabad was circulated, hartals or strikes were called at many places in protest.

CALCUTTA, India, Aug. 1- (UP)—British royal air force planes today bombed a village belonging to Bajauri tribesmen, on the Indian Afghan frontier, because the tribesmen, adhering to Mohammedan traditions of hospitality, refused to hand over three agitators who took refuge with them. The agitators, associates of the “mad fakir,” included an alleged pretender to the throne of Afghanistan. Royal air force planes had flown over the village two days ago dropping leaflets that warned the tribesmen the village would be bombed unless the agitators were handed over by today.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Aug. 1.—(#)--Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh, who are engaged in an aerial survey of northern areas, have returned to Holsteinborg, on the west coast of Greenland, after a flight northward to Ritenbenk, Greenland, a dispatch from Holsteinborg said today. They flew from Godthaab north to Holsteinborg last week after making the former place a base for a series of short flights over the inland ice. Their base ship reached Holsteinborg last Thursday.

AHMEDABAD, India, August 1—re (Tuesday) — Civil authorities, forestalling the intention of the Mahatma Gandhi to lead a march of followers inaugurating a new disobedience movement, early today arrested the aged Indian leader, his wife, his secretary and 32 followers from his ashram, or college of devotees, at Sabarmati. The arrests were made at 1:40 a.m., under the emergency power act, at the bungalow of the Mahatma’s host, Seth Ranchooddass, a wealthy mill owner. Announcement that Gandhi planned a disobedience campaign in which individual acts would replace the mass campaign heretofore practiced was made yesterday. According to the plan Gandhi was to disband the ashram and with the 32 members of the college, his wife, the secretary, Mahadev Desai, and 15 women, start a parade to the village Ras Inkaira district. There the villagers were to be invited to join the new movement. In the eve

AHMEDABAD, India, Aug. (AP)—The Mahatma Gandhi, his wife, and 33 followers were arrested by civil authorities today at the outset of their new disobedience campaign for Indian independence, but their early release on parole was considered likely. Plans to march to the village of Ras in Kaira district, where they hoped to gain converts for the individual movement, were thwarted when Gandhi was arrested at the home of a wealthy mill owner, Seth Ranchooddass. Of considerable importance was the fact that the arrests were made under provisions of ordinary law, whereby they become state prisoners to be detained at the government's pleasure. If a parole is broken, they must stand an open trial. Only recently Gandhi announced he would disband the Ashram, which he called the most precious thing in his life, and that its 32 members would march to Ras. It was planned that if Gandhi were arrested, t

TOKYO, Aug. 1, (®)——-The largest naval estimates in Japan’s naval history were presented to the finance ministry today by the navy ministry for inclusion in the empire’s 1934-35 budget, which is now being drafted, it was learned authoritatively. Included are 180,000,000 yen (currently $50,400,000) for new construction and 75,000,000 ($21,000,000) for the modernization of capital ships. For the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1934, the navy is demanding a total of 680,900,000 yen ($190,000,000), exceeding by 30 per cent the largest previous estimates, those of 1921-22.

Winnipeg, Man., July 31 (4)—Governor John Garland Pollard of Virginia and Miss Violet Elizabeth McDougall, his secretary, were married at the First Presbyterian Church late today. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Gordon McLean. Shortly after the wedding, the Governor and his bride left by train for Minneapolis and Chicago en route to White Sulphur Springs, W. Va. Only relatives and close friends attended the ceremony. The bride, a native of Glengarry County, Ont., was given in marriage by her cousin, Alderman J. A. McKerchar. She was attended by her sister, Miss Bertha McDougall. The bride wore a navy blue gown trimmed in white and a short cape and matching hat. The Governor and his bride met here over the weekend while Mr. Pollard was returning from the Governors’ Conference in California.
| By The Associated Press. | LILLE, France, Aug. 1.—The largest cotton warehouse in Europe, containing 23,000 bales, burned today with an estimated loss of $2,000,000.

1933-09-29.text: London, Sept. 28,—()—Russia again flatly refused Thursday to be drawn into the world wheat agreement despite an offer by the United States and Canada to let the Soviet Union share with them any possible extension during the next year of the limit now set for world exports. The North American countries already had been promised by the other exporters that any boost in the world total, now set at 560,000,000 bushels, which might be provided would not imperil the price lifting program included in the agreement reached incident to the world economic conference sessions. Canada and America met Russia's demand that she must have at least 75,000,000 bushels of the export quota—double her allotment—by offering her 8,000,000 more in the event such an increase was found changed. The Russian delegate, Abraham Gourevitch, left the meeting before its conclusion with the assertion the position of his

WASHINGTON, Sept. 29.—(UP)—Chairman Black of the senate committee investigating ocean mail and ship construction loan contracts today read into the record statistics showing the Hoover and Coolidge administrations authorized in one form or another to the Exports Steamship Corporation subsidies aggregating $45,230,151. Black said the company now owes the government $1,246,188. In addition to the sum identified by Black as the aggregate subsidy there was an item of $40,762,869 representing the difference between the cost to the government of ships purchased by the Export Corporation and the sum paid by the shipping company for those ships. The ships, constructed in wartime, cost $42,114,117 and were sold for $1,361,307. Black informed questioners, however, that this spread did not accurately represent the true value of the ships because it would be impossible to estimate what vessels actua

Jefferson City, Sept. 28,—(P)— The city of Sikeston today lost its fight to oust the Missouri Utilities Company from operating an electricity plant in competition with its municipally-owned system. In an opinion written by Commissioner George H. English the state public service commission denied an application of the city of Sikeston to order the Missouri Utilities Company to abandon its plant in Sikeston. Commissioners William Stoecker and W. M. Anderson concurred in the majority opinion, while Chairman J. C. Collet and J. Fred. Hull dissented, the latter in a separate opinion.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 29.—Credits to Russia by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, and ultimate diplomatic recognition of the Soviet by the United States were understood in informed circles today to hinge upon Russian participation in a world wheat control agreement sought at London. The London agreement would govern acreage, production, exports and imports of the principal wheat growing countries. It is regarded by the administration as “a real treaty of economic peace” and Russian action imperiling it might lead to withholding of credits and recognition by this government. Disappointment was expressed over Russian rejection of a compromise plan submitted in London by John V. A. MacMurray, American delegate, who is returning to confer with officials over the situation created by the Russian action. If Russia insists on a wheat export quota of 75,000,000 bushels, instead of a quota of ab

* LIVERPOOL, Sept. 29 (A) The Bishop of Liverpool, the Rev. A. A. David, used a boxing ring as a pulpit last night to carry on a campaign to increase the congregation of the Merseyside church. At the start of his speech in the Liverpool stadium he said he intended to talk only three minutes—“one round.” Afterwards he saw two bouts, one of which ended in a knockout.

LONDON, Sept. 29.—(AP)—American negotiators were confident today that a world wheat program could be carried on without Russia, if necessary, but nevertheless were hopeful the Soviet Union could still be brought into the export agreement. Russia demands at least 75,000,000 bushels of the export quota, double their allotment, and yesterday refused to accept an American-Canadian offer to share an extension next year of the limit now set for world exports, 560,000,000 bushels. The Americans insisted that Russia's refusal does not threaten anything of the nature of wheat dumping on a scale which would force other nations to withdraw their pledges.

| LEIPZIG, Germany, Sept. 29. —(AP)— Marinus Van Der Lubbe made an unequivocal admission of guilt in the burning of the German Reichstag building at today's session of the case in which four other men are on trial. Judge Wilhelm Buenger announced Van Der Lubbe would give his own version of the burning. Thereupon the defendant, standing with drooping shoulders and downcast eyes, replied hesitantly and reluctantly as Buenger, on a basis of an earlier confession, drew a confirmation from Van Der Lubbe. “Do you admit setting fire yourself to the Reichstag?” the judge demanded. Almost inaudibly Van Der Lubbe added, “I had no intention of so doing when I awoke that day. The idea came to me as I walked past the Reichstag at two o'clock. I spent the afternoon in a suburb returning to the city at eight o'clock.

LEIPZIG, Sept. 29—(UP)—Marinus Van Derlubbe, eccentric young Dutch stone mason, confessed in the supreme court today that he set fire to the Berlin Reichstag and caused a wave of popular anger that swept Adolph Hitler and his Nazis to power. For eight days the red-robed judges conducting the examination of the five defendants in the incendiary trial had led tediously up to the night of Feb. 27, last when the great plenary hall of the Reichstag building burst into flames. Today, after a procession of minor witnesses had testified, the 24 year old Dutchman was recalled. “Did you set fire to the Reichstag building on Feb. 27?” asked presiding justice Wilhelm Buenger. “Yes,” responded Van Derlubbe clearly.

1933-07-11.text: London, July 10-(4)-The steering committee of the World Economic conference today decided tentatively that the meeting would be adjourned on or about July 26, it was said in well-informed quarters. This decision was taken at a meeting of the committee which found that the question whether monetary matters should be discussed remained unbroken. The monetary commission of the conference however at a meeting later today voted 23 to 15 to retain all the original questions on the Agenda for treatment in the further work of the congress. Monetary Vote Loss for France This vote by the monetary group was seen as a defeat for France and her gold allies but the strength of the opposing minority was enough to indicate the size of the difficulty which has arisen over future program. LONDON, July 11.—(4)—After many days of fierce controversy, the steering committee of the world economic conference late today rendered a decision which the gold bloc privately declared virtually kills the monetary agenda and represents a complete victory for the gold group. The committee, constituted of leaders of the parley, adopted a report calling for the discussion of silver, commercial indebtedness, central banking cooperation and other subjects which can be treated without dissension. The American delegation, supported by the British dominions and a number of smaller countries had fought for the inclusion of the full original program in the revised agenda of the congress. It was understood that a gentlemen’s agreement had been reached whereby the conference would be wound up soon without any triumphant shouts by either side.

LONDON, July 11 (AP) — The steering committee of the world economic conference today adopted a report providing that the parley will discuss silver and the question of indebtedness and such other subjects as sub-committees agree can be dealt with without dissension. The course was recommended by the monetary drafting committee and action was taken by adopting this group’s report. James M. Cox of Ohio was a member of the monetary committee, which, he said before the steering committee met, had unanimously agreed on procedure for a future program. The drafting committee indicated in its report which the conference bureau, or steering committee adopted, that in addition to silver, discussions might continue upon resolutions already approved regarding central banking cooperation and the creation of central banks in countries where they do not now exist. London, July 10 (4?)--A Virtual unity of purpose of the Governments of the United States and Great Britain was proclaimed tonight by Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the House of Commons’ closing debate on the Government's policy in the World Economic Conference, Cheers greeted the Chancellor's declaration that “there is no doubt that the avowed policy of this country and the United States are closely parallel to one another.” “It is the declared intention of the Government to pursue by all means in their power any measures which they think will tend toward raising price levels, which we believe to be the first essential,” he said. “I also agree that this country should not depend wholly upon what is done in conjunction with other countries but that we should do what we can to help ourselves. That is what we have been doing and we have met with a considerable measure

LONDON, July 11—(UP)—The world economic conference entered the final phase of its first efforts today with the expectation of continuing another two weeks before adjournment. The conference has been spared from sudden death but is being allowed to live only in a comatose state. The Anglo-American efforts to get full continuation of the conference's work failed except that they forced the gold standard nations to make one concession, that of cooperation between Central banks which in a way involved the gold standard. The outstanding possibilities for concrete accomplishments are for wheat and silver agreement.

LONDON, July 11—Plans for re-cess of the deadlocked world economic conference were advanced further today when the monetary drafting commission reached a unanimous compromise agreement to sidetrack controversial problems. It was understood the committee agreed to place comparatively non-controversial subjects, unaffected by the fluctuation of currencies, as the first topics for discussion. The plan was that when these subjects were exhausted in about two weeks the conference would recess during August at least. Full resumption could be attempted when currency stabilization became possible. James M. Cox, American delegate on the monetary commission, said that both of the regular subcommittees would continue work. The British offered a suggestion that the committees and experts continue their deliberations until fall. 1933-11-28.text: (By ARO ASBSVOEMAVEM FPP HS) Bombay, India, Nov. 28—Mrs. Kasturbai Gandhi, the wife of the mahatma, was arrested for the sixth time today at Annand. Mrs. Gandhi previously has been arrested by Indian government authorities in connection with the civil disobedience campaign conducted by her husband, leader of the Indian national movement.

Berlin, Nov. 22 (7).—Dr. Joaquim Howenfelder, leader of the Nazi German Christian movement, was retired from the Reich's Church ministry today, the latest development in Germany's religious controversy. At the same time, Dr. Friedrich Werner, legal counselor for the Evangelical Reich's church cabinet, also was retired. Then, in a further surprise move, indefinite postponement of the consecration of the Rev. Dr. Ludwig Mustier as Reichbishop was announced. It had been set for December 2. Salisbury, Md, Nov. 2—(AP)—Troops sent by Governor Albert C. Ritchie to arrest nine suspects of the Princess Anne lynching today evacuated the armory here and started back for Baltimore after a mob of more than a thousand persons stormed the building and were repulsed with tear gas bombs and bayonets. The troops took with them four men they arrested in early morning forays into nearby Somerset county, where the lynching occurred Oct. 8. The troops were ordered to Salisbury when State's Attorney John B. Robbins of Somerset county declined to arrest men said by eyewitnesses to have been members of the mob that lynched George Armwood, a Negro, accused of attacking an aged woman. Crowd Swells to 1,000 Three hundred of the soldiers were mobilized in Baltimore last night and arrived in Salisbury shortly before dawn. The arrests followed in short order, although five of those sought could not b

San Jose..-(AP)—-Praise and censure for San Jose’s mob vengeance on the kidnap-slayers of Brooke L. Hart were met here today by official efforts to close their case and wipe out scars of its furious climax. Governors of other states, church leaders and other prominent persons in all parts of the nation were among those who joined in lauding or condemning the mob’s action and the approval of it by Gov. James Rolph, Jr., of California. Disapproval was expressed by Gov. Henry H. Blood of Utah, Gov. Henry Horner of Illinois and Governor Pollard of Virginia. Gov. W. H. Murray of Oklahoma declared the “citizens would not have taken the law into their own hands” if speedier prosecutions in the courts were assured. Rabbi Stephen S. SALISBURY, Md. — (UP) — State militiamen with four alleged lynchers in trucks rolled out of Salisbury today toward Baltimore after a fight in which the soldiers threw more than 100 tear gas bombs at infuriated citizens bent on freeing the four men. The thwarted citizens, who had engaged in wild disorder all morning in front of the armory where the prisoners were held, hurled stones and clubs after the fleeing trucks. The sedan in which Attorney General William P. Lane and Brigadier General Milton A. Reckord were riding was struck by the stones. Several windows were smashed, but the officials' side indicated they were unhurt as they signaled for the troop trucks to hasten through the bedlam of Salisbury’s main street. Coughlin, “radio priest” of Royal Oak, Mich., defending at the hippodrome the Roosevelt money policies... On the other were the crusaders, urging “sound” money and decrying inflation. Coincident with the two meetings a manifesto signed by 37 Columbia University professors was made public. It urged an “expeditious” return to the gold standard by the United States. Still another element was added to the difference of opinion concerning the administration's money policies by a letter to Senator Borah of Idaho in which James P. Warburg, banker, suggested a “modernized” international gold standard. The mass meeting at the hippodrome attracted a crowd which police estimated at 20,000, only 6,500 of whom were able to

Associated Press Staff Writer WASHINGTON, Nov. 27.—(AP)—With instructions from President Roosevelt to keep the currency program going unchanged, Acting Secretary Morgenthau hastened back to Washington today and another high financial official headed down the well-worn path to Warm Springs. A visit by Governor Eugene Black of the Federal Reserve to the president at the Little White House in Georgia set reports buzzing, none of them confirmed, that a new move in the monetary program was in the making. Other developments of the day included: 1. Morgenthau said $8,748,000 of excess governmental funds had been invested in government bonds last week but declined to give comparable figures for such activities over previous periods. 2. Tom K. SAN JOSE, Cal. Nov. 27—(AP)—Frank approval from Governor James Rolph, Jr., and other state officials for giving “a fine lesson to the whole nation” eased the taut nerves of this normally peaceful town today, scene of the lynching of John M. Holmes and Thomas H. Thurmond, confessed kidnaper-slayers of Brooke Hart, beloved San Jose youth. “They'll learn they can’t kidnap in this state,” were the ringing words from the executive office in Sacramento. “If anyone is arrested for the good job, I'll pardon them all.” Such was the assurance from the state’s chief executive as the tense town came to a realization of the seriousness of summary justice dealt out in pioneer fashion by the mob that stormed the ancient jail and seized Holmes and Thurmond. In historic St. James Park, across the street from the jail, the victims were strung up to the cheers of men, women, and children, locking on in car

1933-10-31.text: Washington — (P) — The world price of gold abruptly slumped today in spite of President Roosevelt's announced intention of buying the metal in foreign markets, but nevertheless, the domestic price the RFC will buy was advanced to another new high. While awaiting assurances from London that Mr. Roosevelt's approaching operations would not arouse retaliatory action and precipitate a monetary war, the administration set a price for the day of $32.12 for the yellow metal. By contrast, yesterday's price was $31.96 against a world price of $31.05. Today's world price, converted into dollars at $4.75 1-2 to the pound, the opening exchange rate, was $1.07 less than the domestic quotation. WASHINGTON, Oct. 30—Anxious to avoid an unrestrained monetary war, the administration tonight sought an understanding with Great Britain on the application of President Roosevelt's plan to steady exchanges and increase prices by buying foreign gold. For the London government, Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, treasury expert on international finances, interrupted his conferences on the war debts to talk with American fiscal officials on the economic possibilities behind the presidential plan. Meanwhile, exponents of varied schools of economic thought shook their heads and predicted disappointing results. Slumping markets spoke the opinion of the nation’s stock and grain traders. oe wre ooo WASHINGTON, Oct. 31. (>)— President Roosevelt today expectantly awaited British assurances that his approaching operations in European markets would not arouse retaliatory measures and fire the starting gun for a ruinous race to depreciate currencies. The London government was told in friendly spirit that the chief executive's plan for raising prices here and steadying the dollar abroad was purely a matter of domestic policy dictated by conditions within the country. It could hardly be construed, the British were informed, as a malicious move designed to weaken the position of Great Britain in the world of trade, nor as an unfriendly gesture aimed at any other nation. There were intimations that Britain’s first reaction was sympathetic. Awaiting more definite word from London, Mr. Roosevelt's advisors proceeded busily with preparations for making the first purchase of foreign

LONDON, Oct. 31. (U.P) — The British government is anxious to avert a currency war with the United States, it was stated authoritatively today soon after a mysterious buyer had purchased $1,426,500 worth of South African gold. There was no definite indication that the United States was the buyer of the African gold. Among bullion dealers it was reported there had been no American inquiries for gold. Developments, however, were interpreted in British sources as strengthening belief here that the American policy is likely to lead to a monetary war between the United States and the gold standard nations, of which France is a leader. France is fighting to remain on a gold basis. After the heavy gold purchase, the dollar, which had opened strong, weakened and the pound went up to $4.78, up 2 1/2 cents from the opening figure. The franc in Paris was at 5.899 cents, down from yesterday's close.

| Paris, Oct. 31—(UP) — The French government will refuse to engage in any currency contest with the United States, or to strike at President Roosevelt’s gold buying program, the semi-official newspaper Le Temps indicated today, coincident with London advices that Great Britain was eager to avoid threats of a monetary war. Repudiating a small group of “alarmists” who urged the establishment of a French embargo on gold to protect the nation’s reserves from any American “raid.” Le Temps declared that this procedure would be “the only sure means of demolishing the Franc.” “ The aim of the Washington administration,” it declared, “is not solely to take away French gold. It is simply designed to provoke a drop in the dollar and thus cause a rise in internal prices. Therefore, America will not buy gold in greater quantities than are required to secure the desired results.” The Franc late today

New London, Conn., Oct. 30, (AP) Four men, one of them critically wounded by machine gun fire, were brought to New London today after a lively skirmish that sent an alleged rum runner to the bottom of Long Island Sound and badly damaged a Coast Guard patrol boat. The condition of Charles Foster of Greenport, N. Y., wounded as the speedboat Frances attempted to elude capture behind a smoke screen was reported in a hospital as "critical and chances of recovery slim." He was taken off the Frances, registered out of Newport, R. I., just before the craft sank as a result of a gaping hole opened in her body in a collision with the CG-404. Rescued with Foster were three other members of the speedboat’s crew. They said they were J. H. K. Stevens and Edward Kluge of Atlantic City, N. J., and Frank Lorney of Greenport, N. Y. To avert the same fate met by the four-motored Frances, Coast Guardsmen r

LONDON, OCT. 31 — An unknown buyer bought $1,421,000 worth of South African gold on the London exchange for the open market price which decreased 14.86 cents. The American dollar rose in foreign exchange. There was no indication whether the United States’ new buying policy was concerned with the purchase. The buyer of 115 bars of newly mined South African gold, as soon as the market opened. The price was £1,426,500 at prevailing rates. Today’s London and world price was fixed at 130 shillings or $31.045 at the opening exchange rate of $4.75 1-2 which reflected a decrease of 3 1-2 pence in the pound’s value since last week’s close and 5 cents since yesterday’s opening.

HAMBURG, Germany, Oct. 31 -UP- The nautical institute announced early today that the Graf Zeppelin was reported at latitude 49 north, longitude 23 west, 710 miles west of the English Channel after having been compelled to shift northward because of heavy fog and an east wind. The big German airship is on a return flight from Chicago.

1933-10-22.text: VIENNA, Oct. 20, ()—Orders to shoot to kill Nazi demonstrators were issued today to the police of Dornbirn, in the Voralberg district to impress the populace with the seriousness of the situation. The federal police commissary warned the Dornbirn populace that henceforth anyone refusing to halt when ordered to do so by the police will be fired on, In the recent revival of Nazi activity there has been a tendency shown by the population of some towns in Styria, Voralberg and Carinthia to enjoy the demonstrations rather than prevent them. Forced To Remove Emblems In the Styrian town of Weiz, where streets, houses and billboards suddenly blossomed with Swastika (Nazi) emblems overnight, former Burgomaster Reithope and his wife were forced by gendarmes to scrape them off, Nevertheless the hoisting of Nazi flags from factory chimneys and decorating whole trains with Swastika has continued. MOSCOW, Oct. 21. — Russia displayed unconcealed jubilation today at the prospect of recognition by the United States, and regarded the exchange of letters between President Roosevelt and President Kalinin as the most important event in its recent history. Officials were openly enthusiastic, in contrast to their usual reserve. Popular sentiment was apparent everywhere.

GENEVA, (UP). The League of Nations lost its third member within thirteen months today when Germany handed in her notification of withdrawal. Mexico resigned in September, 1932 and Japan in February of this year. Mexico continues to be represented here, and it is hoped her withdrawal will be annulled before it becomes effective in 1934. But Japan and Germany have ceased all co-operation. The loss of membership has been offset by the adherence to the League of Argentina and Iraq. German Consul General Krauel handed the withdrawal notice to Joseph Avenol, league general secretary, at headquarters today. His action was announced as follows: “Mr. Krauel, the German consul general, presented the following note to the secretary general today: “Sir: In behalf of the German government I have the honor to inform you that Germany hereby declares she withdraws from the League of Nations in accordan

PARIS. () — The cabinet’s chances of surviving appeared slimmer today as the chamber of deputies squabbled, failing to react to the warning of Premier Edouard Daladier that inflation is in sight unless the budget is balanced. An authoritative source said: “Only a miracle can save the government.” Minister of Marine Sarraut already was being discussed as a successor to the premier, with M. Daladier hoping to return to power through support of the right wing when the country sees the franc falling. Both Premier Daladier and Budget Minister Lucten Lamoureaux joined in the inflation warning, as the premier carried on his fight for legislation to balance the budget, on which he has staked the life of his cabinet.

Moscow, Oct. 21 (4)— Russia hailed as a boon to world peace and to better trade relations today its agreement with the United States to negotiate concerning American recognition of the Soviet Union. Events moved swiftly after President Mikhail Kalinin announced he had accepted an invitation from President Roosevelt, dated October 10, and added he would send Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov to Washington to represent the U. S. S. R. Plans were rushed for Litvinov to depart for the United States within a few days. Government officials gathered to consider the points around which the Washington conversations should be centered. As the developments were greeted with cheer and enthusiasm throughout the union, leaders indicated Russia hopes for a 3-fold result from the resumption of official relations, namely: Greatly increased credit facilities; the lifting of American barriers against some o

(Associated Press Staff Writer) MOSCOW, Oct. 21,—(4)—This Russian capital, busy normally with myriad details reaching into the everyday lives of the most remote Soviet peasant, found today in preparations for recognition negotiations with the United States another reason for bustling activity. These conditions involved who should go to Washington with Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov to talk with President Roosevelt, the Soviet platform in the conversations, and a review of industrial and financial details. When M. Litvinov will leave and whom he will take with him have not been announced for the overshadowing fact was the enthusiastically hailed statement that President Roosevelt asked that negotiations looking to recognition be undertaken. VIENNA, Oct. 21. (#)—The German Prince Bernhard von Sachsen-Meiningen and his wife, Princess Margot, were arrested in Carinthia today in connection with an alleged Nazi conspiracy. The arrest was occasioned by the prince’s carrying a Nazi flag on an automobile he drove through the streets of Klagenfurt yesterday. Taken to a police station, he aroused suspicion when he asked permission to telephone to his wife at his castle near Pitzelstaetten, Carinthia. The police, it was alleged, overheard him instruct her to “destroy the documents.” Thereupon, the police, who were listening in, notified the gendarmerie at Pitzelstaetten. --- - A gendarme lorry loaded with 12 men rushed to the castle, arrested the princess, searched the house and grounds and found allegedly incriminating documents. Both of them, Prince Van Schsen-Memmlingen and his wife, Princess Margot, were declared guilty of a Nazi conspiracy against Austria. Police who arrested him in Carinthia because his automobile carried the flag in the streets of Klagenfurt revealed they confiscated incriminating documents, including a letter to Dr. Paul Joseph Goebbels, the German propaganda minister, from them. 1933-06-04.text: Lehourget, France, June 3.—(AP)—Authorities at the flying field here expect James Mattern, the American world flyer, to arrive here by noon Sunday. An oil company has received a request to prepare to refuel the plane and to provide a place for the aviator to get five hours rest. London, June 4, (Sunday)—(AP)—The air ministry reported weather conditions off the coast of Ireland good for Jimmy Mattern's transatlantic flight in an official statement issued today. It is said the weather is mainly fair with few clouds and a good visibility of six to 12 miles. Across the Atlantic a good westerly air current of 26 to 39 miles per hour (Continued on Page 1, Section 2)

WASHINGTON, June 2. ()—The Senate investigation of J. P. Morgan and Company was abruptly recessed for the week-end today after John W. Davis, counsel for the firm, protested against a question directed at Thomas S. Lamont, junior partner, apparently relating to his income tax return. The white-haired Davis, former presidential candidate, leaped to his feet to object when Ferdinand Pecora, aggressive Senate committee counsel, called Young Lamont to the stand and asked him about sales of stock December 30, 1930. “This is not fair play,” Davis protested, asserting that Lamont had not been advised he would be questioned about the stocks. While Lamont sat quietly at the table, and his senior partner—J. P. Morgan—listened intently from the background, Davis and Pecora argued the question. NEW YORK, June 3.—(P)—Bound around the world alone, Jimmie Mattern soared over Newfoundland and headed out over the open sea today seven hours after he lifted his monoplane, Century of Progress, from Floyd Bennett field in Brooklyn at 4:20 a. m. With the wind behind him and fair weather all about, the 28-year-old Texas aviator was sighted at 11:30 a. m. over Lewisporte, N. F., some 1200 miles to the north of New York. Ahead of Post-Gatty Time By not landing at Harbor Grace—the customary stopping point for fliers before they attempt the Atlantic—Mattern gained almost four hours’ advantage on the round-the-world record of 8 days, 15 hours and 51 minutes set by Wiley Post and Harold Gatty in 1931. Following the Lindbergh route, Mattern’s first scheduled stop is Paris, which he expects to reach within 27 hours. Then, after six hours sleep, straight on to Moscow, dipping over the Templehof ai

WASHINGTON, June 3——(AP) Visitors have been barred from the powerhouse at Muscle Shoals, Ala., by order of Major General Lytle Brown, chief of army engineers, because of recurring reports of intended sabotage there. General Brown, asserting that no such activities had occurred as yet, tonight expressed concern lest they take place and ordered that none but known and recognized individuals be admitted. He said that his course was dictated solely by reports that such activities were threatened and that his decision had been made to protect the government's gigantic $150,000,000 property from any who would seek to sabotage it.

SEMINOLE, Okla., June 3—(AP)—The “pretty boy”, listed in a thousand rogues galleries as Charles Arthur Floyd and sought for more than three years by officers in a dozen states, again tonight was the object of a search concentrated in one of his favorite hiding places near Seminole. Early today the elusive outlaw lived up to his ill-fated repute in evading the law by standing off a group of Seminole county officers who apprehended him shortly after midnight. SAN FRANCISCO, June 3.—(AP)—An earthquake, described by residents in outlying sections of the city as “severe,” was felt here about six-forty-five o'clock tonight. A slight shock, felt in the downtown sections, was followed a few seconds later by a more noticeable quake. Residents said the second shock was almost as severe as the recent earth disturbance. No damage was done tonight. The quake apparently was of local character, as it was not felt in nearby cities.

The number of known dead stood at 10 Saturday night. Property damage was estimated at $750,000. The Richfield plant, where the tanks and other apparatus. A survey by oil company and insurance investigators indicated 10 homes were demolished and from 60 to 80 damaged.

San Francisco, June 3. (4) — An earthquake of considerable intensity was felt by residents in the outlying sections of San Francisco tonight, while persons in the downtown section observed a slight temblor. There were no reports of damage. Residents in the districts bordering the n said there were two distinct shocks, one of slight motion, and the second of severe intensity. The shocks apparently were of local character, as nearby cities did not feel the disturbances.

1933-12-20.text: London, Dec. 20. (AP)—The "legal commission of a. teogiry un to the burning of the reichstag," an unofficial organization of investigators, reported today it had concluded that the Nazis themselves, or through others, burned the reichstag building in Berlin last February. The commission conducted its investigation over a period practically concurrent with the trial in Germany of five defendants, all of whom are described by the prosecution as communists, who face the death sentence if found guilty. The actual trial is still in progress in Leipzig. (In the course of the German trial, one of the defendants contended the fire had been caused by Nazis, not by Communists as the Nazi prosecution contends.)

| By The Associated Press. 1 WASHINGTON Dec. 20.—The RFC gold price was retained today at $34.06 an ounce. It was the third time this figure was posted for newly mined domestic metal. -London’s bar gold price was $32.59 on the basis of sterling opening at $5.144%4 to the pound.

| Athens, Greece, Dec. 19. (#)— Samuel Insull was said by his acquaintances today to be planning to go to England when the expiration of his police permit on Jan. 31 forces the former Mid-West Utilities operator to leave his erstwhile refuge here. British authorities in Athens, however, said the 74-year-old former Chicagoan would not be granted a British visa until instructions were received from London. In Toronto his brother, Martin J. Insull, won a delay in his fight against extradition to the United States when the hearing on an appeal was adjourned indefinitely.

London, Dec. 19.— (P) —The Daily Mail's Kalimpong correspondent in Bengal said tonight he was informed from a usually reliable source that the Dalai Lama of Tibet was poisoned. He died Sunday at Lhasa. Lhasa, Tibet. Dec. 19.—The death of the Dalai Lama, the supreme religious ruler of Tibet who was regarded throughout all Buddhist Asia as the reincarnation of a Buddha who died several centuries ago, was announced today. The grand priest had supreme religious power in the country, where the Dalai Lamas, or Grand Lamas, were worshipped as a virtual deity. Lhasa has been the Lamas’ capital for centuries. PARIS, Dec. 20. (UP)—An American man and woman were arrested today on the charge of possessing military documents and photographs as secret police agents sought to break what they believe to be the greatest spy plot since the world war. The Americans were described as Robert Gordon Switz of East Orange and Miss Marjorie Tilley, 22, of New York City. Benjamin Berk, 42, a naturalized Canadian born in the United States, was under arrest and held to be the mastermind of the plot, alleged to be aimed at obtaining secrets of France's defenses. Berkowitz’ wife, Clara, was held also. She was known on the left bank, the artists' colony, as a painter. Almost a score of persons were arrested after secret police agents had investigated reports of a spy plot since last June.

Lhasa, Tibet, Dec. 19.—(AP)—The death of the Dalai Lama, supreme religious ruler of Tibet, who was regarded throughout all Buddhist Asia as the reincarnation of Buddha, was announced today. He died Sunday at the age of 60, but wise men in this mysterious land believe that a Lama does not cease to exist, he merely discards the 'mortal envelope' and his spirit reappears in the person of an infant. The grand priest had supreme civil and religious power in the country, where the Dalai Lama, or Grand Lama, was worshiped as a virtual deity. Lhasa has been the Lamas’ capital for centuries. It is a 'forbidden city' and still remains one of the most mysterious and remote cities on the globe. The late Lama had an unusually adventurous career. He was trained from his earliest days for the high office in a remote monastery. He entered Lhasa as soon as he attained his majority and took the sovereignt

Paris, Dec. 20-(7)-—An American salesman and a naturalized Canadian merchant were held with their wives today by the French police on charges of heading a vast international spy ring reaching into the French ministry of marine itself. Their names were given as: Robert Switz, traveling salesman, born Oct. 26, 1904, East Orange, N. J., and Mrs. Robert Switz, formerly Marjorie Tilley, born Sept. 5, 1911, New York. Another couple arrested, described as naturalized Canadians, was Benjamin Bercowitz, merchant, born May 10, 1891, Jassy, Rumania; and Mrs. Clara Bercowitz, his wife, born Dec. 19, 1903, Bendery, Rumania. * Seal Apartment The American and Canadian couples' apartments were sealed by police pending a search by examining Magistrate Benon as were the living quarters of the other six persons arrested. PARIS (4) — Chancellor Adolf Hitler's German rearmament program, presented to the French government yesterday, was described in authoritative quarters today as failing to give France adequate guarantees of the security she demands. While Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour was studying the document from Berlin in all its implications, Edouard Daladier, minister of war, was planning to extend France's order fortifications to the sea. Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, sent a message to Paul-Boncour asking that he keep Friday and Saturday free for a discussion of disarmament and Germany's attitude. Other leaders will join with Paul-Boncour and Sir John here in conversations through which the British foreign secretary will seek to obtain promises of concessions upon which a settlement of Franco-German differences may be realized.

1933-06-23.text: London, June 23—(P)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald as president of the world economic conference declared in a statement to the press this afternoon that the conference was not going to adjourn but was continuing its work. Mr. MacDonald said in substance that yesterday's developments had cleared the air and paved the way for further progress. He asserted that success of the conference depended on the stabilization of currencies, but pointed out that American difficulties in stabilizing the dollar are very real. In any event currency uncertainties are not going to be allowed to block the conference, the prime minister made clear, and "all the work that can go on is going on." It was a new MacDonald who faced the press. For days he had been fighting to save the conference from collapse over the stabilization issue. All of his knack of bringing warring men together had been exerted, and wh

- The Roosevelt administration is determined that nothing shall hinder its main drive at home. If the London conference can agree upon any measures which will facilitate that program, so much the better. But this government will join in nothing that might retard or endanger it. That is the policy behind the sharp rejection of temporary currency stabilization. It is the policy behind the Couzeus resolution at London urging other governments to go into internal expansion programs similar to America’s. When Prime Minister MacDonald and other foreign visitors came here a few weeks ago they were told in effect: the United States intends to pursue a domestic policy based upon reaching a higher price level using inflation so far as necessary to achieve it and reemployment through public works and industrial control. London, June 23—(A%)-—France proposed a quiet truce at the world’s economic conference today which would enable countries using quotas as weapons against importations to keep them indefinitely. The resolution is considered a counter proposal to the intensive drive by the United States for complete abolition of all embargoes, quotas and arbitrary restrictions. The French suggestion calls upon the nations to undertake not to enact new prohibitions or quotas but permit them to maintain quotas presently in force for an indefinite period. Agricultural products, however, are excluded from the proposed truce. The resolution was debated in a sub-committee considering commercial policies when the French delegate explained the exceptional fall in prices of agricultural products, keeping France from renouncing her right of course to quotas until by means of international organization of production

Associated Press Staff Writer London, June 22.—The American delegation at the world economic conference, having finally banned war debt discussions and made clear today that stabilization of the dollar is impossible at this time, proceeded tonight with a two-fold plan. The objectives were promotion of a plan for eventual return to a workable gold standard, with a feature designed to stabilize silver, and with a program of getting revision in excessive tariffs and arbitrary trade restrictions. American plans were clarified today by an official statement concerning the dollar which announced that currency stabilization cannot be realized at the present. Gold Bloc Reassured Meanwhile, James M. Cox and James P. Warburg of the American delegation were successful in convincing the French and their allies of the European gold bloc that this policy would not lead to an orgy of currency inflation

LONDON, June 23—(U.P)—The big nations are not going to engage in a currency struggle, despite the refusal of the United States to consider immediate stabilization, Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, president of the World Economic Conference, announced today. He made an important statement to the international press not long after an informal conference with Secretary of State Cordell Hull at which the foundations for Anglo-American cooperation were believed to have been laid. MacDonald declared with the greatest emphasis that the conference would not adjourn, and that work would proceed at full speed. He indicated clearly, however, his belief that the final success of the conference depends on eventual stabilization. MacDonald’s statement was regarded as showing that the big powers have momentarily turned their backs on temporary stabilization and established an informal understanding

LONDON, June 23.—(#)—Joseph C. Wedgewood, a labor member, stirred the House of Commons today by telling Neville Chamberlain to his face that “the people of Britain would rather have Franklin Roosevelt as Chancellor of the Exchequer than Neville Chamberlain.” Cries of "No! No! No!" from the government benches answered the labor member's statement. Later Robert Boothby, a conservative, joined in the criticism of Mr. Chamberlain, “When Mr. Roosevelt said he was going to raise prices: the world believed he would do it,” Mr. Boothby said, “but when Mr. Chamberlain said he hoped to raise prices nobody would believe he would do so by his policy.”

HOYLAKE, England, June 23. — George T. Dunlap, jr., sole American survivor in the British amateur golf championship, was eliminated in the semi-final round today 4 and 3 by the veteran British internationalist, Hon. Michael Scott. The slim young American, twice holder of the United States intercollegiate title, held his own with Scott through the first nine holes of the match, which they finished all square, but failed to win a hole on the back nine. Scott took the lead at the 11th to end the match four holes later.

LONDON, June 23. -- The Prince of Wales varied the routine of his busy life but little today in celebration of his 38th birthday. He spent the morning at his Fort Belvedere home, and motored to York House to read hundreds of greetings from all parts of the world. Then he visited Buckingham Palace to receive the congratulations of his royal parents.

1933-10-12.text: BERLIN, Oct. 12—Notice was served on Germany today by the United States, Great Britain, Spain and Holland that attacks on their nationals must cease or the most serious consequences will result to the relations existing between the Teutonic republic and the four protesting powers. The countries complain that after attacks on their nationals, nothing is done by Germany except to extend formal apologies through her foreign office. Expected to Bring Action The notice served today is expected to cause the German official government to take some action other than the customary announcement in the press that foreigners must not be molested if they fail to salute in National Socialist fashion on those occasions when salutes are customary. The government, it is thought, will take some action to assure safety to foreign visitors. Other Protests Made Previously The notice served by the four powers

Geneva, Oct. 11. — Chancellor Hitler of Germany, confronted with staunch opposition to rearming from the United States, France and Great Britain, was forced tonight into a position of deciding whether to accept transformation of the reichswehr without immediate possession of war materials. In a swift moving climax of the day’s disarmament developments, the United States joined England and France in a united position against an increase of German arms.
