'Landon, Oct. 11.—()—Published reports of a mutiny aboard H. M. S. Hood, the world’s largest battle-cruiser, were described tonight in an official statement by the admiralty as “baseless rumors reflecting on the splendid ship's company.” The official statement followed upon a daylong investigation of reported insubordination aboard the giant craft, which carries a complement of more than 1,200 men. She was said to be in home waters on her way to fall maneuvers in the North Sea. The rumors causing the official denial were in no way specific and earlier had been labelled as “ridic-

GENEVA, Switzerland, Oct. 10. (AP) — The main points of difference between the United States, France and Great Britain on how to approach the German arms problem seem to be removed today. Among delegates to the disarmament conference, it appeared established that these three powers had formed a tripartite front firmly convinced that Germany should have no armaments of the type forbidden by the Treaty of Versailles, for its enlarged conscript army. An American spokesman said that the United States' attitude was based upon President Roosevelt’s speech last spring in which he declared that the United States was opposed to any real armament. The American delegation concretely interprets the declaration as a desire to retain the Versailles system of armaments.

Croydon, Eng., Oct. 12—(4)—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh, who has been in England several days without publicly revealing his whereabouts, arrived at the airport here today by automobile on what was described as a private visit to the Imperial airways. It was understood the colonel looked over plans for a landing field and a general method for dealing with the arrival and departure of planes to and from the continent. He then left by automobile for an unrevealed destination.
GENEVA. (2). An official of the League of Nations said Alfred E. Smith was being considered for the post of high commissioner of Jewish refugees.

GENEVA, Oct. 11 (P)—Charles Te Water, president of the League of Nations assembly, told the fourteenth session of the assembly shortly before it was adjourned today that the will to live has asserted itself among the nations of the world. The assembly had been in session since Sept. 25. “Defeatism is being defeated by those powers the innate recovery of which many of us insufficiently discounted in our gloomy prognoses,” the president, who is South African high commissioner in London, declared. “The straitjacket in which the world has been shackled since the great war has been burst,” Te Water added, “and an era of economic restoration has begun.” Then he praised the efforts of the countries to secure national regeneration and, alluding to disarmament, predicted that peace was assured “if the leaders of the great powers change their policies from fear and resentment to a policy of genero

1933-10-21.text: Paris, Oct. 20, (U.P)—Thunderstruck by the prospect of an American embargo on foreign wines and liquors, the French government has cabled the embassy at Washington to protest strongly, it was reported officially today. Reports added that the basis of the protests would be that France could not consider her American war debt position unless the wine and liquor market was open. France has defaulted the last two payments, and has made no provision in the budget to pay the next one due December 15. Exclusion would be a severe blow to one of the more important hopes for French economic recovery.

FAKENHAM, Norfolk, Eng., Oct. 21 (AP)—A young bull, frightened by the traffic, rushed into a small shop where Queen Mary was inspecting goods. The animal was within a few feet of her majesty when a clerk dashed to the rescue and drove it outside. The princess royal and the ladies-in-waiting were with the queen, who was much amused at the incident and continued her shopping.

London, Oct. 21.—(UP)—Maxim Litvinoff, Russian foreign minister, today telegraphed the Soviet embassies at London and Paris to advise him immediately of steamship sailings between now and November 5. It was indicated that Litvinoff intended to leave for Washington to discuss recognition with President Roosevelt at the end of October, pausing briefly at Paris and London where important trade negotiations are proceeding. Soviet officials here expect the conversations at Washington to culminate in an announcement of recognition and an exchange of diplomatic and consular representatives, establishment of a mixed claims commission to settle debts and another committee to perfect a commercial accord and credit arrangements. The stock exchange today showed no noticeable reaction to the Russian-American situation.

Frank M. Kerr, president of the Montana Power company, announced tonight that, although no agreement had been reached, it was "quite probable" the power line for the Fort Peck dam project would be brought to the dam site from a point below the Maroney dam at Great Falls. A large group of engineers, many of them from the war department office at Kansas City, arrived today and tonight to take preliminary steps toward starting actual construction on the huge project, for which the public works administration has allotted $25,000,000. Cost $1,600,000. After a conference with the engineers, Kerr said that if the line were built from the Maroney dam of the power company it would cost approximately $1,600,000. He estimated 50,000 horsepower will be needed for the construction work and said that amount of energy would represent the entire output of the $5,000,000 Maroney dam. It would take 4,000

PARIS, Oct. 20 (P)—French senators urged their government tonight to erect a three-power alliance of France, Great Britain and Italy to supplant the peace pact those nations signed last July with Germany. This development followed the emergence of the opinion among cabinet and parliament members that the four-power agreement was killed by Germany’s resignation from the League of Nations. It was considered likely, meanwhile, that a French plan to draft immediately a disarmament convention regardless of the absence of the Reich will be abandoned. One reason cited for this probability was the theory among some Britons and Americans that the Germans will return to Geneva after the excitement of a German plebiscite on the foreign policy subsides. Under the project, an arms plan would be evolved and given to the Hitler government for unequivocal acceptance or rejection. —e— BERLIN, Oct. 20 (#)

BY STANLEY P. RICHARDSON (Copyright. 1933, by The Associated Press) MOSCOW, Oct. 20 — Russia announced tonight its acceptance of President Roosevelt's proposal to negotiate for the American recognition of the Soviet Union, believing that such action will serve the cause of world peace. In the most cordial terms the Soviet president, Mikhail Kalinin, replied to a message the United States executive sent him on October 10, and announced he would send the foreign commissar, Maxim Litvinoff, to Washington. Peace Is Assailed A foreign office spokesman said that "President Roosevelt's step comes at a moment of a very serious and complicated international situation in which the cause of peace is being assailed in many parts of the world. "I call attention especially," he went on, "to the withdrawal of Germany from the League of Nations and the situation in the Far East. "President Roosevelt's a

Athens, Oct. 21 (UP)—Samuel Insull, 74-year-old American utilities magnate, appeared before the court of appeals today to oppose efforts of the United States government to extradite him to Chicago for alleged violation of the American bankruptcy laws. Insull, backed by a staff of brilliant lawyers, arrived under a police escort at 9:45 from the hospital where he has been detained. Insull sat in the middle of the courtroom before the seats of Chicago Justice Emmanuel Fanykirakis and his associates. Around Insull were grouped his lawyers—Pericles Rallis, noted crime lawyer; Denis Lazarimos and Christos Lalas. Assistant Attorney General Forrest Harkness arrived to represent the United States. Carrying a huge file of papers, he paused to exchange greetings with Insull and his attorneys. He was accompanied by James Calapothakis, former director of the government press bureau, as interpreter.

Paris, Oct. 21. (P)—The defeat of Premier Edouard Daladier’s cabinet loomed menacingly tonight as radical Socialists and Socialists failed to agree on the part of the premier’s budget balancing program providing for a reduction in government employees’ pay. The premier warned the chamber of deputies finance committee that if the budget is not balanced inflation of the franc will be necessary in five or six weeks. And, under the whip lash of the drooping franc, which went to 18.35 francs to the dollar (5.449 cents to the franc) in after-hours trading, compared with an official close of 18.18 francs (5.0550 cents), the main elements of the government's support vainly struggled for a compromise. There also were rumblings in the senate, which wants more economies and less taxes. Premier Daladier in presenting his program earlier this week maintained that if the budget were not balanced a new

1933-10-10.text: GENEVA, Oct. 10. (U.?)--America and England took the joint lead today in an effort to remove a French-German deadlock that threatened the life of the world disarmament conference. Norman H. Davis, chief United States delegate to the conference, and Captain Anthony Eden, chief British delegate, decided at a long meeting to coordinate British-American policy and seek agreement between France and Germany. It was understood that Davis undertook to concentrate his efforts on persuading Germany to abandon her demand for stronger armaments, and that Eden agreed to negotiate with the French. He will ask France to lessen the penalties she seeks to impose on violators during a test period of international armament control. The delegates, as a whole, embarking on a series of private talks, faced the task of changing the entire European political situation in the next six days.

SOERABAYA, Java., Oct. 10 (P)—Well on his way on a flight from England to Australia, Wing Commander Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith arrived here late today. He plans to hop off tomorrow morning for Australia:

LONDON, Oct. 10 (AP).—Douglas Fairbanks is in and out of London so much that even his staff cannot keep track of him, it was said at his headquarters today, so questions about reports that Mary Pickford will seek a divorce from him went unanswered. (An El Paso divorce lawyer said the actress will file suit for divorce in Juarez, Mexico, in about two weeks. Officials of the Mary Pickford company in Hollywood asserted, however, that Miss Pickford has no immediate plans for obtaining a divorce).

WASHINGTON, Oct. 10 (AP)— British war debt spokesmen armed themselves with documents and statistics today for their first effort to persuade the United States that the obligations of the London government to this country should be scaled down. Sir Frederick Leith-Rose, of the British Treasury, with his aides, had an engagement with Undersecretary Dean Acheson at the treasury for the formal opening of negotiations. Accompanying Sir Frederick were Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, and T. K. Bewley, economic expert of the British embassy. Mr. Acheson's assistants were Dr. Frederick Livesay, assistant economic advisor to the state department, and Daniel Bell, commissioner of accounts and deposits, in the treasury. The negotiators were confronted with the problem of reaching a compromise between dominant British sentiment against further war debt payments and the equally emphatic vi

ether with radiograms to Norman Davis at Geneva. What he fears is one grand explosion of the disarmament conference. We have been nursing that incurable ailment along for years. Inner plans are complete to postpone its death quietly a while longer. Our policy there is the same as at the London conference—death by degrees but not by explosions. Now Hitler raises an issue which the powers may not be able to slide out of so easily. The Geneva tricks may be exposed. That would be too bad. He is undisputed master. The “certain things” they want of him should not be hard to fulfill. The only important one is a demand for reorganization of his cabinet to include some of his former adversaries. Apparently our people want the government to have the appearance of a coalition which will be lasting.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Oct. 10--(AP)—Lady Charles Cavendish, the former American dancer, Adele Astaire, has been bereaved by the death of her first child—a girl born Sunday at Lismore Castle, which lived only three hours. Miss Astaire and Lord Cavendish were married in May, 1932.

TOKYO, Oct. 10—(4)—New differences between Russia and Japan rose today to clutter the path to continued peace in the Far East. Tentatively, said a Japanese foreign office spokesman, Japan will content herself with investigation of the circulation at Moscow of documents which allegedly described a Japanese plot to seize the Chinese Eastern railway. Then, he added, “stronger measures may be necessary” unless guarantees of “good faith” immediately are forthcoming. The new threat to peace, like others before it, was born of the protracted wrangling over negotiations for the sale of the railroad. Japan entered the conversations officially as a mediator in the projected sale by Russia to Nippon’s puppet state, Manchukuo. But charges have flared frequently in the Soviet capital that Tokyo was going further—was, in fact, as most lately asserted, joining in a plot to seize the road.

Warsaw, Poland, Oct. 10.—(UP)— Sixty-seven year old President Ignacy Moscicki today married his secretary, Mme. Maria Zagorny, just half his age. The cardinal archbishop of Warsaw solemnized the wedding at 11 a.m. in the ancient little abbey near the presidential palace. Moscicki’s daughter and three officials of his office attended the simple ceremony.

1933-11-07.text: WASHINGTON, NOV. 7. (AP).—President Roosevelt today announced the end of British war debt negotiations without an agreement, but with the payment of $7,500,000 by Great Britain on its December 15 installment. This token payment will be paid in American currency in lieu of the $117,000,000 due from the British in mid-December under the existing agreement. The President announced that in view of the part payment he would not regard the British government as in default. This was the attitude taken last June at which time the British paid about ten per cent of the amount due and that in silver at the rate of fifty cents an ounce to the amount of $11,000,000. In his statement today Mr. Roosevelt said the debt negotiations were concluded without prejudice "until certain factors in the world situation—commercial and monetary—become more clarified." He revealed he had been assured by the British

LONDON. (UP). Great Britain served notice on the world that she will abandon the present tariff truce at once. Announcement of the British denunciation of the truce, which was made effective in a gesture toward economic stability at the world economic conference, was made in the House of Commons. WASHINGTON. (UP). Despite the repudiation of a world tariff truce by Great Britain and some other nations, Secretary of State Hull said that the United States expected to stand by it. He said he considered it effective insofar as it discouraged promiscuous tariff increases.

The upward price swing for newly mined domestic gold was halted at least temporarily today when an RFC price of $32.84 an ounce was set for the metal, representing no change from the previous quotation. The local price came in the face of dispatches from London telling of new gold weakness which had developed there. The London opening slipped off to 129 shillings 11 1-2 pence, representing a drop of one shilling 10 1-2 pence. The United States equivalent of the London price was $31.84 on the basis of sterling opening at $4.90. London Gold Sold Foreign dispatches said that the available supply of bar gold in London, amounting to 490,000 pounds sterling, was reported sold for the continent. Today's disparity in the domestic and world gold price levels has been exceeded on two previous occasions: On October 28 when the spread was $1.25 an ounce, and on October 31 when it amounted to $1.07.

LONDON, (®). Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, asserted during a rally that the “ordinary constitution” has broken down in the United States and that Americans are “practically under a dictatorship.” “It certainly would be interesting,” he declared, “to see what the backwash of America on Germany will be in twelve or eighteen months. Thank God we are not an hysterical nation. The ordinary constitution has certainly broken down in the United States, and they are practically under a dictatorship. Great Britain is the sole guardian of democracy.” He spoke at a luncheon at which Prime Minister MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Simon also gave speeches on the achievements of the national government, on the reopening of parliament after a three months’ recess. “The British national government is the greatest steadying influence in the world,” said MacDonald. The national government

LONDON, Nov. 7 ().—Princess Mary underwent an operation for the removal of her appendix at her Mayfair home today. The King’s surgeon, Sir Stanley Hewitt, operated. The Princess Royal had been suffering from a severe nervous breakdown. A bulletin said “her Royal Highness so far is doing well.”

WASHINGTON, Nov. 7 UP—The Anglo-American war debt negotiations ended today in a "stop gap" agreement whereby the British will make a $7,500,000 "token payment" on their $117,670,000 installment due December 15 and settlement of the major debt problem will be delayed until a more propitious moment. President Roosevelt in announcing the agreement, said he would not consider the British token payment as default. Payment is to be made in United States currency. Thus, if the value of the dollar on Dec. 18 is what it is today, the payment will be worth only about $5,000,000 in terms of gold. Blame World Crisis Announcement of the result of the month-long conversation between Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, British economic expert, and Under Secretary of Treasury Acheson, was made simultaneously at the White House and by the British House of Commons: Uncertainty of world economic and financial condit

London, Nov. 6 (4).—The slump of the American dollar to a new low level of $4.92 in relation to the British pound today aroused fears that the breakdown of Anglo-American war debts discussions may have started an Anglo-American currency warfare. Pressure said to have been caused by nervousness over the future of the dollar pushed the rate from an opening at $4.861, to an after-hours close at $4.88. The official close was $4.90, with $4.92 the extreme level during the day's trading. The financial section anxiously awaited a statement on the war debts Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, will give the House of Commons tomorrow, in the hope it will end the uncertainty.

Amsterdam — (7) — Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and Mrs. Lindbergh returned to Holland, a safe landing near Waalhaven airdrome today, when unfavorable flying conditions prevented them from continuing to Geneva after a flight over Belgium and France in a heavy fog.

1933-01-23.text: LONDON, Jan. 23. (4%—Opposition to the idea of Great Britain returning to the gold standard was strongly featured in today's Anglo-American debt negotiations. Comments were based on Washington dispatches suggesting the United States may use the British debt as a bargaining weapon to force this country back on a gold basis. The United States government's offer to welcome a British debt mission shortly after March 4 was the chief business before today’s cabinet meeting—the first to consider the invitation. The London Times very cordially welcomed the American action but nevertheless shied at the idea of restoring the gold standard.

Washington, Jan. 22—(C?)—The supreme court ruled today that British or Canadian rum running vessels cannot legally be boarded, searched and seized by coast guardsmen when more than one hour's sailing distance from the shore. The decision was handed down in a case brought by Frank Cook, a Canadian. Unusual interest attached to the decision because of frequent friction arising from the search and seizure of Canadian and British vessels by Coast Guardsmen on the lookout for rum runners. The court held that the treaty with Great Britain in 1924, which authorized the boarding of British vessels suspected of liquor smuggling if found within one hour's sailing distance of American shores, had superseded conflictive provisions of the tariff act of 1930. DUBLIN, Irish Free State, ()— More than 100 Irishmen were nursing cracked heads and other injuries suffered in lively political riots Sunday as the De Valera and Cosgrave parties mustered forces for tonight’s final and biggest campaign rallies. Tomorrow the free state elects a new dail éireann. President Eamon De Valera, who will head a torchlight procession in Dublin, was confident of retaining office. Former President William T. Cosgrave, closing his campaign in Cork, was equally sure of regaining the post he lost a year ago. The dail will choose the president. Cosgrave’s Sunday invasion of County Kerry, where De Valera’s fianna fáil is especially strong, led to the worst rioting of the campaign. Many of the injured, however, were only slightly hurt. About fifty previously were injured during the campaign, including seven in Dublin Saturday night. The first row yesterday occurred at Li

Washington, Jan. 20 (P)---The administration tonight began negotiations with Great Britain aimed at a readjustment of the long-troublesome war debts, in accordance with the newly-made Roosevelt-Hoover agreement. Only a few hours after the incoming and outgoing chief executives had decided at the White House to cooperate in bringing British envoys to the American capital early in the new administration, Secretary Stimson called England’s ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, to the State Department and informed him of the developments. Speaks for President-Elect He gave the diplomat no written communication. After making it clear he was acting as a spokesman for Mr. Roosevelt, he informed the ambassador orally and at length of what had passed between Mr. Hoover and the president-elect and of the contents of the statement they later issued. London, Jan. 23—(INS)—The Viscountess Furness, twin sister of Mrs. Reginald C. Vanderbilt of New York, was granted a divorce decree today from Viscount Furness, British shipbuilding magnate, on charges of misconduct. Viscount Furness did not defend the action. The decree was granted on grounds of adultery in Paris, in October, 1932. The Viscountess is also the sister of Mrs. Benjamin Thaw, Jr., of Pittsburgh. She is the former Thelma Morgan Converse and her suit caused a sensation. Lady Furness was granted the costs of the action and the custody of an only child, a boy born in 1929. Her lawyers said she had not lived with her husband since May, 1932. Lady Furness and her sister, Gloria Morgan Vanderbilt, were known as the “Beautiful Morgan Twins.” They are the daughters of Harry Hays Morgan of New Orleans and New York, retired consular official.

DUBLIN, Jan. 23—The rival "armies" backing candidates in Tralee's general election campaign clashed in various parts of the Free State last night and today and filled the final hours of the campaign with rioting and violence. At Tralee, sixty persons were injured last night and former President William T. Cosgrave had a narrow escape when supporters of Eamon De Valera broke up a Cosgrave meeting. Cosgrave is a slight favorite in tomorrow's voting, expected to be heavy. Civic guards, who had succeeded in keeping the "armies" apart most of the campaign, were overwhelmed. Bricks were hurled at political foes and at police alike. The civic guards charged repeatedly with their batons but the battle raged for three hours with fists, bricks and clubs. Supporters of De Valera and the "republican army" wrecked automobiles in which members of the Cosgrave party had come to the meeting. The rioters

| LONDON, Jan. 23.—(U.%—John Galsworthy, 65, famous novelist and playwright, was seriously ill from anaemia today at his home in Hempstead. His illness was said to be due partly to poisoning and partly to overwork. He had not fully recovered from an illness last November, which prevented him from going to Stockholm to receive the Nobel prize for literature. A nephew at Galsworthy’s home said the novelist was “very weak.”

By The Associated Press HALIFAX, N. S. Jan. 23.—The British freight steamer City of Delphi was reported in distress today, 250 miles southeast of Cape Race. A tug was sent to her assistance when she reported she had lost her rudder and was wallowing in heavy seas. The steamer is bound from Shields, England for Philadelphia and New York.

1933-08-15.text: WASHINGTON, Aug. 15.--(UP) — Preliminary negotiations for revision of the British war debt of $4,600,000,000 to the United States will begin early in October, it was learned today at the state department. A representative of the British treasury, probably Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, is expected here shortly after October 1, it was learned. Meanwhile, there may be exploratory talks about the debt between the state department and the British embassy.

Washington, Aug. 15.—()—Secretary Hull said today that international discussion upon the war debt question probably would begin the first part of October when Sir Frederick Leith-Ross, British economic advisor, will come to Washington for a conversation on behalf of Great Britain.

AAIPENG, Honan Province, China. Aug. 15. (P)—One thousand peasants were reported drowned in a few minutes today when dikes of the Yellow River broke and flood waters covered a large area. The stream continued to rage. Dikes north of Kaifeng, a city of 175,000 in northeastern China, were holding against the swirling waters but this community was nearly isolated by floods west and east of here. Inhabitants worked frantically to reinforce the city walls with sandbags should the dikes fail as they have in many other places. The danger that the river will return to its old channel at Lanfent was believed slightly lessened as the waters were said to be remaining principally in the present bed and flowing southward in lesser streams. Prior to 1853 the Yellow River flowed into the Yellow Sea at a point several hundred miles south of its present mouth.

Shanghai, Aug. 15—(#)—Several thousand persons were believed already drowned by the rampant Yellow River as its flooding waters continued spreading today over wide areas along its 2,600-mile course. Breaks in dikes in western Shantung resulted in new floods surging over villages and farms. Fears that the great stream, one of the largest rivers of the world, would renew its old bed through Kiangsu were expressed in dispatches from Kiangsu province. TOKYO, Aug. 10—Testimony regarding a plan to assassinate an American ambassador and consul was offered today during the court martial of ten naval officers charged with assassinating Premier Suyoshi Inukai and other terroristic acts in May, 1932. The witness, Lieut. Kijo Ito, one of the defendants, said two naval officers seriously considered the plot in order to cause friction with America and thereby promote a nationalist and militarist revolution. Still in Hospital Ito testified he was wounded in the Shanghai campaign last year and was still in the hospital. He could not, therefore, participate in the Tokyo raids, culminating in the assassination of the premier. Consequently, he added, he and Lieut. Haruo Oba planned further assassinations as their contribution to the terrorist cause but were arrested as accomplices in the Tokyo outrages before they could act. At that time, he said, t

+ WINNIPEG, Man., Aug. 15 ()— Members of the Winnipeg grain exchange at an emergency session today unanimously decided to establish minimum prices for grain futures and thereby peg the prices of wheat and coarse grains. With a minimum fixed at last night’s closing figures, wheat prices opened sharply higher over a wide range on the grain exchange. Open quotations showed gains of 1 1-8 to 4 1-8 cents over the previous finish. October wheat started the new day at 73 to 73 1/2, December at 74 1/4 to 74 and May at 79 1/4 to 78. The action of the members was taken because of “abnormal conditions surrounding other markets,

Vienna, Austria, Aug. 15 (#)- Reports reaching here and confirmed at Rome told of the assassination in Salonika, Greece, of Hassan Bey Pristina, former premier of Albania. Ibrahim Tselo, a 25-year-old native of Albania, was said to have confessed to police upon his arrest that he killed Pristina yesterday because he wanted to avenge a brother and other relatives.
TOKYO, Aug. 14 (P)—Branchial pneumonia today caused the death of Dr. Frederick Starr, 74, American anthropologist, of Seattle, Wash., at St. Luke's hospital here.

1933-01-10.text: LONDON, Jan. 10 (AP)—The air ministry stated at noon today it had no news of the whereabouts of Bert Hinkler who took off from Feltham, England, early Saturday, on a speed flight to Australia. (A Brindisi, Italy, dispatch today said a sharp lookout was being maintained in that region for Hinkler in view of reports he planned to stop there en route to Australia.)

TOKYO, Jan. 10—-(AP)—Japanese cavalry and infantry units occupied Chiumenkow pass in the great wall of China today, blocking a further pouring of Chinese troops through that famous gate into Jehol. It was the second strategic position taken by the Japanese in a week to block off China from the rich Mongolian province and frustrate Chinese attempts to defend it against impending invasion announced by Japanese military commanders. Occupation of the Chinese city of Shanhaikwan just a week ago by Japanese shut off the eastern gate, only a short distance from where the wall comes down to the sea. Chiumenkow is 12 miles north of Shanhaikwan and near where the 2,000-year-old barrier turns westward. A communique from the Chinchow, Manchuria, headquarters of the Nishi division, said a Japanese column, mostly cavalry, left Shanhaikwan early in the morning and occupied Chiumenkow at 9:15 a.m. This

MADRID (/) — An official report indicated today that simultaneous extremist uprisings throughout Spain against the Republican government apparently have collapsed. Authorities, however, were taking extra precautions in Seville, Barcelona, Cadiz and Madrid to prevent the movement from spreading to railroad, mine and metallurgical workers, who thus far have had no part in the uprising. Unofficial estimates listed 38 persons having been killed and more than 100 wounded in the battles which began Sunday. The battles were centered mainly in attempts to take over police and army quarters in various cities and towns.

BUCHAREST, Jan. 10. — Ten persons were known to have been killed today when an express train crashed into the rear of a local, half a mile outside northern Bucharest station. It was feared the eventual death toll would be between 15 and 20. The last five cars of the local were demolished. Some of the victims were buried from the train into deep snow, while others were imprisoned in wreckage. Troops were rushed to the scene to take charge of rescue work.

By The Associated Press. Madrid, Spain, Jan. 9.———A battle between communists and a large force of civil guards raged tonight in the village of Bugarra in the province of Valencia. The communists had been driven out of the nearby town of Pedralba, where earlier in the day there was a sanguinary fight in which ten rebels and two members of the guard were killed. All told, the extremist movement against the government has resulted in the killing of 35 persons and the wounding of more than 100 in the last two days. Government officials announced tonight that they believed the movement had been crushed, although late reports showed scattered clashes in Barcelona and Cadiz. Machine gun units were en route to Bugarra to reinforce the civil guard. The communists had fortified themselves there. Government officials held police, civil guards and troops in readiness to deal with any fresh outburst

MADRID, Jan. 10.—(UP) — The young Republican government of Spain fought today to quell uprisings allegedly fomented by two of its most bitter enemies—anarchists and monarchists. Newspapers close to the government alleged monarchists financed the extremist outbreaks which cost approximately 30 lives and scores of injured, while authorities took every possible precaution to prevent further disturbances, editors charged monarchists were willing to join communists in attempts to overthrow the administration. More than 100 monarchists were exiled to Villa Cisneros, West Africa, after an unsuccessful attempt at a coup last August. On New Year's Eve, while the Villa Cisneros garrison was celebrating, 29 of the exiles escaped and were reported to have reached French territory in northern Africa. If the reports of monarchist and anarchist cooperation were true, the young Republican government.

wn Jan. 10.—(UP)—Former Premier Pierre Laval intimated strongly to the United Press today that Secretary of State Stimson and Secretary of the Treasury Mills were correct in stating the question of debt revision or annulment did not arise during his conversations with President Hoover in the United States. Laval placed the start of debt differences between France and the United States at the Lausanne reparations conference, which, he insisted, neither he nor President Hoover foresaw. The former premier believed France should not pay the defaulted December debt installment to the United States, or any other debt annuities, until Germany resumes her reparations to France. He made it clear, however, that he was not entering into international debate on war debts. Laval pointed to two documents which he claimed upheld his position. TOKYO, Jan. 9—(AP)—Japanese sources reported today Marshal Chang Hsiao-Liang, military leader charged with defending China’s Northern border, had indicated willingness to negotiate an armistice between the Chinese and Japanese troops in the vicinity of Shanhaikwan. Although Japanese military authorities were keeping an eye on the movements of Marshal Chang’s troops south of Shanhaikwan and in the eastern section of Jeol province, a foreign office spokesman said the Japanese were confident that Marshal Chang “does not desire to fight.” A Rengo (Japanese) news agency dispatch from Chinchow, Manchuria, said that General Nakamura, Japanese commander, had designated Major Chujiro Matura to treat with General Ho Chu-kuo, the Chinese military leader whose command was ousted by the Japanese from Shanhaikwan. The armistice parley, the Rengo correspondent said, will be held near Shanhaikwan.

1933-07-27.text: Washington, July 26.—(4)— In the greatest bid-opening in history, the navy department today received offers for constructing 21 new fighting ships at from $3,000,000 to $25,000,000 each to bring the nation’s sea power to London treaty limit: A dozen firms submitted estimates for one or more classes of war vessels—aircraft carriers, heavy and light cruisers, destroyers and submarines. Immediately, naval experts went to work on the bids, pressing for speedy awards to give employment in shipyards. Bidding on the vessels, always complex, was further entangled today by the new shipbuilding code just signed by the president providing for a maximum work week of 32 hours for concerns having government contracts. As in the past, participants gave a flat bid for one ship and compound figures at lower unit costs for two or more. But in addition, most of the bidders submitted a figure below the flat

Washington (AP)—Farm administrators revealed today that they are planning for an increase of wheat exports from the Pacific coast to the Orient and are prepared to use part of the proceeds of the processing tax on wheat to finance the program. Adjourn Wheat Session London (AP)—Negotiations between wheat delegations of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Australia for restriction of acreage were adjourned today until Aug. 21.

LONDON, July 26.—Leaders of the world economic conference laid their plans tonight for indefinite closing down of the parley tomorrow with a final round of speech-making in which American delegates will plead for international cooperation and continuation of efforts to solve outstanding problems. The steering committee, composed of the first delegates of the more important powers, will submit to the plenary body a resolution empowering Prime Minister MacDonald, as chairman, and other officers of the congress acting as a bureau to keep the international negotiations alive and summon the conference to meet again when they deem it likely to produce useful results. There was little expectation tonight, however, that the conference would reconvene, certainly not at an early date, for most of the delegations were displaying a spirit of defeatism with regard to international economic action. LONDON, July 26.—(#)—Approval of President Roosevelt's bold recovery program was voiced in the British House of Commons tonight by spokesmen of the three principal political camps. The debate, which turned upon the world economic conference on the eve of indefinite adjournment of that gathering, drew from Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, the declaration that the pound sterling is an independent currency, linked neither to gold nor the dollar. Independent speakers of the laborite, liberal and conservative groups declared the United States was not to blame for lack of accomplishments by the economic parley. Roosevelt Defended. "There was no basis on which President Roosevelt could stabilize the dollar with reference to the pound," said the veteran liberal chieftain, David Lloyd George, making one of his now rare appearances in the parliamentary discussions. LONDON — President Roosevelt intervened dramatically at the final plenary session of the world economic conference today to say forcefully and earnestly that it was not a failure and that it was not dead. Delegates were paying little attention to the succession of speakers, reading, some of them with bitter sarcasm, what they thought were funeral orations for the conference. Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister and president of the conference, rose between speeches and announced that Cordell Hull, chief American delegate, soon would read a message from Mr. Roosevelt. Delegates stiffened and became silent. Tomas A. Le Breton, Argentina, read this speech. Then Hull rose and solemnly read the President's statement. Praises MacDonald It was in the form of a message to MacDonald, praising him warmly for his work as president of the conference, “Before the recess of the conference I want y

PORTMARNOOK STRAND, Ireland, July 27.—(UP).—The undercarriage of Charles Ulm’s plane "Faith in Australia" collapsed as it was being refuelled on the beach today for a flight to Harbor Grace, N. F., and New York. Several persons were pinned beneath the wing of the plane and slightly injured. They were sent to a hospital. Police and soldiers attempted to save the plane from the incoming tide.

LONDON, July 27—(4)—Negotiations between wheat delegations of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Australia for restriction of acreage were adjourned today until Aug. 21. London will again be the seat of the discussions of the American proposal to restrict wheat production when the delegations come together again nearly four weeks hence.

London, July 27, (P)—President Roosevelt, in a message to the World Economic Conference read at its dying plenary session today, said he did not regard the conference as a failure. He pledged continuance of United States cooperation. The message was read by Cordell Hull, chief American delegate, as the leaders of delegations rose one by one and gave their versions of the reasons that led to the deadlock and the decision to recess indefinitely after today’s meeting. President Roosevelt's message was brief. It was addressed to Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister, as president of the conference, and it praised his presidency heartily. “Results are not always measured concretely,” the president said. As a result of the conference, the president said, the people in the United States better understood

1933-01-07.text: CHICAGO ~~ All Patrolman John Shannon knows about technocracy is that it’s a suspicious sounding word with Moscow-like associations. He found John Paul Jones and Arthur Streitelmeil distributing handbills announcing a discussion of technocracy at the New England church. He took the two to the station, “Here's a couple of Reds,” he told Capt. Charles McGurn. “They're cooking up a meeting to talk technocracy.” “I don’t know what technocracy is,” said McGurn, freeing the prisoners, “and maybe these fellows don’t, either, but it’s not Communism, Communists don't hold their meetings in churches.”
LONDON, Jan. 7 (INS) — Bert Hinkler, Australian airman, hopped off from Feltham airdrome in Middlesex county, today in an attempt to break the record for a flight from England to Australia.

Shanghai, China, Jan 7. — (AP) — Spread of unofficial war between Japan and China in northern China was regarded in foreign circles Saturday as an imminent possibility. It was estimated that at least 6,000 Japanese troops now were concentrated at Shanhsikwao, China's northern railway terminal which the Japanese captured early this week and Chinese were reported rushing reinforcements to Chinwangtao, the post on the Yellow Sea, ten miles westward. Telegrams were pouring in on the Nationalist government at Nanking from various war lords throughout China asking for orders to march against the Japanese. Chinese leaders here declared they are determined to defend the provinces of Jehol against the anticipated Japanese drive to bring that territory within the Manchurian boundary. They made it clear that a further Japanese advance, either northwestward in that direction from Shanhsikwan or furt

named. Changchun, Manchuria, Jan. 7 (UP)—Clashes between Japanese and Chinese troops in Jehol province appeared imminent today as both armies continued to strengthen their positions in the vicinity of Shanhaikwan. Troops of Marshal Chang Hseuh-liang, young Chinese war lord charged with the defense of the area occupied the towns of Ping Chuan, Lingyuan, Chienkouchen, Piechangyingttze. From Peiping it was learned that volunteer troops have been ordered to take up positions around Chien-suo. The widespread movement of Chinese troops in the region was interpreted as meaning the Chinese will make a determined stand against any effort by Japanese forces to advance into Jehol province. Rumors that the Japanese planned to capture Tientsin next persisted at Peiping despite denials issued at Japanese military headquarters here. All Quiet. SHANGHAI, China, Jan. 7 (A) The national government at Nanking is valiantly seeking to meet the new crisis it is facing as a result of the Japanese occupation of Shanhaikwan and the possibility of further hostilities. In a series of conferences there between civilian and military leaders in which Chiang Kai-Shek, the chief military commander, appeared to dominate, establishment of a future policy with reference to Japan was sought. Although the meetings were secret, it seemed evident that the national government is not desirous of aggravating the situation, instead wishing a quick settlement of the Shanhaikwan incident.

(By The Associated Press) HANGHAI, Jan. 6—The Poet-General Tsai Ting-Kai, who became the national hero of China a year ago when his 19th route army put up a dogged defense against the Japanese in the long battle of Shanghai, appealed today for a chance to lead his men against his old enemy in the Shanhaikwan area. General Tsai offered to take to the field as Chinese leaders and newspapers were bitterly criticizing Marshal Chang Hsiao-Liang, the military leader charged with guarding the northern frontier, on the ground that he had failed to meet the Shanhaikwan emergency. Offers His Services From Hongkong the poet-general telegraphed to the national government that "if Chang Hsiao-Liang has no intention of resisting I will take the 19th route army into north China." The 19th, which bore the brunt of the defense of Shanghai a year ago, now is encamped in Fukien province after a campaign ag

PARIS, Jan. 7 (UP).—John De Habdank Dunikowski, Polish inventor, was sentenced today to two years in prison and fined 100 francs for his attempts to make gold out of sand. He was ordered to refund his financial backers 2,500,000 francs. The court decided “the secret process of turning sand into gold was a combination of absurdities and contradictions.” Dunikowski erected his gold making machine in front of a sand pile in the French patents hall and was given eight days to produce gold. He failed, and was placed on trial.

1933-07-06.text: $77,000,000 more for New Navy WASHINGTON, July 5—/)— A $77,000,000 fleet modernization program intended to lift the United States Navy to new levels of fighting efficiency within London treaty limits was announced today by Secretary Swanson.

By The Associated Press LONDON, July 6—(Thursday).—Great powers of the old and new world agreed early today to suspend the world economic conference until a more propitious time. Admits Defeat Thus, this dismal assembly, called together in an effort to improve economic conditions throughout the world, admitted itself defeated by a violent collision of the monetary policies of the gold countries led by France and of the non-gold countries headed by the United States. The final decision came in a midnight meeting as the gold bloc nations where it was decided the American stand, as reiterated by the United States delegation last evening after cable and telephone communication with President Roosevelt only emphasized the difference, which, temporarily at least, were irreconcilable. LONDON, July 5.—The four principal wheat producing countries of the world, “having agreed in principle on a policy of temporary adjustment of production and trade to world demands,” decided today to determine what measure—if any—of cooperation can be expected from European producing and consuming states on the restriction program. A committee of three men—Thomas Lebreton of Argentina, Stanley M. Bruce of Australia and Frederick E. Murphy of the United States—was set up by the big four to begin negotiations with European states to see what can be done in obtaining their collaboration. (By the Associated Press) Washington, July 5.—Still holding hope of ultimate success for the London economic conference, President Roosevelt received in silence tonight the decision reported from abroad to suspend the parley. His position against the demands of the European gold bloc for immediate stabilization of currencies is final. The chief executive, at the same time, hopes for ultimate stabilization of the world’s monetary system but he is convinced that this cannot be brought about until each nation has stabilized its own currency in relation to its own domestic purchasing power. Mr. Roosevelt maintained close touch with the rapidly shaping events with Chairman Hull of the American delegation concerning the impasse reached at the parley. White House Silent It has been the conviction of the president that the conference which carries the hopes of the world would go ahead to other p

St. Andrews, Scotland, July 6 - Walter Hagen, the American veteran and four-times holder of the title, kept a one-stroke lead in the British open golf championship today by shooting a 72, one under par, for his second round and a total of 140 for 36 holes. A rival American, Ed Dudley, of Concordville, Pa, was on his heels with 70-71—141. Gene Sarazen of New York, the defending champion, tossed away a great chance to overhaul the pace setters by taking 40 strokes for the last nine holes, scoring 73 for his second round and a total of 145, five shots back of Hagen. A six on the short eleventh was disastrous for the champion. Sarazen went into a tie with Leo Diegel, who had 75-70—145 and Joe Eurwood, with 72-73—145. Duplicating Hagen’s great first round, Abe Mitchell, the veteran British professional, gave the gallery a thrill with a 68, five under par, and hurried into third place, two str

London, July 5—(INS)—Secretary of State Cordell Hull talked for half an hour over the trans-Atlantic telephone with President Roosevelt late today as efforts were continued to keep the world economic conference in existence. Hull dismissed all the American delegates except Prof. Raymond Moley, the president’s special envoy, from his suite while the conversation was in progress. Senator James Couzens, James M. Cox, James P. Warburg, Herbert Feis, and others were obliged to cool their heels in the hotel corridor. Prof. Moley and Hull left the hotel at 6 p.m. to confer with Prime Minister MacDonald. Moley announced as he was leaving that he would return to the United States tomorrow as planned. Terrace, B. C., Today—— (P) — On the last half of their flight to Nome, Alaska, members of the "Timmle Mattern rescue plane" were prepared again today to make the difficult hops over Northern British Columbia and into Alaska, with rugged country beneath them. They landed in a hay field near here, about 100 miles east of Prince Rupert, at 3:45 P. M. yesterday after flying from Edmonton, Alta., during the day. Pilot Bill Alexander said they would take off this morning to resume their flight north. Several hours were spent seeking a landing place yesterday after Alexander and his three companions decided poor visibility made hazardous the continuation of the flight to the proposed night stopping place, Whitehorse, Y. T.

1933-08-17.text: Reykjavik, Iceland, Aug. 16 (4) - Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh expect to remain in Iceland until at least Friday when they may fly to England. The couple will await their base ship, the Jelling, due here Friday morning with supplies. Meanwhile, they will continue their Northern aerial route mapping activities with flights in this vicinity. Colonel Lindbergh said last night that England might be their next destination. (The distance to North Scotland is about 600 miles and to England about 850.) The Lindberghs slept last night in their flying machine, lying off Videy, where they landed after a flight from Greenland. They were expected to sleep in the plane again tonight.

LONDON, Aug. 17. — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, hastening back from his vacation in Scotland, arrived today to handle a serious situation resulting from the killing of more than 600 Christian Assyrians by Irak soldiers and Kurdish irregulars on the Irak-Syria frontier. Great Britain, it was learned, made strong representations to the Irak government. The first killings resulted from a rebellion of Assyrian tribesmen but massacres were reported when Irak recruited Kurds to aid its soldiers. The trouble began when Assyrian tribesmen fled across the border to French Syria after refusing to deliver their arms to Irak authorities. The French, it was alleged, after disarming them, restored 500 rifles to the tribesmen, who then returned across the border. Fighting resulted in the recruiting of Kurds, traditional enemies of Assyrians, and their suppression of the little rebellion, apparently

POONA, India, Aug. 17 (AP).— The Mahatma Gandhi refused his evening meal last night and thereby initiated a new fast, H. G. Haig, home member of the legislative council, said in that body today. Haig said Gandhi was informed during the afternoon of certain privileges the Indian government was offering him and that the nationalist leader indicated at first that he would not fast. Later, however, the Mahatma informed the jail superintendent he had changed his mind, Haig declared, adding that he could not give further information. A report circulated that he was still fasting. His decision to abstain from food followed his inability to obtain facilities for continuing his untouchable campaign.

POONA India, Aug. 16.—The threat of a fast until death enabled the Mahatma-Mohandas-K. Gandhi to regain today privileges he formerly had as a political prisoner. Thus he will be able to continue his campaign for the regeneration of “the untouchables,” India’s lowest class. After the mahatma announced at noon that he would start the fast, the British government came forward with a number of concessions. It announced its willingness to provide the Nationalist leader with facilities enabling him to continue, under certain conditions, his campaign to better the status of the “untouchables.” Gandhi's final agreement to the government's terms was awaited this evening. This would enable him to gain his point without missing a single of his frugal meals. He had planned to eat this evening before starting the fast. "I might as well be dead if I am not allowed to proceed with my work, which is my

BANFF, Alberta, Aug. 7.—(U.P.)—Sharp criticism of President Roosevelt's domestic recovery program, with predictions by Oriental nations that it ultimately will fail, developed today at the Institute of Pacific Relations.

Bombay, India, Aug. 17, UR— Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, who began and ended a fast yesterday, was reported today to be tasting again. The government was secretive, Gandhi, at the Yeravda jail in Poone, began a "fast to the death" yesterday because the government would not permit him to conduct in his own way his campaign in favor of the untouchable outcasts. The government relented, and he ended his fast soon after it began.

Bremerhaven, Germany, Aug. 17.— Charles Manger of Los Angeles today was sentenced to three months imprisonment on a charge of involuntary manslaughter in connection with the death of his friend, Karl Werner Heye, III, of New York, aboard the liner Bremen July 30. The sentence, pronounced by a jury which heard the state’s attorney ask for a mild verdict because Manger had “proved himself an upstanding man,” will not take effect until September 30, 1936 if he pays a fine of 3,000 marks ($960) immediately. Manger’s attorney, Dr. Hirschfeld, pleaded that his client completely forgot he had loaded the revolver more than three years ago at Honolulu. The defendant, in a brief plea to the jury, declared he had no intention of killing his friend. When the judge showed him a photograph of Heye, Manger burst into tears. The wording of the sentence was taken by observers to mean that Manger, a unive

HOT SPRINGS, Ark. (4) — A quadruple poisoning that cost the lives of four members of a family was confessed today by a man who identified himself as Mark H. Shank of Akron, Ohio, and begged for leniency, officers announced. The victims were found late yesterday in an automobile which had crashed into a fence near Malvern, Ark., apparently as the driver succumbed. They were identified by officers as Alvin Cooley, 40, of Akron; his wife, Ethel, about 35, and their two sons, Clyde, 11, and Clarence, 7. A third child, Clement, 4, escaped the poison. Shank was arrested in the woods by a posse with bloodhounds about an hour after a farmer, George Clardy, reported seeing the car crash and a man flee from the scene. Shank said the family had eaten spoiled meat, but officers sent the food to chemists for study.

1933-08-29.text: Associated Press Gar Vv rears Washington, D. C.—(AP)--Disposition of America’s bulging wheat crops popped up as a major problem again today, despite action by nature, the agricultural adjustment administration, and more than a score of governments in signing at London a pact to cut down production and reopen foreign markets. While one group in the agriculture department sought to speed up the campaign to reduce American wheat acreage, from another came word that two of the nation's producing areas will have vast “exportable surplus” this year—the Pacific northwest and the southwest. Meanwhile, the export movement of wheat has slowed down to a mere trickle compared with years past, and doubts have arisen whether the wheat acreage reduction plan will offset unofficial reports that farmers not joining in it contemplate increasing their production. LONDON, Aug. 29.—(U.2)—Miss Sunny Lowry, 22, of Manchester, swam the English channel from Cape Gris Nez, France, to St. Margaret’s Bay, England, today, in 15 hours, 39 minutes. She was the first swimmer to make the crossing since 1930. As she fought her way to the English coast, Miss Lowry passed a small parade of eastbound channel swimmers. She entered the water at Cape Gris Nez at 6:36 p.m. yesterday. She arrived well behind the record for women made by Gertrude Ederle in 1926—14 hours, 31 minutes.

HIGHLAND PARK, IL, Aug. 29 (AP).—Miss Virginia Van Wie, of Chicago, defending champion, and Miss Enid Wilson, English title-holder, swept through the first round of the women’s national golf championship today with easy victories. Miss Van Wie defeated Elizabeth Dunn of Indianapolis, by the one-sided margin of 7 and 6, losing only one hole while Miss Wilson, making her third try for the title, submerged Mrs. Marion Turpie Lake of New York, 3 and 2.

| Dover, England, Aug. 29—(7)—The | English Channel was conquered for the first time this year today when Miss Sunny Lowry, 22-year-old Manchester, England, girl, arrived at South Foreland after swimming from Cape Gris Nez, France, in about 15½ hours. She landed, still going strong, at 10:15 a.m., (3:15 a.m. CST.) She started at 6:36 p.m. Monday, (11:30 a.m. CST). Three other swimmers, one of them the American, Charles Zimmy, a legless aspirant to channel honors, started a race across the channel for the Dover town gold challenge cup. The others are Mercedes Gleitz, an Englishwoman who first swam the channel in 1927 after eight failures, and E. H. Temme, another Briton, who in 1927 did the distance in 14 hours, 29 minutes. The Dover cup will be awarded the man or woman who swims from Dover to France in the shortest time this year.

Athens, Greece, Aug. 28 ()—The Athens appeal court today fixed Tuesday morning for hearing the application for formal sanction for Samuel Insull's arrest in connection with American extradition proceedings. The return of the former Chicago utilities operator, who was detained Saturday, is sought in connection with the financial collapse of his interests. The point involved in the pending action is whether he will continue in detention pending the outcome of the extradition proceedings. Insull is confined at a nursing home on advice of physicians.

NEW DELHI, India, Aug. 28. — Northern India was threatened with disastrous floods today when a gigantic volume of water was released into the Shyok and Indus Rivers by the bursting of the great ice barrier known as the Shyok dam in the Himalayas. The Shyok ice dam is 480 feet high. It was formed in 1926, when the Khumdan glacier pushed its way across a mountain gorge near the sources of the Shyok River and formed an ice barrier. Two years later, when last its volume was measured, the lake above the dam had become nine miles long, 1,000 yards wide and twenty-five feet deep. At that time a crack developed in the dam. Villages below were evacuated but there was nothing further than a slight leakage through the crack. The Shyok River rises near the Great Karakoram pass in Kashmir, in far northern India. It is formed of two mountain streams that twist about from their sources 20,000 feet in t

ATHENS, Aug. 29.— The appeals court today ratified as legal the arrest of Samuel Insull, American utilities magnate. Insull was arrested at the request of the American government. Insull’s lawyers contended the arrest was unjustified because Insull had made no effort to evade authorities since the first request for his extradition was made last year. The court had been expected to ratify the arrest on the ground that it was in accordance with the extradition treaty under which the American government asks that Insull be extradited to answer charges that he violated bankruptcy laws. The United States has sixty days within which to convince the court that the request for extradition should be granted. Before announcing the ruling the president of the appeals court informed Insull that he was arrested by virtue of a verbal note from the American legation, accusing him of bankruptcy. No deta

Paris, Aug. 27 (4) - Grave fear of new devaluation of the French franc has been revived in financial circles by the downward slide of the dollar and the pound and concern over possible monetary developments in the United States. The Treasury and the Bank of France still vigorously proclaim that France is firmly on gold, but privately many financiers predict the day is approaching when France will be forced to devalorize to revive crippled business and vanishing foreign trade. Budget Minister Lucien Lamonreaux solemnly pictured a perilous state of the nation’s finances in a speech at Boussae today. He warned the country that not only the present Cabinet but even the French form of government would be in danger unless France succeeds in the tremendous task of balancing the 1933 and 1934 budgets.

1933-05-17.text: LONDON, May 17 (P)—King George may reply personally to President Roosevelt’s appeal for peace and disarmament in order to emphasize the whole-heartedness of British approval, the United Press learned today. The British cabinet was understood to be working on the text of the British reply, King George received President Roosevelt's message at Buckingham Palace last night and was so interested that his inclination was to answer personally.

WASHINGTON, May 17 (UP) World wide reaction to President Roosevelt's appeal for peace and disarmament: London: Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and his government elated; preparing immediate acceptance. Paris: Governmental approval made evident in inspired statement of foreign office. Rome: Italy accepts without reservations, United Press learned on high authority. Moscow: Soviet, elated at tacit American recognition, let it be known plan coincides with own plans. Berlin: Approved if Germany is given arms equality. Buenos Aires: Press comment favorable. Tokio: Roosevelt ignored intentionally or unintentionally Japan's position in Far East, army spokesman said. Japan cannot pledge herself not to cross borders. Mexico City: Government wires acceptance to Roosevelt. Panama City: Panama also wires acceptance. Santiago, Chile: Press comment favorable.

LONDON, May 16.—(UP)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald led the chief powers of the world tonight in warm-hearted acceptance of President Roosevelt's direct appeal for support to the American program for peace. MacDonald, in publicly accepting the Roosevelt peace plan, told members of the Pilgrim Society at a dinner in his honor that the president's bold stroke was “one of the great monuments and landmarks of history.” The plan was accepted unconditionally by Italy, a United Press dispatch from Rome reported, and France fell into line swiftly with an inspired statement in Paris indicating Mr. Roosevelt's message met with instant approval in official circles there. PLYMOUTH, England, May 17.—Robert W. Bingham, arriving today in England to take up his post as United States ambassador, said he agreed absolutely with every syllable of President Roosevelt's plea to the nations of the world. The ambassador, his wife, and (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1.)

Berlin (UP)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler faced the Reichstag and the civilized world today with a demand for 'equality of arms' for Germany. He declared Germany is entitled to demand rearmament unless the other nations fulfill their Versailles treaty obligations and disarm. May Quit League Hailing the Roosevelt peace plan as a constructive step, Hitler agreed to join any non-aggression pact as proposed by President Roosevelt, but refused to adhere to a disarmament agreement, even if reached by a majority of nations, unless Germany’s demand for equality is fully recognized. Otherwise, he declared, Germany will resign from the League of Nations. The Reichstag unanimously approved the speech and then adjourned. Hitler, who led Germany from embittered acceptance of the restrictions of the Versailles treaty to a new aggressive national consciousness, unbent but little in his declaration of Germany

BERLIN, May 17 (UP).—Germany has disarmed in accordance with the Versailles treaty, and now if the other nations refuse to carry out their part of the treaty and disarm too, then Germany is entitled to demand rearmament, Chancellor Adolf Hitler told his parliament today. The tense Reichstag, assembled in the Kroll opera house for the chancellor's vital statement to the world of Germany's position, heard their leader make a forceful presentation of Germany's treaty rights, and demand revision of the hated Versailles treaty. “No European war could improve the present situation,” he said significantly. President Roosevelt's message to the world urging peace and disarmament, he said, “deserves Germany’s warm thanks.” Germany will accept the basis, as far as equality of arms is concerned, of the MacDonald plan which President Roosevelt recommended, he added, and Germany is ready to join any n

PARIS, MAY 17. (AP) — Premier Daladier today declared that France will “gladly join in the generous effort of the President of the United States for which we ardently wish success.” He expressed most sincere satisfaction with the President's message to the world issued yesterday.

Berlin, May 16. (4)—All Germany tonight was on tiptoe of expectation over Chancellor Hitler's address to the Reichstag tomorrow when the Nazi chief will announce German policy on the armaments question and other related international issues. In preparation for this momentous event, the Chancellor today held a private conference with President Von Hindenburg and then retired to seclusion to work out the exact terms of his eagerly awaited pronouncement. Before he saw the aged president, Herr Hitler talked with Count Rudolf Nadolny to learn the latest news of the disarmament negotiations at Geneva. Newspapers and the public generally are intensely interested in the coming declaration by the Chancellor and are deeply concerned to know how it will affect the recent drift of foreign opinion which appeared to be sweeping the Reich toward international isolation. 1933-12-05.text: WASHINGTON, D. C., Dec. 4—Extradition to England of John (Jake the Barber) Factor of Chicago for trial on a charge of participating in an $8,000,000 swindle was approved today by the Supreme Court. The court upheld the action of the seventh circuit court of appeals, directing extradition. Factor fought extradition on the ground that the offense charged against him of having received money, knowing it was fraudulently obtained, was no crime under the laws of Illinois and therefore not extraditable under the treaty with Great Britain. Since the extradition proceedings were begun, Factor and his son claimed to have been kidnapped and held for ransom. At the request of the British government, Factor was taken into custody in Chicago and held for extradition on the charge he was a fugitive from justice. He was charged with having received from the Broad Street Press Ltd. 486,000 pounds, knowi

BATHURST, Gambia, British West Africa (U.P.) — Weather conditions showed improvement Tuesday and gave Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh hope that they might take off soon for their flight of 1,870 land miles (a little over 1,600 sea miles) to Natal, Brazil. Lindbergh has been becalmed. So smooth has been the water that suction caused by the pontoons of his seaplane has held his plane on the surface.

Chicago, Dec. 4 ()—The United States Supreme Court's ruling today that John Factor must return to England for trial comes at a time when much of his fortune, estimated to run high into the millions, has melted away. A three-year legal battle against extradition has cost many thousands of the dollars he allegedly took from British investors in fraudulent stock transactions. He had paid a reported $120,000 to kidnappers of himself and his son. Attorneys for the swarthy, solemn visaged, little man who progressed from bootblack and barber in Chicago to the status of international financier announced they would continue the legal fight.

London—(L.P.)—The British government is unable to accept the assumption that lasting friendship between the Irish Free State and the British Commonwealth of Nations could not be attained on the basis of the present relationship. This was the British government’s reply today to a note from President De Valera of the Irish Free State regarding the relations of the two peoples in the event the Free State were severed from the Commonwealth. The reply was made in the House of Commons today by J. H. Thomas, Dominions Secretary, when he made public notes recently exchanged by London and Dublin. The British answer furthermore declared the government could see no ground for answering a question founded on the assumption indicated. Rum runners, anxious to make a landing be- fore repeal becomes official, were sighted on “rum-row” off the southern New England coast during the early morning. Coast guardsmen reported that the vessels evidently were seeking some place to get rid of their illicit wares before this afternoon.

Madrid, Spain, Dec. 8 —()— A revolutionary general strike was declared in the city of Coria, province of Caceres, 200 miles west of Madrid today. The city, only 20 miles from the Portuguese frontier, is in an isolated mountain region. Telephone and telegraph lines were cut at Coria and National “shock police” were rushed to the scene from the capital.
PARIS, Dec. 4 (AP).—Several deaths were reported in France today as a cold wave swept all Europe. The lakes Paris froze for the first time this year.
— BOSSES 4 TRI 2S WELLINGTON, N. Z., Dec. 5—(4)- Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd's flagship arrived in the harbor late tonight. Byrd is enroute to the Antarctic.

1933-06-07.text: ROME, June 7.—(AP)—The four-power peace pact will give Europe 10 years of peace and security, Premier Mussolini told the crowded Senate today a few minutes after the German government had notified Italy of its complete acceptance of the final text of the treaty. France, Italy and Great Britain agreed to the pact yesterday, and it was scheduled to be initiated later this evening. The Senate, together with the American, British, French and German ambassadors, gave the premier a tremendous ovation as he announced the successful result of 2 months of negotiation over the pact. The new international instrument, Premier Mussolini said, has “produced collaboration by the four great Western powers, upon whom rests the responsibility not only for peace among themselves and in Europe but also for the world.” Outlining the history of the pact since Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Secret

LONDON, June 6.—A special meeting of the British cabinet will be held Friday when the problem of what to do about the American debt payment due June 15 may be decided. Officials intimated today in announcing the summoning of the extraordinary meeting of ministers that the government expects to have by Friday some indication from Washington of what the American government is counting on from London when pay day rolls around. The House of Commons, now in adjournment, will want to have a definite announcement upon the debt question when it re-assembles two days before the payment is due. Several attempts have been in the House to extract a statement from Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, but this

WASHINGTON, June 6 (FP) — Approach of payment day for the European war debtors a week hence stirred a fresh revival of speculation on this controversy today but found President Roosevelt still silent and apparently standing firm for payment of the $144,179,674 due. News that the British cabinet would meet in extraordinary session on Friday to tackle the problem linked with intimations from London that it expected word on the attitude of the United States at that time, brought from the White House only this statement signed by Stephen T. Early, a secretary to the President: “There has been no official word from Great Britain on war debts. Therefore, no official reply is being prepared.” Britain Maneuvering There were indications today, however, that feelers are being put out by the British and that informal talks on the thorny debt question are proceeding. Rome, June 7—Germany’s acceptance of the draft of Premier Benito Mussolini’s 10-year peace treaty was announced today, and it was said that the pact would be initialled here late tonight or tomorrow morning. The treaty would bind Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy, Europe’s leading powers, to keep peace for 10 years. After the initialling there must be additional negotiations before final approval is given and the treaty formally signed.

ABOARD S.S. PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT, en route to London, June 6.—U.P)—A plan to increase materially the price of silver was revealed today as an integral part of the program to be followed by the United States delegates at London next Monday. This project—of particular significance to silver producing states in the West—was part of an informal accord reached with the various nations who sent delegations to Washington in recent weeks to discuss economic topics, it was learned. Agree Tentatively. These nations agreed tentatively to a plan to reduce gold coverage of their currencies, possibly to a minimum of 25 per cent, with 5 per cent of this to be actually in silver, at the option of the central banks. Silver in this instance would be based on an agreed price, to be determined at London. The banks would buy silver as the price falls, (Pentiaued an Sams & Cat 4)

Athens, Greece, June 7.-()-An attempt on the life of Eleutherios Venizelos, who has been premier of Greece eight times since 1910, deeply stirred this little Republic today. The 69 year old veteran statesman narrowly escaped death at the hands of a gunman who fired from an automobile at the motorcar in which M. and Mme. Venizelos were traveling from Amaroussis to Athens late last night. The assailant’s shots killed a personal guard accompanying the former premier and struck Mme. Venizelos, who suffered four serious wounds in the lungs and stomach. The driver of the Venizelos machine was cut by glass from a broken car window. Otherwise unhurt, but in great pain, the chauffeur devotedly stayed at the wheel, and drove the travelers to their destination. The gunman, whose motive was not determined, escaped. Mme. Venizelos was said to be progressing satisfactorily from her injuries later toda

MOSCOW, June 7. (UP)—Soviet officials felt today it was likely Jimmy Mattern had landed his airplane in Chita, Siberia. News of his arrival, however, may be long delayed. Urgent telegrams from Chita often are delayed 10 to 20 hours before reaching Moscow. News of Mattern being sighted over Novosibirsk was telephoned to the United Press bureau here. The telephone line ends at Novosibirsk. Officials of the airdrome there told the United Press that weather conditions were good and there was every reason to believe the flight was proceeding.

| PARIS. (Copyright by U. P.) — The French government does not propose to pay either the defaulted December 15 war debt payment to the United States or the one due June 15, although the cabinet has not formally made its decision, the United Press has learned. The government’s attitude, from an unimpeachable official source, opposes the payments firstly on the grounds the cabinet government would be overthrown by the Socialists-Nationalists in the chamber of deputies, secondly, France has been led to believe Washington would prefer the debtor nations to default rather than to voluntarily grant revisions. It is understood the French also believe a default on the June payment would precipitate a general settlement and aid in the success of the World Economic conference. They believe the conference must be accompanied by a general debt settlement as well as stabilization of currencies. nat _

He visited this newest of America's fighting ships today and reports went out he was ready for a hasty departure for the capital. PARIS, July 1—#)—France intends to remain at the world economic conference and fight for the gold standard regardless of the gold group’s reported threat to walk out, it was declared after today’s cabinet meeting. The ministry enthusiastically approved the action in London of Georges Bonnet, French finance minister and leader of the gold bloc. Camille Chautemps, minister of the interior, said at the conclusion of the meeting that “adjournment of the world economic conference is not foreseen.” He added that France was hopeful President Roosevelt would approve the currency resolution prepared for him by the conference leaders. The cabinet also approved M. Bonnet’s plan to launch a loan to replenish the nearly empty gold reserves. LONDON, July 1.—-(UP)—Trade war between Great Britain and Soviet Russia ended today after the Soviet executive committee liberated and ordered deported two British subjects imprisoned for sabotage after a sensational trial in Moscow. The Soviet embassy notified the British foreign office that the cases of Leslie Thornton and William MacDonald, imprisoned British subjects, had come up in the executive committee meeting in Moscow today and that the sentences had been commuted. Tonight's British official Gazette publishes the king's order revoking the British embargo on Russian imports. The embargo was established in retaliation for the sentencing of MacDonald and Thornton.

1933-10-14.text: Los Angeles, Cal., Oct. 13—: Alice White’s story of a terrific beating at the hands of John Warburton, movie actor from England, was told in a transcript of the comely blond actress' recent testimony before the grand jury, released today. At the same time there was made public the testimony of Martin Biork that he and Russell Brown had been induced by Sidney Bartlett, movie writer and friend of Miss White, to attempt a disfigurement of Warburton in retaliation for the latter's beating of the actress. Biork and Brown were indicted recently for robbing and beating Warburton, but the grand jury took no action against Bartlett, who refused to testify. Miss White testified Warburton beat her so at her home after a Beverly Hills party that her face was frightfully disfigured, her eyes swollen until she could not see and that she had to have a plastic surgeon work on her nose.
