LONDON, Oct. 14—Europe faced a diplomatic crisis of the gravest character today when Germany announced her withdrawal from the League of Nations and the World Disarmament Conference. Worried officials, reluctant to speak, would say only that full responsibility must rest on Germany for anything that might occur, in view of the new peace plan presented to the disarmament steering committee at Geneva only a few minutes before the withdrawal was announced at Berlin. From Geneva came word that even before the withdrawal was announced high American disarmament officials had said that the success or failure of the World Conference depended on Germany’s acceptance or rejection of the Simon plan, endorsed in broad terms by Norman H. Davis, chief United States delegate. The withdrawal confronted the World War allies with a question how far

Owensboro, Ky., Oct. 14, U.P.—The Royal Scot, crack British train, which has been on exhibition at the World's Fair, struck and killed Charles Lee Mitchell, 22, last night at Reed, 15 miles west of here. The train was en route from Louisville to St. Louis on a post-fair tour.

LONDON, Saturday, Oct. 14.-~-UP The Morning Post today said that a “Soviet-Japanese war is ‘inevitable’,” in commenting on the far eastern situation and the disarmament conference at Geneva. Soviet troop trains are reported to be traveling east on the Trans-Siberian railroad every 45 minutes, the Post said. Alleged official Japanese documents concerning the possibility of seizure by Japan of the Chinese Eastern railway in Manchoukuo, jointly operated by Russia and Manchoukuo, were published in Moscow this week and have caused increased friction between the two governments.

Berlin, Oct. 14. ()—By one of the boldest strokes of official action taken since his assumption of power, Chancellor Adolf Hitler today served notice on the League of Nations that Germany will withdraw two years hence, and on the disarmament conference that the Reich no longer finds it possible to continue its attendance. To demonstrate to the world that all Germany stands behind the chancellor's foreign policy, President Paul von Hindenburg ordered the dissolution of the Reichstag and all the state parliaments and set new Reichstag elections for Nov. 12. TOKYO, Oct. 14. (#)—Authoritative sources said here today that Japanese troops were being concentrated at Mukden, Changchun and Harbin in Manchuria. Apparently the concentration was a precautionary measure, ostensibly in preparation for a bandit drive.

PARIS, Oct. 14—(#)—A French spokesman today characterized the announcement of Germany's intention to withdraw from the disarmament conference and the League of Nations as “the gravest news in 20 years.” The news was flashed to the cabinet while it was in session discussing the armaments situation. A foreign office spokesman commented as follows: “France has done what she could to achieve disarmament. Her views are shared by the United States and Great Britain, and now it is perfectly clear where Germany stands.”

BERLIN, Oct. 14 (#)——Chancellor Adolf Hitler in an address to the world, tonight bitterly assailed the treaty of Versailles and again reiterated the conviction of the German people that they are guiltless of blame for the world war. Discussing the close of the great war when the German people in trustful faith and in the assurance of President Wilson’s fourteen points lowered their arms, the Chancellor said: “The people could rightly have expected that from this greatest war a lesson would be drawn of how small were the chances of possible gain in proportion to the magnitude of the sacrifice. “When, therefore, Germany was compelled to destroy her armaments to enable a world disarmament, uncounted millions believed this to be an evidence that a redeeming realization was making headway.” Says Destroyed Arms “The German people,” the Chancellor continued, “destroyed their weapons and fulfill

1933-03-02.text: - LONDON, March 2—The British war department today presented a tentative budget calling for an increase of 1,462,000 pounds sterling over its 1932 expenditures, Presenting the estimate, Lord Holleham, secretary of state for war, pointed out that the economy measures of the past year have “involved a definite loss of efficiency and could not be repeated without serious consequences,” Today's estimate calls for 37,950,000 pounds sterling, as compared with 36,488,000 appropriated for 1932.

Nanking, China, March 1 (4) The Chinese Government announced today that it was making representations to Great Britain concerning the recently ordered British arms embargo against both China and Japan. Announcement of the Government’s action was made after an official spokesman had asserted that the effect of the embargo would be to weaken China, as only a small quantity of arms are produced in this country. The Government spokesman asserted that the embargo should be limited to Japan.

LINGYUAN, Manchuria, March 2 (UP).--Harassed by bitterly fought rear-guard engagements, victorious Japanese troops converged today from six directions upon Chengtehfu, capital of Jehol, in the last phase of the war for subjugation of the province. Flushed with success in the Lingyuan sector, the Japanese predicted confidently they would take Chengtehfu in time to celebrate “Army Day,” March 10, anniversary of the capture of Mukaen in the Turn to Page 2, Column 5.

Berlin, March 1.—(#)—Hermann Goering, minister without portfolio in the Hitler government, declared in a speech tonight the incendiary fire at the Reichstag building Monday night was meant to inaugurate a series of violent acts culminating in a communist revolution. For this reason, he asserted, the government was justified in promulgating its drastic decrees of the last two days, which have placed Germany under virtual martial law. Civil War Looms The cabinet minister said communists have spread handbills calling for the formation of groups for so-called self-protection but really intended to provoke civil war. Communist materials which have been seized, he continued, disclosed forged orders to national socialist storm troopers to be in readiness after the election next Sunday night to seize Berlin by force. They have made this plain in their speeches, meanwhile 60,000 of Hitler’s brown shirted storm troops and Franz Seldte’s steel helmet war veterans are being inducted into the Prussian police force as auxiliaries and action has been taken to assure support of the army. Chancellor Hitler formulated this determination with the statement: “In order to satisfy God and our conscience, we have once more turned to the German people. They themselves are to decide. Berlin, March 2, WPHAn edict regarded as the first official move towards abolition of the German Republican flag was expected today, the News Service Telegraphen Union said. The edict, by the Prussian government, would relieve all Prussian state officials of the obligation to display the Republican black, gold and red colors, Besides permitting use of the banners of the German states, it will also empower Prussian authorities to fly the black, white and red flag of former imperial Germany, the report said.

TOKYO, March 2 (4)~-A Rengo (Japanese) news agency dispatch from Lingyuan today said that the vanguard of the 16th infantry brigade, commanded by Maj. Gen. Tadashi Kawahara, had occupied Sutaoling, which is between Lingyuan and Tingchuan in Jehol province. The dispatch said the troops took over the town at 4:30 o'clock this afternoon, Lingyuan, which was captured yesterday by the Japanese, is approximately 75 miles northeast of Chengtefu, or Jehol City, the capital of the northern Chinese province of Jehol. RENWICK, IOWA, MARCH 2 TWO RENWICK HIGH SCHOOL SENIOR GIRLS WERE KILLED, THE HIGH SCHOOL PRINCIPAL SUSTAINED A BROKEN BACK AND THREE OTHERS WERE INJURED WHEN THEIR CAR OVERTURNED NEAR HERE TODAY. BETTY MARTIN, 17, AND VERL E. KELLING, 16, WERE KILLED, AND MISS ETHEL LINDSAY, PRINCIPAL OF BIRMINGHAM, IOWA, WAS IN A CRITICAL CONDITION AT A FORT DODGE HOSPITAL. 1933-06-02.text: Regent seat. June cor (UP) Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, in his last parliamentary speech before the world economic conference, sounded a warning today that Great Britain will wage unflinching economic warfare on nations that treat her unfairly. Under fire by the labor party, which demanded a statement of policy on payment of the $75,950,000 war debt installment June 15, Chamberlain refused to comply for fear of prejudicing negotiations with the United States. He expressed confidence that the United States was aware of Britain's difficulties and would do nothing to emphasize them or to prejudice the success of the world economic conference. Today's session of the house of commons was its last until June 16, and opposition members were determined to demand information on the government's intentions during the next two weeks, which may become historic. | ABOARD S. & PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT WITH AMERICAN DELEGATION TO LONDON CONFERENCE, June 2 — (AP) — Teamwork was the aim as Secretary of State Cordell Hull called the American delegates to their first formal discussion of the problems to be tackled at the London economic conference. Secretary Hull, who hopes for a fast-moving conference that will bring quick relief to the world, indicated that the United States program coincides with the agenda of the conference. Points emphasized are currency stabilization, a lowering of trade barriers, higher prices, and resumption of capital movements.

Washington — Accepting polite refusals from two Republican independents, President Roosevelt was reported tonight to have requested a third Republican senator—James Couzens of Michigan—to be ready to sail within 48 hours with the American delegation to the London economic parley. Washington—In its own private way, the internal revenue bureau has undertaken a minute check between the reams of testimony and statistics recorded in the Morgan investigation and income tax returns filed by members of that firm. Washington — Acting quickly, the house today voted legal tender money should be used henceforth in the settlement of contractual obligations of the government and the private citizen.

London, June 1. (UP)—A 10 to 7 gamble against death, with the stake the thrill of making airplane flights no one else has made, will be essayed at noon Monday, by J. A. Mollison and his intrepid wife, Amy Johnson, two of Great Britain's foremost aviators. The Mollisons plan to fly from Croydon Airdrome, near London, to Floyd Bennett Field, New York; to rest for one day, then fly to Bagdad, Persia, and back to Croydon—12,000 miles in all. Success would mean making the first two-way Atlantic flight, breaking the non-stop distance record in the New York Bagdad hop and being first to fly from London to New York. In an important debate on foreign affairs, held just ten days before the world parley begins, the chancellor once more refused to disclose the British war debt policy and intimated that the government is awaiting some new move from Washington. Giving great emphasis to the necessity of reviving world trade he expressed the belief that this revival depended upon acceptance of the three main objectives of the world parley. 1933-02-04.text: LONDON, Sept. 5.—Britain hopes to convince American public opinion in the next few weeks that a drastic scaling down or even cancellation of the war debts will not only benefit the United States, but the whole world. It was stated in highest government quarters that Great Britain plans to inaugurate its campaign as soon as Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, returns to the United States. The main purpose will be to counteract any belief in the United States that the debt question merely involves the payment of money owed by Great Britain, which, if not fully discharged, will fall upon the shoulders of the American taxpayer. The cabinet is united behind the views expressed by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer. Berlin—VP— The powerful Catholic parties took their first thrust Friday at Chancellor Adolf Hitler with the allegation that President Paul von Hindenburg was led into dissolving the Reichstag on the basis of false information that they refused to tolerate the Hitler cabinet. Monsignor Ludwig Kaas, leader of the Catholic centrists, in letters of protest to the chancellor and the president, said Hitler’s Junker-Nazi coalition cabinet deliberately broke with the centrists at the height of negotiations, before the dissolution decree was granted by the president. The king summoned a cabinet meeting this morning to discuss extending the state emergency throughout the country. Bucharest and environs were quiet. Widespread labor unrest was responsible for the decrees. Troops were ready to go to Ploesti, center of the important Roumanian Oil Refining industry. Workers invaded the offices, wrecked furniture and attempted to destroy files and records. 1933-12-27.text: (By The Associated Press) Paris, Dec. 27.—France, under threat of reprisals by England, took off the 15 percent exchange surtax on British goods today. The official reason given was that “English money can be considered stable.” It thereby became certain such a tax would not be imposed on American goods, as seemed probable several months ago, when a decree to that effect was prepared but never signed.

LONDON, Dec. 26—(AP)—Stirred by reports its naval strength has been outstripped by the United States and Japan, Great Britain—the belief is growing here—is preparing to launch a large naval building program in 1934. Already the government has announced that the 1933 program has been revised to supply larger and more heavily armed cruisers than were originally projected. Information that six new cruisers are planned has been published in the Sunday Dispatch; owned by Lord Kethermere. Two other newspapers reported five new cruisers are favored by the admiralty, while nearly all agree that an increase in both destroyers and cruisers is in (Continued on Page 3)

WASHINGTON, Dec. 31, — The government gold price was unchanged today at $34.06 an ounce. It was the seventh repetition of this quotation for newly-mined domestic metal. Bar gold in London was worth $32.52 on the basis of sterling opening $5.144 to the pound.

PARIS, Dec. 26.—(4”)--Another one of ten persons held in connection with a wide investigation of an alleged international spy plot protested his innocence before the examining magistrate today. He was Louis Martin, 43, master of many languages, who worked in a secret code room of the navy ministry. Previously, upon his court investigation of what police described as a vast ring of military tipsters, Magistrate M. Benon heard two young Americans, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Switz, declare their innocence. Switz, 29-year-old native of East Orange, N. J., joined his wife, 22, the former Marjorie Tilley, of New York, in declaring that their arrest was a frame-up.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 27 (P)--General Tsai Ting-Kai, commander of the famous 19th Route Army, and two of his co-leaders in the Fukien revolt, were reported in flight today after a heavy aerial bombardment of their quarters in the rebel city of Foochow by Nanking government aviators. The bombardment centered on the headquarters of the revolutionary "people's government." For three days heavy bombs dropped on buildings believed to harbor the rebels. At the conclusion of the bombardment, in which at least 50 persons, all of them Chinese, were killed and heavy property damage was suffered, the Nanking government confidently predicted an early collapse of the Fukien revolt. Generals Tsai, Chen Ming-Shu and Li Chi-Sen were in hiding outside the city, it was reported.

Paris, Dec. 27—(2)—In a national funeral at a Paris railroad station France paid a last farewell to the victims of the Lagny train disaster today as the deaths of two women raised fatalities to 202. - An enormous crowd gathered in the great, black-draped under

Moscow, Dec. 26. (®)—Alexander Troyanovsky, Soviet Russia's first ambassador to the United States, left Moscow tonight in a race against time in order to sail to America on the same boat as William C. Bullitt, United States ambassador to Russia. Troyanovsky departed hurriedly in response to insistent urgings from Bullitt that they travel on the same ship, although state plans for his work were not completed here. Bullitt is returning to Washington after making plans for an embassy in Moscow. He is to sail from Havre December 30 on the liner Washington.

| PARIS, Dec. 27.—%)}—France’s drive to line up allies in defense of the League of Nations and against German rearmament entered a new phase today. - Henceforth, under a decision made at a meeting of French national defense ministers, an understanding will exist that there are to be no direct talks with Chancellor Adolf Hitler on arms. The government will keep an ear open, however, for what the German chancellor may say through the regular diplomatic channels.

1933-11-26.text: VIENNA, Nov. 25.— Tension on the Austro-German frontier near Salzburg increased greatly today as a result of the shooting of a German soldier on the Tyrolese border near Kitzbühel. The German legation filed a protest with the foreign office and at the same time the director of security at Salzburg added to the border patrol and closed the frontier to everybody except a few considered beyond suspicion of political activities. The Austrian government began a complete investigation of the incident, which occurred yesterday. One version said three fascist home guard patrols saw 20 Germans approaching them on skis and shouting “Hail Hitler!” Believing they faced an attack, the Austrian patrols opened fire. Surveyors and photographers were sent to help a commission decide whether the episode occurred on German or Austrian soil. Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss (Continued on Page 6, Col. 7.)

BERLIN, Nov. . A secret visit of the French ambassador Andre Francois-Poncet to Chancellor Adolph Hitler and their conference, reportedly on Germany's return to disarmament discussions, aroused intense interest tonight. It was understood that Hitler, who six weeks ago today startled the world by withdrawing from the Geneva disarmament conference and the league, requested the conversation and that the French envoy readily accepted the invitation. News Leaks Out The two met yesterday and news of the interview leaked out only by accident in governmental circles, much to the chagrin of M. Francois-Poncet who, it was said, wished, like Hitler, that nothing be said about it. The reason offered for the secrecy was that France yesterday was without a government following (Continued on page six)

Premier Camille Chautemps started forming a “crisis cabinet” tonight in the face of a mounting clamor for the rescue of the franc from perils of an unbalanced budget and dwindling gold reserves. As the second choice of President Albert Lebrun, the veteran lawyer, legislator, and minister was said to be seeking a ministry that would last until the veteran Edouard Herriot would again be ready to take the helm. Chautemps' cabinet would be dedicated to a program of “public safety at home and national security abroad.” Political forecasters had set Chautemps’ ministerial for December 17 so that M. Herriot, whose government fell in December on his advocacy of a debts payment to the United States, could avoid another debt default, an extremely embarrassing issue for Herriot. In the meantime, his radical socialist party:

PARIS, Nov. 25.—(UP)—Camille Chautemps, minister of the interior under Albert Sarraut, was making a valiant attempt tonight to form a republican union government with former Premier Édouard Herriot in a keystone position. Chautemps told the United Press that he was hopeful of completing his cabinet by tomorrow afternoon in time to permit its publication in the Official Journal Monday. The most important development in his plans for the new government, which, like that of his predecessors, Sarraut and Daladier, must stand or fall on the rock of a 6,000,000,000-franc deficit, was his proposal to enlist Herriot as a minister of state without portfolio. Herriot would make his residence at the Quai d'Orsay, as the super-statesman of France, in a position looking over both the domestic and foreign policies of the nation. Chautemps was endeavoring to bring together the same coalition of faction
MADRID, Nov. 26 (Sunday) (4. -~-Discovery of a nationwide syndicalist revolutionary plot, scheduled to begin Monday, was announced early today by the government.

BERLIN, Nov. 25 (4)—The ousting of an evangelical church cabinet member and the resignation of three noted theological professors from the Nazi German Christian movement led many churchmen tonight to believe that only a miracle can prevent a schism in the Protestant ranks. Thousands asked whether "Chancellor Hitler will interfere and try to compel the warring factions to stick together, or will he, as a political leader, keep hands off in this religious quarrel?" At the same time 460 pastors and churchgoers in Westphalia wrote to Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller that they declined to take orders from the reich’s church government and Bishop Adler of Westphalia. German Christians in Thuringia announced today their determination to secede from the Nazi church regime "because of questions of principle." The fight between the Nazi faction headed by Dr. Joachim Hossenfelder, leader of the German C

San Jose, Calif. (7)—Thomas H. Thurmond and John M. Holmes, confessed kidnapers-slayers of Brooke Hart, were lynched here last night by a mob of 100 men who smashed their way into the county jail after a two hour battle to seize the pair. 6,000 See Lynching A whooping, cheering crowd, estimated at 6,000 persons, looked on. Thurmond, first to confess, was unconscious when dragged to St. James park, 100 yards from the jail, partially stripped and hanged to a tree. Holmes, a powerful man, fought for his life in vain. Twice he wrenched his hands free and lifted the noose from his head but the third time it was put there to stay and, still kicking, he was yanked into the air. In the glare of torches and flashlights the bodies dangled for half an hour or so—a macabre picture for the thousands who had assembled swiftly after the news of the lynching movement had spread through the city. WARM SPRINGS, Ga, (UP). President Roosevelt has ordered Ambassador William C. Bullitt to proceed at once to Russia to establish the new relations with the Soviet government. The ambassador left Warm Springs to sail next Wednesday, with orders to return “as soon as practicable.” This action was all that was forthcoming from the presidential vacation retreat despite the array of financial and recovery leaders here. To all appearances the president gave no other serious attention to government business on this Saturday. Sunday Secretary Ickes, public works administrator, arrives. And, thus, Mr. Roosevelt will have with him the leaders of the recovery and financial programs. It offers ample opportunity for a thorough checkup on the domestic situation, including the complex commodity dollar monetary program, and to all appearances the president is well satisfied with the trend of events. 1933-10-03.text: (Copyright, 1933, By United Press) WASHINGTON, Oct. 3. — Preliminary moves toward a monetary “truce” with Great Britain will be made during war debt negotiations opening here Thursday, the United Press was informed by a high authority today. The groundwork will be laid during these talks, it was stated, for a monetary conference between the United States and Great Britain in London before the end of the year. Little progress is anticipated toward settlement of the debt question because of current political and economic obstacles but it is expected that headway will be made toward world monetary stability. Under present plans, an agreement for stability of the dollar and the pound will be sought within the next few months. With these two largest non-gold currencies definitely linked, it is expected to be a comparatively easy matter to tie other unstable currencies. American monetary and f

SAGA BEACH, Ont., Oct. 3.—The attempt of Capt. and Mrs. James A. Mollison, England’s famous flying couple, to take off for Bagdad in an attempt on the long distance record, failed today when the left undercarriage of their plane, Seafarer II, cracked. The accident occurred on their second attempt to get their heavily loaded plane into the air. The Mollisons were in no danger. They climbed out and told the crowd of 600 at the beach that it would take two days to repair the carriage.

GLASGOW, Oct. 2.—(4)—Jubilant over the favorable recommendation of army engineers, residents of northeastern Montana tonight were talking of the possibility of a new era in this section should the Fort Peck water storage project be finally approved. “This means a new deal for northeastern Montana,” said Mayor Leo B. Coleman, chairman of the local project committee. The dam, the site of which is 20 miles southeast of here, on the Missouri River, would serve to control the flow of the Missouri, provide water for irrigation and make possible the development of power. Army engineers have estimated the value of the power possibilities at $29,500,000. Jobs for 25,000, Word of the favorable report by army engineers immediately caused attention to be focused on the employment possibilities. It has been ‘Continued on Page 2, Col. 2.)

GENEVA, Oct. 2.——A report that the world depression is gradually lifting and the economic situation especially in the United States, is steadily improving, was heard today by the economic commission of the League of Nations assembly. The official report, read by Augusto Schmidt, the Estonian minister to Rome and the commission's reporter, declared production was increasing and unemployment decreasing. The delegates expressed great satisfaction at the reading of the statements.

| MONTVILLE, Me., Oct. 3, (P)— Phyllis Rowell, 16, of this town and Fred B. Jackson, 34, were shot to death early today by a jealous suitor of the girl, who then committed suicide. The slayer was Elwood Kane, 35, also of Montville. Kane accosted Jackson as he was driving Miss Rowell and her sister home from a dance, and the shooting followed.

VIENNA (#) — Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss was shot and wounded today in what authorities described as an attempted assassination. A youthful gunman found the chancellor in the Parliament building — seat of the parliamentary government Dollfuss shelved August 3. The assailant fired twice, both shots taking effect. However, surgeons said the chancellor was “not dangerously wounded.” The youth was placed under arrest. One of the shots lodged in the chancellor's arm, police announced as they began an examination of the prisoner whom they said had been identified as an ex-soldier. Drastic action against both Nazis and Socialists was expected as police launched a drive to round up all political suspects. Authorities were not able immediately to determine whether the gunman was a Nazi or a Socialist. The chancellor had been attending a meeting of Christian Social party leaders in the Parliamen

Oslo, Norway, Oct. 3—-(AP)— Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh hopped today on a flight to Stavanger, a seaport in southwest Norway. The American fliers arrived Sunday by plane from Tallinn, Estonia, and spent two days in sightseeing here. Yesterday they were granted an audience by King Haakon VII, and later Colonel Lindbergh visited the army aviation field fifteen miles away, where he inspected various types of planes.

HAVANA, Oct. 3—Heavily armed soldiers patrolled the capital’s streets today, civilians moved warily, tense with fear, after the bloodiest twenty-four hours in recent Cuban history. The United States cruiser Richmond and two American destroyers were at anchor in the harbor within gunshot from shore, and the battleship New Mexico was immediately outside the harbor ready to move in at any time. Bodies of about 100 persons: soldiers, sailors, officers, revolutionary students and civilians, were on the morgue slabs, victims of the National Hotel battle between rebel officers and their own enlisted men and of innumerable shooting affrays throughout the city. Few were sanguine enough to believe that yesterday's fighting marked the last bloodshed in Cuba's groping effort to find the new freedom that was to follow the overthrow nearly two months ago of the despot, Gerardo Machado. 1933-07-20.text: London — Great Britain, the United States and several other great powers have agreed to a tariff truce to remain effective until the world economic conference finally is wound up, regardless of the duration of the coming recess, it was understood tonight. However, it was understood any nation could withdraw after July 31 on one month's notice.

London, July 19.—(#)—Senator Key Pittman of Nevada received some encouragement for his silver revival plans today as the World Economic conference moved steadily toward adjournment, July 27, one committee after another deciding to postpone consideration indefinitely on their problems. The Nevada senator achieved the acceptance by a sub-committee of part of his proposals for increasing the use of the white metal in subsidiary coinage and preventing further debasement of silver money. Limit Set The silver agreement, however, is finally dependent upon conclusion of an arrangement between the chief producers and holders, before April 1, 1934. Although the silver resolution as adopted dropped Mr. Pittman’s proposal for optional use of silver for one-fifth of currency reserves, the Nevadan was optimistic about the matter. “What it means,’’ he said in ex- iCoantinned on Page ?)

London, July 20. — Failure of efforts to conclude a world wheat control agreement, last hope of the World Economic Conference for a major accomplishment, was indicated today. Delegates sought a compromise under which problems of acreage restrictions, reduction of tariffs and relaxation of import quota restrictions might be left for debate at a meeting at Geneva in September. At a two hour meeting today, nations interested in wheat appointed a committee of six to draft a compromise, reconciling proposals of import nations with demands of export nations. Australia, Canada and a Danubian delegate will represent the exporters; Great Britain, France and Italy the importers. One by one the planned agreements have proven impossible, after refusal of the United States to stabilize its currency, hopes for tariff agreements were gone. London, July 20 (UP)—Failure of efforts to conclude a world wheat control agreement, last hope of the world economic conference for a major accomplishment, was indicated today. One by one the planned agreements have proven impossible. After refusal of the United States to stabilize its currency, hopes for tariff agreements were gone. But conferees thought agreements on several commodities were possible before the conference recesses July 27. Senator Key Pittman, Democrat, Nevada, indicated in a speech today before the Silver Subcommittee that an agreement to control silver might be delayed for a month or two by discussion of technical questions. Now coffee, sugar, tin and cocoa subcommittees have adjourned without reaching agreements. The Silver subcommittee had hoped to reach agreement and the wheat negotiators, trying to plan an increase in prices, seemed for a time on the verge of agr

Moscow, July 19 (®) — Wiley Post, American globe-circling flier, came down at Rukhlovo, Siberia, about 300 miles short of his scheduled halting place, Blagoveschensk, at 2:52 p. m. today Moscow time (6:32 a. m., E. S. T.) bad weather forcing him to interrupt his round the world flight. The aviator's plane, the Winnie Mae, was slightly damaged in brushing against the treetops shortly before the arrival at Rukhlovo. Clouds of mist forced the American to hug the ground dangerously, but despite the mishap he made a perfect landing. Near Exhaustion, Post, who left Irkutsk at 7 a. m. Moscow time, was very near exhaustion when he brought his ship down at the Siberian town which lies between Chita and Blagoveshensk, having denied himself needed rest along the route in an effort to set a new record for the round-the-world air trip. His arrival at Rukhlovo set at rest anxieties which had been felt

Berlin, July 20.—In an endeavor to find Marxist parties’ funds and to ascertain who have foreign bank accounts, police officials advertised today that a reward would be given persons divulging such information. The move is preliminary to the confiscation of the sums as provided for in a cabinet decree issued last week ordering the seizure of private fortunes and even citizenship rights of “enemies of the state and the people.” The advertisements referred principally to a socialist war chest which, it was apparent from the plea to the public, has evaded the best efforts to find it. Strong Weapon The decree, probably the strongest weapon yet placed at the disposal of Nazi officials, only legalized methods—so far as political parties are concerned—which had long been used. In view of the government's flood of complaints about ancestry, hundreds of thousands of citizens are expected to take

MOSCOW, July 20—There was a possibility today that Wiley Post and Jimmie Mattern may race from Alaska to New York as a climax to their world flights. Post took off from Khabarovsk, Siberia, for North America today in his plane, the Winnie Mae, and Mattern is believed to have left Anadyr, Siberia—where he was lost June 14 after taking off for Nome from Khabarovsk—in a Soviet rescue plane. The former stayed in Khabarovsk only long enough to fuel then flew on, nearly exhausted. He hopes to make Fairbanks, Alaska, non-stop. At Nome Mattern expects to get a new plane to replace the one destroyed when he was forced down on Anadyr Peninsula.

MOSCOW, July 20.—(UP)—Aviator Levanevsky, of the Russian arctic air service, planned to take off from Anadir, Siberia, today, for Nome, Alaska, with James J. Mattern, stranded American world flyer. Mattern hoped to continue his world flight from Nome. Levanevsky arrived at Anadir July 18, after waiting for days for the weather to improve over the Okhotsk Sea. Levanevsky was missing for some time, and fear was felt for his safety because of the fog hanging over the dangerous Okhotsk Sea stretch of his.

Northampton, Mass.—The funeral of Calvin Coolidge will be held Saturday morning at 10:30 in Edwards Congregational church, of which he was a member. The body will be taken by automobile cortege to Plymouth, Vt., where the committal service will be held at 1 o'clock. Capital Shocked Washington, D. C.—Amazement and sorrow mingled in a brief stricken capital Thursday night as it united with the nation in mourning Calvin Coolidge, whose death shocked the White House, the congress and the citizen in the street. LONDON, Jan. 6 (P)—The passing of Calvin Coolidge was the outstanding item of the front pages of today’s London newspapers, which printed lengthy obituaries while several editorialized. Tributes to his personal character were abundant. Views were also expressed that he had not displayed or had not the opportunity to display great political capacity. The London Times editorially remarked that “Singular good fortune” made him president in a period of unprecedented prosperity. It continued: “He owed it more to his luck than to his wisdom that he had not occupied the White House in the succeeding years of misery and ruin. * * * This lonely, inarticulate, simple, shrewd man was not of today but had the fine qualities of the best type of American plain citizen of the past.” The Daily Mail said: “Never faced with the necessity of making heroic decisions, his task was to keep the ship of state o

BEVERLY HILLS, Val, Jan. d-- (a) — Mrs. Carrie Guggenheim, 74, widow of Isaac Guggenheim, New York copper magnate, died at her residence here today from a sudden heart attack. Mrs. Guggenheim, who had lived here since the death of her husband in Southampton, England, eight years ago, had been ill about five months. The family formerly resided in New York. Three daughters survive. They are Mrs. Helene Glorney and Mrs. Clarence B. Hewes, both of London, and Mrs. Beulah Splegelberg of New York. They were not here at the time of their mother’s death. Mrs. Guggenheim's secretary said funeral services and cremation would be held Sunday, the ashes to remain here.
London, England, Jan. 6.--A violent earthquake threw the population of Athens, Greece, into a panic, according to an exchange telegraph dispatch. Little damage was reported.

SHANGHAI (4) — Two days of quiet on the Shanhaikwan battlefront was broken today with a renewal of hostilities between Japanese and Chinese forces. Rifle fire broke out on the battle line extending from one mile west of Shanhaikwan to near the limits of the city of Chinwangtao, the seaport which is several miles southwest of Shanhaikwan. The opposing armies faced each other from opposite banks of the Tashih river. Driven from the walled city of Shanhaikwan, China's northern railway exit, the Chinese were reported bringing up reinforcements from Tientsin on the railroad which passes through Chingwangtao. Japanese warships were gathering in the Chingwangtao harbor and today additional Japanese troops and ammunition were reported having been brought into Shanhaikwan from Manchuria. Further operations on the scale of the terrific three-day bombardment and street battle for possession of Shan

PARIS, Jan. 4—().-The body of Jack Pickford, motion picture actor and brother of the famous Mary, who died here yesterday, will be returned to the United States aboard the steamship Europa, which sails Saturday. Funeral plans were not announced here, It was presumed the body was being sent to California.

PARIS, Jan. 6 P—Criticism was mingled with praise in this morning's newspaper tributes to former President Coolidge. The following were outstanding comments: Petit Journal: “He deserved his prestige and was an ideal president.” Echo de Paris (By “Pertinax,” Andre Geraud, the foreign editor): “Coolidge did not know Europe. As concerns France, his ignorance and hostility unfortunately were fairly evident.” Ere Nouvelle (organ of former Premier Edouard Herriot): Coolidge really was the author of that policy which clashes with our taste for order and logic.” Former Premier Laval said he “participated in the sorrow of American citizens.”

Shanghai, Jan. 6.—(#)—(Friday)—Sino-Japanese hostilities were renewed, reports from Chingwangtao said, when Chinese and Japanese troops exchanged rifle fire today from opposite banks of the Tashih river, between that city and Shanhaikwan. Dispatches said additional Japanese troops and ammunition arrived at Shanhaikwan, with the resulting widespread belief that further operations were destined to eventuate.

1933-01-11.text: LONDON, Jan. 10 (#)—For the second night in succession a dismal heavy pea-green fog shrouded London and suburban areas and complicated the police search for Samuel Furnace, whom the police charge with the slaying of his friend, Walter Spatchett, who first was identified as Furnace himself. The body of the victim was burned in such a manner that murder was not suspected at first, leading to the identification of the body as that of the man who is now sought. Scotland Yard forces now are considering additional alternatives which Furnace faced when confronted with the problem of disappearing after Spatchett’s death. One of these is that he may have succeeded in disguising himself as a woman, and another that he may be hidden by some friend who is bringing him food and providing shelter. Several times Furnace has been reported to have been seen near London, with the police close behind.

LONDON, Jan. 11—(P)—A ghostly fog-shrouded dawn found Scotland Yard's host of police relentlessly pursuing Samuel Furnace today in the most minute search London and the surrounding territory ever have undergone in criminal annals, "PERFECT CRIME" He is sought as the slayer of his friend, Walter Spatchett, whose body was burned in such a manner that murder at first was unsuspected and the victim was identified as Furnace himself. Throughout the huge London zone which contains a larger population than any other equal area in the world, officers in plain clothes conducted an almost microscopic examination. They combed highways and byways. They visited hotels, lodging houses, inns, roadhouses, coffee stalls, hospitals, and in some instances, private dwellings. Police disguised in the nondescript apparel of down-and-outers mingled with denizens of the underworld, listening for a word which mi

MOSCOW, Jan. 11.—(#)-- Four men were sentenced to death today and three others to ten years in prison for stealing jam from a government warehouse. The manager of the warehouse and three employees are to be shot, three other employees will go to a prison camp in the most remote region of the country, and two others must spend three years in jail for the crime, which was characterized as “causing great harm to the workers’ supply.”

Moscow, Jan. 10—(#)—A challenge was cast to “the capitalist world” today by Joseph V. Stalin in the industrial program he has mapped out for Russia for the next five years. The Bolshevik chieftain announced a 16 percent increase in general production over last year as this year’s goal of the socialist nation. The annual average increase for the second five-year plan, now being inaugurated must be 13 or 14 percent, he said. This, he declared, “would be impossible in capitalist countries.” Stalin announced his plan in a speech before a joint meeting of the communist party central committee and the central control committee. Claiming “the successful fulfillment of the first five-year plan,” he declared its aim “was to change the country from one with the technique of the middle ages to one of contemporary technique—to make the nation independent of the whims of capitalism.” He admitted the

Sinaida Woelkow Commits Suicide Because of Ill Health, Berlin—(4)—Sinaida Woelkow, daughter of Leon Trotsky, the exiled Russian revolutionary, committed suicide last week "on account of illness," a note she left on her dresser disclosed today. The woman, whose identification was made public yesterday, was reported to have lost her passport when Soviet citizenship was withdrawn from Trotsky and his family. The only message she left said: "Be good to my boy. I have taken my life on account of illness." She died of gas asphyxiation. Her six-year-old son survives.

TOKYO, Jan. 11 —(#)—The Japanese Government today replied to a Chinese protest against the occupation of Shanhaikwan with the statement that Japan "expressly reserves the right to make demands" in connection with any settlement. The protest from the Chinese Nationalist Government was received earlier today. The Japanese reply held the Chinese garrison entirely responsible for the outbreak of hostilities at Shanhaikwan, China’s northern railway terminal, on the night of January 1. BOXER PROTOCOL CLAUSE IN JAPAN'S CHAT. Although the reply did not mention the Boxer protocol of three decades ago, under which foreign powers were permitted to place troops in North China to keep the Peiping - Shanhaikwan Railway open, a foreign office spokesman believed provisions of this protocol would be among Japan's reserved "demands." These provisions, which the foreign office spokesman outlined Monday, de

PARIS, Jan. 10.—(AP)—Exactly what President Hoover said to former Premier Pierre Laval when they discussed the debts in Washington in 1931, became an important issue today as parliament reconvened for a session which may bring the downfall of the government. Senator Damecour, dean of the upper house, declared in the senate that the American president clearly informed Laval the United States would proceed with revision of the debts if France consented to reduce her reparations claims against Germany. Discussion of the debt issue revived as the government faced a dangerous parliamentary situation growing out of Finance Minister Cheron’s proposals to balance the budget by providing new taxes amounting to 5,453,000,000 francs ($218,120,000). In his speech before the upper house, Senator Damecour declared Senator William E. Borah had admitted the accuracy of his statement that President Hoove

Stalin's recent statement that the Soviet government is preparing for war removed the last possibility that Japan might sign a non-aggression pact with Russia, a government spokesman in Tokyo said today. The Soviet government demonstrated that while it was asking Tokio to sign the pact, it was shifting its entire industrial five-year plan to prepare for war, the spokesman said. The demand of the Japanese military for huge appropriations in the current budget was due to the knowledge of the change in the Soviet program, according to the spokesman. Stalin's speech, to which the spokesman referred, was delivered before the central executive committee of the Soviet Union and was the first pronouncement in 18 months by the virtual dictator of the Soviets. Stalin told the committee that the far eastern crisis and the failure of "certain neighbors" to sign non-aggression pacts forced the Soviet

1933-04-07.text: Washington, April 6-4#)--A fateful gathering of European statesmen at Washington in coming days was in the making tonight as President Roosevelt called for “realistic action” to help the world, and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, the first to come, sent word he would sail for New York a week from Saturday. Broad plans on the part of the president aimed at solving the world’s greatest ills by personal conversations with the chieftains of the leading nations took on definite shape with information from a high official quarter that France already has been approached on the matter of sending especial representatives here and that a formal invitation will be sent to Paris soon. From the same authoritative source came disclosure that German and Italian spokesmen also will be welcomed here and that the Roosevelt administration will be glad to receive the representatives of any

BY MUGEN LIONS, (United Press Staff Correspondent) MOSCOW, April 7—One of the chief motives behind Great Britain's exceptionally strong protests against the arrest of six of her citizens in Russia is the desire to prevent American recognition of the Soviet government, Soviet spokesmen charged today. British conservatives are apparently hopeful that Washington would hesitate to assume relations with the Soviet at a moment when London threatened to limit its relations, the spokesmen declared. Certain American groups opposed to Russian recognition are benefiting by renewed attacks against the GPU (secret political police), the Soviet judiciary system, and the Soviet regime in general, they said. The spokesmen cited certain editorial passages in the British press to support their charge. The threatened British embargo and the strained relations of the Soviet with Germany offer American busin

LONDON, (/)—Possibility of a war debt moratorium when the next payment to the United States becomes due in June was seen by several British newspapers today. Desires for a moratorium were reflected in reports of President Roosevelt’s invitation to Prime Minister MacDonald to visit Washington and the latter’s acceptance. Mr. MacDonald is expected to leave April 15. “The result of the visit cannot be otherwise than good,” commented the Daily Mail.

Tientsin, China, April 7 (AP)— Chinese dispatches said today that British marines had been landed at Chinwangtao to protect British property here as a result of renewed hostilities in that sector. The Chinese here said Japanese aviators were bombing towns along the Lwan river.

LONDON, April 7.—The government’s Russian embargo bill went to the House of Lords today after receiving final approval of the House of Commons. It is expected to become effective April 18 but the government made it clear it hoped never to have to use its provisions. The bill was requested as a government weapon to be used to protect the interests of six British engineers who are to be tried soon in Russia on charges of espionage and sabotage. The House of Commons passed the measure by a vote of 291 to 41 last night. The British government contends the engineers have no chance for a trial and that the charges were manufactured to provide a “show” to draw attention from Soviet industrial difficulties.

Washington, April 7.---(UP)—While President Roosevelt prepared for a visit from Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, arrangements progressed today for receiving representatives of France and perhaps other nations. Assuring Mr. Roosevelt that “I am most touched by your friendly invitation,” MacDonald notified the president that he would sail for the United States April 15 aboard the Berengaria. He will be a guest at the White House. Similar conversations appeared likely between Mr. Roosevelt and envoys of France, Italy, Japan and Germany. Informed sources predicted an invitation to Premier Daladier of France either to visit the United States himself or send a delegation may be extended today. Mr. Roosevelt has told Ambassador Paul Claudel of France that he would be glad to receive a French representative. Ambassador Augusto Rosso of Italy also was told by the state department

LONDON, April 6 (#)— The house of commons gave third reading Thursday night to the government bill which would empower the cabinet to declare an embargo on Russian trade agreement. The measure was sent to the house of lords and it is expected to become effective April 18 on the expiration of the present Anglo-Russian trade agreement. The embargo would be applied only as a weapon in dealing with the cases of the six British engineers who are facing trial in Russia on charges of espionage and sabotage, it was indicated.

PARIS, April 1. (AR) — France will send a delegation to Washington to participate in the conversations between President Roosevelt and Premier MacDonald of Great Britain, it was officially announced today. Premier Daladier and Foreign Minister Paul-Boncour, who conferred today, will be unable to go, a high official said. The spokesman added that because of internal political reasons it was highly improbable that former Premier Herriot would go and that he still expected Andre De La Boulaye, new French ambassador to America, to speak for the government. No invitation has been received yet from President Roosevelt, but the matter of sending experts to Washington to participate in a preliminary meeting preparatory to the forthcoming world economic conference was discussed with Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large. The government accepted Mr. Davis’ proposal that the experts be disp

1933-02-03.text: | LONDON, Feb. 3.— (UP) — The British cabinet today entrusted negotiations with the United States for war debt revision to a committee of five cabinet members headed by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald. Other members of the committee are: Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer. Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, who negotiated the present debt funding agreement with America. Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade. The committee was charged with completing negotiations with the United States for discussion of war debts and was made jointly responsible for advising the government of the negotiations. Baldwin's appointment caused considerable surprise as the Baldwin settlement is still the subject of severe criticism by political opponents. It was announced MacDonald would accept the chairmanship of the world economic con

Woking, Eng., Feb. 3.—(4)—With the same simple austerity which characterized his life, the body of John Galsworthy was brought today from his home for cremation here. The hearse carried a plain oak casket on each side of which lay a large laurel wreath tied with red, green and white ribbons. The absence of flowers was by request of the family. The widow, other members of the family, a few friends and the family servants attended a brief service in the chapel.
Geneva, Feb. 3, UR - A final attack led by the British delegation today killed the French plan before the World Disarmament Conference general commission.

(By the Associated Press) Qelin, Feb. 2.—Chancellor Adolf Wile, who took over the cares of government four days ago, renewed today his plea for four years of power, challenging his countrymen to “crucify me or do anything else to me” if his policies have not succeeded in that time. While he was talking to foreign newspaper correspondents, the police, by his order, were raiding Communist meeting places and the homes of suspected Communists, arresting anyone implicated in the serious disturbances which have been continuing since the Hitler government was formed. The chancellor interrupted a working schedule which has left him very few hours of rest to outline for the foreign press the broad principles up. “The other side had things all their own way for 14 years, and look at the result!” he told his visitors. “Give us four years, the legal period of a Reichstag, and then let the country si

- "TOKIO, Feb. 3.—The Japanese government was reported today to have learned informally that President-elect Roosevelt was considering American recognition of Soviet Russia, and Japanese sources made it clear that such action would be considered “unfortunate” here. Several candidates for United States ambassador to Moscow are being considered, it was reported in diplomatic quarters. The Japanese felt that American recognition of Russia would connote support of Moscow's anti-Japanese policy in Asia. Yousuke Matsuoka, Japanese delegate at Geneva, was understood to have reported to the government that there was little hope for conciliation of the Manchurian dispute, and to have asked instructions regarding withdrawal from the League of Nations. The foreign ministry was understood to have replied that Japan will not decide on withdrawal until the league assembly makes its report.

BERLIN, Feb. 3.—An emergency decree providing death or long prison terms for political terrorists was considered by the government of Adolf Hitler today to curb increasing fights and fatal street brawls. A similar decree was promulgated last summer and had the desired effect of restraining political outbreaks. The decree was withdrawn when the country became quiet politically. Reports early today indicated that the disturbances were continuing in several parts of Germany, especially in the Rhineland, despite police precautions. Many cities followed Berlin's example and banned open air meetings likely to create political excitement. The government was reported to plan a meeting of prime ministers of all the German states to discuss action against Communists and means of counteracting political disturbances generally. Berlin police who occupied Liebknecht House, local Communist headquarter

TOKYO, Feb. 2—(AP)—It became apparent today from newspaper comment and unofficial discussions that Japan, faced with the prospect of possible withdrawal from the League of Nations on account of the Manchurian dispute, was determined to retain islands which she holds in the Pacific Ocean under League mandate. Admiral Osumi, minister of the navy, declined to answer directly whether Japan would retain the islands in event of withdrawal from the League, but navy circles were insistent that they be held. The islands are located between the Philippines and the United States and are important in the Japanese navy's plan for domination of the western Pacific.

PARIS, Feb. 3—Premier Edouard Daladier avoided a definite stand on war debts and touched only lightly on other foreign problems in his ministerial declaration, completed today to be read to the chamber of deputies this afternoon. The premier based his bid for a vote of confidence on handling of domestic problems, chiefly balancing the budget. If parliament votes confidence in the new government today, Daladier and Minister of Finance Georges Bonnet will promise to submit a definite financial program to the chamber Tuesday. The fate of the cabinet depended on the attitude of the Socialists, who overthrew the last two ministries.

1933-03-17.text: ROME, March 17.—(4)—Hopes of the world for disarmament and relief from the threatening anarchy on frontiers of European countries turned toward Rome today as final preparations were made for the British-Italian conference this week-end. Italy, which has been silent for so long while watching its neighbor, France, carrying on its negotiations for a united front with England and the United States, proposes to keep the center of the stage for some time to come. Other government chiefs will follow Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of England, to this city, Premier Mussolini's newspaper Il Popolo D'Italia declares. Mussolini’s paper did not state what other government leaders would arrive, nor when, but Hitler of Germany has been mentioned as a possible caller. MacDonald, who put new life in the disarmament conference yesterday with a plan for armaments reductions specifying definite limits on

London, March 17 (AP)—Andrew W. Mellon, ending a year’s service as United States ambassador here, and Yosuke Matsuoka, who represented Japan in the League of Nations debate over the Manchurian issue, left on the same boat train today to take the steamship Leviathan for the United States. Matsuoka is returning to Japan via the United States. It is understood he considers his American visit highly important. He expects to discuss the far eastern situation and Japanese-American relations with influential leaders from President Roosevelt down.

Geneva, Switzerland, March 16. —(P)—With a boldness and fervor which stirred the weary disarmament conference to fresh life, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today submitted a new scheme for a treaty which would reduce the fighting strength of France and other powers and permit Germany and her former allies to augment their military forces. To counter-balance this proposed concession on the part of the armed powers, the British leader advocated an agreement for a consultative pact by the signatories to the Kellogg anti-war treaty and under its terms. Thus the United States is invited to interest herself in any breach or threat of a breach of the peace of the world. Mr. MacDonald explained that contributions to peace must be made by both the armed and unarmed nations and he appealed directly to France and Germany to abandon their fear and to cultivate (Continued on Page 2)

GENEVA, March 17—(UP)—Tired from his emotional appeal to the disarmament conference, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald prepared to leave today for his momentous conference with Premier Mussolini in Rome. The same tense political situation hung over Europe as conference delegates hotly, but unofficially, discussed MacDonald's sweeping proposals. Though all realized that something would have to be done to relieve a situation brought about by the rise of the Nazis in Germany and the general suspicion of nations and groups of nations toward one another, MacDonald's proposals did not meet with widespread approval. He urged a reduction of continental armies, a naval holiday until 1935 when a world naval conference would be held, abolition of military and naval aviation, and permission to Germany to double her armed forces to 200,000 men. Officially the delegates commented pleasantly on the boldn

TOKYO, Mar. 17, (UP)—Japanese bombing planes swooped down on Chinese positions along the Luan river south of Hsifengkow today, dropping their missiles of death, dispatches to the newspaper Asahi said. Planes following close behind dropped printed leaflets urging the Chinese to withdraw. Japanese troops were in possession of both Hsifengkow and Panchiakow, the dispatches said. Hand to hand fighting was reported from the former city where Japanese columns under Maj. Gen. Hattori united to repulse Chinese counterattacks.

By The Associated Press. Berlin, Germany, March 16.—Hjalmar Schacht was reappointed to his old post as president of the Reichsbank today, succeeding Hans Luther, who submitted his resignation to Chancellor Hitler. Dr. Schacht headed the bank from 1923 to 1930, resigning because of dissatisfaction with the final draft of the Young Plan as it was agreed upon at The Hague. Dr. Luther succeeded him. Regulations of Reichsbank prevent removal of its president for political reasons and Dr. Luther retired voluntarily, but he has been in conflict with the government recently over the program for financing work to relieve unemployment. Apparently this disagreement made it impossible for him to continue in office. Dr. Schacht has a wide background of banking experience. In the years since the war he has been particularly active in attempts to stabilize banking and currency in this country. It was h

TOKIO, March 17.10 P+ Japan's interest in world peace will not be lessened by her withdrawal from the League of Nations, Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida told a special committee of the privy council today. Uchida pledged Tokyo's continued participation in the Geneva Disarmament Conference and other peaceful enterprises, supported by the League. Japanese bombing planes swooped down on Chinese positions along the Luan River south of Haifengkow today, dropping their missiles of death. Dispatches to the newspaper Asahi said planes following close behind dropped printed leaflets, urging the Chinese to withdraw.

Washington, March 17 (®)— Beer of at least 3.05 per cent alcohol by mid-April was in prospect today as house leaders discussed what to do about amendments the senate inserted in the beer-wine-revenue bill before passing it last night. Some Democrats responsible for what the house does had said they would insist upon allowing 3.02 per cent alcohol by weight instead of the 3.05 the senate approved, and added they thought, too, that wine had no place in the measure. One of these was Representative McCormick (D., Mass.) who had charge of the beer bill when it went through the house. “I’ll use every bit of my influence to oppose those senate amendments,” he told newspaper men. Speaker Rainey and Democratic floor leader Byrns reserved public expressions of their views until they could confer. President Roosevelt’s attitude also was asked. The leaders knew that if they rejected the senate amend

1933-12-31.text: | Brussels, Dec. 30.—- (AP) — Fog rolling in from the coast was believed responsible for a crash today of the Imperial Airways London-bound plane Apollo which fell like a flaming coffin with 10 dead after colliding with a wireless pylon near Ruysselde, 14 miles from Bruges. An official description of the accident said the craft fell “like a mortally wounded bird” and that the absence of any cry from within the cabin led to the belief that all inside, including eight passengers said to be Britons, were killed instantly. Five members of the air station staff were burned about the face and hands in attempting a rescue. Bodies of the victims were charred. The tragedy occurred between Ostend and Bruges at 1:05 p.m. The craft, used on the Cologne-Brussels-London route, was flying from Brussels, where five of the passengers boarded it. The others were taken on at Cologne. The Dead The passenger

PARIS, Dec. 30—(AP)—An- are Francois-Poncet, the French ambassador to Germany, left for Berlin today with a memorandum containing France's refusal of Chancellor Hitler's disarmament proposals and the declaration that “disarmament is still possible.” In a final talk with the envoy, Foreign Minister Joseph Paul-Boncour reiterated the French “determination” to resist any change in the League of Nations and to conduct arms negotiations through its medium only.

SINAIA, RUMANIA, Dec. 30.—(@)—An explosion in the royal pavilion and an attempt to slay the assassin of Premier Ion G. Duca marked this city’s farewell today to the body of the government leader who was killed yesterday. Mourners thronging the railroad station, where the pavilion is located, were thrown into a panic. One child was slightly injured but property damage was slight. Shortly afterward the late premier’s brother-in-law, Radux Polizu, entered the station guard room, snatched out a pistol and fired several shots at Nicholas Constantinescu, the student assassin, but he was overpowered and led away. In view of the small damage done by the explosion police were inclined to believe it was a grenade similar to a smoke bomb either planted in the pavilion to create confusion or dropped there last night by Constantinescu or his alleged confederates in an attempt to escape. All three car

Miami, Dec. 30 (4)—Exhausted from battling rain squalls and choppy winds, Frances Mareelis and Helen Richey landed at 10:47 a.m. today, completing the longest sustained flight for women, 237 hours and 52 minutes. The women took off December 20th from the municipal airport and equalled the previous record of eight days, four hours and five minutes at 5:08 p.m. Thursday, establishing the new mark officially one hour later. The fliers came in with a graceful landing in the face of a brisk wind.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 30. (AP)— President Roosevelt, in a proclamation tonight, returned to the state banking authorities sole supervision over the non-member banking structure. He amended a proclamation issued last March whereby all banks were brought under supervision of the administration when the banking emergency was declared. The prohibitions in the previous regulations pertaining to the holding of gold, hoarding, and dealing in foreign exchange, were continued in tonight’s order. Inasmuch as the treasury has acted on all requests for licensing member banks of the federal reserve system, and as the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation likewise has acted on all applications to it for insurance, it was deemed appropriate, in the proclamation, that the state authority in each state should exercise the sole responsibility for the institutions not members of the federal reserve system. The

Washington, Dec. 30.—(P®)— President Roosevelt today approved a code to govern the vast retail food and grocery trade, composed of 480,000 stores in every city and town, and then completed the NRA’s organization of the country’s entire retail trade. It was the 182nd code of fair competition to be approved by the chief executive. With its signature by the president, NRA closed down until after New Year’s leaving nearly 50 other codes at the White House. Two hundred and fifty more were being perfected after hearings, and 40 additional hearings were docketed for the first part of next month, Effective Soon The grocery code will take effect January 6. The code generally paralleled the one governing general retail trade and its twin ruling drug stores. ‘Loss leaders,’ the articles offered below cost to bring in customers, are prohibited. Nothing except perishable, damaged or similarly cheapen

SHAWNEE, Okla., Dec. 30. (>) The “Tri-State Terror,” Wilbur Underhill—killer, bank robber, machine gunner and prison breaker—lay in a dying condition tonight, his body almost riddled by police bullets, and law enforcement agencies checked off another name on the dwindling list of southwestern bad men still at large. “I don't think I can live,” he told his bride, a pretty brunette whom he married at Coalgate, Okla., several weeks ago. Hospital physicians expressed the belief that the outlaw would not live, and officers voiced amazement that Underhill had been able to escape from a house where he was trapped and wounded in a gunfight early today. Bleeding from more than half a dozen wounds and scantily clad, Underhill ran from the house under a hail of lead and found refuge in a furniture store. Four hours later he was found hiding in a bed in the rear of the store. He surrendered without

- Washington, Dec. 30. (AP)— Secretary Ickes, in a statement published today, estimated 5,000,000 persons had received pay envelopes from rolls financed by the public works administration during the first six months of its operation and that this total “will continue to mount.” The public works administrator listed 4,000,000 as employed by the Civil Works Administration, and original Civilian Conservation Corps roster of 300,000, and a public works payroll that totalled 750,540 men on December 9. “This figure is now approaching the million-man mark,” he said. “and will continue to mount as a result of action already taken.” The administrator explained that only $145,000,000 remained unallotted out of the PWA’s original $3,300,000 fund, but that “another army of men now unemployed” would be given work before the total was finally expended.

1933-02-28.text: TOKYO, Feb. 28 ()—The British government's embargo on new arms shipments to Japan and China has caused that country to momentarily replace the United States in the villain’s role of the international drama as seen through Japanese eyes. America’s failure to follow suit was regarded as surprising. Keen resentment at yesterday's announcement by Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon of Great Britain was manifested in official circles. Authorities, however, agreed Japan was self-sufficient and that the embargo would only handicap China.

Washington, Feb. 27 ()—A strong likelihood that France as well as Great Britain will be allowed to present its plea for war debt revision was seen tonight in the wake of conferences between Cordell Hull, the incoming secretary of state, and the envoys of those two nations. At the same time it was disclosed that Paul Claudel, the veteran poet-ambassador of France, is soon to be recalled and one of the leading figures in the French ministry of foreign affairs sent to take his place at Washington. Slated to succeed Claudel is Andre Lefebvre de la Boulaye, now assistant director of political affairs in the foreign ministry, well-known in Washington diplomatic circles, he was second secretary of the French embassy during the war and later served as counselor. Claudel gave guarded confirmation to the report that such a move is on foot as he left a conference with Senator Hull at the new secret

= s #°= bd Once more the outstanding developments in the dispute between China and Japan have taken place off the battlefield. Great Britain announced the application of a temporary embargo on the shipment of arms and ammunition to either country. Permission to fill contracts already placed will be sanctioned, however. The French government was represented as willing to participate in any embargo provided both Great Britain and the United States take part, but the American Congress blocked President Hoover's proposal for executive power to apply an embargo. The issue also is under discussion by the League of Nations. Meantime, the fighting in Jehol continued. Japan admitted that the Chinese resistance had stiffened but asserted that the advance had not been stemmed and that Jehol City would fall within 10 days. Chinese dispatches, on the contrary, reported that the 19th Route Army had bl

LONDON, Feb. 27 (#)—A virtual embargo on the shipment of arms and ammunition to Japan and China was announced today by Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary, in the House of Commons. There is one condition—orders and contracts already placed by the two countries will be completed and shipped with the sanction of the government. Coincident with his announcement the foreign secretary stated that in no circumstances would Great Britain allow herself to be drawn into the conflict. It was felt that in this statement lies the key to the whole policy of virtual embargo. It was said unofficially that should an actual state of war between China and Japan come about, the Japanese navy easily would be able to seize shipments of arms to China and that if sometime that shipment happened to be in a British bottom it would be very difficult to escape involvement.
