KHABAROVSK, Siberia, June 29. (AP)—Soviet guards and sailors continued to search for Jimmie Mattern north of here today, but the belief grew the American aviator had been forced down southwest of Khabarovsk, whence he took off for Alaska June 15. Aviation experts believe the Texan had not reached the Aleutian Islands and that he could not have crashed near Okhotsk Sea, because the visibility was good when he left here to continue his projected world flight. He carried a rifle, ammunition, and fishing tackle, so if he were forced down on a remote island safely he could easily survive for a

Winnipeg, Man.—(AP)—Jimmy Mattern, American round-the-world flier, left Winnipeg at 6:30 a.m. (EST) today, bound for Toronto by way of Pembina, N.D., and Duluth. Mattern rode in a plane piloted by Pat Reid, Canadian airman. They expected to be in Toronto this evening.

1933-07-24.text: London, July 24.—(/P)—Far from dead, the world economic conference may live many years as a result of today's decision by the steering committee to remain in permanent session here although the conference will take recess Thursday. Prime Minister Ramsey McDonald insisted the action be taken. Behind him was the full support of Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Secretary Hull looks on the conference not as having failed but as a series of conferences of which the London parley is only a starter. Today's decision called for the original members of the steering committee to attend meetings and Jas. M. Cox will be able to represent the United States as he will stay here several weeks after the recess starts. The nations whose delegates on the steering committee will not be in London will be represented by their ambassadors here. Senator Key Pittman expects five great silver producing nations t

Bridgeport, Conn.—()— Britain’s famous flying couple—Captain Jim and Amy Johnson Mollison—awakened at the Bridgeport hospital this morning, refreshed and smiling again at life. After nine hours’ sleep, they regarded more cheerfully the crack-up in the salt marsh last night which ended their flight over the north Atlantic, and friends said they were in good spirits. Their plane “Seafarer,” in which they flew from Pendine, Wales, planning to start over the ocean again in Baghdad, and thence back to England, lay in swampy grass (Continued on Page 10)

Bridgeport, Conn.—(AP)—James and Amy Mollison’s “greatest gamble” has put them in a hospital. The British empire’s famous flying couple crashed last night near the end of the first leg of what was to be a triangular flight from Wales to New York, thence to Bagdad and thence back to England. Today, Mr. and Mrs. Mollison were recovering from cuts and bruises. Their black biplane Seafarer was badly damaged, but probably not beyond repair. Physical exhaustion caused the accident after the Mollisons had flown thirty-nine hours from Pendine Sands, Wales, to within sixty miles of New York. Their gasoline nearly gone, they tried to bring the plane down on a runway at Bridgeport airport, only to have it shoot into marshlands and turn over. “I was so tired I didn't know where I was headed,” Mollison whispered as mechanics carried him and his wife away on stretchers made from fabric torn from the S

By United Press America and the world were thrilled today by the daring feats of a host of airmen. Jim and Amy Mollison, Britain's first fliers, were up in a Bridgeport swamp after a remarkable flight across the north Atlantic from Pendine Sands, Wales. They were only 80 miles short of New York, their goal, when they ran out of gasoline and were forced to land. General Italo Balbo was prepared to lead his squadron of 24 Italian seaplanes on the first leg of the return flight to Italy. The squadron was ready to fly to Shediac, N. B., today if weather permitted. Wiley Post, American flier, just returned from a record-breaking flight around the world, received the enthusiastic applause of his countrymen. Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh were at Godthaab, Greenland, where they planned a series of flights to explore the Greenland coast. They may go to Iceland in their work of charting a new

‘BY THE ASSOC FICS? London, July 23.—Cordell Hull, American secretary of state, insisting that the work of the world economic conference scarcely even had been started, was reliably reported today to be convinced that the recess of the parley must be definitely limited to assure a reconvening. The secretary's position was claimed to be that an indefinite adjournment after next Thursday would leave such uncertainty over the fate of the world congress that resumption of the work would be jeopardized. Suggests Three Months Mr. Hull was understood to have under consideration a recommendation that the recess be for a maximum period of three months, with the steering committee authorized to call the nations together earlier should it decide this is desirable. Meanwhile Senator Key Pittman’s pact between eight silver producing and holding countries seeking to raise the price of the white metal

BRIDGEPORT, Conn., UP)—Jim and Amy Mollison, Great Britain's “flying sweethearts,” who ended their courageous and perfect flight across the North Atlantic from Pendine Sands, Wales, in a swamp adjoining the Bridgeport airport, hope to continue on to New York Monday. Mechanics who examined the wreckage of their plane, however, believed it was damaged beyond repair. The exhausted fliers were put to bed at Bridgeport hospital Sunday night after they had been treated for slight cuts and bruises. Hospital authorities thought they were in such a nervous state after their 39 hours in the air that it would be impossible for them to fly before Tuesday. Both Jim and Amy expressed the bitterest disappointment at not reaching Floyd Bennett airport, their goal, and were determined to continue on at the earliest possible moment. They were forced down 80 miles short of their goal when their fuel was ex

BRIDGEPORT, Conn., JULY 30—After conquering the North Atlantic and flying within 60 miles of their goal, the British air aces, Amy and Jim Mollison, crashed their black cabin biplane near the airfield here tonight, but escaped with slight injuries. “The couple, who had set out from Pendine, Wales, yesterday in an effort to fly non-stop to New York, circled the airport five times in an apparent effort to find a safe landing place. The airport is in the village of Stratford, near here. Captain Mollison told the doctor at the Bridgeport hospital that he had run short of fuel while coming down the coast. He said he saw the lights of the Bridgeport airport and decided to land there. He circled the field five times before he put the plane down. The airport was lighted on the chance that they might halt there and Fred Moller, airport manager, was atop the administration building when the ship a

Bridgeport, Conn., July 23. —()—Jim and Amy Mollison, who set out from Wales with hopes of being the first persons to make a non-stop flight from Great Britain to New York, crashed here tonight within 60 miles of their goal. After successfully crossing the north Atlantic and speeding down the New England coast, the flyers cracked up at 9 p.m. eastern standard time, after 39 hours in the air. The Plunge Captain Mollison, a sturdy Scotsman, known to his friends as “Dour Jim,” and his wife, the former Amy Johnson, were headed for {Continued on Page 7}

1933-11-14.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 10. (2)—A price of $33.20 an ounce for RFC purchases of newly mined gold was set today, an increase of five cents over yesterday and a new high. The figure was six cents less than the London price of gold converted into dollars at the opening exchange rate of $5.13. Previously the domestic price has been held at a point well above the world figure. The weakening dollar, however, carried the London price above the domestic price for the first time late yesterday.

London — (?) — The Daily Mail said today that the British government contemplated calling a further disarmament conference elsewhere than in Geneva, but the foreign office in Downing Street discredited the report. It was said that the report was based on Premier MacDonald's speech, made in the House of Commons, urging that Germany resume its arms negotiations, interrupted when the Reich withdrew from the disarmament conference and the League of Nations at Geneva. Want Germany In. The Mail's article followed the sensational threat by Arthur Henderson, made Monday night in the House of Commons, to resign as president of the conference. It said the British government has not given up hope of getting Germany back into some kind of disarmament talks. The thought was, the writer said, that Germany might agree to resume disarmament conversations provided she were not called back to Geneva—which

London, Nov. 14—(®)—The British admiralty today announced revision of its 1938 naval program to include new type 9,000-ton cruisers with increased armaments and one cruiser of the 5,200-ton Arethusa class. Sir Bolton Meredith Eyres Monell, first lord of the admiralty, made a statement of this decision of the admiralty in the House of Commons. He said the decision was made after reviewing the latest cruiser programs of other countries and “following the most anxious consideration and with much regret.” Eyres Monell emphasized that the United States and Japan, under the terms of the London naval treaty, were entitled to build the ships which those two countries contemplated but that, nevertheless, it would be the policy of the British government, by agreement, to restrict the vessels of larger sizes as much as possible. He also said it would be the British policy to reduce the maximum size

By the Associated Press. A threat of Sir Arthur Henderson, president of the world disarmament conference, to resign his post "unless there is a change in the present situation" resounded in European capitals last night. It marked the climax of a heated debate in the House of Commons in which the British government’s policy in Geneva was severely criticized. In Geneva, Henderson’s statement was interpreted as motivated by the failure of the various governments to seek in earnestness a way out of the arms deadlock caused by Germany's withdrawal. A statement read in London on behalf of Sir Arthur said, "no results are likely to be achieved by the attitude adopted by delegations at a recent meeting, and it is useless for me to remain here (at Geneva) for months unless the attitude changes." At Rome, newspapers and semi-official circles saw little chance for Germany's reversal on its disarmam

LONDON, Nov. 14 (U.P)—The British naval program will be revised to include the building of three new cruisers, Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, announced today in the House of Commons.

LONDON, Nov. 15.—Great Britain took the stand today that it is up to Germany to make a move to save the peace of Europe. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald himself confirmed before the House of Commons that Britain is marking time, but warned she is ready to point a finger of blame at any country responsible for a breakdown in peace efforts. Arthur Henderson, in a personal message read to the house, threatened to quit as president of the World Disarmament Conference unless governments change their attitude regarding arms. The announcement came as a sensation and as a climax to a debate on disarmament in which the British government's policy at Geneva was severely criticized. Sir Stafford Cripps, Labor party colleague of Henderson, wound up the debate for the opposition and read the veteran peace worker's message, Most Unsatisfactory “I have not decided to resign,” it said, “but the present

LONDON, Nov. 14. (4)—The Duke of Atholl, on trial for an alleged violation of the lotteries act, rested his case with a Bow Street police magistrate today on a plea of not guilty, he said. His attorney, Norman Birkett said the defense would call no evidence. Sir Rollo Graham Campbell, chief metropolitan magistrate, presiding over the hearing, said that in view of the importance of the case he would take time to consider his judgment, put it into writing, and give his decision on a date to be fixed by the opposing counsel. “The Duke honestly believed,” said Norman Birkett, “that apparently he has invented a method enabling him to get around the provisions of the lottery act which hitherto stood the test of 270 years.” Behind the summons against the 66-year-old Duke lay the scheme launched by him to fund British hospitals a portion of the 10-shilling notes that annually find their way to I

MANSFIELD, O., Nov. 14.—Police today were on the trail of two men, who they believe hurled the bomb which wrecked the mailing room of the Mansfield News-Journal Sunday. The newspaper was on the streets as usual the following day with a front-page editorial denouncing the gangsters who are believed to have been responsible for the bombing. Editor George J. Kochenderfer has been conducting a crusade against the underworld element in the city and the attempt to wreck his presses was believed to have been a retaliatory move. Police were also investigating a report that a man was seen running rapidly away from the News-Journal building shortly after the explosion and that four strangers had been loitering near the plant at midnight Saturday.

1933-08-10.text: Hourly reports on the frenzied political strife in Cuba, held back from any thought of intervention today as the Spanish and British governments, looking to America as protector of Cuban liberty and order, protested to American Ambassador Sumner Welles against loss of Spanish lives and destruction of British property. America has the responsibility under the Platt Amendment of maintaining Cuban liberty and resorting to intervention if necessary to restore order after the breakdown of effective government. State Department officials insisted that this country still was not considering sending troops to the strife-torn island. The Spanish and British protests indicated to observers here that the outside world was inclined to hold the United States responsible for Cuban conditions. Although declaring they had received no instructions from the State Department to prepare for intervention, th

__ NEW YORK, Aug. 10.—(?)—President Machado of Cuba has a name interesting in its English translation. His full name, Gerardo Machado y Morales means, literally, “Gerald Hatchet and Morals.” It is pronounced “Herr-ar’ Dough, Mah-Chah’-Dough y Moreahl’-Ace.” The “y Morales” comes from the Spanish practice of adding the surname of his mother.

LISBON, Portugal. Aug. 9 (PF) — Twenty-three seaplanes of the Italian trans-Atlantic air squadron arrived here this afternoon from the Azores where, on the departure early this morning, one of the ships overturned, resulting in the death of one member of its crew and the injury of three. General Italo Balbo, leader of the expedition which now has crossed and recrossed the Atlantic, was in the first of three groups to descend on the River Tagus. A welcoming throng, which included many Italians, cheered.

Lisbon, Portugal, Aug. 10 (UP) — General Italo Balbo and the crew of his fleet of seaplanes rested today and prepared to take off for ancient Ostia, the seaport of Rome, Saturday morning on the last stage of the greatest mass flight in history. Plans have been made at Rome for a triumphal reception of the fleet, now totaling but 23 planes because of the crash of the I-Rani at Ponta Del Gada, in the Azores Islands, when the fleet took off for Lisbon yesterday. The aviators were saddened by the death of Lieutenant C. Squaglia in the crash of the I-Rani, but were eager to be home. With but five hours' sleep in the Azores after a flight from Newfoundland, the crews were exhausted when they arrived here yesterday afternoon. On the flight to Ostia the fleet's course lay across Portugal and Spain, over the Mediterranean north of the Balearic Islands and across the Tyrrhenian Sea to the Italian

Lisbon, Portugal.—-(AP)—Sorrow over the death of a comrade in the Azores dimmed for members of Gen. Italo Balbo’s seaplane squadron the happiness they otherwise would have found in preparations today for completing their flight to America and back. The airmen prepared to fly directly to Ostia, Rome's new port, where thousands of Italians were expected to do them homage and escort them in triumphal procession to Rome. Twenty-three planes of the fleet arrived here yesterday. The twenty-fourth was damaged in taking off at Ponta Delgada, Azores, causing the death by drowning of Lieut. Enrico Squagila, relief pilot, and injuries to three others.

Charleroi, Aug. 9 (4)—Their strike over wages and hours settled by NRA mediators, 450 employees of the Fort Pitt Glass Company went back to work today. D. R. Hormel, one of the mediators, told the workers the glass industry code will be arranged shortly and he urged them to go back to work with the assurance that their demands will be considered.

TRIER, Germany (AP) — Four Saar district residents, alleged to have refused to "surrender" and to have fired on a frontier guard when crossing the border were jailed Thursday. Five German communists were arrested at the same time and charged with cooperating with foreign communists.

HAVANA, Aug. 10 —(AP)—The question whether President Machado shall resign his post to bring peace to Cuba, now under a formally declared war, today was placed before the national executive committee on General Machado’s Liberal party. The executive committee met to consider the formula of peace presented by Ambassador Welles acting as mediator between the Machado party and opposition forces. Differences within the party over the mediation proposal widened as the liberal conference got under way and it appeared that old party lines might be obliterated. Meanwhile the general strike which brought the conflict over Machado to a head continued unbroken with food becoming scarcer.

1933-12-17.text: LONDON, Dec. 16 (UP)— A prominent member of the American colony here received a demand for payment of the British income tax. His reply was prompt and to the point: "I am prepared to make a token payment of 10 percent in silver at 50 cents an ounce." He has not yet received a reply from the treasury.

PARIS, DEC. 20. (AP) — An American salesman and his wife and a naturalized Canadian couple were under arrest today, charged by the French police with heading an alleged espionage service reaching into the French ministry of marine itself. Ten arrests in all were made and the police said one other leader whom they did not name had escaped. The American salesman was described by police as Robert Switz, 28, born in East Orange, N. J. He was arrested without a fight and police said they believed him to be the chief of a band of ten persons, including five women, all of whom are held. The gendarmes said they found 19,000 francs in Switz’s room together with a number of military documents. They said others of the alleged ring were preparing to flee when they were caught in the round-up. Arrested with Switz was his wife, formerly Marjorie Tilley, 22, of New York. Another couple arrested were de

BERLIN, Dec. 20.—(UP)—Medical experts announced today that 400,000 persons, half of the men and half women, would be subjected to sterilization soon under the Nazi law for prevention of diseased progeny. Fifty per cent of those affected were said to be suffering from congenital feeble-mindedness. Total expenses of the sterilization were estimated at 14,000,000 marks ($5,264,000), costing 20 marks for each man and 50 for each woman.

HALIFAX, N. S., Dec. 16 (A.-- Rescue ships combed the graveyard of the Atlantic tonight in search of four men, believed to be adrift in a dory since their ship, the Gloucester fishing schooner Elien T. Marshall, burned to the water's edge off Cape Sable, N. S., yesterday, resulting in the death of at least three men. Three companions of the missing men drowned and 19 others had been saved. Eight of the latter were picked up by a Danish steamer while 11 had made shore by their own efforts after battling wind and sea for nearly 20 hours in open boats.

Paris, Dec. 16.—(4?)—Premier Mussolini's suggestion that the League of Nations should be reformed met with the answer from France, Poland, and the Little Entente today that the fundamentals of the league must not be tampered with. The Italian leader had asked for changes in the setup of the league in order to permit the entrance of Germany into international disarmament discussions; today’s developments indicated a united front opposing his suggestion. Would Mean War "Joseph Paul-Boncour, foreign secretary of France, and Dr. Edouard Benes, foreign secretary of Czechoslovakia and virtual spokesman for the other two countries in the Little Entente—Yugoslavia and Rumania—emerged from a series of conferences to declare that destruction of the League of Nations would open the doors to war.

Strengthening his economic recovery program, President F. D. Roosevelt has extended the re-employment agreement as well as concentrating various units of the national recovery agencies. Extension of the blanket codes for four months, continues to May, 1934, President Roosevelt has announced, and is designed to cover with temporary codes the 30 per cent of the nation’s industries which have not yet come under the permanent organization of the NRA. He said: “In the midst of winter and with many persons out of work it is essential that the new year should not bring with it any letdown in the recovery program in the trades and industries.” He established a policy of tying together under the direction of one leader, Frank C. Walker, the recovery machinery, including the NRA, the several farm rehabilitation agencies and the Home Loan Corporations.

GREENVILLE, Tex., Dec. 20. (4) — Two persons were trapped and lost their lives and four of six persons who jumped from a second-story window were injured today when fire destroyed the McBride hotel at Lone Oak. Clem Wilburn, 53, crippled operator of a shoe shop, and a blind man believed to be Dr. Roberts, who had been a guest at the hotel three weeks, were burned to death. Claudie Thompson, operator of a cafe on the ground floor of the building, said the fire started when he attempted to light an oil stove. An oil burner had been left on and oil had dripped on the floor.

(By the Associated Press) The man-in-the-street’s measuring rod of recovery—jobs and pay envelopes—went up Wednesday for a reading. From many centers where the clutch of joblessness has left its mark came evidence that part of the huge sums allotted by government and private enterprises and local relief groups was finding its way into needy purses. From other sectors the word was not glowing but nowhere, so far as news reports covering the entire country showed, was the outlook gloomy. Nowhere in the country does it appear any possibilities for making jobs are being overlooked. All sorts of work, from tooting an oompa-oompah in beer garden bands to serving as special traffic cops on coasting lanes, are finding ready applicants. Tools Scarce An actual scarcity of the trinity of tools emblematic of manual labor—picks, axes and shovels—has been found in North Carolina. Work that means jobs

1933-11-22.text: LONDON, Nov. 22 — (U.P) — King George, finishing a state speech to the new session of parliament yesterday, stood in his ermine robes before his throne and heard John McGovern, hot-headed Labor member of Commons, shout that those present were parasites, living on the suffering of the poor. "You are a gang of lazy, idle parasites, living on the wealth other people create," shouted McGovern. The King and Queen, the Queen in her famous crown jewels, were standing in front of their thrones. They looked straight ahead, ignoring the incident as the angry former plumber from Glasgow shouted his impromptu denunciation of the gathering. The King had revived both international and domestic affairs in his brief speech.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 22—(AP)—A price of $33.76 per ounce was fixed today for RFC purchases of newly mined gold, unchanged from yesterday. With the dollar again in a slump, this figure was below the world price of gold, $34.41 at London on a basis of sterling opening at $5.44 to the pound, The dollar later showed some improvement and recovered to $5.41, only to depreciate again to $5.45. The London gold price in dollars changed accordingly.

London, Nov, 21 (4)—The age-old pageant of regal splendor with which Parliament opened a new session reached an unexpectedly dramatic denouement in the cries of "Shame!" uttered by a Laborite member as King George ended his traditional speech from the throne. Before a throng of princes and diplomats, clad in ermine and gold, the Monarch pledged his Government's continued efforts to "promote and sustain by every means in their power peace in the world" and "promote a return of the nation step by step to conditions which will permit easing present burdens." "What about the means test and unemployment cuts?" cried the Laborite, J. McGovern, as His Majesty turned and offered his arm to Queen Mary, ignoring the shout. "You are a gang of lazy, idle parasites—living on wealth created by other people," McGovern shouted. "You ought to be ashamed of yourselves! It's a shame—all this, while people

MOSCOW, Nov. 22 (4)—Thirteen persons were reported killed in an airplane disaster today at Kharkov. The dead were reported to include the chief pilot and mechanic and several Kharkov aviation officials, but beyond these bare facts no details were given out. This is the second major aviation disaster in the Soviet Union in the past few months. Sept. 5 eight executives of the aviation industry were killed in a plane crash at Podolsk. Among the dead were three of Russia’s leading aviation figures. Six-Motored Ship The K-7 was a six-motored monoplane without the orthodox fuselage. Instead, all accommodations for luggage and fuel space as well as controls were in the wings. Only a slight framework of steel composed the structure on which the rudder was anchored. For Big Load The great airplane was designed to carry 128 persons including its crew. It was designed with sleeping accommodations f

GENEVA, Nov. 22. ()—The steering committee of the disarmament conference voted today to suspend the parley until January. In the meantime international diplomacy is to be given full play in its efforts to save the disarmament conference from oblivion and to bring Germany, which withdrew last month from the negotiations, back into the conversations. The committee unanimously accepted a statement by Arthur Henderson of Great Britain, president of the conference, which said there shall be "parallel and supplementary effort between the various states and the full use of diplomatic machinery conducted energetically to advance in every possible way the work of the conference." The committee decided that the governments concerned will keep Henderson informed as to the results of these diplomatic efforts and the president furthermore is to decide how far the work of the committee should be carri

MOSCOW, Nov. 22.—The world’s largest airplane, just completed, crashed at Kharkov yesterday, killing fourteen persons, according to dispatches reaching here today. Details of the accident were not available. The gigantic plane, named the K7, was an all-metal ship with six motors, and was built to carry 120 passengers.

Horta Azores, Nov. 22—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh who flew here yesterday from Lisbon planned to take off tomorrow for a return flight to the continent by way of the Island of St. Michael. Whether the return to the continent would preclude a projected flight back to the United States by way of Bermuda was not indicated.

PARIS. VH— Chancellor Hitler offered peace security to France Wednesday in an interview published in the newspaper La Matin. In return he asked equality for Germany which he said could be “realized by stages when details are talked over.” To give security to France, the chancellor said, he would “willingly do anything not involving dishonor or danger to my country.” He said he was convinced once the question of the Saar is settled, there is nothing which can oppose Germany to France.

1933-11-15.text: Valentia, Ireland, Nov. 15—(P)—Ships steamed today from all directions to assist the little British freighter Saxilby, whose crew of 27 men had taken to lifeboats after waging a losing battle against a storm 300 miles off the Irish coast. Leading the rescue efforts was the great liner Berengaria, regarded as one of the most important factors in the sea battle for life. Hearing the distress call from the little cargo ship, she changed her course and rushed at a speed of 20 knots toward the last reported position of the Saxilby. Nearer the Saxilby, but unable to aid, is another British freighter, the S. St. Quentin with her steering gear disabled. Her crew was working frantically to repair the damage but she asked some other ship to stand by until she could make repairs.

Valentia, Ireland.—(AP)— Battling a southeasterly gale on the Atlantic, two British steamers reported themselves in distress between 300 and 400 miles off this coast today. They were the Saxilby, a 3,630-ton vessel bound for Port Talbot, and the St. Quentin, a 3,528-ton ship bound from Swansea to Montreal. The American steamer Coelleda wirelessed around 11 o'clock this morning that she had got in touch with the Saxilby by wireless and that the Saxilby said she was trying to get her boats away. Nothing, however, was heard thereafter.

Landon, Nov. 15 (UP)!—A screeching northwesterly gale crashed across the north Atlantic from southern Ireland to mid-ocean today, endangering shipping, and left two British steamships in distress. The ships involved were the Saxilby, which was abandoned by her crew of 27, and the St. Quentin with a crew of 28. Both are freighters. Each of the ships was about 500 miles west of southern Ireland, the St. Quentin perhaps 160 miles north of the Saxilby.

LONDON, Nov. 14 (#)—The British government announced today it intended to build larger warships within the limits of the 1930 Naval Treaty, to meet the construction programs of the United States and Japan. This announcement was made in the House of Commons today by Sir Bolton Meredith Eyres Monsell, the first lord of the admiralty. He made the point that Japan and the United States were building bigger cruisers. He said the admiralty had revised its 1933 program to include two new type 9,000-ton cruisers with increased armament and one cruiser of the £200,000 Arethusa class and that revision had been made “following the most anxious consideration and with much regret.”

ABOARD THE U. S. CRUISER CHESTER, Off the California Coast, Nov. 15 (7)—The use of rigid dirigibles as an operating unit of the navy was put to test today when the world’s greatest skyship, the U. S. S. Macon, had its maiden experience with the United States fleet at sea in maneuvers. The Macon moved with a powerful high seas fleet, formed as a Blue force of superior power, moving in attack against the area between San Luis Obispo and San Diego. This area was defended by a fast-striking force of inferior power, designated as the Brown fleet. An airdrome of the clouds, rather than a scout, was the role of the Macon. Its eyes and its weapons were the airplanes the great skyship carries. The dirigible itself found its duty to lie in concealment. Not only were the Macon’s planes scouting and observation planes, but theoretically they were bombardment planes. Scouting and attack planes of the

ROME, Nov. 14 (UP).—Premier Benito Mussolini, abolishing at one stroke ancient Italian parliamentary system; today announced dissolution of the chamber of deputies, and the turning over of national legislative powers to a system of trade and commercial guilds. The guilds, through their central council, and embracing industry, labor and commerce, will replace the chamber in the new “corporate state” evolved by Mussolini on the foundations of Fascism. Mussolini's speech confirmed the setting up of a new political system. After reviewing the “history” of capitalism, which, he said, embraced three phases, the “dynamic, the static and the decadent,” and declaring that the rise of the cartel and trust from 1870 on marked the decline of the old system, Mussolini turned to modern life. “The United States,” he declared, “was the first nation to raise an insurmountable customs barrier, and she was

PARIS, Nov. 14—(?)—French fears of Chancellor Hitler's danger to peace were openly acknowledged by Joseph Paul-Boncour, minister of foreign affairs, in the chamber of deputies today. He declared German “exaltation” was “fraught with adventurous possibilities.” “It is perhaps,” he said, “a menace to European stability.”

Vienna, Nov. 14—(P)—United States Minister Earle warned today that American sympathy for Austria would be immediately forfeited if this country goes anti-Semitic. The diplomat said the United States looked sympathetically upon Austria's growth and independence and is anxious to help Austria in every way, but he cautioned against anti-Semitism. “Ninety-five per cent of all Americans,” he said, “are either fugitives from persecution or descendants of people who crossed the ocean because of religious or racial persecution. They cannot co-operate sympathetically with a country where people are persecuted on account of birth. He told newspapermen that he had communicated this friendly warning to representatives in all provinces of Austria during his recent motor tour and said: “I was assured that there was politically no anti-Semitism anywhere in Austria except Vienna.”

1933-04-25.text: By The Associated Press. LONDON, April 25.—Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain announced in presenting his budget to the House of Commons today that no provision will be made this year for war debt payments to the United States or for receipts from foreign debtors. This is the same policy Britain followed in last year’s budget. Special provision was necessary for the debt installment paid to the United States last December.

1. Former Premier Herriot of France, after conference with President Roosevelt, says enthusiastically that the latter laid down a complete program, including disarmament, world economic stabilization, and war debts. 2. President Roosevelt and Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain, who announced that their conversations had “admirably served” the purpose of mapping the territory to be covered at the world economic conference, plan final talk late today. 3. President Roosevelt, in talks with Premier Bennett of Canada, is expected to seek a pact for control of world wheat production. 4. Disarmament conference reopens at Geneva, buoyed by moral support afforded by economic conversations at Washington. 5. Opening date for the world economic conference is expected to be set by the organization committee which meets Saturday in London. 6. Senator Reed, Pennsylvania, leads Republican opposit

LONDON, April 25.—(U.R)—No provision for paying war debts to the United States are made in the current budget, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told the House of Commons today. Explaining the omission, Chamberlain said ‘it must be obvious’ that no figures on war debts ‘can be considered final,” indicating Britain's confidence in a coming revision. WOULD HAVE MATTERED Chamberlain said if it had not been for the Dec. 15 war debt payment of $95,550,000 which Britain met, there would have been a deficit for 1932-33 of only $12,705,000 (with the pound at $3.85) instead of $123,200,000 as at present. The Lausanne agreement, Chamberlain said, suspended certain reparations and war debts due to Britain. “They are at present in suspense,” he said. “Sooner or later a final settlement will be made which will determine their distribution as well as that of our debt to the United Stat

Washington, April 25.—(U.P)—Former Premier Herriot of France found President Roosevelt's conversational ability in French “so good that I was ashamed to try my few words of English.” Most of last night's conversations between the two were carried on in French without the use of an interpreter. The State Department assigned two interpreters to the White House for the occasion, but Mr. Roosevelt waved them aside. M. Herriot today said the president’s knowledge of French was equal to that of a very bright pupil after five years of study.

The Chancellor aroused cheers with a declaration that every member of the House, irrespective of party, earnestly prayed for the success of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's mission in Washington. He absolved the Washington government of charges that have been made by some commentators to the effect that America abandoned the gold standard for the purpose of arming itself with a bludgeon for the Roosevelt-MacDonald discussions. If the budget works out as Mr. Chamberlain anticipates, Britain will come through the year with a surplus of 1,291,000 pounds ($4,900,000). WASHINGTON, April 25, — A powerful movement to increase the use of silver as money and so augment the purchasing power of millions gained headway today in the American-French-British conversations. Vast reservoirs of the white metal lie stagnant in India, China and Mexico. Economists are seeking means of translating this silver into purchasing power for goods in a gold-famished world. If their recommendations are applied to America, millions of bills backed by gold would be withdrawn from circulation and replaced by silver dollars, half-dollars, quarters and dimes. The purpose of enlarging the use of silver would be two-fold: 1. To increase the demand for it and so raise both its market price and purchasing power. 2. To relieve the strain on gold. The world has only $11,600,000,000 worth of the yellow metal. Economists consider the supply inadequate to the needs of international business

War debts, reciprocal trade agreements and silver monetization proposals assumed places of prominence today in the economic discussions between President Roosevelt and representatives of Great Britain, France and Canada. While it became apparent that France would not oppose a bi-metal monetary standard, it was learned that Canada is prepared to discuss reciprocal commercial agreements with the United States. In connection with the American inflation program, an amendment proposing an $8,000,000,000 silver certificate issue at a ratio of 33 to 1 with gold was revealed in Congress. Bi-partisan support was being sought. Conferences of American, British, and French experts on world economic affairs continued. President Roosevelt, Prime Minister MacDonald and Former Premier Herriot will join this evening in their first three-cornered discussion of the current international series. Prime Minis

President Roosevelt and Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain jointly announced ‘deep satisfaction’ with the results of their conversations. Former Premier Edouard Herriot of France began his formal talk with the president in the evening, with a separate meeting also arranged between Herriot and MacDonald. At the American capital arrived, also Richard B. Bennett, premier of Canada, who will be a White House guest upon MacDonald's departure. Credit Inflation While the statesmen conferred the senate went deeper into the sharp-edged debate on the pending bill for American credit and currency inflation. In New York, Chicago, New Orleans and elsewhere, financial and commodity markets continued their upward march, wheat, cotton and scores of stocks hitting new highs for the year. 1933-05-31.text: Epsom Downs, Eng. May 31.—(/P) Lord Derby’s Hyperion, the second choice at 100 to 11 today, won the 150th running of the English Derby today before a crowd of 250,000 including the king and queen. King Salmon carrying the silks of Sir H. Cunliffe Owen was second and the Victor Emmanuel’s American owned Statesman third. Twenty-four ran. Hyperion ridden by Tommie Weston gave Lord Derby his third victory in the event founded by his ancestors in 1780. The last time he won was in 1924. Scarlet Tiger owned by Lord Durham was fourth. Hyperion finished four lengths in front of King Salmon. Another length separated Statesman from King Salmon. King Salmon was reported 7 to 1 in the betting.

LONDON, May 31 (AP)--The Roosevelt administration's intention of being a “good neighbor,” as expressed by Ambassador Robert W. Bingham in a Memorial Day address, was hailed today as presaging a new era of Anglo-American co-operation. Mr. Bingham, speaking before the Pilgrim's Society, reviewed ‘the phenomenal recovery” in the United States since President Roosevelt's inauguration, and maintained that “this indefinitely enlarges the influence which the United States has to offer on behalf of world peace and world recovery.” Warm approval was expressed in British newspapers. “I believe that civilization, as we have known and enjoyed it, cannot exist much longer unless burdens which oppress mankind are lifted soon,” the ambassador said. “In this, the great crisis in human history, I repeat I believe the foundation of hope of our world lies in whole-hearted, concerted action between Great Br
Washington — Senator La Follette of Wisconsin, like Senator Johnson of California, has declined an invitation to serve on the American delegation to the London economic conference.

WASHINGTON, May 30.—(/)— President Roosevelt tonight announced a delegation of six men for the London economic conference and a staff of advisers and experts to carry out his program. Ralph W. Morrison of San Antonio, Texas, was named by the president as the sixth man to fill out the delegation. Others previously named include Secretary Hull, chairman; James M. Cox, former governor of Ohio, vice chairman; Chairmen Pittman and (Continued on Page 2, Col. 2.)

KPSOM DOWNS, England, May 31. - Lord Derby's Hyperion won the 150th running of the historic derby today before a roaring crowd of some 80,000 persons, among them the king and queen. Sir Hugo Cunliffe-Owen's King Salmon was second. The American-owned Statesman, owned by Victor Emanuel, was third and Lord Durham's Scarlet Tiger was fourth. The stirring test of approximately a mile and a half over the ups and downs and turns of the difficult course was run over a hard track and under ideal weather conditions. The Prince of Wales and Prince George arrived a few minutes before the start. Lord Derby's victory was the third for the house of Stanley, which founded the race. The 12th Earl of Derby won it in 1787, eight years after the inaugural. The present Lord Derby won it with Sansovino in 1924. Hyperion proved himself far superior to his field, winning by four lengths in an easy canter.

LONDON—May 31—(UP)—Hopeful of achieving a four power agreement for restriction in wheat acreage before the world economic conference, June 12, representatives of the United States, Argentina, Australia and Canada, began negotiations here today under the chairmanship of Henry Morgenthau, Jr. An acreage restriction of considerably more than 10 per cent is the aim of the United States, it was reported reliably. A stiff fight is ahead, however, to gain the approval of Canada and Australia for a reduction of even a little as 10 per cent for two years. Chances were considered fair for some sort of acreage agreement before the world economic conference. All delegates agreed to the utmost secrecy so far as the press is concerned.

LONDON (U.P.)——The Prince of Wales and the new United States ambassador, Robert W. Bingham, joined in heralding the end of America’s policy of isolation in speeches at a Pilgrims society dinner Tuesday night. Speaking publicly for the first time since his arrival in England, Bingham said the United States was prepared to lower tariffs and join in political cooperation with other nations. Toasting Bingham, the Prince of Wales said: “I believe that in the midst of this great catastrophe, Americans realize with us that under the economic system now existing no country can prosper in isolation. The difficulties through which we are passing are showing us our dependence on others. If the present suffering has the effect of bringing home to us the evils of economic nationalization it will be a blessing in disguise.” Bingham said: “Americans have learned the fallacy of the belief that the highe

Epsom Downs, Eng, May 31 — For the third time in the history of the Earls of Derby, those who started the world's famous turf event 150 years ago, the English Derby Wednesday was won by Lord Derby. His horse, Apsley, backed at 6 to 1, caused his silks to a record-breaking victory over 23 of Britain's finest thoroughbreds, a crowd of 250,000 including the Queen cheering him to victory in one and one-half minutes in 2:34 2-5 seconds, which is 2 seconds faster than the record made by Blue Bonnet in 1927 and equalled the closing year by Pelican. The race was worth to the winner £10,000 (about $50,000). King Salmon carrying the silks of Sir H. C. Fetherstonhaugh was second, the winner Emanuel's American-bred statesman third, and Scarlet Taper fourth.

1933-07-05.text: WASHINGTON, July 4—(AP)— President Roosevelt tonight cabled fresh instructions to the American delegation at the London economic conference to put forth every effort to keep the parley going. Returning to the White House from his two weeks' vacation cruise, Mr. Roosevelt took up immediately the latest reports from the troubled economic parley. He decided to send a message to the American conferees and the new instructions were coded and dispatched through the navy department. It was said authoritatively that Mr. Roosevelt had every confidence that the conference would not break up and that the American delegation would act to keep it in progress. The text of the Roosevelt cable was not disclosed and it was reiterated that any news regarding the conference must come from London. The president’s confidence in a continuation of the struggling conference became known even as the most pessimi

WASHINGTON, July 5 aM President Roosevelt, plunging into the task of his office again after a seagoing vacation, indicated today he was confident that the London economic conference would survive its present impasse. At the same time, it was made clear that the president intends to stand unflinchingly by his decision not to enter a stabilization agreement at this time and intends to follow a three point currency program: 1.--The United States is not ready to export gold 2. It is not ready to enter into agreements looking to the creation of a stabilization fund. 3. It is not ready for a stabilization fund. The president's opinion over the future of the conference was in contrast to the gloom prevailing at London. He appeared hopeful of success of the world meeting after holding a significant trans-Atlantic conversation shortly before noon with Secretary of State Hull, a delegation he

Washington, July 8.—(7)—President Roosevelt Wednesday put his every ounce of force behind the domestic recovery campaign after transmitting the American delegation to strive for continuance of the London economic conference. Back in the White House from more than two weeks on the open seas, the vacation-rested president immediately studied pessimistic reports from London and requests for fresh instructions. Before going to bed Tuesday night he dispatched a message telling the delegation to use every means to keep the deadlocked party going. There was, however, no intimation at the White House of any modification in his stand against immediate stabilization of currencies. That was the stand which provoked gold-bloc nations to move for quick adjournment of the conference. Cabinet officers got calls to report Wednesday to the president. LONDON, July 5.—(U.P)—Delegates representing the United States, Canada, Australia, and Argentina today reached agreement in principle on a "policy of temporary adjustment" to raise wheat prices. The text of a communique issued by the "big four" delegates was: "The four overseas wheat exporting countries—Argentina, Australia, Canada and the United States—today agreed in principle on a policy of temporary adjustment of production and trade to world demand, with the view of improving the price of wheat and liquidating the surplus stocks now hanging over the market. "They recognize, however, that a solution of the wheat problem depends upon the co-operation of European countries." It was rumored that the agreement provided for a 15 percent reduction of acreage for two years, or a reduction of exports 15 percent for two years. But it was said officially that it was not necessary at this time

St. Andrews, Scotland. July 3. (P) - Walter Hagen, the American veteran who has won the British crown four times, today shot into the lead with a spectacular 68, five under par, for the first round of the British Open golf championship. His total was only a stroke short of the course record set by William (Pat) Nolan, Irish pro, in the qualifying competition, and he took the lead from Cyril J. H. Tolley, British amateur, who had a 70 for his first round. — Sarazen trailed Hagen today by four strokes, shooting a 72.

LONDON, July 5.—(?)—The American delegates had been in telephonic communication with Washington this afternoon, the impression prevailed in important American quarters that the major part of the world economic conference would recess this week, leaving committees to carry on the technical work, possibly at Geneva. In some delegation quarters it was believed that the movement to recess could be blocked in the plenary session of the parley but that there was no point in trying to continue the full conference until the world monetary situation became easier. The steering committee of the conference was scheduled to meet tomorrow morning to act on the proposal for adjournment submitted yesterday by Hendryk Colijn, prime minister of Holland.

LONDON, (P)—"Revaluation of the dollar in terms of American commodities is an end from which the government and the people of the United States cannot be diverted," said a statement issued tonight by the American delegation at the world monetary and economic conference. The statement was handed to the secretary-general of the League of Nations in explanation of President Roosevelt's monetary stand. Temporary currency stabilization, the communique continued, would be "artificial and unreal."

1933-07-16.text: ROME, —O)— The four-power European peace pact was signed here today by Premier Mussolini and representatives of France, Germany and Great Britain. The accord which is designed to guarantee tranquility among European nations for 10 years facilitates reduction of armaments and leads in improvement of economic conditions. The instruments were given official approval of the four powers in Il Duce’s huge office in Palazzo Venezia.

LONDON, July 1. (UP) —The United States favors indefinite adjournment of the world economic conference, it was said authoritatively today. Delegates were said to feel that to fix a specific date for reassembling after the recess to be taken July 27 would be putting indirect pressure on the United States to stabilize its currency by whatever date named, This, it was said, would interfere with the government's determination on a domestic recovery program, It had been said previously that the United States favored adjournment to a definite date. It was said also the delegation had asked President Roosevelt for rush instructions whether he intended to institute a “commodity dollar” with a sliding gold content or go back on the gold standard. Unless he committed himself, it was said, then there was danger that the conference might adjourn for good, Today it was understood that the president h

London, July 15.—(AP)—The United States today made last-minute preparations to save something of its tariff truce and world price-raising program as the world economic conference moved toward the final fortnight’s work. With prospects of the salvage of important results regarded in some quarters as meager, however, the American delegation had entered its discussions of a separate movement of several Western Hemisphere nations to try to form a new world economic bloc. It was reliably reported in Latin-American circles that Ralph W. Morrison of the American delegation had participated in discussions exploring the prospect of a joint agreement of several American nations to grant mutual trade concessions, possibly along the lines of the Ottawa agreement between Great Britain and the Dominions. PARIS, July 15. (7) — Jeanette MacDonald, film actress, accepted an apology today in place of the $8,000 damages she sought from Andre Ranson, a French magazine writer, on a charge of defamation of character. The suit resulted from the account of an imaginary interview with Miss MacDonald appearing in a weekly magazine, Fantasie.
Torbay, Newfoundland, July 15—Wiley Post, American round-the-world flier, passed seaward from here on his flight toward Europe this afternoon.

NEW YORK, July 15.—Capt. F. L. Sears went down with his burning ship, the tanker Citgo Service Petrol, in the Atlantic off Wilmington, N. C., last night, while two other American merchant ships stood by and rescued 34 members of the crew. Two other men went down with Captain Sears. They were reported killed aboard before the ship sank. One was an engine wiper, George Binninger. The name of the other was not immediately available. The rescue ships were the tanker Gulf Gem and the steamer Tri-Mountain. The Gulf Gem saved 24 members of the Petrol crew and the Tri-Mountain 10. Immediately after the Petrol sank, enveloped in flames with Captain Sears alive and at his post, the Gulf Gem turned off her course to put in with the survivors, some of whom were injured, at Charleston, S. C. It was presumed the Tri-Mountain accompanied her.

NEW YORK, July 15. (®)—Wiley Post, bound around the world for a second time, was racing across the Atlantic tonight with two Lithuanian fliers who hopped off at dawn from their native land without governmental sanction. Post, confident of shattering the world record of 8 days, 15 hours and 51 minutes which he and Harold Gatty set two summers ago, left Floyd Bennett field in his pursuit of white monoplane, Winnie of Oklahoma, at 4:10 a.m. In Berlin Sunday A plane believed to be that of the stocky Oklahoma City aviator was reported at 1:10 p.m. heading out over the Atlantic from Torbay, Newfoundland. He is due in Berlin, his first scheduled stop, between 5 a.m. and noon tomorrow. The Lithuanians, Stephen Darius and Stanley Girenas of Chicago, made a surprise start in their orange and black monoplane at 5:24 a.m., an hour and 14 minutes after Post had taken off. FLOYD BENNETT FIELD, N. Y. (UP)—Two flying teams hopped off on transatlantic flights Saturday, one heading for Berlin on the first leg of a round-the-world race, the other steering a course to Kaunas, Lithuania. Wiley Post, with a robot pilot as his companion, set out in the famous plane Winnie Mae in an attempt to lower the record of eight days, 15 hours, 51 minutes for an around the world flight he set with Harold Gatty two years ago. His first planned stop was Berlin, thence on to Novosibirsk, Russia; Khabarovsk, Russia; Fairbanks, Alaska; Edmonton, Alberta, and New York. Post hoped to complete the flight in six days. The Lithuanian team, Captain Stephen Darius and Stanley T. Girenas, began their flight without official permission and faced the possibility of losing their licenses as a result. 1933-07-02.text: London, July 3—President Roosevelt, seizing confident personal leadership of the world economic conference, told in a telegram published today by Secretary of State Cordell Hull, what he is trying to do for America and the world. Explaining forcefully and frankly why the United States would not endanger its price raising efforts in order to join Europe in stabilizing currencies, the president said: “The old fetishes of so-called international bankers are being replaced by efforts to plan national currencies with the objective of giving those currencies continuing purchasing power which does not greatly vary in terms of commodities and the need of modern civilization. “Let me be frank in saying the United States seeks the kind of dollar which a generation hence will have the same purchasing and debt paying power as the dollar value we hope to attain in the near future,” he declared. “That

B., July 1, (PP) President Roosevelt started back from his vacation cruise today aboard the trim cruiser Indianapolis, with his thoughts again turning to work and more particularly to the London economic conference. Before boarding the new 10,000 ton fighting ship of the American fleet late this afternoon, the presi- dent made it definitely known that he has sanctioned no formal agree- ment at London on stabilization of currency. Not Ready Very apparently, Mr. Roosevelt is watching closely the troubled econ- omic parley just as apparently he is not ready to enter any compact on currency stabilization just now — the demand of the gold bloc headed by France. LONDON, July 1.—Great Britain and Soviet Russia patched up their immediate differences tonight with the result that both countries canceled their trade embargoes and the two British engineers held in prison at Moscow were released. The peace agreement came after consultations between Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and the Soviet diplomats, Jean Maisky, ambassador at London, and Maxim Litvinov, foreign commissar. The embargo on Russian goods coming into British ports was laid down April 19, the day after the two British engineers were found guilty by a Moscow court of espionage and sabotage. Three of the British engineers were expelled from Russia but L. C. Thornton and W. L. MacDonald were sentenced to three and two years imprisonment, respectively.

CHICAGO, July 1—(4)—Kidnappers held ‘Jake the Barber' Factor captive tonight for a reported $150,000 ransom after a bold pre-dawn coup of international complications that echoed the downfall of the Al Capone dynasty. The erstwhile bootblack and barber on Chicago’s west side—who is wanted in England on charges of a $7,000,000 stock fraud—was seized from an automobile near a suburban gambling inn early today. His wife and his son, Jeronie, as well as a group of friends in other automobiles, saw a sextet of heavily armed men. (Continued on Page 8, Col. 3.)

LONDON—The chief European gold countries issued a joint statement today confirming their “firm intention” of remaining on the gold standard at the present gold parities. The statement was signed by the French, Belgians, Dutch, Italians, Polish and Swiss. The statement said each government would demand that its central bank remain in close cooperation with the central banks of the others to ensure a maximum effectiveness of their gold standard policies. Designed as a reply to President Roosevelt's monetary message, the statement was signed by the representatives of the six gold governments after a conference at the headquarters of the Italian delegation, to which Finance Minister Guido Jung hurried by airplane from Londonderry.

AERRY, were gee AMSTERDAM, July 1 (®)—Tragedy marked the arrival here today of the Italian air armada of 25 seaplanes en route to Chicago. One of the ships capsized on striking the water, resulting in the death of Sergeant Quintavelle and the injury of three other members of the crew. General Balbo, the youthful bearded leader of the squadron, and his companions were much disturbed at the loss of life. Shortly after midnight, however, he talked with attaches of the meteorological institute of Holland and then ordered the pilots to be ready to leave their hotel at 5 a.m. (11 p.m. E.S.T. Saturday), for Londonderry, Ireland, forty minutes later. The commander of the ill-fated craft, Flight Lieutenant Baldini, was stated to be suffering from concussion. BERLIN, Germany.— (UP) — Wolff's (German) Agency Saturday night published an official statement denying that Chancellor Adolf Hitler had joined the new National Protestant church after abandoning his Roman Catholic faith. The Wolff's announcement read: “In the entire world reports have been circulated that Chancellor Hitler has joined the Evangelical church. These are a fantasy and lies. Hitler belongs now, as previously, to the Catholic church and has no intention of leaving it.” The announcement spread rapidly through German church circles and Protestant authorities wondered if the head of the government in embracing Protestantism would also claim the title of summus episcopus—head bishop—which was the ka

My The Associated Press : MUNICIPAL AIRPORT, LOS ANGELES, July 1.—Rocketing westward from New York, Colonel Roscoe Turner, veteran racing pilot of Hollywood, won the cross-country dash of the national air races today with a time of 11 hours, 30 minutes. Half an hour behind him came Jimmie Wedell, the New Orleans plane designer and speed pilot, to take second place. Turner's flight broke his own record by 1 hour 3 minutes, and was 33 minutes ahead of the Pacific coast pilot set last fall. In the wake of these two were four other fliers, one the trans-Atlantic pilot, Amelia Earhart, all forced out of the grueling race. One, Russell Boardman, holder of the American long distance flying record set in a flight from New York to Istanbul, lay in an Indianapolis hospital, seriously injured by the crash of his ship. 1933-02-08.text: LONDON, Feb. 8—Payment in a lump sum of 100,000,000 pounds (about $399,000,000 at current exchange), to the United States in full and final settlement of Great Britain's war debt was proposed today in the House of Commons. This payment would include the $95,000,000 paid last December 15. The proposal was advanced by Geoffrey Mander, a liberal. He made it in an indirect manner in the form of a question to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, so as to conform to parliamentary procedure. Mr. Mander asked whether the Chancellor would consider the advisability of such a proposal.

CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa, Feb. 8.—(4)—The British fliers, Squadron Leader O. R. Gayford and Flight Lieutenant G. ib Nicholeets, landed at Walfish Bay at 4:40 p. m. (10:40 a. m., E. T.) today after setting a new long-distance non-stop record. They beat the American long distance mark established by Russell Boardman and Jean Polando by more than 300 miles. They were in the air 57 hours and 2 minutes.

By Associated Press One British plane set a new world flying record, another cracked up in an attempt to beat a lesser mark and a third was still apparently in the running today for another record. The two-year-old mark for a straight line, non-stop hop, set by the Americans, Russell Boardman, and John Polando, fell as the British officers, O. R. Gayford and G. E. Nicholetts, neared the end of a 6,198 mile two-day marathon from Cramwell, England to Cape Town, South Africa. Captain J. A. Mollison, the only aviator to span the north Atlantic alone from east to west, was last reported resting at Thies, Senegal on the west coast of Africa, on his projected flight from near London to Natal, Brazil. Victor Smith, young South American, failed in his attempt to beat Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison’s record for the England-South Africa flight by stages, when his plane cracked up today in landing at Ora

Capetown, South Africa, Feb. 8. (UP)—Two British Royal Air Force fliers brought their big monoplane down at Walvis Bay, on the west coast of Africa 800 miles north of Capetown today, after setting a new world’s straight-line distance record on a flight from London. Squadron Leader Oswald R. Gayford and Flight Lt. Gilbert F. Nicholetts, who left Cranwell Airdrome, England, on Monday at 7:15 a.m. g.m.t., landed at Walvis Bay at 4:40 p.m. today after a flight of approximately 5,175 miles without a stop. They thus exceeded by 163 miles (unofficial figures)—the previous record of 5,012 miles set by Russell Boardman and John Polando on their flight from the United States to Istanbul, Turkey, in 1931.

London, Feb. 17.--(4?)-- The case of the mysterious prisoner in the Tower of London is exciting such public interest that the government is to be asked in the House of Commons next week to make a public announcement concerning him. This evening the war department disclosed that the prisoner is Lieutenant N. Baillie-Stewart of the Seaforth Highlanders. The statement said he probably will be court-martialed early next month. The charges against him were not specified. (A dispatch from London last week said it was understood that an officer of the Seaforth Highlanders had been imprisoned, allegedly for violation of the Official Secrets Act. Most of the officers of the Seaforth Highlanders hold high social rank, and the organization is known as one of the most proud in the empire's service.)

London, Feb. 7.—(AP)—After the “big five” of the cabinet and Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador to the United States, had completed a preliminary survey of the debt problem today, it was learned that suggestions that a lump sum between $1,250,000,000 and $2,000,000,000 be paid to the United States contemplated that this payment would cover all European war debts and not merely Britain's. Such a lump sum, it was said in authoritative quarters, would mean scaling down the war debts in accordance with the reparations policy adopted at the Lausanne conference, which virtually ended reparations payments from Germany. The total European debt to the United States was funded at more than $11,000,000,000. - LONDON, Feb. 7.—(AP)—Four fliers—three of them British and the other a young South African—were well on their way tonight toward record-breaking goals. Victor Smith, 19 years old, started from Southampton at 7:10 a.m. (2:10 a.m. e.s.t.) today in an attempt to beat Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison’s time for the England-to-Cape Town flight. He has a “stiff job” before him, he said, and, if he succeeds, he intends to settle down and work in his father’s factory. LONDON, Feb. 8 — A majority of the British parliament favors an indefinite moratorium on war debts owed the United States, including the June 15 payment, the political correspondent of the Daily Mail indicated today. The moratorium would not involve a return to the gold standard or tariff concessions to the United States, the Daily Mail said. The following three courses of action were said to have been discussed by members of the cabinet and the ambassador to Washington, Sir Ronald Lindsay: An indefinite moratorium. Capitalization of the war debt in a lump sum to be decided on through negotiations with the United States. The parliamentary majority was said to oppose flat default and to favor a moratorium beginning June 15, if the forthcoming negotiations at Washington have not resulted in a debt agreement by that time. 1933-09-25.text: VHAPARRA, Cuba, Sept. 25 (P) - American officials of the Chaparra sugar mill sought safety today in the yacht club, near American destroyer Hamilton and a British freighter anchored in Puerto Padre Bay, as a general strike spread through most of the province. A small party of United States marines landed Sunday at Puerto Padre to obtain supplies, and after returned to the destroyer. Workers and soldiers stood guard at the Chaparra and Deli mills and other properties. There was no violence, but strikers cut wires of the Chaparra telephone and power company, plunging more than ten towns into darkness.

PASADENA, Cal., Sept. 25.—Creation of matter as a visible process was foreseen today by scientists at the California Institute of Technology. Researches here and by scientists at Cambridge, England, indicate that pure motion has been transformed into solid matter through the medium of radium, it was said. The experiments have been photographed. Physicians explained that their observations indicate that a fast-traveling radium ray can be converted into two electrical particles, one the negatively charged electron, the other the positively charged positron. When the conversion is completed, virtually no motion of the original ray remains. The electron and the positron, on a recent discovery of science, compose the essence of all matter, the basic substance of creation, scientists say. Glasgow, Sept. 23.— (AP) —Governor Frank H. Cooney will ask the public works administration for a state loan of between $5,000,000 and $10,000,000 to be used in constructing about 500 small irrigation dams in Montana, he announced here today. The state, the governor said, will loan the money to individuals for the small projects. Governor Cooney, State Engineer J. S. James and State Relief Director T. C. Spaulding are en route to Washington to present to the administration plans for building 164 flood control and irrigation projects costing about $42,828,000. The party toured the Fort Peck dam and reservoir site area this afternoon. Governor Cooney will ask approval of a $60,000,000 loan to construct the dam across the Missouri River at Fort Peck while he is in Washington. The chief executive expressed himself as being enthusiastically in favor of the project and said that the members of

NEW YORK, 5. (P)-- New York has definitely taken the lead away from London as the world's leading market for silver. Active speculation in this metal has within the past few days boosted the price to within the highest level in more than three years. Buying here has been so insistent that New York prices have recently gone to a substantial premium over London. Were this premium to widen somewhat, it would undoubtedly swell the already large imports of the metal. Although thus far it has not been large enough to leave a profit of payment of freight and insurance across the Atlantic. Having touched 10% cents an ounce at the end of last week (with futures nominally quoted as high as 43 cents), the long-negotiated restoration in price of silver bullion has made marked progress since last December when it touched 24.4 cents, the lowest in history. Dr. Mowinckel, president of the League council, declared further that the four-power peace pact recently signed by Germany, Italy, France and Britain can aid considerably in a “torn and divided Europe, where liberty of thought and personal liberty are not everywhere secure.” Another surprise was occasioned by the election of Charles te Water, South African high commissioner in London, to be president of the assembly. He defeated Francisco Castillo Najera of Mexico. The election of Najera, former president of the League council, had generally been forecast since there was no other candidate until today when during a recess Scandinavian delegates proposed te Water. (By United Press). Geneva, Sept. 25.—The United States dollar was barred as a medium of exchange by the League of Nations today in carrying on League work. The League’s supervisory commission ruled against the League paying out contributions in American dollars because of the loss entailed in conversion of Swiss francs.

Geneva, Sept. 25 (UP) — The League of Nations met today for its 14th assembly. Joseph Goebbels, German minister of propaganda, his safety assured by a heavy Nazi guard, prepared to defend his country against attacks and demand that Germany be permitted to rearm if her neighbors did not disarm themselves. Goebbels arrived by airplane last night. At the airport his bodyguard presented him with an armful of roses. Countering Goebbels was chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss of Austria, anti-Nazi, who said his principal concern was to defend Austria's position if anyone raised the Nazi question. He visited Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, to discuss the attitude to be taken when Goebbels raises the armament problem. He was expected to confer with Norman H. Davis, American disarmament delegate.

LENINGRAD, Russia (UP)—Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh left in their seaplane at 2:39 p.m., Monday for Moscow, planning to make a dangerous landing in the Moscow River. The flight is one of 400 miles. Lindbergh was warned by Russian aviators that the river was not suitable for a landing. He replied that he would try it, and fly back here if he found a landing practicable.

1933-10-08.text: LONDON, Oct. 7.—UPI—Postponement of the world disarmament conference was considered today while European statesmen faced a crisis brought about by a German demand for armament equality with other powers. So serious was the situation that some statesmen speculated on the possibility of the conference adjourning in failure with an armament race and the threat of a catastrophic war on the background. In view of the new emergency, it was thought Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy might invite the premiers of Great Britain, France and Germany to a conference in northern Italy. The British cabinet will meet Monday to consider its policy.

Campbelton Harbor, Scotland, Oct. 8 (*)—Two seamen were fatally injured and 14 others seriously hurt by a terrific explosion followed by fire aboard the submarine L-26 today. Of those injured, five suffered from poisonous gases. The members of the crew, who had just taken their places in the mess room for the midday meal, were thrown in all directions by the blast, originating in the adjacent battery room. Authorities believe the blast was caused by water reaching the batteries, which were being recharged, through a hole in the hull. The submarine had reached the landlocked area after being grounded five hours yesterday evening on the rocks at Kintyre peninsula.

LONDON, Oct. 7. (AP)— Death cast an unexpected shadow today over the colorful ceremony of the changing of the guard at Buckingham Palace—witnessed by thousands of American tourists annually, as an automobile out of control crashed into the throng of spectators, injuring three men fatally and four others seriously. With a crash heard within earshot, F. H. Hills, 45, apparently sideswiped another machine and careened full tilt into the crowd. With Hills slumped over the wheel, the automobile finally came to a stop after snapping off a lamp post. Amid mingled with the strains of a lively tune a band was playing while the ceremony continued through the chaos as relief was rushed to the injured. All the dead were aircraftsmen from the Royal Air Force station at Andover. The three, sightseeing in London, were Aircraftsman Marsh, killed outright or at least so seriously injured he died in an am

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Sept. 8. —(4)—The party of former President William T. Cosgrave voted unanimously today to merge with the center party and the national guard, forming the United Ireland party. This fusion would bring together the opposition to President de Valera. The national guard, led by General Eoin O'Duffy, has been the center of considerable conflict in the Free State recently, as it has been accused by the de Valera government of seeking to establish a dictatorship, and on this ground has been outlawed.

SOUTHAMPTON, England, Oct. 7 (P)—Professor Albert Einstein sailed for New York tonight on the liner Western Land with his wife, who had embarked at Antwerp. The couple is en route to Princeton, N. J., where Dr. Einstein will carry out scientific studies and lecture. Special precautions were taken by the steamship officials to prevent possible trouble as the physicist embarked. Einstein recently went to England from Belgium after a Nazi organization was alleged to have put a price upon his head.
