He made the accusation in an address directed to the American people, speaking in English. “Certain financial interests in the United States are unfriendly—they are sworn enemies of our people—and they are engaged in a campaign of destruction, issuing false propaganda and fighting us step by step.” President Grau said, “They have been at the back of our army problem, just solved under unfortunate circumstances. You know these American interests. They have also brought havoc to their own fellow citizens and yours.

PARIS. (U.P)—Herman P. Behn, president and co-founder of the International Telephone & Telegraph Corp., died today at Saint Jean de Luz. He had been critically ill for weeks and was 53 years old. Behn and his brother, Sosthenes, founded the international system after a sensational rise in business. Interests of the corporation are in the United States, Mexico, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Spain, China and other places, including Postal Telegraph and Cable Co. and all American cables.

BERLIN, Oct. 7 —(P— The ministry of justice in a detailed memorandum explaining the Nazi aims concerning the German penal code today announced its intention to authorize physicians to end the tortures of incurable patients. The memorandum, still lacking the force of law, proposed that “it shall be made possible for physicians to end the tortures of incurable patients upon request, in the interests of true humanity.” This proposed legal recognition of euthanasia, or the method of peaceful death, raised a number of fundamental problems of a religious, scientific and legal nature. The Catholic newspaper Germania hastened to observe: ‘to accept this method of shortening the sufferings of incurables who are tormented by pain.” In Lutheran circles, too, life is considered something which God alone can take. A large section of the German people, it was expected in some interested circles, might

1933-11-13.text: LONDON, Nov. 18. ()—British treasury officials, says the Daily Mail, are beginning to think President Roosevelt was bluffing about buying gold abroad. They think, inasmuch as no trace of gold purchases by the President can be found, that he merely was relying on the psychological effect of a bluff to depreciate the dollar, the Mail added.

BERLIN, Nov. 13 (#)—Adolf Hitler was armed with the almost unanimous support of his people today to press his bold drive toward a new deal for Germany. More than 90 per cent of the qualified voters cast ballots in yesterday's Reichstag election and foreign policy plebiscite and well over 90 per cent of those electors rang up a resounding “ja” (yes) for the chancellor and his program. Today the entire nation joined in a celebration of the event hailed by Nazi party leaders as a “miracle of Germany becoming one people.” No sooner had the result been indicated than propaganda Minister Goebbels, whose work figured large in the big turnout at the polls, called for a day-long demonstration. Reichstag Also Friendly Jubilant Nazis saw Hitler increase the party following from 17 to 40 million voters as they contrasted yesterday’s results with the elections of last March 5. Besides, he got another

Moscow, Nov. 13 (#)—Japanese imperialists are charged with creating an armed base in Manchukuo in a manifesto issued by the far eastern section of the Communist party, Warning that Russia is prepared to act quickly in the event of Japanese attempts of aggression in the Far East, the manifesto said: "Our airfleet is prepared to deal decisive blows at enemy centers of population. With such an array of terrible armament, the Soviet Union would readily kill any desire to compete against our program of peaceful labor." Issued Nov. 1—two days before Russia protested to Tokyo against the alleged flight of Japanese army planes over Soviet territory—the manifesto emphasized Russia's desire for peace. But, it added, Japan will lay herself open to "immeasurable catastrophe" if her imperialists put their policies into effect. As this manifesto, newest development in extended differences, was discuss

Madrid, Nov. 13—(7)—Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh landed safely today near Candelas De Tuy, province of Pontevedra on a flight across Spain. Original reports were that the American fliers, who took off from Santona, Spain, for Portugal, had been forced down near the little village at the foot of the mountains. The province of Pontevedra is one of the most mountainous in Spain. Its woody heights are still the haunts of wolves and wild boars although the country about Candelas De Tuy is regarded as a perfect garden of vineyards and dairy farming. The ruins of abbeys and castles, hundreds of years old, are among the famous antiques of the province. Despite its picturesque delights, however, the area is not extremely well supplied with communication facilities.

Berlin, Nov. 13,—Overwhelming endorsement of Chancellor Hitler’s foreign policies and the Nazi regime came in returns from the German election yesterday in what was obviously the largest vote in the history of the nation. The final vote, as reported by Woli’s agency, showed well over 90 per cent of the ballots in favor of Nazi political domination and an even larger proportion of “yeses” on the national plebiscite. The final vote exceeded 90 per cent of the qualified electors, which numbered 45,106,168. The vote count stood: For the Nazi slate of candidates in the Reichstag: 39,621,437 or 92.2 per cent; invalid votes, 3,845,125 or 7.8 per cent; total 42,969,562. In the plebiscite: ‘Yes,’ 40,583,430 or 93.5 per cent; “No,” 2,052,100 or 4.7 per cent; invalid 789,999 or 1.8 per cent; total 43,425,529. BERLIN, (UP)—Flags flew through Germany Monday in celebration of a victory at the polls for Chancellor Adolf Hitler and his Nazis that was expected to have important repercussions on internal politics and German foreign policy. Nearly 44,000,000 Germans turned out afoot, on bicycles, in motor cars to jam cafes, restaurants and other polling places to vote approval of Hitler’s withdrawal from the League of Nations and disarmament conference and to elect 660 Nazi candidates to a one-party Reichstag. The final official vote was: Plebiscite: 43,439,046 voted, for withdrawal: 40,588,804 (93.5 percent); against withdrawal: 2,100,181 (4.8 percent); spoiled ballots: 750,061 (1.7 percent). Reichstag: 42,975,009 voted. For Nazi candidates: 39,626,647 (92.8 percent); spoiled ballots: 3,348,862 (7.2 percent). Cadiz, Spain, Nov. 12.—(#)—A spectacular attempt to assassinate Jose Antonio Primo de Rivera, leader of Spanish fascists and son of Spain's late dictator, brought death to one man and serious injury to four others in the neighboring town of San Fernando today. The man killed by the bullet aimed at De Rivera was Sigismundo Garea Mantilla. Under the cover of an exuberant ovation with which 2,000 persons greeted De Rivera and other speakers at a fascist meeting, a lone, unidentified assailant fired several shots at the speakers’ platform from the audience. Assassin Escapes Pandemonium seized the audience. In the confusion, the assassin escaped from the building, sending another bullet into Henriques Costa Congorg, who tried to stop him.

Vigo, Nov. 13. (UP)—Customs officials at Tuy, near Caldelas de Tuy, announced today that Col. and Mrs. Lindbergh had landed safely in the Mino river. Some concern had been felt for their safety upon reports that an unidentified plane had crashed near the little watering place where the American fliers alighted.

1933-08-28.text: EXMOOR CLUB, Highland Park, Ill, Aug. 28 (4).--Shattering a record that had stood for 36 years, Enid Wilson of England shot a brilliant 76 today in the qualifying round of the women's national golf championship. Miss Wilson, making her third and perhaps final bid for the American title, got her record-breaking score and probably the medal with a great finish of two birdies and an eagle. The former low qualifying record that had stood for years was 77, held by four players.

ENNIS, County Clare, Irish Free State. (UP). While President de Valera held a large mass meeting here through a ninety minute downpour, General O'Duffy played hide and seek with civic guards and addressed a secret gathering of his blue shirt organization at Bandon. After the Bandon meeting, O'Duffy went to Beal-Nablath, where fifty civic guards met him and prevented him from addressing a scheduled meeting of the proscribed national guard. The question of the moment for Ireland, declared President De Valera, is "whether you are going to have a government of the people, by the people and for the people or a government controlled by an individual who appoints himself." The president said a small group was trying to get into power by force but there was no hope of any such system being voluntarily accepted by the Irish people.

(Ry The Associated Press) LONDON, AUG. 28--AN AIR CIRCUS PLANE FLYING UPSIDE DOWN AND CLOSE TO THE GROUND STRUCK A MOTOR CAR AT ABERDEEN, SCOTLAND YESTERDAY. THE ROOF WAS RIPPED OFF THE AUTOMOBILE AND THE PLANE CRASHED IN A RIVER BUT BOTH THE PILOT AND THE OCCUPANTS OF THE CAR ESCAPED INJURY.

(Copyright 1933 by United Press) London, Aug. 28.—(UP)—The British Labor Party hopes to rise to power at the next general election with a new deal platform that incorporates many of the ideas President Roosevelt has inaugurated in the United States. “At the next general election, probably not before October, 1931, the party, frankly socialistic, will ask the British public to give it a majority in the House of Commons and a mandate that calls for the nationalization of transportation, banking, agriculture and coal mining. Labor party experts are at work on plans that envisage a closely coordinated socialistic state, in which the profits that go now to private owners would be used for the benefit of all. Some plans are still in a formative stage, although the theory has been perfected. Projects already worked out include: Transportation: Coordinated under

HYDE PARK—President Roosevelt entered the final week of his vacation today with grave problems, domestic and international, confronting him. The Chief Executive was to meet Montague Norman, governor of the Bank of England, and George Harrison, head of the New York Federal Reserve Bank. It was believed they would discuss the broad question of currency stabilization. It was made clear, however, that Mr. Roosevelt's position was to be that of an interested listener. The visit of the two bankers was at their own request, it was said. That the complex world monetary situation will be surveyed in all its ramifications was regarded as a foregone conclusion with government officials charged with guiding American policies. It was not thought a new monetary policy might result. Only last week the White House said it was not interested in dollar fluctuations on foreign exchanges, but only in the in

Berlin—(A)— Germans regarded as handwriting on wall today the broad hints of two leaders regarding restoration of the monarchy and the reich’s claims to the Saar territory. Venerable President Paul von Hindenburg said he was thinking of his “Kaiser, the King and Lord” when he accepted as a gift from East Prussia a forest estate adjoining his ancestral home at Neudeck. Chancellor Adolph Hitler told a crowd of 200,000 that Germany, without wanting a new war or proposing to annex anything foreign, would never renounce her claims to the Saar. “The flying chancellor,” in his swift airplane, flew to both gatherings about 700 miles apart—the demonstration at Niederwald mountain near the southwestern border, and exercises for von Hindenburg at Tannenberg, near the eastern extremity. ATHENS, Aug. 28.— A Turkish beauty of 30—Mme. Vouyindjoglou, wife of an Istanbul export merchant—entered the Samuel Insull case today as the “mystery woman.” Mme. Vouyindjoglou was keenly interested Saturday when the 73-year-old utilities magnate was arrested on a charge of violating the United States bankruptcy law, and she has been active in his behalf since. Not only did she visit Insull at the hospital where he is under detention awaiting an extradition hearing, but she consulted Greek officials and Insull’s lawyers regarding his case. She was his first visitor at police headquarters where he was taken after his arrest. Mrs. Insull left for Paris two weeks ago, about the time that Mme. Vouyindjoglou's friendship for the aged Insull first became a topic for conversation in Athens. Mme. Vouyindjoglou accompanied Insull to nearly all social functions, her husband visits Athens on busine

PARIS, Aug. 28. (U.P)—Premier Édouard Daladier, on a tour of inspection of the new “great wall” of defenses believed impregnable, served notice today that France was determined to guarantee Austria's political and economic independence. As he left Paris to motor to Metz, and thence to inspect the new fortifications along the frontier, Daladier made a plain statement of French policy to the United Press. “I am examining the new defenses personally,” he said, “to make sure that our defensive system is of the fullest efficiency. “We want only peace and order. No victorious people, after such a long and cruel war as that in which we engaged from 1914 to 1918 ever made so many sacrifices afterward as has France, due to her policy of European conciliation. “It is our duty to assure our liberty, which is respected because we are known to be capable of defending it. “We should also see that the

1933-03-14.text: Washington, March 14.—(A.P.)—The American government has informed Great Britain that it will press for legislation permitting the president to declare an arms embargo against any nation in the world. The statement of American policy was made through the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay. Great Britain yesterday withdrew an arms embargo declared several days ago against China and Japan. Its revocation followed failure of any other nation to take similar action. The embargo also caused some complaint on the ground that it placed China at a disadvantage as compared to Japan with its already full supply of war materials. President Roosevelt is expected to ask enactment of the arms embargo legislation at the special session of congress, although probably not in a special message.

GENEVA, March 14.—UP—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of England may visit Rome to confer with Premier Mussolini in an effort to save the rapidly crumbling arms conference, it was learned today. Increasing tension throughout Europe since the rise to full power of the Hitlerites in Germany has resulted in renewed efforts to rescue the conference. Decisions intended to leave Germany with no possible excuse for re-arming were confidently expected to be reached here before the end of the week. Should such decisions be undertaken without the most careful preparation and establishment of a united front, the action might mean the complete collapse of the conference.

MOSCOW, March 13—(AP)—An official communique tonight said that six Englishmen and 25 Russians, including eight officers and employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers company, a British electrical firm, were arrested on charges of participating in a conspiracy to damage electric power stations. This was the first explanation given by the government for the arrests Saturday and Sunday by the Soviet secret police, who took four British subjects and four other employees of the firm into custody after raids on its offices. The alleged sabotage plot resulted in damage to areas served by electric power stations, the communique said. Allan Monkhouse, the company director here, and Charles Nordwell, who were among the Englishmen arrested, were released after a preliminary investigation. Four British subjects remained in custody tonight.

| GHANGCHUNG, Manchuria, Mar 14—(UP)—China today ordered 16 full divisions of troops into position along the great wall, determined to hold it against Japan. It was reported Chiang Kai-Shek, Generalissimo of Chinese armies had taken personal command.

LONG BEACH, Cal., March 14 —(P)— Newborn business life stirred in this quake-ridden city today with the echo of Friday’s devastating earth shocks still in the ears of the populace. All banks which could complete temporary repairs meeting with the approval of building inspectors planned to open at 10 a.m., 88 hours after the first quake and 11 days after Gov. James Rolph Jr. declared a state bank holiday. A few opened Monday and allowed withdrawals of $15 a person.

Los Angeles, Calif—A fairly severe settling quake rocked southern California at 11:06 a. m. today. It was the first disturbance of any consequence since 4:21 a. m. No new damage was reported immediately.

NEW YORK, March 14 (P)—Call him Uncle Samson now! A fortnight since, he was a pale and weary Uncle Sam, tugging about in economic delirium, staggering from over-draughts at the flagon of fear and sick from the grog of dissipated confidence. Today the laugh was back on his lips, his eyes flashed with new hope, the financial snarls were being combed from his sparse chin whiskers, and he faced his destiny with courage in his heart and a song in his soul. The hair of this Samson, clipped short by Delilahs of little faith, already had sprouted anew, and the blood of trade, slowed to faint pulse by bank holidays, pounded again through his veins, a positive sign of certain convalescence. WASHINGTON — Secretary Woodin said today bank deposits were exceeding withdrawals generally in the cities where banks were being reopened and that “the era of fear” was completely passed. He made his statement after reports had come to the federal reserve board of progress toward opening hundreds of banks in the country today. At about the same time, the senate banking committee was approving the Robinson bill to allow state banks to borrow from the federal reserve, but with the understanding that the measure was not to be pressed if it were found that present laws met the needs. Referring in his talk with newspapermen to the fact that the banks had started reopening on March 13, Woodin said: “The people have been co-operating with us magnificently. I am beginning to believe a superstition I have long maintained—that is that 13 is my lucky number.” “In a little while the stress of the pr

1933-08-18.text: BAGDAD, Iraq. (—Killing of over six hundred Assyrian Christians in conflicts with Kurds and Iraqi forces in Northern Iraq, climaxed an international situation in which England, former mandatory power over Iraq, has been moved to take a hand. Three hundred and fifteen bodies were found at the village of Simel. Three hundred or more were discovered in the vicinity of Doguk.

New London, Conn. Aug. 18 (UP)—A 150-ton yacht, the "Felicia," with a crew of ten and carrying several thousand cases of liquor, was captured by a coast guard cutter today near Fishers Island and towed to customs docks here. The "Felicia," 111 feet long and with an eighteen-foot beam, is owned by Jesse H. Metcalf, Providence, R.I., according to coast guard officials. The craft and cargo will be taken to New York tomorrow. The capture was made without resistance as the yacht was passing through "The Race," at the eastern point of the island. The names of the captain and crew were not disclosed.

OSLO, Norway, Aug. 18 (UP).— Government investigation was ordered today of unconfirmed reports that fishermen have found wreckage of the seaplane in which Roald Amundsen, discoverer of the South Pole, disappeared while flying to the rescue of the dirigible Italia, wrecked in the Arctic in 1928. The reports said the wreckage of the plane had been found between Bear Island and Tromsø, whence the Amundsen party set out June 18, 1928. Amundsen, Commandant Rene Gilbaud of the French navy, Lieutenant Lief Dietrichsen and three others set out in a French navy seaplane to rescue the crew of the Italia, which General Umberto Nobile of Italy took to the Arctic. The two-motored Farman seaplane never was heard from.

PARIS, Aug. 18 UP—Government dispatches reported that 25 French soldiers, most of them native troops, were killed the week in clashes aimed at cleaning up the last rebel strongholds in the Atlas mountains. Thousands of insurgents have surrendered to the 25,000 troops engaged in the warfare.

BERLIN, Aug. 17 (#)—Dr. Daniel Mulvihill, of the Long Island College of Medicine, Brooklyn, N. Y., was struck in the face upon failing to salute a Nazi detachment on Unter den Linden late Tuesday night. His injuries were not serious and he was able to return to his hotel. The American consulate has been informed. Dr. Mulvihill arrived in Germany two weeks ago and has been studying in a Berlin hospital.

Johnson's blunt warning there would be “no exceptions whether large or small.” The code, when approved, will be administered without fear of favor,” Johnson said to the automobile men. “It is a matter of regret that the code does not include 100 percent of the manufacturers, and I hope that this condition will not long continue.” Immediately afterward, disciplinary powers will be applied under the law. The recovery chieftain said he was still to take the production- supervision oil code to President Roosevelt today but was ready to correct any mistakes pointed out by oil men during the numerous complaints filed with him. CHICAGO, Aug. 18. (4)—Secretary Wallace today outlined the government’s emergency hog program for buying 5,000,000 swine, employing meat packers to process them, and distributing the meat to the needy. In an address at the Century of Progress exposition, he said that the program will be ready to go into effect in a few days and that he expects it to boost purchasing power in the corn belt substantially. The plan should increase prices of swine, possibly 25 to 30 per cent, he asserted, and at the same time provide relief to farmers heavily stocked with swine but with short feed supplies due to drought. The program calls for purchase of 4,000,000 pigs weighing 25 to 100 pounds at from 6 to 9 cents a pound, and 1,000,000 sows soon to farrow, weighing a minimum of 275 pounds, at market prices on the day marketed plus a bonus of $4. The purchases are to be complete by about October 1. They wi

CHICAGO, Aug. 18. (P) — Ten race horse owners, managers, trainers, and employees were indicted by the federal grand jury today on charges that they violated narcotic laws in “doping” horses. Among the principal defendants were A. A. Baroni, described as an owner of race horses, Jack Howard, manager for a stable owned by his wife, and Benjamin Creech, also manager for a stable owned by his wife. The indictments followed investigations at Chicago race tracks by federal government agents. Three minor defendants in the case have pleaded guilty and were sentenced to penitentiary terms on charges that they violated the Harrison anti-narcotic act by supplying “dope” to owners and trainers.

1933-03-04.text: Developments in the banking situation today were: New York and Illinois, followed by the New England states and scattering other states declared banking holidays. The effect was to make the moratorium newly nationwide. The New York Stock Exchange, the Chicago Board of Trade, and all other stock exchanges in the country were closed. Leading foreign exchanges suspended trading in American dollars and foreign banks refused to cash American checks and drafts. Financial officers of the government held conferences during the inauguration festivities at which they considered means of composing the situation. Several federal reserve banks announced compliance with the state moratoria. Citizens took the situation calmly. Credit was extended to them by tradespeople and others where cash was lacking. Tokyo, March 3.—-(#)——The few schools and temples still standing in the area of destruction were converted into hospitals to care for the hundreds of persons injured by earthquake, tidal wave and fire which devastated the northwestern section of the main Japanese island, today, leaving 1,535 known dead. Late tonight the full casualty list had not been compiled, as communications with many sections remained broken. It was feared that the death total would be materially increased. Reports showed that 7,930 homes had been destroyed and that the tidal wave had wrecked or carried to sea 1,570 small boats. Snow Impedes Relief A heavy snowfall impeded efforts to send relief to the stricken area by airplanes, which were forced to turn back. The navy came to the rescue, however, and doctors and medical supplies were landed from five destroyers. An engineer battalion and two cavalry regiments were

SHANGHAI, SATURDAY, March 4 (P)--Chinese sources said that Japanese troops entered Jehol City Friday afternoon and found defenders of the capital demoralized. Verification on the report that the Japanese war machine had achieved its objective after a relentless march across the Chinese province of Jehol was not immediately given.

HANGHAI, March 4—(Saturday)—(AP)—Latest reports reaching here Saturday afternoon said that Chinese troops are offering stiff resistance to Japanese invaders who seek to conquer Jehol City, the capital of Jehol province.

TOKIO, March 4.—Every government agency was called upon today to hasten relief for stricken seaside provinces where more than 1,500 persons lost their lives and 3,000 homes were destroyed by earthquakes, tidal waves and fire. Snow storms added to the discomfort of thousands of homeless, and every hospital was jammed with the injured. Japanese military units assumed charge of the relief work. Refugees were organized into groups. Army doctors and nurses treated the injured, and agencies for the distribution of emergency food supplies and for the housing of the homeless were organized. Railroads were required to carry relief supplies without charge and the government issued an order suspending the collection of taxes in the stricken districts.

TOKYO, March 4.— Army, navy and civilian relief workers today plunged into the immediate task of providing shelter for 50,000 persons made homeless by earthquake, tidal waves and fire which devastated the northeastern section of the main Japanese island Friday, leaving 1,535 known dead. The majority of those whose homes were destroyed spent a cold and fearful night in the open or else in unheated and unlighted shelters in the midst of the wreckage left by receding waves. Occasional after-shocks revived their terrors, and there were harrowing scenes outside improvised hospitals when thousands sought their lost children or other relatives. Along the coast, bodies began drifting ashore today. Authorities in the Prefecture of Iwate said at least 20 villages in that prefecture had been wiped out. WASHINGTON, Mar. 4.—(AP)—Franklin D. Roosevelt became president today in a setting vibrant with the gravity of national responsibilities, and declared in his inaugural address he was prepared to submit a program of drastic remedies to cure the nation’s economic ills. He took the oath at 1:06 p. m. Cheered by thousands as he pronounced the words of his faith from the north steps of the capitol, the new president added that if congress did not help to carry this program into fulfillment, he would ask that wartime powers be vested in the presidency. He outlined only in general terms the program he had in mind, but named among his objectives new safeguards for banking and against speculation. His induction into office was the high moment of an old-time inaugural, to which one of the largest crowds in history had come. Vice President Garner had taken the oath of office nearly an hour before h

Roosevelt tomorrow as the leader to whom the nation and the world look in this hour of need. Thousands Wait Thousands of his fellow-citizens eagerly awaited the hour that will bring to him the honors accorded in years gone by to his acknowledged heroes, from Jefferson to Cleveland, Theodore Roosevelt and Wilson. A mighty expectancy pervaded

1933-03-18.text: (EDITOR'S NOTE: During the stirring domestic events of the last fortnight, a crisis of tremendous importance has arisen in Europe, the significance of which has been missed by many newspaper readers because of absorption in affairs at home. The incredible war talk of 1914 is being revived. The continent is aflame with suspicion and intrigue. The nations are splitting into two camps. The following story by the general European news manager of the United Press gives the background of what has been happening. As in 1914, the British government is listening to divided opinions. There is firstly, advocacy that Britain avoid becoming embroiled in continental troubles; secondly, advocacy of an immediate, unequivocal declaration that Britain will support any European nation which is the victim of aggression. Europe Divided As in 1914, the Balkan "powder barrel" needs only a spark to set off a da

LONDON, March 17.—A break in diplomatic relations between Great Britain and Soviet Russia was anticipated today in both business and political circles. This is the second crisis in the affairs of the two countries within five months. This time it was the arrest of six British subjects employed in Moscow, which is considered likely to cause a recall of the British ambassador. An embargo on Russian goods is also viewed as a possibility to take effect when the present trade agreement with the two countries expires April 16. In the meantime hope of world disarmament and relief from the threatening tension on frontiers of European countries turned toward Rome as final preparations were made for a British-Italian conference this week-end.

ROME, Mar. 18. (U.P)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and his Foreign Minister, Sir John Simon, arrived in Rome today for a series of conferences which may determine the momentous issue of war or peace in Europe. Premier Benito Mussolini, a dominant figure in the parleys upon which the fate of Europe's disarmament conference now hangs, met the British officials at the Ostia airport, and after a brief word of welcome, saw them escorted to the British Embassy. With MacDonald also was his daughter, the attractive Ishbel MacDonald, who has often accompanied her father on his diplomatic missions, and upon whom he leans as an ever-present aide in time of stress. The importance of the mission was emphasized by the fact that the last stage of the journey was made by air from Genoa, in a giant plane piloted by the dashing Italo Balbo, Mussolini's youthful air minister. MacDonald's

MOSCOW, March 19 (4)—Four British subjects charged with ‘wrecking activities’ in connection with their work on electrical projects in Russia will be subjected to a public trial within a month. Protests of the British government were ignored by Soviet authorities in making the decision. A government statement said ‘no pressure or menace’ from Great Britain would dissuade it. Thirty-five other employees of the Russian branch of the British Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical company, all of them native Russians, are also facing trial. (In a similar recent trial of three German engineers and 59 Russian associates, the Germans escaped with acquittals after long prosecution but many of the Russians were executed.) The British subjects who will be tried are L. C. Thornton, chief erecting engineer; W. H. MacDonald, engineer; John Cushney, engineer, and a fitter named Gregory. Two other British offi

ASSOCIATED PRESS Via PRTILer Washington, March 17 (AP) — American statesmen poring over the far reaching British disarmament proposal tonight found themselves faced with a vital decision as to whether the United States should commit itself to join in solving any disputes which might arise between nations which have signed the famous pact of Paris. This question stood out as the most important from an American viewpoint of all the matters covered in the plan presented yesterday by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain. Accord On Provisions On the provisions dealing with specific steps toward reduction of armies, navies and war materials, the American government found itself in general accord as most of these proposals closely resembled suggestions made previously by President Hoover and endorsed in general by Mr. Roosevelt. On the other hand, part one of the MacDonald plan deal

- WASHINGTON, Mar. 17. UR— Secretary of Navy Swanson said today he wished to build the United States Navy up to London treaty limits immediately, but that no construction program has yet been completed. He said he had not discussed a building program thoroughly with President Roosevelt, and had not even had an opportunity to summon bureau chiefs in the Navy Department for consultation on such a plan. The Secretary said he would first have to determine how much money would be available for the Navy before considering any form of construction—warships or aircraft.

By EAMONN DE VALERA President of the Irish Free State Copyright, 1933, by United Press Dublin—On behalf of the Irish people I desire once more to send hearty greetings for St. Patrick’s day to our kindred and all our friends in the United States. We in Ireland are watching with intense interest and sympathy the efforts of the American people to end the depression from which they, in common with the rest of the world, are suffering. We earnestly pray that those efforts will be crowned with success. Ireland is perhaps suffering less from economic evils of the time than any of the great industrial countries; but here, too, the task of remedying those evils becomes the chief preoccupation of the people. We are endeavoring to establish an order of things which will provide a means of secure livelihood for all our citizens, banish unemployment and save the homes of Ireland from the miseries un

1933-12-02.text: - FISHGUARD, Wales, Dec. 2 (4). The British steamer Deebank wirelessed today she had rescued the 26 members of the crew of the Spanish steamer Gloria, sinking in the Irish Sea. The Deebank went to the assistance of the Spanish ship when the Gloria reported her engineroom and two holds were flooded. When the last man had been transferred, members of the Gloria's crew said she could only live another hour.

BATHURST, GAMBIA, British Africa, Dec. 2—(U.P)—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh fueled his seaplane for a long flight today. Lindbergh declined to say what his next destination would be. It was believed that he might start for Natal, Brazil, at dawn tomorrow.

GLASGOW, Scotland, Dec. 2.—(UP)—Thirty thousand cases of Scotch whiskey went to New York today aboard the liner Cameronia, 1ones bottles, enough for five million or more highballs. The ship is due at New York at noon December 10. The American consul unexpectedly issued a permit for the shipment 10 days ago. Distillers were caught napping, but rose to the occasion nobly. They had the whiskey and bottles but not enough labels, and emergency lots were printed. Dockers worked throughout yesterday loading practically every hold in the ship with whiskey. Distillers said that similar shipments will follow all through the month.

Warm Springs, Ga. Dec. 1—President Roosevelt filed away new monetary reports today and devoted himself to Warm Springs business and celebrations. He drove to town to participate in the flag-raising on the main street. While there he was shown a one-sentence report of stories from London of currency agreement between the United States and Great Britain. He smiled and then chuckled, apparently referring to the many reports on the carefully-guarded monetary program of the President for a "managed currency." Of course, as pointed out yesterday by Ambassador Bingham in London, the United States and Great Britain are pursuing similar monetary policies, buying and selling gold in the international exchange.

London, Dec. 2.—(AP)—The Daily Mail said today that President Eamonn de Valera of the Irish Free State was understood to have clearly declared to the British government his intention to go forward with plans for creating an Irish republic. The declaration was made, it was said, in a communication answering a recent statement before the House of Commons by Dominion Secretary J. H. Thomas. If the Irish Free State is to enjoy the privileges of membership in the British Commonwealth of Nations, Thomas warned, it must accept the responsibilities. The British government has sent a reply to de Valera’s communication, the paper said, adding that it seemed the time has arrived when a definite decision on relations of the Irish Free State with the Commonwealth must be made. The Mail said it was believed Britain would place the situation before the other members of the empire for consideration and

Glasgow, Dec. 1.—(4)—The first shipment of Scotch whisky to leave for the United States since before prohibition will depart tomorrow morning in the liner Cameronia. Totaling 40,000 cases, it is the largest consignment of whisky ever to leave Scotland for overseas export.

The Hague, Dec. 2 (.—Sir Cecil Hurst of Great Britain was elected President of the Permanent Court of International Justice today, succeeding Mineichiso Adachi of Japan. Sir Cecil will hold the office from January 1934 to December 1938.

Paris, Dec. 2 (P)—Police massed like troops before the chamber of deputies today while hungry marchers paraded in freezing cold and demanded “work and bread.” Inside, in the stifling atmosphere of the chamber, Premier Camille Chautemps appealed to patriotism to balance the budget and save the franc. The government head made his appeal in a ministerial declaration in which he asked that the French currency be preserved for the public safety. The fate of the cabinet hung in the balance of a proposed vote of confidence in which a majority had pledged themselves to his support. The test was to come with a vote on Chautemps’ cuts of governmental expenditures. Governmental employees were threatening a nationwide strike if salaries were reduced. Even though the vote of confidence were received, observers predicted the government's early downfall.

1933-02-26.text: WASHINGTON, (UP).—The secrecy which for nearly a year has hidden early activities of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation ended today with a report to the house detailing loans totaling $1,171,983,307. The great lending agency, set up to save the nation’s financial structure, disclosed that during the first six months of its existence it made more than 5,000 advances to great corporations, banks and railroads. The disclosure was forced by a house resolution sponsored by Rep. Edgar Howard, (Dem. Neb.). For months the corporation has fought publicity, holding it would be dangerous to its borrowers. Today, over strenuous protests, it submitted to clerk of the house South Trimble a voluminous, detailed report on its activities from its beginning on February 2 to July 21, 1932. Loans since July 21 have been published monthly. It detailed advances made to small county banks; to great railroa

The major Japanese offensive to conquer the province of Jehol, involving 90,000 invaders divided into three spearheads, thrust toward the interior Saturday from the eastern border of the province, along which every important town was flying the flags of Japan and Manchukuo. The advance was carried on in snow a foot deep, and—judging from the reports sent back to Chin-chow—the attackers encountered little resistance. The fourteenth infantry brigade under the command of Major General Hattori was advancing from Suichung Saturday night along the road leading to Wukungfu. Strong resistance was anticipated at the point where the road enters Jehol by Marshal Chang Hsiao-Liang’s 19th brigade there. Along the roads southwest of Kallu and northwest of Chaiyang the Japanese and Manchukuoans claimed a steady and almost unimpeded progress. Indianapolis, Feb. 25 (AP)—Repeal of Indiana's prohibition enforcement law will bring an early decrease in the state's penal institution population. Paul V. McNutt, young governor, said today that soon after he affixes his signature to the bill erasing the “bona dry” law from the statute books he will pardon or parole about 400 persons serving sentences on liquor charges. Governor McNutt expects to sign the repeal bill early next week. It was passed by the state senate yesterday after having been voted in the house of representatives several days ago. The governor said he would request penal institution authorities to check the sentences of all prisoners and to recommend pardons for those convicted of liquor law violations other than public intoxication and driving while intoxicated. “If these men were kept in prison after the liquor law is repealed they would be political prisoners,” sa

DENVER, Feb. 2.—(P)—At the approach of midnight tonight—zero hour in the Boettcher kidnaping case—this mile high metropolis of the Rockies was stirred by the spreading of the largest dragnet in its history... a ae Peace officers, augmented by 4000 Volunteers from the American Legion and service clubs, by the precinct workers of the major political parties and by an aroused citizenry, were carrying their search for the kidnapers of Charles Boettcher II, heir to millions, to every house in greater Denver. Midnight was the zero hour because Claude K. Boettcher, father of the missing heir, fixed it as the limit of time in which he would treat with the men who accosted young Boettcher and his wife in the driveway of their home the night of Feb. 12, carried off the husband and thrust into the hand of the trembling woman a demand for $60,000 ransom. By The Associated Press. Denver, Colo, Feb. 25.—Claude K. Boettcher stood firm tonight in his decision to seek out and punish the abductors of his son, Charles Boettcher, 2nd, if he was not returned home unharmed by midnight for the demanded $60,000 ransom. "I have stated my proposition," the wealthy father said, "I have no cause for retreat from it." He previously had asserted he would spend his life and his fortune to track down the kidnappers. No Contact With Kidnappers Boettcher said he had not heard from the kidnappers since his ultimatum of Thursday that he would pay the ransom demanded if and when his son was released. Boettcher disclosed the selection of the Rev. D. B. Dagwell, dean of the Cathedral of St. John’s, as an intermediary in the case was made by the extortionists themselves. Miami, Fla., Feb. 25.—(C?)—Mayor Anton Cermak of Chicago rallied today after a blood transfusion and at 5:15 p.m. his physicians said he had maintained the gain made as a result of the treatment. He was sleeping at that hour and his daughters, who have kept vigil at his hospital room door, went to their Miami Beach home, cheered by news that their father's condition had improved. In Oxygen Tent. Cermak was in an oxygen tent, a treatment decided on this morning. He took nourishment—the first by mouth in twenty-four hours—late today and his physicians issued this bulletin: “He is sleeping after having taken the first nourishment by mouth in the last twenty-four hours. “His temperature is 99.4, pulse 128, respiration 26.” Dr. Frederick Tice of Chicago, one of the attending physicians, said after the transfusion: “I have been completely downcast, but I am more encouraged now.” However, anoth

©SAN BENITO, Tex., Feb. 25— (Pi—A bizarre scheme of five youths to steal a plane for use on a flight to Yucatan, Mexico, was revealed by prosecutors today as the background for the airplane slaying of Lehman Nelson, 33-year-old flying instructor, and the subsequent suicide of Erin McCall, 21. With the filing of attempted theft charges against four youths here, D. S. Purl, district attorney, made known that two boys had tried to take the plane from its Harlingen hangar Tuesday night, only two days before Nelson, substitute for Bill Williams, consented to give McCall a lesson to augment his nine hours of flying time. One Charged With Murder The accusations were filed against Gaylord Pitts, 19; Clois Lawson, 17; Earl Dodson, 17, and Vernon Bryant. Dodson also was charged with murder in connection with Nelson’s death while flying the plane over San Benito. McCall and Dodson had been rooming

WASHINGTON, Feb. 25—(AP)— After considering for two days the resignation of Joshua Reuben Clark, United States ambassador to Mexico, President Hoover today accepted his retirement without public comment, effective immediately. There was speculation in the capital tonight that Clark might possibly be renamed to this post by the incoming President, particularly in the light of praise given him from Latin American sources. There was no apparent solid base, however, for these reports. The Mexican chamber of commerce has drafted a resolution asking that Clark be returned, but Roosevelt spokesmen here, including Cordell Hull, incoming Secretary of State, have declined to comment.

1933-03-31.text: Moscow, March 31.—(/)—British Ambassador Sir Esmond Ovey was crossing the Russian border today on a trip to London from which he may never return, at least in his present official capacity. He is to report to the British government on the arrest of six British subjects here on charges of sabotage in connection with their work on electrical projects. It was said on high authority that it is very likely Sir Esmond is leaving for good. (British newspapers were speculating on the possibility of a ban on Russian imports, cancellation of trade treaty negotiations already suspended and severance of diplomatic relations with Russia.) The Russian foreign office was not represented when virtually the entire Moscow diplomatic corps gathered at the station last night to bid Sir Esmond and his family farewell. As the train pulled out all present lifted their hats in a silent gesture. At least two of

| PARIS, March 31 (4) — Premier Mussolini's plan to assure peace in Europe was made public here today and was disclosed as a proposal for a six-point pact. It provided: 1. Four-power collaboration for peace by Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany: 2. Acceptance of the principle of revision of treaties in accordance with the League of Nations covenant, “in a spirit of mutual understanding and solidarity of reciprocal interests’; 3. Great Britain, France and Italy—in the event of the failure of full disarmament (by which Germany would realize equality)—pledge gradual realization of equality for Germany, Austria, Hungary and Bulgaria; 4. The following if a common line of action by the four powers in world affairs; 5. Effectiveness of the accord for 10 years, when it will be automatically renewable unless denounced; 6. Registration of the accord with the League of Nations.

TANDON, March 29 (Pi) — Sir Esmond Ovey, ambassador at Moscow, has been called home to report in person on the arrest of six British subjects employed by the Metropolitan-Vickers electrical company who are charged with sabotage by the Russian government. The newspapers, which regard the incident as of considerable importance to relations between the two governments, speculated today on the possibility of a ban on Russian imports, cancellation of negotiations for a new trade treaty with Russia, and perhaps of a severance of diplomatic relations. Sir Esmond, it was said, leaves Moscow tonight and will reach here on Sunday. For the past two weeks, since the men were arrested in Moscow, Leningrad and elsewhere, he has been in frequent communication with the government as his negotiations for their release continued. The present intention is that he will return to Moscow before long unless th

Washington, March 31 Bette: Secretary of Navy Swanson today said he had arranged to confer tomorrow with President Roosevelt on a navy building program. Swanson favors building the fleet up to London Treaty limits as quickly as possible.

Dagenham, England, March 31 (UP) Continued shutdown of the Ford automobile works was regarded as likely today following refusal of more than half the employees of the Briggs body works to return to the night shift. Briggs workers demanded the same wages as those paid in the Ford factory and abolition of the piece-work system. Two thousand men were expected to go on strike at the Briggs works today.

BERLIN, March 31.—(P)—Nazi storm troopers today cleared Berlin law courts of Jewish judges and attorneys. Among those ousted was Chief Justice Kurt Soelling. Reports from the United States that Chancellor Hitler’s Nazi party might be persuaded at the last minute to refrain from launching its drastic economic war on Jewry tomorrow seemed only to add fuel to the fire today. A new proclamation defined the action as the beginning of a war on the entire Jewish race of the world. A party declaration said it will be fought “until victory is ours.” The Jews, their backs to the wall as their last appeals for mercy fell on deaf ears, have visualized their financial ruin and ultimate isolation from German cities and towns. Such elaborate plans were being made for the beginning at 10

BERLIN, Mar. 31 (UP)-Twenty-four hours before their scheduled nation-wide boycott of Jewish industry and commerce, Nazi storm troopers mobilized today for mass action in every city of Germany. In last minute instructions issued through boycott committees set up by the Hitlerites to manage the boycott it was emphasized that tomorrow's action is not a government but a party activity. Thousands of civilian party members were summoned to “duty” to take the place of storm troopers who are office holders and who will not be able to participate in the picketing of Jewish shops. Nazi storm troopers occupied the first division of the Berlin criminal court today and asked judges, lawyers, and clerks of Jewish origin, to quit their posts. The ensuing evacuation resulted in a docket jam which caused adjourning of the court for the weekend.

1933-02-12.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., Fed. 9.—England had no idea they would kick up such a fuss just by suggesting that they settle in cash. The senate howled, how dare you offer us cash, so I guess England will just have to keep on owing us. Here is one for the book. Hollywood is having its first divorce forced on it. That old rich Oklahoma Indian that lives out here, the government wants him to divorce his wife. Well they are happy and don't want to be divorced. The government claims they could pick him out a cheaper wife. He says he doesn't want a cheap wife, I imagine the Indian agents would like to marry him themselves. So poor old Hollywood, they won't let you live happy if you want to. Yours, WILL ROGERS,

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil, Feb. 11—(4)—Capt. J. A. Mollison, British flier, landed here at 11:50 a.m. (9:50 a.m. Eastern Standard Time) today from Caravellas, Brazil. The long distance flier reached Caravellas yesterday after completing a flight across the South Atlantic from West Africa to Natal.

Doctors and nurses did what they could for the injured, and everywhere the relatives of men still missing poked about in the ruins. More than 300 were in the hospitals with serious injuries, and 1,200 or more were slightly hurt. Neunkirchen, Saar, Germany—(P)—Blind to the dangers of tottering walls, rescue workers dug frantically Saturday into the debris of a wide area in this industrial city of 49,000 population, still finding bodies of persons killed and maimed in Friday’s huge gas tank explosion. At dawn authorities computed casualties as follows: Dead: Known, 61; estimated, 196 to 200. Seriously injured: Nearly 390, Slightly injured: About 1,200. Tokyo, Feb. 11—()—Japan is preparing a reply to the League of Nations’ inquiry on discontinuance of the present Manchukuo regime, which will be a proclamation to the world in vigorous, unmistakable terms, of Japan's determination to maintain the independence of Manchukuo regardless of cost. Government sources also disclosed today that Japan will proclaim in advance its refusal, under any circumstances, to be restrained or deflected from this policy by the league’s recommendations. (When conciliation of disputes fails, the league covenant provides the league to make its own report and recommendations for action). Although the league committee of nineteen requested a simple “yes” or “no” answer to its one question of whether Japan would agree to discontinuance of the present Japanese-sponsored Manchukuo government in Manchuria, Japan is seizing upon the occasion to publicize her Manchurian

TOKIO, (UP).—— Rear Admiral William V. Pratt’s decision to keep the American Atlantic fleet, as well as the Pacific fleet in Pacific waters until July 1, 1934, is due to American uneasiness over the Japanese situation, authoritative sources here believed today. It was said unofficially that it would be difficult to give any other interpretation to the admiral’s announcement, which was expected to revive talk of a possible Japanese-American war. Admiral Pratt said it would cost $410,000 to return the Atlantic fleet to the east coast while the navy faces the necessity of absolute economy and gave the desire for economy as the reason for the decision. The decision had been expected by the Japanese. They believed American authorities would not want to return the Atlantic fleet to its eastern base with the possibility of having to return to the Pacific at any time.

EUNKIRCHEN, Saar Territory, Germany.—(#)—The number of dead from Friday's explosion of a gas tank at the Neunkirchen iron works slowly mounted Saturday to 68 and police said that the total was not likely to be greatly exceeded. So far as the authorities were able to tell, there were no Americans or other foreigners among the victims. Police estimated that 160 persons had been seriously injured and more than 369 slightly hurt. Distraught residents of the ruined working class section of the city near the iron works poked about in the wreckage of their homes, looking for remnants of their property. There were many strange and pathetic sights. One woman after a long search, walked away with a rescued kitten; another salvaged a birdcage. The works management stated that all danger of further explosions was not yet over. Hence the work of clearing away the debris proceeded with greatest cautio

GENEVA (UP)—Thirty thousand Japanese troops are approaching their allotted positions for a Japanese drive on Jehol province, the Chinese delegation to the League of Nations charged Saturday. The troops transported from Korea are almost ready to attack at Kilu Fushin and Shankaihwan, the Chinese alleged. The last of 24 Japanese troop trains were said to have reached Chinese soil. The Chinese said 220 railway cars were used for conveyance of troops, 288 cars for arms and ammunition and provisions, and 50 cars for artillery and machine guns. TOKIO (UP)—Japanese delegates to the League of Nations will be instructed to return home soon, well-informed quarters understood today. TOKYO, Feb. 11.—()—An emphatic refusal to drop the state of Manchukuo which Japan set up after driving the Chinese out of Manchuria is in preparation as this government’s reply to a League of Nations proposal for settlement of the dispute over that territory. It will be a proclamation to the world in unmistakable language that Japan is determined to maintain Manchukuo’s independence regardless of the consequences. It will assert that this country will refuse under any circumstances to be restrained or deflected from its Manchurian policy of recommendations which a League committee completed today after several weeks of deliberation. To Restate Position This information came from government sources which explained that the cabinet will take the opportunity, when it replies to the League, of restating its Manchurian position for the edification of the rest of the world. 1933-03-09.text: Paris.—(AP)—French fears that Germany may announce she intends to rearm are likely to be one of the principal topics of the talks here today between Premier MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon of England and Premier Daladier of France. The French seek to forestall such a possibility by a big power pronouncement against Germany. The British statesmen will meet Premier Daladier for the first time since the formation of the new French government. They will leave tonight for Geneva for disarmament discussions. It was understood here the British leaders are seeking a five-power conference in Geneva to wind up the disarmament situation. A strong joint effort to obtain some practical results at Geneva is expected to result from their conversations with M. Daladier. Other international problems are likely to be discussed but the disarmament question predominates.
Lympne Airdrome, England, Mar. 9 U.R—Victor Smith, South African airman, hopped off today on his third attempt to set a flight record to South Africa. The record is now held by Amy Johnson Mollison.

BERLIN, March 9—Charles Messersmith, consul general of the United States at Berlin, today handed the Prussian chief of police, Magnue Von Levetzow, a memorandum concerning attacks on American citizens here. The memorandum cited attacks on six citizens—all since Sunday—in their domiciles or on the streets. Five of the six attacked were of Jewish descent. In each case the men attacking the Americans were dressed in Nazi uniforms. Max Schussler, an American operating a real estate business in Berlin, told the United Press he and his wife were awakened at 2 a.m. by four men carrying revolvers, who forced him to sign a cancellation of an eviction order against one of his Nazi tenants. Two of the men, he said, wore brown uniforms and the Swastika insignia of the Nazi forces. They described themselves as policemen. American authorities took affidavits from the Schusslers. COURTHOUSE, Miami, Fla. March 7. (*)—Arraignment of Giuseppe Zangara on charges of the murder of Mayor Anton J. Cermak of Chicago was set for 9 a.m. Thursday. The date was set by Circuit Judge Thompson on agreement of attorneys. The date was set soon after Zangara was led into the courtroom by officers. He wore a figured yellow shirt and the same sport trousers and shoes he wore on his last appearance in court, when he was sentenced to 80 years in prison for shooting at Pres. Roosevelt last Feb. 15 and the wounding of three other persons.

(By The Associated Press) MIAMI, Fla., March 6.—A bullet intended for President Roosevelt brought death to Mayor Anton J. Cermak of Chicago in a hospital here today and about 10 hours later Giuseppe Zangara, the assassin, was indicted for first degree murder. The mayor died at 6:57 a.m., after 19 days of suffering with the wound and many complications it caused. Almost immediately the Dade County grand jury met and began hearing testimony on which it based the murder indictment returned about 5 p.m. Arraigned Tuesday Circuit Judge Uly O. Thompson announced Zangara, a naturalized Italian, will be arraigned at noon tomorrow. Conviction carries the death penalty by electrocution. The assassin, already under 80 years’ prison sentence for firing on Roosevelt and wounding three other persons, was not brought into the courtroom today nor did the grand jury question him. C.—(AP)—President Roosevelt's emergency bank bill was submitted to Congress today, carrying out his program for controlled expansion of the currency and resumption of normal banking under his regulation. The bill would ratify the executive orders issued by the president and continue his authority over the banking situation; provide for concentration of the nation’s gold supply in the federal reserve banks; penalize hoarding; and provide for controlled expansion of the currency. Senator Robinson of Arkansas, the democratic leader, said he was convinced the bill was sound, and that, if “passed today, will assure the opening of many banks both national and state on tomorrow that are now closed.” Senate leaders planned to submit the measure immediately to committee after organization of the senate, with a view to reporting it back within an hour or two and passing it in time f

Washington, March 8.—(/P)—The 73rd congress, dominated by democrats and pledged to support President Roosevelt’s proposals, assembles tomorrow in extraordinary session to enact the new administration’s emergency banking program. Preparing to meet the executive's demand for speedy action, both senate and house democrats and republicans rushed their organization plans today. First Message Either late tomorrow or early Friday, Mr. Roosevelt will send his first message to congress.
