Washington, March 7 (Thursday) (AP) — President Roosevelt predicted early today "immediate" resumption of banking activities throughout the country as a result of the enactment of an emergency bill speedy passage of which had just been pledged him by congressional leaders. "I have been in conference with members of the Senate and House and have talked over with them a measure which has been carefully studied and prepared and which will immediately relieve the situation and at once start banking operations throughout the entire country," a statement issued by the President said. Drive On Hoarders Meanwhile, the Treasury launched a drive upon gold hoarders with a thinly concealed threat of publishing their names. At Secretary Woodin's direction, orders went forward to the twelve Federal Reserve banks to report the names of all persons who have withdrawn gold from member banks since Februar

1933-11-09.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 9. (P)—The administration watched its gold operations club the dollar to a record low level today and then added another dime to the price it will pay for the metal when newly mined in the United States. London dispatches told of an overnight drop of 4% cents in the exchange value of the dollar as against the pound, opening at $4.98¼. As the trading progressed the dollar fell to $5.01¼. Meanwhile, the price of gold at London was reduced, but the change in the dollar-pound relationship caused an increase in this quotation when converted into dollars. Today it was $32.78, at the $0.0114 point of the exchange quotation, compared with $32.63 yesterday. The domestic quotation was increased from $33.05 to $33.15. While yesterday’s quotation was 69 cents above the London figure, today’s was 52 cents. In the fortnight that the administration has been buying newly mined gold, it

NEW YORK, Nov. 9—(1)—James D. Mooney, vice-president in charge of overseas operations for the General Motors company, said on his return from Europe on the Tex today that Germany was making substantial and England amazing progress in economic recovery. “The progress that has been made in England, particularly during the past year,” he said, “is little short of amazing. The English have capitalized their forced departure from the gold standard with intelligence and resourcefulness, and they have fortified the advantages derived in this regard by adhering rigorously to their traditional belief in low prices on domestic consumer goods. “Germany is also making substantial progress in her economic recovery, and France is continuing to hold her place after the United States and England as the third best automotive market in the

LONDON, Nov. 9—QU.P!—The pound sterling reached the $5 mark in foreign exchange trading today, setting a new post-war high record. Opening at $4.98%, the pound went to $5 in the first 45 minutes of trading. Then it moved to $3.01. French francs, which had opened at 80 9-16, went to 80 5-8. The pound rose further to $5.014. Today’s gold price was set at 130 shilling 11 pence a fine ounce ($32.82) including a premium of nine pence on the French franc, a reduction of 11 pence or 23 cents from yesterday’s price. Gold bars worth $2,060,000 were ie After the gold price was set, the pound went back to $5.01. The dollar recovered further losses and the pound in afternoon trading receded to $4.99%.

Washington, Nov. 5 —(UP)— The dollar was driven down to new low levels today in line with President Roosevelt's currency depreciation policy, designed to thrust upward commodity prices through raising the price of newly-mined gold. The dollar went above $5 to the pound in the London foreign exchange market today, bringing the dollar to the lowest value in more than 60 years.

' New York, Nov. 9—(#)—James Roosevelt, son of the president, returned on the liner Rex today from a six weeks vacation tour of Europe, which included social calls on Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain, President Lebrun of France, Premier Mussolini of Italy, and the Pope. He said he didn't believe foreign officials would be anything but polite about his father to him, but he added that “they did seem enthusiastic about his program.” He added too that “we didn't really discuss things, though.” Roosevelt was accompanied by his wife. He said he was much impressed with the cheerfulness displayed in England and Italy. “There they are on the upswing,” he said, “and they seem to be in no particular hurry about it.” “There is a greater desire, on the part of the man in the street, for peace than ever before. The attitude is ‘we don't want to fight and even if we do who is going to pay for

— PARIS (4) — Wine sellers are sad instead of joyful at the end of prohibition in the United States, because it was explained today, they believe imitations masquerading as vintages will kill the taste for French wines before they start marketing them. Further, the sellers were said to fear that renewed calls for another French default on the war debt payment, Dec. 15, will stimulate an anti-French feeling.

GENEVA. (CP). Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and Mrs. Lindbergh, touring Europe by airplane, slept here after a flight from Rotterdam, Holland. They landed in the Swiss capital, on the little lake in front of the Nautical club, three hours after taking off from the Dutch city. Hugh R. Wilson, American minister to Switzerland, and many government officials were members of the welcoming crowd. Scores of cheering persons narrowly escaped a plunge into the lake when a pontoon upon which they had swarmed to catch a glimpse of the aviator threatened to capsize.

MOSCOW. (Ur), SOVIET RUSSIA with its customary gusto celebrated the sixteenth anniversary of the most important date on its calendar—the October revolution—coincident with the scheduled arrival in the United States of its foreign commissar, Maxim Litvinoff. Newspapers found space to refer prominently to this coincidence despite the fact that their columns were filled with praises of the “socialist construction” and the forward march of the Soviet Union in world affairs. Meanwhile, in the Red Square the Red legions of the proletariat paraded in another day-long demonstration in which approximately one million persons were estimated to have participated.

1933-03-28.text: Washington, March 27. -(P)- At both the White House and the State Department today, representatives of America’s biggest war debtors - Great Britain and France - engaged in economic discussions of world import. The opinion that France will pay its $19,000,000 war debt installment due last December 15 was expressed to newspaper men by one of the callers upon President Roosevelt, a member of the French chamber of deputies. His Personal View. In making this prediction, the French legislator, Jacques Stern, also a Paris banker, emphasized that it was his own personal view and that he had not been personally in touch with conditions in France for the last two weeks. Stern voted for the payment last December. Ambassador Paul Claudel, who introduced Stern to the president, said war debts had not figured in their 20-minute conversation, although other economic matters were discussed. The French

— DIAMUDE, Belgium, March 28. —UP—The British Imperial Airways passenger plane, City of Liverpool, with 15 persons aboard, crashed in flames today at Essen. All on board were killed. Police after an hour's effort recovered five bodies. It was assumed the remaining seven were dead. * An eye-witness to the disaster saw bodies falling from the flaming plane before it crashed, indicating they had jumped. Some bodies were found 300 feet from the wreckage. After the flames died, searchers found three gold watches in the wreckage. The victims comprised one Belgian, three Germans and 11 English.

London, Mar. 28.—(UP)—The "Flying Mollisons" will attempt a spectacular crossing of the North Atlantic by air this summer, and at the same time try to establish a new long-distance record, 'Jim' Mollison said today. If his attempt is successful, he and Amy Johnson, who is Mrs. Mollison, will settle down on a farm and attempt no more exciting exploits. "We intend to fly to New York," Mollison said, "perhaps in April and perhaps not until June. We will await good flying weather, preferably at a time when there is a full moon. Our limit will be as far east as our machine will carry us, however, and New York will not be our ultimate objective when we leave London. "After we get back to England there will be no more excitement and no more flying."

LONDON, Mar. 28 — (*) — The trial of Lieutenant Norman Baillie-Stewart was concluded this evening with acquittal of the defendant on three charges of attempting to gather military information. The acquittal was in keeping with instructions of the judge advocate in summing up the case. The remainder of the court's findings, however, were reserved for submission to higher military authorities. Lieutenant Baillie-Stewart had been charged on ten counts in previous court-martials; a verdict in this form has meant a failure to acquit on charges in which acquittal was not specified. Some time may elapse before the entire finding in the case becomes known. Military rules prescribe the referring of the case to higher authorities. Lieutenant Baillie-Stewart himself came smartly to attention when the court returned from deliberating on his case. He heard the announcement of the verdict without nota

| Paris, Today.— (P)— Premier Daladier, supported by a cheering chamber of deputies, today defended Premier MacDonald of Great Britain and Premier Mussolini of Italy against an opposition attack in the chamber on the Italian premier’s four-power peace plan. The attack culminated in an expression by Deputy Henry Franklin-Bouillon that the four-power peace plan was “abominable collusion between Mr. MacDonald and Signor Mussolini.” By a vote of 369 to 212 the chamber postponed discussion of interpellations made to the foreign affairs committee, and particularly concerning Premier Mussolini's four-power plan. The premier refused to discuss the plan but pledged the parliament that nothing would be done and nothing concluded without its knowledge. He declared, ‘France fears no menace on any frontier.” Foreign Minister Paul-Boncour, who in a speech Sunday declared ‘peace or war is at stake in t

UTICA, N. Y. March 28 (AP)— If the king of England still wants that rarest stamp in the world, a British Guiana one cent issue valued at $50,000 for which he was outbid once by Arthur Hind of Clark Mills, he will have the opportunity again soon. Hind’s internationally known stamp collection is to be sold. He had refused $400,000 for his United States collection alone. Mr. Hind died a few weeks ago in Florida.

DIXMUDE, Belgium, March 28 - A giant British passenger and cargo plane crashed to earth near here during a severe storm today, with a probable loss of 15 lives. The plane, owned and operated by the Imperial Airways, Ltd, was en route from Brussels to London. The huge tri-motored craft left Haran field, Brussels, at 1:36 p. m., carrying 12 passengers and a crew of three, including a pilot, mechanic and radio operator. As the plane roared over Lesens in a heavy storm, peasants in the field noticed it was in difficulty. When less than two miles from Dixmude, the ship began to lose altitude speedily. One person was seen to jump from the descending plane with a parachute. The parachute failed to open and the victim plunged like a plummet to death. Shortly afterward, the plane fell to earth with a terrific crash. Peasants from the surrounding countryside rushed to the scene, while ambulances c

GENEVA, March 27 (#)—The disarmament conference adjourned for the Easter holidays today after adopting the new British disarmament and security plan as a basis for subsequent discussions with a view of concluding a general convention. The debate showed general approval of the British draft in its broad lines. Hugh Gibson, representing the United States, did not participate in the discussion. The French delegate said his government was willing to accept the British plan “as a basis for friendly discussion” and Germany’s representative said Berlin welcomed the scheme as a means of obtaining Germany’s ambition for arms equality.

1933-04-27.text: NEW YORK (?)--Premier Ramsay MacDonald of England, sailed homeward Thursday leaving behind a solemn plea to the American and British people to pull together in a struggle back to prosperity. Addressing the Pilgrims Wednesday night, MacDonald called for joint effort to defeat what he termed “influence of disruption” rampant in the world. He emphasized he was asking for no “alliance.”

BY the Associated Press. Washington, D. C., April 26.—President Roosevelt is preparing to send to Congress a resolution on the war debts understood to give him authority to grant a moratorium on payments until after the London economic conference. The move is said authoritatively to be conditional only upon French agreement first to meet their defaulted Dec. 15 interest payment of $19,261,432. This is being gone into thoroughly by the President in his White House talks with former Premier Herriot of France. Enabled to End Tension Exactly what form the resolution would take has not yet been decided by the President but it would be so drawn as to enable him to end the tension created by the approach of payments totaling some $144,000,000 June 15 in the face of French and British warnings that they would make no more payments under the present settlement terms. The President's goal is the r

(By the Associated Press) New York, Apr. 26.—Prime Minister Macdonald expressed the hope tonight that the United States and Great Britain will “sit on the same side of the table” at the forthcoming international economic conference. Addressing the Pilgrims of the United States, the prime minister said “No greater blessing can come upon the nations of this world than that Great Britain and America should remain in affectionate relations.” Coming to New York late today, the minister bade America farewell amidst a brilliant setting. Notables of the financial world surrounded him: J. P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Thomas W. Lamont. Society crowded into the boxes of the Waldorf-Astoria grand ballroom. The prime minister's daughter, Miss Ishbel Macdonald, entered the center box as the band played “Dixie.” This was their last night in America. The prime minister said President Roosevelt “hinted a

LONDON, Apr. 27.—The dollar, which was “left to look after itself” when America went off the gold standard, appears to be coming back in favor now that the MacDonald-Roosevelt conversations have been closed in favorable circumstances. Speculators who sold the dollar short some time ago are hurriedly covering as a result of the proposed increase in Britain’s exchange equalization fund. They, along with other purchasers, were in the market today and the quotation appreciated five cents, closing at $3.74 to the pound.

By RAYMOND CLAPPER United Press Staff Correspondent WASHINGTON, (UP)—With Britain and France firmly enlisted in the battle for economic recovery, President Roosevelt Thursday marched ahead into new territory in his quest for international action to heal the ailing world. First in order in another busy day was a long initial discussion with Prime Minister Bennett of Canada, here as the representative of the United States’ second largest customer, Tariff adjustments and other means of increasing Canadian-American trade to the mutual benefit of both countries were important on the schedule for this talk. Plans for bettering the price of the great output of wheat and silver from Canadian and American farms and mines also were slated for consideration. Offers of war debt revision, a consultative pact to help preserve peace in exchange for real arms reduction, and scaling down of tariffs now s

GENEVA, Switzerland, April 26 —(AP)— Norman H. Davis, special American delegate to the disarmament conference, told that body today his government had the whole question of a consultation pact under advisement. A recently submitted British plan for disarmament which aimed to coordinate efforts to promote an established peace through consultations and methodical cooperation when peace may be threatened or broken, he said, "introduces a new element for us" which the United States government is now considering. "Our ability to make collaboration effective will depend in large part on the measure of disarmament we now may be able to achieve," the American ambassador-at-large declared. These remarks were interpreted by other delegates as indicating that the United States was disposed to strengthen the Briand-Kellogg treaty by an agreement to participate in a consultation pact. The suggestion

Statesmen of the world grappled in Washington and abroad today with disarmament, currency and war debt phases of international economic problems. Development of an Anglo-French monetary alliance aimed at keeping the English pound depreciated and the French on a gold standard added to the significance of the economic conversations of Washington between former Premier Herriot and President Roosevelt. Disarmament questions centered abroad at Geneva where Norman Davis, American delegate, succeeded in having the disarmament conference seek arms reduction before security pacts. Payments of this year’s war debts wholly in silver was proposed in the Senate. A revision of the debts before June 15 appeared likely.

PARIS, April 26—-(4)—France moved today toward what financial experts hope will be a three-power financial pact with the United States and Great Britain for the stabilization of currencies. A French financial plan by which that portion of the British equalization fund which is in francs will be loaned to the French Treasury to tide over the present need is under negotiation in Paris and London. Premier Édouard Daladier, meanwhile, was represented by a member of his immediate circle as being willing to ask Parliament for credits to pay the $19,000,000 war debt interest due the United States last December 15 if President Roosevelt would offer a war debts moratorium for the duration of the World Economic Conference. Premier Daladier, it was said, feels that if President Roosevelt can obtain such a holiday from the present Congress he believes conditions made when the French Parliament Dec.

1933-04-29.text: WASHINGTON, April 28 (P)— A four-power campaign for a new economic order and for disarmament was organized tonight by President Roosevelt as he concluded the first phase of his international negotiations. France and Canada took their places beside Great Britain and the United States during the day in the effort for economic stability and arms reduction to be made at the London economic conference and the Geneva arms reduction parley. War debts—the thorn in relations between the United States and European debtors—also came up in a "most frank and friendly" talk today between President Roosevelt and Edouard Herriot, special envoy of France. As in the case of Great Britain no agreement or plan was proposed but a joint statement from the President and M. Herriot said the exchange of views "will undoubtedly help in determining the steps to be taken hereafter." Future negotiations were hoped f

LONDON, April 29.—U.P)—A world tariff truce will be proposed by Norman Davis, American ambassador at large, to the organizing committee of the World Economic conference which meets here this afternoon, it was learned from semi-official sources today. Ambassador Davis arrived here at noon by plane from Paris. He will remain until Wednesday, and expects to hold important conferences on disarmament with Sir John Simon, British secretary for foreign affairs.

FLORENCE, Italy, April 28.—(p)— The charred body of Bert Hinkler, Australian airman lost last January in a projected England-to-Australia flight, was found by two charcoal burners today in the woods at Pratomagno near the charred wreckage of his airplane. The airman's passport was found on the body. Pratomagno is in a heavily wooded area at an altitude of 4700 feet.

PARIS, April 28—(#)—A loan of 30,000,000 pounds (approximately $114,000,000 currently) for six months to the French treasury at 2 1-2 per cent. interest by a group of English banks was negotiated today. Meanwhile, the question of paying the December and June debt installments to the United States was brought sharply to the fore in government quarters. Details of the loan arrangement were mostly worked out during the last visit to London of George Bonnet, French Finance Minister. He conferred there with officials of the Bank of England, but it was stated semi-officially tonight that the British treasury will play no part in the loan operations. Although earlier in the week the information was that the Bank of France and the British Equalization Fund would play a part in the negotiations, it was stated the loan as finally arranged, was purely between individual British banks and the French

FLORENCE, Italy, April 29— A body found near the wreckage of an airplane in the mountain fastness near Castel-Franco in Tuscany, was definitely identified today as that of Bert Hinkler, famous Australian flier, who disappeared several weeks ago during an attempt to regain the England-Australian record. The body was identified through a passport and other documents. Apparently his plane had nose-dived into the mountain side. Only a small amount of gasoline was in the tanks, and the oil supply was exhausted.

WASHINGTON, April 28 — The state department announced today that President Roosevelt had instructed Ambassador Norman Davis to propose a worldwide economic conference. At a committee meeting in London today, Davis suggested that the nations of the world enter a gentlemen's agreement not to raise tariff barriers before or during the economic conference. The dates of the conference were set by the London committee for June 7.

PARIS, April 29.—(?)—A loan of 300,000,000 pounds ($114,000,000) for the French treasury from a group of English banks was announced by Finance Minister Georges Bonnet. The finance ministry said the loan carried the possibility of repayment at the end of three months and forbade negotiations of securities given to the banks by the treasury. The Bank of France also guaranteed the loan.

CASTEL SAN NICOLO, Italy. Bert Hinkler, noted Australian speed pilot, apparently crashed head-on into a mountainside in the middle of the afternoon of January 7, when he was killed here. This was learned today when an Associated Press correspondent reached the scene where Italian charcoal burners found the body and shattered plane yesterday. The discovery came early four months after the famous airman started his attempt to regain the speed record for the England-Australia flight. Contrary to first reports, the body was not burned. It was mangled, however, and thrown thirty feet from the plane on the mountain, Varco di Roeca. A watch found in Hinkler's pocket stopped at 3 p.m. indicating he flew over here in broad daylight, but it was recalled that a storm was then raging in this region. (Hinkler left Feltham airdrome in Middlesex, England, at 2:10 a.m. January 7). Hinkler's body lies in

1933-05-05.text: (By the Associated Press) The American dollar decreased in value today in foreign exchange markets, hitting its lowest quotation in relation to the British pound since Britain left the gold standard in September, 1931. New York—Sterling opened at $4.00, an overnight gain over the dollar of 6 cents. The quotation subsequently dipped. London—After dropping to $4.01 to the pound, the dollar closed stronger at $3.97, a falling off of more than 6 cents from yesterday's close. Paris—The dollar hit a new low, closing at 21.20 francs. Berlin—The dollar reached an all-time low of 3.54 marks.

WASHINGTON, May 5. (#)— President Roosevelt's selection of delegates for the London world economic conference took more definite shape today with authoritative word that one member will be James M. Cox, former governor of Ohio and 1920 Democratic presidential nominee. His name has figured in speculation previously, but this was the most definite assertion in quarters that should know, that a decision had been reached. Cox has declined to comment and White House announcement is awaited. It was also said that Ralph W. Morrison of San Antonio, Texas, financier and ranchman who was a heavy contributor to the Roosevelt-Garner campaign, will be asked to become one of the American representatives. A White House invitation to Representative John McDuffie of Alabama, chairman of the house insular committee, to go to London was declined. McDuffie is understood to have said he found it necessary to

WASHINGTON, May 4—American efforts to prepare the way for genuine contributions to world business recovery at the London economic conference next month were redoubled tonight in the face of reports from abroad which accentuated the difficulties involved. Earnest conversations with Italian and Argentine envoys invited here by the president were pursued at the State Department and the White House while the cables were kept busy with official messages to London where Norman H. Davis, ambassador-at-large, is working for agreement of European nations to an armistice on tariff wall boosting between now and the conference opening June 12. Undersecretary William Phillips of the State Department said France had made three reservations, reserving the right to raise its tariffs to meet depreciation of currencies, specifying that the truce shall not apply to tariff measures now before its parliament

LONDON, May 5.—Premier MacDonald in two long cabinet sessions today failed to swing his ministers to support the American proposal for a world tariff truce effective immediately. The American proposal was that the customs armistice should begin at once and continue throughout the world economic and monetary conference. The prime minister's failure to obtain his cabinet’s approval for this action was authoritatively learned after a full day of negotiations on the tariff issues. The first conversations upon the proposal were between MacDonald and Norman H. Davis, the American ambassador-at-large. Thereafter the suggestion was discussed by the prime minister and his cabinet in morning and afternoon sessions. Later the same question was treated at a conference between Davis and Sir Robert Van Sittart, permanent undersecretary of state for foreign affairs.

London, May 5, W.P.--The English pound, unsupported by the government's huge equalization fund, soared in value today and at 2 p.m. was quoted at $4.00, up from an opening of $3.92. Presumably due to profit-taking, the quotation dropped quickly back to $3.09. The dollar was at its lowest level since England went off the gold standard. At the latest quotation, Britain saw the trade advantage which she had held over the United States by the depreciated pound — which at one time fell below $3.20 — dwindling to the vanishing point. While the dollar depreciated sharply, gold standard currencies improved fractionally in relation to sterling. The French franc gained 3-18 to 84 9-16 compared to yesterday's close.

LONDON, May 5.—(UP)— The dollar was driven down today to its lowest point, since America abandoned the gold standard by a furious rush of selling from here and on the continent. The pound, not supported by the government's huge equalization fund, opened at $3.92, soared to a high of $4.0014 at 2 P.M., and closed at $3.98, a gain of seven cents from yesterday's close. The dollar was similarly weak in Paris, Berlin, Rome and other centers.

CHANGCHUN, Manchuria, May 5.—(UP)—With an army swollen to 30,000 troops Gen. Liu Hkueti-Tang, Manchu military leader, deserted the captured Chahar provincial city of Doolnar and started a march southward toward the Great Wall of China, according to advices received here today. His first conquest was reported at Kayuan, important town midway between Dolonar and Changchiakou, Great Wall gateway. The town apparently was captured, the advices reported.

TOKIO, May 5—Formation of a permanent joint committee with Manchukuo and Russia to settle future controversies such as the present Manchu-Soviet rail dispute was proposed today by Japan. The plan was suggested by Konstantin K. Yurenev, Soviet ambassador to Tokio, who asked the foreign office to take a direct hand in settling Moscow's dispute with Manchukuo over ownership of Chinese Eastern railway rolling stock. Yurenev said Russia would not object to the principle of such a joint committee and asked Vice Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita to draw up a concrete proposal. Arita today conferred with Foreign Minister Yasuya Uchida who then discussed the matter with the war office before deciding the government would take part in an issue which previously it had insisted was one for Russia and Manchukuo to settle between themselves.

1933-04-18.text: Moscow, April 18.—(P)—Just before the court retired today to consider its verdict in the Metropolitan-Vickers sabotage, William L. MacDonald reiterated his guilt, all the other British prisoners stoutly affirmed their innocence, and all the Russian defendants abjectly threw themselves on the mercy of the court. The Russians admitted all the charges against them. These varying statements were made individually to the court by the defendants just before the judges retired to make their decision. Limping to the microphone in front of the judges' stand, his ascetic face unusually pale, MacDonald—the first of the British defendants called—stood with his hands in his trouser pockets, looked Judge Vassili Ulrich squarely in the eye, and in Russian declared: "I confessed and I have nothing to add." John Cushny, the next Englishman, spoke in English as did the remainder of his British colleagues.

82 ASSOCIATED PRESS| Rivers on a spring spree wallowed over lowlands in northern New England, southern Indiana, northeast Arkansas and the Mississippi delta today while the weather staged a crazy exhibition. Snow in California and cold in Dixie were among the special demonstrations of what April can do. At St. Johnsbury Center, Vermont, residents were aroused at midnight and told to prepare for a flight before the unruly Passumpsic. Rain in torrents and melting snow helped the river out of its banks. The Ipswich threshed about in Massachusetts and the Connecticut rose in New Hampshire. The White, Wabash and Ohio rivers were swollen by persistent rains in Indiana and a highway between Seymour and Louisville, Ky., had to be closed because of high water. Down in the Mississippi delta, the Tallahatchie, Yazoo and several other perennial miscreants chased valley dwellers to high ground. The M

Chicago, April 17.—(AP)—Worn and haggard from his nocturnal tours of underworld haunts, John Factor, fighting extradition to England for fraud, today declared he would comply with any ‘reasonable’ demand for the safe return of his kidnapped son, Jerome, 19. The speculator whom England wants for allegedly bilking investors of several million dollars, said he talked on the telephone with his son, a university student, 36 hours after he had been seized last Wednesday night. “They are treating me all right so far,” Jerome told his father, “But hurry up with the money, or it will be tough for me.” Factor had not established actual contact with the abductors, he said, nor had negotiations reached the stage of a ‘go-between.’ Factor's secretary late this afternoon received a telephone call purporting to come from Jerome's kidnappers, “This is the kidnappers,” the caller said, “Tell Jack to get

MOSCOW. April 17 — (P) — A “five-year plan of sabotage” by six British electrical engineers on trial for bribery, sabotage and espionage was charged tonight by the counsel for three of their Russian co-defendants. The accusation was made at the beginning of the defense summation, shortly after Prosecutor Andrey Vishinsky asked that charges against Albert W. Gregory be dismissed but that the five other British employees of the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical company be convicted. Speculation regarding the possible verdicts included ten-year sentences for two of the Britons, a possible three-year sentence for one of them, and death sentences for two of the Russians. It was speculated also that the other nine Russians would be given various prison terms and that two Britons would probably be released and bound over. The session tonight was devoted to pleas by four defense attorneys, all of

Boston, April 18. (AP)—New England rivers, swollen to roaring, muddy torrents by continued rain and, in northern sections, by melting snow, today were at their highest stage since the disastrous floods of 1927. As the waters rose, inundating lowlands, blotting out roads, flooding cellars and creeping nearer to bridge structures, the weather bureau predicted additional rain for tonight and Wednesday. In Vermont, scene of the most serious flood damage in 1927, anxiety grew today as rivers in the narrow valleys left their beds, to sweep across highways and lap at doorsteps of countless homes. In New Hampshire, Vermont and Massachusetts, other streams, including the great Connecticut River, were at flood stage.

BY BOGHRNE LAUNS, (United Press Staff Correspondent.) MOSCOW, April 18—The revolutionary tribunal trying six Englishmen and 11 Russians for high crimes against the Soviet, retired at 3:30 p. m. today to consider a verdict. William MacDonald, one of the British citizens made a second confession of guilt when called upon for his final statement today. "I confessed my guilt," he told the tribunal. "I have nothing more to add." MacDonald's terse statement was given in an electrified room where defense attorneys had just pleaded for extenuation for the six British and 11 Russian defendants. When he sat down, the court called upon John Cushney, another of the Englishmen. "I will leave this courtroom as honest a man as when I entered it," Cushney declared. Allan Monkhouse was called next. (Turn to Page 6—No. 5.)

LONDON, (U.P)---The British government shifted to a conciliatory attitude toward Russia today, and there were indications from Downing St. that England would not maintain an embargo on Russian trade if the Soviet did no more than deport the Britons on trial for sabotage. The cabinet met this afternoon in special session to consider the Russian situation. The government was holding its cards up its sleeve, but it was intimated that even if a temporary embargo was imposed, it would be lifted if the Soviet permitted all the accused Englishmen to return to Great Britain. The belief prevailed generally today that whatever sentences might be imposed on those of the Englishmen whom the Soviet tribunal con- (Continued on page 3)

Colomb-Bechar, Algeria, April 18.—(UP)—Violent sand storms over the Sahara Desert interrupted search for Captain William N. Lancaster, British flier, today. Lancaster has been missing six days on a projected flight from London to Cape Town. It is feared he was forced to land in the Sahara. He was acquitted of murder in Miami, Fla., recently.

1933-05-22.text: Rome, May 22—(AP)—Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy have swung into line in support of Premier Mussolini's plan for the maintenance of European peace for ten years untrammeled by desires to force their will on any other nation. Informal agreements to a revised version of the four power pact first proposed by the premier in March was given yesterday by the four nations. Its main points: One, collaboration among the four powers to preserve peace for ten years without intention to impose any solution on any smaller nation. Two, the statement that post war treaties revision is a possibility but only under article 16 of the covenant of the league of nations. Three, the mention of disarmament only as a desirable necessity without specific recommendations. Four, an agreement to abide by article 10 of the covenant protecting territorial integrity and independence of league members against

Rome, May 22.—A treaty binding Europe’s leading powers to keep the peace for 10 years awaited formal initialing by diplomats today after approval by representatives of the contracting nations—Italy, Great Britain, France and Germany. Mussolini wrote the pact months ago. He revived it this weekend as an ideal, and perhaps essential, basis for agreement by the disarmament conference at Geneva and the world economic conference at London in June. So swiftly did he obtain approval by representatives of the powers that, when the news was flashed out last night, it was greeted with skepticism. Drafts of the pact were due to arrive today at London, Paris, Berlin and Geneva. The plan was for representatives of the contracting nations to initial the treaty at Geneva. Mussolini prepared to announce its approval to the deputies today and, if all went well, to proclaim his success over a radio hook-u

WASHINGTON, May 22. (P). — President Roosevelt was expected to decide definitely today whether to ask Congress for complete power to scale down tariffs through accords with other nations at the London economic conference. His Secretary of State, Cordell Hull, was called in for a thorough examination of the international situation. From this meeting was due the tariff decision and completion of the conference delegation which Hull will lead. Negotiating reciprocal agreements with other powers and simultaneous lowering of the tariff walls is a London objective of the president. For its accomplishment he had two courses: to obtain full power from Congress in advance, or to negotiate the treaties and submit them to the legislature later.

LONDON, May 22. (P)—Acceptance by Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy of the draft of Premier Benito Mussolini's ten-year peace pact was announced officially today. The draft was accepted at Rome by representatives of the nations concerned, but formal initialling and eventual signature remained to be accomplished. Britain and France, it was said, reserved the right to make changes in the Mussolini pact at Geneva. It was assumed by officials that the approval at Rome of Hermann Goering, who holds cabinet rank in Germany, meant Germany was satisfied with the pact as it stands. Mussolini, the author, naturally approved. Sir John Simon and Joseph Paul Boncour, British and French foreign ministers now at Geneva, will examine the draft as it was approved at Rome. Then, after they consult their governments from Geneva, it is intended that the pact shall be initialled there. An official sta

WASHINGTON, May 22.—United States officials today viewed the European four-power peace agreement as strengthening the cause of international cooperation for disarmament and economic reconstruction. Secretary of State Hull’s advisors represented him as feeling that acceptance by Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy of the plan for assuring peace in Europe for 10 years should improve the prospects at Geneva for favorable consideration of President Roosevelt's proposals for world security and disarmament. Officials likewise believed the four-power agreement would create a more favorable background for the London conference at which the nations of the world will seek cooperative means of stimulating business. (By The Associated Press) Mussolini’s four-power pact, aiming to guarantee peace in Europe for at least 10 years, has been informally accepted by France, England, Germany, and Italy. Two important provisions which raised a chorus of protests to the original pact two months ago by France and her eastern allies, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and Rumania, have been so altered as to be practically eliminated, Rome reports disclosed. Instead of providing a pledge of gradual arms ‘equality’ for Germany, Austria, Hungary, and Bulgaria, it mentions the disarmament question only generally, leaving the MacDonald disarmament plan to take care of this matter. WASHINGTON, May 22. (P)—The name of Chairman McReynolds, of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, was definitely listed on the American delegation to the London economic conference by observers here today. President Roosevelt is nearing completion of the delegation of seven. He is looking for Republicans to join with Secretary Hull, James M. Cox of Ohio, and Chairman Pittman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, who have already been named... An offer has been made to Senator Johnson (R., Cal.) and an early decision by him is in prospect, but there is no indication whether he will go.

United Press Staff Correspondent GENEVA, May 22.—(U.P)— The United States called on all nations today to disarm drastically, and offered to consult and co-operate with other powers in the punishment of aggressors. The offer was regarded here as marking the end of America’s traditional policy of isolation. President Roosevelt, boldly taking leadership of the world’s efforts for peace, even proposed to abandon his nation’s cherished neutrality in the event peace is threatened, and virtually offered to scrap the bulk of the powerful American navy, army and military air forces, if other nations will do the same. The President’s dramatic and sweeping proposals were presented to the general commission of the world arms conference by Norman H. Davis, his special ambassador to Europe. Warning that another war threatens if armament races are not stopped, Davis called on the nations for immediate

1933-12-12.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 12. ()—The war debt payment due the United States from France, Dec. 15 amounts to $22,200,926 of which $2,354,434 is principal and $19,855,487 interest. The French payment is second only in amount to that owed this month by Great Britain amounting to $117,670,765. London has announced its intention of making a token payment in dollars of $7,500,000. France has never made a token payment. Last June her default amounted to $46,738,000 and the previous December $19,261,000. Debt payments due the United States Dec. 15 from all foreign debtors aggregate $153,024,327 of which $106,405,636 is interest and $46,618,691 principal.

London, Dec. 12--(U.R)—investigation of the rapidity with which certain private financial concerns receive the daily Washington gold price in advance of official announcement of the figure was understood today to center around one or more American brokerage houses. In banking circles it was learned today that at least 20 banks and brokerage houses receive a “flash” from the United States each day, generally between 2:40 p.m. and 5 p.m. (from 9:40 to 9:45 a.m., e.s.t.) It was reported today that one large American brokerage house, with a branch in London, is “frequently slightly ahead” of the other financial services. Upon some occasions, it appears, London has been advised of the day's gold price five minutes before the American public is aware of the figure. The price is announced daily at 9:45 a.m. e.s.t. in Washington. The concern named as being peculiarly fortunate in the rapidity wi

CHICAGO. (UP). The plea of an English authoress, Rosita Forbes, stood between James Larue, 22, and return to Florida to complete a five year sentence on the chain gang. Miss Forbes’ sympathies were aroused by Larue’s impassioned plea that a return to the chain gang meant a living death for a crime he contends he did not commit. She employed attorneys to defend him. Florida officers who obtained extradition papers for Larue in Springfield were to arrive here Friday to seek custody of him. His attorneys planned to ask a judge to prevent his return thru habeas corpus proceedings. Their principal hope is an appeal for humanitarianism, rather than for legal rights. Larue was sentenced to the chain gang on a plea of guilty to breaking into a deserted orange grove hut to sleep. He contended he pleaded guilty when told that he would be proved guilty if he refused, but on assurance he would be gr

PARIS. (UP) — France will completely ignore her debt installment due the United States December 15, the United Press learned today. Unless there is a last minute revision of the government’s attitude, it is probable France will not even dispatch a note explaining her default as she did July 15. The cabinet, discussing the economics of national finances today touched only briefly on the United States treasury’s memorandum to debtor powers and “failed to take any action.” Members of the cabinet asserted circumstances are unchanged since July. France feels she is obliged to defer payments until offered a new debt arrangement.

Madrid, Dec. 11. (P)—The menace of a general strike today occupied Spain, already clouded by three days of revolt and bloodshed in twelve of its fifty provinces. As acts of violence diminished after the capture by government troops of a rebel garrison in the Villanueva military barracks, the government turned its attention toward the strike threats. At nightfall, a nation-wide official report said order was restored in practically all troubled areas and that the strike was decreasing in importance as Socialists ordered intimidated workers to return to their posts. Commerce and industry functioned almost as normal. The cruiser squadron at Ferrol, a naval base, received orders to be ready to sail at a moment’s notice in the event force was necessary in any port. (A dispatch from Gibraltar said it was rumored there a detachment of Spanish Foreign Legion would be brought to Spain. British to

Berlin, Dec. 12—(7)—The German reichstag met today for the shortest session in its history—seven and one-half minutes. The new parliament was practically a Nazi body; women and Jews were completely absent. The absence of Chancellor Adolf Hitler, who was at Wilhelmshaven, was equally notable. Hermann Goering, Prussian premier, was re-elected president of the reichstag and was the only speaker. He confined his remarks to recording a unanimous sentiment for the nomination of himself and three vice presidents. Then he led the house in a full-throated “Heil Hitler!” and adjourned the session “until further notice.”

Wellington, N. Z., Dec. 12. (UP) —The freighter Jacob Ruppert, principal ship of Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd’s south polar expedition, sailed from the spring climate of New Zealand today for the Ross Sea and the ice barrier that covers Antarctica. Byrd hoped that the Ruppert would overtake, on its way to his base, the Bear of Oakland, on which most members of the expedition had sailed previously, and to spend Christmas at his permanent base, Little America, in the Bay of Whales. Most of the expedition members were on the Bear. The Ruppert has the supplies, including the twin-engined airplane and the autogyro which Byrd plans to use in exploratory polar flights. Byrd was aboard the Ruppert.

By The Associated Press Wellington, N. Z., Dec. 12.—Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd sailed yesterday with his second expedition to the Antarctic, where a party of scientists and explorers will make a two year study of the South Polar regions from their base at “Little America.”

1933-08-12.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, Aug. 12. — (Saturday) — General Owen O'Duffy, organizer and leader of the blue-shirted national guard, today canceled a parade scheduled for Sunday announced as in honor of three late Irish leaders after the government had issued an order banning the demonstration. O’Duffy announced that instead he was planning organization of church parades in many districts the following Sunday. Not So A denial of reports that the opposition to President de Valera is planning a coup d'état was issued today by William T. Cosgrave, former president of the council.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 11—(AP) In its second major rate decision in a week, the Interstate Commerce Commission today voted 6 to 4 against reducing charges on bituminous coal from Pennsylvania, Maryland and northern West Virginia mines to eastern trunk lines and New England territories. The decision followed that of last Saturday in which the commission refused to grant a blanket reduction in all freight rates. One of the reasons given in both cases was that the roads could not stand a cut financially. The commission said today the record showed “the adverse effect that even a slight reduction in the rates would have on defendants’ (railroads) financial condition, which is serious.” It also upheld existing rates on bituminous coal from the same mines to New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore for export in foreign and coastwise trade, and dismissed complaints against these and interstate track-del

NEW YORK, Aug. 12.—(AP)— Capt. Jimmie Mollison never says quit. The British flier sailed for London last night to rush work on a new plane, in which he and his wife, the former Amy Johnson, are expected to seek a long distance record. The plane will be a duplicate of one in which the Mollisons flew the Atlantic only to crash at Bridgeport, Conn. Mrs. Mollison will stay in this country a while, inspecting aviation developments.

ROME, Aug. 12 (#)— The entire city quit its daily routine early today to prepare a happy welcome for General Italo Balbo's returning air armada. Everywhere there were flags and placards eulogizing the aviators, whose final lap on their round trip to Chicago began from Lisbon at 6:30 a.m. today (1:30 a.m., BE. 8, T.). Special excursion trains brought thousands upon thousands of Italians who came to participate in the festivities, in which an important detail will be a triumphant procession, not seen since the time of the Caesars, through the arch of Constantine. Hundreds went to Ostia, Rome's nearby port, where the fleet will land. Anxiety had been felt over the condition of Gen. Giuseppe Valle, chief of staff of the air ministry, who was injured near Nazareth, Spain, when his plane fell into the sea. Six other passengers were slightly hurt. All were taken to a hospital in Valencia, Spain

LISBON, Portugal, Aug 12.—(UP)—General Italo Balbo and his fleet of 28 seaplanes took off today for Ostia, the port of Rome on the Tiber river, to receive a triumphant welcome after their double transatlantic flight. General Balbo, as usual leading the armada, left the water in his plane Balbo at 6:10 a. m., (2:10 a. m. EDT) and the last plane rose at 6:40 (2:40 EDT). The crews went to bed at 9 o'clock last night at Balbo’s order, in order that they should have sufficient rest for the 1150 mile flight across Portugal, Spain, the Mediterranean and Tyrrhenian Sea to Ostia, 15 miles down the Tiber from Rome. Balbo, accompanied by the Italian minister, left his hotel at 4:40 a. m. and proceeded to the Terreiro do Paço pier where thousands of the populace waited to bid him and his men farewell. He entered a motor boat, followed by his aides.

OSAKA, Japan, Aug. 12 — The Shanghai correspondent of the Mainichi Shimbun sent a dispatch today saying the United States was secretly strengthening the Manila naval base in contravention to the Washington Treaty. The dispatch was printed under a sensational headline. It asserted all of the labor on the naval base was being done by life-term convicts brought from America. And it gave as its authority for the information one of these convicts who had escaped. The work at the naval base, the correspondent said, would result in greatly strengthening it. Various Japanese have talked about the United States violating its commitments by increasing its naval facilities in the Pacific. These stories have been met with denials in Washington.

Rome, Aug. 11. (47) - Thousands of persons came to Rome today to participate in the welcoming ceremonies for General Italo Balbo and his seaplane squadron, expected home tomorrow from their round-trip flight across the Atlantic to Chicago. Before ending their flight from Lisbon the squadron will swoop over the capital and then alight at Fiumicino seaport, near Ostia, where Premier Mussolini will receive the fliers and treat them to Fascist honors - a Mussolinian embrace. On Sunday morning the group will be received by the King.

Lisbon, August 12. (6).—Cheered by virtually the entire population of Lisbon, the Italian air armada took off to-day on the last lap of its flight from Italy to Chicago and return. Confident of negotiating the 1,400 miles between here and Ostia, Italy, in record time, General Italo Balbo and the squadron’s twenty-three sea-planes roared off to the East shortly after dawn brightened the waters of the Tagus river, where the huge flying boats had been moored. Rounding Cape St. Vincent a little more than an hour after leaving Lisbon, the armada passed over the straits and circling the Southern coast of Spain, headed toward the Balearic Islands, to the East. The visibility here was poor and the prevailing wind to the East.

1933-12-24.text: Seattle— () — The weatherman brought the perfect Christmas gift to the weather-soaked Pacific northwest today—colder temperatures to stem the floods which have caused 13 deaths and made thousands homeless. General belief was felt in Washington, Oregon and British Columbia, although traffic by rail and motor was still paralyzed in western Washington. Fifteen cities and towns were inundated in whole or in part. Scores more were isolated except to airplanes and some rivers kept on rising, adding to flood damage already of tremendous extent. Building An Ark William Greenwood, “the prophet of doom,” of Olympia, Wash., who is building an ark and predicting a deluge that will wipe life from the earth, chuckled grimly anent the inundation of a few hundred thousand acres in the northwest and said “it’s only a sign.” A genuine flood will occur in 1938, he declared in warning sinners to prepare for

Paris, Dec. 22. — (P) During talks today of Joseph Paul-Boncour and Sir John Simon, the French and British foreign ministers, France stood by her guns against German rearmament and Premier Mussolini's demands for changes in the League of Nations. British support for at least a part of the French program was announced in French quarters. Brussels, Dec. 22.—(#)—By a vote of 86 to 50 in the house today voted 759,000,000 francs (currently about $53,789,000) in extraordinary credits for fortifications and modernization of armaments.

Reading, Sept. 4—Automobile accidents claimed two lives over the weekend. Mrs. Clara E. White, 58, Shillington, died of a fractured skull in a hospital today. She was struck by an automobile as she alighted from a street car near her home Sunday night. George Swoyer, 63, died of a crushed skull at another hospital last night. He was injured as a fire truck, returning from a fire company picnic, sideswiped a pole on the Pricetown road about three miles north of Reading.

TOKYO. A son, the long awaited crown prince of the imperial family of Japan, was born today to Empress Nagaku amid rich medieval The first male child of Emperor Hirohito and the empress brought great rejoicing among their 95 million subjects, whom the newcomer, if he lives, someday will rule as the 125th mikado. The birth was at 6:59 a.m. at the shrine hospital of the Three Sisters.

Leipzig, Germany, Dec. 23 (UP)— Marinus Van Der Lubbe, 24, was sentenced to death by hanging today for burning the Reichstag building February 27. His four fellow defendants, all communists, were acquitted. Slumped down in his chair, moronic, looking like a clothed animal, Lubbe, the Dutch stone mason who proved an enigma throughout the trial, heard the supreme court verdict without interest. Four Acquitted The four acquitted were Ernest Torgler, former whip of the communist party in the Reichstag; George Dimitroff, effervescent ex-leader of the Bulgarian communist party; Wassil Taneff, 36, Bulgarian shoemaker, and Blacoi Popoff, 31, Bulgarian student. They showed less emotion than those packed in the dingy, dark courtroom to see the end of a trial that may take a place among the most famous of modern times. Torgler’s mother and wife were in the front row. The others were without relativ

At the same time the court freed communists whom the state had held to be responsible with Van Der Lubbe. This ended one of the most spectacular trials in German history. Van Der Lubbe did not appear to take any notice of the verdict. ATHENS, Greece, Dec. 23 (?)— Samuel Insull, former American utility operator, today filed an appeal with the Supreme State Council against the government's decision that he must leave Greece by January 31. Insull was served Thursday with notice that the government would make no further extension of his police resident permit, already extended by a previous order from the becca expiration date, December. The United States, however, had given no indication of what its next move would be in attempting to extradite Insull to face charges growing out of the collapse of his utilities holdings.

PARIS, Dec. 23.—(#)—Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gordon Switz, young Americans, declared vigorously today that their arrest on suspicion of being “tools of an international spy ring” was a police “frameup” and the result of a “plant.” They were heard separately by Magistrate Benon. During the grilling examination they protested their innocence and asserted that supposedly incriminating documents found by police did not belong to them. The 29-year-old native of East Orange, N. J., maintained that the affair “looked like a scenario well played.” His 4-hour examination left him nearly exhausted. Mrs. Switz told the American consul, Robert D. Murphy, that the evidence against them was “put there as a plant.” Murphy, who was not present during the hearing of the husband, will make a report to Washington regarding the examination. The meeting of the couple after a separation of almost a week was an aff

1933-02-18.text: Rome, Feb. 17 (P) The Giornale d'Italia today published the text of what it called a virtual ultimatum that France, with Great Britain’s adhesion, sent to Vienna giving the Austrian government a fortnight in which to get rid of arms and supplies allegedly concentrated in that country in violation, the paper says, of the treaty of St. Germain. The note was kept secret, the Giornale d'Italia said, because responsible French circles realized it was “excessively forceful,” and do not wish to lay themselves open to public judgment. On Feb. 11 (A dispatch from Paris said that the note was presented February 11, and was mainly in the nature of a request for information as to the state of arms shipment in Hungary.) The note evidently referred to the reported shipment of 40,000 rifles and 200 machine guns from Italy to Austria recently, although it did not mention the specific

London, Feb. 18—(AP)—The Reuters news agency correspondent at Doorn, Holland, telegraphed today that the former kaiser's wife, Princess Hermine, left with a secretary for Berlin with the announced object of opening a fancy goods fair there. The correspondent continues: “However, it is considered highly probable that the princess will endeavor to effect meetings with leaders of the nationalist coalition (Hitler government), others in nationalistic circles and former members of the nobility, who will be invited to a tea party, at which no doubt the actual political problems regarding possible restoration of the monarchy will be discussed.” The message states the ex-kaiser is in excellent health, cutting wood daily. He is receiving numerous telegrams from all parts of the world, it added, “but mostly from Germany from nationalistic circles there.”

London, Feb. 18.—Official quarters today confirmed that Great Britain and France had made joint representations to Austria that a recent arms shipment from Italy violated the treaty of St. Germain. The communication requested that the arms be returned to Italy or destroyed by a certain date. It was stated that the note was in no sense an ultimatum, but was in the nature of a friendly request.

LOS ANGELES, Feb. 17—(AP)—Motion pictures or the law call to William James Guy, the smiling young Welsh adventurer who was acquitted at Long Beach last night of the killing of Walter Wanderwell. In the county jail where he is detained pending deportation to England as an alien illegally in the United States, Guy said today he planned to return to Southern California under the immigration quota and attempt to “crash the movies or try to be a lawyer.” “As for the Wanderwell mystery,” he said, “I have no idea who killed him. His widow, Aloha, once said a thousand persons might have wanted to do the job. That is correct.” Guy was nonchalant about the murder trial.

(By the Associated Press) Geneva, Feb. 17. — The League of Nations told the whole world today by its own wireless telegraph of the plan of its leaders for a pronouncement of solemn censure upon Japan for her military action against China, and for a peaceful settlement of the dangerous conflict in the Far East. Yosuke Matsuoka, special counsel for Japan, announced less than an hour after publication of the league's proposals that his government would not accept the recommendations for peace. "There never was any question of Japan's accepting the report," he said. "To protect Manchukuo we must possess the chief town of Jehol. The only way to get peace is for the Chinese to withdraw their troops from Jehol. "We will fight if we have to. I have heard that there are about 150,000 Chinese troops in Jehol, but one Japanese is worth ten Chinese. All Chinese soldiers are bandits." Avoids Question

TOKYO, Feb. 18—A government summons to Yosuke Matsuoka, Japanese delegate at Geneva, to return here by way of Siberia, the shortest route, to assist in the final stages of Japan's secession from the League of Nations is likely to compel Matsuoka to abandon a projected trip to the United States, a government spokesman said today. This matter was still unsettled but the cabinet might decide to consult Matsuoka personally before taking final action on withdrawal from the league, in which event the delegate will be called home immediately after the anticipated acceptance by the league assembly of its report on Manchuria next week. The cabinet postponed further discussion of the league question until Monday, permitting Premier Viscount Makoto Saito to present the decisions thus far reached to Prince Saionji, last surviving member of the council of the Genro, the highest seat of power in the E

GENEVA, (UP) — Japanese delegates to the League of Nations today received instructions from Tokio to “reject unequivocally” the report and recommendation on the Manchurian situation. TOKIO, (U.P)—Japanese withdrawal from the League of Nations will be postponed at least temporarily, it was indicated today when a cabinet meeting scheduled to discuss withdrawal was cancelled. Later it was announced the cabinet would meet in extraordinary session Monday, presumably to discuss the impending military action toward “policing” Jehol province. Foreign Minister Uchida ordered Yosuke Matsuoka, chief league delegate, to return to Japan via Siberia, instead of visiting the United States en route home. Matsuoka had been expected to spend several weeks in America conferring with government officials and prominent individuals. The orders to Matsuoka indicated that the league question would not be settle

GENEVA, Feb. 18.—(UP)—Colombia invoked Article XV of the League of Nations covenant today for settlement of the Leticia dispute with Peru. The League Council will meet Monday to begin consideration of the dispute. Article XV provides for investigation of a dispute between League members and recommendation for settlement. It was invoked in the Manchurian dispute between Japan and China.

1933-12-26.text: BOSTON, Dec. 25.—(#)—Santa Claus came today to 70 lonely lighthouses and coast guard stations strung along the New England coast from Boston to Monhegan Island—off the coast of northeastern Maine. This particular Santa Claus’ other name is Captain “Bill Wincapaw, widely known New England aviator. He and four others flew in a big seaplane hundreds of miles through frigid, howling winds, to bring a bit of cheer, a bit of contact with the outside world, a change in the monotony of the existences to those who spend their lives safeguarding others. At each station was dropped a package containing newspapers, magazines, and a pound of fresh coffee—the gift of Adriel Bird, Boston business executive, who has interested himself in Wincapaw’s attempts to bring cheer at Christmas to humanity's lonely outposts along the wilderness of the state.

PARIS. (P). The horror of Saturday night's railroad catastrophe saddened Christmas day for France. Twenty-three bodies of the 196 known victims remained unidentified, some so mutilated it was doubted if their identity could ever be established. An indication of the frightful shock of the crash of the Strasbourg Flier into the fogbound Nancy Express seventeen miles from here was the fact that 165 passengers in wooden cars of the express were killed outright. Thirty-one died in hospitals later with the death list likely to go above 200. As investigators continued what loomed as a long inquiry into the worst railroad disaster in the history of France, both the engineer and fireman of the flier remained in prison, charged with homicide by imprudence. President Lebrun, bareheaded and pale with emotion, passed before 160 caskets in the basement of the East Paris station. He also visited hospit

PARIS, Dec. 26. (AP)—Cabinet ministers, their Christmas saddened by the most tragic railway accident in French history, made plans today for a national funeral tomorrow morning for victims of the Lagny wreck. After 60 hours of work, construction gangs this morning cleared the second track of the line where the Strasbourg Express, traveling at more than 60 miles an hour, plowed through the wooden coaches of the Paris-Nancy train, and traffic proceeded normally past the wreck scene. There were 191 known dead today, with 90 desperately injured in hospitals here and at Meaux. The dead lay in the Chapel Ardente under the eastern station here in the dim light of holy candles. Many of the children, lying in the long rows of dead, still clutched Christmas teddy bears and dolls. Inquiry into the cause of the wreck continued to center on the operation of safety signals. These failed in a test yest
One Way To Travel. ‘ IRKUTSK, U. S. S. R.—Five Red Army soldiers have set out from here on skis for Moscow, a distance of more than 3,000 miles. They hope to reach the capital in 86 days.

| Barcelona, Dec. 26 — (AP) — Thousands of mourners passed today before the bier of Col. Francisco Macia, 74, dead President of Catalonia. The body of the Catalonian leader, who achieved political autonomy for his province in his lifetime of political service, lay in state in the St. George Salon of the Parliamentary building. | It is expected more than 300,000 persons would attend the last rites tomorrow. At the head of the mourning procession will be President Alcala Zamora of Spain. _ The sorrow of Catalonia was expressed dramatically as hundreds of women wailed and prayed in and about the building where the body of Macia lay. Huge banks of flowers were piled above his casket, | His death occurred yesterday following an operation for relief from intestinal disorders.
ROME, Dec. 26—(UP)—Furio Nicolet today claimed a world record for altitude in a one-seater airplane. He reached 10,008 meters (32,826 feet).

Rome—(/)—Princess Marie celebrated her 19th birthday today deluged with good wishes and presents. She passed the day in the royal villa with her parents, King Victor Emmanuel and Queen Elena. Last fall Princess Maria began to assume the responsibilities of the only remaining royal offspring residing in Rome. She appeared at several public ceremonies at the head of her suite of ladies and gentlemen of the court. Previously her appearances at the opera, benefits and other functions were under the chaperonage of the queen or of elder married sisters. Reports of her imminent engagement have been recurrent. Her name has been linked most persistently with that of Archduke Otto, pretender to the throne of Hungary, and the Infante Juan, son of the former King Alfonso of Spain, and heir-pretender to the Spanish throne.

ST. JOHN'S, N. P., Dec. 26.—(7)— The bodies of four members of the crew of the Newfoundland schooner Monica Hartnery drifted ashore near Rose Blanche light on the southern coast of Newfoundland today, following a weekend storm. Scattered bits of wreckage carried to land with the bodies pointed to the schooner’s fate. She was believed to have been overturned Saturday night or Sunday morning as she proceeded along the coast with five men aboard.

1933-09-14.text: "LONDON, Sept. 14—Orders to Kill at sight any of the 33 internationally known Germans recently deprived of citizenship have been posted at the London club for Nazis, the Daily Herald charged today. “If you meet one of them kill him, and if he is a Jew break every bone in his body,” reads a notice displayed prominently at the club, the newspaper asserted. Photographs of each of the 33 exiles were on the notice, it was said. Those named in the alleged order include Philip Scheidemann, first chancellor of the republic of Germany; Otto Wels, former chairman of the German socialist party, and Lion Feuchtwanger, author. Three of the 33 political outlaws arrived in London yesterday to attend a mock trial today satirizing the forthcoming trial of five men for the burning of the Reichstag building. These three are Rudolph Breit-scheid, former leader of the German parliamentary socialist party; Ge

AUSTIN, Sept. 13.—Controversial subjects, such as the manner in which state relief money shall be administered and whether Texas’ stringent anti-trust laws should be liberalized, were topmost on the legislator’s slate, as the first called session was about to convene. The legislative halls, deserted since June 1, when the regular session adjourned after 143 days of continuous work, took on activity tonight as senator and house members came in. Predicts Warm Session Coke Stevenson, speaker of the house, predicted on his arrival that this would be a “warm” session. Lieutenant Governor Edgar Witt will be here in time to call the senate to order at noon tomorrow. Governor Miriam A. Ferguson's official proclamation giving her reasons for convening the legislature in extraordinary session will be ready after a quorum is reported present. Whether Governor Ferguson planned to send up her message

Tokyo, Sept. 14, (Thursday) — Count Yasuya Uchida, resigned today as Foreign Minister of Japan. Koki Hirota, former Ambassador to Moscow, was named his successor. Count Yasuya Uchida, former Ambassador to the United States and a former acting Premier of Japan, is a veteran statesman who has held a score of important posts in the Japanese government. He is a former minister to Peking, former Ambassador to Austria-Hungary and Russia, and one time President of the important South Manchuria railway. He has been for many years a staunch advocate of naval parity and recently said that Japan would stick to an “iron principle” of armament equality in the naval conference scheduled for 1935. He made plain at this time Japan would avoid taking positive steps aiming at the abrogation of the Washington and London Naval treaties.

WINNIPEG, Man, Sept 14—At an emergency meeting held on the trading floor of the Winnipeg grain exchange, the members voted today to remove pegged prices which were placed on wheat and oats, Aug. 15. The vote, which was unanimous, was taken 10 minutes after the exchange had been opened. Trading was halted while the members expressed themselves on the Aug. 15 Motion, which placed minimum levels for the grains.

Berlin, Sept. 14, UR—The Nazi government’s answer to foreign criticism will be a gigantic internal propaganda campaign designed to solidify national spirit, it was revealed today. Plans call for 150,000 public meetings within two months. Chancellor Adolf Hitler will lead the campaign. Every Nazi in high government office will be required to make 15 speeches and those not in the government, 25. The campaign will begin October 1.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Sept. 14 -(AP).—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh said today that he and Mrs. Lindbergh probably will remain two more days in this country and then sail for the United States. The colonel will make a final report on a proposed air route across the North Atlantic by way of Greenland after reaching New York. The couple has been here several days after charting such a route.

WINNIPEG — Minimum price "pegs" for wheat in the Winnipeg grain market were removed today. They had been in effect since August 15. Removal of the "peg" sent prices down immediately, but they rallied quickly. October wheat, on which the minimum price had been set at 170 cents a bushel, dropped to 66 and then snapped back to 70. December futures, pegged at 71 cents, declined to 71, but rallied to 72. Quiside buying showed a big increase as a result of the strength at Chicago.

(By The Associated Press) Poona, India, Sept. 14—The Mahatma Gandhi promised today to ‘refrain from aggressive civil disobedience acts and not to court reimprisonment until August 3, 1934, even though he believes this restraint is a ‘bitter cup of agony.” He gave this assurance to Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, a nationalist leader like Gandhi, after they ended protracted talks.

1933-10-30.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 30 (UP).—The government today raised its price on newly mined American gold to $31.96 an ounce from the $31.82 level of Saturday. The price was an advance by 14 cents an ounce. Today’s Washington price was 55 cents above the world price set in London on the basis of the early low for the pound. President Roosevelt turned to the purchase of foreign gold today to realize his determination to raise domestic commodity prices, if not in one way in another. His policy was to boost commodities by raising the price of gold through forced depreciation of the dollar in world markets. The same objective was sought last week by purchases at a premium of newly mined domestic gold. The plan for world operations raised the possibility of a spectacular international poker game in which the stakes would be the almost immeasurable resources of the participating nations. By The Associated Press Stocks shot up and then slipped back on the New York stock exchange Monday and the dollar dropped in value abroad as President Roosevelt’s plan to buy gold on the world market met varying reactions in the leading capitals. The American dollar closed in London at $4.79 in relation to the British pound, a drop of 734 cents. At the low price of the day, $4.82, the dollar was down more than 10 cents. The London Herald, meanwhile, expressed the belief that foreign interests were taking means to oppose the American President’s monetary plan, hinting that the Bank of England and the Bank of France had joined to buy dollars, thus counteracting any sharp drop of the American currency abroad. French financial interests foresaw danger to the gold supply of the Bank of France. Paul Reynaud, former finance minister, talked of a limited gold embargo, while one newspaper came ou

Jerusalem, Oct. 29.—(AP)—British police battled twice today against crowds of excited Arabs attempting to demonstrate against Jewish immigration at the gates of this cosmopolitan holy city. At least two Moslems were reported killed in the second clash, making a total of 27 dead and more than 200 injured in the rioting in Palestine in the last two days. Besides two native policemen killed Friday, 18 British police have been injured, three seriously. Indications today were that the Arab movement was spreading beyond the Holy Land with unconfirmed reports of demonstrations at Damascus, Syria, and Amman, the capital of Transjordania. The first clash today was at the Damascus gate in the morning and the second at the Jaffa gate this afternoon. At the Jaffa gate the police fired on the rioters, a number of casualties resulting in the mob. The police said they did not use their guns at the Dama

PARIS, (UP).—Maxim Litvinoff, Russian foreign commissar and emissary to the United States, intends to sail for America Wednesday, either on the British liner Berengaria, or the French liner, Champlain, the United Press learned today. Litvinoff’s decision not to sail on the Berengaria was made “for political reasons,” it was understood. The Russian diplomat, “missing” over the weekend, had motored from Berlin to Hanover, stopping over at Magdeburg, and arriving here on the North Express at 10:25. One of his first activities in the French capital was to pay a visit of respect to the bier of Paul Painleve, French war-time premier. He was accompanied by the Soviet Ambassador, Valerian Dovgalevsky.

PARIS, Oct. 30. — France mourned today the last of her wartime premiers, Paul Painlevé, and prepared to accord him the honor of burial in the Pantheon, reserved for her greatest men. Painlevé died yesterday after a long illness. His body will lie in state during the week, and will be buried Saturday with full national honors. It was Painlevé, who as premier in 1917, named Ferdinand Foch as generalissimo of the army, coordinated the Western Front and organized the Salonica front, on which there had been but desultory fighting. Welcomed Lindbergh In 1927, as minister of aviation, Painlevé welcomed Charles A. Lindbergh after his New York-Paris flight. Lindbergh was here today on his first visit since then. Painlevé also, as minister of war, greeted American troops who arrived in France in 1917. Painlevé was premier three times, and served in the cabinet ten times. He was seven times ministe

PARIS, Oct. 30.—()—Abruptly bringing to an end the mystery which had surrounded his movements for hours, Maxim Litvinoff, Russian foreign commissar, arrived here today en route to the United States. He was reported to have left Berlin for Paris yesterday, but he did not arrive on the train he was believed to have taken and it was not until he showed up of his own accord that it was generally known what had happened to him. His plans for sailing to the United States, where he is to confer with President Roosevelt regarding possible American recognition of Russia, remained veiled in secrecy. He made no appointments here, but it was said he might see Foreign Minister Paul-Boncour and associates pointed out he would have to get a visa to go on to the United States.

Paris, Oct. 30—Col. Charles A. Lindbergh today revisited Le Bourget Air Field, where he landed after his historic flight from New York in 1927. He inspected the Lindbergh Memorial at the field and the slab that marks the spot where he first touched French soil. He recognized several airport officials who were present when he landed. Laughingly, Lindbergh disclaimed the remark attributed to him when he landed: “I am Charles A. Lindbergh.” Lindbergh’s visit was unannounced and only a few airline passengers recognized him, compared to the milling thousands who welcomed him in 1927.

Paris, Oct 30. —Col. Charles A. Lindbergh revisited with his wife today the scene of his first taste of world fame. They motored to Le Bourget field where “the Lone Eagle” showed Mrs. Lindbergh the tablet-marked spot where he landed six years ago — a solo trans-Atlantic hop. The trip to the airfield followed a visit to the home of Paul Painleve where the Colonel expressed his sorrow at the death of the aviation enthusiast who as war minister in the Poincare cabinet received the flier at the time of his historic first arrival.
